problems.whyOnTest: Money and change: one amount is spent and another is received, so each step must go the right way.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A locker code is one letter, A or B, followed by two different digits chosen from 1, 2 and 3. For example, A31 is a code. How many different codes are there?

choices.misconception: I thought A13 and A31 were the same code because they use the same digits, so I found only 3 for each letter.
I added the choices, 2 + 3 + 2, instead of letting every branch split again.
I thought each digit place had only 2 choices because the code has two digits, so 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.
I let the two digits be the same, like A11, but the digits must be different.

hints: Pick the letter first, then the first digit, then the second digit.
Draw a tree: 2 branches for the letter, then 3 branches for the first digit, then branches for the second digit, which can be any digit except the one already used. Count the ends.
Each letter gives the first digit 3 choices, and each of those leaves 2 choices for the second digit.

solutions.reliable: Codes starting with A: A12, A13, A21, A23, A31, A32, which is 6 codes. Codes starting with B: the same 6 with B in front. In all 6 + 6 = 12. The idea to keep: a tree that branches at every choice counts all the codes, and each level can have its own number of branches.
solutions.elegant: 2 choices for the letter, 3 for the first digit, then 2 for the second digit: 2 x 3 x 2 = 12. The idea to keep: when every branch at a level splits the same way, multiply the choices at each step.

problems.whyOnTest: Tree diagrams: the second digit has one fewer choice than the first, so each level of the tree must be counted on its own.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each side of a triangle is 4 cm long. An ant walks all the way round the edge of the triangle two times. How far does the ant walk?

choices.misconception: I gave the length of one side, not the whole walk.
I walked along one side two times instead of all the way round two times.
I found the distance once round the triangle and forgot that the ant goes round two times.
I thought a triangle has 4 sides, like a square, so once round is 16 cm.

hints: How far is it once all the way round?
The distance all the way round a shape is all its sides added together. A triangle has 3 sides. Find the distance once round, then think about twice round.
Once round is 4 + 4 + 4 cm.

solutions.reliable: Once round the triangle is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 cm. Twice round is 12 + 12 = 24 cm. The idea to keep: find the distance once round first, then repeat it.
solutions.elegant: Going round twice means walking along 6 sides of 4 cm each: 6 x 4 = 24 cm. The idea to keep: count all the sides walked.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter: the distance round a shape adds every side, and stopping after one side or one lap is the usual mistake.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle 8 cm long and 4 cm wide is cut into two equal squares. Kai adds up the distances all the way round both squares. What total does he get?

choices.misconception: I added 8 + 4, which only goes half way round the rectangle, and forgot about the cut.
I found the distance round only one square.
I gave the distance round the rectangle, but the cut makes a new edge on each square.
I added the new 4 cm cut edge only once, but both squares get that edge.

hints: How long is each side of the squares?
The cut makes a new edge, and that edge belongs to both squares. Find the side of each square, find the distance round one square, then add the two.
Each square is 4 cm by 4 cm, so the distance round one square is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 cm.

solutions.reliable: Cutting an 8 cm by 4 cm rectangle into two equal squares gives two squares with sides of 4 cm. The distance round one square is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 cm. Two squares give 16 + 16 = 32 cm. The idea to keep: work out the new shapes first, then measure them.
solutions.elegant: The distance round the rectangle is 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 24 cm. The cut adds a 4 cm edge to each square, so the total is 24 + 4 + 4 = 32 cm. The idea to keep: cutting a shape keeps all the old edges and adds the cut twice, once for each piece.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter: a cut adds a new edge to both pieces, so the pieces together go further round than the whole shape did.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What number is 1 more than 199?

choices.misconception: I added 1 to the last 9, wrote 0, and forgot to carry the 1 into the tens.
I added 1 ten instead of 1 one.
I added 1 hundred instead of 1 one.
I added 1 to the last 9 and wrote 10 in that place, so I got 19 followed by 10.

hints: What happens after 9 ones?
When the ones go past 9 they make a new ten, and when the tens go past 9 they make a new hundred. Add the 1 to the ones and follow what happens to each place.
199 is 1 hundred, 9 tens and 9 ones. One more one makes 10 ones, which is another ten.

solutions.reliable: 199 is 1 hundred, 9 tens and 9 ones. Adding 1 makes 10 ones, which is 1 more ten. Now there are 10 tens, which is 1 more hundred. That leaves 2 hundreds, 0 tens and 0 ones: 200. The idea to keep: when a place reaches ten, it becomes 1 of the next place, and that can happen more than once.
solutions.elegant: Count on: 197, 198, 199, 200. The idea to keep: counting on past a hundred is a quick check of a carry.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value: adding 1 to 199 makes the ones and then the tens roll over, and stopping after the first carry is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Max writes the number 47. Then he swaps its two digits to make a new number. How much bigger is the new number than 47?

choices.misconception: I saw the tens digit go up from 4 to 7, which is 3 tens, and forgot that the ones digit went down by 3.
I worked out 74 - 47 by taking the smaller ones digit from the bigger one, 7 - 4, instead of regrouping.
I gave the new number, not how much bigger it is.
I added 47 and 74 instead of finding the difference.

hints: What is the new number?
Find the difference between the new number and 47. Count up from 47 in tens and then in ones, or think about what happens to the tens and to the ones separately.
The new number is 74. Count up from 47 in tens: 57, 67. Then count on in ones to 74.

solutions.reliable: The new number is 74. Count up from 47 to 74: from 47 to 67 is 20, and from 67 to 74 is 7. So 74 is 20 + 7 = 27 bigger than 47. The idea to keep: counting up in tens, then in ones, is a safe way to find a difference.
solutions.elegant: The tens digit goes up by 3, which adds 30, but the ones digit goes down by 3, which takes away 3. So the change is 30 - 3 = 27. The idea to keep: look at each place separately, then put the changes together.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value: swapping digits changes the tens and the ones at once, and a digit in the tens place is worth ten times as much.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Half of Leo's toy cars are red. Then he gets 4 more cars, all red. Now he has 10 red cars. How many toy cars does he have now?

choices.misconception: I found how many red cars Leo had at the start and stopped there.
I gave the number of red cars now, not the number of all his cars.
I found how many cars Leo had before he got the new ones.
I thought half of his cars are still red, so I doubled 10.

hints: How many red cars did Leo have before the new ones?
Work backwards: take away the new red cars to find the red cars at the start. Half the cars were red then, which tells you how many cars he had. Then add the new cars back on.
At the start Leo had 10 - 4 = 6 red cars, and that was half of his cars.

solutions.reliable: Before the new cars, Leo had 10 - 4 = 6 red cars. That was half of his cars, so he had 6 + 6 = 12 cars. Then he got 4 more, so now he has 12 + 4 = 16 cars. The idea to keep: a fraction belongs to one moment in the story, so use it only for that moment.
solutions.elegant: The cars that are not red never change. At the start they were the other half, so there are 6 of them, the same as the 6 red cars then. Now he has 10 red cars and 6 other cars: 10 + 6 = 16. The idea to keep: look for the part of the story that stays the same.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of a quantity: half was true before the new cars came, and doubling 10 uses the fraction at the wrong moment.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, Kim starts at 23. She jumps back 2 steps at a time and lands exactly on 15. How many jumps does she make?

choices.misconception: I counted the numbers Kim stands on, including 23 where she starts.
I found the distance from 23 to 15 and forgot that each jump is 2 steps.
I counted all the numbers from 15 to 23, including both ends.
I multiplied the distance 8 by 2 instead of sharing it into jumps of 2.

hints: How far is it from 23 back to 15?
Find the distance between the start and the end first. Each jump covers 2 of those steps, so share the distance into jumps of 2. Be careful not to count the numbers she lands on.
From 23 back to 15 is 8 steps. Each jump is 2 steps.

solutions.reliable: Write the landings: start at 23, then 21, 19, 17, 15. Kim makes one jump to each of 21, 19, 17 and 15, which is 4 jumps. The idea to keep: count jumps, not landing spots, because the starting spot is not a jump.
solutions.elegant: From 23 to 15 is 23 - 15 = 8 steps. Jumps of 2 cover that in 4 jumps, since 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. The idea to keep: the distance shared into the jump size gives the number of jumps.

problems.whyOnTest: Number lines: a jump is a gap between two numbers, so counting the numbers landed on, including the start, gives one too many.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pattern goes 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, and so on. What number comes next?

choices.misconception: I added 1 to 11, because the very first jump in the pattern was 1.
I added 4 again, the same jump as the last one.
I added the two numbers before, 7 + 11.
I thought each number doubles, like 1, 2, 4, so I doubled 11.

hints: Look at how much the pattern grows each time.
Write the jump between each pair of neighbours: from 1 to 2, from 2 to 4, and so on. Then look at how the jumps themselves change.
The jumps are 1, 2, 3, 4. What is the next jump?

solutions.reliable: The jumps are 1, 2, 3 and 4, so each jump is 1 more than the one before. The next jump is 5, and 11 + 5 = 16. The idea to keep: when a pattern does not grow by the same amount each time, look at the jumps and find their pattern.

problems.whyOnTest: Continuing a pattern: the start looks like doubling, so checking every jump between neighbours is what shows the real rule.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cake looks the same on both sides of a line through its middle. It has 4 cherries on the left side and 1 cherry on the line. How many cherries does it have?

choices.misconception: I only counted the cherries on the left side of the line.
I added the cherry on the line to the left side but forgot the right side.
I doubled the 4 cherries on the left but forgot the cherry on the line.
I doubled the cherry on the line too, as if it had a partner on the other side.

hints: What does the right side of the cake look like?
Each cherry on one side has a matching cherry on the other side. A cherry sitting on the line is its own match, so it is counted only once.
The right side has 4 cherries, the same as the left. Add the left side, the right side and the one cherry on the line.

solutions.reliable: The right side matches the left side, so it also has 4 cherries. That makes $4 + 4 = 8$ cherries off the line. The cherry on the line has no partner, so add it once: $8 + 1 = 9$. The idea to keep: in a symmetric picture, things off the line come in pairs, and things on the line are counted once.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetry doubles everything off the mirror line but not what sits on it, and that one detail is where young solvers slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many of the letters in the word ZEBRA can be folded along a straight line so that the two halves match exactly?

choices.misconception: I only looked for up-and-down fold lines, and only A has one.
I only looked for fold lines going across, and found only E and B.
I counted Z because it looks the same when turned round, but turning is not folding.
I thought every capital letter has a fold line somewhere and counted all five.

hints: Try both kinds of fold: up-and-down and across.
Check each letter on its own. A fold line can go up and down or across the middle. A letter that only looks the same after turning it round does not count.
A folds up and down. E and B fold across the middle. Z only matches when it is turned round, and R does not match at all. Count the letters that fold.

solutions.reliable: Check each letter. Z: no fold line works, it only looks the same when turned halfway round. E: folds across the middle. B: folds across the middle. R: no fold works. A: folds up and down. So E, B and A can be folded, which is 3 letters. The idea to keep: test every letter for both up-and-down and across fold lines, and do not mix up folding with turning.

problems.whyOnTest: Students must test two directions of fold and keep turning symmetry separate from folding symmetry, two classic traps.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A strip has 4 squares in a row. Mia colours one or more squares so the strip looks the same when turned round flat, end to end. How many different strips can she make?

choices.misconception: I thought only colouring all 4 squares works.
I found the two end squares and the two middle squares but forgot colouring all four.
I also counted the strip with no squares coloured, but Mia colours at least one.
I counted every way to colour exactly 2 of the 4 squares, without checking the turn.

hints: When the strip turns round, where does the first square go?
Turning the strip end to end swaps the first square with the last, and the second with the third. So squares that swap must be coloured the same. Think of the strip as two pairs.
The end pair can be coloured or not, and the middle pair can be coloured or not. List the choices and remove the one where nothing is coloured.

solutions.reliable: Number the squares 1, 2, 3, 4. Turning the strip end to end puts square 1 where square 4 was, and square 2 where square 3 was. So squares 1 and 4 must match, and squares 2 and 3 must match. The choices are: colour the end pair only, colour the middle pair only, or colour both pairs. Colouring nothing is not allowed. That is 3 strips. The idea to keep: find which parts swap places, and colour each swapping group all the same.
solutions.elegant: Only two things are really chosen: the end pair (yes or no) and the middle pair (yes or no). That gives $2 \times 2 = 4$ ways, and one of them colours nothing, so $4 - 1 = 3$. The idea to keep: symmetry cuts a big count down to a few free choices.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetry turns four squares into two pairs, and the student who sees the pairs can list every strip in seconds.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Leo picks either one fruit or one biscuit for a snack. The fruit can be an apple or a pear. The biscuit can be plain, chocolate or jam. How many different snacks are there?

choices.misconception: I only counted the two kinds of snack, fruit or biscuit.
I only counted the biscuits and forgot the fruit.
I multiplied 2 by 3, as if Leo picks a fruit and a biscuit together.
I counted the 5 snacks and also counted fruit and biscuit as two more.

hints: Does Leo get a fruit and a biscuit, or just one thing?
Draw a tree. The first branch is fruit or biscuit. Under fruit, draw a branch for each fruit. Under biscuit, draw a branch for each biscuit. Count the ends of the branches.
Under fruit there are 2 ends: apple and pear. Under biscuit there are 3 ends: plain, chocolate and jam. Add the ends.

solutions.reliable: Leo takes only one thing. If he picks fruit, there are 2 snacks: apple or pear. If he picks a biscuit, there are 3 snacks: plain, chocolate or jam. Altogether $2 + 3 = 5$ snacks. The idea to keep: when you choose one thing OR another, add the ways; multiply only when you choose one thing AND another.

problems.whyOnTest: The word "either" means add, not multiply, and a tree diagram shows the difference at a glance.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sam throws a ball at a basket until one goes in, but he stops after 3 throws anyway. Each throw goes in or misses. In how many different ways can his throws go?

choices.misconception: I only looked at the first throw: in or miss.
I only counted the ways that end with the ball going in and forgot that all 3 throws could miss.
I counted 2 ways for each of the 3 throws and added them, 2 + 2 + 2.
I thought Sam always throws 3 times, so I counted every way 3 throws can go.

hints: Can Sam stop after just one throw?
Draw a tree. Each throw has two branches, in or miss. A branch that goes in stops there. Only a miss carries on, and the tree stops after 3 throws.
In stops at once. Miss then in stops after two throws. After two misses, the third throw can go in or miss, and both end the turn. Count the branch ends.

solutions.reliable: Write I for in and M for a miss. If the first throw goes in, Sam stops: I. If it misses, he throws again, and a second throw that goes in stops him: MI. After two misses he throws a third time, and that ends his turn either way: MMI or MMM. That is 4 ways. The idea to keep: in a tree diagram, stop a branch as soon as the rule says stop.
solutions.elegant: Each way is fixed by when the first ball goes in: on throw 1, throw 2, throw 3, or never. That is 4 ways. The idea to keep: sometimes you can count the stopping points instead of drawing every branch.

problems.whyOnTest: A tree whose branches stop early tests whether students follow the stopping rule or just multiply by 2 for every throw.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three lamps stand in a row. Each lamp is on or off. Two lamps next to each other are never both on. In how many different ways can the row of lamps look?

choices.misconception: I only counted the rows with exactly one lamp on.
I forgot the row with all three lamps off.
I only crossed out the row with all three lamps on.
I counted every on-and-off row and forgot the rule about neighbours.

hints: Is it allowed for every lamp to be off?
Make a tree: first lamp on or off, then the second, then the third. Cross out a branch as soon as two neighbours are both on. Count what is left.
With no lamps on there is 1 row. With one lamp on there are 3 rows. With two lamps on, they must not touch, so only the two end lamps work. Three lamps on is never allowed.

solutions.reliable: Sort by how many lamps are on. None on: 1 way. One on: it can be the left, middle or right lamp, 3 ways. Two on: they cannot be neighbours, so they must be the two end lamps, 1 way. Three on: impossible, since neighbours would be on together. Total $1 + 3 + 1 = 5$. The idea to keep: sort the cases by size and check the rule in each case.
solutions.elegant: All 8 on-and-off rows are possible without the rule. The rows that break the rule are on-on-off, off-on-on and on-on-on, which is 3 rows. So $8 - 3 = 5$. The idea to keep: sometimes it is quicker to count the bad cases and take them away.

problems.whyOnTest: A rule that forbids neighbours forces careful listing, and the all-off row is the case most students forget.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The distance all the way round a square is 12 cm. How long is one side of the square?

choices.misconception: I shared 12 among 3 sides, forgetting that a square has 4 sides.
I halved 12, as if a square had only 2 sides.
I took away 4 for the four sides instead of sharing 12 into 4 equal parts.
I multiplied 12 by 4 instead of dividing it by 4.

hints: How many sides does a square have, and are they equal?
A square has 4 equal sides, and the distance round it is all 4 sides added together. Share the total equally between the sides.
Find the number that, added 4 times, makes 12.

solutions.reliable: A square has 4 equal sides. Going all the way round adds all 4 sides, so 4 equal sides make 12 cm. Since $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12$, each side is 3 cm. The idea to keep: the distance round a square is 4 equal sides, so share it into 4 to find one side.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards from the distance round to one side checks that a student knows what the distance round really is.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana cuts a 2 cm square off one corner of a paper square with 6 cm sides. What is the distance all the way round the shape that is left?

choices.misconception: I took away the 2 cm and 2 cm cut off the outside edges, but forgot the two new 2 cm edges inside the corner.
I added the two new 2 cm edges but did not take away the 2 cm and 2 cm cut off the outside edges.
I added all four sides of the small square to the 24 cm of the big square.
I worked out 6 times 6, which counts the small squares inside, not the distance round.

hints: Walk all the way round the new shape and write down each side.
Draw the shape after the corner is gone. Cutting the corner takes away two bits of the old edge but makes two new edges. Compare what is lost with what is gained.
Put the cut corner at the top right and start at the bottom left. Go 6 cm along the bottom, 4 cm up, 2 cm in, 2 cm up, 4 cm along the top and 6 cm down. Add these sides.

solutions.reliable: Put the cut corner at the top right. Going round from the bottom left corner, the sides are 6 cm along the bottom, 4 cm up, 2 cm in, 2 cm up, 4 cm along the top and 6 cm down. That is $6 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 24$ cm, the same as the whole square. The idea to keep: list every side of the new shape, including the new edges made by the cut.
solutions.elegant: The new edge going across is as long as the 2 cm missing from the top, and the new edge going up is as long as the 2 cm missing from the side. So nothing is lost and nothing is gained: the distance round is still $6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24$ cm. The idea to keep: cutting a square out of a corner makes the shape smaller but keeps the distance round the same.

problems.whyOnTest: Cutting a corner out of a square leaves the distance round unchanged, which surprises students who expect a smaller shape to have a shorter border.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ella puts 12 square tiles, each with sides of 1 cm, together to make one rectangle. What is the largest possible distance all the way round her rectangle?

choices.misconception: I added the length 12 and the width 1, but only once each.
I used the 3 by 4 rectangle, which gives the smallest distance round.
I stopped at the 2 by 6 rectangle and did not try one long row.
I counted the top and the bottom of one long row but forgot the two short ends.

hints: Which rectangles can 12 tiles make?
List every rectangle: rows times tiles in a row must make 12. Work out the distance round each one and compare. Long, thin shapes have more edge on the outside.
The rectangles are 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4. For 1 by 12, go round: 12 along the top, 1 down, 12 along the bottom, 1 up.

solutions.reliable: The rectangles made of 12 tiles are 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4. Their distances round are $12 + 1 + 12 + 1 = 26$ cm, $6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16$ cm and $4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14$ cm. The largest is 26 cm. The idea to keep: the same tiles can have very different distances round, and a long thin shape has the most.
solutions.elegant: Every tile edge that touches another tile is hidden. A single row hides the fewest edges, only 11 joins, so it shows the most outside: $12 \times 4 = 48$ edges, minus $2 \times 11 = 22$ hidden ones, gives 26. The idea to keep: to make the outside long, make the tiles touch as little as possible.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparing all rectangles with the same tiles shows that area and distance round are different things.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A class has 12 girls and 9 boys. Today 4 of the girls are at home sick. How many girls are in class today?

choices.misconception: I found how many more girls than boys there are.
I gave the number of girls at home, not the girls in class.
I took the 4 away from the boys instead of the girls.
I took the 4 away from all 21 children instead of only the girls.

hints: Read the question again: who is it asking about?
The question is only about girls. The number of boys does not change the answer. Use only the numbers about girls.
There are 12 girls in the class and 4 of them are not there. Take 4 away from 12.

solutions.reliable: The question asks only about girls, so the 9 boys are not needed. There are 12 girls and 4 are at home, so $12 - 4 = 8$ girls are in class. The idea to keep: decide what the question asks for before you use any numbers, and leave out numbers that do not belong.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo questions often include a number that is not needed, and the student must pick out what is really asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lily is 7 years old. In 3 years, her brother will be twice as old as Lily is now. How old is her brother now?

choices.misconception: I worked out Lily's age in 3 years instead of her brother's age now.
I found the brother's age in 3 years and forgot to go back to now.
I doubled Lily's age in 3 years, 10, to get 20, then took away 3.
I doubled Lily's age in 3 years and stopped there.

hints: Is the doubling about Lily now, or Lily in 3 years?
Find what the brother's age will be in 3 years first. The sentence compares it with Lily's age today. Then work backwards to today.
Twice Lily's age now is 14, so in 3 years the brother will be 14. Today he is 3 years younger than that.

solutions.reliable: Lily is 7 now, so twice her age now is 14. That is how old her brother will be in 3 years. Today he is 3 years younger: $14 - 3 = 11$. Check: in 3 years he is 14, and 14 is twice 7. The idea to keep: mark which time each age belongs to, and answer for the time the question asks about.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems test whether a student keeps track of "now" and "later" and answers the time actually asked about.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Dad cuts a long stick into 5 pieces. Each cut goes straight across just one piece. How many cuts does he make?

choices.misconception: I drew the stick but missed the cut between the last two pieces.
I thought each piece needs its own cut, so 5 pieces need 5 cuts.
I counted the two ends of the stick as cuts as well as the cuts in between.
I thought every piece needs two cuts, one at each end.

hints: Draw the stick and mark the cuts.
Draw a line for the stick and split it into 5 pieces. The cuts are the marks between pieces. The two ends of the stick are not cuts.
Between 5 pieces in a row there is one gap after each piece except the last.

solutions.reliable: Draw the stick split into 5 pieces. The cuts sit between neighbouring pieces: between pieces 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 3 and 4, and 4 and 5. That is 4 cuts. The idea to keep: in a row, the gaps between things are one fewer than the things.

problems.whyOnTest: The gap-versus-piece question is the gentlest form of the off-by-one trap, and a quick drawing settles it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rope is folded in half. Then it is cut twice, straight across both layers, in two different places away from the fold. How many pieces of rope are there?

choices.misconception: I forgot about the fold and cut a straight rope in 2 places.
I counted the 4 places where the rope is cut, not the pieces.
I counted 2 pieces in each of the 3 parts of the folded rope, but the part with the fold is still one piece.
I thought each cut splits both layers into 2 pieces each, so each cut makes 4 pieces, and 4 + 4 = 8.

hints: Draw the rope opened out again after the cuts.
The folded rope has 2 layers, so each cut goes through the rope in 2 places. Draw the rope straight, mark every cut point, then count the pieces between and outside the marks.
Two cuts through 2 layers make 4 cut points on the straight rope. A rope with 4 cut points falls into the pieces between the marks plus the two end pieces.

solutions.reliable: The folded rope has 2 layers, so each cut goes through the rope in 2 places. Two cuts make 4 cut points. Opened out, a straight rope with 4 cut points splits into $4 + 1 = 5$ pieces. The middle one of these is the bent piece that went round the fold. The idea to keep: unfold the picture and count the cut points; on a single line, there is one more piece than cut points.
solutions.elegant: Look at the folded rope. The two cuts split it into 3 parts. The part with the fold is one bent piece, and each of the other 2 parts has 2 layers, so 2 pieces each: $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$. The idea to keep: a piece that goes round a fold stays in one piece.

problems.whyOnTest: Students cannot see inside the folded rope, so drawing it opened out is the only safe way to count the pieces.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many even numbers are there from 10 to 20, counting 10 and 20 too?

choices.misconception: I left out 10 and 20, the two numbers at the ends.
I counted the odd numbers, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19.
I worked out 20 minus 10 instead of counting the even numbers.
I counted every number from 10 to 20, odd ones too.

hints: Count in twos, starting at 10.
Even numbers go up in steps of 2. Start at 10, keep adding 2, and stop at 20. Count every number you say, including both ends.
Say them: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20. Count them on your fingers.

solutions.reliable: Count in twos from 10: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20. That is 6 even numbers. The idea to keep: list numbers by steps of 2 and include both ends when the question says so.
solutions.elegant: From 10 to 20 there are 11 numbers. They start and end with an even number and take turns even, odd, even, so the even ones are one more than the odd ones: 6 even and 5 odd. The idea to keep: when a list starts and ends on even, the evens win by one.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting evens in a range tests the step-of-2 idea and the end-point trap together.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Children in a class make pairs, and one child is left without a partner. Then 3 more children join, and everybody makes pairs again. How many children are left without a partner now?

choices.misconception: I thought adding children never changes whether one is left over, so it is still 1.
I paired two of the new children and left the third one and the old child alone.
I added the 3 new children to the 1 left over and did not pair any of them.
I thought I needed to know how many children were in the class.

hints: Was the number of children odd or even at first?
One child left over means the class had an odd number of children. Think about what happens when you add an odd number to an odd number.
The 1 child left over and the 3 new children make 4 children. Can 4 children all find partners?

solutions.reliable: At first one child is left over, so the class has an odd number of children. Adding 3, another odd number, gives an even number, and an even number of children can all be paired. So 0 children are left over. Check with a small class: 5 children leave 1 over, and $5 + 3 = 8$ children make 4 pairs. The idea to keep: odd plus odd is even, so you can answer without knowing the size of the class.
solutions.elegant: Keep the old pairs as they are. The 1 child left over and the 3 newcomers make 4 children, which is 2 more pairs, with nobody left. The idea to keep: only the leftovers matter.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity answers this without the class size, and students must trust that a missing number is not needed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia has a 1-cent coin, a 2-cent coin and a 5-cent coin. She picks exactly two of the coins. How many different amounts of money can she make?

choices.misconception: I also counted taking all three coins, which is more than two.
I counted picking the 1 then the 2 and picking the 2 then the 1 as different.
I listed every amount using one, two or three coins.
I added up all three coins instead of picking two.

hints: Which coin does Mia leave behind?
List the pairs in order so you miss none: start with the 1-cent coin and pair it with each bigger coin, then do the same for the 2-cent coin. Then add each pair.
The pairs are 1 and 2, 1 and 5, and 2 and 5. Add each pair and check that the totals are all different.

solutions.reliable: The pairs are 1 + 2 = 3, 1 + 5 = 6 and 2 + 5 = 7 cents. The three totals are all different, so there are 3 amounts. The idea to keep: list pairs in a fixed order so that none is missed or counted twice.
solutions.elegant: Picking two coins out of three is the same as choosing which one coin to leave out, and there are 3 ways to do that. The idea to keep: sometimes it is easier to count what you leave out.

problems.whyOnTest: A short, careful list beats guessing, and the order of picking does not make a new pair.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ben writes 10 as a sum of three different numbers, none of them 0, like 1 + 2 + 7. Changing the order does not make a new sum. How many sums can he write?

choices.misconception: I only looked for sums that start with 1 and missed 2 + 3 + 5.
I also counted sums with two equal numbers, like 2 + 4 + 4.
I counted each sum three times, once starting with each of its numbers.
I counted every order of the numbers as a new sum.

hints: Write each sum with the smallest number first.
Always write the numbers from smallest to largest so each sum is written only one way. Start with the smallest number 1, then try 2, and so on.
Smallest number 1: 1 + 2 + 7, 1 + 3 + 6, 1 + 4 + 5. Smallest number 2: try 2 + 3 + 5. Can the smallest number be 3?

solutions.reliable: Write each sum from smallest to largest. Smallest 1: 1 + 2 + 7, 1 + 3 + 6, 1 + 4 + 5. Smallest 2: 2 + 3 + 5 (2 + 4 + 4 repeats a number). Smallest 3: the other two would be at least 4 and 5, and 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 is too big. So there are 4 sums. The idea to keep: put each list in order, smallest first, and go through the smallest number one value at a time.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing in a fixed order is the skill that makes counting reliable, and it stops repeats from sneaking in.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A ribbon is 24 cm long. Kim cuts off a quarter of it. How long is the piece that she cuts off?

choices.misconception: I found half of the ribbon instead of a quarter.
I found the piece that is left, not the piece she cut off.
I took away 4 cm, thinking a quarter means 4.
I multiplied by 4 instead of sharing into 4 equal parts.

hints: A quarter means one of how many equal parts?
A quarter is one of 4 equal parts. Split the ribbon into 4 equal pieces and take one of them.
Four equal pieces must add up to 24 cm. Find the number that, added 4 times, makes 24.

solutions.reliable: A quarter is one of 4 equal parts. Since $6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24$, each part is 6 cm, so the piece Kim cuts off is 6 cm. The idea to keep: a quarter means share into 4 equal parts and take one.
solutions.elegant: Half of 24 is 12, and half of that is 6. The idea to keep: a quarter is half of a half.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of a length are the first step to fractions as numbers, and "quarter means 4" is the common slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A box has 12 crayons. Half of them are red and a third of them are blue. The rest are green. How many crayons are not green?

choices.misconception: I worked out the green crayons, but the question asks for the ones that are not green.
I only counted the blue crayons.
I only counted the red crayons.
I took a third of the 6 crayons left after the red ones, so I got only 2 blue.

hints: A third of what: all 12 crayons, or what is left?
Both fractions are parts of the whole box of 12. Find the red crayons and the blue crayons from 12, then read the question again: it asks for crayons that are not green.
Half of 12 is 6 red. A third of 12 is 4 blue. Crayons that are not green are the red ones and the blue ones together.

solutions.reliable: Half of 12 is 6, so 6 crayons are red. A third of 12 is 4, so 4 crayons are blue. The crayons that are not green are the red and blue ones: $6 + 4 = 10$. (The green ones are $12 - 10 = 2$.) The idea to keep: take each fraction of the same whole, and read the question again before you answer.

problems.whyOnTest: Two fractions of one whole plus a "not" in the question make this a two-step problem with a trap at each step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Leo has plenty of 1-cent, 2-cent, 5-cent and 10-cent coins. He wants to pay exactly 27 cents using as few coins as possible. How many coins does he use?

choices.misconception: I made 25 cents with 10 + 10 + 5 and forgot the last 2 cents.
I used two 1-cent coins at the end instead of one 2-cent coin.
I started with 5-cent coins: five of them make 25, then one 2-cent coin.
I counted the cents instead of the coins.

hints: Start with the biggest coin you can.
To use few coins, use big coins first. Take as many 10-cent coins as fit, then 5-cent coins, then 2-cent coins, then 1-cent coins.
Two 10-cent coins make 20. Then 7 cents are left. One 5-cent coin leaves 2 cents.

solutions.reliable: Use the biggest coins first. Two 10-cent coins make 20 cents, leaving 7. One 5-cent coin leaves 2. One 2-cent coin finishes it. So $10 + 10 + 5 + 2 = 27$ uses 4 coins. Three coins are not enough, since the three biggest coins give only $10 + 10 + 10 = 30$, and no three coins from the list make exactly 27. The idea to keep: for fewest coins, take the biggest coin that still fits, again and again.

problems.whyOnTest: Paying with the fewest coins rewards working from the biggest coin down, and checking that fewer is impossible.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben and Cal stand on a number line. Ana is 3 to the left of Ben. Cal is 5 to the right of Ben. Cal stands at 17. Where does Ana stand?

choices.misconception: I found where Ben stands and stopped there.
I went 3 to the left of Cal instead of 3 to the left of Ben.
I found Ben at 12 and then went 3 to the right instead of the left.
I went to the right both times, 17 + 5 + 3.

hints: Whose place on the number line do you already know?
Draw a number line and mark Cal. Work backwards: Cal is to the right of Ben, so Ben is to the left of Cal. Then find Ana from Ben, not from Cal.
Ben is 5 to the left of Cal, so Ben is at 12. Ana is 3 to the left of Ben. Count 3 steps left from 12.

solutions.reliable: Cal is 5 to the right of Ben, so Ben is 5 to the left of Cal: $17 - 5 = 12$. Ana is 3 to the left of Ben: $12 - 3 = 9$. Check: from 9, 3 steps right is 12, where Ben is, and 5 more steps right is 17, where Cal is. The idea to keep: draw the number line, find who each clue is measured from, and move the right way.
solutions.elegant: Ben stands between Ana and Cal, so Ana is $3 + 5 = 8$ to the left of Cal: $17 - 8 = 9$. The idea to keep: when one point is between two others, the two gaps add up to the whole gap.

problems.whyOnTest: Clues measured from different people and in both directions test whether a student can keep a number line straight.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Stack 1 is 1 can. Stack 2 has rows of 2 and 1 cans. Stack 3 has rows of 3, 2 and 1 cans, and so on. How many cans are in stack 5?

choices.misconception: I only counted the bottom row of stack 5.
I worked out stack 4 instead of stack 5.
I put 6 cans in the bottom row, one more than the stack number.
I gave every row of stack 5 the same 5 cans.

hints: How many cans are in the bottom row of stack 5?
Each stack has a bottom row as long as the stack number, and each row above has one can fewer, up to 1 can at the top. Add the rows.
Stack 5 has rows of 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 cans. Add them.

solutions.reliable: Stack 5 has rows of 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 cans, so it has $5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15$ cans. Check with the pattern: stacks 1 to 4 have 1, 3, 6 and 10 cans, and each new stack adds a new bottom row one longer than before, so stack 5 adds 5 to make $10 + 5 = 15$. The idea to keep: see how each picture is built from the one before.
solutions.elegant: Pair the rows: $5 + 0$, $4 + 1$, $3 + 2$ each make 5, and there are 3 pairs, so 15. The idea to keep: pairing numbers to the same total makes adding quick.

problems.whyOnTest: Growing patterns test whether a student sees what each new step adds, not just the last number.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana has 9 stickers. That is 4 fewer than Ben has. How many stickers do Ana and Ben have together?

choices.misconception: I took 4 away from 9 to find Ben's stickers and stopped there.
I found Ben's stickers and stopped before adding Ana's.
I took 4 away for Ben, getting 5, then added 9 + 5.
I thought Ben also has 9 and added 9 + 9, forgetting his 4 extra.

hints: Who has more stickers, Ana or Ben?
Draw two bars. Ben's bar is longer than Ana's by 4. Find Ben's number first, then add both bars, because the question asks for both children together.
Ana has 4 fewer than Ben, so Ben has 4 more than Ana: 9 + 4. Then add Ana's 9.

solutions.reliable: "Ana has 4 fewer than Ben" means Ben has 4 more than Ana, so Ben has $9 + 4 = 13$. Together they have $9 + 13 = 22$. The idea to keep: turn "fewer than" into a picture of two bars before choosing to add or take away.
solutions.elegant: Together is two of Ana's 9 plus Ben's extra 4: $9 + 9 + 4 = 22$. The idea to keep: in a bar model, the longer bar is the shorter bar plus the difference.

problems.whyOnTest: The word "fewer" tempts students to take away, and a bar model shows that Ben actually has more.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a two-digit number, the tens digit is 3 more than the ones digit, as in 52. How many such two-digit numbers are there?

choices.misconception: I forgot 30, because its ones digit is 0.
I thought every tens digit from 1 to 9 could start such a number.
I also counted numbers whose ones digit is 3 more than the tens digit, like 14.
I counted every number twice, once for each order of its digits, like 41 and 14.

hints: Which digits can the ones digit be?
Go through the ones digit from 0 upwards and add 3 to get the tens digit. Stop when the tens digit would be bigger than 9.
Ones digit 0 gives 30, ones digit 1 gives 41, and so on. The tens digit can go up to 9.

solutions.reliable: Try each ones digit and add 3 for the tens digit: 0 gives 30, 1 gives 41, 2 gives 52, 3 gives 63, 4 gives 74, 5 gives 85, 6 gives 96. A ones digit of 7 would need a tens digit of 10, which is impossible. So there are 7 numbers. The idea to keep: list by one digit in order and check both ends, including 0.
solutions.elegant: The tens digit must be at least 3 and at most 9, so it can be 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9: that is 7 choices, and each gives exactly one number. The idea to keep: count the choices for one digit when the other is fixed by it.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles need both ends checked, and the number ending in 0 is the one students most often miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Jo has one minute left and 3 blank questions. She knows one answer, has a hunch about another, and no idea about the third. Wrong answers cost nothing. What should she do?

choices.text: answer none of them, as there is no time
choices.misconception: I thought a minute was too short, but marking a choice takes only a few seconds.

choices.text: answer only the one she knows
choices.misconception: I thought guessing was risky, but a wrong answer costs nothing.

choices.text: answer the two she has some idea about
choices.misconception: I left the third one blank, but a blank scores zero for sure and a guess might score.

choices.text: it depends on how many points each one is worth
choices.misconception: I thought guessing a big question was riskier, but nothing is taken off for any wrong answer.

hints: What does a blank score?
Compare a blank with a guess. A blank always scores nothing. A guess might be right and costs nothing if it is wrong. So a guess is never worse than a blank.
Mark the answer she knows, mark her hunch, and mark any choice for the last one. All three take only seconds.

solutions.reliable: A blank always scores zero. A marked answer scores if it is right and loses nothing if it is wrong, so marking is never worse than leaving a blank. Jo should mark the one she knows, mark her hunch, and pick any choice for the third. The idea to keep: when wrong answers cost nothing, never leave a question blank.

problems.whyOnTest: Knowing that a blank can only score zero is a free gain on every Kangaroo paper.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A wrong answer scores 0, like a blank. Kit and Remy get the same 5 questions right. Kit also guesses on 3 more; Remy leaves those blank. Which sentence must be true?

choices.text: Kit always scores more than Remy.
choices.misconception: I thought at least one of the guesses would always be right, so Kit must get more.

choices.text: Remy always scores more than Kit.
choices.misconception: I thought leaving a question blank is safer, so the blanks must give more points.

choices.text: Kit could score less than Remy.
choices.misconception: I thought each wrong guess takes points away, so Kit could fall behind.

choices.text: They always get the same score.
choices.misconception: I thought guesses are only luck, so they never count for any points.

choices.text: Kit never scores less than Remy.

hints: What happens to Kit's score if all 3 guesses are wrong?
Compare the two children question by question. On the 5 shared questions they score the same. On the other 3, a blank scores 0, and a guess scores 0 or more. Then read each sentence carefully.
If every guess is wrong, Kit and Remy tie. If any guess is right, Kit is ahead. Which sentence fits both cases?

solutions.reliable: On the 5 questions they both got right, they score the same. On the other 3 questions, Remy scores 0. Kit scores 0 for a wrong guess and points for a right one, so Kit scores 0 or more there. If all of Kit's guesses are wrong they tie, and otherwise Kit is ahead. So Kit can never score less than Remy, but Kit does not always score more. The idea to keep: when wrong answers cost nothing, a guess can only help, so never leave a blank.

problems.whyOnTest: It states the rule behind never leaving a blank, and the choices separate "never less" from "always more", which students often mix up.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A contest has 24 questions. With one minute left, Max has answered 19 and cannot solve the rest. Wrong answers and blanks both score 0. How many more should he guess?

choices.misconception: I thought a blank was safer than a guess, so he should not guess at all.
I counted 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 and got 6, but question 19 is already answered.
I gave the number of questions he has already answered.
I gave the number of questions in the whole contest.

hints: Can a guess ever lose him points?
A wrong answer scores the same as a blank, so every guess can only add points. Max should guess on every question he has not answered. Count how many those are.
He has answered 19 of the 24 questions. Count on from 19 to 24 by the jumps, not the numbers.

solutions.reliable: A wrong guess scores 0, exactly like a blank, and a right guess scores points. So Max should guess on every question he has not answered. He has answered 19 of 24, so $24 - 19 = 5$ are left. He should guess on all 5. The idea to keep: when wrong answers cost nothing, fill in every blank before time runs out.

problems.whyOnTest: Using the last minute to fill every blank is free points, and the trap answers come from fearing a guess or miscounting what is left.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ivy draws a house: a square with a triangle roof sitting exactly on its top side. The roof's two slanted sides are equal. How many lines of symmetry does the house have?

choices.misconception: I thought a line straight across the middle works too, because it works for the square.
I thought the roof has 3 lines of symmetry, like a triangle with all sides equal.
I counted the lines of symmetry of the square and forgot the roof.
I added the 4 lines of the square and 3 lines for the triangle.

hints: Picture folding the whole house, roof and all.
A line of symmetry must work for the whole shape at once. Try each line that works for the square and check whether the roof matches on both sides of it too.
Fold the house straight down the middle, through the top of the roof. Now try folding across the middle, or corner to corner. Does the roof land on itself?

solutions.reliable: A fold straight down the middle goes through the tip of the roof. The two slanted sides are equal, so the halves match. A fold across the middle would put the roof onto the bottom of the square, which has no roof, so it fails. Corner-to-corner folds also move the roof onto a side of the square. So there is exactly 1 line of symmetry. The idea to keep: a line of symmetry must work for every part of the shape.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding a piece to a shape can destroy symmetry, and students who count the lines of each part separately fall into the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three equal squares make an L shape: two squares side by side, and one more square on top of the left one. How many lines of symmetry does the L shape have?

choices.misconception: I only tried lines going straight up and down or straight across, and none of those work.
I thought the two lines of the rectangle made by the bottom squares still work for the L.
I thought each of the three squares adds one line of symmetry.
I counted the lines of symmetry of one square and forgot the rest of the shape.

hints: Do not only try lines that go straight up or straight across.
A line of symmetry can be slanted. Draw the L and try a fold through its corner square, from corner to corner, and check where the two arms land.
Fold along the slanted line through the corner square of the L. The arm going up lands on the arm going right.

solutions.reliable: Fold straight down or straight across and the halves do not match, because the L has one arm sticking up and one sticking out to the side. Now fold along the slanted line through the corner square, from its outer corner to its inner corner. The corner square folds onto itself and the two arms land on each other. No other line works, so the L has exactly 1 line of symmetry. The idea to keep: always check slanted lines too.

problems.whyOnTest: Students look only for upright lines of symmetry, and this shape has a single slanted one, so it tests looking in every direction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pie is cut into 16 pieces. Dad eats 2 pieces, Mom eats 4 pieces and Ivy eats 3 pieces. How many pieces do Mom and Dad eat altogether?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many more pieces Mom ate than Dad.
I worked out how many pieces were left after all three had eaten.
I added everyone, Ivy too, but the question only asks about Mom and Dad.
I took Mom and Dad's pieces away from 16, which is how many they did not eat.

hints: Who does the question ask about?
Read the question again before you calculate. Some numbers are there that you do not need. Use only the people the question names.
The question names only Mom and Dad. Add Dad's 2 pieces and Mom's 4 pieces. Ivy and the 16 are not needed.

solutions.reliable: The question asks only about Mom and Dad. Dad eats 2 and Mom eats 4, so together they eat $2 + 4 = 6$ pieces. The 16 pieces and Ivy's 3 pieces are extra facts. The idea to keep: find exactly what is asked before you start adding.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo questions often carry extra numbers, and finding which ones the question needs is a skill on its own.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Children wait in a line for the slide. Tara is 7th from the front. Ken is 3 places behind Tara. How many children are in front of Ken?

choices.misconception: I counted only the children standing between Tara and Ken.
I took 3 away from 7 instead of adding, as if Ken were in front of Tara.
I counted the children in front of Tara instead of in front of Ken.
I counted the 6 children in front of Tara and the 2 between them, but forgot Tara herself.

hints: First find Ken's place in the line.
Places behind means further from the front, so add. Once you know which place Ken is in, think about how many children come before that place.
Ken is 7 + 3 = 10th from the front. Being 10th means some children are ahead of him. How many?

solutions.reliable: Tara is 7th. Ken is 3 places behind her, so count 8th, 9th, 10th: Ken is 10th. The children in front of Ken are those in places 1 to 9, which is 9 children. The idea to keep: the 10th person has 9 people in front, so check whether the question wants a place or a number of people.
solutions.elegant: Count directly: 6 children are in front of Tara, then Tara herself, then the 2 children between Tara and Ken. That is $6 + 1 + 2 = 9$.

problems.whyOnTest: A place in line and the number of people in front differ by one, and this checks you answer the question that was actually asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tom stands 5 dominoes in a line. Each is 3 cm thick, with a 1 cm gap between neighbours. How long is the whole line, end to end?

choices.misconception: I added the 5 dominoes and forgot the gaps between them.
I added one gap of 1 cm for the whole line instead of one between every two dominoes.
I put a gap after every domino, even after the last one.
I put a gap between the dominoes and also one at each end of the line.

hints: Draw the 5 dominoes and mark the gaps.
Gaps only go between neighbours, so there is one fewer gap than dominoes. A quick sketch shows exactly how many gaps there are. Then add the dominoes and the gaps.
The 5 dominoes make 15 cm. Drawing them shows 4 gaps, one between each pair of neighbours. Add the gaps.

solutions.reliable: The dominoes are $5 \times 3 = 15$ cm thick altogether. Between 5 dominoes there are 4 gaps, so the gaps add 4 cm. The line is $15 + 4 = 19$ cm long. The idea to keep: in a row of things, there is one gap fewer than things.
solutions.elegant: Think of each of the first 4 dominoes with the gap behind it: that is 4 cm each, so 16 cm. The last domino has no gap behind it and adds 3 cm, making 19 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Gaps between objects are a classic off-by-one, and drawing the row is the reliable way to count them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana cuts a rectangle of brownies with 2 straight cuts from the left edge to the right edge and 3 from the top edge to the bottom edge. How many pieces are there?

choices.misconception: I added the number of cuts, 2 + 3.
I multiplied the number of cuts, 2 times 3, instead of the number of strips.
I added the 3 rows and the 4 columns instead of multiplying them.
I counted a strip on each side of every cut, which made 4 rows and 5 columns.

hints: How many rows do the 2 side-to-side cuts make?
Draw it. Cuts that go across split the tray into rows, and cuts that go down split it into columns. Count the rows and the columns, then count the pieces in the grid.
The 2 cuts across make 3 rows. The 3 cuts down make 4 columns. Every row is split into 4 pieces.

solutions.reliable: Two cuts from left to right split the brownies into 3 rows. Three cuts from top to bottom split them into 4 columns. Each of the 3 rows has 4 pieces, so there are $3 \times 4 = 12$ pieces. The idea to keep: a strip has one more piece than it has cuts, so draw the cuts and count the pieces.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks the one-more rule for cuts and strips, and drawing the grid beats juggling the numbers of cuts.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each sheet of a book has an odd page on the front and the next page on the back, like 1 and 2. Tim tears out pages 5 to 12. How many sheets is that?

choices.misconception: I thought page 5 is on the back of page 4, so I counted sheets 4 and 5, 6 and 7, and so on up to 12 and 13.
I took 5 away from 12 instead of counting the sheets.
I counted the pages, not the sheets.
I thought each page was a whole sheet with two sides, so I doubled the 8 pages.

hints: Which page is on the back of page 5?
Every sheet starts with an odd page and ends with the next even page. Pair the pages up from 5 to 12, then count the pairs.
The sheets are 5 and 6, then 7 and 8, then 9 and 10, then 11 and 12.

solutions.reliable: Page 5 is odd, so it is on the front of a sheet with page 6 on the back. The pages pair up as 5 and 6, 7 and 8, 9 and 10, 11 and 12. That is 4 sheets. The idea to keep: odd and even numbers take turns, so a run that starts odd and ends even splits neatly into pairs.
solutions.elegant: There are 8 pages from 5 to 12, starting with an odd page and ending with an even one, so they fill whole sheets: 8 pages make 4 sheets.

problems.whyOnTest: Odd and even numbers take turns, and pairing them correctly is the whole problem, while pairing an even page with the next odd one gives an extra sheet.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag has 5 balls numbered 2, 3, 5, 8 and 9. Max takes out two balls and adds their numbers. How many of the different pairs he could take give an even total?

choices.misconception: I thought only two even numbers add to an even total, so only 2 and 8 works.
I counted the even balls, 2 and 8, instead of the pairs.
I found the pairs of odd balls but forgot that 2 and 8 also make an even total.
I counted the pairs that give an odd total instead.

hints: When is the total of two numbers even?
Two odd numbers make an even total, and so do two even numbers. An odd and an even make an odd total. Sort the balls into odd and even, then count the matching pairs.
The odd balls are 3, 5 and 9. The even balls are 2 and 8. Pairs of odd balls: 3 and 5, 3 and 9, 5 and 9. Is there a pair of even balls?

solutions.reliable: List all 10 pairs: 2+3, 2+5, 2+8, 2+9, 3+5, 3+8, 3+9, 5+8, 5+9, 8+9. The even totals are 10 from 2+8, 8 from 3+5, 12 from 3+9 and 14 from 5+9. So 4 pairs give an even total. The idea to keep: odd plus odd and even plus even are both even.
solutions.elegant: Only whether each number is odd or even matters. Three odd balls make 3 odd pairs, and two even balls make 1 even pair. That is $3 + 1 = 4$ pairs, with no adding needed.

problems.whyOnTest: Knowing when a total is even lets you count without adding every pair, and the trap is forgetting that two odd numbers make an even total.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sam sticks all 18 of his square stickers on a page to make one rectangle with no gaps. A turned rectangle counts as the same. How many different rectangles can he make?

choices.misconception: I only thought of 3 rows of 6, because the long thin ones did not look like rectangles to me.
I found 2 rows of 9 and 3 rows of 6, but forgot the single row of 18.
I counted 1, 2, 3 and 6 rows as four rectangles, but 6 rows of 3 is 3 rows of 6 turned around.
I counted 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18 rows as six rectangles, counting each turned one again.

hints: Try 1 row first, then 2 rows, and keep going.
Make an orderly list by the number of rows. Each row must have the same number of stickers, with none left over. Stop when the rectangles start repeating as turned versions.
1 row of 18 works. 2 rows of 9 works. 3 rows of 6 works. 4 and 5 rows do not share 18 equally. 6 rows of 3 is the 3-by-6 rectangle turned around.

solutions.reliable: List by rows: 1 row of 18, 2 rows of 9, 3 rows of 6. Four rows and five rows do not work, because 18 stickers do not share equally into them. 6 rows of 3, 9 rows of 2 and 18 rows of 1 are the same three rectangles turned around. So there are 3 rectangles. The idea to keep: list in order and stop when the list starts to repeat.

problems.whyOnTest: A careful list is the tool here, and turned shapes counted twice is the classic overcount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A spinner shows 1, 2 and 3. Ben spins it twice: the first spin gives the tens digit, the second the ones digit. How many of his possible numbers are bigger than 20?

choices.misconception: I only counted the numbers in the twenties and forgot the ones starting with 3.
I left out 22 and 33, because I thought a number could not use the same digit twice.
I listed the numbers from 21 up but stopped at 32 and forgot 33.
I counted every number he could make, even the ones smaller than 20.

hints: Which first spins give a number bigger than 20?
A tree diagram helps: branch for the first spin, then for the second. Numbers bigger than 20 must start with 2 or 3. Count the branches below those.
Starting with 2: 21, 22, 23. Starting with 3: 31, 32, 33. Count them.

solutions.reliable: Numbers starting with 1 are 11, 12, 13, all smaller than 20. Starting with 2 gives 21, 22, 23, and starting with 3 gives 31, 32, 33, all bigger than 20. That is 6 numbers. The idea to keep: a tree diagram makes sure every branch is counted once.
solutions.elegant: There are 2 good first spins, 2 and 3, and each can be followed by any of 3 second spins. That is $2 \times 3 = 6$.

problems.whyOnTest: It joins a tree diagram to place value, and repeated digits like 22 are the case students forget.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two equal rectangles, each 5 cm long and 3 cm wide, are joined along their long sides to make one bigger rectangle. How far is it all the way around the bigger rectangle?

choices.misconception: I added one long side and one short side of the big rectangle, 5 + 6, and stopped.
I gave the distance around just one of the small rectangles.
I joined them along their short sides, which makes a rectangle 10 cm long and 3 cm wide.
I added the distances around both small rectangles, counting the sides that are now hidden inside.

hints: Draw the two rectangles joined along their long sides.
Work out the length and width of the new, bigger rectangle from the drawing. Sides that touch are now inside, so they are not part of the distance around.
The big rectangle is still 5 cm long, but it is 3 + 3 = 6 cm wide. Go round it: 5, 6, 5, 6.

solutions.reliable: Joining along the 5 cm sides stacks the rectangles, so the big rectangle is 5 cm long and $3 + 3 = 6$ cm wide. All the way around is $5 + 6 + 5 + 6 = 22$ cm. The idea to keep: when shapes are joined, the touching sides go inside and stop counting.
solutions.elegant: Each small rectangle measures 16 cm around, so 32 cm for both. Joining hides one 5 cm side from each rectangle, so take away $5 + 5 = 10$ cm: $32 - 10 = 22$ cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Joining shapes hides the touching sides, and which sides touch changes the answer, so drawing the joined shape is the reliable step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square garden has sides of 4 m. A path 1 m wide runs all the way around the outside. How far is it all the way around the outer edge of the path?

choices.misconception: I took 1 m off each side, as if the path were inside the garden.
I gave the distance around the garden, not around the outside of the path.
I added the path's 1 m just once to the garden's 16 m.
I added 1 m to each side once, but the path sticks out at both ends of every side.

hints: Draw the garden with the path around it.
The outer edge of the path is a bigger square. Find the length of its side by looking at one side of the drawing: the path adds width at both ends. Then go all the way around.
Across the drawing you meet 1 m of path, 4 m of garden, then 1 m of path. So the big square has sides of 6 m.

solutions.reliable: The outer edge is a square. Each side is 1 m of path, plus 4 m of garden, plus 1 m of path, which is 6 m. All the way around is $6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24$ m. The idea to keep: a border adds its width at both ends of every side, so draw it before you add.
solutions.elegant: Each of the 4 garden sides grows by 2 m, so the distance around grows by $4 \times 2 = 8$ m: $16 + 8 = 24$ m.

problems.whyOnTest: A border adds its width twice to every side, and a quick drawing shows it where mental arithmetic misses it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A vase holds 19 flowers. 5 are red, some are blue and the rest are yellow. There are 3 more yellow flowers than red flowers. How many flowers are blue?

choices.misconception: I found the number of yellow flowers and stopped there.
I took away the 5 red ones and then only 3 for the yellow ones.
I added the red and yellow flowers but forgot to take them away from 19.
I only took away the red flowers, so I counted blue and yellow together.

hints: How many yellow flowers are there?
Draw a bar for all the flowers, split into red, yellow and blue. Work out the yellow part from the red part first. The blue part is what is left of the whole.
Yellow is 5 + 3 = 8. Red and yellow together are 5 + 8 = 13. Take that away from 19.

solutions.reliable: There are $5 + 3 = 8$ yellow flowers. Red and yellow make $5 + 8 = 13$ flowers. The blue flowers are the rest: $19 - 13 = 6$. The idea to keep: in a part-whole problem, find every known part first, then take them all from the whole.

problems.whyOnTest: Part-whole problems with a hidden step check that you find every part before subtracting, and three trap answers stop one step early.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Pia has 3 more shells than Sam. Then Sam finds 7 more shells and Pia finds 2 more shells. Who has more shells now, and how many more?

choices.misconception: I got the right difference, but gave the lead to Pia because she was ahead at the start.
I added Pia's 2 shells to her lead of 3 and forgot Sam's 7 shells.
I took Pia's lead of 3 away from Sam's 7 but forgot that Pia also found 2.
I compared the 7 and the 2 that they found and forgot that Pia started 3 ahead.

hints: Draw two bars, with Pia's bar 3 longer.
Only the difference between the bars matters. Track how each new find changes the gap: shells Pia finds make her lead bigger, and shells Sam finds make it smaller.
Pia starts 3 ahead. Her 2 new shells make her 5 ahead. Then Sam finds 7 shells, which is 2 more than her lead.

solutions.reliable: Pia starts 3 ahead. When Pia finds 2 shells, she is 5 ahead. When Sam finds 7 shells, he catches up 5 and goes 2 past her. So Sam has 2 more shells. Check with numbers: if Sam had 4 and Pia 7, then Sam has 11 and Pia has 9. The idea to keep: in a comparison, follow the gap, not the totals.
solutions.elegant: Sam found $7 - 2 = 5$ more shells than Pia did. That beats Pia's head start of 3 by 2, so Sam leads by 2.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparison bar models reward following the gap, and every trap answer comes from dropping one of the three changes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia has 20 cents. She buys a ruler for 9 cents and an eraser for 6 cents. How much money does she have left?

choices.misconception: I found how much more the ruler costs than the eraser.
I only took away the ruler and forgot the eraser.
I only took away the eraser and forgot the ruler.
I worked out what she spent, not what she has left.

hints: She buys two things. What do they cost together?
Find what she spends on both things, then take that from what she had. Check that the question asks for money left, not money spent.
The ruler and eraser cost 9 + 6 = 15 cents. Take 15 away from 20.

solutions.reliable: Together the ruler and eraser cost $9 + 6 = 15$ cents. Mia had 20 cents, so she has $20 - 15 = 5$ cents left. The idea to keep: add up what is spent, then take it from what you had.
solutions.elegant: Count on from 15 to 20: 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 is 5 more, so 5 cents are left.

problems.whyOnTest: Two-step money problems check that you include every purchase and report change, not cost.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Stickers cost 6 cents each. Tom pays using only 10-cent coins, and he must not get any change. What is the smallest number of stickers he can buy?

choices.misconception: I bought one sticker with one coin and forgot that he would get 4 cents back.
I found the number of coins he pays with, not the number of stickers.
I found that 10 stickers works, but there is a smaller number that works too.
I found how many cents he pays, not how many stickers he buys.

hints: Count up in sixes. When do you land on a ten?
With only 10-cent coins and no change, the total cost must be exactly 10, 20, 30 and so on. List the costs of 1, 2, 3 stickers and keep going until one fits.
The costs go 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first cost that is a whole number of tens is 30 cents.

solutions.reliable: List the cost: 1 sticker is 6 cents, 2 are 12, 3 are 18, 4 are 24 and 5 are 30. The first of these that is exactly some 10-cent coins is 30 cents, paid with 3 coins. So the smallest number of stickers is 5. The idea to keep: list in order and stop at the first one that works.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve: check the choices. 1 sticker costs 6 cents, which needs change. 5 stickers cost 30 cents, three coins exactly. 10 stickers also work, but 5 is smaller.

problems.whyOnTest: It tests a careful list against a money rule, and two trap answers give the coins or the cents instead of the stickers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which number has 5 ones and 2 tens?

choices.misconception: I wrote the digits in the order I read them, 5 first and then 2.
I added the 5 and the 2 together.
I wrote 2 tens as 20 and then wrote the 5 after it.
I wrote 25 and then put a 0 on the end because tens end in zero.

hints: Which digit goes in the tens place?
Write the tens digit on the left and the ones digit on the right, whatever order the words come in.
2 tens means 20. 5 ones means 5. Put them together: 20 and 5.

solutions.reliable: 2 tens is 20 and 5 ones is 5, so the number is $20 + 5 = 25$. The words give the ones first, but the tens digit still goes on the left. The idea to keep: each digit goes in its place, not in the order you hear it.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value is the base of all arithmetic, and giving the ones first catches students who write digits in the order they hear them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sticks come in bundles of 10. Ana has 3 bundles and 14 loose sticks. Ben has 4 bundles and 2 loose sticks. Who has more sticks, and how many more?

choices.misconception: I counted each bundle as 1 stick, so Ana had 17 and Ben had 6.
I compared only the loose sticks, 14 and 2.
I wrote Ana's sticks as 34, forgetting that her 14 loose sticks make another bundle.
I compared only the bundles: Ben has 1 more bundle, which is 10 more sticks.

hints: Can Ana make another bundle from her loose sticks?
Turn both amounts into ordinary numbers before comparing. Ten loose sticks make one more bundle, so regroup first. Then compare the two totals.
Ana has 30 sticks in bundles and 14 loose, so 44. Ben has 40 in bundles and 2 loose, so 42.

solutions.reliable: Ana has $30 + 14 = 44$ sticks. Ben has $40 + 2 = 42$ sticks. So Ana has $44 - 42 = 2$ more. The idea to keep: when there are 10 or more ones, regroup them into a ten before comparing.
solutions.elegant: Ana's 14 loose sticks make 1 bundle and 4 loose, so she has 4 bundles and 4 loose. Ben has 4 bundles and 2 loose. The bundles match, and Ana has 2 more loose sticks.

problems.whyOnTest: Regrouping 10 ones into a ten is the heart of place value, and comparing bundles alone points the wrong way.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A box has 15 pencils. One third of the pencils are blue. How many pencils are blue?

choices.misconception: I thought one third means just 1 pencil.
I thought one third means 3 pencils, because of the 3 in a third.
I found the pencils that are not blue.
I took 3 away from 15 because a third has a 3 in it.

hints: A third means one of three equal shares.
To find a third of a group, share the whole group equally into 3 piles. One pile is a third.
Share 15 pencils into 3 equal piles. Each pile has 5.

solutions.reliable: One third means sharing into 3 equal parts and taking one part. 15 shared into 3 equal parts is 5 in each, because $5 + 5 + 5 = 15$. So 5 pencils are blue. The idea to keep: a fraction of a group means equal sharing, not taking away.

problems.whyOnTest: Finding a fraction of a group is equal sharing, and the trap answers use the 3 as a number of pencils.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Grandma bakes some cookies. She gives half of them to Ana and a quarter of them to Ben. Ana gets 4 more cookies than Ben. How many cookies did Grandma bake?

choices.misconception: I found how many cookies Ben gets, not how many Grandma baked.
I thought the 4 extra cookies were half of all the cookies.
I found how many cookies Ana and Ben get together and thought that was all of them.
I found that Grandma baked 16 cookies and then added the 4 extra cookies again.

hints: How much bigger is a half than a quarter?
Draw a bar for all the cookies and split it into 4 equal parts. Ana gets 2 parts and Ben gets 1 part. The difference between their shares is a number of parts you can see.
Ana's 2 parts are 1 part more than Ben's 1 part. So 1 part, a quarter, is the 4 extra cookies.

solutions.reliable: Split the cookies into 4 equal parts. Ana gets half, which is 2 parts. Ben gets a quarter, which is 1 part. Ana has 1 part more, and that part is 4 cookies. So each part is 4 cookies, and all 4 parts are $4 \times 4 = 16$ cookies. Check: Ana gets 8, Ben gets 4, and 8 is 4 more than 4. The idea to keep: turn fractions into equal parts of a bar, then find what one part is worth.
solutions.elegant: Half take away a quarter is a quarter, so a quarter of the cookies is 4. The whole is four quarters: 16.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparing two fractions of the same whole needs a picture of equal parts, and the trap answers stop at a part instead of the whole.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A snail is at 12 on a number line. It crawls along the line to 5. How many steps does it crawl, if each step goes from one number to the next?

choices.misconception: I counted only the numbers in between, leaving out both 12 and 5.
I counted the numbers from 12 down to 5, both ends included, instead of the steps between them.
I gave the number where the snail started.
I added 12 and 5 instead of finding the distance between them.

hints: Count the jumps, not the numbers.
The distance between two numbers on a number line is the number of steps between them. Take the smaller number away from the bigger one, or count the jumps one at a time.
Jump from 12 to 11, 11 to 10, and so on until you reach 5. Count each jump once.

solutions.reliable: The steps go 12 to 11, 11 to 10, 10 to 9, 9 to 8, 8 to 7, 7 to 6 and 6 to 5. That is 7 steps, the same as $12 - 5 = 7$. The idea to keep: the distance on a number line counts the jumps, so the starting number is not counted.

problems.whyOnTest: Distance on a number line is a difference, and counting the marks instead of the jumps gives one too many.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An arrow makes a quarter turn each step. In steps 1 to 4 it points up, right, down and left, then keeps turning the same way. When does it point up for the third time?

choices.misconception: I thought the arrow comes back to up every 3 steps, so I counted 1, 4, 7.
I counted up, right, down, left, up as 5 steps in each round, so I counted 1, 6, 11.
I thought up comes on steps 4, 8 and 12, as if the round started at step 4.
I did not count step 1 as the first time, so I found the fourth time instead of the third.

hints: After step 4, what does the arrow do in step 5?
The arrow repeats a pattern of 4 directions. Find the steps where it points up: the first one is step 1, and each next one comes a full round later.
It points up in step 1, then 4 steps later in step 5, then 4 steps after that.

solutions.reliable: The pattern up, right, down, left repeats every 4 steps. Step 5 starts a new round, so the arrow points up in steps 1, 5, 9 and so on. The third time is step 9. The idea to keep: in a repeating pattern of 4, the same picture comes back every 4 steps, starting from where it first appears.
solutions.elegant: Write the list: 1 up, 2 right, 3 down, 4 left, 5 up, 6 right, 7 down, 8 left, 9 up. The third up is step 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeating patterns are about the length of the cycle, and the trap answers each use a cycle that is too long, too short or started in the wrong place.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana makes hollow square frames, one tile wide, from square tiles. The first three have 3, 5 and 7 tiles along each side. She keeps going. How many tiles does the next frame need?

choices.misconception: I counted 9 tiles along the top and bottom and 8 down each side, so one corner on each side was counted twice.
I counted 9 tiles on each of the 4 sides, so every corner tile was counted twice.
I counted 9 tiles on each of the 4 sides and then added the 4 corner tiles again.
I counted a full 9 by 9 square and forgot the frame is hollow.

hints: How many tiles along each side does the next frame have?
The sides grow 3, 5, 7, so the next frame has 9 tiles along each side. Count the tiles in a frame carefully: each corner tile belongs to two sides, so count it only once.
The frames have 8, 16 and 24 tiles. Each new frame adds the same number of tiles. Or count the 9-tile frame directly: top, bottom, then the tiles left on each side.

solutions.reliable: The sides go 3, 5, 7, growing by 2 each time, so the next frame has 9 tiles along each side. Count it: 9 tiles on the top and 9 on the bottom. Each side then needs only 7 more tiles, because its two corner tiles are already counted. That is $9 + 9 + 7 + 7 = 32$ tiles. Check with the pattern: the frames have 8, 16 and 24 tiles, adding 8 each time, and $24 + 8 = 32$. The idea to keep: corner tiles belong to two sides, so count them only once.
solutions.elegant: Count 4 sides of 9 tiles, which is 36, then take away the 4 corner tiles that were counted twice: $36 - 4 = 32$.

problems.whyOnTest: Growing frames test whether corner tiles are counted once, and the classic trap of four times the side double-counts every corner.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A lamp starts off. Each button press switches it on or off. Monday to Friday, Ivy presses it 2, 1, 1, 2 and 2 times. On how many days is it on at bedtime?

choices.misconception: I counted the days when she pressed an odd number of times that day, Tuesday and Wednesday, and forgot the lamp keeps its state from the day before.
I counted the days when she pressed an even number of times that day, because I thought even meant on.
I thought the lamp started on, so I counted the days it would be on if it began on, which are the days it is really off.
I thought every press turns the lamp on, so it is on every day.

hints: The lamp does not reset at night. Keep a running count.
Two presses bring the lamp back to how it was. So only the total number of presses so far matters: an odd total means on, an even total means off.
