solutions.reliable: Any $k$ balls add up to at least $1 + 2 + \dots + k$, and you might draw exactly those. With 13 balls the unluckiest total is $91 < 100$, so 13 balls are not enough. With 14 balls the smallest possible total is $105 \ge 100$, so 14 balls always suffice. The transferable idea: to be certain, plan for the worst possible draw.

problems.whyOnTest: Certainty means beating the unluckiest case, and the trap is reasoning from typical or lucky draws instead.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A long strip of paper has parallel straight edges. It is folded flat along a straight crease that makes an angle of 65° with the bottom edge. What acute angle do the edges of the folded-over part make with the edges of the part that stayed in place?

choices.misconception: I gave 90° - 65°, the angle between the crease and a line at right angles to the edge.
I thought the folded edge makes the same angle with the bottom edge as the crease does.
I gave 180° - 65°, the angle on the other side of the crease, without reflecting anything.
I found the angle $2 \times 65^\circ$ correctly but gave the obtuse angle instead of the acute one.

hints: Folding is a reflection in the crease.
A reflection keeps the angle with the mirror line the same size but puts it on the other side. Find the angle between the bottom edge and its reflection in the crease, then take the acute one.
The bottom edge makes 65° with the crease on one side, and its image makes 65° with the crease on the other side.

solutions.reliable: Folding reflects the folded part in the crease. The bottom edge makes $65^\circ$ with the crease, so its image makes $65^\circ$ with the crease on the other side. The angle between the edge and its image is $65^\circ + 65^\circ = 130^\circ$, so the acute angle between the two lines is $180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ$. The other edge of the folded part is parallel to this image, so it makes the same angle. The transferable idea: a fold is a reflection, and a reflection doubles the angle to the mirror line.

problems.whyOnTest: A fold is a reflection, so the angle to the crease doubles, and the slips are forgetting to double it or giving the obtuse angle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A convex polygon has interior angles that are all different whole numbers of degrees. What is the largest number of sides it can have?

choices.misconception: I took the exterior angles of a polygon to add up to 180° and fitted $1 + 2 + \dots + 18 = 171$ under that total.
I solved $n(n + 1)/2 = 360$, got about 26.3 and rounded up to 27, but 27 different exterior angles need at least 378°.
I counted how many different whole numbers an interior angle can be, 1° to 179°, and ignored the angle sum.
I let every exterior angle be 1°, forgetting that the interior angles, and so the exterior angles, must all be different.

hints: Look at the exterior angles instead of the interior ones.

The exterior angles of a convex polygon add up to 360°. If the interior angles are different whole numbers, so are the exterior angles. Make the exterior angles as small as possible to fit in as many as you can.
The smallest possible exterior angles are 1°, 2°, 3° and so on. Find the largest $n$ with $1 + 2 + \dots + n \le 360$.

solutions.reliable: Each exterior angle is 180° minus an interior angle, so the exterior angles are different positive whole numbers of degrees, and they add up to 360°. With $n$ sides they total at least $1 + 2 + \dots + n = n(n + 1)/2$. Since $26 \times 27 / 2 = 351 \le 360$ but $27 \times 28 / 2 = 378 > 360$, there are at most 26 sides. And 26 is possible: take exterior angles 1°, 2°, ..., 25° and 35°, which are different and add up to $325 + 35 = 360$, giving interior angles 179°, 178°, ..., 155° and 145°. A convex polygon with any such exterior angles exists, because the side lengths can be chosen to close the shape. The transferable idea: an extremal question about angles often becomes easy after switching to exterior angles, whose sum is fixed.

problems.whyOnTest: Switching from interior to exterior angles turns a polygon question into fitting different whole numbers under a fixed total of 360.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten counters lie in a row: five black ones followed by five white ones. A move swaps a black counter with the white counter directly to its right. Moves are made, in any order, until no move is possible. How many moves are made in total?

choices.misconception: I counted the 9 gaps between neighbouring counters and allowed one swap for each gap.
I thought each of the ten counters moves exactly once.
I counted every pair of counters, $\binom{10}{2} = 45$, but only pairs with a black counter to the left of a white one ever swap.
I counted each swap twice, once for the black counter and once for the white one.

hints: Look at pairs made of one black and one white counter.
Find a quantity that every move changes by exactly one, such as the number of pairs with a black counter somewhere to the left of a white one. It fixes the number of moves in any order.
At the start all $5 \times 5$ black and white pairs have the black counter on the left. Each move fixes exactly one such pair, and the process stops only when none are left.

solutions.reliable: Call a pair made of one black and one white counter out of order if the black one is to the left of the white one. At the start all $5 \times 5 = 25$ such pairs are out of order. A move swaps two neighbours, so it changes the order of exactly that one pair and no other: the count drops by exactly 1. If any pair is out of order, somewhere a black counter has a white counter directly to its right, so a move is still possible; the process therefore stops exactly when the count reaches 0. So exactly 25 moves are made, whatever their order. The transferable idea: a quantity that changes by exactly one per move counts the moves for you.
solutions.elegant: Each white counter must end up to the left of every black counter, and in one move it passes exactly one black counter. Each of the 5 white counters passes 5 black ones, so there are $5 \times 5 = 25$ moves. The transferable idea: count how many times each object must overtake another.

problems.whyOnTest: A process with free choices still has a fixed length when some quantity drops by exactly one each move, which turns a search into a count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers can NOT be the sum of the digits of a perfect square?

choices.misconception: I tried the squares up to $15^2$, none had digit sum 19, so I decided it was impossible, but $17^2 = 289$ works.
I thought the digit sum of a square, like a square itself, can never be 2 more than a multiple of 4, but $43^2 = 1849$ has digit sum 22.
I listed the remainders of squares on division by 9 as only 0, 1 and 4, forgetting 7, which comes from $4^2 = 16$.
I checked the squares up to $100^2$ and found no digit sum of 28, but $134^2 = 17956$ has it.

hints: A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by 9.
Prove impossibility by contradiction: if some square had that digit sum, the square would leave a particular remainder on division by 9. Check which remainders squares can actually leave.
Squares leave remainder 0, 1, 4 or 7 on division by 9. Find the remainders of 19, 22, 24, 25 and 28.

solutions.reliable: A number leaves the same remainder on division by 9 as its digit sum. The squares of 0, 1, ..., 8 leave remainders 0, 1, 4, 0, 7, 7, 0, 4, 1, so every square leaves remainder 0, 1, 4 or 7. The choices leave remainders 1 (for 19), 4 (for 22), 6 (for 24), 7 (for 25) and 1 (for 28). Only 24 has a remainder that no square can have, so no square has digit sum 24. The others really occur: $17^2 = 289$, $43^2 = 1849$, $67^2 = 4489$ and $134^2 = 17956$ have digit sums 19, 22, 25 and 28. The transferable idea: to show something never happens, find a remainder that it would force and that is impossible.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders on division by 9 prove that a digit sum is impossible for every square, while searching small cases misleads.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A radio host chooses 3 songs from a list of 9 for a show, and the order does not matter. Song A must be one of the three, but song B must not. In how many ways can she choose the songs?

choices.misconception: I made sure song A was chosen but forgot to leave out song B, so I chose the other 2 songs from 8.
I left out both song A and song B and chose all 3 songs from the other 7.
I left out song B but did not make sure that song A was chosen, so I chose 3 songs from 8.
I counted every choice of 3 songs from 9 and ignored both conditions.

hints: Once song A is in, how many places are left to fill?
Deal with the conditions first: put song A in, cross song B off the list, and then count the free selections from the songs that are left.
Two more songs are needed, chosen from the 7 songs that are neither A nor B.

solutions.reliable: Song A is in, so 2 more songs are needed. Song B is out, so they come from the other 7 songs: $\binom72 = 21$ ways. The transferable idea: settle the forced and forbidden items first, then count the free choice.
solutions.elegant: Check by complement: of the $\binom83 = 56$ choices without song B, $\binom73 = 35$ also leave out song A, so $56 - 35 = 21$ include it. The transferable idea: a complement count is a quick second method.

problems.whyOnTest: Forced and forbidden items shrink a selection before any counting, and each distractor forgets one of the two conditions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three of the 8 corners of a cube are chosen. In how many ways can this be done so that the three chosen corners are the vertices of a right-angled triangle?

choices.misconception: I counted the triangles whose sides are all face diagonals, but those are equilateral, not right-angled.
I only counted right-angled triangles lying in a face of the cube, 4 in each face, and missed the ones that cut through the inside.
I subtracted only 4 equilateral triangles, thinking there is just one regular tetrahedron inside the cube, but there are two.
I counted every choice of three corners and forgot that some of the triangles are equilateral.

hints: What shapes can three corners of a cube make?
Count the complement: every triangle on the corners of a cube turns out to be either right-angled or equilateral. Count all choices of three corners, then subtract the equilateral triangles.
There are $\binom83 = 56$ choices. An equilateral triangle has three face diagonals as its sides, and it is cut off by the three face diagonals around one corner.

solutions.reliable: Take a cube with edge 1. Two corners are at distance 1, $\sqrt2$ or $\sqrt3$. Checking the possible triangles, the sides are 1, 1, $\sqrt2$ or 1, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$, both right-angled by Pythagoras, or $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt2$, which is equilateral. Each corner has exactly three face-diagonal neighbours, and they form one equilateral triangle, so there are 8 equilateral triangles, one for each corner. All $\binom83 = 56$ choices give a triangle, since no three corners of a cube lie on a line, so $56 - 8 = 48$ are right-angled. The transferable idea: when almost everything qualifies, count what does not and subtract.
solutions.elegant: Count directly. Right angles inside a face: 6 faces with 4 triangles each, 24. Triangles with sides 1, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$: choose one of the 4 long diagonals and any of the other 6 corners, 24. Total $24 + 24 = 48$. The transferable idea: sort the triangles by side lengths and count each type.

problems.whyOnTest: Classifying the few triangle shapes a cube allows turns the count into one subtraction, and the trap is missing triangles that cut through the cube.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mixing 1 litre of drink P with 2 litres of drink Q gives a drink that is 40% juice. Mixing 2 litres of P with 1 litre of Q gives a drink that is 50% juice. What percentage of drink P is juice?

choices.misconception: I wrote $p + 2q = 40$ and $2p + q = 50$, forgetting that each mixture has 3 litres, and solved to get $p = 20$.
I solved the equations correctly but gave the percentage of juice in drink Q.
I averaged the two mixtures, which gives the juice in a half-and-half mix, not in drink P.
I assumed the mixture with more P is close enough to P itself and gave its percentage.

hints: Write the amount of juice in each 3-litre mixture.
Let P be $p\%$ juice and Q be $q\%$ juice. Each mixture gives one equation for the litres of juice. Solve the pair, for example by adding and subtracting the equations.

solutions.reliable: Let P be $p\%$ juice and Q be $q\%$ juice. The first mixture holds $\frac{p + 2q}{100}$ litres of juice in 3 litres, so $p + 2q = 120$. The second gives $2p + q = 150$. Subtracting, $p - q = 30$; adding, $3p + 3q = 270$, so $p + q = 90$. Hence $p = 60$ and $q = 30$. Check: $(60 + 2 \times 30) / 3 = 40$ and $(2 \times 60 + 30) / 3 = 50$. The transferable idea: in a mixture, the amounts of the ingredient add up, not the percentages.

problems.whyOnTest: Weighted averages combine amounts of juice rather than percentages, and two mixtures give two equations to solve.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to $\sqrt{5050^2 - 5049^2}$?

choices.misconception: I treated $\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}$ as if it were $a - b$.
I simplified $5050^2 - 5049^2$ to 5050, forgetting that it equals $(5050 - 5049)(5050 + 5049)$, and took the square root.
I wrote the square root of $5050 + 5049$ as $\sqrt{5050} + \sqrt{5049}$, which is about 71 + 71.
I found that $5050^2 - 5049^2 = 10099$ but forgot to take the square root.

hints: Do not square 5050. Factorise instead.
Use the difference of two squares, $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, to turn the expression under the root into a manageable number, then estimate its square root.

solutions.reliable: $5050^2 - 5049^2 = (5050 - 5049)(5050 + 5049) = 10099$. Since $100^2 = 10000$ and $101^2 = 10201$, the square root is between 100 and 101 and very close to 100. The transferable idea: factorise a difference of squares before doing any arithmetic, then estimate.

problems.whyOnTest: One factorisation turns huge squares into a number whose root is easy to estimate, and the distractors come from misusing square roots.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lamps numbered 1 to 360 are all off. Ana flips the switch of every lamp whose number is a multiple of 9. Then Ben flips the switch of every lamp whose number is a multiple of 12. How many lamps are on at the end?

choices.misconception: I counted every lamp that was flipped at least once, $40 + 30 - 10$, but lamps flipped twice are off again.
I took the lamps flipped by both to be the multiples of $9 \times 12 = 108$ and removed them from both counts: $40 + 30 - 2 \times 3$.
I counted the lamps flipped at least once and took the overlap to be the multiples of 108: $40 + 30 - 3$.
I added Ana's 40 lamps and Ben's 30 lamps, forgetting that some lamps were flipped by both.

hints: What happens to a lamp whose switch is flipped twice?

A lamp ends up on exactly when it was flipped by exactly one of the two people. Count each person's lamps, find the overlap carefully using the least common multiple, and remove the overlap from both counts.
Multiples of 9: 40. Multiples of 12: 30. Multiples of both 9 and 12 are the multiples of 36: 10.

solutions.reliable: A lamp is on at the end exactly when its switch was flipped once. Ana flips $360 / 9 = 40$ lamps and Ben flips $360 / 12 = 30$. A lamp is flipped by both when its number is a multiple of both 9 and 12, that is a multiple of their least common multiple 36: 10 lamps. These appear in both lists and end up off, so the lamps that are on number $(40 - 10) + (30 - 10) = 50$. The transferable idea: exactly one of two sets is the two counts minus twice the overlap.
solutions.elegant: Follow Ben's turn: after Ana, 40 lamps are on. Of Ben's 30 lamps, the 10 multiples of 36 were on and go off, and the other 20 were off and come on. That leaves $40 - 10 + 20 = 50$. The transferable idea: track how each step changes the count instead of recounting from scratch.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting exactly one of two sets needs the overlap removed twice, and the overlap of multiples of 9 and 12 is the multiples of 36, not 108.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many six-digit numbers can be made by arranging the digits 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 and 4 so that the two 1s are not next to each other and the two 2s are not next to each other?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the 24 arrangements with both pairs together instead of adding them back.
I subtracted the 120 arrangements with a pair together but did not add back the 24 arrangements that were subtracted twice.
I added back the arrangements with both pairs together but counted only 12 of them, wrongly dividing $4!$ by 2.
I counted every arrangement of the six digits and ignored the rule.

hints: How many arrangements are there with no rule at all?
Overcount, then correct: subtract the arrangements where the 1s touch and where the 2s touch, then add back those subtracted twice. Glue a touching pair into one block to count them.
With no rule: $\frac{6!}{2! \times 2!} = 180$. With the 1s glued together: $\frac{5!}{2!} = 60$, and the same for the 2s. With both pairs glued: $4! = 24$.

solutions.reliable: Without the rule there are $\frac{6!}{2! \times 2!} = 180$ arrangements. Gluing the two 1s into one block leaves 5 items, with the two 2s alike, so $\frac{5!}{2!} = 60$ arrangements have the 1s together; likewise 60 have the 2s together. The arrangements with both pairs together are arrangements of two blocks and the digits 3 and 4, so there are $4! = 24$ of them, and they were subtracted twice. The answer is $180 - 60 - 60 + 24 = 84$. The transferable idea: subtract the bad cases, then add back what was subtracted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Two forbidden adjacencies overlap, so plain subtraction overcorrects, and the test is adding back exactly the arrangements removed twice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A short stick holds 4 beads in a row, and each bead is red, green or blue. Turning the stick end to end reverses the order of the beads. Two sticks count as the same if one becomes the other when turned. How many different sticks are there?

choices.misconception: I removed the 9 sticks that read the same both ways and halved the rest, $(81 - 9)/2$, but forgot to add those 9 back.
I halved the 72 sticks that read differently each way and then counted each of the 9 symmetric sticks twice.
I removed the 9 sticks that read the same both ways but did not halve the others.
I counted all $3^4$ colourings and did not merge a stick with its reverse.

hints: Which sticks look exactly the same after turning?
Pair each colouring with its reverse. Most pairs contain two different colourings that must count once, but some colourings are their own reverse and must not be halved.
A colouring is its own reverse when bead 1 matches bead 4 and bead 2 matches bead 3: $3 \times 3 = 9$ such colourings.

solutions.reliable: There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings. A colouring reads the same both ways when beads 1 and 4 match and beads 2 and 3 match: $3 \times 3 = 9$ of them, each a stick on its own. The other 72 colourings pair up with their reverses, giving $72 / 2 = 36$ sticks. The total is $9 + 36 = 45$. The transferable idea: under a symmetry, halve only the objects that the symmetry moves.
solutions.elegant: Average the number of colourings that each move leaves unchanged: doing nothing fixes 81 and turning fixes 9, so there are $(81 + 9)/2 = 45$ sticks. The transferable idea: the number of patterns up to a symmetry is the average number of colourings each move fixes.

problems.whyOnTest: Dividing by the symmetry only works for objects that the symmetry moves, and the symmetric ones are where students go wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The nine numbers $1 \times 2, 2 \times 3, 3 \times 4, \dots, 9 \times 10$ are written on a board. A move erases two numbers $a$ and $b$ and writes $\frac{ab}{a + b}$ in their place. After eight moves only one number is left. What is it?

choices.misconception: I found that the reciprocals add up to $\frac{9}{10}$ and gave that, forgetting to turn it upside down.
I telescoped the reciprocals to $1 + \frac{1}{10}$ instead of $1 - \frac{1}{10}$, then turned the result upside down.
I stopped the telescoping at $\frac{1}{9}$, getting $1 - \frac{1}{9} = \frac{8}{9}$, then turned it upside down.
I kept only the last term, $\frac{1}{10}$, of the telescoping sum and turned it upside down.

hints: Look at $\frac{1}{a}$ and $\frac{1}{b}$ rather than at $a$ and $b$.
Find an invariant: the reciprocal of the new number is the sum of the reciprocals of the two erased numbers. So some total never changes. Compute that total at the start.
$\frac{1}{k(k + 1)} = \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k + 1}$, so the reciprocals of the nine numbers add up to $1 - \frac{1}{10}$.

solutions.reliable: The new number has reciprocal $\frac{a + b}{ab} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$, so a move replaces two reciprocals by their sum and the sum of the reciprocals of all the numbers on the board never changes. At the start it is $\frac{1}{1 \times 2} + \frac{1}{2 \times 3} + \dots + \frac{1}{9 \times 10} = (1 - \frac{1}{2}) + (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}) + \dots + (\frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{10}) = \frac{9}{10}$. At the end there is one number $x$ with $\frac{1}{x} = \frac{9}{10}$, so $x = \frac{10}{9}$. The transferable idea: when a move combines two numbers, look for a quantity whose total the move preserves.

problems.whyOnTest: The order of moves is irrelevant once the preserved quantity is found, and here it is the sum of reciprocals, which then telescopes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts with $a_1 = 1$, and each later term is given by $a_{n+1} = 2a_n + n$. What is $a_{10}$?

choices.misconception: I found that $a_n + n + 1$ doubles each time, but subtracted only $n = 10$ from $3 \times 2^9$ and forgot the extra 1.
I subtracted only 1 from $3 \times 2^9$, forgetting that the amount to subtract grows with $n$.
I found that $a_n + n + 1 = 3 \times 2^{n-1}$ but forgot to subtract $n + 1$ at the end.
I applied the rule one time too many and gave $a_{11}$.

hints: Work out the first few terms and compare them with powers of 2.
Look for a shift that turns the rule into pure doubling: add a simple expression in $n$ to every term so that the new numbers just double. Then undo the shift at the end.
The numbers $a_n + n + 1$ run 3, 6, 12, 24 and so on, doubling each time.

solutions.reliable: Compute term by term: $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 3$, $a_3 = 8$, $a_4 = 19$, $a_5 = 42$, $a_6 = 89$, $a_7 = 184$, $a_8 = 375$, $a_9 = 758$ and $a_{10} = 2 \times 758 + 9 = 1525$. The transferable idea: with only ten steps, careful direct computation is reliable, and a pattern can check it.
solutions.elegant: Let $b_n = a_n + n + 1$. Then $b_{n+1} = (2a_n + n) + (n + 1) + 1 = 2(a_n + n + 1) = 2b_n$, and $b_1 = 3$, so $b_n = 3 \times 2^{n-1}$ and $a_{10} = 3 \times 512 - 11 = 1525$. The transferable idea: shift a recursion so that the extra term disappears.

problems.whyOnTest: A doubling rule with an extra term becomes pure doubling after a shift, and the slips come in undoing the shift.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag holds 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are taken out at random, one after the other, without putting the first one back. What is the probability that the two balls have different colours?

choices.misconception: I counted the 6 pairs of one red and one blue ball but divided by the 20 ordered draws, mixing unordered and ordered counting.
I worked out the probability that the two balls have the same colour, which is the opposite of what was asked.
I treated the draws as if the first ball were put back before the second, so I used $2 \times \frac35 \times \frac25$.
I thought that same colour and different colours are two outcomes and so must be equally likely.

hints: Count pairs of balls, or think of the two draws in order.

Solve it two ways to be safe: count unordered pairs directly, and separately find the chance of the same colour and subtract it from 1. Use the same kind of counting in the top and bottom of each fraction.
There are $\binom52 = 10$ pairs of balls, and $3 \times 2 = 6$ of them are one red and one blue.

solutions.reliable: There are $\binom52 = 10$ equally likely pairs. A mixed pair is one of the 3 red balls with one of the 2 blue balls: 6 pairs. The probability is $\frac{6}{10} = \frac35$. Check by complement: two reds, $\binom32 = 3$ pairs; two blues, 1 pair; so the same colour has probability $\frac{4}{10}$ and different colours $1 - \frac{4}{10} = \frac35$. The transferable idea: confirm a probability with a second method, and keep ordered and unordered counting consistent.
solutions.elegant: In order: red then blue has probability $\frac35 \times \frac24 = \frac{3}{10}$, and blue then red $\frac25 \times \frac34 = \frac{3}{10}$, so the total is $\frac35$. The transferable idea: when the order of events matters, add the orders separately.

problems.whyOnTest: Two quick methods, direct and complement, agree only if ordered and unordered counts are not mixed, which is the classic slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three different numbers are chosen from $1, 2, 3, \dots, 11$. In how many ways can this be done so that their sum is even?

choices.misconception: I only counted the choices of three even numbers.
I added $\binom62 + 5$ instead of multiplying for two odd numbers and one even number, then added the 10 all-even choices.
I counted two odd numbers with one even number, but forgot that three even numbers also give an even sum.
I counted the choices with one or three odd numbers, which are exactly the ones with an odd sum.

hints: How many of the numbers 1 to 11 are odd?
Casework on parity: a sum of three numbers is even exactly when an even number of them are odd. Count the case with no odd numbers and the case with two odd numbers separately, then add.
There are 6 odd and 5 even numbers. Three evens: $\binom53$. Two odds and one even: $\binom62 \times 5$.

solutions.reliable: The numbers 1 to 11 include 6 odd and 5 even numbers. The sum is even when 0 or 2 of the chosen numbers are odd. No odd numbers: $\binom53 = 10$. Two odd and one even: $\binom62 \times 5 = 15 \times 5 = 75$. The total is $10 + 75 = 85$. The transferable idea: split a selection by parity and multiply the choices within each case.
solutions.elegant: Check by complement: all $\binom{11}{3} = 165$ choices, minus the odd sums, which are three odd numbers ($\binom63 = 20$) or one odd and two even ($6 \times \binom52 = 60$), leaves $165 - 80 = 85$. The transferable idea: the complement gives an independent check on a casework count.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity casework organises a selection count, and forgetting the all-even case or confusing odd and even sums are the common slips.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A café sells 12 kinds of drink and 7 kinds of pastry. Each of 1000 customers buys exactly one drink and one pastry. What is the largest number $k$ for which we can be certain that at least $k$ customers chose exactly the same drink and pastry?

choices.misconception: I added one to my answer, as in the usual pigeonhole rule, but that step belongs to finding how many customers are needed, not how many must share.
I added the 12 drinks and 7 pastries to get 19 combinations instead of multiplying, then divided 1000 by 19 and rounded up.
I gave the number of different drink and pastry combinations instead of how many customers must share one.
I worked out how many customers guarantee that two share a combination, which answers a different question.

hints: How many different drink and pastry combinations are there?
Pigeonhole: the combinations are the boxes and the customers are the objects. If every box held fewer than $k$ customers, how many customers could there be at most?
There are $12 \times 7 = 84$ combinations, and $84 \times 11 = 924$.

solutions.reliable: There are $12 \times 7 = 84$ combinations. If every combination were chosen by at most 11 customers, there would be at most $84 \times 11 = 924 < 1000$ customers, so some combination is chosen by at least 12. And 12 is the most we can promise: the 1000 customers could be spread with 76 combinations chosen 12 times and 8 chosen 11 times, since $76 \times 12 + 8 \times 11 = 912 + 88 = 1000$, and then no combination has 13. The transferable idea: with $N$ objects in $B$ boxes, some box holds at least $N / B$ rounded up.

problems.whyOnTest: The general pigeonhole principle needs the right number of boxes, here a product, and rounding up rather than down.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Cards numbered 1 to 100 lie face down. You take cards without looking. What is the smallest number of cards you must take to be certain that three of them have consecutive numbers, such as 41, 42 and 43?

choices.misconception: I split the cards into 33 groups of three consecutive numbers and took one card from each group plus one more.
I worked out how many cards guarantee two consecutive numbers, not three.
I took two cards from each of the 33 groups 1 to 3, 4 to 6, up to 97 to 99, and added one, forgetting that card 100 can also be held safely.
I avoided four numbers in a row instead of three, keeping three of every four cards, and then added one.

hints: How many cards can you hold without having three consecutive numbers?
Worst case: find the largest collection of cards with no three consecutive numbers, then add one. To prove that one more always works, split 1 to 100 into blocks that each force a run.
Two cards from each of the blocks 1 to 3, 4 to 6, ..., 97 to 99, together with card 100, make 67 cards with no three consecutive numbers.

solutions.reliable: The cards 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, ..., 97, 98 and also 100 are $2 \times 33 + 1 = 67$ cards with no three consecutive numbers, so 67 cards are not enough. Now take any 68 cards. Card 100 is at most one of them, so at least 67 come from the 33 blocks $\{1, 2, 3\}, \{4, 5, 6\}, \dots, \{97, 98, 99\}$. If each block held at most 2 of them, there would be at most 66, so some block holds all three of its numbers, which are consecutive. The answer is 68. The transferable idea: a worst-case answer needs both a bad example one short of it and an argument that it always works.

problems.whyOnTest: A guarantee needs the largest bad collection plus one, and the leftover card 100 is the detail that separates 67 from 68.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: For which of these values of $n$ does the equation $x^2 - 3y^2 = n$ have NO solution in integers $x$ and $y$?

choices.misconception: I thought $x^2 - 3y^2$ can never be negative because squares are never negative, but $1^2 - 3 \times 1^2 = -2$.
I thought $x^2 - 3y^2$, like a square, can never be 2 more than a multiple of 4, but $5^2 - 3 \times 1^2 = 22$.
I thought a multiple of 3 forces both $x$ and $y$ to be multiples of 3, making the left side a multiple of 9, but $6^2 - 3 \times 1^2 = 33$.
I listed the remainders of $x^2 - 3y^2$ on division by 8 and missed 5, which comes from $0 - 3$, but $7^2 - 3 \times 2^2 = 37$.

hints: Squares leave only a few possible remainders when divided by a small number.
Argue by contradiction: assume a solution exists and compare the remainders of both sides on division by a small number. Division by 3 rules out none of the choices, so try division by 4.
On division by 4, $-3y^2$ leaves the same remainder as $y^2$, so $x^2 - 3y^2$ behaves like $x^2 + y^2$, which leaves 0, 1 or 2.

solutions.reliable: Every square leaves remainder 0 or 1 on division by 4. Since $-3y^2 = y^2 - 4y^2$, the number $x^2 - 3y^2$ leaves the same remainder as $x^2 + y^2$, which is 0, 1 or 2, never 3. As $7 = 4 + 3$ leaves remainder 3, the equation $x^2 - 3y^2 = 7$ has no integer solution. The others do: $1^2 - 3 \times 1^2 = -2$, $5^2 - 3 \times 1^2 = 22$, $6^2 - 3 \times 1^2 = 33$ and $7^2 - 3 \times 2^2 = 37$. The transferable idea: when one divisor gives no contradiction, try another small one.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders on division by 3 do not separate the choices, so the student must find the divisor, here 4, that gives a contradiction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class of 30 students, 19 like football and 17 like tennis. Let $m$ be the smallest possible number of students who like both sports, and $M$ the largest possible number. What is $m + M$?

choices.misconception: I found only the smallest possible number, $19 + 17 - 30$, and gave that.
I found $m = 6$ and $M = 17$ correctly but gave their difference instead of their sum.
I assumed every student likes at least one sport in both cases, so I used 6 for the largest number too.
I found only the largest possible number, when every tennis fan also likes football.

hints: When is the overlap smallest, and when is it largest?
Inclusion-exclusion: the number who like at least one sport is 19 + 17 minus the overlap, and it can be at most 30. The overlap also cannot be bigger than the smaller group.
The overlap is at least $19 + 17 - 30 = 6$ and at most 17.

solutions.reliable: The number who like football or tennis is $19 + 17 - b$, where $b$ students like both. This is at most 30, so $b \ge 6$, and $b = 6$ happens when every student likes at least one sport. Also $b \le 17$, since only 17 like tennis, and $b = 17$ happens when every tennis fan also likes football; then 19 like at least one sport and 11 like neither. So $m = 6$, $M = 17$ and $m + M = 23$. The transferable idea: inclusion-exclusion with a cap on the total gives the smallest overlap, and the smaller set gives the largest.

problems.whyOnTest: Inclusion-exclusion runs backwards here to bound an unknown overlap, and the slips are finding only one bound or combining them wrongly.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A, B and C are three different non-zero digits. The six three-digit numbers that can be made from them, ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB and CBA, add up to 3552. What is the largest possible value of ABC?

choices.misconception: I found the digit sum $A + B + C = 16$ and gave that as the answer.
I found the smallest possible value of ABC instead of the largest.
I divided 3552 by 6 and took the average of the six numbers as ABC.
I made ABC as large as possible with digit sum 16 but used the digit 0, which is not allowed.

hints: How many times does each digit appear in the hundreds column?
Each digit appears twice in each of the three columns, so the total is a fixed multiple of $A + B + C$. Find the digit sum first, then build the largest number allowed.
The total is $2 \times 111 \times (A + B + C) = 222(A + B + C)$.

solutions.reliable: Each digit appears exactly twice in each place, so the six numbers add up to $222(A + B + C)$. Then $A + B + C = 3552 / 222 = 16$. To make ABC as large as possible take $A = 9$; then $B + C = 7$ with B as large as possible and both digits non-zero and different, so $B = 6$ and $C = 1$ ($B = 7$ would need $C = 0$). So ABC is 961. Check: $961 + 916 + 691 + 619 + 196 + 169 = 3552$. The transferable idea: in a sum of digit rearrangements, each digit appears equally often in each place.

problems.whyOnTest: Sums of digit rearrangements collapse to a multiple of the digit sum, after which the question is careful choice under the non-zero rule.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A convex polygon has one interior angle of $90^\circ$, and every other interior angle is $150^\circ$. How many sides does the polygon have?

choices.misconception: I wrote the angle sum as $180(n-1)$ instead of $180(n-2)$, which gave $30(n-1) = 90$.
I found that nine angles of $150^\circ$ are needed but forgot to count the $90^\circ$ corner as a side too.
I worked out $(360 - 90) \div 30 = 9$ and then added 2, because the angle-sum formula has an $n - 2$ in it.
I ignored the $90^\circ$ angle and used a regular polygon with all angles $150^\circ$, which has 12 sides.

hints: Look at the angle outside each corner instead of inside it.
The exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to $360^\circ$. Turn each interior angle into its exterior angle, then count how many of each kind you need.
The $90^\circ$ corner has an exterior angle of $90^\circ$ and each $150^\circ$ corner has an exterior angle of $30^\circ$. So $90 + 30k = 360$, where $k$ is the number of $150^\circ$ corners.

solutions.reliable: Each exterior angle is $180^\circ$ minus the interior angle, so the polygon has one exterior angle of $90^\circ$ and the rest are $30^\circ$. Exterior angles of a convex polygon add up to $360^\circ$, so $90 + 30k = 360$, giving $k = 9$. With the $90^\circ$ corner the polygon has $9 + 1 = 10$ sides. Check with interior angles: $90 + 9 \times 150 = 1440 = 180 \times (10 - 2)$. The transferable idea: exterior angles always total $360^\circ$, which is often quicker than the interior-angle formula.
solutions.elegant: Using the interior sum directly: $90 + 150(n-1) = 180(n-2)$ gives $30n = 300$, so $n = 10$. The exterior-angle route avoids the algebra because $360^\circ$ does not depend on $n$.

problems.whyOnTest: Exterior angles total $360^\circ$ for every convex polygon, a fixed number that turns a polygon with mixed angles into a one-line count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The six interior angles of a convex hexagon, measured in degrees, are whole numbers. Listed from smallest to largest, each angle is the same amount bigger than the one before. What is the largest possible size of the biggest angle?

choices.misconception: I treated the average angle, $120^\circ$, as the third angle in the list, so I used $120 + 3d < 180$ and got $d = 19$.
I let the step be any whole number and took $d = 23$, the largest with $120 + 2.5d < 180$, without checking that the angles are then not whole numbers.
I only made sure the biggest angle was a whole number less than $180^\circ$ and did not check that the six angles could fit the pattern.
I allowed the biggest angle to be $180^\circ$, but a convex polygon has every interior angle smaller than $180^\circ$.

hints: What do the six angles of any hexagon add up to?
Call the smallest angle $a$ and the step $d$. The angle sum gives one equation. Check whether it allows $d$ to be odd, then push the biggest angle as close to $180^\circ$ as allowed.
The angles are $a, a + d, \dots, a + 5d$ with sum $6a + 15d = 720$, so $2a + 5d = 240$. That forces $d$ to be even. Write $d = 2e$: then $a = 120 - 5e$ and the biggest angle is $120 + 5e$.

solutions.reliable: The angles of a hexagon add up to $720^\circ$. With smallest angle $a$ and step $d$: $6a + 15d = 720$, so $2a + 5d = 240$. Since $2a$ and $240$ are even, $5d$ is even, so $d$ is even, say $d = 2e$. Then $a = 120 - 5e$ and the biggest angle is $a + 5d = 120 + 5e$. Convexity needs $120 + 5e < 180$, so $e < 12$ and $e \le 11$. With $e = 11$ the angles are $65, 87, 109, 131, 153, 175$, which add up to $720$. The biggest angle is $175^\circ$. The transferable idea: when the unknowns must be whole numbers, check what the equation says about parity before maximising.
solutions.elegant: The angles are symmetric about their mean $120^\circ$: the biggest is $120 + 2.5d$. For this to be a whole number, $2.5d$ must be whole, so $d$ is even. The largest even $d$ with $120 + 2.5d < 180$ is $d = 22$, giving $175^\circ$.

problems.whyOnTest: An angle-sum fact meets a whole-number condition, and the 5-point idea is noticing the parity restriction before pushing the biggest angle up to the limit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: $ABCDEFGHI$ is a regular nine-sided polygon, with its vertices labelled in order. The diagonals $AD$ and $BF$ cross at the point $P$. What is the size of angle $APB$?

choices.misconception: I halved only the arc $AB$, $40^\circ$, and forgot the arc on the other side of $P$.
I halved only the arc $DF$, $80^\circ$, and forgot the arc $AB$.
I added the arcs $AB$ and $DF$, $40^\circ + 80^\circ$, but forgot to halve the total.
I assumed the angle between two diagonals equals an interior angle of the nonagon, $140^\circ$.

hints: Draw the circle through all nine vertices.
Each side of the nonagon cuts off an arc of $40^\circ$. Angles at a point on the circle are half the arc they stand on. Find two angles of triangle $ABP$ that way.

Angle $BAP$ is angle $BAD$, which stands on arc $BD$ (two sides, $80^\circ$), so it is $40^\circ$. Angle $ABP$ is angle $ABF$, which stands on arc $AF$ not containing $B$ (four sides, $160^\circ$), so it is $80^\circ$.

solutions.reliable: Put the nonagon in its circle; each side cuts off an arc of $360^\circ \div 9 = 40^\circ$. In triangle $ABP$, angle $BAP = \angle BAD$ stands on arc $BCD$ of $80^\circ$, so it is $40^\circ$. Angle $ABP = \angle ABF$ stands on arc $FGHIA$ of $160^\circ$, so it is $80^\circ$. Then angle $APB = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 80^\circ = 60^\circ$. The transferable idea: in a regular polygon, every angle between vertices is a multiple of half the arc of one side.
solutions.elegant: Two chords crossing inside a circle make an angle equal to half the sum of the arcs they cut off. Angle $APB$ faces arc $AB$ ($40^\circ$) and its vertical angle faces arc $DF$ ($80^\circ$), so $APB = (40 + 80) \div 2 = 60^\circ$.

problems.whyOnTest: Regular polygons live on a circle, and inscribed-angle facts turn any angle between diagonals into simple counting of sides.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A whole number $N$ leaves remainder 7 when it is divided by 9. What remainder does $N^2 + 5N$ leave when it is divided by 9?

choices.misconception: I worked out the remainder of $N^2$ only, $49 = 45 + 4$, and forgot to add the $5N$ part.
I treated $N^2$ as if it left the same remainder as $N$, so I added $7 + 35 = 42$, which leaves 6.
I thought the remainder stays 7 whatever you do to $N$.
I worked out the remainder of $5N$ only, $35 = 27 + 8$, and dropped the $N^2$ part.

hints: You may replace $N$ by any number that leaves remainder 7.
Remainders can be added and multiplied: only the remainder of $N$ matters, not $N$ itself. Work with the remainder in place of $N$, then reduce at the end.

solutions.reliable: Write $N^2 + 5N = N(N + 5)$. Here $N$ leaves remainder 7 and $N + 5$ leaves remainder 12, that is 3. A product leaves the same remainder as the product of the remainders: $7 \times 3 = 21 = 18 + 3$. So the remainder is 3. Check with $N = 7$: $49 + 35 = 84 = 81 + 3$, and with $N = 16$: $256 + 80 = 336 = 333 + 3$. The transferable idea: in a remainder question, replace each number by its remainder before doing any arithmetic.
solutions.elegant: Only the remainder matters, and $7 = 9 - 2$, so $N$ behaves like $-2$. Then $N^2 + 5N$ behaves like $4 - 10 = -6$, which is remainder $9 - 6 = 3$.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders survive adding and multiplying, so a question about an unknown number reduces to arithmetic with its remainder.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when $3 + 3^2 + 3^3 + \dots + 3^{100}$ is divided by 7?

choices.misconception: I saw that each block of six remainders adds up to 21, a multiple of 7, and assumed the 100 terms make whole blocks.
I found that 4 terms are left over after the full blocks, but I took the last four remainders of the cycle, $6 + 4 + 5 + 1 = 16$, instead of the first four.
I found the remainder of the last term only, $3^{100}$, which leaves 4, instead of the remainder of the whole sum.
I thought every power of 3 leaves remainder 3, so I used $100 \times 3 = 300 = 294 + 6$.

hints: Find the remainders of the first few powers of 3 on division by 7.
The remainders of powers repeat in a cycle. Add one full cycle of remainders, see what that total does, then deal with the terms left over after the full cycles.
Powers of 3 leave remainders $3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1$, then repeat. One cycle adds up to $21$, a multiple of 7. Since $100 = 6 \times 16 + 4$, only the first four remainders of a cycle are left over.

solutions.reliable: Powers of 3 leave remainders $3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1$ on division by 7, and then the cycle repeats, since $3^6 = 729 = 7 \times 104 + 1$. Each full cycle of six terms adds up to $3 + 2 + 6 + 4 + 5 + 1 = 21$, a multiple of 7. The 100 terms make 16 full cycles (96 terms) followed by $3^{97}, 3^{98}, 3^{99}, 3^{100}$, which leave remainders $3, 2, 6, 4$. These add up to $15 = 14 + 1$, so the remainder is 1. The transferable idea: when remainders cycle, a full cycle often adds up to a multiple of the divisor, so only the leftover terms matter.
solutions.elegant: The sum is $S = \frac{3^{101} - 3}{2}$, so $2S = 3^{101} - 3$. As $101 = 6 \times 16 + 5$, $3^{101}$ leaves the same remainder as $3^5 = 243 = 238 + 5$, so $2S$ leaves remainder $5 - 3 = 2$. The only remainder that doubles to 2 is 1, so $S$ leaves remainder 1.

problems.whyOnTest: Huge sums of powers become small once remainders cycle, and a full cycle that adds up to a multiple of the divisor simply disappears.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: For how many whole numbers $n$ from 1 to 100 is $n^6 - 1$ divisible by 7?

choices.misconception: I counted the multiples of 7, which are exactly the numbers that do not work.
I only counted the $n$ for which $n^3 - 1$ is a multiple of 7 and forgot that $n^3 + 1$ can be the multiple instead.
I only checked up to 98, the last multiple of 7, and missed 99 and 100.
I used the rule that $n^6$ always leaves remainder 1 on division by 7, but it fails when $n$ is itself a multiple of 7.

hints: Only the remainder of $n$ on division by 7 matters.
Check the seven possible remainders $0, 1, \dots, 6$ of $n$ and find the remainder of $n^6$ in each case. Then count how many numbers from 1 to 100 have the good remainders.
$n^6 - 1 = (n^3 - 1)(n^3 + 1)$. Cubes leave remainder 0, 1 or 6 on division by 7, and 0 happens only when 7 divides $n$.

solutions.reliable: Write $n^6 - 1 = (n^3 - 1)(n^3 + 1)$. Checking remainders: $1^3, 2^3, 4^3$ leave remainder 1 ($1, 8, 64$) and $3^3, 5^3, 6^3$ leave remainder 6 ($27, 125, 216$), so for these $n$ one of the two brackets is a multiple of 7. If 7 divides $n$, then $n^6 - 1$ leaves remainder 6. So $n^6 - 1$ is divisible by 7 exactly when 7 does not divide $n$. From 1 to 100 there are 14 multiples of 7, leaving $100 - 14 = 86$. The transferable idea: test every remainder once and the answer holds for all numbers.
solutions.elegant: Fermat's little theorem says $n^6$ leaves remainder 1 on division by 7 whenever 7 does not divide $n$. So every $n$ except the 14 multiples of 7 works: 86.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainder tables settle questions about infinitely many numbers, and the factorisation tempts students to count only half the cases.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts $a_1 = 3$, $a_2 = 5$, and each later term is the term before it divided by the term two places before it, that is $a_{n+2} = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}$. What is $a_{2027}$?

choices.misconception: I worked with 2026 instead of 2027, which leaves remainder 4 on division by 6, so I took the 4th term.
I counted the first term as term 0, so remainder 5 pointed me to the sixth term of the cycle.
I thought the terms alternate, so every odd-numbered term would equal $a_1 = 3$.
I assumed the sequence repeats every 3 terms, and 2027 leaves remainder 2 on division by 3, so I took $a_2 = 5$.

hints: Work out the first eight terms carefully.
A rule applied again and again can bring back the starting pair of terms. Find the length of the cycle, then use the remainder of 2027 on division by that length.
The terms are $3, 5, \tfrac{5}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{5}, \tfrac{3}{5}, 3, 5, \dots$, so the cycle has length 6.

solutions.reliable: Compute: $a_3 = \frac{5}{3}$, $a_4 = \frac{5/3}{5} = \frac{1}{3}$, $a_5 = \frac{1/3}{5/3} = \frac{1}{5}$, $a_6 = \frac{1/5}{1/3} = \frac{3}{5}$, $a_7 = \frac{3/5}{1/5} = 3$, $a_8 = \frac{3}{3/5} = 5$. Since $a_7, a_8$ repeat $a_1, a_2$, and each term depends only on the two before it, the sequence repeats every 6 terms. As $2027 = 6 \times 337 + 5$, $a_{2027} = a_5 = \frac{1}{5}$. The transferable idea: when a two-term rule brings back the starting pair, the whole sequence is periodic and remainders do the rest.
solutions.elegant: For any start $a_1 = p$, $a_2 = q$, the rule gives $\frac{q}{p}, \frac{1}{p}, \frac{1}{q}, \frac{p}{q}$ and then $p, q$ again, so the period is always 6. Here $a_5 = \frac{1}{a_2} = \frac{1}{5}$.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules that bring back their starting values turn a question about term 2027 into a question about a remainder.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The first term of a sequence is 2. Each later term is found by doubling the term before it and then subtracting 1. What is the 10th term?

choices.misconception: I saw the differences 1 and 2 between the first terms and assumed they go up by 1 each time, so I added $1 + 2 + \dots + 9 = 45$ to 2.
I saw that each term is 1 more than a power of 2, but I used $2^8 + 1$, which is the 9th term.
I saw the powers of 2 and used $2^9$, but forgot that every term is 1 more than a power of 2.
I matched the power to the term number and used $2^{10} + 1$, which is the 11th term.

hints: Write out the first five terms before looking for a pattern.
Compare each term with a nearby power of 2. Once you have a formula, test it on the first few terms so that the power matches the position in the sequence.
The terms are $2, 3, 5, 9, 17, \dots$, each 1 more than $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$. So the $n$th term is $2^{n-1} + 1$.

solutions.reliable: The terms are $2$, $2 \times 2 - 1 = 3$, $2 \times 3 - 1 = 5$, $9$, $17$, $33$, $65$, $129$, $257$, $513$. Each is 1 more than a power of 2: the $n$th term is $2^{n-1} + 1$, so the 10th term is $2^9 + 1 = 513$. The transferable idea: when a rule doubles and then adjusts, subtract the number the rule leaves unchanged (here 1, since $2 \times 1 - 1 = 1$), and only the doubling remains.

problems.whyOnTest: A double-and-adjust rule hides a pure doubling sequence once you shift by the number the rule leaves unchanged.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A function $f$ on the positive whole numbers satisfies $f(1) = 1$ and, for every $n \ge 1$, $f(2n) = f(n)$ and $f(2n + 1) = f(n) + 1$. For how many whole numbers $n$ from 1 to 100 is $f(n) = 3$?

choices.misconception: I listed the numbers with $f(n) = 3$ in base 2 but only went up to five binary digits, the numbers below 32.
I counted numbers with three 1s among six binary digits, $\binom{6}{3}$, and forgot the numbers from 64 to 100.
I counted correctly but stopped at 99 and missed 100, which is 1100100 in base 2.
I counted all seven-digit binary numbers with three 1s, $\binom{7}{3}$, without removing the two that are bigger than 100.

hints: Work out $f(n)$ for $n = 1$ to $8$. What do the values count?
Doubling a number adds a 0 to the end of it in base 2, and doubling and adding 1 adds a 1. So $f(n)$ counts something about the binary form of $n$. Then count with a selection.
$f(n)$ is the number of 1s in the binary form of $n$. Numbers up to 127 have at most seven binary digits, so there are $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ with three 1s. Now remove those above 100.

solutions.reliable: Small values: $f(1) = 1$, $f(2) = 1$, $f(3) = 2$, $f(4) = 1$, $f(5) = 2$, $f(6) = 2$, $f(7) = 3$. In base 2, $2n$ is $n$ with a 0 written after it and $2n + 1$ is $n$ with a 1 after it, so $f(n)$ is the number of 1s in the binary form of $n$. Numbers from 1 to 127 use the seven place values $1, 2, 4, \dots, 64$, and choosing three of them gives $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ numbers. Those above 100 must use 64 and two more adding to at least 37: only $64 + 32 + 8 = 104$ and $64 + 32 + 16 = 112$ (note $64 + 32 + 4 = 100$ is allowed). So the answer is $35 - 2 = 33$. The transferable idea: when a rule halves its input, think in base 2.

problems.whyOnTest: Inferring what a recursive rule really computes, here binary digit counts, turns a long calculation into a quick selection count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A function $f$ gives these values: $f(1) = 1$, $f(7) = 2$, $f(12) = 6$, $f(16) = 5$ and $f(30) = 8$. Following the same rule, what is $f(36)$?

choices.misconception: I listed the divisors of 36 in pairs and dropped 6, because it pairs with itself.
I listed the divisors of 36 in pairs and counted 6 twice, once for each place in $6 \times 6$.
I wrote $36 = 12 \times 3$ and multiplied $f(12) \times f(3) = 6 \times 2$, but 12 and 3 share a factor.
I thought $f(36) = 3 \times f(12)$ because 36 is three times 12.

hints: Why might 7 give 2 while 16 gives 5?
Test a rule against every example, not just one. A prime giving 2 and a square giving an odd number are strong clues about counting something related to $n$.
$f(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$: 12 has 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 and 16 has 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Now list the divisors of 36.

solutions.reliable: The rule is: $f(n)$ is the number of whole numbers that divide $n$. Check: 1 has one divisor; 7 has 1 and 7; 12 has six; 16 has 1, 2, 4, 8, 16; 30 has 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. The divisors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36, so $f(36) = 9$. The transferable idea: a rule must fit every example, and odd outputs here point to perfect squares.
solutions.elegant: With $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$, a divisor is $2^a 3^b$ with $a, b \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, giving $3 \times 3 = 9$ divisors.

problems.whyOnTest: Inferring a rule means testing it on every example; divisor counts are a natural candidate, and perfect squares are where counting slips happen.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Look at these facts: $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 + 1 = 5^2$, $\ 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 + 1 = 11^2$, $\ 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 6 + 1 = 19^2$. Following the same pattern, $10 \cdot 11 \cdot 12 \cdot 13 + 1$ is the square of which number?

choices.misconception: I continued the list 5, 11, 19, 29, ... by its differences but stopped one line early, at the line that starts with 9.
I noticed the product of the outside numbers matters and used $10 \times 13 = 130$, but forgot to add 1.
I used the product of the two middle numbers, $11 \times 12$, but forgot to take 1 away.
I continued the list 5, 11, 19, 29, ... by its differences one line too far, to the line that starts with 11.

hints: How is 5 related to the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4?
Look for a formula connecting each square root to the four numbers in its product. Compare it with the product of the outer two numbers or of the inner two.
$5 = 1 \times 4 + 1$, $11 = 2 \times 5 + 1$, $19 = 3 \times 6 + 1$: the square root is the product of the outer numbers plus 1.

solutions.reliable: In each line the number being squared is the product of the first and last numbers plus 1: $1 \times 4 + 1 = 5$, $2 \times 5 + 1 = 11$, $3 \times 6 + 1 = 19$. So $10 \cdot 11 \cdot 12 \cdot 13 + 1$ should be $(10 \times 13 + 1)^2 = 131^2$. Check: $10 \cdot 11 \cdot 12 \cdot 13 = 17160$ and $131^2 = 17161$. The transferable idea: guess a rule from examples, then confirm it on the case you need.
solutions.elegant: With $m = n^2 + 3n$: $n(n+3) = m$ and $(n+1)(n+2) = m + 2$, so the product plus 1 is $m(m + 2) + 1 = (m + 1)^2$. For $n = 10$, $m + 1 = 131$.

problems.whyOnTest: A pattern guessed from three lines can be confirmed by algebra; spotting which pair of factors controls the square is the key step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: These lines are all true: $$3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$$ $$10^2 + 11^2 + 12^2 = 13^2 + 14^2$$ $$21^2 + 22^2 + 23^2 + 24^2 = 25^2 + 26^2 + 27^2$$ The pattern continues. One line begins with $210^2$. What is the largest number squared in that line?

choices.misconception: I gave the last number on the left-hand side instead of the last number on the right.
I gave the line ten squares on the left and nine on the right, one too few on each side.
I gave the right-hand side as many squares as the left-hand side, eleven.
I assumed each line runs right up to where the next line begins, and the next line begins at 253.

hints: How many squares are on each side of line $k$?
Find a formula for the first number of line $k$ by looking at 3, 10, 21 and their differences. Solve for the line that starts at 210, then count its squares on each side.
Line $k$ starts at $k(2k + 1)$, with $k + 1$ squares on the left and $k$ on the right. $k(2k + 1) = 210$ gives $k = 10$.

solutions.reliable: Line $k$ has $k + 1$ squares on the left and $k$ on the right, so $2k + 1$ consecutive numbers in all. The first numbers 3, 10, 21 have differences 7, 11, so the next difference is 15 and the line starts at 36; in general line $k$ starts at $k(2k + 1)$: $1 \times 3$, $2 \times 5$, $3 \times 7$. Solving $k(2k + 1) = 210$ gives $k = 10$, because $10 \times 21 = 210$. That line uses the 21 numbers from 210 to 230, so its largest number is 230. The transferable idea: find the rule for where each line starts and how long it is, then jump straight to the line you need.
solutions.elegant: The numbers $3, 10, 21, 36, \dots$ are every second triangular number, and 210 is the 20th triangular number, so it starts line 10. Line 10 holds $2 \times 10 + 1 = 21$ numbers, ending at $210 + 20 = 230$.

problems.whyOnTest: Rules inferred from a few lines must cover both where a line starts and how long it is; the 5-point step is using both to jump far ahead.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many triangles have their three vertices among the vertices of a regular 10-sided polygon, but share no side with the polygon?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 80 triangles with a side of the polygon, but that counted each triangle with two such sides twice.
I counted the triangles with exactly one side of the polygon instead of those with none.
I counted the triangles with at least one side of the polygon, which are the ones to remove.
I only removed the 10 triangles made of three neighbouring vertices and forgot the triangles with just one side of the polygon.

hints: Count all triangles first, then the ones you do not want.

Count triangles that use a side of the polygon by choosing the side and then the third vertex. Some triangles use two sides, so they are counted twice; correct for that before subtracting from the total.
There are $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ triangles. Side first, then third vertex gives $10 \times 8 = 80$, but the 10 triangles of three neighbouring vertices were counted twice.

solutions.reliable: There are $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ triangles in total. Choose one of the 10 sides and any of the other 8 vertices: $10 \times 8 = 80$. A triangle made of three neighbouring vertices uses two sides and was counted twice; there are 10 of these. So $80 - 10 = 70$ triangles use at least one side, and $120 - 70 = 50$ use none. The transferable idea: when a count by 'choose this, then that' can reach the same object twice, find exactly which objects are double counted and subtract them once.
solutions.elegant: Count directly: pick the first vertex in 10 ways, and the other two must leave gaps of at least one vertex. The 7 non-neighbours split into choices of two non-adjacent vertices in a line of 7, giving $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ ways; each triangle is counted 3 times, so $10 \times 15 \div 3 = 50$.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting by sides counts some triangles twice, and the 4-point step is spotting exactly which ones before using the complement.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In how many ways can $1000$ be written as a product $a \times b \times c$ of three positive whole numbers, if the order of the factors does not matter? For example, $2 \times 4 \times 125$ and $125 \times 2 \times 4$ count as the same way.

choices.misconception: I left out every product that uses the factor 1, such as $1 \times 8 \times 125$.
I only counted the products in which the three factors are all different.
I counted the 100 ordered products and divided by 6, rounding up, but products with repeated factors are not counted 6 times.
I forgot the product $10 \times 10 \times 10$, where all three factors are equal.

hints: First count the products where order does matter.
Count ordered triples using the prime factors $2^3 \cdot 5^3$. Dividing by 6 only works for triples with three different numbers, so count the triples with repeated numbers separately and correct.

Ordered triples: share three 2s among three factors in $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ ways, and the same for the 5s, so 100. Triples with two equal factors $a, a, c$ need $a^2$ to divide 1000: $a = 1, 2, 5$ (and $a = 10$ gives all three equal).

solutions.reliable: Since $1000 = 2^3 \cdot 5^3$, an ordered triple shares out three 2s and three 5s among three places, each in $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ ways, so there are $100$ ordered triples. All equal: only $10 \times 10 \times 10$, counted once. Exactly two equal, $a \times a \times c$ with $c \ne a$: $a^2$ must divide 1000, so $a = 1, 2, 5$, giving $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1000$, $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 250$, $5 \cdot 5 \cdot 40$; each appears in 3 orders, using 9 ordered triples. The remaining $100 - 1 - 9 = 90$ ordered triples have three different factors, each counted 6 times: 15 ways. Total $1 + 3 + 15 = 19$. The transferable idea: divide by the number of orders only after separating the objects that have fewer orders.

problems.whyOnTest: Overcounting and correcting is only safe when every object is overcounted equally; triples with repeated factors are the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three of the eight corners of a cube are painted red. Two painted cubes count as the same if one can be turned to look exactly like the other. How many different painted cubes are there?

choices.misconception: I sorted the red corners into 'all on one face' or 'not all on one face', and missed that the second kind splits into two shapes.
I counted the triangle with an edge, a face diagonal and a long diagonal and its mirror image as different, but a turn takes one to the other.
I took the $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ choices and divided by 8, the number of corners.
I counted every choice of three corners, $\binom{8}{3}$, and forgot that turning the cube makes many of them the same.

hints: The three red corners form a triangle. What lengths can its sides have?

Any two corners of a cube are joined by an edge, a face diagonal or a long diagonal through the middle. Sort the red triangles by their three side types and check each type is one shape up to turning.
The possible triangles are: edge, edge, face diagonal (all on one face); three face diagonals; and edge, face diagonal, long diagonal. Check the counts add up to 56.

solutions.reliable: Two corners are joined by an edge (length 1), a face diagonal ($\sqrt{2}$) or a long diagonal ($\sqrt{3}$). Three red corners form a triangle of one of these types: (1) edge, edge, face diagonal, three corners of one face: $6 \times 4 = 24$ choices; (2) three face diagonals, an equilateral triangle cut off around one corner: 8 choices; (3) edge, face diagonal, long diagonal: the remaining $56 - 24 - 8 = 24$ choices. In types (1) and (3) only the 'do nothing' turn keeps such a triangle in place, so the cube's 24 turns make 24 different copies of one triangle, which is the whole type. In type (2) the 3 turns about a long diagonal keep the triangle in place, so the 24 turns make 8 copies, again the whole type. So there are 3 different cubes. The transferable idea: up to symmetry, classify by something turning cannot change, such as distances, then check each class is a single shape.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting up to rotation means classifying by invariants such as distances; dividing the raw count by something is the tempting wrong shortcut.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An equilateral triangle tile is split into four smaller equilateral triangles by joining the midpoints of its sides. Each small triangle is painted red, yellow or blue; colours may repeat. Two tiles count as the same if one can be turned in its plane to look exactly like the other; flipping is not allowed. How many different tiles are there?

choices.misconception: I grouped the colourings in threes but left out the 9 tiles whose three corner triangles share one colour.
I divided all $3^4 = 81$ colourings by the 3 turns, but the 9 tiles with three matching corners look the same after every turn.
I also counted a tile and its mirror image as the same, but flipping over is not allowed.
I counted every way to paint the four triangles and did not treat turned copies as the same.

hints: Which small triangle stays in place when the tile is turned?
A turn moves the three corner triangles round in a cycle. Most colourings have three different turned copies, but some look the same after every turn: count those separately.
The middle triangle never moves. There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings. In 9 of them the three corners share a colour, and such a tile is unchanged by turning; the other 72 fall into groups of 3.

solutions.reliable: The middle triangle stays in place, and a turn through a third of a full turn moves the three corner triangles round a cycle. There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings in all. If the three corners have the same colour (3 choices), the tile looks the same after every turn; with 3 choices for the middle this gives 9 tiles, each in a group of its own. Any other colouring changes under both turns, so it has exactly three different turned copies, and the other $81 - 9 = 72$ colourings give $72 \div 3 = 24$ tiles. In total $9 + 24 = 33$. The transferable idea: when counting up to turning, count the colourings that a turn leaves unchanged separately before dividing.
solutions.elegant: Burnside's lemma: average the number of colourings that each turn leaves unchanged. Doing nothing fixes all 81, and each of the other two turns fixes the 9 with matching corners, so the count is $(81 + 9 + 9) \div 3 = 33$.

problems.whyOnTest: Dividing by the number of turns only works for objects with no symmetry of their own, so the exceptions must be counted on their own.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pizza shop offers 6 different vegetable toppings and 5 different meat toppings. A customer chooses 4 different toppings, including at least one vegetable topping and at least one meat topping. How many different choices are possible?

choices.misconception: I removed the choices with only vegetable toppings but forgot to remove the choices with only meat toppings.
I removed the choices with only meat toppings but forgot to remove the choices with only vegetable toppings.
I counted every choice of 4 toppings from 11 and ignored the condition.
I picked one vegetable, one meat and then any two others, $6 \times 5 \times \binom{9}{2}$, which counts the same choice several times.

hints: Which choices break the rule?
Count all selections of 4 toppings from 11, then subtract the selections that are all vegetable or all meat. This is complementary counting.
There are $\binom{11}{4} = 330$ selections, $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ all vegetable and $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ all meat.

solutions.reliable: All selections of 4 from 11 toppings: $\binom{11}{4} = 330$. The bad ones use only one kind: all vegetable $\binom{6}{4} = 15$, all meat $\binom{5}{4} = 5$. So $330 - 15 - 5 = 310$. Check by cases: 1 vegetable and 3 meat $6 \times 10 = 60$; 2 and 2: $15 \times 10 = 150$; 3 and 1: $20 \times 5 = 100$; total $310$. The transferable idea: 'at least one of each' is usually easiest as everything minus the selections that miss a kind.

problems.whyOnTest: 'At least one of each' invites an overcount by fixing one of each first; the complement gives a clean answer in one step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A positive number $x$ satisfies $x + \dfrac{1}{x} = 3$. What is the value of $x^5 + \dfrac{1}{x^5}$?

choices.misconception: I worked out $x^4 + \frac{1}{x^4} = 7^2 - 2 = 47$ and stopped one power too early.
I multiplied $x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2} = 7$ by $x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} = 18$ but forgot that the product also contains $x + \frac{1}{x}$, which must be taken away.
I multiplied $7 \times 18 = 126$ and then added $x + \frac{1}{x} = 3$ instead of subtracting it.
I raised both sides to the fifth power and assumed that $\left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right)^5 = x^5 + \frac{1}{x^5}$.

hints: Solving for $x$ works but is slow. Build up the powers instead.
Squaring or multiplying expressions of the form $x^k + \frac{1}{x^k}$ gives a higher power plus a lower one you already know. Find a route to the fifth power in as few steps as possible.
$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2} = 3^2 - 2 = 7$ and $x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} = 3^3 - 3 \times 3 = 18$. Then $\left(x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2}\right)\left(x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3}\right) = x^5 + \frac{1}{x^5} + x + \frac{1}{x}$.

solutions.reliable: Let $s_k = x^k + \frac{1}{x^k}$, so $s_1 = 3$. Squaring gives $s_1^2 = s_2 + 2$, so $s_2 = 7$. Cubing gives $s_1^3 = s_3 + 3s_1$, so $s_3 = 27 - 9 = 18$. Multiplying, $s_2 s_3 = x^5 + x + \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{x^5} = s_5 + s_1$, so $s_5 = 7 \times 18 - 3 = 123$. Check with the rule $s_{k+1} = 3s_k - s_{k-1}$: $s_4 = 3 \times 18 - 7 = 47$ and $s_5 = 3 \times 47 - 18 = 123$. The transferable idea: in the 5-point block, look for an identity that builds the answer from what is given before solving for the unknown.
solutions.elegant: Multiplying $x + \frac{1}{x}$ by $x^k + \frac{1}{x^k}$ gives $s_{k+1} + s_{k-1}$, so $s_{k+1} = 3s_k - s_{k-1}$. Starting from $s_0 = 2$ and $s_1 = 3$, the values run $2, 3, 7, 18, 47, 123$.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetric expressions in $x$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ can be built from $x + \frac{1}{x}$ alone, turning a quadratic with surds into three lines of arithmetic.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Zoe has 6 minutes left. Question A (5 points) needs 6 more minutes; she has already spent 6 on it. Questions B and C (4 points each) would take 3 minutes each. She guesses any question she does not finish: right with probability $\frac{1}{5}$, and wrong costs nothing. What is her largest expected score from the three?

choices.misconception: I chose to finish A and forgot the guessing points on B and C.
I finished A because I had already spent 6 minutes on it, giving $5 + 0.8 + 0.8$, but the time already spent is gone whichever plan I choose.
I solved B and C but forgot to add the guessing points for A.
I solved B and C and then also added guessing points for them, $0.8 + 0.8$, as well as 1 point for guessing A.

hints: Only the remaining 6 minutes matter. The time already spent is gone.
List the plans that fit in 6 minutes and work out the expected score of each: a solved question scores its full points, a guessed one scores one fifth of its points on average.
Finishing A: $5 + \frac{4}{5} + \frac{4}{5} = 6.6$. Solving B and C: $4 + 4 + \frac{5}{5} = 9$.

solutions.reliable: In 6 minutes Zoe can either finish A or solve both B and C. (Solving just one of B and C gives $4 + 0.8 + 1 = 5.8$, which is worse.) Finishing A gives 5 points plus guesses on B and C worth $\frac{4}{5}$ each on average: $6.6$. Solving B and C gives 8 points plus a guess on A worth $\frac{5}{5} = 1$: $9$. So the largest expected score is 9. The 6 minutes already spent on A are spent in every plan, so they should not affect the choice. The transferable idea: in time triage, compare plans only on the time you still have; time already spent is not a reason to carry on.

problems.whyOnTest: Time already spent on a question is gone; the triage decision depends only on the points each remaining minute can still earn.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sheet of paper is $0.1$ mm thick. Imagine that it could be folded in half 30 times, doubling the thickness each time. Which of these is closest to the thickness of the folded stack?

choices.misconception: I added 0.1 mm for each fold, $30 \times 0.1 = 3$ mm, instead of doubling each time.
I treated $2^{30}$ as $30 \times 2^{10}$, about 30 000, which gives about 3 m.
I used $2^{30} \approx 10^6$, as if $(10^3)^3$ were $10^6$, which gives about 100 m.
I found about $10^8$ mm but divided by 1000 to change millimetres into kilometres, when 1 km is $10^6$ mm.

hints: How many times thicker is the stack after 30 doublings?
Thirty doublings multiply the thickness by a power of 2. Estimate that power using a power of 2 that is close to a power of 10, then change millimetres into kilometres with care.
$2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$, so $2^{30} \approx 10^9$. The stack is about $0.1 \times 10^9 = 10^8$ mm, and there are $10^6$ mm in a kilometre.

solutions.reliable: Each fold doubles the thickness, so 30 folds multiply it by $2^{30} = (2^{10})^3 = 1024^3$, a little more than $10^9$. The stack is about $0.1 \times 10^9 = 10^8$ mm thick. One kilometre is $1000 \times 1000 = 10^6$ mm, so the stack is about $100$ km thick (more exactly, about 107 km). The transferable idea: estimate powers of 2 with $2^{10} \approx 10^3$, and convert units one factor of 1000 at a time.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeated doubling grows far faster than intuition suggests, and $2^{10} \approx 1000$ makes its size easy to estimate.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two upright poles, each 4 m tall, stand on flat ground. A 10 m rope is tied to both tops. Its middle is pulled down until it just touches the ground, so each half is a straight line from a pole top to that point. How far apart are the poles?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the two pole heights from the rope, $10 - 4 - 4 = 2$, as if the rope ran straight down each pole.
I found the ground distance from one pole to the point where the rope touches, 3 m, and forgot the other half.
I used the whole 10 m rope as the long side of one right triangle with height 4 m, so I got $\sqrt{100 - 16} = 2\sqrt{21}$.
I assumed the poles are as far apart as the rope is long.

hints: Draw the poles, the rope and the ground.
The rope and the poles make two matching right triangles. In each one you know the upright side and the sloping side, so Pythagoras gives the side along the ground.
Each half of the rope is 5 m and each pole is 4 m, so each triangle has ground side $\sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3$ m.

solutions.reliable: By symmetry the rope touches the ground halfway between the poles. Each half of the rope, 5 m long, is the sloping side of a right triangle whose upright side is a 4 m pole. Its side along the ground is $\sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3$ m. The two triangles together give a distance of $3 + 3 = 6$ m between the poles. The transferable idea: draw the picture first, and a symmetric picture often splits into two matching right triangles.

problems.whyOnTest: A quick sketch turns a wordy description of a rope into two matching 3, 4, 5 right triangles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A train travels at a steady $90$ km/h. How many metres does it travel in 1 minute 20 seconds?

choices.misconception: I treated 90 km/h as 90 metres per second and multiplied by 80 seconds.
I converted 90 km/h to metres per second by multiplying by 3.6 instead of dividing.
I wrote 1 minute 20 seconds as 1.2 and then treated it as 1.2 hours, getting 108 km.
I turned the speed into 1.5 km per minute but then treated 1 minute 20 seconds as 80 minutes.

hints: Put the speed and the time into matching units first.
Convert the speed to metres per second, or convert the time to hours, before multiplying. Check the answer is a sensible distance for a train in just over a minute.
$90$ km/h is $90000$ m in $3600$ s, which is $25$ m/s. The time is $80$ s.

solutions.reliable: $90$ km/h means $90000$ m every $3600$ s, which is $25$ m/s. In 1 minute 20 seconds, which is 80 seconds, the train travels $25 \times 80 = 2000$ m. Check in hours: $80$ s is $\frac{80}{3600} = \frac{1}{45}$ h, and $90 \times \frac{1}{45} = 2$ km. The transferable idea: convert to matching units before multiplying, and re-read mixed times such as minutes and seconds carefully.

problems.whyOnTest: Unit slips are the cheapest marks to lose: mixed minutes and seconds and the km/h to m/s factor are both tested here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ann can paint a fence alone in 3 hours, and Ben can paint it alone in 6 hours. They start painting together at their usual rates. After 30 minutes Ben takes a 30-minute break while Ann keeps painting, then Ben comes back and they finish the fence together. How long does the whole job take?

choices.misconception: I let Ann paint $\frac{1}{3}$ of the fence during the break, a full hour's work, although the break lasts only 30 minutes.
I ignored Ben's break and used their combined rate for the whole job.
I mixed up who was resting and let only Ben paint during the break.
I added the 30-minute break on top of 2 hours, as if no painting happened during the break.

hints: Think about what fraction of the fence each person paints in one hour.
Add rates, not times. Split the job into stages: both painting, Ann alone during the break, then both again. Work out how much of the fence is done in each stage.

Together they paint $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ of the fence per hour. In the first hour they paint $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{12}$ of it.

solutions.reliable: Ann paints $\frac{1}{3}$ of the fence per hour and Ben $\frac{1}{6}$, so together they paint $\frac{1}{2}$ per hour. In the first 30 minutes they paint $\frac{1}{4}$. During the break Ann alone paints $\frac{1}{6}$. After 1 hour, $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{12}$ is done, leaving $\frac{7}{12}$. Together this takes $\frac{7}{12} \div \frac{1}{2} = \frac{7}{6}$ hours, which is 1 hour 10 minutes. The whole job takes 2 hours 10 minutes. Check: Ann paints for $\frac{13}{6}$ hours, which is $\frac{13}{18}$ of the fence, and Ben for $\frac{10}{6}$ hours, which is $\frac{5}{18}$; together that is the whole fence. The transferable idea: in work problems add rates, never times, and handle each stage separately.
solutions.elegant: Ann paints for the whole time $t$ hours and Ben for $t - \frac{1}{2}$ hours, so $\frac{t}{3} + \frac{t - 1/2}{6} = 1$. Multiplying by 6 gives $3t - \frac{1}{2} = 6$, so $t = \frac{13}{6}$ hours, which is 2 hours 10 minutes.

problems.whyOnTest: Work problems test whether you add rates rather than times, and a break simply removes one worker's rate for a while.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Car A leaves a town at 9:00 at 60 km/h. Car B leaves the same town at 9:30 along the same road at 80 km/h. Car C leaves the town at 10:00 along the same road at a steady speed and passes A and B at exactly the same moment. What is the speed of car C, in km/h?

choices.misconception: I found where B catches A, 120 km away at 11:00, but divided by the 2 hours since 9:00 instead of C's 1 hour.
I took the average of the speeds of A and B.
I found where B catches A, 120 km away, but divided by the 1.5 hours since 9:30 instead of C's 1 hour.
I assumed the speeds go up by 20 km/h each time a car leaves later.

hints: When can one car pass two others at the same moment?
C can only pass A and B together when A and B are side by side, which is when B catches A. Find that time and place, then the speed C needs to get there.
B catches A when $80(t - \frac{1}{2}) = 60t$, with $t$ in hours after 9:00. That gives $t = 2$, at 11:00, 120 km from town.
