What is left is 48 - 16 = 32 square centimetres. The transferable idea: the area of a shape with pieces removed is the whole area minus the pieces.
solutions.elegant: What is left is a plus shape: a middle strip 8 by 2, with strips 4 by 2 above and below it, so 16 + 8 + 8 = 32.

problems.whyOnTest: Cut-out regions are found by subtracting from the whole, and the distractors mix up side lengths with areas.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these words looks exactly the same after the page is turned upside down with a half turn?

choices.misconception: I picked MOM because it reads the same backwards, but a half turn changes each M into a W.
I thought E looks the same upside down, but a half turn makes it face the other way.
I checked that T is the same on both sides, but upside down its bar ends up at the bottom.
I thought D stays a D upside down, but a half turn makes its curved side face left.

hints: A half turn changes two things about a word, not just one.
Turning a word upside down reverses the order of the letters and also turns each letter over. Check both: the reversed word must match, and every letter must still be itself after a half turn.
Reading backwards is not enough. Test each letter: does M stay M upside down? Does N stay N? Does O?

solutions.reliable: A half turn puts the last letter first and also turns each letter upside down. All five words read the same backwards, so the order is fine for each; the test is the letters. M becomes W, E faces the other way, T has its bar at the bottom and D faces left. N and O both look the same after a half turn, so NOON is unchanged. The transferable idea: a half turn reverses order and rotates each piece, so check the pieces as well as the order.

problems.whyOnTest: Half-turn symmetry is not the same as reading backwards, and every distractor here reads the same backwards.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The plan shows a building made of cubes, seen from above. Each number tells how many cubes are stacked on that square. How many squares can be seen in the view from the front?

figure.alt: A plan of a 3 by 3 square seen from above, with the back edge at the top and an arrow at the bottom showing the front. The numbers of cubes on each square, left to right, are: back row 1, 4, 1; middle row 1, 1, 1; front row 2, 1, 3.

choices.misconception: I only counted the tallest stack, 4, as if it hid everything else.
I added only the front row, 2 + 1 + 3, but taller stacks behind it also show.
I took the tallest stack in each row, which gives the view from the side, not from the front.
I added all the numbers, which counts every cube instead of only the squares seen from the front.

hints: From the front, stacks in the same column hide behind one another.
Looking from the front, each column of the plan becomes one column of the view. A column shows as tall as its tallest stack, so find the tallest number in each column and add them.
The left column has stacks 1, 1 and 2, so it shows 2 squares tall. The middle column has 4, 1 and 1. The right column has 1, 1 and 3.

solutions.reliable: From the front, the three stacks in each column line up one behind another, and you see only the tallest. The left column shows 2 squares, the middle column 4, the right column 3. The front view has 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 squares. The transferable idea: a view of a stacked plan keeps the tallest stack along each line of sight.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning a plan with heights into a view tests whether you know which stacks hide behind which.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 3 by 3 by 3 cube is built from 27 small cubes. The cube in the middle of each face is pulled out, and so is the centre cube. How many small cubes remain?

choices.misconception: I counted the cubes that were pulled out instead of the cubes that are left.
I pulled out the six face middles but forgot the cube at the very centre.
I forgot the top and bottom faces, so I only pulled out four face middles and the centre cube.
I counted only the three faces I can see at once, so I pulled out three face middles and the centre cube.

hints: How many faces does a cube have?
Count how many small cubes are removed, then take that away from 27. Every face has one middle cube, and the centre cube is one more on top of those.
A cube has 6 faces, so 6 face middles come out, and then the centre cube makes 7 removed in all.

solutions.reliable: A cube has 6 faces, and each face has one middle cube, so 6 small cubes come out. The very centre cube is one more, so 7 are removed. That leaves 27 - 7 = 20. The transferable idea: count what is removed carefully, including the parts you cannot see, then subtract from the whole.
solutions.elegant: What is left is the 8 corner cubes and the 12 edge-middle cubes, because those are the only small cubes that are neither a face middle nor the centre: 8 + 12 = 20.

problems.whyOnTest: Building with unit cubes rewards counting hidden faces and hidden cubes, which is exactly what the wrong totals forget.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tiles 2 squares long and 1 square wide are placed on a 5 by 5 board, each covering exactly two squares, with no overlaps. What is the largest number of tiles that fit?

choices.misconception: I placed tiles only in a 4 by 4 corner, which holds 8, and thought the rest of the board was wasted.
I fitted two tiles across each row of five and left the last column empty, but tiles also fit down that column.
I filled each row with two tiles and then fitted only one tile in the empty last column of five squares.
I divided the 25 squares by 2 and rounded up, but a tile cannot hang off the board.

hints: Each tile covers two squares. How many squares does the board have?
Find a limit first: the tiles always cover an even number of squares, but the board has an odd number. Then try to build a layout that reaches that limit, leaving only one square empty.
25 squares means at most 12 tiles, with one square uncovered. Two tiles across each row fill four columns; the fifth column of 5 squares still takes 2 tiles standing up.

solutions.reliable: Each tile covers 2 squares and the board has 25, so at most 24 squares can be covered, which is 12 tiles, with one square left over. It can be done: put two tiles across each of the five rows, filling the first four columns with 10 tiles, then stand 2 tiles up in the last column, leaving one square empty. So the answer is 12. The transferable idea: find an upper limit by counting, then show a layout that reaches it.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions reward a two-part argument: count to find a limit, then build an example that meets it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Through how many degrees does the minute hand of a clock turn between 3:10 and 3:35?

choices.misconception: I used 1 degree for each minute, but a full turn of 360 degrees takes 60 minutes.
I used 5 degrees for each minute because the minute marks are counted in fives.
I counted the six numbers the hand points at or passes, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, instead of the five gaps between them.
I used 30 degrees for each minute, but 30 degrees is one gap between two numbers, which is 5 minutes.

hints: Where does the minute hand point at 3:10, and where at 3:35?
The minute hand makes a full turn of 360 degrees in 60 minutes, and the 12 numbers split that turn into 12 equal gaps. Find the size of one gap, then count how many gaps the hand moves across.
At 3:10 the minute hand points at 2 and at 3:35 it points at 7. One gap between numbers is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees.

solutions.reliable: At 3:10 the minute hand points at the 2, and at 3:35 it points at the 7. That is 5 gaps between numbers. The 12 gaps share 360 degrees, so each gap is 30 degrees, and the hand turns 5 x 30 = 150 degrees. The transferable idea: on a clock face each gap between numbers is 30 degrees, and you count gaps, not numbers.
solutions.elegant: The minute hand turns 360 degrees in 60 minutes, which is 6 degrees a minute. From 3:10 to 3:35 is 25 minutes, and 25 x 6 = 150 degrees.

problems.whyOnTest: Clock geometry tests that one gap between numbers is 30 degrees and that you count gaps, not numbers, when a hand turns.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A farmer says: "Not all of my 6 sheep are white." She is telling the truth. Which of these must be true?

choices.text: None of her sheep is white.
choices.misconception: I thought "not all are white" means the same as "none are white".

choices.text: At least one of her sheep is not white.
Exactly one of her sheep is not white.
choices.misconception: I thought "not all" means "all but one", but more than one sheep could be another colour.

choices.text: At least one of her sheep is white.
choices.misconception: I thought some sheep must still be white, but all six could be another colour.

choices.text: Most of her sheep are white.
choices.misconception: I pictured a flock that is mostly white, but the farmer did not say how many are white.

hints: What would make the farmer's sentence false?
"Not all are white" is false only when every single sheep is white. So for it to be true, there must be at least one sheep that breaks the pattern. Check each choice against that.
If all 6 were white, she would be lying. So at least one sheep is not white, and that is all you know.

solutions.reliable: The statement "not all of my sheep are white" would be false only if all 6 were white. Since it is true, at least one sheep is not white. Nothing else is fixed: she could have one, three or even all six sheep that are not white. So only "at least one is not white" must be true. The transferable idea: "not all" means "at least one is not", nothing more.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo checks whether you read "not all" precisely, and each wrong choice reads more into it than it says.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The 3rd day of a month is a Monday. The month has 31 days. On what day of the week is the 31st?

choices.misconception: I counted both the 3rd and the 31st, making 29 days, so I went one day too far.
I treated the 1st of the month as the Monday instead of the 3rd.
I moved on 31 days from the 3rd instead of 28.
I divided 28 by 7 to get 4 and moved on 4 days instead of 4 whole weeks.

hints: How many days after the 3rd is the 31st?
The days of the week repeat every 7 days. Find how many days pass from the 3rd to the 31st, then see how many whole weeks that is and how many days are left over.
From the 3rd to the 31st is 31 - 3 = 28 days, and 28 days is exactly 4 weeks.

solutions.reliable: From the 3rd to the 31st is 31 - 3 = 28 days. Since 28 = 4 x 7, that is exactly 4 whole weeks with nothing left over, so the 31st falls on the same day as the 3rd: Monday. The transferable idea: for days of the week, only the remainder after dividing by 7 matters.
solutions.elegant: The 10th, 17th, 24th and 31st are each one week after the one before, so all of them are Mondays, like the 3rd.

problems.whyOnTest: Calendar questions test remainders on division by 7, and the distractors come from counting days off by one or moving the wrong amount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class of 30 children, two fifths walk to school and one third come by bus. The rest come by car. How many children come by car?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many children walk and stopped there.
I took one fifth of 30 for the walkers instead of two fifths.
I took away the walkers but forgot the children who come by bus.
I took away the bus children but forgot the walkers.

hints: Find how many children walk and how many take the bus.
A fraction of 30 is found by dividing 30 into equal parts and taking the right number of them. Work out the walkers and the bus children separately, then take both groups away from 30.
One fifth of 30 is 6, so two fifths is 12. One third of 30 is 10. Now take both groups away from 30.

solutions.reliable: One fifth of 30 is 6, so two fifths is 12 walkers. One third of 30 is 10 bus children. Together that is 22, so 30 - 22 = 8 children come by car. The transferable idea: turn each fraction into a number of children first, then subtract all the known groups from the whole.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of a quantity are tested in two steps here, and each distractor stops after one step or misreads one fraction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pile of 10 sheets of paper is 1 mm thick. How tall is a pile of 5000 of these sheets?

choices.misconception: I divided 5000 by 1000 instead of by 10.
I got 500 mm but divided by 100 to change it to centimetres instead of by 10.
I thought each sheet was 1 mm thick, so I got 5000 mm, which is 5 m.
I thought each sheet was 1 cm thick, so I got 5000 cm, which is 50 m.

hints: How many piles of 10 sheets make 5000 sheets?
Group the sheets in tens, since each ten is 1 mm. That gives the height in millimetres. Then change the millimetres into a more sensible unit, remembering 10 mm make 1 cm.
5000 sheets is 500 groups of 10, so the pile is 500 mm. There are 10 mm in a centimetre.

solutions.reliable: 5000 sheets make 5000 / 10 = 500 groups of ten, and each group is 1 mm, so the pile is 500 mm. Since 10 mm make 1 cm, 500 mm is 50 cm. That is about the height of a table leg, which is believable for a big stack of paper. The transferable idea: choices that differ by a factor of ten test units, so check the size makes sense.

problems.whyOnTest: The choices are powers of ten apart, so this tests sense of size and unit changes, not long arithmetic.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cake recipe uses 250 g of flour. How many kilograms of flour are needed to bake 12 of these cakes?

choices.misconception: I found 3000 g but divided by 100 instead of by 1000 to change grams into kilograms.
I knew 250 g is a quarter of a kilogram, but I multiplied 12 by 4 instead of dividing 12 by 4.
I found 3000 g but divided by 10 instead of by 1000 to change grams into kilograms.
I worked out the flour in grams and forgot to change it into kilograms.

hints: The recipe is in grams, but the question asks for kilograms.
First find the flour for 12 cakes in the unit you are given. Then re-read the question and change the answer into the unit it asks for, using 1000 g in a kilogram.
12 cakes need 12 x 250 = 3000 g of flour. Now turn 3000 g into kilograms.

solutions.reliable: 12 cakes need 12 x 250 = 3000 g of flour. There are 1000 g in a kilogram, so 3000 g is 3 kg. The transferable idea: re-read the question for its unit before choosing, because the number in the wrong unit is almost always one of the choices.
solutions.elegant: 250 g is a quarter of a kilogram, so 4 cakes use 1 kg, and 12 cakes use 12 / 4 = 3 kg.

problems.whyOnTest: The answer in grams is offered as a trap, so this checks the habit of matching the unit the question asks for.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Using each of the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3 exactly once, how many different four-digit numbers can be made? A four-digit number cannot start with 0.

choices.misconception: I counted only the numbers that start with 1 and forgot the ones that start with 2 or 3.
I thought only 3 orders start with 0, but after the 0 the other three digits can go in 6 orders.
I took away only 0123, but every order that starts with 0 is not a four-digit number.
I counted every order of the four digits, including the ones that start with 0.

hints: Which digits are allowed in the first place?
Fill the four places from left to right. Count the choices for the first digit, remembering it cannot be 0, then the choices left for each later place, and multiply.
The first digit can be 1, 2 or 3, so there are 3 choices. Once it is chosen, 3 digits are left for the second place, including the 0.

solutions.reliable: The first digit can be 1, 2 or 3: 3 choices. The second digit can be any of the 3 digits left, including 0, then 2 choices remain for the third digit and 1 for the last. So there are 3 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 18 numbers. The transferable idea: fill the place with a rule first, then multiply the choices for the other places.
solutions.elegant: The four digits can be put in order in 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 ways. Those starting with 0 are the 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 orders of 1, 2 and 3 after it. So 24 - 6 = 18 are four-digit numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Arrangements with one rule test whether you place the restricted digit first, and the distractors forget or undercount the orders the rule removes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five children hold a table tennis contest. Every two children play each other exactly twice. How many games are played in total?

choices.misconception: I only counted the games of one child: 4 opponents, twice each.
I counted each pair of children once and forgot that every pair plays twice.
I counted 4 opponents twice for each of the 5 children, but that counts every game from both sides.
I multiplied 5 by 5 and doubled, as if each child also played themselves.

hints: How many different pairs of children are there?
Count the pairs so that each pair is counted once: the first child pairs with every other child, the next with the ones not yet paired, and so on. Then use the fact that each pair plays twice.
The pairs number 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, and each pair plays 2 games.

solutions.reliable: List the pairs without repeats: the first child with 4 others, the second with 3 new ones, then 2, then 1. That is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 pairs. Each pair plays twice, so there are 10 x 2 = 20 games. The transferable idea: count pairs once each, then multiply by what each pair does.
solutions.elegant: Each child plays 4 opponents twice, which is 8 games. 5 x 8 = 40 counts every game once for each of its two players, so there are 40 / 2 = 20 games.

problems.whyOnTest: Pairs counting tests whether each pair is counted once, and two games per pair catches anyone who stops at the pairs.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ben is 5 cm taller than Ana. Cal is 3 cm shorter than Ben. Ana is 120 cm tall. How tall is Cal?

choices.misconception: I took both the 5 cm and the 3 cm away from Ana's height.
I made Ben 5 cm shorter than Ana and then added 3 cm for Cal.
I found Ben's height and stopped.
I added both the 5 cm and the 3 cm to Ana's height.

hints: Whose height can you work out first?
Turn each sentence into a sum or a difference, starting from the one person whose height you know. "Taller" means add, "shorter" means take away, and each sentence compares two particular people.
Ben is 120 + 5 = 125 cm. Cal is 3 cm shorter than Ben, not shorter than Ana.

solutions.reliable: Ana is 120 cm and Ben is 5 cm taller, so Ben is 125 cm. Cal is 3 cm shorter than Ben, so Cal is 125 - 3 = 122 cm. The transferable idea: translate each comparison into an operation on the right person, in the order the facts allow.
solutions.elegant: Cal is 5 cm up and then 3 cm down from Ana, so 2 cm taller than Ana: 120 + 2 = 122 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparison sentences test careful translation, and each wrong height comes from adding or subtracting the wrong way.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia had three times as many shells as Leo. Then Mia gave Leo 6 shells, and now they both have the same number. How many shells did Leo have at the start?

choices.misconception: I thought Mia had 6 more than Leo at the start, but giving 6 away closes a gap of 12.
I found how many shells each of them has at the end.
I worked out how many shells Mia had at the start, not Leo.
I found how many shells they have altogether.

hints: When Mia gives shells to Leo, by how much does the gap between them shrink?
Giving 6 shells moves Mia down 6 and Leo up 6, closing a gap of 12. Draw Leo as one bar and Mia as three equal bars, then re-read whose number, and at what moment, the question asks for.
Mia's extra two bars make the gap, and the gap is 12, so each bar is 6.

solutions.reliable: Giving 6 shells lowers Mia by 6 and raises Leo by 6, so the difference between them was 12. Mia had three times Leo's amount, so the difference is two of Leo's amounts. Two of Leo's amounts make 12, so Leo had 6 and Mia had 18. Check: after the gift both have 12. The question asks for Leo at the start: 6. The transferable idea: in a problem with many numbers, find what is actually asked, and expect the other numbers to be among the choices.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve: if Leo had 6, Mia had 18; after Mia gives 6, both have 12. The other choices fail at once.

problems.whyOnTest: Several true numbers appear on the way to the answer, so this tests reading which one the question asks for.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A frog on the middle rung of a ladder jumps up 3 rungs, down 5, then up 7, and lands on the top rung. How many rungs does the ladder have?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many rungs are above the middle one and stopped.
I counted the rungs from the middle to the top, including the middle one, but forgot the rungs below.
I doubled the 5 rungs above the middle but forgot to count the middle rung itself.
I added all the jumps, 3 + 5 + 7, without noticing that the 5 rungs went down.

hints: Draw the ladder and mark the middle rung.
Track the frog's moves from the middle rung to find how many rungs lie above it. A middle rung has as many rungs above it as below it, and is itself one more rung.
Up 3, down 5, up 7 puts the frog 5 rungs above the middle, so there are 5 rungs above the middle and 5 below.

solutions.reliable: From the middle, the frog goes up 3, down 5 and up 7, ending 3 - 5 + 7 = 5 rungs above the middle. That rung is the top, so there are 5 rungs above the middle. Because it is the middle rung, there are 5 rungs below it too. The ladder has 5 + 1 + 5 = 11 rungs. The transferable idea: draw a quick diagram so you remember the middle rung itself.

problems.whyOnTest: A sketch makes the middle rung visible, and the distractors are what you get by losing it or stopping halfway.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three cubes weigh the same as two balls. One ball and one cube together weigh 50 grams. How many grams does one cube weigh?

choices.misconception: I divided 50 by 5 because the first fact has 3 cubes and 2 balls.
I split the 50 grams equally, as if a ball and a cube weighed the same.
I found the weight of a ball instead of a cube.
I worked out what three cubes weigh, which is one side of the balance, not one cube.

hints: Try doubling the second fact: what do two balls and two cubes weigh?
Two balls and two cubes weigh 100 grams. Swap the two balls for something the first fact says weighs the same, so only cubes are left. Then share the weight among the cubes.
Two balls weigh the same as three cubes, so two balls and two cubes weigh the same as five cubes, which is 100 grams.

solutions.reliable: One ball and one cube weigh 50 g, so two balls and two cubes weigh 100 g. Two balls weigh the same as three cubes, so this is the same as five cubes. Five cubes weigh 100 g, so one cube weighs 20 g. Check: a ball is 50 - 20 = 30 g, and three cubes (60 g) balance two balls (60 g). The transferable idea: on a balance, swap things of equal weight until only one kind is left.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve: if a cube is 20 g then a ball is 30 g, and 3 x 20 = 2 x 30. No other choice balances.

problems.whyOnTest: Balance puzzles reward swapping equal weights until one kind of object remains, and the distractors stop or split too soon.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rope 40 m long is cut into two pieces. One piece is 6 m longer than the other. How long is the longer piece?

choices.misconception: I found the shorter piece instead of the longer one.
I cut the rope in half and ignored the 6 m difference.
I cut the rope in half and then added the whole 6 m to one half.
I took the 6 m away from 40 m and called that the longer piece.

hints: Draw two bars, one 6 m longer than the other.
Take the extra 6 m off the longer bar so the two bars are equal. Share what is left of the rope between them, then put the 6 m back onto the longer one.
40 - 6 = 34 m shared equally gives 17 m for each equal bar.

solutions.reliable: Take the extra 6 m away: 40 - 6 = 34 m is shared equally, so each equal part is 17 m. The shorter piece is 17 m and the longer piece is 17 + 6 = 23 m. Check: 23 + 17 = 40 and 23 - 17 = 6. The transferable idea: in a sum-and-difference problem, remove the difference, halve, then add it back.
solutions.elegant: The answer is 3 m above the halfway point of 20 m, because the 6 m gap is split evenly on either side: 20 + 3 = 23 m.

problems.whyOnTest: Sum and difference problems test a bar model, and each wrong length is one slip in that model.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A three-digit number has three different digits, none of them 0, and its digits add up to 8. What is the difference between the largest and the smallest such number?

choices.misconception: I only used the digits 1, 3 and 4, so I worked out 431 - 134 and missed the digits 1, 2 and 5.
I found the smallest number, 125, but for the largest I used 431 and missed 521.
I found the largest number, 521, but for the smallest I used 134 and missed 125.
I let digits repeat, so I worked out 611 - 116, but the digits must be different.

hints: Which groups of three different digits, with no 0, add up to 8?

List the digit groups, starting from the smallest digit 1. For each group, the largest number puts the digits from biggest to smallest, and the smallest number from smallest to biggest. Compare across groups.
The groups are 1, 2, 5 and 1, 3, 4. The largest numbers they make are 521 and 431, and the smallest are 125 and 134.

solutions.reliable: Three different digits from 1 to 9 that add to 8 must include 1, since 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 is already too big. The other two add to 7 and are different and not 1: 2 and 5, or 3 and 4. So the groups are 1, 2, 5 and 1, 3, 4. The largest number is 521 (bigger than 431) and the smallest is 125 (smaller than 134). The difference is 521 - 125 = 396. The transferable idea: list every digit group first, then pick the extremes across all the groups.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles test complete casework, and each distractor comes from using only one digit group or ignoring a rule.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana picks five different odd numbers, each smaller than 12, and adds them up. Which of these could be her total?

choices.misconception: I checked that the total is odd but not that it is big enough; the smallest possible total is 25.
I took 6 away from the total of all six odd numbers, but the number left out must itself be odd.
I added all six odd numbers smaller than 12 instead of only five.
I checked that the total is odd but not that it is small enough; the largest possible total is 35.

hints: How many odd numbers are smaller than 12?
There are only six odd numbers below 12, so choosing five means leaving exactly one out. Find the total of all six, then see what happens when one odd number is removed.
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36. Ana leaves out one of these six odd numbers, so her total is 36 minus an odd number.

solutions.reliable: The odd numbers below 12 are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11, which add to 36. Ana uses five of them, so she leaves one out, and her total is 36 minus one of these: 35, 33, 31, 29, 27 or 25. Of the choices only 31 is on that list, by leaving out 5. The transferable idea: when you must choose almost all of a small set, think about the one you leave out.
solutions.elegant: Five odd numbers always add to an odd total, which rules out 30 and 36. The total is between 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25 and 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 35, which rules out 23 and 37.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity rules out the even totals, but bounding is needed too, so this tests using both checks.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A red light flashes every 3 seconds and a blue light flashes every 5 seconds. They flash together right now. How many more times will they flash together in the next 50 seconds?

choices.misconception: I counted the flash together happening right now as one of the times.
I added 3 and 5 and thought they flash together every 8 seconds.
I divided 50 by 5, which counts only the flashes of the blue light.
I found that they flash together every 15 seconds and gave that instead of how many times.

hints: When is the first time after now that both lights flash?
Both lights flash at a time that is a multiple of 3 and also a multiple of 5. Find the smallest such time, then count its multiples up to 50, leaving out the flash happening now.
The first common time is 15 seconds. After that come 30 and 45; the next, 60, is too late.

solutions.reliable: The red light flashes at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ... seconds and the blue light at 5, 10, 15, ... seconds, so they first meet again after 15 seconds. They then meet at 30 and 45 seconds, and 60 is past 50. That is 3 more times. The transferable idea: events that repeat every a and every b seconds coincide at the common multiples of a and b.
solutions.elegant: 3 and 5 share no factor, so they coincide every 3 x 5 = 15 seconds, and 50 contains three full 15s.

problems.whyOnTest: Common multiples tested in a story, with traps for the starting flash and for reporting the gap instead of the count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, A is at 18 and B is at 66. C is halfway between A and B, and D is halfway between A and C. What number is at D?

choices.misconception: I found half of the distance from A to C, but forgot to start counting from 18.
I found the distance from A to C and gave that instead of the position of D.
I found where C is and stopped.
I went halfway between C and B instead of between A and C.

hints: Find C first. How far is it from A to B?
Halfway between two numbers is found by halving the distance between them and adding that to the smaller number. Do this once for C, then again for D, using A and C.
A to B is 48, so C is 18 + 24 = 42. Now A to C is 24, and half of that is 12.

solutions.reliable: From 18 to 66 is 48, so C is 18 + 24 = 42. From 18 to 42 is 24, so D is 18 + 12 = 30. The transferable idea: a midpoint is the starting number plus half the distance, and a distance is not a position.
solutions.elegant: D is a quarter of the way from A to B. A quarter of 48 is 12, and 18 + 12 = 30.

problems.whyOnTest: Midpoints on a number line test the difference between a distance and a position, which is where the distractors come from.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A list of numbers starts 4, 10, 16, 22, and each number is 6 more than the one before. What is the 10th number in the list?

choices.misconception: I added 6 only eight times, one step too few.
I multiplied 9 by 6 and forgot to add the starting 4.
I multiplied 10 by 6 and forgot the list starts at 4.
I added 6 ten times to the 4, but the 4 is already the first number.

hints: How many steps of 6 are there from the 1st number to the 10th?
Each number is the first number plus some steps of 6. Count how many steps you take to reach the 2nd and the 3rd number, find the rule, and use it for the 10th.
The 2nd number is 4 plus one 6, the 3rd is 4 plus two 6s, so the 10th is 4 plus nine 6s.

solutions.reliable: The 1st number is 4, the 2nd is 4 + 6, the 3rd is 4 + 2 x 6, so the 10th is 4 + 9 x 6 = 4 + 54 = 58. The transferable idea: the nth number in a list that goes up by the same step is the first number plus one fewer than n steps.

problems.whyOnTest: Arithmetic sequences test the one-fewer step count, and the distractors are each slip around it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a hundred square, 1 to 10 fill the top row, 11 to 20 the next, and so on. Ana starts on 23, moves 3 squares down, then 2 squares left. Where does she land?

choices.misconception: I added 1 for each square down, as if moving down worked like moving right.
I mixed up the moves and went 2 squares down and 3 squares left.
I counted the starting row as one of the three, so I only went 2 rows down.
I moved 2 squares right instead of left.

hints: What happens to a number when you move one square down?
In a grid with rows of 10, moving down one square adds 10 and moving left one square takes away 1. Apply each move in turn, starting from 23.
Three squares down from 23 is 23 + 30 = 53. Now move 2 squares left.

solutions.reliable: Each row has 10 numbers, so one square down adds 10 and one square left takes away 1. Three squares down from 23 is 23 + 30 = 53, and two squares left is 53 - 2 = 51. Check: 51 is in the same column as 21, two columns to the left of 23. The transferable idea: in a grid with rows of n, moving down adds n and moving left takes away 1.

problems.whyOnTest: Number grids test the link between row length and the size of a vertical step, and each distractor misreads one move.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Hana has a ribbon 40 cm long. She cuts off a fifth of it. How many centimetres of ribbon are left?

choices.misconception: I took away 5 cm, as if a fifth meant 5 centimetres.
I took away a quarter of the ribbon instead of a fifth.
I cut the ribbon in half instead of taking off a fifth.
I found the fifth that was cut off and gave that instead of the piece that is left.

hints: First find how long the piece that is cut off is.
A fifth means one of five equal parts. Find one part, then check whether the question asks for the piece cut off or the piece left.
One fifth of 40 cm is 40 divided by 5 = 8 cm. Take that away from the whole ribbon.

solutions.reliable: A fifth of 40 cm is 40 divided by 5 = 8 cm, so 40 - 8 = 32 cm are left. The transferable idea: find one equal part first, then read again whether the question wants the part taken or the part left.

problems.whyOnTest: Finding a fraction of a quantity, here a fifth of a length, is one step, and the length of the piece cut off is offered as the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Kofi's bean plant is 1 metre and 8 centimetres tall. How tall is it in centimetres?

choices.misconception: I added the 1 and the 8 without changing the metre into centimetres.
I counted a metre as 10 centimetres, so I added 10 and 8.
I put the 8 in the tens place, as if the plant were 1 metre and 80 centimetres.
I thought a metre is 1000 centimetres, the way a kilometre is 1000 metres.

hints: How many centimetres make one metre?
Change the metre into centimetres first, then add on the extra centimetres. Watch which place the 8 belongs in.
1 metre is 100 centimetres, so the plant is 100 centimetres and 8 more.

solutions.reliable: 1 metre is 100 cm, so 1 metre and 8 cm is 100 + 8 = 108 cm. The transferable idea: change every part into the same unit before you add, and keep each digit in its proper place.

problems.whyOnTest: Changing metres into centimetres is a one-step conversion, and the place-value slip that gives 180 is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a balance, 1 melon weighs the same as 4 oranges, and 1 orange weighs the same as 2 plums. How many plums weigh the same as 1 melon?

choices.misconception: I divided 4 by 2 instead of swapping each orange for 2 plums.
I gave the number of oranges and did not swap them for plums.
I added the 4 and the 2 instead of multiplying them.
I swapped the oranges for 8 plums but kept the 4 oranges on the pan as well.

hints: Replace each orange with something you already know it balances.
On a balance you can swap one thing for anything that weighs the same. Swap the oranges one at a time and count what ends up on the pan.
The melon balances 4 oranges, and each of those oranges can be swapped for 2 plums.

solutions.reliable: The melon balances 4 oranges. Each orange balances 2 plums, so the 4 oranges balance 4 x 2 = 8 plums. The transferable idea: on a balance you can swap anything for something that weighs the same, one step at a time.

problems.whyOnTest: Swapping one equal weight for another is the basic move of every balance puzzle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these gives an odd answer?

choices.misconception: I thought odd plus odd gives an odd number, but two odd numbers always add to an even number.
I thought an odd number times an even number stays odd, but multiplying by an even number always gives an even answer.
I mixed up the rule and thought an even number minus an even number could be odd.
I looked only at the first number, 11, which is odd, and ignored the even 12.

hints: Look at whether each number is odd or even, not at its size.
Odd and even follow fixed rules for adding, taking away and multiplying. Decide each one from the last digits alone.
Odd + odd is even, even + odd is odd, and any multiplication with an even number in it is even.

solutions.reliable: Work each one out: 18 + 31 = 49, 15 + 27 = 42, 23 x 4 = 92, 36 - 14 = 22 and 11 x 12 = 132. Only 49 is odd. The transferable idea: when unsure, a quick full calculation settles it, but the last digit is all that decides odd or even.
solutions.elegant: Use the rules: odd + odd is even, even - even is even, and a product with an even number in it is even. Only 18 + 31 adds one even and one odd number, so it is the only odd answer. The transferable idea: odd or even can be decided without the full answer.

problems.whyOnTest: The odd and even rules for sums and products let you answer without calculating, which is what this probes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a calendar page, the dates of a month are written in rows of 7, one square for each day of the week. Which date is directly above the 26th?

choices.misconception: I took away 10, as if the calendar had rows of 10 like a hundred square.
I took away 8, which moves up one row and also one square to the left.
I moved one square to the left instead of one row up.
I moved down a row instead of up, so I added 7.

hints: How many dates are in each row of the calendar?
Each row holds 7 dates, so moving straight up one row always changes the date by the same amount. Work out that jump and which way it goes.
Going up one row lands on the date that is 7 smaller.

solutions.reliable: Each row has 7 dates, so the square directly above any date holds the date that is 7 smaller: 26 - 7 = 19. Check: the date directly below the 19th is 19 + 7 = 26. The transferable idea: in a grid with rows of n, one step up means take away n and one step left means take away 1.

problems.whyOnTest: Patterns in a grid: seeing that one row up means taking away the row length is the core idea, and the hundred-square habit of using 10 is offered as a trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A photo 6 cm long and 4 cm wide is stuck flat onto a card 10 cm long and 7 cm wide, inside its edges. How many square centimetres of card can still be seen?

choices.misconception: I took away the lengths and the widths, 10 - 6 = 4 and 7 - 4 = 3, and multiplied 4 x 3.
I took the distance around the photo, 20 cm, away from the distance around the card, 34 cm.
I found the area of the photo and stopped there.
I found the area of the whole card and forgot to take away the part the photo covers.

hints: Find the area of the whole card before thinking about the photo.
The card that can be seen is the whole card minus the part under the photo. Find each area separately, then subtract.
The whole card covers 10 x 7 square centimetres and the photo covers 6 x 4.

solutions.reliable: Whole card: 10 x 7 = 70 square cm. Photo: 6 x 4 = 24 square cm. Still seen: 70 - 24 = 46 square cm. It does not matter where on the card the photo sits. The transferable idea: the area of a region with a piece covered or cut out is the whole area minus that piece.

problems.whyOnTest: Area by subtraction, whole minus the covered part, is the simplest form of the shaded-region idea.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to 49 x 21?

choices.misconception: I added 49 and 21 instead of multiplying them.
I rounded to 50 x 20 and multiplied 5 by 2, but put back only one of the two zeros.
I rounded 21 down to 10 instead of to 20.
I rounded to 50 x 20 and then wrote one zero too many.

hints: Round each number to a nearby number that is easy to multiply.
Estimating means swapping awkward numbers for round ones close to them. Choose roundings that change each number only a little, then count the zeros carefully.
49 is close to 50 and 21 is close to 20.

solutions.reliable: 49 is about 50 and 21 is about 20, so 49 x 21 is about 50 x 20 = 1000. The exact answer is 1029, which is indeed closest to 1000. The transferable idea: round to friendly numbers, multiply the front digits, then count the zeros.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimating to the nearest choice saves time, and the usual slips with zeros are all offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The houses on one side of a street are numbered 3, 7, 11 and so on, going up by 4 each time: the 1st house is number 3. Which house is number 31?

choices.misconception: I counted only the houses between number 3 and number 31 and left out both of those houses.
I counted the 7 jumps of 4 from number 3 to number 31, but the 1st house comes before any jump.
I worked out 31 divided by 4, which is about 8, and then added 1 for the first house.
I took 3 away from 31 and gave the difference between the house numbers instead of the house's place.

hints: Write the house numbers out in order and count them.
This is a sequence with a start number and equal jumps. Count how many jumps of 4 take you from 3 to 31, then remember the 1st house needs no jump.
From 3 to 31 is 28, which is 7 jumps of 4.

solutions.reliable: List them: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31. Number 31 is the 8th in the list, so it is the 8th house. The transferable idea: when the list is short, writing every term out and counting is the safest method.
solutions.elegant: From 3 to 31 is 31 - 3 = 28, and 28 divided by 4 = 7 jumps. The 1st house needs no jump, so 7 jumps lead to the 8th house. The transferable idea: the position of a term is one more than the number of jumps from the first term.

problems.whyOnTest: In an arithmetic sequence, counting the jumps and adding 1 for the first term finds a term's position, and both off-by-one slips are offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Kofi, Lena, Ravi and Yusuf each play a different instrument: drum, flute, piano or violin. Lena plays piano. Kofi plays neither flute nor drum. Ravi does not play drum. Who plays the drum?

choices.misconception: I used only the two clues that mention the drum, which leaves Lena and Yusuf, so I thought it could not be decided.
I read the clue about Kofi as saying he plays the flute or the drum, and picked the drum.
I crossed out Kofi and Ravi but forgot that Lena already plays the piano.
I missed the word 'not' in the clue about Ravi.

hints: Start with the clue that tells you something for certain.
Use an elimination grid with a row for each child and a column for each instrument. Each tick crosses out the rest of its row and column.
Lena has the piano, so Kofi, who plays neither flute nor drum, must play the violin.

solutions.reliable: Lena plays piano. Kofi cannot play flute or drum, and the piano is taken, so Kofi plays violin. Ravi does not play drum, and piano and violin are taken, so Ravi plays flute. That leaves the drum for Yusuf. The transferable idea: settle the certain facts first, because each one removes options for everyone else.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination grids test whether every clue, including the plain fact about Lena, is used to cross out options.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: I am a two-digit number. My tens digit is 3 more than my ones digit, and my two digits add up to 11. What number am I?

choices.misconception: I found the tens digit and gave it as the whole answer.
I read the clue as 'the tens digit is 3' and chose 8 to make 11.
I found the digits 7 and 4 but put the bigger one in the ones place.
I split 11 as evenly as I could and ignored the clue about 3 more.

hints: Which pairs of digits add up to 11?
List the digit pairs that make 11, then test each pair against the other clue. Keep track of which digit goes in the tens place.
The pairs are 2 and 9, 3 and 8, 4 and 7, 5 and 6. Only one pair differs by 3.

solutions.reliable: Digit pairs adding to 11: 2 and 9, 3 and 8, 4 and 7, 5 and 6. Only 4 and 7 differ by 3. The tens digit is the bigger one, so the number is 74. The transferable idea: list everything that fits one clue, then test the list against the other clue.
solutions.elegant: Take the difference of 3 away from the total first: 11 - 3 = 8. Share 8 equally: 4 and 4. The ones digit is 4 and the tens digit is 4 + 3 = 7, so the number is 74. The transferable idea: remove the difference, share equally, then add the difference back.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles test whether you can satisfy two conditions at once and keep each digit in the right place.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A red ribbon is 3 times as long as a blue ribbon. The red ribbon is 16 cm longer than the blue one. How long is the blue ribbon?

choices.misconception: I split the 16 cm into 4 equal parts, counting the blue part as well as the three red parts.
I thought the blue ribbon was the 16 cm difference itself.
I found the length of the red ribbon instead of the blue one.
I multiplied the 16 cm difference by 3.

hints: Draw the blue ribbon as one bar and the red one as three such bars.
In a bar model the difference is the part of the red ribbon that sticks out beyond the blue one. Count how many blue-length bars make up that difference.
The red ribbon sticks out by 2 blue lengths, and those 2 lengths make 16 cm.

solutions.reliable: Draw blue as 1 bar and red as 3 equal bars. Red is longer by 2 bars, so 2 bars = 16 cm and 1 bar = 8 cm. The blue ribbon is 8 cm, and the red one is 24 cm, which is indeed 16 cm longer. The transferable idea: in a bar model the difference is only the bars that stick out, not all of them.

problems.whyOnTest: Bar models turn 'times as long' and 'longer by' into one picture, and the trap of sharing the difference into 4 parts is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: From a tree, Pia walks 4 squares east and 3 north and buries a coin. The well is 2 squares east and 5 north of the tree. Which walk takes Tom from well to coin?

choices.misconception: I found the right numbers of squares but went north, without noticing that the coin is further south than the well.
I added the coin's position and the well's position together instead of finding the difference between them.
I found the walk from the coin to the well, which is the trip the wrong way round.
I gave Pia's walk from the tree, but Tom starts at the well, not at the tree.

hints: Deal with east-west and north-south separately.
Find how far east of the tree the coin and the well are, and how far north. Compare the well with the coin in each direction to see which way Tom must go.
The coin is 4 east and 3 north of the tree, and the well is 2 east and 5 north. Compare 4 with 2, and 3 with 5.

solutions.reliable: East-west: the coin is 4 squares east of the tree and the well only 2, so Tom goes 4 - 2 = 2 squares east. North-south: the coin is 3 squares north of the tree and the well is 5, so the coin is further south and Tom goes 5 - 3 = 2 squares south. The transferable idea: on a grid, compare two places one direction at a time, and the bigger number tells you which way to go.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid coordinates: describing one point from another means comparing across and up-down separately, which is the heart of lattice reasoning.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from today?

choices.misconception: I worked out 2 extra days but counted them backwards from Wednesday.
I thought 100 is a round number, so it must be a whole number of weeks and the day would not change.
I counted today as the first of the 100 days, so I ended one day short.
I threw away the 14 whole weeks but then started counting the 2 extra days from Thursday instead of from Wednesday.

hints: What day is it exactly 7 days from today?
The days of the week repeat every 7 days, so whole weeks can be thrown away. Only the days left over after the whole weeks move you on.
100 days is 14 whole weeks, which is 98 days, and 2 days more.

solutions.reliable: 14 weeks is 14 x 7 = 98 days, so 98 days from today is again a Wednesday. Two more days: Thursday, then Friday. The answer is Friday. The transferable idea: in any repeating cycle, only the remainder after the whole cycles matters.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders and modular cycles: a day-of-the-week question is the remainder after dividing by 7, and the off-by-one counting slip is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four flags, coloured red, blue, green and yellow, are hung in a row. The red flag must be at one of the two ends. How many different orders are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted only the two places the red flag can go and forgot to arrange the other flags.
I put the red flag at the left end only and forgot it could go at the right end.
I started from all 24 orders and took away only the orders with red in second place, forgetting third place.
I ignored the rule about the red flag and counted every possible order.

hints: Put the red flag in place first.
Place the flag with the rule first, then count the ways to arrange the others in the places left. Do this for each end and add the results.
With red at the left end, the other three flags can be arranged in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways.

solutions.reliable: Red at the left end: the other three flags fill the three places left in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways. Red at the right end: another 6 ways. Total 6 + 6 = 12. The transferable idea: place the object with the rule first, then arrange the rest.
solutions.elegant: With no rule there are 24 orders, and red is equally likely to be in each of the 4 places, so it is at an end in 2 out of 4 places: half of 24, which is 12. The transferable idea: symmetry can turn a rule into a simple fraction of the total.

problems.whyOnTest: Placing the restricted object first is the standard way to count arrangements that come with a rule.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A leaky tap drips 50 millilitres of water every minute. How much water drips from it in 2 hours? Give your answer in litres.

choices.misconception: I worked out how much drips in one hour and forgot the second hour.
I changed 6000 millilitres into litres by dividing by 100 instead of by 1000.
I changed 6000 millilitres into litres by dividing by 10 instead of by 1000.
I worked out 6000 millilitres and wrote the number down without changing it into litres.

hints: How many minutes are in 2 hours?
Find the amount in millilitres first, then re-read the question to see which unit the answer must be in. Changing millilitres into litres is the last step.
2 hours is 120 minutes, so the tap drips 120 x 50 millilitres.

solutions.reliable: 2 hours is 2 x 60 = 120 minutes. 120 x 50 = 6000 millilitres, and 6000 millilitres = 6 litres because 1000 millilitres make 1 litre. The transferable idea: before choosing an answer, re-read the question and check the unit it asks for.

problems.whyOnTest: Check units and re-read: a question that wants a different unit from the working catches students who stop one step early.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lena thinks of a number. Multiplying it by 3 gives the same answer as adding 10 to it. What is Lena's number?

choices.misconception: I took the 10 from the question to be the number itself.
I added 3 and 10 as if both were amounts to add.
I gave the answer after multiplying by 3, not the number Lena started with.
I multiplied the 10 by the 3 instead of finding Lena's number.

hints: Try a small number and see whether both ways give the same answer.
Write the sentence as a balance: three lots of the number on one side, one lot and 10 more on the other. Take the same thing away from both sides.
Three lots of the number equal one lot plus 10, so two lots of the number must make 10.

solutions.reliable: Test the choices: 5 x 3 = 15 and 5 + 10 = 15, which match. For 10: 30 and 20 do not match, and the others fail the same way. So Lena's number is 5. The transferable idea: put each answer choice back into the sentence, and both sides must agree.
solutions.elegant: Three lots of the number equal one lot plus 10. Remove one lot from each side: two lots make 10, so one lot is 5. The transferable idea: turn the words into a balance and remove the same amount from both sides.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning a sentence into a balance of equal amounts is the first step towards every equation.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana writes a three-digit number. Its digits are all different and add up to 12, and its hundreds digit is the sum of the other two. What is the largest number she could have written?

choices.misconception: I ignored the rule about the hundreds digit and made the largest number with different digits that add up to 12.
I used 6 and 0 for the last two digits, forgetting that all three digits must be different.
I stopped at the first pair I found for the last two digits, 4 and 2, without looking for a bigger tens digit.
I found the digits 6, 1 and 5 but put the 5 last, which does not make the largest number.

hints: How does the hundreds digit compare with the total of all three digits?
The hundreds digit and the other two digits together make 12, and those two parts are equal. Find the hundreds digit first, then try pairs for the last two digits, biggest tens digit first.
The hundreds digit is half of 12, which is 6, so the tens and ones digits add up to 6.

solutions.reliable: The hundreds digit is the same as the tens and ones digits added together, so the 12 splits into two equal halves: the hundreds digit is 6, and the other two digits add up to 6. The pairs that add up to 6 are 6 and 0, 5 and 1, 4 and 2, and 3 and 3. The pair 6 and 0 repeats the 6, and 3 and 3 repeats the 3, so neither is allowed. For the largest number, put the biggest allowed tens digit, 5, next: 651. Check: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12 and 5 + 1 = 6. The transferable idea: use the strongest clue first to fix one digit, then list what is left.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit-constraint puzzles: spotting that the hundreds digit must be half the digit total is the key idea, and each broken rule is offered as a trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a scale, 1 key and 2 coins weigh 14 g, while 2 keys and 1 coin weigh 16 g. All keys weigh the same, and so do all coins. What does one key weigh?

choices.misconception: I found the weight of one coin instead of one key.
I found that a key and a coin weigh 10 g together and split it equally between them.
I halved 16 g, as if the two keys made up all of that weight.
I found the weight of one key and one coin together and stopped there.

hints: Try putting everything from both weighings on the scale together.
Combining both weighings gives equal numbers of keys and coins. That tells you what one key and one coin weigh together, which you can compare with one of the weighings.
Together, 3 keys and 3 coins weigh 30 g, so 1 key and 1 coin weigh 10 g.

solutions.reliable: Compare the two weighings. The second has one more key and one fewer coin, and it is 2 g heavier, so a key is 2 g heavier than a coin. In the first weighing, a key and 2 coins make 14 g: that is 3 coins and 2 g more, so 3 coins weigh 12 g and a coin is 4 g. A key is 4 + 2 = 6 g. Check: 6 + 4 + 4 = 14 and 6 + 6 + 4 = 16. The transferable idea: compare two balances to see what one swap is worth.
solutions.elegant: Put both weighings together: 3 keys and 3 coins weigh 30 g, so 1 key and 1 coin weigh 10 g. The second weighing is that pair plus one more key: 10 g + key = 16 g, so a key is 6 g. The transferable idea: combining balances can make a simpler group appear.

problems.whyOnTest: Two balance facts with mixed objects need an idea, combining or comparing them, not just a single swap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mei has fewer than 50 shells. In rows of 2, 3 or 4 there is always 1 shell left over. In rows of 5 there are none left over. How many shells does she have?

choices.misconception: I found the first number that leaves 1 over for rows of 2, 3 and 4, and forgot to check rows of 5.
I looked for a number that fits rows of 4 and rows of 5 exactly and forgot the shell left over.
I found a number that 2, 3 and 4 all divide but forgot the 1 shell left over.
I took the largest number under 50 that leaves 1 over for rows of 2, 3 and 4, without checking rows of 5.

hints: Take away the shell that is left over. What can you say about the rest?
If 1 is always left over, then one fewer shell would fit rows of 2, 3 and 4 exactly, so it is a common multiple. List those, add 1, and test rows of 5.
The common multiples of 2, 3 and 4 below 50 are 12, 24, 36 and 48.

solutions.reliable: One fewer than the number of shells is a multiple of 2, 3 and 4, which means a multiple of 12: 12, 24, 36 or 48. Adding 1 gives 13, 25, 37 or 49. Only 25 fits rows of 5 exactly. Mei has 25 shells. The transferable idea: always 1 left over means one fewer is a common multiple.

problems.whyOnTest: Recognising a common multiple hidden behind a remainder is the idea this question tests.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The big square is made of 36 equal small squares. What is the area of the shaded square, measured in small squares?

figure.alt: A 6 by 6 grid of small squares. A tilted shaded square has one corner on each side of the big square, each 2 small squares along from a corner of the big square. This leaves four white corner triangles, each with a short side of 2 and a long side of 4 along the edges of the big square.

choices.misconception: I took away four whole 2 by 4 rectangles instead of four triangles that are each half of one.
I counted only the small squares that lie completely inside the shaded square.
I found the total area of the four white corner triangles instead of the shaded square.
I treated each corner triangle as half of a 2 by 2 square, which made the triangles too small.

hints: Look at the white parts instead of the shaded part.
The shaded area is the big square minus the four white corner triangles. Each white triangle is half of a rectangle you can see on the grid.
Each white triangle is half of a 2 by 4 rectangle, so it covers 4 small squares.

solutions.reliable: The big square covers 36 small squares. Each white corner triangle is half of a 2 by 4 rectangle, so it covers 8 divided by 2 = 4. The four triangles cover 16. The shaded square covers 36 - 16 = 20 small squares. The transferable idea: when a shape is awkward, find the easy area around it and subtract.

problems.whyOnTest: A tilted shape cannot be counted square by square, so it tests whether you think to subtract the pieces around it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At a party, every guest shook hands exactly once with every other guest. There were 15 handshakes in all. How many guests were at the party?

choices.misconception: I added 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 and gave the biggest number, but that is the handshake count for 6 guests.
I halved the 15 handshakes because each one uses two people, then rounded up.
I thought there was one guest for each handshake.
I doubled the 15 handshakes because each handshake has two people in it.

hints: Count the handshakes for 3 guests, then for 4 guests. What pattern appears?
Each new guest who arrives shakes hands with everyone already there. Build up the total one guest at a time until it reaches 15.
With 2 guests there is 1 handshake. A 3rd guest adds 2 more, a 4th adds 3 more, and so on.

solutions.reliable: Add guests one at a time: 2 guests make 1 handshake, the 3rd guest adds 2 (total 3), the 4th adds 3 (total 6), the 5th adds 4 (total 10) and the 6th adds 5 (total 15). So there were 6 guests. The transferable idea: build a pair count up one person at a time.
solutions.elegant: Each of the guests shakes hands with everyone else, and each handshake is counted once by each of its two people. So the number of guests times one fewer than that is 2 x 15 = 30, which is 6 x 5. There were 6 guests. The transferable idea: count from each person, then halve for the double count.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards from a handshake total tests whether you understand how pairs grow, and the classic off-by-one is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sofia read a third of her book on Monday and a quarter of the whole book on Tuesday. On Tuesday she read 4 pages fewer than on Monday. How many pages does the book have?

choices.misconception: I found the number of pages she read on Monday instead of the number in the whole book.
I found the pages she still has to read after Tuesday instead of the whole book.
I found that one twelfth of the book is 4 pages, but then I worked out the 7 twelfths she read over both days instead of the whole book.
I found the number of pages she read on Tuesday instead of the number in the whole book.

hints: Split the book into equal parts that both a third and a quarter fit.
Use 12 equal parts: a third of the book is 4 of those parts and a quarter is 3 of them. Compare Monday with Tuesday in parts.
Monday was 4 parts and Tuesday was 3 parts, so the 4 pages are exactly 1 part.

solutions.reliable: Cut the book into 12 equal parts. A third of the book is 4 parts and a quarter is 3 parts. Monday's reading was 1 part more than Tuesday's, and that difference is 4 pages, so 1 part is 4 pages. The whole book is 12 parts, which is 12 x 4 = 48 pages. Check: a third of 48 is 16, a quarter of 48 is 12, and 16 - 12 = 4. The transferable idea: to compare two fractions of the same whole, cut the whole into equal parts that both fractions fit, then find what one part is worth.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of a quantity: comparing a third and a quarter of the same book means finding equal parts that both fit, which is what makes this a 5-point problem.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a club, every child who plays chess also plays tennis. 8 children play chess, 13 play tennis and 5 play neither. How many children are in the club?

choices.misconception: I took the chess players away from the tennis players as if they had been counted twice, then added the 5.
I counted the tennis players but forgot the children who play neither game.
I added the chess and tennis players, which counts the chess players twice, and forgot the 5.
I added all three numbers, which counts every chess player twice.

hints: Can a child play chess without being one of the tennis players?
Read the first sentence precisely: it puts every chess player inside the tennis group. Draw the chess group as a circle inside the tennis circle.
All 8 chess players are already among the 13 tennis players.

solutions.reliable: Every chess player plays tennis, so the 8 chess players are already counted among the 13 tennis players. Children who play at least one game: 13. Add the 5 who play neither: 13 + 5 = 18. The transferable idea: every A is also B means the A group sits inside B, so it must not be added again.

problems.whyOnTest: Reading 'every chess player also plays tennis' precisely decides how the groups overlap, which is the whole problem.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A block 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 2 cubes tall is built from small cubes. The whole outside of the block is painted. How many small cubes have paint on exactly one face?

choices.misconception: I thought no cube can be in the middle of a face because the block is only 2 cubes tall.
I counted the middle cubes of the top face and forgot the bottom face.
I counted the corner cubes, which have three painted faces.
I counted the cubes with exactly two painted faces.

hints: Every small cube is in either the top layer or the bottom layer.
A cube with exactly one painted face sits in the middle of a face, touching no edge of the block. Check each of the six faces for such cubes.
On the 4 by 3 top face, the cubes that touch no edge form a 2 by 1 strip.

solutions.reliable: Every cube is in the top or bottom layer, so each has its top or bottom face painted. It has only that one face painted if it touches none of the four sides: on a 4 by 3 layer that is the middle 2 by 1 strip, 2 cubes. Top and bottom layers give 2 + 2 = 4. The side faces are only 2 cubes tall, so every cube on them lies on an edge. Check: 8 corner cubes, 12 with two faces and 4 with one face make all 24 cubes. The transferable idea: one painted face means the middle of a face, away from every edge.

problems.whyOnTest: Painted-block questions test whether you can picture which cubes sit on edges, and a block only 2 tall changes the usual picture.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers of sweets can be shared equally among 9 children, with none left over?

choices.misconception: I remembered 9 x 22 as 196, but 9 x 22 is really 198.
I added the digits to get 12, which divides by 3, and mixed up the test for 3 with the test for 9.
I thought any number ending in 9 can be split into 9 equal groups.
I thought a number starting with 9 hundreds can always be split into nines.

hints: Add up the digits of each number.
A number divides exactly by 9 when its digits add up to a multiple of 9. Use that test on each choice instead of dividing.
The digit sums are 16, 12, 9, 15 and 14. Only one of these is a multiple of 9.

solutions.reliable: Use the digit-sum test for 9: 1 + 9 + 6 = 16, 4 + 2 + 6 = 12, 5 + 1 + 3 = 9, 5 + 1 + 9 = 15, 9 + 0 + 5 = 14. Only 513 has a digit sum that is a multiple of 9, and indeed 513 = 9 x 57. The transferable idea: the last digit tests for 2, 5 and 10, but for 3 and 9 you must add the digits.

problems.whyOnTest: Knowing which divisibility test to use, and that the last digit says nothing about 9.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bug sits on a point of a huge square grid. Each step takes it along a grid line to a neighbouring point. For how many points is its shortest walk exactly 3 steps?

choices.misconception: I only counted the points 3 steps away in a straight line, up, down, left and right.
I counted the straight-line points and the walks of 2 steps one way and 1 step the other, but forgot 1 step one way and 2 steps the other.
I found the 4 points in one corner region, including the ones on the lines, and multiplied by 4, so I counted the straight-line points twice.
I counted every point on the edge of the 7 by 7 square around the bug, but the corners of that square are 6 steps away.

hints: Sort points by how many steps go sideways and how many go up or down.
A shortest walk mixes sideways steps and up-or-down steps that add up to 3. Do casework on how many are sideways, and in each case count the directions it could go.
3 sideways and 0 up or down gives 2 points; 2 and 1 gives 4 points; 1 and 2 gives 4 points; 0 and 3 gives 2 points.

solutions.reliable: Split the 3 steps into sideways and up-or-down. 3 sideways, 0 up-or-down: left or right, 2 points. 2 sideways, 1 up-or-down: 2 x 2 = 4 points. 1 sideways, 2 up-or-down: 4 points. 0 sideways, 3 up-or-down: 2 points. Total 2 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 12. The transferable idea: on a grid, split a walk into its across part and its up part and do casework on the split.
solutions.elegant: The points form a diamond around the bug. Each of its four sides runs from one tip to the next and holds 4 points, and the 4 tips are each shared by two sides, so 4 x 4 - 4 = 12. The transferable idea: when you count around a closed shape, subtract the corners you counted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid distance is not straight-line distance, and counting the diamond of points needs careful casework without double-counting.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Coins come in 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 cents. What is the smallest number of coins that make exactly 87 cents?

choices.misconception: I only counted the coins worth 10 cents or more and forgot the 7 cents.
I made 87 as 50 + 20 + 10 + 7, forgetting there is no 7-cent coin.
I made the 7 cents from a 5-cent coin and two 1-cent coins instead of a 5 and a 2.
I made the 7 cents from seven 1-cent coins.

hints: Start with the biggest coin that fits.
To use as few coins as possible, take the largest coin that does not go over the amount still to pay, and repeat until nothing is left. Check each coin you write really exists.
50 cents leaves 37, then 20 leaves 17, then 10 leaves 7.

solutions.reliable: Take the biggest coin each time: 50 (37 left), 20 (17 left), 10 (7 left), 5 (2 left), 2 (0 left). That is 5 coins. Fewer is impossible. The 10, 20 and 50 cent coins only make whole tens, so the 1, 2 and 5 cent coins must make 7, 17, 27 or more. Making 7 takes at least 2 small coins (5 + 2), and then the other 80 cents takes at least 3 coins, since no two coins add up to 80. Making 17 or more from small coins already takes at least 4 coins, and the rest needs at least 1 more. The transferable idea: for the fewest coins, pay with the largest coin that fits, again and again.

problems.whyOnTest: Making an amount with the fewest coins, where the leftover few cents are where mistakes happen.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven children in a circle are numbered 1 to 7. Child 1 passes a ball to child 2, who passes it to child 3, and so on around. Who has the ball after 30 passes?

choices.misconception: I knew 28 passes bring the ball back to child 1 and forgot the other 2 passes.
I took the remainder of 30 divided by 7 as the child's number, but the ball started at child 1, not child 0.
I divided 30 by 7 and moved the ball on by the answer, 4, instead of by the remainder.
I thought it takes 8 passes to get round the circle and back to child 1.

hints: How many passes bring the ball back to child 1?
Every full trip round the circle brings the ball back to where it started. Take away as many full trips as you can, then count on the passes that are left.
7 passes take the ball once round, so after 28 passes it is back with child 1.

solutions.reliable: Seven passes take the ball once round the circle and back to child 1. After 4 x 7 = 28 passes child 1 has it again. The last 2 passes take it to child 2 and then child 3. The transferable idea: in a repeating cycle, strip off the full cycles and count only the remainder, starting from the right place.

problems.whyOnTest: Positions in a repeating cycle, where the starting point decides whether the remainder is off by one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Stamps are worth 1, 2 and 5 cents. In how many different ways can you make exactly 10 cents? (The order of the stamps does not matter.)

choices.misconception: I left out the 1-cent stamps and only used 2-cent and 5-cent ones.
I only counted the ways that use at least one 5-cent stamp.
I forgot about the 5-cent stamps.
I forgot the way that uses two 5-cent stamps.

hints: Sort the ways by how many 5-cent stamps they use.
Do casework on the biggest stamp: no 5-cent stamps, one, or two. In each case the rest is made from 1s and 2s, so count how many 2-cent stamps can be used.
With no 5s, use 0 to 5 two-cent stamps. With one 5, use 0 to 2 two-cent stamps. With two 5s, nothing else.

solutions.reliable: Case 0 fives: the 10 cents is made of 2s and 1s, with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 twos, so 6 ways. Case 1 five: 5 cents of 2s and 1s, with 0, 1 or 2 twos, so 3 ways. Case 2 fives: 1 way. Total 6 + 3 + 1 = 10. The transferable idea: in a making-amounts count, fix the biggest piece first and count the rest case by case.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting ways to make an amount needs casework organised by the largest coin, or ways get missed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: 47 children go on a trip by car. Each car carries 4 children as well as its driver. What is the smallest number of cars needed?

choices.misconception: I gave the number of children left over after filling the cars, not the number of cars.
I rounded 47 down to 40 before dividing by 4.
I divided 47 by 4 and threw the leftover children away.
I thought the driver took one of the 4 seats, so only 3 children fit in each car.

hints: What happens to the children left over after filling the cars?
Divide the children into groups of 4. A remainder means some children still have no car, so think about whether to round the answer up or down.
47 divided by 4 is 11 with 3 left over. Those 3 children still need a car.

solutions.reliable: 47 divided by 4 is 11 with remainder 3. Eleven full cars carry 44 children, and the other 3 children need one more car, so 12 cars. The transferable idea: in a sharing problem, decide what the remainder means before you write the answer.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders in real situations: when everybody needs a seat, a leftover forces you to round up.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mr Lee sets out 24 chairs in equal rows: at least 2 rows, with at least 2 chairs in each. How many ways are there? (3 rows of 8 and 8 rows of 3 differ.)

choices.misconception: I counted 3 rows of 8 and 8 rows of 3 as the same arrangement.
I listed the factor pairs of 24, including 1 and 24, and counted each pair only once.
I allowed one long row of 24 chairs, forgetting the rule of at least 2 rows.
I counted all eight factors of 24, including 1 row of 24 and 24 rows of 1.

hints: The number of rows must divide 24 exactly.
List the factors of 24 in order. Each factor could be the number of rows, but check both rules: the number of rows and the number of chairs in a row must each be at least 2.
The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. Using 1 row or 24 rows breaks a rule.

solutions.reliable: The number of rows must be a factor of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24. One row breaks the 'at least 2 rows' rule, and 24 rows would leave 1 chair a row, which breaks the other rule. That leaves 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 rows, so 6 arrangements. The transferable idea: list factors in order so none are missed, then apply every condition to the list.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing factors systematically, then filtering by the conditions in the question, which is where most errors happen.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Bo and Cy each always lie or always tell the truth. Ana: "Exactly one of us lies." Bo: "Exactly two of us lie." Cy: "All three of us lie." How many lie?

choices.misconception: I believed all three of them without checking whether their sentences can all be true together.
I believed Ana, without noticing that Bo and Cy would then both be liars, which makes two.
I believed Cy, but if Cy told the truth, Cy would not be a liar.
I thought there was not enough information to tell.

hints: Can Cy be telling the truth?
The three sentences give different numbers, so at most one of them can be true. Test each child as the only truth-teller and check whether the number of liars then matches what that child said.
Cy cannot be truthful, because then Cy would be a liar. If Ana is the only truthful one, there are two liars, not one.

solutions.reliable: The sentences give different numbers, so at most one is true. Cy cannot be telling the truth, since a truthful Cy would be one of three liars. If all three lied, there would be 3 liars and Cy would be right, which is impossible. If Ana alone told the truth, there would be 2 liars, not 1. If Bo alone tells the truth, there are 2 liars, Ana and Cy, which matches Bo. So there are 2 liars. The transferable idea: assume one speaker is truthful and check whether the whole picture agrees with itself.

problems.whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles reward testing each possibility for consistency rather than trusting any one sentence.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag holds 3 kg of rice. How many portions of 250 g can be filled from it?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many 250 g portions fit in 1 kg, not in 3 kg.
I thought 250 g was half a kilogram.
I wrote 3 kg as 30,000 g, with one zero too many.
I multiplied 3 by 250 instead of dividing.

hints: How many grams are in a kilogram?
Put both amounts in the same unit before you divide. Then ask how many portions fit into the whole bag.
1 kg is 1,000 g, so the bag holds 3,000 g. Four portions of 250 g make 1,000 g.

solutions.reliable: 3 kg is 3 x 1,000 = 3,000 g. Each portion is 250 g, and 4 portions make 1,000 g, so 3,000 g fills 3 x 4 = 12 portions. The transferable idea: change to one unit first, then divide.
solutions.elegant: 250 g is a quarter of a kilogram, so each kilogram gives 4 portions and 3 kg give 12. The transferable idea: spot a friendly fraction of the bigger unit.

problems.whyOnTest: Unit conversion between kilograms and grams, with the multiply-instead-of-divide and dropped-step slips offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Counting numbers fill rows, each row one number longer than the row before: 1, then 2 3, then 4 5 6, and so on. What is the first number in row 8?

choices.misconception: I thought each row starts 2 more than the row before, so I counted 1, 3, 5 and onwards.
I found the first number in row 7, not row 8.
I added the row lengths 1 to 7 and forgot that row 8 starts one after that.
I found the last number in row 8 instead of the first.

hints: Where does row 7 end?
Each row ends where the numbers used so far run out. Add up how many numbers the earlier rows hold, and the next row starts just after that.
Rows 1 to 7 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 numbers altogether.

solutions.reliable: Rows 1 to 7 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 28 numbers, so row 7 ends with 28. Row 8 starts with 29. Check by listing the first numbers: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, 29, growing by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. The transferable idea: in a table filled row by row, the start of a row is one more than the total of the rows before it.
solutions.elegant: The first numbers grow by 1 more each time: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, 29. The transferable idea: list the differences and the next term falls out.

problems.whyOnTest: Locating an entry in a number triangle, where row 7 and the last number of row 8 are both tempting near misses.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a table, a 5 by 5 layer of cubes has a 3 by 3 layer centred on it and 1 cube on top. How many cubes are hidden from above and from every side?

choices.misconception: I thought every cube in the bottom layer shows at a side or on top, and only counted the cube under the top one.
I found the hidden cubes in the bottom layer but forgot the one under the top cube.
I thought the whole 3 by 3 middle layer was hidden, as well as the middle of the bottom layer.
I counted the cubes that can be seen instead of the ones that are hidden.

hints: Look at each layer separately.
A cube is hidden only if another cube covers its top and other cubes surround all four of its sides. Check which cubes in each layer are on the edge and which are covered from above.
