In the bottom layer, the 3 by 3 middle is covered by the middle layer. In the middle layer, only the centre cube is covered.

solutions.reliable: Bottom layer: the outer ring of 16 cubes shows at the sides, and the inner 3 by 3 block of 9 cubes is covered by the middle layer and surrounded, so 9 are hidden. Middle layer: its 8 outer cubes show at the sides and on top, but its centre cube is under the top cube and surrounded, so 1 is hidden. The top cube is visible. Hidden cubes: 9 + 1 = 10. The transferable idea: count hidden cubes layer by layer, asking whether each one is covered on top and on every side.
solutions.elegant: The cubes you cannot see form a smaller pyramid inside: a 3 by 3 layer with 1 cube on top, 9 + 1 = 10. The transferable idea: the hidden part of a stepped shape is often a smaller copy of it.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting hidden cubes means picturing the inside of a solid, layer by layer, which pictures alone never show.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Without a calculator, work out 25 x 7 x 4.

choices.misconception: I multiplied 25 by 7 and forgot the 4.
I multiplied 25 by 4 and forgot the 7.
I added the three numbers instead of multiplying them.
I worked out 25 x 4 as 1,000 instead of 100.

hints: Two of these numbers make a round number when multiplied.
You can multiply numbers in any order. Pair the two that give a round number first, then the last step is easy.
25 x 4 = 100, and then 100 is multiplied by 7.

solutions.reliable: Multiply in a friendly order: 25 x 4 = 100, and 100 x 7 = 700. The transferable idea: in a product, look for a pair that makes 10, 100 or 1,000, and do that pair first.

problems.whyOnTest: Regrouping a product to make a round number first turns a hard multiplication into an easy one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tower A is 3 m taller than B. C is 2 m shorter than A. D is 4 m taller than C. How many metres taller is the tallest tower than the shortest?

choices.misconception: I found how much taller D is than A and stopped there.
I thought A was the tallest and found how much taller it is than B.
I thought C was the shortest, so I gave the 4 m between C and D.
I just added up the three numbers in the clues, 3, 2 and 4.

hints: Give tower B a height and work out the others.
Put all four towers on one number line by measuring each from the same starting tower. Then the tallest and shortest can be read off directly instead of guessed.
If B is 0, then A is 3, C is 1 and D is 5.

solutions.reliable: Measure from B. A is 3 m above B, C is 2 m below A, so 1 m above B, and D is 4 m above C, so 5 m above B. In order from shortest: B, C, A, D. The tallest, D, is 5 m taller than the shortest, B. The transferable idea: place everything on one line measured from a single reference point.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering from relative clues needs one common reference, and each partial comparison is offered as a trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers between 300 and 600 have three different digits that are all odd?

choices.misconception: I added the choices for each place, 2 + 4 + 3, instead of multiplying them.
I only counted the numbers in the 300s and forgot the 500s.
I made the last two digits different from each other but forgot they must also differ from the first digit.
I let digits repeat, so I counted 2 x 5 x 5.

hints: Which digits can go first?
Fill the places one at a time, starting with the most restricted one, the hundreds. For each later place, count how many odd digits are still unused, then multiply.
The first digit must be 3 or 5. Then 4 odd digits are left for the tens place.

solutions.reliable: The hundreds digit is odd and between 3 and 5, so it is 3 or 5: 2 choices. The tens digit is one of the other 4 odd digits, and the ones digit is one of the 3 odd digits still unused. That makes 2 x 4 x 3 = 24 numbers. The transferable idea: fill the most restricted place first, then multiply the choices left for each place.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles reward filling the most restricted place first, and adding instead of multiplying is the classic slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia counts backwards from 100 in sixes: 100, 94, 88, and so on. What is the first number she says that is less than 50?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 6 from 50 instead of counting down from 100.
I took 9 sixes away from 100 but used 6 x 9 = 52.
I assumed she would land on the number just below 50.
I gave the last number she says before going below 50.

hints: Keep counting back by 6 and write each number down.
Each step takes away the same amount, so you can either keep listing or work out how many sixes fit between 100 and 50. Make sure the number you give is below 50, not just close to it.
The list goes 100, 94, 88, 82, 76, 70, 64, 58, 52, and then one more step.

solutions.reliable: Listing: 100, 94, 88, 82, 76, 70, 64, 58, 52, 46. The first number below 50 is 46. Check: 100 - 9 x 6 = 100 - 54 = 46. The transferable idea: in a sequence with a constant step, the number after k steps is the start minus k steps.
solutions.elegant: From 100 down to 50 is 50, and 8 x 6 = 48, so 8 steps reach 52, just above 50. One more step gives 46. The transferable idea: divide the distance by the step to jump close to the target.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting in equal steps and stopping at the right term, with the last term above the line as the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many different 1 by 3 strips of three squares, going across or down, can be found on a 4 by 4 grid?

choices.misconception: I counted how many strips fit on the grid at the same time without overlapping.
I only counted the strips that go across.
I thought a strip can start in any of the first 3 squares of a row or column.
I counted each strip twice, once from each end.

hints: How many places can a strip slide to in one row?
Strips may overlap, so slide a strip along one row and count its positions. Every row and every column works the same way, so multiply, and remember both directions.
In a row of 4 squares, a strip of 3 can start in square 1 or square 2.

solutions.reliable: In one row of 4 squares, a 1 by 3 strip fits in 4 - 3 + 1 = 2 positions. There are 4 rows, giving 8 strips across, and by the same reasoning 8 strips down. Total 16. The transferable idea: count positions by sliding, not by cutting the grid up.

problems.whyOnTest: Sliding-window counting: overlapping positions count, so cutting the grid into pieces undercounts.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A clock with hands but no numbers hangs opposite a mirror. In the mirror, the clock seems to show exactly 4 o'clock. What time is it really?

choices.misconception: I flipped the clock top to bottom instead of left to right.
I thought a mirror shows the time without changing it.
I counted back 4 from 12 but counted the 12 itself as the first step.
I turned the clock upside down, which moves each hand to the opposite side.

hints: A mirror swaps left and right, but keeps the 12 at the top.
Picture the hour hand being reflected in the line from 12 to 6. A hand that is some hours past 12 on one side ends up the same number of hours before 12 on the other.
In the mirror the hour hand is 4 hours clockwise from 12. On the real clock it is 4 hours anticlockwise from 12.

solutions.reliable: The mirror swaps left and right, so the line from 12 to 6 stays put and everything else flips across it. The minute hand stays on 12. An hour hand 4 hours clockwise from 12 in the mirror is really 4 hours anticlockwise from 12, which is 8. So it is really 8 o'clock. The transferable idea: a left-right reflection sends hour h to 12 - h.
solutions.elegant: Mirror time and real time always add up to 12 hours on the hour: 4 + 8 = 12. Check with an easy case: at 6 o'clock the hand points straight down and looks the same in a mirror, and 6 + 6 = 12. The transferable idea: test a rule on a case you can see.

problems.whyOnTest: Reflections on a clock face: knowing which line stays fixed in a mirror and what that does to the hour hand.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Bo and Cal sit on a bench with 4 seats, so one seat stays empty. In how many different ways can they sit?

choices.misconception: I only counted which seat stays empty and forgot the children can swap places.
I only counted the orders of the three children and forgot the empty seat can move.
I thought the empty seat had to be at one of the two ends.
I gave each child 4 choices of seat, letting two children share a seat.

hints: Let the children choose seats one at a time.
Ana picks a seat first, then Bo picks from the seats left, then Cal. Multiply the numbers of choices, remembering that a seat cannot be used twice.
Ana has 4 seats to choose from, then Bo has 3 and Cal has 2.

solutions.reliable: Ana can take any of the 4 seats, Bo any of the 3 left and Cal any of the 2 left, so 4 x 3 x 2 = 24 ways. The transferable idea: when people choose places one after another, the number of choices drops by one each time.
solutions.elegant: Choose the empty seat (4 ways), then arrange the three children in the other three seats (3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways): 4 x 6 = 24. The transferable idea: treat the empty seat as a fourth, invisible person.

problems.whyOnTest: Arrangements with more places than people, where both the empty seat and the order of the children must be counted.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A heart beats about 70 times every minute. Which of these is closest to the number of times it beats in one whole day?

choices.misconception: I multiplied 70 by the 24 hours and forgot that each hour has 60 minutes.
I worked out the beats in one hour only, not a whole day.
I worked out 70 x 60 as 420 instead of 4,200, then multiplied by 24.
I multiplied by 60 twice, as if I needed seconds as well as minutes.

hints: How many minutes are in one day?
Change a day into minutes using hours, then multiply by the beats per minute. Round the numbers so the multiplication is easy, because the choices are far apart.
There are 60 minutes in an hour and 24 hours in a day. One hour is 70 x 60 = 4,200 beats.

solutions.reliable: One hour has 70 x 60 = 4,200 beats. A day has 24 hours, and 4,200 x 24 is about 4,000 x 25 = 100,000. The exact value is 100,800. The transferable idea: chain the unit changes one at a time, then estimate.
solutions.elegant: Round to 70 x 60 x 24, about 70 x 1,500 since a day has about 1,440 minutes. That is about 105,000, nearest to 100,000. The transferable idea: knowing a day is about 1,400 minutes makes many estimates quick.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimating a large total by chaining unit conversions, where a dropped zero or a missing step is easy to spot by size.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The pattern grows like this, adding a square to the end of each arm at every stage. Which stage uses exactly 61 squares?

figure.alt: Three stages of a growing plus shape. Stage 1 is a middle square with one square on each of its four sides, 5 squares. Stage 2 has arms 2 squares long, 9 squares. Stage 3 has arms 3 squares long, 13 squares.

choices.misconception: I thought each stage has 5 squares more than the stage before, starting from 5, and divided 61 by 5.
I took away the 5 squares of stage 1 and divided the rest by 4, forgetting to count stage 1 itself.
I divided 61 by 4, got 15 and a bit, and rounded up.
I worked out the number of squares in the arms, not the stage number.

hints: Look at the middle square and the four arms separately.
Find what stays the same from stage to stage and what grows. Write the number of squares for any stage using its arms, then work backwards from 61.
Every stage has 1 middle square, and in stage n each of the 4 arms has n squares.

solutions.reliable: Stage n has 1 middle square and 4 arms of n squares, so 4n + 1 squares: 5, 9, 13 for stages 1, 2, 3, matching the picture. For 61 squares, 4n = 60, so n = 15. Check: 4 x 15 + 1 = 61. The transferable idea: split a growing shape into the part that stays the same and the parts that grow.
solutions.elegant: Each stage adds 4 squares to stage 1's 5. From 5 to 61 is 56 more, which is 14 more stages after stage 1, so stage 15. The transferable idea: count the steps, then add the starting stage back.

problems.whyOnTest: Seeing the structure of a visual pattern, then running its rule backwards from a total.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An ice cream shop sells 3 flavours, in a cone or a cup, with or without sprinkles. How many different ice creams can be ordered?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the 2 choices of cone or cup by the 2 choices of sprinkles and forgot the flavours.
I added the 3 flavours and the 2 holders and forgot about sprinkles.
I multiplied the flavours by cone or cup and forgot about sprinkles.
I added the choices, 3 + 2 + 2, instead of multiplying them.

hints: Draw a small tree for one flavour.
Every flavour can go with every holder, and each of those can go with or without sprinkles. Choices made one after another multiply.
One flavour gives 2 x 2 = 4 different ice creams.

solutions.reliable: Each of the 3 flavours can go in a cone or a cup, giving 3 x 2 = 6 combinations. Each of those can have sprinkles or not, giving 6 x 2 = 12 ice creams. The transferable idea: independent choices multiply.

problems.whyOnTest: The multiplication principle with three independent choices, where adding instead of multiplying is the classic slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A long paper strip is folded in half, then in half again, then in half a third time. It is then unfolded. How many fold lines can be seen?

choices.misconception: I counted one fold line for each fold.
I counted only the fold lines made by the last fold.
I thought every fold makes two new fold lines.
I counted the pieces of paper between the fold lines, not the fold lines.

hints: Try it with just one fold, then two.
Work out small cases first and look for a pattern. Each fold goes through every layer, so think about how the number of sections changes, then turn sections into lines between them.
One fold gives 2 sections and 1 line. Two folds give 4 sections and 3 lines.

solutions.reliable: Each fold doubles the number of sections: 2, then 4, then 8. The fold lines are the boundaries between neighbouring sections, and 8 sections in a row have 7 boundaries. So there are 7 fold lines. The transferable idea: try one and two folds first, then count gaps between pieces, which is one less than the pieces.
solutions.elegant: Each fold adds as many new lines as there were layers: 1, then 2, then 4, making 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. The transferable idea: count what each step adds.

problems.whyOnTest: Trying small cases reveals the doubling pattern, and pieces versus lines is the classic off-by-one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Eggs are packed in boxes of 5. Today's eggs fill some boxes with 4 eggs left over. Tomorrow there will be exactly twice as many eggs. How many will be left over then?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many eggs today's leftovers are short of a full box.
I doubled how many eggs are short of a full box and gave that, not the eggs left over.
I thought the number left over stays the same when the eggs double.
I doubled the 4 left over and forgot that 5 of them fill another box.

hints: Try it with a real number of eggs, like 9.
Doubling the eggs doubles the full boxes and doubles the leftovers. The doubled full boxes are still full, so only the doubled leftovers need packing again.
Twice 4 leftover eggs is 8 eggs, and 5 of those fill one more box.

solutions.reliable: Doubling the eggs gives twice as many full boxes, which are still full, plus twice the 4 leftovers, which is 8 eggs. Those 8 fill one more box with 3 to spare. So 3 eggs are left over. Check with 9 eggs: 18 eggs make 3 boxes and 3 over. The transferable idea: to find the remainder of a double, double the remainder and reduce it again.
solutions.elegant: Try a small case: 4 eggs today means 8 tomorrow, one box and 3 over. Any other number of full boxes today just adds full boxes. The transferable idea: when the answer cannot depend on the unknown, test the easiest case.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders behave predictably under doubling, and the unreduced 8 is the natural trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four marks are made between 20 and 60 on a number line, splitting the part between them into equal pieces. What number is at the mark closest to 60?

choices.misconception: I found the length of each piece, not the number at the mark.
I found the mark closest to 20 instead of the one closest to 60.
I took the halfway point, but with four marks there is no mark exactly in the middle.
I thought 4 marks make 4 equal pieces, so I used pieces of 10.

hints: Draw it: how many pieces do 4 marks make?
Sketch the line with the two ends and the marks between them, and count the gaps. Share the whole distance equally among the gaps, then step back from 60.
4 marks between the ends make 5 equal pieces. The distance from 20 to 60 is 40.

solutions.reliable: Four marks between the ends make 5 equal pieces. The distance is 60 - 20 = 40, so each piece is 8. The marks are at 28, 36, 44 and 52, so the one closest to 60 is 52. Check: 52 + 8 = 60. The transferable idea: n marks between two ends make n + 1 gaps.

problems.whyOnTest: Equal spacing on a number line, with the marks-versus-gaps slip as the main trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cinema room has 28 seats. 19 people come in and sit down. Then 5 people leave and 8 more come in and sit down. How many seats are empty now?

choices.misconception: I worked out 28 take away 19 and forgot about the people who left and the people who came in later.
I mixed up the second step: I added the 5 who left and took away the 8 who came in, so I thought 16 people were sitting.
I added the 5 seats that were freed to the 9 empty seats but forgot the 8 people who came in after that.
I worked out how many people are sitting in the room, not how many seats are empty.

hints: The question asks about seats, not people.
First find how many people are sitting after everyone has come and gone, then compare that with the number of seats. Re-read the question before choosing.
After the changes there are 19 - 5 + 8 = 22 people sitting. The room has 28 seats, so 28 - 22 = 6 seats are empty.

solutions.reliable: Follow the people: 19 come in, 5 leave, which leaves 14, then 8 more come in, which makes 22. Each person fills one seat, so the empty seats are 28 - 22 = 6. The transferable idea: when a story has several steps, finish by checking that your number answers the question that was asked, here seats rather than people.
solutions.elegant: Follow the empty seats instead: 28 - 19 = 9 are empty, the 5 who leave make 14 empty, and the 8 who arrive leave 14 - 8 = 6 empty.

problems.whyOnTest: Several-step stories tempt you to stop at the number of people; the question asks for empty seats, so reading the final question is the whole skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each cake needs 3 eggs and 2 cups of flour. Kim has 20 eggs and 11 cups of flour. She bakes as many cakes as she can. How many eggs are left over?

choices.misconception: I found how many cups of flour are left over, not how many eggs.
I looked only at the eggs, thought she could bake 6 cakes, and forgot that the flour runs out first.
I found how many cakes the eggs alone are enough for, not how many eggs are left.
I found how many eggs she uses, not how many are left over.

hints: Which runs out first, the eggs or the flour?
Work out how many cakes the eggs allow and how many the flour allows; the smaller number is how many she bakes. Then answer the question that is asked, which is about eggs.
The eggs are enough for 6 cakes, but the flour only for 5, since 6 cakes need 12 cups. She bakes 5 cakes, using 15 eggs, so 20 - 15 = 5 eggs are left.

solutions.reliable: Eggs: 20 eggs are enough for 6 cakes (18 eggs), with 2 to spare. Flour: 11 cups are enough for 5 cakes (10 cups), with 1 to spare. Kim can bake only 5 cakes, because the flour runs out first. Those 5 cakes use 5 x 3 = 15 eggs, which leaves 20 - 15 = 5 eggs. The transferable idea: find what limits the story, then check that your final number answers the question that was asked.

problems.whyOnTest: Several numbers in the story answer other questions; finding what runs out first and then reading what is asked is the skill being tested.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Bo and Cy share 30 sweets. Ana gets 4 more than Bo, and Bo gets 4 more than Cy. How many more sweets does Ana get than Cy?

choices.misconception: I used only one clue, that Ana gets 4 more than Bo, and forgot that Bo also gets 4 more than Cy.
I worked out how many sweets Cy gets instead of how many more Ana gets.
I worked out how many sweets Bo gets and gave that as the answer.
I worked out how many sweets Ana gets, not how many more she gets than Cy.

hints: Do you need to know how many sweets each child gets?
The question asks only for a difference. Follow the two clues from Cy up to Ana, and ask whether the total of 30 is needed at all.
Ana gets 4 more than Bo, and Bo gets 4 more than Cy, so Ana gets 4 + 4 = 8 more than Cy. The 30 is not needed.

solutions.reliable: Solve fully as a check. Bo gets 4 more than Cy and Ana gets 8 more than Cy, so three equal shares plus 12 make 30. The three equal shares make 18, so Cy gets 6, Bo gets 10 and Ana gets 14. Ana gets 14 - 6 = 8 more. The transferable idea: read what is asked before computing, because a difference can often be found without the full solution.
solutions.elegant: The difference comes straight from the clues: 4 more, then 4 more again, is 8 more. The total of 30 is extra information.

problems.whyOnTest: Contests reward noticing that the question asks for a difference; the total is a distraction, and solving everything invites giving one child's share.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A straight path is 20 m long. Trees stand along both sides of it, one every 5 m, with a tree at each end of each side. How many trees are there?

choices.misconception: I divided 20 by 5 and counted only the gaps along one side of the path.
I counted the trees on one side correctly but forgot the other side of the path.
I added a tree at each end to the 4 gaps along one side, counting the end trees twice, and forgot the other side.
I counted the 4 gaps on each side as 4 trees, forgetting that each row has one more tree than gaps.

hints: Draw one side of the path and mark where the trees stand.
A sketch shows that the trees sit at the ends of the gaps, so one row has one more tree than gaps. Then remember the path has two sides.
One side has 20 ÷ 5 = 4 gaps, so 5 trees: at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 m. Both sides together have 5 + 5 = 10 trees.

solutions.reliable: Mark one side: trees at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 metres, which is 5 trees. The other side is the same, so there are 5 + 5 = 10 trees. The transferable idea: draw a quick sketch to see that a row has one more post than gaps, and to remember every part of the picture.

problems.whyOnTest: A sketch exposes both traps at once: trees outnumber gaps by one, and the path has two sides.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Children stand in a line. Zoe is 7th from the front. Sam is behind Zoe, with exactly 3 children between them. Sam is 6th from the back. How many children are there?

choices.misconception: I added 7 and 6 and took away 1, as if Zoe and Sam were the same child.
I added Zoe's place from the front and Sam's place from the back, 7 and 6, without thinking about the children between them.
I added the 3 children between them to Zoe's place and forgot the extra step to reach Sam, so I put him 10th from the front and worked out 10 + 6 - 1.
I found that Sam is 11th from the front, then added the 6 from the back without taking away 1, so I counted Sam twice.

hints: Draw the line of children and mark Zoe first.
Mark Zoe's place from the front, then the 3 children behind her, then Sam. His place from the front and his place from the back overlap in one child: Sam himself.
Zoe is 7th, the next 3 children are 8th, 9th and 10th, so Sam is 11th from the front. He is also 6th from the back, so there are 11 + 6 - 1 = 16 children, since Sam is counted twice.

solutions.reliable: Number the places from the front. Zoe is in place 7 and the 3 children between are in places 8, 9 and 10, so Sam is in place 11. Sam is 6th from the back, so 5 children stand behind him, and there are 11 + 5 = 16 children. Check: Zoe, in place 7 of 16, is 10th from the back. The transferable idea: a quick sketch of positions shows overlaps that simply adding the numbers hides.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding the given numbers ignores where the children really stand; drawing the line is the reliable way to handle places counted from both ends.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten 2s are multiplied together: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times \dots \times 2$. What is the last digit of the answer?

choices.misconception: I added the ten 2s instead of multiplying them, got 20, and took its last digit.
I miscounted along the pattern and found the last digit for nine 2s instead of ten.
I saw the pattern 2, 4, 8, 6 and stopped after two full rounds, forgetting the last two 2s.
I counted the first 2 as step zero of the pattern, so I went one step too far.

hints: Find the last digit for one 2, then two 2s, then three 2s.
Try small cases. Only the last digit matters each time you multiply by 2 again, so look for a pattern in the last digits and see where the tenth one falls.
The last digits go 2, 4, 8, 6, then 2, 4, 8, 6 again, then 2, 4. The tenth is 4. Indeed, ten 2s multiply to 1024.

solutions.reliable: Small cases: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, ... The last digits go 2, 4, 8, 6 and then repeat. Two full rounds use eight 2s and end on 6; the ninth 2 gives 2 and the tenth gives 4. Check by multiplying: ten 2s make 1024, which ends in 4. The transferable idea: when a calculation is long, work out the first few cases and let the pattern carry you the rest of the way.
solutions.elegant: Five 2s make 32, which ends in 2, and 2 x 2 ends in 4. So ten 2s, which is 32 x 32, ends in the same digit as 2 x 2: 4.

problems.whyOnTest: Nobody expects you to multiply ten 2s fast; trying one, two, three 2s reveals a short repeating pattern, the habit this checks.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 10 are written on a board. Again and again, Kim rubs out two numbers and writes their sum minus 1 instead. When one number is left, what is it?

choices.misconception: I thought each step takes away 2, one for each number rubbed out.
I took away 1 for each of the 10 numbers, but going from ten numbers to one takes only 9 steps.
I took away 1 only once, as if Kim did the rubbing out a single time.
I added up 1 to 10 and forgot that each step takes 1 away from the total.

hints: Try it with just 1, 2 and 3 first.
Watch what happens to the total of all the numbers on the board at each step, and count how many steps it takes to go from ten numbers down to one.
The total starts at 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55. Each step lowers the total by exactly 1 and leaves one number fewer, so there are 9 steps. The last number is 55 - 9 = 46.

solutions.reliable: Small case: with 1, 2, 3, rub out 1 and 2 and write 2, leaving 2 and 3, then write 2 + 3 - 1 = 4. That is the total 6 minus 1 for each of the 2 steps. In general each step lowers the total by 1 and removes one number. Ten numbers need 9 steps, and 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55, so the last number is 55 - 9 = 46, whatever order Kim chooses. The transferable idea: try a tiny case, then look for a quantity that changes in a predictable way.
solutions.elegant: The total 55 drops by exactly 1 per step, and 9 steps turn ten numbers into one, so the last number is 46.

problems.whyOnTest: The process looks too long to follow, but a tiny case shows the total falls by 1 each step, the kind of idea 5-point problems test.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana is 3 times as old as her brother. In 4 years, their ages will add up to 32. How old is Ana now?

choices.misconception: I found her brother's age and gave that instead of Ana's age.
I added the 4 years only once instead of once for each child, so I thought their ages now add up to 28.
I found how old Ana will be in 4 years instead of how old she is now.
I took 8 away from 32 and gave the total of their two ages now.

hints: You can test each answer choice in the story.
Back-solve: take a choice for Ana's age, find her brother's age from the first sentence, add 4 years to each of them, and check whether the total is 32.
Try 18: her brother is 6. In 4 years they will be 22 and 10, which add up to 32. So Ana is 18.

solutions.reliable: Test the choices. 6: brother 2, in 4 years 10 + 6 = 16, no. 18: brother 6, in 4 years 22 + 10 = 32, yes. 21: brother 7, in 4 years 25 + 11 = 36, no. 22 is not 3 times a whole number, no. 24: brother 8, in 4 years 28 + 12 = 40, no. Ana is 18. The transferable idea: when the choices are numbers, putting each one back into the story is often faster than setting the problem up.
solutions.elegant: In 4 years each child is 4 years older, so their ages now add up to 32 - 8 = 24. Ana is 3 shares and her brother 1 share, so 4 shares make 24, one share is 6, and Ana is 18.

problems.whyOnTest: Age puzzles look like algebra, but with five choices, testing each one in the story is a reliable contest method for young solvers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Zara thinks of an even two-digit number. It is 3 times as big as its two digits multiplied together. What is her number?

choices.misconception: I checked only that 15 is 3 times 1 x 5 and forgot that the number must be even.
I added the digits instead of multiplying them, since 3 x (2 + 7) = 27, and I forgot that the number must be even.
I checked only that 36 is even and is 3 times 12, without checking that its digits multiply to 18, not 12.
I found that the digits 2 and 4 work but wrote them in the wrong order, and 42 is not 3 times 4 x 2 = 8.

hints: Each answer choice can be tested against both rules.
Back-solve: for each choice, check that it is even, then multiply its two digits together and multiply that by 3. Only one choice passes both tests.
24 is even. Its digits multiply to 2 x 4 = 8, and 3 x 8 = 24. So Zara's number is 24.

solutions.reliable: Test each choice on both rules. 15: 3 x 1 x 5 = 15, yes, but 15 is odd. 24: even, and 3 x 2 x 4 = 24, yes. 27: odd, and 3 x 2 x 7 = 42, no. 36: even, but 3 x 3 x 6 = 54, no. 42: even, but 3 x 4 x 2 = 24, no. The number is 24. The transferable idea: when back-solving, test every choice against every condition, not just the first one.
solutions.elegant: Go through the tens digit. With tens digit 1, the number is 10 more than its ones digit and also 3 times it, so the ones digit is 5, giving 15, which is odd. With tens digit 2, the number is 20 more than its ones digit and also 6 times it, so the ones digit is 4, giving 24.

problems.whyOnTest: A rule about multiplying digits is hard to set up at this level, but testing five choices against both rules is quick and exposes the choices that pass only one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a quiz, wrong answers lose no points. Each question has 5 choices and only one is right. Leo guesses all 20 questions at random. About how many should he expect to get right?

choices.misconception: I thought guessing never gets anything right, so it is not worth doing.
I divided 20 by 4, the number of wrong choices, instead of by 5, the number of choices.
I thought a guess is right half of the time, like tossing a coin.
I worked out how many he should expect to get wrong instead of right.

hints: How likely is a single random guess to be right?
One guess among 5 choices is right about 1 time in 5. Use that to share out the 20 questions, and compare with leaving them blank.
About 1 guess in every 5 is right. 20 questions are 4 groups of 5, so Leo should expect about 4 right answers, which is 4 more than if he left them blank.

solutions.reliable: With 5 choices, a random guess is right about 1 time in 5. Twenty questions make 4 groups of 5, so Leo should expect about 4 right. Leaving the questions blank would score nothing, and wrong answers cost nothing, so guessing can only help. The transferable idea: when wrong answers cost nothing, a guess is always worth more than a blank.

problems.whyOnTest: When wrong answers lose nothing, a blank wastes points: random guessing earns about one right answer in every five, for free.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A toy train goes once around its track in 45 seconds. How long does it take to go around 8 times? Give your answer in minutes.

choices.misconception: I thought 45 seconds is nearly a minute, so I counted each lap as one whole minute.
I wrote 360 seconds as 36 minutes by just dropping the zero.
I worked out the time in seconds and forgot to change it into minutes.
I used 60 seconds for each lap instead of 45, and left the answer in seconds.

hints: Check which unit the answer must be given in.
Find the total time in seconds first, then change seconds into minutes using how many seconds make one minute.
8 laps take 8 x 45 = 360 seconds. A minute is 60 seconds, and 360 ÷ 60 = 6, so the train takes 6 minutes.

solutions.reliable: Eight laps take 8 x 45 = 360 seconds. Since 60 seconds make a minute, 360 seconds is 360 ÷ 60 = 6 minutes. The transferable idea: re-read the unit the question asks for before choosing, because the number in the wrong unit is usually waiting among the choices.
solutions.elegant: Four laps take 4 x 45 = 180 seconds, which is exactly 3 minutes, so 8 laps take 6 minutes.

problems.whyOnTest: The answer in seconds, 360, sits among the choices; checking the unit the question asks for is what separates right from nearly right.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A snail crawls 3 cm every minute. How far does it crawl in one hour? Give your answer in metres.

choices.misconception: I thought a metre is 1000 cm, so I divided 180 by 1000.
I thought an hour has 100 minutes, so I got 300 cm, which is 3 m.
I changed 180 cm into metres by dropping just one zero.
I found the distance in centimetres and forgot to change it into metres.

hints: Find the distance in centimetres first, then check the unit.
Work out how many minutes are in one hour and find the distance in centimetres. Then change centimetres into metres using how many centimetres make one metre.
One hour is 60 minutes, so the snail crawls 60 x 3 = 180 cm. 100 cm make 1 m, so 180 cm is 1.8 m.

solutions.reliable: In 60 minutes the snail crawls 60 x 3 = 180 cm. There are 100 cm in a metre, so 180 cm is 1 m and 80 cm, which is 1.8 m. The transferable idea: when a question changes units twice, do one change at a time and re-read the unit asked for at the end.

problems.whyOnTest: It needs two unit changes, minutes to hours and centimetres to metres, and each slip lands on a choice, so checking units is the skill tested.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag holds 4 marbles. Each marble is red or blue. How many different bags are possible, if only the number of marbles of each colour matters?

choices.misconception: I counted only the bag that is all red and the bag that is all blue.
I left out the two bags that use only one colour.
I forgot the bag with no red marbles at all.
I multiplied 2 colours by 4 marbles instead of listing the bags.

hints: List the bags by how many red marbles they have.
Systematic listing: the number of red marbles decides the whole bag, because the rest are blue. Go through every possible number of red marbles, including the smallest and the largest.
The bag can have 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 red marbles, with the rest blue. That gives 5 different bags.

solutions.reliable: Count the red marbles: 0 red and 4 blue, 1 red and 3 blue, 2 red and 2 blue, 3 red and 1 blue, 4 red and 0 blue. That is 5 bags. The transferable idea: list in order of one quantity, from its smallest to its largest value, and include both ends.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing in order shows that only the number of red marbles matters, and checks that the all-red and all-blue bags are not forgotten.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A digital clock shows times from 1:00 to 1:59. For how many of these times does each digit get bigger from left to right, like 1:37?

choices.misconception: I counted only the choices for the middle digit, 2, 3, 4 or 5, and forgot to count the last digit.
I counted only the times whose middle digit is 2 and stopped there.
I thought the middle digit could go only up to 4, so I left out times like 1:56.
I forgot the middle digit can be at most 5, so I counted times like 1:78 that a clock never shows.

hints: Look at the digit just after the colon. What values can it take?
List systematically by the middle digit. For each possible middle digit, count the last digits that are bigger than it, remembering what a clock can really show.
Middle 2: last digit 3 to 9, 7 times. Middle 3: 6 times. Middle 4: 5 times. Middle 5: 4 times. Total 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 22.

solutions.reliable: The middle digit must be bigger than 1 and, on a clock, at most 5, so it is 2, 3, 4 or 5. Middle 2: the last digit is 3 to 9, 7 times. Middle 3: 4 to 9, 6 times. Middle 4: 5 to 9, 5 times. Middle 5: 6 to 9, 4 times. Total 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 22. The transferable idea: fix one position at a time and count the rest, checking which digits are really allowed.

problems.whyOnTest: A careful list by the middle digit avoids both misses and impossible times; the clock's limit on the minutes is the detail most students forget.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Home has 3 paths to the park and 1 straight to the shop. The park has 2 paths to the shop. How many routes go from home to the shop, visiting no place twice?

choices.misconception: I counted the 3 paths to the park and the straight path, and forgot the choice from the park to the shop.
I added 3 and 2 instead of multiplying, and forgot the straight path.
I counted the routes through the park but forgot the path straight to the shop.
I treated the straight path as a fourth path to the park, so I multiplied 4 by 2.

hints: Draw a tree: what are the choices for the first step?
Start a tree with every possible first step. Each route through the park branches again at the park; the straight path does not branch at all.
Through the park: 3 paths, each followed by 2, so 3 x 2 = 6 routes. Straight: 1 route. Total 6 + 1 = 7.

solutions.reliable: Split the routes by their first step. Through the park: each of the 3 paths to the park can be followed by either of the 2 paths to the shop, so 3 x 2 = 6 routes. Straight to the shop: 1 route. Total 6 + 1 = 7. The transferable idea: in a tree, multiply along a branch that splits again and add the separate branches.

problems.whyOnTest: Real trees mix multiplying along branches with adding separate branches; the straight path tests whether students know when to add.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three lily pads are called A, B and C. A frog on A makes 3 jumps, each time to one of the other two pads. In how many ways can it finish on B?

choices.misconception: I counted only the trips whose first jump goes to B.
I thought exactly half of all the trips must end on B.
I counted every trip that does not end back on A, including the ones ending on C.
I counted every possible trip of 3 jumps, wherever it ends.

hints: Draw a tree starting at A, with two branches for each jump.
Each jump gives two branches, so 3 jumps make a small tree. Write the pad reached at each step and count only the branches that finish on B.
The trips that finish on B are A, B, A, B and A, B, C, B and A, C, A, B. That is 3 ways.

solutions.reliable: Tree from A. Jump 1 goes to B or C. From B the frog can go to A or C, and from C to A or B. Jump 3 can land on B only if jump 2 did not. The trips are A, B, A, B and A, B, C, B and A, C, A, B. A trip that is on B after 2 jumps, A, C, B, must leave B on jump 3. So there are 3 ways. The transferable idea: draw the whole tree and keep only the branches that finish where the question asks.
solutions.elegant: Work backwards: just before the last jump the frog must be on A or C. After 2 jumps it is on A in 2 ways (A, B, A and A, C, A) and on C in 1 way (A, B, C). Each can then jump to B, so 2 + 1 = 3.

problems.whyOnTest: A tree of 8 trips is small enough to draw but too big to hold in your head, exactly when a tree diagram earns its place.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A lock code has 3 digits. The first digit is odd, the second is even, and the third is 0 or 5. How many different codes are there?

choices.misconception: I multiplied only the choices for the first and last digits and forgot the middle one.
I added the choices, 5 + 5 + 2, instead of multiplying them.
I multiplied the choices for the first two digits and forgot the last one.
I did not count 0 as an even digit, so I used only 4 choices for the middle digit.

hints: Count the choices for each digit on its own.
Each digit is chosen without affecting the others, so the multiplication principle applies. Be careful about which digits count as even.
First digit: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, so 5 ways. Second: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, so 5 ways, because 0 is even. Third: 2 ways. Total 5 x 5 x 2 = 50.

solutions.reliable: Odd digits: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, which is 5. Even digits: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, which is also 5, because 0 is even. Last digit: 0 or 5, which is 2. Every choice goes with every other choice, so there are 5 x 5 x 2 = 50 codes. The transferable idea: when choices are made one after another and do not affect each other, multiply the numbers of choices.

problems.whyOnTest: Independent choices multiply, and the hidden trap is that 0 is an even digit, which turns a routine count into a careful one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five dots are drawn: the four corners of a square and the centre of the square. How many triangles have all three of their corners on these dots?

choices.misconception: I counted only the triangles made from corners of the square and forgot the ones that use the centre.
I noticed that one diagonal gives three dots in a straight line, but forgot that the other diagonal does too.
I counted every way to choose 3 of the 5 dots, but three dots on a diagonal make a straight line, not a triangle.
I counted each triangle that uses the centre twice, once from each of its two square corners.

hints: Split the triangles into those that use the centre and those that do not.
Casework: count the triangles made from three corners, then the triangles made from the centre and two corners. Watch out for three dots that lie on one straight line.
Three corners: 4 triangles. The centre and two corners: 6 pairs of corners, but the 2 pairs of opposite corners lie on a straight line through the centre, so only 4 triangles. Total 4 + 4 = 8.

solutions.reliable: Case 1, no centre: choosing 3 of the 4 corners is the same as leaving one corner out, so there are 4 triangles. Case 2, with the centre: choose 2 corners, which can be done in 6 ways. Opposite corners lie on a diagonal through the centre, so those 2 choices make straight lines, not triangles. That leaves 4. Total 4 + 4 = 8. The transferable idea: split the count into cases and check each case for choices that do not really work.
solutions.elegant: There are 10 ways to choose 3 of the 5 dots. Only the 2 diagonals put three dots in a line, so there are 10 - 2 = 8 triangles.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework with a catch: three dots on a line make no triangle, and spotting the two diagonals is what separates the right count from 10.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each domino shows two numbers from 0 to 4, maybe equal, like 2 and 2. Order does not matter. A full set has every possible domino once. How many dominoes is that?

choices.misconception: I counted the pairs of different numbers and forgot the doubles, like 2 and 2.
I left out the 0 and 0 domino, thinking a domino that shows nothing does not count.
I counted 1 and 3 and 3 and 1 as different dominoes, and I forgot the doubles.
I paired every number with every number in order, 5 x 5, so I counted most dominoes twice.

hints: Count dominoes with two different numbers and doubles separately.
Two different numbers on a domino are like two people shaking hands: count each pair once, not in both orders. Then add the dominoes that show the same number twice.
Pairs of different numbers from 0 to 4: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Doubles, from 0 and 0 up to 4 and 4: 5. Total 10 + 5 = 15.

solutions.reliable: List by the smaller number. Smallest 0: (0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (0, 4), which is 5. Smallest 1: (1, 1) to (1, 4), which is 4. Smallest 2: 3. Smallest 3: 2. Smallest 4: only (4, 4), which is 1. Total 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. The transferable idea: count pairs like handshakes, each one once, and then add any special cases such as doubles.
solutions.elegant: The 5 numbers make 5 x 5 = 25 ordered pairs. The 5 doubles appear once each, and the other 20 appear twice, as 1 then 3 and 3 then 1. So there are 5 + 20 ÷ 2 = 15 dominoes.

problems.whyOnTest: It is the handshake count in disguise, with a twist: a domino can pair a number with itself, which a handshake cannot.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A flag has 3 stripes, one above another. Each stripe is red, white or blue, and two stripes that touch must be different colours. How many different flags are possible?

choices.misconception: I gave the two lower stripes 2 choices each and multiplied, but forgot the 3 choices for the top stripe.
I used each colour exactly once, but the top and bottom stripes may match because they do not touch.
I gave every stripe only 2 choices, even the top one, which can be any of the 3 colours.
I gave the top and middle stripes 3 choices each and forgot about the bottom stripe.

hints: Choose the colours one stripe at a time, from the top down.
Use the multiplication principle stripe by stripe. The top stripe can be any colour; each stripe below only has to be different from the one just above it.
Top: 3 choices. Middle: any colour except the top one, so 2 choices. Bottom: any colour except the middle one, so 2 choices. Total 3 x 2 x 2 = 12.

solutions.reliable: The top stripe can be red, white or blue: 3 choices. Whatever it is, the middle stripe can be either of the other 2 colours. The bottom stripe must differ only from the middle one, so it also has 2 choices, and it may match the top. Total 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 flags. The transferable idea: when each choice limits only the next one, count the choices step by step and multiply.
solutions.elegant: Flags using three different colours: 3 x 2 x 1 = 6. Flags whose top and bottom match: 3 colours for those two stripes and 2 for the middle, so 6. Total 6 + 6 = 12.

problems.whyOnTest: A rule about touching stripes changes the count at each step, which tests whether students apply the multiplication principle carefully.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: If Max gives Kim 5 stickers, they will have the same number. If instead Kim gives Max 5 stickers, Max will have 3 times as many as Kim. How many stickers does Max have?

choices.misconception: I found how many more stickers Max has than Kim, not how many Max has.
I found how many stickers Kim has instead of how many Max has.
I found how many each child would have after Max gives 5 away, not how many Max has now.
I found how many stickers Max would have after Kim gives him 5, not how many he has now.

hints: After Max gives away 5, they are equal. How far apart are they now?
Translate each sentence into a fact about the gap between the two children. The first sentence gives the gap now; use it to find the gap after Kim gives 5, then use the 3 times fact.
Max has 10 more than Kim. If Kim gives 5, Max has 20 more than Kim and also 3 times as many, so Kim would have 10 and Max 30. So now Kim has 15 and Max has 25.

solutions.reliable: If Max gives 5 and they become equal, Max has 5 + 5 = 10 more than Kim. If Kim gives Max 5 instead, the gap grows to 10 + 10 = 20. Then Max has 3 times as many as Kim, so the gap of 20 is 2 lots of Kim's new amount: Kim would have 10 and Max 30. Before that gift, Kim has 15 and Max has 25. Check: if Max gives 5, both have 20. The transferable idea: turn each sentence into a fact about the difference, and draw bars if it helps.
solutions.elegant: Test the choices: if Max has 25, the first sentence makes Kim 15, and then Kim giving 5 leaves 10 against 30, which is 3 times as many. No other choice works.

problems.whyOnTest: Each sentence hides a fact about the gap between the children; translating "gives 5 and they are equal" into "a gap of 10" is the key step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A big cube built from 27 small cubes stands on the floor in a corner, touching both walls. How many small cubes cannot be seen from anywhere in the room?

choices.misconception: I thought the whole bottom layer is hidden because it sits on the floor.
I thought each of the three layers hides 4 cubes, but the top layer can be seen completely.
I thought only the top layer can be seen, forgetting the two sides that face the room.
I counted the cubes that can be seen instead of the ones that cannot.

hints: Which faces of the big cube face into the room?
Only the top and the two sides away from the walls can be seen. A small cube is hidden only if it is on none of those three faces. Count layer by layer.
Take away the top layer and the two open sides: what is left is a block 2 by 2 by 2 in the corner, which is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cubes.

solutions.reliable: Layer by layer from the bottom. In the bottom layer, the cubes along the two open sides can be seen, which leaves a 2 by 2 square of 4 hidden cubes in the corner. The middle layer is the same: 4 hidden. The top layer can all be seen from above. Total 4 + 4 + 0 = 8. The transferable idea: count hidden cubes layer by layer, deciding for each one whether any of its faces can be seen.
solutions.elegant: Peel off the top layer and the two open side layers, and a 2 by 2 by 2 cube is left tucked in the corner: 8 hidden cubes.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting what cannot be seen forces a careful picture of which faces are exposed, the core of every hidden-cube question.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm is cut into two rectangles by one straight cut parallel to the 5 cm sides. What do the two perimeters add up to, in cm?

choices.misconception: I assumed the cut was in the middle and gave the perimeter of only one of the pieces.
I thought cutting does not change the total distance around, so I gave the big rectangle's perimeter.
I added the 5 cm cut only once, but it is an edge of both pieces.
I added the cut as if it were 8 cm long, parallel to the long sides, and counted it twice.

hints: Think about which edges are new after the cut.
Each piece keeps part of the old outline, and the cut becomes an edge of both pieces. Start from the big perimeter and add what the cut creates.
The old outline, 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm, is shared between the pieces. The 5 cm cut is an edge of both pieces, so add 5 twice: 26 + 10 = 36 cm.

solutions.reliable: Try a cut 3 cm from one end: the pieces are 3 by 5 and 5 by 5, with perimeters 16 cm and 20 cm, which add up to 36 cm. Any other position gives the same total, because the old outline of 26 cm is shared between the pieces and the cut adds 5 cm to each. The transferable idea: when a shape is cut, the old outline is shared and every cut line is counted twice.
solutions.elegant: The cut appears in both perimeters, so the total is 26 + 2 x 5 = 36 cm wherever the cut is made.

problems.whyOnTest: Cutting a shape changes the total perimeter; seeing that the cut counts twice is the idea, and it works wherever the cut is made.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A staircase has 24 steps. Leo climbs it 2 steps at a time and Mia 3 steps at a time, both starting at the bottom. How many steps does neither of them step on?

choices.misconception: I found the steps that both of them step on, not the steps that neither of them steps on.
I took away only the 12 steps Leo uses and forgot the steps that Mia uses.
I found the steps that at least one of them steps on.
I counted the steps they do not both step on, taking only the 4 shared steps away from 24.

hints: Which steps does Leo use? Which steps does Mia use?
Leo uses the even steps and Mia uses every third step. Some steps are used by both, so do not count them twice before finding the steps that nobody uses.
Leo: 12 steps. Mia: 8 steps. Both: 6, 12, 18 and 24, which is 4 steps. Used by at least one: 12 + 8 - 4 = 16. Used by neither: 24 - 16 = 8.

solutions.reliable: Leo steps on 2, 4, ..., 24, which is 12 steps. Mia steps on 3, 6, ..., 24, which is 8 steps. Both step on 6, 12, 18 and 24, which is 4 steps. So 12 + 8 - 4 = 16 steps are used by at least one of them, and 24 - 16 = 8 steps are used by neither: 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23. The transferable idea: check whether the question asks for both, either or neither before you calculate, because each of those counts is waiting among the choices.
solutions.elegant: The unused steps are the odd steps that are not multiples of 3. In each block of 6 steps only the 1st and the 5th are unused, and 24 steps make 4 blocks, so 4 x 2 = 8.

problems.whyOnTest: Both, either and neither each give a different count, and all of them appear as choices, so the question rewards reading which one is asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these shapes has exactly one line of symmetry?

choices.misconception: I noticed only the line straight down the middle, but a square folds onto itself in 4 different ways.

choices.text: a rectangle that is not a square
choices.misconception: I checked only the fold from top to bottom, but a rectangle also folds onto itself from side to side, so it has 2 lines.

choices.text: a triangle with all three sides equal
choices.misconception: I checked only the line from the top corner down, but each corner has a line like that, which makes 3.

choices.text: a parallelogram with no right angles and with two long and two short sides
choices.misconception: I thought folding along a diagonal matches the two halves, but they only match after a half turn, so it has no line of symmetry.

choices.text: a triangle with exactly two equal sides

hints: Imagine folding each shape so the two halves match exactly.
A line of symmetry is a fold that puts one half exactly on top of the other. For each shape, count every such fold, not just the first one you notice.

Square: 4 folds. Rectangle: 2. Triangle with three equal sides: 3. Slanted parallelogram: 0, since a diagonal fold does not match. Triangle with exactly two equal sides: just 1, through the corner between the equal sides.

solutions.reliable: Count the folds that match exactly. A square has 4 (two through the middles of opposite sides, two along the diagonals). A rectangle that is not a square has 2. A triangle with three equal sides has 3. A slanted parallelogram has none: folding along a diagonal does not make the halves line up. A triangle with exactly two equal sides has exactly 1, from the corner between the equal sides to the middle of the opposite side. The transferable idea: a line of symmetry is a fold that matches exactly, so test every possible fold before deciding.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks that symmetry means a fold that matches exactly, and that students count every fold rather than stopping at the first, or seeing one in a parallelogram.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers have digits that add up to 5? For example, 203 is one of them, because $2 + 0 + 3 = 5$.

choices.misconception: I counted the groups of digits, like 5, 0, 0 and 4, 1, 0, instead of all the numbers each group can make.
I left out every number with a 0 in it, like 410 and 500.
I never let the tens digit be 0, so I missed numbers like 302, 401 and 500.
I let the first digit be 0, as in 041, but then the number is not a three-digit number.

hints: The first digit cannot be 0. Try each possible first digit in turn.
Casework on the hundreds digit: once it is chosen, the tens and ones digits must add up to what is left. Remember that the tens digit or the ones digit can be 0.
If the hundreds digit is 5, only 500 works. If it is 4, the other two digits add up to 1: 410 and 401. Keep going down to a hundreds digit of 1.

solutions.reliable: The hundreds digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, but not 0. Hundreds digit 5: the other two digits add up to 0, so only 500. Hundreds digit 4: they add up to 1: 410, 401, that is 2. Hundreds digit 3: they add up to 2: 320, 311, 302, that is 3. Hundreds digit 2: they add up to 3: 230, 221, 212, 203, that is 4. Hundreds digit 1: they add up to 4: 140, 131, 122, 113, 104, that is 5. Total $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$. The transferable idea: split the count into cases by the most limited digit, then count each case on its own.
solutions.elegant: When the tens and ones digits must add up to a number $k$, the tens digit can be $0, 1, \ldots, k$ and the ones digit is then fixed, so there are $k + 1$ choices. As the hundreds digit goes 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, the rest add up to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, giving $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$.

problems.whyOnTest: Choosing the most limited digit as the case to split on, and remembering that 0 is allowed after the first place, is the core of digit casework.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In how many two-digit numbers is one digit exactly twice the other digit? For example, 36 is one of them.

choices.misconception: I only counted numbers where the tens digit is the smaller one, like 12, and forgot 21.
I stopped at 3 and 6 and forgot that 4 and 8 also work.
I also used the pair 5 and 10, which adds 2 more numbers, but 10 is not a single digit.
I counted each number twice, once for each of its two digits.

hints: Start with the smaller digit and see what the bigger one must be.
Casework on the smaller digit: for each choice, the bigger digit is fixed. Then decide how many two-digit numbers each pair of digits makes.
The pairs are 1 and 2, 2 and 4, 3 and 6, 4 and 8. Each pair can be written in two orders.

solutions.reliable: Let the smaller digit be 1, 2, 3, 4, ... Its double must also be a single digit, so the smaller digit is at most 4: the pairs are 1 and 2, 2 and 4, 3 and 6, 4 and 8. (The digit 0 only pairs with itself, and 00 is not a two-digit number.) Each pair gives two numbers: 12 and 21, 24 and 42, 36 and 63, 48 and 84. That is $4 \times 2 = 8$ numbers. The transferable idea: fix the smaller part first, so every case is found exactly once.

problems.whyOnTest: Choosing a clear case variable, here the smaller digit, makes sure every number is counted once and none is missed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At a party, 4 girls and 3 boys meet. Each girl shakes hands once with each boy, and every two girls shake hands once. Boys never shake hands. How many handshakes are there?

choices.misconception: I only counted the handshakes between two girls and forgot the girls shaking hands with the boys.
I only counted the girl and boy handshakes and forgot that the girls also shake hands with each other.
I counted the girl and boy handshakes as $4 + 3 = 7$ instead of $4 \times 3 = 12$, then added the 6 between girls.
I counted the handshakes between the boys, 3, instead of the handshakes between the girls, 6.

hints: There are two kinds of handshake here. Count each kind on its own.
Split into girl and boy handshakes, where each girl meets each boy, and girl and girl handshakes, where each pair of girls meets once. Add the two kinds.
Each of the 4 girls shakes hands with 3 boys: $4 \times 3 = 12$. The pairs of girls are $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$.

solutions.reliable: Girl and boy handshakes: each of the 4 girls shakes hands with each of the 3 boys, so there are $4 \times 3 = 12$. Girl and girl handshakes: the first girl shakes hands with 3 others, the second with 2 new ones, the third with 1 new one, so $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$. No boy and boy handshakes. Total $12 + 6 = 18$. The transferable idea: when pairs come in different kinds, count each kind separately and add.
solutions.elegant: All 7 children would make $6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21$ handshakes. The only missing ones are between the boys: $2 + 1 = 3$. So $21 - 3 = 18$.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting pairs by sorting them into kinds, or counting all pairs and removing the forbidden ones, is the heart of handshake problems.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five teams play a tournament; every two teams meet once. A win gives 2 points, a loss 0, and a draw 1 point each. What is the total of all teams' points at the end?

choices.misconception: I worked out the most points one team can get, 4 games times 2 points, instead of the total for all teams.
I counted the 10 games correctly but gave only 1 point for each game.
I counted the games as $5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15$, starting from 5 instead of 4, and then gave 2 points for each game.
I said each team plays 4 games, so $5 \times 4 = 20$ games, but that counts every game twice.

hints: Look at one single game. How many points does it hand out?
Every game gives out the same number of points whatever happens, so the total depends only on how many games there are. Count the pairs of teams.
A win hands out $2 + 0 = 2$ points and a draw $1 + 1 = 2$ points. The number of pairs of 5 teams is $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$.

solutions.reliable: In every game, 2 points are handed out: 2 and 0 for a win, or 1 and 1 for a draw. So the total is 2 times the number of games. The first team plays 4 others, the second plays 3 new ones, the third 2, the fourth 1: $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$ games. The total is $10 \times 2 = 20$ points. The transferable idea: find something every game shares, then the results of the games do not matter.
solutions.elegant: Each team plays 4 games, which looks like $5 \times 4 = 20$ games, but every game has two teams, so it was counted twice: 10 games, and $10 \times 2 = 20$ points.

problems.whyOnTest: It tests counting pairs and spotting that every game gives the same points, so the total does not depend on who won.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A row in a cinema has 10 seats. Three friends want to sit in three seats next to each other in that row. How many different groups of three seats could they choose?

choices.misconception: I took away 1 from 10, as if they needed only two seats next to each other.
I counted one group starting at every seat, but a group cannot start at seat 9 or 10.
I found the 8 groups and then multiplied by 3 because there are 3 friends, but each group is just one choice of seats.
I counted the 8 groups and also the 6 orders the friends can sit in, but the question only asks which seats.

hints: Where can the leftmost seat of the group be?
Counting by position: name each group by its first seat, then find the last seat a group of three can start at without running off the row.
A group can start at seat 1, 2, 3 and so on, up to seat 8, which uses seats 8, 9 and 10.

solutions.reliable: Name each group by its leftmost seat. Starting at seat 1 uses seats 1, 2, 3. Starting at seat 8 uses seats 8, 9, 10. Starting at seat 9 would need a seat 11, which does not exist. So the starting seat is 1, 2, ..., 8, giving 8 groups. The transferable idea: a block of length $k$ in a row of $n$ fits in $n - k + 1$ positions.

problems.whyOnTest: Sliding a block along a row and counting its starting places is the basic move behind every counting by position problem.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 30-day month starts on a Monday, in rows of 7. Ella boxes two dates that share a side, like 3 and 4, or 3 and 10. How many boxes can she draw?

choices.misconception: I only counted pairs with one date above the other and forgot the pairs side by side.
I only counted pairs side by side in a row and forgot the pairs with one date above the other.
I left out the short last row, so I missed the three boxes that use 29 or 30.
I counted pairs like 7 and 8 as side by side, but 8 starts a new row, so they do not touch.

hints: Draw the calendar. Count the side-by-side pairs and the up-and-down pairs separately.
Name each box by its first date, the left or top one. How many side-by-side boxes fit in a full row of 7? A date has a partner below only if the date 7 later is on the calendar.
A full row of 7 dates gives 6 side-by-side boxes, and the last row, 29 and 30, gives 1. Up-and-down boxes have a top date from 1 to 23.

solutions.reliable: The rows are 1 to 7, 8 to 14, 15 to 21, 22 to 28, then 29 and 30 under 22 and 23. Side by side: each full row of 7 dates has 6 neighbouring pairs, so the 4 full rows give $4 \times 6 = 24$, and the last row adds 1 (29 and 30), making 25. Pairs like 7 and 8 do not count, because 8 starts a new row. One above the other: a date has a partner directly below it when the date 7 later is on the calendar, so the top date can be 1 to 23, giving 23 boxes. Total $25 + 23 = 48$. The transferable idea: name each block by its first square, count the starting places, and check the edges separately.
solutions.elegant: The numbers 1 to 30 make 29 pairs of neighbours, but 4 of them (7 and 8, 14 and 15, 21 and 22, 28 and 29) break across a row, leaving 25. Up-and-down pairs are $d$ and $d + 7$ with $d + 7 \le 30$, so $30 - 7 = 23$. Total $25 + 23 = 48$.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting overlapping blocks by their first square, and handling the row breaks and ragged last row of a calendar, is classic counting by position.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle is divided into 8 equal small rectangles, arranged in 2 rows of 4. How many rectangles of any size can be found in the picture?

choices.misconception: I only counted the 8 small rectangles and none of the bigger ones made from several pieces.
I counted the rectangles inside one row, $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$, and forgot the other row and the tall ones.
I counted 10 rectangles in each row but forgot the rectangles that are two rows tall.
I counted 10 in each row, but for the two-rows-tall rectangles I only counted the 4 tall columns.

hints: Sort the rectangles by how tall they are.
A rectangle is fixed by choosing its left and right edges from the vertical lines and its top and bottom edges from the horizontal lines. Count the choices for each, or count row by row.
In one row there are $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$ rectangles. Rectangles one row tall: top row or bottom row. Rectangles two rows tall: 10 more.

solutions.reliable: One row tall: inside a single row of 4 pieces there are 4 rectangles of width 1, 3 of width 2, 2 of width 3 and 1 of width 4, so 10. There are two rows, giving 20. Two rows tall: the same 10 widths and positions, stretched over both rows, giving 10. Total $20 + 10 = 30$. The transferable idea: sort hidden shapes by size or by height so that none is counted twice or missed.
solutions.elegant: There are 5 vertical lines and 3 horizontal lines. Choose 2 vertical lines in $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$ ways and 2 horizontal lines in $2 + 1 = 3$ ways: $10 \times 3 = 30$ rectangles.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting hidden rectangles by sorting them by size, or by choosing their edges, is a favourite Kangaroo counting idea.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Kai builds a cube wall 5 long, 3 tall and 2 thick. He removes an archway 1 cube wide and 2 tall from the middle of the bottom, right through. How many cubes are left?

choices.misconception: I only counted the front layer that I could picture, 15 cubes, and took away its 2 archway cubes.
I only counted the front layer of the wall and forgot the archway too.
I took away 4 cubes from the front layer and 4 from the back layer, but each layer only loses 2.
I only took the archway out of the front layer, but it goes right through, so the back layer loses 2 cubes as well.

hints: How many cubes does the whole wall have before the archway?
Count the full block as length times height times thickness. Then count the cubes removed: the archway goes through every layer of the thickness, not just the one you can see.
The full wall has $5 \times 3 \times 2 = 30$ cubes. The archway removes 2 cubes from the front layer and 2 from the back layer.

solutions.reliable: The full wall is $5 \times 3 = 15$ cubes in each layer, and there are 2 layers, so 30 cubes. The archway is 1 cube wide and 2 cubes tall, so it takes 2 cubes out of each layer. It goes right through, so both layers lose 2: that is 4 cubes. $30 - 4 = 26$. The transferable idea: count a solid layer by layer, including the layers you cannot see.
solutions.elegant: Each layer becomes $15 - 2 = 13$ cubes, and there are 2 identical layers: $2 \times 13 = 26$.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks that the student counts the hidden back layer of a solid, not just the face they can picture.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square with sides of 6 cm is cut into two equal rectangles. What is the perimeter of one of the rectangles?

choices.misconception: I halved the perimeter of the square, 24 cm, but the cut adds a new 6 cm side to each rectangle.
I gave the perimeter of the whole square instead of one rectangle.
I added the cut to the perimeter of the square, $24 + 6 = 30$, which is the length of all the lines, not one rectangle.
I added the perimeters of both rectangles together instead of giving one.

hints: Draw it. How long and how wide is one rectangle?
Perimeter means the distance all the way round one shape. Find the two side lengths of one rectangle, then add all four sides.
Each rectangle is 6 cm long and 3 cm wide, so go round: 6, 3, 6, 3.

solutions.reliable: Cutting the square in half gives two rectangles that are 6 cm long and $6 \div 2 = 3$ cm wide. The perimeter of one is $6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18$ cm. The transferable idea: when a shape is cut, each piece gets a new side along the cut, so you cannot just halve the perimeter.

problems.whyOnTest: Cutting a shape changes perimeter in a way it does not change area, which is a common trap in Kangaroo geometry.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five equal squares are placed side by side in a row to make a rectangle. The perimeter of the rectangle is 60 cm. What is the area of one square, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found the side of one square, 5 cm, and gave that instead of the area.
I thought the rectangle has $5 \times 4 = 20$ sides of a square around it, so I got a side of 3 cm, but the inside sides are not on the edge.
I only counted the 10 square sides along the top and bottom and forgot the 2 short ends, so I got a side of 6 cm.
I found the area of the whole rectangle, not of one square.

hints: Walk round the rectangle. How many square sides do you pass?
The perimeter is made of whole sides of the small squares. Count how many of them lie on the outside edge, then share the perimeter between them to find one side.
Along the top there are 5 sides, along the bottom 5, and 1 at each end: 12 sides in all.

solutions.reliable: The outside edge of the rectangle is made of square sides: 5 along the top, 5 along the bottom and 1 at each end, so 12 sides. They add up to 60 cm, so one side is $60 \div 12 = 5$ cm. The area of one square is $5 \times 5 = 25$ square centimetres. The transferable idea: only the outside edges count towards a perimeter, the sides that touch inside do not.
solutions.elegant: The rectangle is 5 sides long and 1 side tall, so its perimeter is $2 \times (5 + 1) = 12$ sides. $60 \div 12 = 5$, and $5 \times 5 = 25$.

problems.whyOnTest: It tests knowing which edges belong to a perimeter, and keeping side length and area apart.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these words, written in capital letters, has an up-and-down line of symmetry, so its left half is a mirror image of its right half?

choices.misconception: I thought any word that reads the same backwards has a mirror line, but the letter N itself is not symmetric up and down.
I saw that D and E each have a line of symmetry, but their lines go across, not up and down.
I checked that every letter has an up-and-down mirror line, but the word does not read the same backwards.
I thought S has a mirror line because it looks the same after a half turn, but turning is not the same as reflecting.

hints: Two things must both be true for the whole word to have a mirror line.
For an up-and-down mirror line through the middle, the word must read the same backwards, and every single letter must be symmetric about an up-and-down line. Check both for each word.
T and O are both symmetric about an up-and-down line. N, D, E and S are not.

solutions.reliable: A mirror line down the middle swaps the first letter with the last, the second with the second last, and so on, and also flips each letter. So two things are needed: the word reads the same backwards, and each letter has its own up-and-down mirror line. NOON reads the same backwards, but N is not symmetric up and down. DEED reads the same backwards, but D and E only have across lines. OHIO has symmetric letters, but backwards it reads OIHO. SOS: S has no mirror line at all. TOOT reads the same backwards, and T and O are each symmetric up and down. So TOOT works. The transferable idea: the symmetry of a whole shape needs the symmetry of its parts and of their arrangement.

problems.whyOnTest: It probes the difference between a line of symmetry, a half-turn and a word that reads the same backwards.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana draws a rectangle that is longer than it is tall, so not a square. She adds one diagonal, from a corner to the opposite corner. How many lines of symmetry does her drawing have?

choices.misconception: I thought the diagonal itself is a mirror line, but folding a long rectangle along its diagonal does not make the corners meet.
I counted the two lines of symmetry of the rectangle, but forgot that each one moves the diagonal to the other corner pair.
I counted the rectangle's two lines and added the diagonal as a third.
I counted the two middle lines and both diagonals of the rectangle as mirror lines.

hints: A rectangle alone has two mirror lines. Does each one still work?
Test every possible line: reflect the whole drawing, including the diagonal, and see whether you get exactly the same drawing. Remember that a long rectangle is not symmetric about its own diagonal.
Reflecting in the up-and-down middle line sends a diagonal from top left to bottom right onto the other diagonal, from top right to bottom left.

solutions.reliable: A rectangle that is not a square has exactly two lines of symmetry: the up-and-down middle line and the across middle line. Say the diagonal joins the top-left and bottom-right corners. Reflecting in the up-and-down line sends it to the line from top right to bottom left, which is not drawn, so that line no longer works. Reflecting in the across line does the same. The diagonal is not a mirror line either: folding a long rectangle along a diagonal does not make the corners land on each other. So the drawing has 0 lines of symmetry. The transferable idea: adding a line to a shape can destroy symmetries, so test each mirror line on the whole drawing.
solutions.elegant: The drawing still looks the same after a half turn, but a half turn is not a mirror line. Every mirror line of the rectangle swaps the two diagonals, so none of them keeps the drawing the same: 0.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks that symmetry is tested on the whole figure, and that a diagonal is not a mirror line of a long rectangle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On squared paper, P is 3 squares right of O and 1 square up. The paper is turned a quarter turn clockwise around O. Where is P now, compared with O?

choices.misconception: I turned the paper anticlockwise instead of clockwise.
I flipped P over an across line through O instead of turning it.
I made a half turn instead of a quarter turn.
I flipped P over an up-and-down line through O instead of turning it.

hints: Turn each of the two moves on its own.
In a quarter turn clockwise, every direction turns too: right becomes down, and up becomes right. Turn the walk from O to P one step at a time.
The walk 3 right becomes 3 down, and the walk 1 up becomes 1 right.

solutions.reliable: Think of the walk from O to P: 3 squares right, then 1 square up. A quarter turn clockwise turns every direction: right turns into down, and up turns into right. So the walk becomes 3 squares down and 1 square right. P is now 1 square right and 3 squares down from O. You can check with a clock hand: pointing right (at 3) and turning a quarter clockwise, it points down (at 6). The transferable idea: to turn a point, turn the path that leads to it.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning a point about a centre by turning each step of its path is the basic tool for rotation questions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The net in the picture is folded to make a cube. Which letter ends up on the face opposite the shaded square?

figure.alt: A cube net of six squares arranged like a staircase going down to the right. The shaded square is at the top left. Square M is to its right. Square K is below M. Square F is to the right of K. Square W is below F. Square H is to the right of W.

choices.misconception: I picked the square furthest from the shaded one in the net, thinking the furthest square must be opposite.
I thought the square that touches the shaded one only at a corner folds round to the opposite side.
I picked the square right beside the shaded one, but squares that share an edge in a net become neighbours on the cube.
I followed the diagonal line of squares and used the skip one rule along it, but that rule only works along a straight row.

hints: Choose one square to be the bottom, then fold the others up.
Nets and folding: fix one face as the base, fold its neighbours up as walls, then work out where each remaining square lands. Squares sharing an edge in the net are always neighbours on the cube.
Put K on the bottom. Then M is the back and F is the right side. The shaded square, joined to M, becomes the left side.

solutions.reliable: Put K on the table as the bottom. M is joined to the top of K, so it folds up as the back wall. F is joined to the right of K, so it folds up as the right wall. The shaded square is joined to the left of M, so it folds forward to become the left wall. W is joined below F, so it becomes the front wall, and H, the last square, is the top. The left wall (shaded) is opposite the right wall, F. The transferable idea: fix one face, fold its neighbours, and opposite faces are never neighbours in the net.
solutions.elegant: In a staircase net like this one, each square is opposite the square three steps further along the staircase: shaded, M, K, F. So F is opposite the shaded square.
