problems.whyOnTest: Folding a net in your head by fixing one face and building the cube around it is the core skill behind every net question.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Pens cost 3 euros each and pencils cost 2 euros each. Lila bought 9 things in total, some pens and some pencils, and paid 23 euros. How many pens did she buy?

choices.misconception: I found that 1 pen and 10 pencils cost 23 euros, but did not check that this is 11 things, not 9.
I found that 3 pens and 7 pencils cost 23 euros, but did not check that this is 10 things, not 9.
I found the number of pencils, 4, instead of the number of pens.
I found that 7 pens and 1 pencil cost 23 euros, but did not check that this is only 8 things, not 9.

hints: Try each answer. What else must you check besides the price?
Back-solve: for each choice, the number of pencils is 9 minus the number of pens. Work out the total cost and keep the choice that makes exactly 23 euros.
If she bought 5 pens, she bought 4 pencils. Check: $5 \times 3 + 4 \times 2$.

solutions.reliable: Try the choices, remembering that pens and pencils together make 9. 1 pen and 8 pencils cost $3 + 16 = 19$. 3 pens and 6 pencils cost $9 + 12 = 21$. 4 pens and 5 pencils cost $12 + 10 = 22$. 5 pens and 4 pencils cost $15 + 8 = 23$. That works, so she bought 5 pens. The transferable idea: when you back-solve, check every condition in the question, not just one.
solutions.elegant: If all 9 things were pencils she would pay 18 euros. She paid 5 euros more, and swapping a pencil for a pen adds 1 euro, so she swapped 5 times: 5 pens.

problems.whyOnTest: Back-solving from the choices is fast, but only if every condition is checked; several choices here meet the price alone.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ben has three cards showing the digits 2, 5 and 8. He makes numbers by placing one, two or all three of the cards in a row. How many different numbers can he make?

choices.misconception: I only counted the numbers that use all three cards.
I counted which cards are used, 3 single cards, 3 pairs and 1 group of three, but forgot that changing the order makes a new number.
I counted the one-card and two-card numbers but forgot the numbers that use all three cards.
I counted the two-card and three-card numbers but forgot that a single card is a number too.

hints: Count the one-card, two-card and three-card numbers separately.
Systematic listing: for each length, list the numbers in order of their first digit so none is missed or repeated. Then add the three lengths.
One card: 2, 5, 8. Two cards: 25, 28, 52, 58, 82, 85. Three cards: there are 6.

solutions.reliable: One card: 2, 5, 8, that is 3 numbers. Two cards: 25, 28, 52, 58, 82, 85, that is 6 numbers. Three cards: 258, 285, 528, 582, 825, 852, that is 6 numbers. Total $3 + 6 + 6 = 15$. The transferable idea: split a listing by size and list each group in a fixed order, so nothing is missed.
solutions.elegant: For two cards: 3 choices for the first, 2 for the second, so 6. For three cards: $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$. Add the 3 single cards: 15.

problems.whyOnTest: Organised listing, split by the number of cards used, is exactly what stops students missing or repeating cases.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A spinner shows the numbers 1, 2 and 3, each equally often. Zara spins it twice and adds the two numbers. In how many of the possible outcomes is the sum 4?

choices.misconception: I only found 2 then 2 and missed 1 then 3 and 3 then 1.
I counted 1 then 3 and 3 then 1 as the same outcome, but the first and second spins are different.
I counted 2 then 2 twice, as if the two 2s could be swapped, but swapping them gives the same outcome.
I counted all the possible outcomes instead of only those with a sum of 4.

hints: Write down every outcome as first spin, then second spin.
A tree diagram: three branches for the first spin, and three for the second spin from each. Read along each path and pick the ones whose sum is 4.
The paths are 1 then 1, 1 then 2, 1 then 3, 2 then 1, and so on. Check which add to 4.

solutions.reliable: The tree has 3 branches for the first spin and 3 for the second, so 9 outcomes. Those with sum 4 are 1 then 3, 2 then 2, and 3 then 1. That is 3 outcomes. The transferable idea: in a tree diagram the order of the spins matters, so 1 then 3 and 3 then 1 are different paths.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing a tree keeps order straight and stops both double counting and missing outcomes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Cubes stand on a 2 by 2 square. The front view shows heights 3 (left) and 1 (right). The side view shows 3 (front) and 2 (back). What is the largest possible number of cubes?

choices.misconception: I added the heights in the front view, $3 + 1 = 4$, as if the front view shows every cube.
I added the heights in the side view, $3 + 2 = 5$, as if the side view shows every cube.
I put no cubes on the back right square, but 1 cube fits there without changing either view.
I added the front view and the side view together, $4 + 5 = 9$, but those views show some of the same cubes.

hints: Draw the 2 by 2 square from above and give each place a height.
Each stack is limited twice: by its half in the front view and by its row in the side view. For the most cubes, make every stack as tall as both limits allow.
The stack at front left can be 3 tall, at back left 2, at front right 1, at back right 1.

solutions.reliable: Call the four places front left, back left, front right, back right. A stack can be no taller than its half in the front view and no taller than its row in the side view. Front left: at most 3 and at most 3, so 3. Back left: at most 3 and at most 2, so 2. Front right: at most 1 and at most 3, so 1. Back right: at most 1 and at most 2, so 1. These heights do give exactly the two views, so the largest number is $3 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7$. The transferable idea: each view gives an upper limit, so the largest building takes the smaller limit for every stack.

problems.whyOnTest: Combining two views into a plan of heights, and seeing that views limit but do not fix the count, is the key idea of view problems.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A clock shows exactly 11 o'clock. Some time later, its hour hand has turned through exactly $90^\circ$. What time does the clock show now?

choices.misconception: I turned the hour hand backwards, anticlockwise, from 11 to 8, but clock hands always turn clockwise.
I thought of the minute hand, which turns $90^\circ$ in 15 minutes, but the hour hand is much slower.
I thought the hour hand turns $90^\circ$ in one hour, but that is how far it turns in 3 hours.
I counted three numbers starting with 11 itself, 11, 12, 1, but the hand must move across 3 gaps between numbers.

hints: How many degrees does the hour hand turn in one hour?
A full turn is $360^\circ$, and the hour hand takes 12 hours to make it. Work out the turn for one hour, then how many hours make $90^\circ$.
One hour turns the hour hand $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees, so $90^\circ$ takes 3 hours.

solutions.reliable: The hour hand makes a full turn of $360^\circ$ in 12 hours, so it turns $360 \div 12 = 30^\circ$ every hour. To turn $90^\circ$ it needs $90 \div 30 = 3$ hours. Three hours after 11 o'clock is 12, then 1, then 2, so the clock shows 2 o'clock. The transferable idea: the hour hand moves $30^\circ$ for every hour, and you count the gaps between the numbers, not the numbers.
solutions.elegant: $90^\circ$ is a quarter of a full turn, and a quarter of the 12 hours on the face is 3 hours. 11 o'clock plus 3 hours is 2 o'clock.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning an angle into hours on a clock face, and keeping the hour hand and the minute hand apart, is standard clock geometry.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a pictogram, a whole circle stands for 4 children and half a circle for 2. Swimming has 3 and a half circles and football has 5. How many more children chose football than swimming?

choices.misconception: I took away the numbers of circles, $5 - 3 = 2$, and forgot that each circle stands for 4 children.
I counted the half circle as 1 child instead of 2, so I thought 13 children chose swimming.
I ignored the half circle, so I thought only 12 children chose swimming.
I added the two rows together instead of finding the difference.

hints: Turn each row into a number of children first.
Reading a pictogram: multiply the number of whole circles by what one circle stands for, and remember to include the half circle. Then answer the question that was asked, which is a difference.
Football: $5 \times 4 = 20$. Swimming: $3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$.

solutions.reliable: Football has 5 whole circles: $5 \times 4 = 20$ children. Swimming has 3 whole circles and a half: $3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$ children. The difference is $20 - 14 = 6$. The transferable idea: read the key first, and turn every symbol, including part symbols, into numbers before comparing.
solutions.elegant: Football has one and a half circles more than swimming. One circle is 4 children and half a circle is 2, so the difference is $4 + 2 = 6$.

problems.whyOnTest: Reading a pictogram key, including half symbols, and answering "how many more" is everyday data reading on the test.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Picture 1 is a square with a star in its top left corner and 1 dot. Each new picture moves the star one corner clockwise and adds a dot. What does picture 10 look like?

choices.text: The star is in the top right corner, with 9 dots
choices.misconception: I counted only the 9 dots added after picture 1 and forgot the dot that picture 1 already has.

choices.text: The star is in the top right corner, with 10 dots
The star is in the top right corner, with 11 dots
choices.misconception: I added 10 new dots to picture 1, but from picture 1 to picture 10 there are only 9 new pictures.

choices.text: The star is in the bottom right corner, with 10 dots
choices.misconception: I moved the star 10 times, but from picture 1 to picture 10 it only moves 9 times.

choices.text: The star is in the bottom left corner, with 10 dots
choices.misconception: I moved the star anticlockwise instead of clockwise.

hints: The star and the dots change separately. Follow each one on its own.
The star goes round 4 corners, so its place repeats every 4 pictures. The dots simply go up by 1 each time. Count how many moves there are from picture 1 to picture 10.
From picture 1 to picture 10 there are 9 moves, which is 2 full trips round the square and 1 more corner. Picture 1 has 1 dot and picture 2 has 2 dots, so picture 10 has 10 dots.

solutions.reliable: The star: it is in the top left corner in pictures 1, 5 and 9, because every 4 moves bring it back. Picture 10 is one move after picture 9, so the star is in the top right corner. The dots: picture 1 has 1 dot, picture 2 has 2 dots, and so on, so picture 10 has 10 dots. Picture 10 has the star in the top right corner and 10 dots. The transferable idea: when a pattern changes two things at once, follow each change on its own and then put them together.
solutions.elegant: The star is in the top right corner in pictures 2, 6, 10, and so on, every 4 pictures starting from picture 2. Every picture has as many dots as its number. So picture 10: top right, 10 dots.

problems.whyOnTest: A pattern that changes two things at once, one going round a cycle and one that keeps growing, is a common Kangaroo trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben and Cleo each always tell the truth or always lie. Ana: "Ben tells the truth." Ben: "Exactly one of Ana and me lies." Cleo: "Ben lies." How many of them lie?

choices.misconception: I believed everyone without checking, but if Ana and Ben both told the truth, Ben's sentence would be false.
I found that Ana must lie, but I still thought Ben could tell the truth, even though Ana's lie means Ben lies.
I found that Ana and Ben lie, and then thought Cleo must lie too, but she says Ben lies, which is true.
I tried Ana telling the truth, reached a contradiction, and gave up instead of trying Ana as a liar.

hints: Suppose Ana tells the truth. What follows?
Truth-tellers and liars: assume one person is a truth-teller and follow the consequences. If you reach a contradiction, that person must be a liar. Then go through the others.
If Ana told the truth, Ben would tell the truth, so Ana and Ben would be the same kind, and Ben's sentence would be false. So Ana lies.

solutions.reliable: Suppose Ana tells the truth. Then Ben tells the truth. But then Ana and Ben are the same kind, so Ben's sentence is false, which a truth-teller cannot say. So Ana lies. Then her sentence is false, so Ben lies. Check Ben: Ana and Ben are both liars, so they are not different, and his sentence is false, as a liar's should be. Cleo says Ben lies, which is true, so Cleo tells the truth. Ana and Ben lie: 2 liars. The transferable idea: assume, follow, and throw away any assumption that leads to a contradiction.
solutions.elegant: Ana says Ben tells the truth. If Ana is truthful, Ben is truthful; if Ana lies, Ben lies. Either way they are the same kind, so Ben's sentence is false and Ben lies. Then Ana lies too, and Cleo is right: 2 liars.

problems.whyOnTest: Assuming a speaker is truthful and following it to a contradiction is the standard method for truth-teller and liar puzzles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven children queue up. Ana is 3rd. Bo is behind Ana, with exactly 2 children between them. Cal is directly in front of Bo. Dev is last. How many children are between Cal and Dev?

choices.misconception: I put everyone in the right place but did not count Bo, who stands between Cal and Dev.
I put Bo 2 places behind Ana, in 5th place, but then there is only 1 child between them, not 2.
I counted Cal and Dev themselves as well as the child between them.
I counted the children in front of Cal instead of the children between Cal and Dev.

hints: Draw seven boxes in a row and number them from the front.
Ordering from clues: place the fixed people first, then use the clues about gaps and neighbours one at a time. Count only the places strictly between the two children.
Ana is in place 3. With 2 children between, Bo is in place 6. Cal is directly in front, in place 5.

solutions.reliable: Number the places 1 to 7 from the front. Ana is in place 3. Exactly 2 children stand between Ana and Bo, so places 4 and 5 are between them and Bo is in place 6. Cal is directly in front of Bo, in place 5. Dev is last, in place 7. Between places 5 and 7 there is only place 6, where Bo stands. So 1 child stands between Cal and Dev. The transferable idea: draw the line with numbered places and translate "between" into places, not differences.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning words like "between" and "directly in front of" into exact positions is the key skill in ordering puzzles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 4 by 4 floor is covered exactly, with no gaps or overlaps, by square tiles of sizes 1 by 1, 2 by 2 and 3 by 3. What is the fewest tiles possible?

choices.misconception: I divided the 16 squares by 9, the size of the biggest tile, and rounded up to 2, but no two tiles can fill the floor.
I put a 2 by 2 tile in each corner and squeezed a fifth one into the middle, but the four corner tiles already fill the floor.
I put the 3 by 3 tile down first and counted the 7 small tiles for the strip left over, but forgot to count the big tile itself.
I started with the biggest tile, 3 by 3, but then the strip left over is only 1 square wide and needs 7 small tiles.

hints: Biggest first is not always best. What is left after a 3 by 3 tile?
Tiling: try a layout with a 3 by 3 tile and a layout without one, and count the tiles in each. Then use area to check that fewer tiles cannot work.
A 3 by 3 tile leaves a strip 1 square wide, which only 1 by 1 tiles fit. Without a 3 by 3 tile, each tile covers at most 4 small squares.

solutions.reliable: Case 1, a 3 by 3 tile is used: only one fits, and it leaves an L-shaped strip 1 square wide. Only 1 by 1 tiles fit in that strip, which has $16 - 9 = 7$ squares, so this uses $1 + 7 = 8$ tiles. Case 2, no 3 by 3 tile: every tile covers at most 4 small squares, so at least $16 \div 4 = 4$ tiles are needed, and four 2 by 2 tiles, one in each quarter of the floor, cover it exactly. So the smallest number is 4. The transferable idea: taking the biggest piece first can backfire, so compare cases and use area to show when fewer pieces are impossible.
solutions.elegant: Four 2 by 2 tiles cover the floor exactly. Three tiles cannot work: without a 3 by 3 tile they cover at most $3 \times 4 = 12$ squares, and with one, the rest is a strip 1 square wide that needs 7 small tiles.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions reward testing whether the biggest piece really helps, and using area to show that fewer pieces are impossible.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A farmer packs eggs into boxes of 6, with no eggs left over. Which of these numbers of eggs could she have?

choices.misconception: I checked that the digits add up to a multiple of 3, but forgot the number must also be even.
I thought any number ending in 6 can be shared into sixes.
I only checked that the number is even and forgot it must also be a multiple of 3.
I knew 18 is a multiple of 6 and thought writing another digit after it keeps it a multiple of 6.

hints: A multiple of 6 is a multiple of two smaller numbers at once.
Divisibility by 6: the number must be divisible by 2 (it is even) and by 3 (its digits add up to a multiple of 3). Check both rules for every choice.
The digit sums are 9, 9, 10, 13 and 13. Which numbers with a digit sum of 9 are even?

solutions.reliable: A number is divisible by 6 exactly when it is divisible by 2 and by 3. Divisible by 2 means even; divisible by 3 means the digit sum is a multiple of 3. 126: even, $1 + 2 + 6 = 9$, so yes, and $126 = 6 \times 21$. 135: digit sum 9 but odd, no. 136: even but digit sum 10, no. 148: even but digit sum 13, no. 184: even but digit sum 13, no. The answer is 126. The transferable idea: test divisibility by 6 with both the rule for 2 and the rule for 3.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks combining two divisibility rules, since a number must pass both the test for 2 and the test for 3 to be a multiple of 6.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The hour hand of a clock points exactly halfway between the 10 and the 11. Where does the minute hand point?

choices.misconception: I thought halfway between two numbers meant a quarter of the hour had gone, so I put the minute hand on 3.
I thought the minute hand points at the number the hour hand has just passed, so I chose 10.
I thought the minute hand points at the number the hour hand is moving towards, so I chose 11.
I thought the minute hand is on 12 whenever the hour hand is near a number, as it is at an o'clock time.

hints: How far through the hour has the hour hand gone?
The hour hand moves from one number to the next in exactly one hour. Work out what fraction of that hour has passed, then find where the minute hand is after that fraction of a turn.
Halfway from 10 to 11 means half of the hour after 10 o'clock has passed, so the time is half past 10. After half an hour the minute hand has made half a turn from 12.

solutions.reliable: The hour hand takes one hour to move from the 10 to the 11. Halfway there means half an hour has passed since 10 o'clock, so the time is 10:30. In half an hour the minute hand turns half way round the clock, from 12 to 6. The transferable idea: the hour hand's position between two numbers tells you the fraction of the hour that has passed.
solutions.elegant: Picture 10:30 on any clock: the minute hand points straight down at 6 and the hour hand sits halfway between 10 and 11. Reading the clock backwards from the hour hand gives the same picture.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks that the hour hand creeps between numbers in step with the minute hand, which students who only read o'clock times miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At 2:30, what is the smaller angle, in degrees, between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock?

choices.misconception: I found how far the hour hand has turned from 12, $2.5 \times 30 = 75$, instead of the angle between the two hands.
I counted the 3 number spaces from the 3 to the 6 and forgot the half space between the hour hand and the 3, $3 \times 30 = 90$.
I put the hour hand exactly on the 2, as at 2 o'clock, and counted 4 spaces from the 2 to the 6, $4 \times 30 = 120$.
I measured the long way round, from the 6 past the 9 and the 12 to the hour hand, which is $8.5 \times 30 = 255$.

hints: Where exactly is the hour hand at half past two?
The minute hand is on the 6. The hour hand has moved part of the way from the 2 towards the 3. Count the number spaces between the two hands, then use the angle for one space.

At 2:30 the hour hand is halfway between the 2 and the 3. From it to the 6 is half a space and then 3 more spaces. One space is $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees, so the angle is $15 + 3 \times 30 = 105$ degrees.

solutions.reliable: At 2:30 the minute hand points at the 6. The hour hand has gone half of the way from the 2 to the 3, so it sits halfway between them. From the hour hand to the 3 is half a space, and from the 3 to the 6 is 3 spaces: three and a half spaces in all. Each space is $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees and half a space is 15 degrees, so the angle is $90 + 15 = 105$ degrees. The transferable idea: place the hour hand between the numbers first, then count spaces of 30 degrees.
solutions.elegant: Measure both hands from 12. The minute hand is halfway round, at 180 degrees. The hour hand turns 30 degrees an hour, so after two and a half hours it is at $2.5 \times 30 = 75$ degrees. The angle between them is $180 - 75 = 105$ degrees.

problems.whyOnTest: Clock angles test whether you remember that the hour hand creeps forward between the numbers instead of sitting on one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a normal die, opposite faces add up to 7. Three dice lie on a table. Their top faces show 2, 4 and 5. What is the total of their three bottom faces?

choices.misconception: I added the top faces, $2 + 4 + 5 = 11$, instead of the faces underneath.
I thought opposite faces add up to 8, so I found $6 + 4 + 3 = 13$.
I thought the bottom face shows the next number after the top, so I added $3 + 5 + 6 = 14$.
I added 7 for each die, $3 \times 7 = 21$, and forgot to take away the top faces.

hints: Each bottom face is opposite one top face.
Opposite faces make 7, so each bottom face is 7 take away its top face. You can find the three bottoms one at a time, or use the total of all six faces at once.
The bottoms are $7 - 2 = 5$, $7 - 4 = 3$ and $7 - 5 = 2$. Add these three numbers.

solutions.reliable: Work die by die. Under the 2 is $7 - 2 = 5$, under the 4 is $7 - 4 = 3$, under the 5 is $7 - 5 = 2$. The bottoms add to $5 + 3 + 2 = 10$. The transferable idea: on a die, knowing one face tells you the face opposite it.
solutions.elegant: Each die's top and bottom add to 7, so the three tops and three bottoms together make $3 \times 7 = 21$. The tops make 11, so the bottoms make $21 - 11 = 10$.

problems.whyOnTest: Dice questions on the test lean on one fact, opposite faces add to 7, and reward using it as a total rather than one face at a time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a die, opposite faces add up to 7. Lily sees the top (1), the front (2) and the right face. Her three hidden faces add up to 14. What is on the right face?

choices.misconception: I found the hidden face that makes 14 with the 6 and the 5, which is 3, but that is the face opposite the right face, not the right face itself.
I thought the right face is opposite the front, so I gave $7 - 2 = 5$, but two opposite faces can never be seen at the same time.
I thought the right face is opposite the top, so I gave $7 - 1 = 6$, but two opposite faces can never be seen at the same time.
I worked out that the three faces Lily sees add up to $21 - 14 = 7$ and gave that total, forgetting to take away the 1 and the 2.

hints: Which faces are hidden, and which seen face is each one opposite?
Each hidden face is opposite one of the faces Lily sees, and every pair of opposite faces makes 7. You can use all six faces together, or find the hidden faces one at a time.
All six faces add up to $3 \times 7 = 21$, so the three faces Lily sees add up to $21 - 14 = 7$. The top and the front make $1 + 2 = 3$, so the right face shows $7 - 3 = 4$.

solutions.reliable: The hidden faces are the bottom, the back and the left. The bottom is opposite the 1, so it shows 6. The back is opposite the 2, so it shows 5. The three hidden faces add up to 14, so the left face shows $14 - 6 - 5 = 3$. The right face is opposite the left, so it shows $7 - 3 = 4$. Check: 4 is not opposite the 1 or the 2, so it can sit next to both of them. The transferable idea: every hidden face is the partner of a face you can see.
solutions.elegant: The three pairs of opposite faces make $3 \times 7 = 21$ in all. Take away the 14 that is hidden: the faces Lily sees make 7. So the right face is $7 - 1 - 2 = 4$.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks using opposite faces making 7 both one pair at a time and as a total of 21, a favourite move in dice questions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia cuts a paper cube with 1 cm edges along some of its edges and lays it flat as one piece made of 6 squares. What is the perimeter of the flat shape?

choices.misconception: I pictured the six squares as a 2 by 3 block, which cannot fold into a cube, and found its perimeter of 10.
I gave the number of edges of the cube, 12, instead of the perimeter of the flat shape.
I took 1 cm off the total of 24 for each of the 5 joins, but each join hides two sides, one from each square.
I added up all the sides of the six squares, $6 \times 4 = 24$, forgetting that sides where two squares join are not on the outline.

hints: Does the answer depend on which net Mia makes?
Six squares have 24 sides in all. Count how many places two squares stay joined in a net of a cube, then remember each join hides two sides from the outline.
A net of a cube has its 6 squares joined in exactly 5 places, because a cube has 12 edges and 7 of them are cut. Each join hides 2 sides, so take $5 \times 2$ from 24.

solutions.reliable: Try the cross-shaped net: a column of four squares with one square on each side of the second square. Walking round its outline gives 14 sides of 1 cm. Every net works the same way: the six squares have $6 \times 4 = 24$ sides, and in a net the squares stay joined in exactly 5 places. Each join hides two sides, so the perimeter is $24 - 10 = 14$ cm. The transferable idea: count the sides, then subtract twice the number of joins.
solutions.elegant: Mia cuts 7 of the cube's 12 edges, since 5 must stay joined to hold 6 squares in one piece. Each cut edge becomes two pieces of outline, one on each side of the cut, so the perimeter is $7 \times 2 = 14$ cm, whatever net she makes.

problems.whyOnTest: Nets reward thinking about how the squares join, not drawing every net; here one count of joins answers the question for all of them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cube-shaped box with no lid is opened out flat in one piece. Each face is a 3 cm by 3 cm square. What is the area of the flat piece, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found the area of only one square face, $3 \times 3 = 9$.
I multiplied the number of faces by the side length, $5 \times 3 = 15$, instead of by the area of a face.
I counted only the four side faces and forgot the bottom of the box, $4 \times 9 = 36$.
I counted six faces as if the box had a lid, $6 \times 9 = 54$.

hints: How many faces does a cube box without a lid have?
Opening the box out does not change the cardboard, so the flat piece has the same faces as the box. Count those faces, then find the area of one face.
The box has a bottom and four sides, so 5 square faces. Each face has area $3 \times 3 = 9$ square centimetres. Multiply 5 by 9.

solutions.reliable: A cube has 6 faces; with no lid the box has 5: a bottom and four sides. Unfolding keeps every face, so the flat piece is 5 squares. Each square is $3 \times 3 = 9$ square centimetres, so the area is $5 \times 9 = 45$. The transferable idea: a net has exactly the faces of the solid, no more and no fewer.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks that a net is made of the solid's faces, here with one face missing, joined to a simple area calculation.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each square of a 2-row, 3-column grid holds a stack of at least one cube. The pictures show the stacks from the front and from the right. How many cubes are there?

figure.alt: Two views of the stacks. From the front: three columns of cubes, 2, 3 and 1 cubes tall from left to right. From the right: two columns, 1 and 3 cubes tall from left to right.

choices.misconception: I counted only the cubes in the front view, $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$, as if all the stacks stood in one row.
I put the front view in the tall row and only one cube in the short row, forgetting that every square has at least one cube.
I added the cubes in the two views, $6 + 4 = 10$, but some cubes appear in both views.
I copied the front view into both rows, $2 \times 6 = 12$, which makes the short row too tall for the view from the right.

hints: Start with the view from the right. What does it tell you about each row?
One row is never taller than 1 cube, and every square has a cube, so you know that row exactly. Then use the front view to work out the stacks in the other row.

The short row has 1 cube on each square: 3 cubes. The front columns of 2 and 3 must be stacks in the tall row, and the column that is 1 tall has 1 cube there too. So the tall row has $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$ cubes, and the total is $3 + 6 = 9$.

solutions.reliable: From the right, one row is 1 cube tall and the other is 3 tall. In the short row every square has at least one cube but no stack is taller than 1, so it has exactly 1 cube on each square: 3 cubes. From the front the columns are 2, 3 and 1 tall. The short row only reaches 1, so the stacks of 2 and 3 must be in the tall row. In the last column both stacks are 1 tall. So the tall row has 2, 3 and 1 cubes: 6 cubes. Total: $3 + 6 = 9$. The transferable idea: start with the view that pins down a whole row, then let the other view fill in the rest.

problems.whyOnTest: Views of a solid test whether you can rebuild the stacks from two flat pictures and see which cubes each view hides.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 5 by 6 rectangle of squared paper is cut along the grid lines into squares. The squares do not all have to be the same size. What is the smallest number of squares?

choices.misconception: I found square numbers that add up to 30, $25 + 4 + 1$, and did not check that a 5 by 5, a 2 by 2 and a 1 by 1 square fit together into the rectangle.
I found four square numbers that add up to 30, $16 + 9 + 4 + 1$, but a 4 by 4, a 3 by 3, a 2 by 2 and a 1 by 1 square cannot fit together into a 5 by 6 rectangle.
I started with the biggest square, 5 by 5, and then cut the 5 by 1 strip left over into 5 small squares, $1 + 5 = 6$.
I used only 2 by 2 and 1 by 1 squares: 6 big ones fit, and the 6 small squares left over make $6 + 6 = 12$.

hints: Is cutting the biggest possible square first always best?
Try the biggest square first and look at what is left over. Then try squares that are a bit smaller but leave no thin strips. Remember the areas of the squares must add up to 30.

Cut the top 3 rows into two 3 by 3 squares side by side, and the bottom 2 rows into three 2 by 2 squares: 5 squares. Four is impossible: the only four square numbers that add to 30 are 16, 9, 4 and 1, and a 3 by 3 square never fits beside a 4 by 4 one in this rectangle.

solutions.reliable: Cutting a 5 by 5 square first leaves a 5 by 1 strip that needs 5 tiny squares, 6 squares in all. Better: cut the top 3 rows into two 3 by 3 squares and the bottom 2 rows into three 2 by 2 squares. That is 5 squares, and the areas check: $9 + 9 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 30$. Can it be done with fewer? The areas must add up to 30. Two squares never make 30. Three squares only make 30 as $25 + 4 + 1$, and the 5 by 5 leaves a strip 1 square wide, too thin for the 2 by 2. Four squares only make 30 as $16 + 9 + 4 + 1$, and beside the 4 by 4 there is only 1 free row and 2 free columns, too thin for the 3 by 3. So 5 is the smallest. The transferable idea: biggest-first can leave thin strips, so check what really fits, not just the areas.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions test whether you check what physically fits instead of trusting the areas or the biggest-first habit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A paper strip is folded in half, then in half again. One straight cut is made across it, through all the layers, away from the folds. How many pieces are there?

choices.misconception: I thought one straight cut always makes two pieces, however the paper was folded.
I thought folding in half twice makes only 2 layers, so the cut went through the strip in 2 places.
I worked out there are 4 layers, so the strip is cut in 4 places, but I forgot that 4 cuts make one more piece than cuts.
I thought each of the 4 layers is cut into 2 separate pieces, giving $4 \times 2 = 8$.

hints: How many layers of paper does the scissors go through?
Each fold in half doubles the layers. A cut through every layer cuts the unfolded strip in that many places. Then think of a straight strip cut in several places: how many pieces?
After two folds there are 4 layers, so the strip is cut in 4 places. Cutting a strip in 4 places gives one more piece than the number of cuts.

solutions.reliable: One fold in half makes 2 layers; folding again makes 4 layers. The cut goes through all 4 layers, so when the strip is opened it has been cut in 4 different places. A strip cut in 4 places falls into $4 + 1 = 5$ pieces. You can check with a real strip of paper: the three middle pieces each have a fold in them and the two end pieces do not. The transferable idea: count layers to count cuts, then remember that cuts in a strip make one more piece.
solutions.elegant: Small cases: no fold, one cut, 2 pieces. One fold gives 2 layers, 2 cuts, 3 pieces. Two folds give 4 layers, 4 cuts, 5 pieces. The pieces are always one more than the layers.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding and cutting questions reward tracking layers rather than picturing the final shape, and the fence-post step catches the hasty.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six children sit round a table. Each child always tells the truth or always lies. Every child says: "The child on my left is a liar." How many liars are at the table?

choices.misconception: I assumed everyone was telling the truth because they all said the same thing.
I checked only what the liars said and used the pattern liar, truth-teller, truth-teller, which gives 2 liars.
I checked only what the truth-tellers said and used the pattern truth-teller, liar, liar, which gives 4 liars.
I thought that if everyone says the same thing, they must all be liars.

hints: What is true about the child to the left of a truth-teller? Of a liar?
Check both kinds of child. A truth-teller's claim must be true, and a liar's claim must be false. Work out what each one says about its left neighbour, then go round the table.
A truth-teller has a liar on its left. A liar's claim is false, so a liar has a truth-teller on its left. So the children must alternate all the way round the table.

solutions.reliable: Take any child. If the child tells the truth, the child on the left really is a liar. If the child lies, the statement is false, so the child on the left tells the truth. So going round the table the children alternate: truth-teller, liar, truth-teller, liar, and so on. With 6 seats this works and gives 3 liars and 3 truth-tellers. Check that all six statements fit: each truth-teller has a liar on the left and each liar has a truth-teller on the left. The transferable idea: test both kinds of speaker and look for the pattern they force.
solutions.elegant: Two liars cannot sit side by side, and nor can two truth-tellers, so the two kinds must alternate. Six seats in a circle split evenly: 3 liars.

problems.whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles check whether you test both cases, true and false, instead of trusting the statement; a circle adds a pattern to spot.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One of Ann, Ben and Cal took the last cookie. Ann: "It was Ben or Cal." Ben: "It was not me." Cal: "It was Ann." Only one of them tells the truth. Who took it?

choices.misconception: I believed Cal because he named one person directly, and I did not check how many statements were then true.
I believed both Ann and Ben, so I decided it was Cal, but then two children would be telling the truth.

choices.text: Ann or Cal, the clues do not decide
choices.misconception: I worked as if exactly one child was lying, and then both Ann and Cal fitted.
I tested only Ann and Cal as the cookie-taker, found two true statements each time, and gave up.

hints: Try each child in turn as the cookie-taker.
There are only three possibilities. For each one, decide whether each of the three statements is true or false, then count the true statements. Keep the case with exactly one.
If Ann took it, Ben and Cal are both right. If Cal took it, Ann and Ben are both right. Now check Ben.

solutions.reliable: Test each possibility. If Ann took it: Ann is wrong, Ben is right, Cal is right, so 2 truths. If Cal took it: Ann is right, Ben is right, Cal is wrong, so 2 truths. If Ben took it: Ann is right, Ben is wrong, Cal is wrong, so exactly 1 truth. Only Ben fits. The transferable idea: when there are few possibilities, test each one against every clue.
solutions.elegant: Ann and Cal can never both be right, since one blames Ben or Cal and the other blames Ann. So the single true statement is Ann's or Cal's, which means Ben's "It was not me" is false.

problems.whyOnTest: It checks reading each statement precisely and counting truths case by case, the core move in every liar puzzle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lea, Max and Noor have different bags (red, blue, green) and fruits (apple, banana, cherry). The apple is in the red bag. Max's is blue. Lea's isn't green. Noor hasn't got the banana. Who has?

choices.misconception: I missed the clue that Noor does not have the banana.
I forgot that the apple is in the red bag, so I let Lea have the banana in her red bag.
I mixed up the bag clue and gave Max the green bag instead of the blue one.
I missed the clue that Lea's bag is not green, so I let Lea take the green bag and the banana.

hints: Start with the bags: which clue fixes a bag straight away?
Settle the bag colours first, because two clues are about bags. Then the apple clue links one bag to a fruit, and the last clue settles the other two fruits.
Max has blue, and Lea's bag is not green, so Lea has red and Noor has green. The apple is in the red bag, so Lea has the apple. Noor has no banana.

solutions.reliable: Bags first. Max has the blue bag. Lea's bag is not green, and blue is taken, so Lea has red. That leaves green for Noor. The apple is in the red bag, so Lea has the apple. The banana and cherry go to Max and Noor, and Noor has no banana, so Noor has the cherry and Max has the banana, in his blue bag. Check every clue: apple in red, Max blue, Lea not green, Noor no banana. The transferable idea: fix the attribute with the most clues first, then link the rest.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination grids test using every clue and settling the most-constrained item first, which keeps a two-attribute puzzle short.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four books stand on a shelf. Green is left of red. Blue is right of red. Yellow is between green and red. Which book is third from the left?

choices.misconception: I read the shelf from the right end and also forgot the yellow book, so from the right I had blue, red, green.
I counted from the right end of the shelf instead of from the left.
I forgot the yellow book, so I lined up green, red, blue and took blue as the third book.
I thought 'between' did not say exactly where the yellow book goes, so I decided the order was not fixed.

hints: Draw four spaces and place the books one clue at a time.
Draw the shelf as a row of four spaces. Put green before red, blue after red, then fit yellow into the gap between green and red. Only one order uses all four spaces.
Green must come before yellow, which comes before red, and blue comes after red. So from the left the order is green, yellow, red, blue.

solutions.reliable: Green is somewhere left of red, and yellow is between them, so we have green, yellow, red in that order. Blue is to the right of red, so it goes last. The shelf from the left reads green, yellow, red, blue, and the third book is red. The transferable idea: draw the line and place the items, rather than holding them in your head.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering clues test turning words like left of and between into a drawn line, and counting from the correct end.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Rosa, Pia, Quinn, Sam and Tom ran a race with no ties. Pia finished after Rosa but before Quinn, and Sam right after Quinn. Tom was neither first nor last. How many orders are possible?

choices.misconception: I thought the clues fix the whole order, but Pia and Tom can swap places.
I forgot that Tom cannot be last, so I also allowed Tom to finish after Sam.
I ignored the clue about Tom, so I let him go in any gap except between Quinn and Sam.
I counted every order of Pia, Quinn and Tom in the middle three places, ignoring that Quinn must come right before Sam.

hints: Who can be first? Who can be last?
Write Rosa, Pia, Quinn, Sam in their forced order, with Quinn and Sam glued together. Then list every gap where Tom could go, and cross out the ones the clues forbid.
Tom cannot go before Rosa, because then he is first, or after Sam, because then he is last, or between Quinn and Sam. That leaves two gaps.

solutions.reliable: The clues force Rosa before Pia before Quinn, with Sam right after Quinn: Rosa, Pia, Quinn, Sam. Tom must be added somewhere. The possible gaps are before Rosa, between Rosa and Pia, between Pia and Quinn, between Quinn and Sam, and after Sam. Before Rosa makes Tom first and after Sam makes him last, both forbidden, and between Quinn and Sam breaks the clue that Sam is right after Quinn. Two orders remain: Rosa, Tom, Pia, Quinn, Sam and Rosa, Pia, Tom, Quinn, Sam. The transferable idea: build the forced order first, then list where the free item can go.
solutions.elegant: Rosa must be first and Sam must be last, since nobody else can be. Quinn is right before Sam, so fourth. Pia and Tom fill second and third in either order: 2 orders.

problems.whyOnTest: Ranking clues probe careful use of words like right after and neither; asking how many orders checks that nothing is assumed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When a class stands in rows of 6, there are 4 children left over. In rows of 5, there are also 4 left over. Which of these could be the number of children?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the 5 in each row by the 4 left over, $5 \times 4 = 20$.
I multiplied the 6 in each row by the 4 left over, $6 \times 4 = 24$.
I checked rows of 6, where 28 leaves 4, but forgot to check rows of 5, where it leaves 3.
I checked rows of 5, where 44 leaves 4, but forgot to check rows of 6, where it leaves 2.

hints: Test each choice. Both conditions must hold.
Instead of solving from scratch, try each answer choice. Divide it into rows of 6 and look at the leftover, then into rows of 5. Only one choice leaves 4 both times.
Rows of 5 leave 4 for numbers ending in 4 or 9, so only 24, 34 and 44 survive. Now check rows of 6 for those three.

solutions.reliable: Check every choice. 20: rows of 6 leave 2. 24: rows of 6 leave 0. 28: rows of 6 leave 4, but rows of 5 leave 3. 34: rows of 6 make 5 rows of 30 with 4 left, and rows of 5 make 6 rows of 30 with 4 left. 44: rows of 6 leave 2. Only 34 works. The transferable idea: when the choices are numbers, testing them can be faster than solving.
solutions.elegant: Take away the 4 extra children and the rest fill rows of 6 and rows of 5 exactly, so that number is a multiple of 30. The class could be $30 + 4 = 34$.

problems.whyOnTest: Back-solving from the choices is a real contest skill: checking five numbers can be quicker and safer than building the answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers use only the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, with each digit bigger than the digit before it, like 135?

choices.misconception: I counted the numbers whose digits go up and also those whose digits go down, like 531.
I let a digit repeat as long as the digits never went down, so I also counted numbers like 113 and 222.
I counted every number with three different digits from 1 to 5, $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$, not just the ones going up.
I counted every three-digit number made from these digits, $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$, ignoring the rule.

hints: List them in order, starting with the ones that begin with 1.
Work systematically by first digit. Fix the first digit, then list the possible second digits in increasing order, then the third. This way nothing is missed or repeated.
Starting with 1: 123, 124, 125, 134, 135, 145, which is 6. Starting with 2: 234, 235, 245. Starting with 3: 345.

solutions.reliable: List by first digit. Starting with 1: 123, 124, 125, 134, 135, 145, which is 6 numbers. Starting with 2: 234, 235, 245, which is 3. Starting with 3: 345, which is 1. A number cannot start with 4 or 5, since it needs two bigger digits after. Total: $6 + 3 + 1 = 10$. The transferable idea: fix the first position and list in order so the list checks itself.
solutions.elegant: Choose any three different digits from 1 to 5; there is exactly one way to write them in increasing order. So count the ways to leave out two of the five digits: 10.

problems.whyOnTest: Systematic listing is the base skill under all counting; a rule like increasing digits tests whether the list is organised enough to be complete.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A snack is one drink and one fruit. With milk you can have an apple, a pear or a plum; with juice, only an apple or a pear. How many different snacks are there?

choices.misconception: I counted only the two drinks and forgot that each drink comes with a fruit.
I counted only the snacks with milk and forgot the ones with juice.
I used 2 fruits for each drink, $2 \times 2 = 4$, as if milk had only two fruits too.
I multiplied 2 drinks by 3 fruits, as if every fruit went with both drinks.

hints: Draw a branch for each drink first.
A tree diagram fits here because the choices after milk are not the same as after juice. Draw the two drink branches, then the fruit branches from each one, and count the ends.
The milk branch splits into 3 fruits. The juice branch splits into 2 fruits. Every end of the tree is one snack.

solutions.reliable: Draw a tree. From milk come apple, pear and plum: 3 snacks. From juice come apple and pear: 2 snacks. The tree has $3 + 2 = 5$ ends, so there are 5 snacks. The transferable idea: when the later choices depend on the earlier one, add the branches instead of multiplying.

problems.whyOnTest: Tree diagrams test when you may multiply and when you must add branches, since unequal branches break the multiplication shortcut.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a 3 by 3 grid, the top-left and top-middle squares are shaded. How many more squares, at least, must be shaded so that both middle lines and both diagonals are mirror lines?

choices.misconception: I only made the picture match across the up-and-down middle line, so I shaded just the top-right square.
I gave the picture a half turn and shaded the two squares the shaded ones land on, but a half turn is not a mirror line.
I shaded all four corners but forgot that the top-middle square needs copies on the other three sides.
I made the picture symmetric across and down only, and forgot to check the two diagonal lines.

hints: Where does each shaded square go when reflected in each line?

Reflect each shaded square in all four mirror lines, and keep reflecting the new squares too, until nothing new appears. Corner squares only ever land on corners; middle-of-side squares land on middles of sides.
The top-left corner forces all four corners. The top-middle square forces all four middle-of-side squares. That is 8 squares in all, and 2 are already shaded.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting the top-left corner in the up-and-down line gives the top-right corner; reflecting those in the across line gives the bottom two corners. So all 4 corners must be shaded. Reflecting the top-middle square in the across line gives the bottom-middle; in a diagonal it goes to the left-middle or right-middle. So all 4 middle-of-side squares must be shaded. The picture is then every square except the centre, which is symmetric in all four lines. That is 8 shaded squares, 2 already done, so 6 extra. The transferable idea: a figure with several mirror lines must contain every image of every part.
solutions.elegant: The four lines of a square swap the four corners among themselves and the four side-middles among themselves. One shaded corner means all four; one shaded side-middle means all four: $4 + 4 - 2 = 6$ extra.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetry questions test applying every mirror line, not just the obvious one, and noticing which squares can swap places.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ava's summer holiday lasts 30 days, numbered 1 to 30. She wants to choose 7 days in a row for a trip. How many different choices does she have?

choices.misconception: I counted how many whole weeks fit into 30 days, as if the trips could not overlap.
I left out the two trips that start on day 1 or end on day 30.
I took 7 away from 30 and forgot to add 1 for the trip that starts on day 1.
I thought every day could start a trip, but a trip starting after day 24 runs past day 30.

hints: Count the possible first days of the trip.
Each trip is fixed by the day it starts. Find the earliest possible first day and the latest one that still fits 7 days inside the holiday, then count the days from one to the other.
The first trip is days 1 to 7. The last trip ends on day 30, so it starts on day 24. Count the start days 1 to 24.

solutions.reliable: A trip is decided by its first day. It can start on day 1, covering days 1 to 7. The latest start is day 24, covering days 24 to 30, because starting on day 25 would need day 31. The start days 1, 2, ..., 24 give 24 choices. The transferable idea: count sliding windows by counting where they can start.
solutions.elegant: Small case: a 7-day trip in a 7-day holiday has 1 choice, in an 8-day holiday 2 choices. Each extra day adds one choice, so 30 days give $30 - 7 + 1 = 24$.

problems.whyOnTest: Sliding-window counting checks the off-by-one step: the windows are one more than the difference of the lengths.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, A is at 12 and B is at 48. Point C lies between them and is 3 times as far from A as from B. What number is at C?

choices.misconception: I put C 3 times as far from B as from A, which places it a quarter of the way from A instead of three quarters.
I found the distance from A to C, three quarters of 36, which is 27, and forgot to add it to 12.
I put C halfway between A and B, ignoring the 3 times.
I split the gap of 36 into 3 equal parts instead of 4 and went 2 parts from A, $12 + 24 = 36$.

hints: How far apart are A and B?
C splits the gap from A to B, and the piece next to A is 3 times the piece next to B. Draw the gap as 4 equal parts: 3 from A to C, 1 from C to B.
The gap is $48 - 12 = 36$, split into $3 + 1 = 4$ equal parts of 9. C is 3 parts, 27, to the right of A.

solutions.reliable: The distance from A to B is $48 - 12 = 36$. C is 3 times as far from A as from B, so think of 4 equal parts: 3 from A to C and 1 from C to B. Each part is $36 \div 4 = 9$. So C is $3 \times 9 = 27$ to the right of A, at $12 + 27 = 39$. Check: C to B is $48 - 39 = 9$, and 27 is 3 times 9. The transferable idea: turn 'times as far' into equal parts of the gap, then count from the right end point.

problems.whyOnTest: Number line questions test turning distances into equal parts and remembering to start from the end point, not from zero.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square napkin is folded in half and then in half again, making a smaller square with sides of 10 cm. What is the perimeter of the napkin when it is unfolded?

choices.misconception: I found the side of the unfolded napkin, 20 cm, and stopped before working out the perimeter.
I gave the perimeter of the folded square, $4 \times 10 = 40$, not the unfolded napkin.
I unfolded only one fold, getting a 20 cm by 10 cm rectangle with a perimeter of 60 cm.
I doubled the side once for each fold, making it 40 cm and the perimeter $4 \times 40 = 160$, but each fold works in one direction only, so the side doubles just once.

hints: Unfold one fold at a time. What happens to the shape?
Each fold in half halves one direction only. Undo the second fold, then the first, and keep track of both side lengths. Then find the distance all the way round.
Undoing one fold gives a rectangle 20 cm by 10 cm. Undoing the other fold gives a square 20 cm by 20 cm. Its perimeter is 4 sides of 20 cm.

solutions.reliable: The two folds go in different directions, because the result is a square. Unfold one: the 10 cm square becomes a 20 cm by 10 cm rectangle. Unfold the other: it becomes a 20 cm by 20 cm square. The perimeter is $4 \times 20 = 80$ cm. The transferable idea: undo folds one at a time, tracking each direction separately.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding questions test running a process backwards one step at a time, and noticing that a fold changes only one direction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A film starts at 17:45 and lasts 1 hour 50 minutes. At what time does it end?

choices.misconception: I added 50 minutes to 45 minutes and wrote the extra 35 minutes, but forgot to add the hour that came from the 95 minutes.
I added the hours and the minutes separately and did not change 95 minutes into 1 hour and 35 minutes.
I rounded 1 hour 50 minutes up to 2 hours and forgot to take the extra 10 minutes back off.
I rounded up to 2 hours, then added 10 minutes instead of taking them away.

hints: An hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
Add the hour first, then the minutes, and change any 60 minutes into an hour. Or round the film to 2 hours and correct for the extra minutes at the end.
17:45 plus 1 hour is 18:45. Adding 15 minutes reaches 19:00, and 35 more minutes are still to add.

solutions.reliable: Add the hour: 17:45 becomes 18:45. Now add 50 minutes in two steps: 15 minutes takes the clock to 19:00, and the other 35 minutes take it to 19:35. The transferable idea: when adding times, jump to the next full hour first, since an hour has 60 minutes.
solutions.elegant: 1 hour 50 minutes is 10 minutes less than 2 hours. Two hours after 17:45 is 19:45; take off 10 minutes to get 19:35.

problems.whyOnTest: Time arithmetic tests working in sixties instead of hundreds, a unit slip that costs many students easy points.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

choices.misconception: I paired 11 with 19, 12 with 18, 13 with 17 and 14 with 16 to make four 30s, but forgot to add the 15 in the middle.
I counted ten tens to make 100 and then added the ones 1 to 9, which is 45, but there are only nine numbers.
I thought there were ten numbers, which makes five pairs of 30.
I made five pairs of 30 by pairing 15 with itself, and then added the 15 again.

hints: Pair the numbers from the outside in.
Numbers that are the same distance from the middle add to the same total. Pair the first with the last, the second with the second last, and see what is left over.
11 + 19, 12 + 18, 13 + 17 and 14 + 16 each make 30. That is four 30s, and 15 has no partner.

solutions.reliable: Pair from the outside: $11 + 19 = 30$, $12 + 18 = 30$, $13 + 17 = 30$, $14 + 16 = 30$. That is $4 \times 30 = 120$, and the middle number 15 is left over, so the total is $120 + 15 = 135$. The transferable idea: pair numbers to make round totals, and watch for an unpaired middle.
solutions.elegant: There are nine numbers and their middle one is 15, so their average is 15. The total is $9 \times 15 = 135$.

problems.whyOnTest: Clever regrouping turns a long sum into a few round numbers; the odd count tests whether you notice the unpaired middle term.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three boxes hold 52 marbles in all. The second box has 4 more marbles than the first. The third box has twice as many as the first. How many marbles are in the third box?

choices.misconception: I found the number in the first box, 12, and stopped.
I found the number in the second box, $12 + 4 = 16$, instead of the third.
I took the extra 4 away twice, once for the second box and once for the third, so I shared 44 into 4 bars of 11 and doubled it to get 22.
I forgot the 4 extra marbles, so I shared 52 into 4 equal bars of 13 and doubled it to get 26.

hints: Draw one bar for the first box.
Draw the first box as one bar. The second is one bar plus 4, the third is two bars. Take away the extra 4 and share what is left among the bars.
There are 4 equal bars and an extra 4. So the 4 bars make $52 - 4 = 48$, and one bar is 12.

solutions.reliable: Draw the first box as one bar. The second box is one bar and 4 more. The third box is two bars. Altogether: 4 bars and 4 marbles make 52. So 4 bars make 48 and one bar is 12. The third box has two bars: $2 \times 12 = 24$. Check: $12 + 16 + 24 = 52$. The transferable idea: draw equal bars, remove the extras, then share.

problems.whyOnTest: Bar models make part-whole problems visual; three parts with a difference and a multiple test drawing before calculating.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Cubes are stacked in towers on a 3 by 3 square. From the front, from the right and from above, Leo sees a full 3 by 3 square. What is the fewest cubes possible?

choices.misconception: I used three towers of 3 placed so that each row and each column has one, but forgot that from above all 9 squares must be covered.
I made the whole front row and the whole left column 3 tall, using 5 tall towers when 3 are enough.
I used three tall towers for the front view and three different tall towers for the side view, then 1 cube on the other 3 squares.
I filled the whole 3 by 3 by 3 block, which works but is not the smallest.

hints: What does the view from above tell you about every square?
From above, every square must have at least one cube. From the front and the side, every row and every column needs one tower of 3. Use as few tall towers as possible, each doing two jobs.
Put towers of 3 on a diagonal: each tall tower fills one row and one column. The other 6 squares need just 1 cube each.

solutions.reliable: From above Leo sees all 9 squares, so every square has at least 1 cube. From the front each of the 3 columns must look 3 tall, so each column of squares needs a tower of 3 somewhere; from the side the same holds for each row. One tall tower can serve one row and one column, so at least 3 tall towers are needed, and 3 are enough if they sit on a diagonal. The other 6 squares get 1 cube each. Total: $3 \times 3 + 6 \times 1 = 15$. The transferable idea: let each tall stack do two jobs at once, and fill every other square as lightly as allowed.

problems.whyOnTest: Three views at once test reasoning about what each view forces; the smallest count needs each tall tower to serve a row and a column.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A jar holds 45 beads. Some are red, some are blue, and 9 are green. There are as many red beads as blue beads. How many red beads are there?

choices.misconception: I took away the 9 green beads and then shared the other 36 among three colours instead of two.
I shared all 45 beads equally among the three colours, as if there were as many green beads as red.
I found the 18 red beads and then added the 9 green beads to them.
I took away the 9 green beads and stopped, forgetting to split the rest between red and blue.

hints: Which beads are not red or blue?
Draw a bar for the whole jar. Cut off the green part, then split what is left into two equal parts, one red and one blue.
Without the green beads there are $45 - 9 = 36$ beads, shared equally between red and blue.

solutions.reliable: Take away the green beads: $45 - 9 = 36$ beads are red or blue. Red and blue are equal, so each is $36 \div 2 = 18$. Check: $18 + 18 + 9 = 45$. The transferable idea: remove the part you know, then split what is left into equal parts.

problems.whyOnTest: A part-whole bar model: remove the known part first, then split the rest into equal parts.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Half of Ana's marbles is the same number as one third of Bo's marbles. Together they have 40 marbles. How many marbles does Bo have?

choices.misconception: I found the size of one equal part, $40 \div 5 = 8$, and stopped there.
I worked out how many marbles Ana has instead of Bo.
I thought half and a third being equal meant they have the same number, so I split 40 in half.
I thought Bo has three times as many as Ana, so I split 40 into 4 parts and took 3 of them.

hints: Call the equal amount one block.
If half of Ana's marbles is one block, Ana has two blocks. If a third of Bo's is one block, Bo has three blocks. Draw the blocks and use the total.
Ana has 2 blocks and Bo has 3 blocks, so 5 equal blocks make 40 marbles.

solutions.reliable: Let one block be the number that is half of Ana's marbles and also a third of Bo's. Then Ana has 2 blocks and Bo has 3 blocks, 5 blocks in all. Since 5 blocks make 40, one block is 8. Bo has $3 \times 8 = 24$. Check: Ana has 16, half of 16 is 8, and a third of 24 is 8. The transferable idea: turn "a fraction of one equals a fraction of another" into equal blocks.
solutions.elegant: Try the choices: if Bo has 24, Ana has 16, and half of 16 equals a third of 24, both 8. No other choice works, so the bar model and back-solving agree.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning a statement about equal fractions into equal blocks is the bar-model idea behind many harder sharing problems.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A lemonade costs 45 cents and a cookie costs 30 cents. Jo buys 2 lemonades and 3 cookies and pays with a 2-euro coin, which is 200 cents. How many cents change does she get?

choices.misconception: I mixed up the numbers and bought 3 lemonades and 2 cookies, which cost 195 cents.
I only counted the 2 lemonades, 90 cents, and took that from 200.
I added one lemonade and one cookie, 75 cents, and forgot to multiply by how many she bought.
I worked out how much she spent, 180 cents, instead of her change.

hints: Find the total cost first.
Work out the cost of the lemonades and of the cookies separately, add them, then take the total away from what she paid.
Two lemonades cost $2 \times 45 = 90$ cents and three cookies cost $3 \times 30 = 90$ cents.

solutions.reliable: Lemonades: $2 \times 45 = 90$ cents. Cookies: $3 \times 30 = 90$ cents. Total: $180$ cents. Change: $200 - 180 = 20$ cents. The transferable idea: change is what you paid minus the full cost, so find the full cost first.

problems.whyOnTest: Money problems test a multi-step chain: price times quantity, total, then change, and the question asks for the last step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Kai's money box holds only 10-cent and 20-cent coins. There are 15 coins, worth 210 cents in total. How many 20-cent coins are there?

choices.misconception: I found that 210 is 60 more than 150, but then divided 60 by 20 instead of by 10.
I thought there would be about the same number of each coin, so I halved 15 and rounded up.
I worked it out correctly but gave the number of 10-cent coins instead of 20-cent coins.
I found how many 20-cent coins fit into 210 cents, 10 of them with 10 cents over, and forgot that there must be 15 coins in all.

hints: What if every coin were a 10-cent coin?
Start with all 15 coins as 10-cent coins and see how far short of 210 you are. Each swap to a 20-cent coin adds the same amount.
Fifteen 10-cent coins make 150 cents, which is 60 cents short. Each swap adds 10 cents.

solutions.reliable: If all 15 coins were 10-cent coins, they would make 150 cents. We need 60 cents more. Swapping one 10-cent coin for a 20-cent coin adds 10 cents, so we need $60 \div 10 = 6$ swaps: 6 coins of 20 cents and 9 of 10 cents. Check: $6 \times 20 + 9 \times 10 = 120 + 90 = 210$. The transferable idea: start from an easy guess and count how many swaps fix the total.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve from the choices: 6 coins of 20 cents and 9 of 10 cents make exactly 210 cents with 15 coins. Each other choice gives the wrong total.

problems.whyOnTest: Two kinds of coins with a known count and total: the swap method is a classic way to solve it without algebra.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three parcels weigh 1 kg 400 g, 850 g and 2 kg 750 g. How much do they weigh altogether? (1 kg = 1000 g.)

choices.misconception: I added only the kilograms, 1 + 2, and forgot about the grams.
I added the grams to get 2000 g but counted that as only 1 kg.
I read 850 g as 8 kg 50 g, so I added 1400 g, 8050 g and 2750 g.
I thought there are 100 grams in a kilogram, so the 2000 g made 20 kg, giving 23 kg.

hints: Add the grams on their own first.
Add the kilograms and the grams separately, then change every 1000 grams into one more kilogram.
The grams are $400 + 850 + 750 = 2000$ g, which is 2 kg.

solutions.reliable: Kilograms: $1 + 2 = 3$ kg. Grams: $400 + 850 + 750 = 2000$ g $= 2$ kg. Total: $3 + 2 = 5$ kg. The transferable idea: add each unit separately, then carry over whenever the smaller unit makes a whole larger one.
solutions.elegant: Pair the grams that make round numbers: $850 + 750 = 1600$ g, and $1600 + 400 = 2000$ g. So the grams give exactly 2 kg.

problems.whyOnTest: Mixed units need a careful carry: 1000 grams make a kilogram, just as 10 ones make a ten.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pancake recipe uses 3 cups of milk, and one cup holds 250 ml. Leo makes the recipe 3 times. Milk is sold in 1-litre cartons. How many cartons must he buy?

choices.misconception: I worked out the milk for just one recipe, 750 ml, which fits in one carton.
I found he needs 2250 ml, which is 2 and a quarter litres, and rounded down to 2.
I counted the cups of milk, 3 times 3, instead of the cartons.
I thought 1 litre is 100 ml, so 2250 ml needed 22 and a half cartons, which I rounded to 23.

hints: How many cups does he use in all?
Find the total milk in millilitres, change it to litres, and remember he cannot buy part of a carton.
He uses $3 \times 3 = 9$ cups, which is $9 \times 250 = 2250$ ml.

solutions.reliable: Three recipes use $3 \times 3 = 9$ cups. Nine cups hold $9 \times 250 = 2250$ ml. One litre is 1000 ml, so 2 cartons give only 2000 ml, which is not enough. He must buy 3 cartons. The transferable idea: when you can only buy whole packs, round up, not to the nearest.
solutions.elegant: Four cups of 250 ml make exactly 1 litre. Nine cups is two full litres and one more cup, so he needs a third carton.

problems.whyOnTest: Converting millilitres to litres and then rounding up to whole cartons is a two-step trap common in Kangaroo word problems.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The pictogram shows how many apples a stall sold on four days. How many apples did it sell altogether?

figure.alt: A pictogram of apples sold on four days. A key shows that one whole circle stands for 4 apples. Monday has 3 whole circles. Tuesday has 2 whole circles and a half circle. Wednesday has 4 whole circles. Thursday has 1 whole circle and a half circle.

choices.misconception: I worked out that the symbols make 11 whole circles, but forgot that each circle stands for 4 apples.
I left out the half circles and only counted the 10 whole ones.
I counted each half circle as just 1 apple.
I counted each half circle as a whole circle, making 12 circles.

hints: Look at the key, and at the half circles.
Each whole circle means 4 apples, so a half circle means half of 4. Count the symbols, then multiply.
There are 10 whole circles and 2 half circles, which is 11 whole circles in all.

solutions.reliable: Monday $3 \times 4 = 12$, Tuesday $2 \times 4 + 2 = 10$, Wednesday $4 \times 4 = 16$, Thursday $4 + 2 = 6$. Total: $12 + 10 + 16 + 6 = 44$. The transferable idea: read the key first, and work out what a part of a symbol is worth.
solutions.elegant: Two half circles make one whole, so there are 11 whole circles in all, and $11 \times 4 = 44$.

problems.whyOnTest: Pictograms test reading a key and handling a part-symbol, the two steps students most often skip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The chart shows how many cups of cocoa a cafe sold each day. From one day to the next day, what was the biggest increase in the number of cups sold?

figure.alt: A bar chart of cups of cocoa sold on five days. The vertical axis is gridded in ones and labelled 0 to 14 in steps of 2. Monday 6, Tuesday 12, Wednesday 3, Thursday 10, Friday 14.

choices.misconception: I worked out the first rise, from Monday to Tuesday, and stopped there.
I compared Friday with Monday, the last bar with the first, instead of neighbouring days.
I found the biggest change between neighbouring days, but that was the fall from Tuesday to Wednesday, not a rise.
I took the shortest bar away from the tallest bar, 14 minus 3.

hints: Compare each day only with the day just before it.
Write down the change for each pair of neighbouring days, and mark which ones go up and which go down. The question wants the biggest one that goes up.
The changes are: up 6, down 9, up 7, up 4.

solutions.reliable: Read the bars: 6, 12, 3, 10, 14. Changes: Monday to Tuesday up 6, Tuesday to Wednesday down 9, Wednesday to Thursday up 7, Thursday to Friday up 4. The biggest increase is 7. The transferable idea: re-read whether the question wants a rise, a fall, or any change.

problems.whyOnTest: Reading a bar chart carefully and answering exactly what is asked: a rise between neighbouring days, not just the biggest gap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bus has 26 passengers. At the first stop, 9 get off and 5 get on. At the second stop, 7 get off and 12 get on. How many passengers are on the bus now?

choices.misconception: I worked out the first stop correctly but forgot about the second stop.
I mixed up the two kinds: I added the people who got off and took away the people who got on.
I mixed up getting on and off at the first stop, but did the second stop correctly.
I added every number in the problem, as if everyone who got off also stayed on.

hints: People getting off make the number smaller.
Go one stop at a time: take away the people who get off, then add the people who get on.
After the first stop there are $26 - 9 + 5 = 22$ passengers.

solutions.reliable: First stop: $26 - 9 + 5 = 22$. Second stop: $22 - 7 + 12 = 27$. The transferable idea: follow the story in order, one change at a time.
solutions.elegant: Altogether $9 + 7 = 16$ got off and $5 + 12 = 17$ got on, so the bus gained 1 passenger: $26 + 1 = 27$.

problems.whyOnTest: A multi-step story where each step changes the total, testing careful tracking of increases and decreases.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A garden has 6 rows of 8 tulips. Of these, 15 are red, and there are twice as many yellow tulips as red ones. The rest are white. How many tulips are white?

choices.misconception: I read "twice as many" as "2 more", so I took the yellow tulips as 15 + 2 = 17.
I took away 15 for the red tulips and only 15 for the yellow ones, forgetting to double.
I worked out the number of yellow tulips and gave that as the answer.
I only took away the red tulips and forgot the yellow ones.

hints: How many tulips are there in the whole garden?
Find the total first, then the number of yellow tulips, then take away both red and yellow to leave the white ones.
There are $6 \times 8 = 48$ tulips and $2 \times 15 = 30$ yellow ones.

solutions.reliable: Total: $6 \times 8 = 48$. Yellow: $2 \times 15 = 30$. Red and yellow together: $15 + 30 = 45$. White: $48 - 45 = 3$. The transferable idea: in a part-whole story, find the whole, find every known part, and subtract.
solutions.elegant: Red and yellow together are three times the red, $3 \times 15 = 45$, so white is $48 - 45 = 3$.

problems.whyOnTest: Several small steps in a row, where "twice as many" and "the rest" each hide a step that is easy to miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Pens cost 3 euros each, or 8 euros for a pack of 4. Nia needs at least 11 pens, and spare pens are fine. What is the least amount she can spend, in euros?

choices.misconception: I worked out that a pen in a pack costs 2 euros and multiplied by 11, but pens cannot be bought for 2 euros on their own.
I bought exactly 11 pens, 2 packs and 3 single pens, and did not think of buying a spare.
I bought one pack of 4 and then 7 single pens.
I bought 11 single pens, without using any packs.

hints: Do you have to buy exactly 11?
Compare the price of a pack with the price of the same number of single pens. Then list the ways to get at least 11 pens and cost each one.
Two packs and 3 single pens cost $16 + 9 = 25$ euros. Is a third pack cheaper than 3 single pens?

solutions.reliable: Packs are cheaper per pen, so use as many as sensible. Two packs give 8 pens; 3 more single pens cost 9 euros, total 25 euros. A third pack instead costs only 8 euros and gives 12 pens, total $3 \times 8 = 24$ euros. Four packs cost 32, and fewer packs cost more (1 pack and 7 singles is 29, 11 singles is 33). The least is 24 euros. The transferable idea: when spares are allowed, buying a little more can cost less.
solutions.elegant: Three single pens cost 9 euros, but a whole pack of 4 costs only 8 euros, so whenever you would need 3 single pens, a pack is cheaper. That gives 3 packs for 24 euros.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparing deals needs a careful list of options, and the trap is assuming you must buy exactly what you need.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers can be divided exactly by 12?

choices.misconception: I thought a number divides by 12 if it starts with the digits 1 and 2.
I thought a number divides by 12 when its last two digits, here 36, make a multiple of 12.
I thought a number divides by 12 when its digits add up to 12.
I thought dividing by 12 only needs the number to divide by 2 and by 6, and 618 does.

hints: 12 is 3 times 4.
A number divides by 12 exactly when it divides by both 3 and 4. Use the digit-sum rule for 3 and the last-two-digits rule for 4.
For 540, the digits add to 9 and the last two digits make 40.

solutions.reliable: Check 3 (digit sum) and 4 (last two digits). 128: digit sum 11, fails 3. 236: digit sum 11, fails 3. 471: odd, fails 4. 618: 18 is not a multiple of 4, fails 4. 540: digit sum 9 passes 3, and 40 is a multiple of 4, so 540 divides by 12 ($540 = 12 \times 45$). The transferable idea: to test a number like 12, split it into factors with no common factor, here 3 and 4, and test each.

problems.whyOnTest: Divisibility by 12 combines the rules for 3 and 4; the trap is that 2 and 6 share a factor, so they are not enough.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Using each of the digits 1, 2, 3 and 4 exactly once, Max makes four-digit numbers. How many of these numbers can be divided exactly by 4?

choices.misconception: I found the three possible endings, 12, 24 and 32, but forgot the first two digits can be swapped.
I found the endings 12 and 32 but missed 24, then swapped the first two digits.
I counted the even numbers, the ones ending in 2 or 4, as if every even number divides by 4.
I counted all the numbers that can be made, without checking which divide by 4.

hints: Only the last two digits matter for 4.
A number divides by 4 when its last two digits make a multiple of 4. List the possible endings from these digits, then count the ways to fill the front.
The endings can be 12, 24 or 32. Each leaves two digits for the front.

solutions.reliable: The last two digits must be a multiple of 4 made from two different digits of 1, 2, 3, 4: that gives 12, 24 and 32 (but not 14, 34, 42 or the others). For each ending, the two leftover digits can go in front in 2 orders. Total: $3 \times 2 = 6$. They are 3412, 4312, 1324, 3124, 1432, 4132. The transferable idea: use the divisibility rule to fix the end, then multiply by the ways to fill the rest.

problems.whyOnTest: The last-two-digits rule for 4 turns a long list into a short count: fix the ending, then multiply.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

choices.misconception: I thought that adding and taking away numbers that are so close together cancels out to nothing.
I worked out $1000 - 999 = 1$ and thought the whole thing would come to that same 1.
I made pairs that each give 1, but only counted two of the three pairs.
I thought each pair like $1000 - 999$ makes 2, because the numbers go down by 2 each time.

hints: Look at the numbers two at a time.
Group the calculation into pairs: a number minus the number just below it. Each pair is easy to work out.

solutions.reliable: Group into pairs: $(1000 - 999) + (998 - 997) + (996 - 995) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3$. The transferable idea: regroup a long calculation into pairs that are easy to work out.

problems.whyOnTest: Clever regrouping turns a scary calculation with big numbers into three easy pairs.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana adds up all the numbers from 1 to 10. Bo adds up all the numbers from 11 to 20. How much bigger is Bo's total than Ana's?

choices.misconception: I thought Bo's total is just 10 more, because his numbers start 10 higher.
I worked out Ana's total and gave that as the answer.
I worked out Bo's total and stopped there.
I added both totals together instead of finding the difference.

hints: Match each of Bo's numbers with one of Ana's.
Pair 11 with 1, 12 with 2, and so on. Each of Bo's numbers is bigger than its partner by the same amount. Count the pairs.
There are 10 pairs, and in each pair Bo's number is 10 bigger.

solutions.reliable: Ana: $1 + 2 + \dots + 10 = 55$. Bo: $11 + 12 + \dots + 20 = 155$. Difference: $155 - 55 = 100$. The transferable idea: two lists that match up term by term differ by the sum of the gaps.
solutions.elegant: Pair each of Bo's numbers with one of Ana's: 11 with 1, 12 with 2, up to 20 with 10. Each pair differs by 10, and there are 10 pairs, so Bo is $10 \times 10 = 100$ ahead without adding anything up.
