The transferable idea: in a tree, a rule that bans one combination removes one path, not a whole branch.
solutions.elegant: Count shirt by shirt: red goes with 2 shorts, yellow with 2, and blue and white with 3 each, so 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 10.

problems.whyOnTest: Crossing out a whole branch instead of one path, or adding instead of multiplying, are the classic tree-counting slips.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sam tosses a coin and writes H for heads or T for tails each time. He stops as soon as he gets two heads in a row, or after his fourth toss, whichever comes first. For example, THH is one possible record. How many different records are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted only the records that end with two heads in a row: HH, THH, TTHH and HTHH.
I counted only the records with no two heads in a row, the ones where Sam runs out of tosses.
I counted only the records that are four tosses long and forgot the short ones, HH and THH.
I listed every pattern of four tosses and ignored that Sam stops early after two heads in a row.

hints: Draw a tree, and end a branch as soon as it shows HH.
Each toss splits a branch into H and T, but a branch ends early the moment it has two heads in a row. Count the ends of all the branches, short ones included.
HH ends after 2 tosses and THH after 3. Five branches are still going after 3 tosses.

solutions.reliable: Build the tree. After 2 tosses, HH stops: 1 record. After 3 tosses, of the branches still going (HT, TH, TT), only THH stops: 1 record. The branches still going after 3 tosses are HTH, HTT, THT, TTH and TTT, which is 5 branches, and each splits in 2 at the fourth toss: 10 records. Total 1 + 1 + 10 = 12. The transferable idea: in a tree with a stopping rule, count the ends of the branches, wherever they end.
solutions.elegant: Start from all 16 four-toss patterns. The 4 patterns beginning HH all collapse into the single record HH, and the 2 beginning THH collapse into THH. So 16 - 4 - 2 + 1 + 1 = 12.

problems.whyOnTest: A tree whose branches can stop early tests whether you count every ending, not just the longest paths.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many different triangles have whole-number side lengths and a perimeter of 14? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as the same triangle.

choices.misconception: I thought a triangle had to have three different side lengths, so I only kept 3, 5, 6.
I let the two shorter sides add up to exactly the longest side, like 2, 5, 7, which lies flat.
I counted the same triangle again each time its sides were listed in a different order.
I listed every way to split 14 into three whole numbers and never checked whether they make a triangle.

hints: List sides from shortest to longest, and try longest sides one at a time.
Casework on the longest side keeps the list complete. The two shorter sides must add up to more than the longest, so the longest side is less than half the perimeter.
The longest side is less than 7 and at least 5. Try longest side 6, then longest side 5.

solutions.reliable: List the sides from shortest to longest. For a triangle the two shorter sides must add up to more than the longest, so the longest side is less than half of 14, which means at most 6. It is also at least 5, because three sides each 4 or less add up to at most 12. Longest side 6: the other two add to 8 and are at most 6: 2 and 6, 3 and 5, 4 and 4. Longest side 5: the other two add to 9 and are at most 5: only 4 and 5. That gives 2-6-6, 3-5-6, 4-4-6 and 4-5-5: 4 triangles. The transferable idea: split into cases by the largest part, and check the triangle rule once, on the longest side.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework on the longest side, plus the rule that two sides must beat the third, is the standard way to count triangles without gaps or repeats.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers have digits that multiply to 12? For example, 341 is one of them.

choices.misconception: I found the three sets of digits, 1-2-6, 1-3-4 and 2-2-3, and forgot that each set can be arranged in several orders.
I missed the digits 1, 3, 4, so I only counted 6 orders of 1, 2, 6 and 3 orders of 2, 2, 3.
I missed the set 2, 2, 3 because I only looked for three different digits.
I counted 6 orders for 2, 2, 3 as well, not noticing that swapping the two 2s gives the same number.

hints: First find which sets of digits work, then count orders.
Split into cases by the set of three digits. Three different digits can be ordered in several ways, but a set with a repeated digit has fewer different orders.
The sets are 1, 2, 6 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 2, 3. Count the orders of each separately.

solutions.reliable: No digit can be 0, and every digit must divide 12. The sets of three digits with product 12 are 1, 2, 6 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 2, 3 (1, 1, 12 fails because 12 is not a digit). Three different digits give 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 orders each, so 12 numbers from the first two sets. The set 2, 2, 3 gives only 3 orders: 223, 232, 322. Total 6 + 6 + 3 = 15. The transferable idea: in casework, count each case by its own rule, and watch for repeated items, which reduce the number of orders.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework by digit set, then counting orders, rewards a careful list and punishes mishandling a repeated digit in either direction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a die, opposite faces add up to 7. A die sits on a table with 1 on top, 2 on the face towards you and 3 on the right. It is tipped over once to the right, then once away from you. Which number is now on top?

choices.misconception: I thought tipping one way and then another way would undo each other, so 1 came back to the top.
I did the first tip correctly, which puts 4 on top, and forgot the second tip.
I thought tipping away from me brings the back face up to the top, when it is the front face that comes up.
I thought two tips turn the die upside down, so the bottom face 6 ends up on top.

hints: Track just two faces: the top and the one facing you.
When a die tips to the right, the face on its left rises to the top. When it tips away from you, the face towards you rises. Use the rule about opposite faces to name the hidden ones.
The left face is 7 - 3 = 4, so after the first tip 4 is on top and 2 still faces you.

solutions.reliable: At the start: top 1, front 2, right 3, so left 4, back 5, bottom 6. Tipping to the right rolls the top over onto the right and lifts the left face up, so 4 is on top. The front face stays at 2, because the die rolled sideways. Tipping away from you rolls the top over to the back and lifts the front face up, so 2 is now on top. The transferable idea: for a rolling die, ask which face rises, and it is always the face on the side opposite the direction of the roll.
solutions.elegant: The second tip lifts whatever faces you, and a sideways tip never changes the face towards you. So the answer is simply the original front face, 2.

problems.whyOnTest: Rolling a die tests whether you can track faces through turns, using the opposite-faces rule for the ones you cannot see.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a die, opposite faces add up to 7. A die sits on a table showing 5 on top and 3 on the face towards you. What is the sum of the numbers on its left face and its right face?

choices.misconception: I found the bottom face 2 and the back face 4 and added those instead of the left and right faces.
I added the two numbers I was given, 5 and 3.
I took 21 and subtracted the top and front, which adds up the left, right, bottom and back faces together.
I thought I needed to know which number is on the left before I could find the sum.

hints: Where are the left and right faces compared with each other?
Left and right are opposite faces, just like top and bottom. Think about what the rule for opposite faces says, whichever numbers they turn out to be.
Left and right are a pair of opposite faces, and every pair of opposite faces has the same total.

solutions.reliable: The left face and the right face are opposite each other, and on this die every pair of opposite faces adds up to 7. So the left and right faces add to 7, even though we cannot tell which is which. (Top 5 with bottom 2, and front 3 with back 4, use up the other two pairs, so left and right are 1 and 6 in some order.) The transferable idea: notice when a question only needs a total, which can be fixed even when the separate values are not.

problems.whyOnTest: The given numbers are a distraction, and the opposite-faces rule answers the question directly, a common shape for 3-point dice questions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A net is made of 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. It folds up into a closed solid with no gaps or overlaps. How many edges does the solid have?

choices.misconception: I counted the sides around the outside of the flat net, but two outside sides join up to make one edge.
I counted the 3 sides of each triangle and then 2 long sides of each rectangle, so each long edge shared by two rectangles was counted twice.
I counted all 18 sides of the pieces and took away only the 4 fold lines, as if the other sides did not pair up.
I counted every side of every piece, but each edge of the solid is where two sides meet.

hints: Count the sides of all five pieces together.
When the net folds up, every edge of the solid is made by two sides of the pieces meeting. Count all the sides first, then allow for that pairing.
The pieces have 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 18 sides altogether. Each edge uses two of them.

solutions.reliable: The solid is a triangular prism: two triangle ends joined by three rectangles. The two triangles give 3 + 3 = 6 edges, and three long edges run between their corners, giving 9 edges in all. The transferable idea: every edge of a closed solid is shared by exactly two faces, which lets you count edges from the flat pieces.
solutions.elegant: The pieces have 2 x 3 + 3 x 4 = 18 sides. Every edge of the closed solid is shared by exactly two faces, so there are 18 / 2 = 9 edges, without needing to picture the solid at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Nets test whether you can see flat pieces becoming a solid, and halving the total number of sides is a reliable way to count edges.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seen from directly above, a building made of unit cubes looks like a full 3 by 3 square. Seen from the front, it looks 3 cubes tall on the left, 2 cubes tall in the middle and 1 cube tall on the right. What is the largest number of cubes the building can contain?

choices.misconception: I counted only the cubes I can see in the front view, 3 + 2 + 1, and forgot the stacks behind them.
I used only the view from above and put one cube on each of the 9 squares.
I found the smallest possible number of cubes instead of the largest.
I filled a whole 3 by 3 by 3 block, which would look 3 cubes tall all the way across from the front.

hints: Behind each part of the front view are three stacks.
The front view only shows the tallest stack in each strip of three squares running away from you. To make the most cubes, make every stack as tall as its strip allows.
The three stacks in the left strip can each be 3 tall, the middle strip 2 tall, the right strip 1 tall.

solutions.reliable: From the front, the height you see on the left is the tallest stack among the three squares of the left strip running away from you, and the same for the middle and right strips. The view from above says every one of the 9 squares has at least one cube. For the most cubes, make all three stacks in the left strip 3 tall, all three in the middle strip 2 tall, and all three in the right strip 1 tall: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18. This still looks like a full 3 by 3 square from above and shows heights 3, 2, 1 from the front. The transferable idea: a view only fixes the tallest stack behind each point, so the largest count fills every hidden stack up to that height.

problems.whyOnTest: Two views never pin down a solid exactly, so the test asks for the largest or smallest count to see whether you know what a view hides.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A strip 2 squares tall and 5 squares long is to be covered exactly by five 1 by 2 tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps. Each tile may stand upright or lie flat. In how many different ways can this be done?

choices.misconception: I counted 1 way with no flat tiles, 4 ways with one stacked pair of flat tiles, and 6 ways to pick 2 of the 4 places for two stacked pairs, without noticing that neighbouring places overlap.
I found the pattern 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 for longer and longer strips and took one term too many.
I treated each of the 4 places where a stacked pair of flat tiles could go as simply used or not, 2 x 2 x 2 x 2, without checking overlaps.
I thought each of the 5 columns could be filled in 2 ways on its own, upright or flat, giving 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2.

hints: Try shorter strips first: 2 by 1, 2 by 2, 2 by 3.
Look at the left end. Either one upright tile covers the first column, or two flat tiles stacked together cover the first two columns. That links each strip to the two shorter strips.
Strips of length 1, 2 and 3 have 1, 2 and 3 tilings. Each new count is the sum of the two before it.

solutions.reliable: Look at the leftmost column not yet covered. Either one upright tile fills it, or a flat tile covers its top square, and then the square below can only be covered by another flat tile directly underneath. So flat tiles always come in stacked pairs covering two neighbouring columns. Count by the number of stacked pairs: none gives 1 tiling; one pair can sit in columns 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 or 4-5, giving 4; two pairs fit without overlapping in columns 1-2 and 3-4, 1-2 and 4-5, or 2-3 and 4-5, giving 3. Total 1 + 4 + 3 = 8. The transferable idea: in a tiling count, decide what covers one end, which breaks the problem into smaller cases.
solutions.elegant: An upright tile at the left end leaves a 2 by 4 strip, and a stacked pair leaves a 2 by 3 strip. So the count for length 5 is the count for length 4 plus the count for length 3. Starting from 1 and 2 for lengths 1 and 2, the counts go 3, 5, 8.

problems.whyOnTest: Small tiling counts grow in a pattern, and seeing that each strip builds on the two shorter ones is a classic 5-point idea.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A long strip of paper is folded in half, and then folded in half again, so it is 4 layers thick. Two straight cuts are made across the folded strip, neither of them on a fold. How many pieces of paper are there now?

choices.misconception: I ignored the folding and counted two cuts across a single strip, which gives 3 pieces.
I worked out what one cut does to the folded strip and forgot about the second cut.
I counted the places where the unfolded strip is cut, but there is one more piece than there are cuts.
I thought each cut makes 5 pieces, so two cuts make 5 + 5, but the two cuts share pieces between them.

hints: Unfold it in your head: where along the strip is it cut?
Each cut goes through every layer, so it cuts the unfolded strip in several places. A strip cut in some number of places falls into one more piece than that number.
Each cut goes through 4 layers, so the unfolded strip is cut in 4 places per cut.

solutions.reliable: The folded strip has 4 layers, and a straight cut across it goes through each layer once, making 4 cuts in the unfolded strip. Two cuts make 8 cut points, all at different places along the strip because neither cut is on a fold. A strip cut at 8 points falls into 8 + 1 = 9 pieces. The transferable idea: when folded paper is cut, unfold the cuts, count the cut points along the strip, and add one.
solutions.elegant: Check the rule on a smaller case you can test with real paper: one fold and one cut gives 2 cut points and 3 pieces. The same rule, pieces equal cut points plus one, gives 8 + 1 = 9 here.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding multiplies every cut, and the unfold-then-count method avoids both forgetting layers and the off-by-one at the end.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ada, Bo, Cy and Di each either always tell the truth or always lie. Ada says: "Bo is a liar." Bo says: "Cy is a liar." Cy says: "Di is a liar." Di says: "Ada and Bo are both liars." Who tells the truth?

choices.misconception: I assumed Ada lies and followed the chain to Di, but never checked whether Di's own statement then holds.
I decided Di was telling the truth because Bo really is a liar, forgetting that both needs Ada to be a liar too.
I thought that in a chain of people calling each other liars, they must all be lying.

choices.text: It could be Ada and Cy, or it could be Bo and Di
choices.misconception: I saw that the chain alternates whichever way it starts and did not test either case against Di's statement.

hints: Suppose Ada lies, and follow the chain.
Each statement about one person passes truth or lies along the chain. Try both possibilities for Ada, and keep only the one where Di's statement agrees with what Di is.
If Ada lies, then Bo tells the truth, Cy lies and Di tells the truth. Check Di's claim in that case.

solutions.reliable: Suppose Ada lies. Then Bo is not a liar, so Bo tells the truth, so Cy lies, so Di tells the truth. But then Di's statement "Ada and Bo are both liars" must be true, and Bo is not a liar. That is impossible, so Ada tells the truth. Then Bo lies, Cy tells the truth and Di lies. Check Di: "Ada and Bo are both liars" is false because Ada tells the truth, which fits Di being a liar. The truth-tellers are Ada and Cy. The transferable idea: in liar puzzles, try one case, follow every statement, and throw out the case that contradicts itself.

problems.whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles test whether you follow a chain of consequences all the way and check the last statement rather than stopping early.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six different whole numbers, each bigger than 0, add up to 22. Which of these statements must be true?

choices.text: The largest of the numbers is 7

choices.misconception: I started from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and assumed the 6 had to stay in the list.

choices.text: Exactly three of the numbers are even
choices.misconception: I counted the even numbers in 1 to 6 without noticing that the 6 has to change.

choices.text: Several different lists of six numbers are possible
choices.misconception: I thought there must be many ways to share out 22, and did not test what happens if a small number is missing.

choices.text: No such list of six numbers exists
choices.misconception: I saw that 1 to 6 already adds up to 21 and thought there was no room to change anything.

hints: What is the smallest total six different whole numbers can have?
The six smallest different whole numbers already add up to almost 22. Suppose one of the numbers 1 to 5 is missing, and show that the total is then too big.
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, so there is only 1 to spare. Where can that 1 go?

solutions.reliable: The six smallest different whole numbers bigger than 0 are 1 to 6, which add up to 21. Suppose one of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 were missing from the list. Then the best we can do is the other five of 1 to 6 together with 7, and the total is at least 28 - 5 = 23, which is too much. So 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are all in the list, and the sixth number is 22 - 15 = 7. The list must be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, so the largest number is 7. The transferable idea: assume the opposite, show it forces the total over the limit, and the assumption is ruled out.
solutions.elegant: There is only 1 to spare above the smallest possible total of 21, so exactly one number of 1 to 6 goes up by 1. Raising any number except the 6 would make two numbers equal, so the 6 becomes a 7.

problems.whyOnTest: Pushing numbers to their smallest possible values and showing nothing else fits is the heart of many 5-point arguments by contradiction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a test, a wrong answer costs nothing. Kai has 4 unanswered 5-point questions, each with 5 choices. On every one he can rule out one choice he knows is wrong, and he guesses among the rest. On average, how many points will his guesses earn him?

choices.misconception: I thought a guess is worth the same as a blank, because a guess might be wrong.
I worked out that he expects 1 correct answer, 4 times 1 in 4, and forgot each one is worth 5 points.
I worked out the average for one question, 5 points times 1 in 4, and forgot there are four questions.
I used a 1 in 5 chance on each question, forgetting that he has ruled one choice out.

hints: After ruling one out, how many choices are left on each question?
With no penalty, a guess on average earns its chance of being right times the points it is worth. Add that up over all the questions.
Each guess has a 1 in 4 chance, and each question is worth 5 points, so each guess is worth 5/4 points on average.

solutions.reliable: Each question has 4 choices left, so a guess is right 1 time in 4. On average each guess earns 5 x 1/4 = 1.25 points, and four questions give 4 x 1.25 = 5 points. A blank earns 0. The transferable idea: with no penalty for a wrong answer, every guess is worth more than a blank, and ruling out a choice makes it worth even more.
solutions.elegant: Four guesses, each with a 1 in 4 chance, give one correct answer on average, and one correct answer is worth 5 points.

problems.whyOnTest: Math Kangaroo takes nothing off for a wrong answer, so knowing what a guess is worth turns blanks into real points.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which number is made of 3 thousands, 14 hundreds, 5 tens and 12 ones?

choices.misconception: I treated 14 hundreds as 140, mixing up hundreds and tens.
I wrote 4 in the hundreds place for the 14 hundreds and dropped the extra thousand.
I added 5 for the 5 tens instead of 50.
I wrote 2 in the ones place for the 12 ones and dropped the extra ten.

hints: Turn each part into an ordinary number before adding.
Some parts have more than 9 of a kind, so they spill over into the next place. Write each part as a plain number, then add them all.
14 hundreds is 1400 and 12 ones is 12. Add 3000, 1400, 50 and 12.

solutions.reliable: 3 thousands is 3000, 14 hundreds is 1400, 5 tens is 50 and 12 ones is 12. Adding: 3000 + 1400 + 50 + 12 = 4462. The transferable idea: when a place holds 10 or more, regroup it into the next place up before writing the digits.
solutions.elegant: Regroup first: 14 hundreds is 1 thousand and 4 hundreds, and 12 ones is 1 ten and 2 ones. That makes 4 thousands, 4 hundreds, 6 tens and 2 ones: 4462.

problems.whyOnTest: Places holding more than 9 test whether you understand regrouping, not just reading digits off in order.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each box in the four-digit number 5□3□ is filled with a digit (the two digits may be the same). The number must be divisible by both 4 and 9. How many different numbers can be made?

choices.misconception: I found one number that works and stopped without looking for others.
I tested divisibility by 4 by checking that the last digit is 0, 4 or 8, instead of checking the last two digits.
I thought divisible by 4 just means even, so I let the last digit be 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
I used the rule for 3, a digit sum that is a multiple of 3, instead of the rule for 9.

hints: Use the last two digits for 4 and the digit sum for 9.
Divisibility by 4 depends only on the number made by the last two digits, which narrows down the last box. Then the digit sum must be a multiple of 9, which fixes the other box.
The last two digits must make 32 or 36. Then 5 + box + 3 + 2, or 5 + box + 3 + 6, must be 18.

solutions.reliable: For 4: the last two digits make a number from 30 to 39 that is divisible by 4, so they are 32 or 36. For 9: the digit sum must be a multiple of 9. With last digit 2, the sum is 10 plus the missing digit, which must be 18, so the digit is 8: 5832. With last digit 6, the sum is 14 plus the missing digit, which must be 18, so the digit is 4: 5436. That is exactly 2 numbers. The transferable idea: apply the most restrictive rule first, then let the next rule fix what is left.

problems.whyOnTest: Combining two divisibility rules, and using each one correctly, is a staple of Kangaroo number questions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A three-digit number has three different digits, and its tens digit is the sum of its hundreds digit and its units digit. What is the largest such number?

choices.misconception: I found the smallest such number instead of the largest.
I made the units digit the sum of the other two digits instead of the tens digit.
I made the hundreds digit the sum of the other two digits instead of the tens digit.
I forgot that the three digits must all be different, and 9 + 0 = 9 repeats the 9.

hints: Make the hundreds digit as big as you can, then check.
Go greedy on the hundreds digit, but remember the tens digit is a sum, so it can be at most 9. Test each choice of hundreds digit against the rule that all digits differ.
With hundreds digit 9, the units digit must be 0 and the tens digit is then 9 again. Try hundreds digit 8.

solutions.reliable: The tens digit equals hundreds plus units, and it is at most 9. Hundreds digit 9 forces units digit 0 and tens digit 9, which repeats the 9, so it fails. Hundreds digit 8: units 0 gives tens 8, a repeat, while units 1 gives tens 9, and 891 has three different digits. No number starting with 8 can have a tens digit bigger than 9, so 891 is the largest. The transferable idea: to find the largest, fix the leading digit as high as the rules allow, then the next digit, checking every rule as you go.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles reward a greedy search from the left, but only if every condition is checked, including that the digits differ.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A ribbon is cut into two pieces. The long piece is 3 times as long as the short piece, and it is also 24 cm longer than the short piece. How long was the ribbon before it was cut?

choices.misconception: I found the length of the short piece and gave that.
I took the long piece to be 24 cm, so the short one was 8 cm, but 24 cm is the difference, not the long piece.
I found the length of the long piece and forgot to add the short one.
I took the short piece to be 24 cm, so the long one was 72 cm, but 24 cm is the difference between them.

hints: Draw a bar for each piece, made of equal blocks.
Draw the short piece as one block and the long piece as three equal blocks. The extra part of the long bar is exactly the 24 cm difference.
The difference is 2 blocks, which is 24 cm, so one block is 12 cm.

solutions.reliable: Short piece = 1 block, long piece = 3 blocks. The long piece is 2 blocks longer, and that is 24 cm, so 1 block is 12 cm. The ribbon is 1 + 3 = 4 blocks, which is 48 cm. Check: the pieces are 12 cm and 36 cm, and 36 is 3 times 12 and also 24 more. The transferable idea: a bar model turns 'times as long' and 'longer by' into blocks you can count.

problems.whyOnTest: Part-whole problems mix a ratio with a difference, and a bar model shows exactly which blocks the difference covers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Beads are threaded in the repeating pattern red, blue, green, blue, blue, red, blue, green, blue, blue, and so on. How many of the first 83 beads are blue?

choices.misconception: I counted the beads that are not blue instead of the blue ones.
I counted 16 full rounds of 5 beads with 3 blue each and forgot the 3 beads left over.
I took the 3 leftover beads from the end of the pattern, green, blue, blue, instead of from the start.
I rounded 83 divided by 5 up to 17 full rounds, as if the last round were complete.

hints: How many beads are in one round of the pattern?
Split the 83 beads into complete rounds of the pattern plus a few left over. Count the blues in the complete rounds, then look at the leftover beads, which start a new round.
83 = 16 x 5 + 3. The 3 leftover beads are red, blue, green.

solutions.reliable: One round is 5 beads, 3 of them blue. 83 = 16 x 5 + 3, so there are 16 full rounds with 16 x 3 = 48 blue beads, then 3 more beads that start a new round: red, blue, green, with 1 blue. Total 48 + 1 = 49. The transferable idea: for a repeating pattern, divide by the length of one round and read the remainder from the start of the pattern.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeating patterns test dividing with a remainder and then reading the leftover from the correct end of the cycle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bakery packs muffins in boxes of 6 and sells only full boxes. Muffins left over at the end of a day are given away. On Monday it bakes 100 muffins, and on Tuesday it bakes 10 more than on Monday. How many full boxes does it sell over the two days?

choices.misconception: I worked out Tuesday's boxes only and forgot to add Monday's.
I used 100 muffins for both days and forgot that Tuesday had 10 more.
I added both days' muffins first, 210, and divided by 6, but Monday's leftovers are given away and cannot help fill a box on Tuesday.
I rounded each day's boxes up, to 17 and 19, as if a part-full box could be sold.

hints: Work out each day on its own.
Leftover muffins do not carry over to the next day, so each day is a separate division with a remainder. Count only the full boxes each day, then add.

solutions.reliable: Monday: 100 muffins fill 16 boxes (96 muffins), with 4 left over and given away. Tuesday: 110 muffins fill 18 boxes (108 muffins), with 2 left over. Total 16 + 18 = 34 boxes. The transferable idea: in a multi-step problem, notice when a remainder is thrown away at each step instead of being saved up.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding first and dividing once looks quicker, but the leftovers here do not combine, so the order of the steps changes the answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five children each either always tell the truth or always lie. Each of them says: "Among the other four children, there are more liars than truth-tellers." How many of the five tell the truth?

choices.misconception: I assumed that children who all say the same thing must all be liars, without checking that the statement would then be true.
I checked that one truth-teller's statement works but never checked what the four liars would be saying.
I found that there are 3 liars and gave that instead of the number of truth-tellers.
I thought several different numbers of truth-tellers could work, without testing each one.

hints: Pick a number of liars, then check one truth-teller and one liar.
A truth-teller sees every liar among the others, while a liar sees one liar fewer, since a liar does not count themselves. Write what each kind needs, and find the total that satisfies both at once.
A truth-teller needs at least 3 liars among the other four. A liar's statement must be false, so a liar sees at most 2 other liars.

solutions.reliable: Let L be the number of liars. A truth-teller sees L liars among the other four, and needs more liars than truth-tellers, so L is at least 3. A liar sees L - 1 liars among the others, and the statement must be false, so L - 1 is at most 2, which means L is at most 3. If there is at least one of each kind, L is at least 3 and at most 3, so L = 3 and 2 children tell the truth. The other cases fail: if all five told the truth, each would see 0 liars, making the statement false; if all five lied, each would see 4 liars and 0 truth-tellers, making the statement true. So exactly 2 tell the truth. The transferable idea: in liar puzzles about counts, write the condition for a truth-teller and for a liar separately and find the count that meets both.
solutions.elegant: Test 2 truth-tellers and 3 liars: a truth-teller sees 3 liars and 1 truth-teller, so the statement is true, as it should be; a liar sees 2 liars and 2 truth-tellers, so the statement is false, as it should be. Every other total fails one of these two checks.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting liars tests whether you check the statement from both kinds of speaker, since a liar sees one fewer liar than a truth-teller does.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A table has rows numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on. Row 1 lists 1. Row 2 lists 2, 4. Row 3 lists 3, 6, 9. In general, row n lists the first n multiples of n. How many of the first 40 rows contain the number 36?

choices.misconception: I paired up the factors of 36 as 1 and 36, 2 and 18, 3 and 12, 4 and 9, and counted one row for each pair, but forgot 6 times 6, which pairs 6 with itself.
I left out only row 1, assuming every other row whose number is a factor of 36 reaches 36.
I counted every factor of 36, forgetting that row n stops at n times n.
I counted both numbers of each of the 5 factor pairs of 36 as rows, so 6 was counted twice and short rows were included.

hints: Which rows could contain 36 at all?
36 can only appear in a row whose number divides 36. But each row stops at its own number times itself, so check that 36 is not past the end of the row.
Row n reaches 36 only if n times n is at least 36, so n must be at least 6. Which factors of 36 are 6 or more?

solutions.reliable: 36 is in row n exactly when n divides 36 and 36 is not past the last entry, n times n. So n must divide 36 and be at least 6. The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36, and those that are 6 or more are 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36. All are within the first 40 rows, so 5 rows. Check one that fails: row 4 is 4, 8, 12, 16 and stops long before 36. The transferable idea: in a table, find the rule for what a row contains and the rule for where it stops, and apply both.
solutions.elegant: Each factor pair of 36 puts 36 in exactly one row, the row of the larger factor: 36 x 1 is in row 36, 18 x 2 in row 18, 12 x 3 in row 12, 9 x 4 in row 9 and 6 x 6 in row 6. Five pairs give five rows.

problems.whyOnTest: Table questions often hide two rules, what a row contains and where it stops, and missing either one lands on a listed choice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A standard die, whose opposite faces add up to 7, sits on a table with 1 on top and 2 on the face pointing towards you. You tip it over away from you three times in a row. Which number is on top now?

choices.misconception: I thought three tips bring the die all the way round, so the 1 comes back to the top.
I followed only the first tip, where the face pointing towards me rolls up to the top.
I thought the top number goes up by one with each tip, so 1 became 4.
I followed two tips, which puts the old bottom face on top, and forgot the third tip.

hints: Follow one tip at a time. Which face rises to the top?
When a die tips away from you, the face pointing towards you rolls up to the top. Only four faces take turns on top; use opposite faces adding to 7 to name the hidden ones.
The faces that come to the top in turn are the one towards you (2), then the bottom (6), then the far face, which is opposite 2, so 7 - 2 = 5.

solutions.reliable: Tipping away from you turns the die over its far bottom edge: the face towards you moves up to the top, the top moves to the far side, the far side moves to the bottom and the bottom comes round to face you. Only four faces take part: top 1, front 2, bottom 6 (opposite 1) and back 5 (opposite 2). After one tip 2 is on top, after two tips 6, after three tips 5. The transferable idea: when a die rolls in one direction only the four faces in that ring move, and opposite faces adding to 7 names the ones you cannot see.
solutions.elegant: Three quarter turns forward end in the same place as one quarter turn backward. Tipping the die once towards you would bring the far face to the top, and the far face is opposite 2, so it shows 5.

problems.whyOnTest: Dice questions test tracking faces in your head, using opposite faces adding to 7 to name the faces you cannot see.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Towers of cubes stand on a grid of 2 rows and 3 columns. From left to right, the back row has towers of 1, 3 and 2 cubes, and the front row has towers of 2, 1 and 1 cubes. Looking from straight in front, you see a flat shape made of squares. How many squares does it have?

choices.misconception: I gave the height of the tallest tower instead of counting the squares in the view.
I counted only the front row and forgot that taller towers behind it show above it.
I added the tallest tower in each row, 3 and 2, instead of looking at each column.
I counted one square for each tower, which is the view from above, not from the front.

hints: Look at one column at a time, front and back together.
From the front, a back tower hides behind the front tower in its column unless it is taller. So each column shows as many squares as its taller tower. Do this for all three columns and add.
The columns show the taller of 1 and 2, the taller of 3 and 1, and the taller of 2 and 1: that is 2, 3 and 2 squares.

solutions.reliable: Each column of the front view is as tall as the taller tower in that column, because the shorter one is hidden behind it. Left column: the taller of 1 and 2 is 2. Middle column: the taller of 3 and 1 is 3. Right column: the taller of 2 and 1 is 2. The view has 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 squares. The transferable idea: a view from one side keeps only the tallest tower in each line of sight.

problems.whyOnTest: Views questions check that you know what hides behind what: from the front, only the tallest tower in each column counts.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Floor tiles are equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons, all with the same side length. Which set of tiles can fit together around a single point, with no gaps and no overlaps?

choices.text: one hexagon, two squares and one triangle

choices.misconception: I gave the triangle a corner of 90 degrees, the same as a square, so the corners seemed to add to 360.
I took a hexagon's corner to be 135 degrees, so 135 + 135 + 90 seemed to make 360.
I treated the hexagon's corner as a right angle, so four right angles seemed to fill the point.
I took a triangle's corner to be 45 degrees, half a right angle, so four of them and two squares seemed to make 360.

hints: What must the corners meeting at one point add up to?
The corners around a point must total exactly 360 degrees. Find the corner angle of each kind of tile, then add up each set and see which one makes exactly 360.
A triangle's corner is 60 degrees, a square's is 90 and a hexagon's is 120. Add each set: only one reaches exactly 360.

solutions.reliable: The angles meeting at a point make a full turn, 360 degrees. The corners are: triangle 60, square 90, hexagon 120 (a regular hexagon splits into 6 equilateral triangles, and each of its corners is made of two 60-degree angles). Now add: three squares and a triangle make 330; two hexagons and a square make 330; a hexagon and three squares make 390; four triangles and two squares make 420; a hexagon, two squares and a triangle make 120 + 180 + 60 = 360. The transferable idea: tiles fit around a point exactly when their corner angles add to 360.
solutions.elegant: Measure every corner in triangle corners: a triangle is worth 1, a square 1 and a half, a hexagon 2, and a full turn 6. A hexagon (2), two squares (3) and a triangle (1) make exactly 6; every other set misses.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions come down to one fact, that angles around a point make 360 degrees, plus knowing the corner of each regular shape.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A paper strip of 8 equal squares in a row is numbered 1 to 8 from left to right. The right half is folded onto the left half, so 8 lies on 1. The folded strip is folded the same way again. A hole is punched through square 1 and all layers on it. Which squares have holes when unfolded?

choices.misconception: I followed the first fold but forgot the second one, so I only had two layers.
I thought all the holes stay in the left half of the strip, where the folded stack sat.
I thought the four holes would be spread out evenly, one in every second square.
I made the second fold put the pile next to square 1 on top of it, instead of the pile at the far end of the folded strip.

hints: Write down which squares lie on top of each other after the first fold.
After the first fold, 8 is on 1, 7 on 2, 6 on 3 and 5 on 4. The second fold brings the short strip’s far end onto its first square. Find every square in the pile over square 1.
The second fold puts the pile of squares 4 and 5 onto the pile of squares 1 and 8.

solutions.reliable: Track the squares. The first fold lays the right half on the left, end to end: 8 on 1, 7 on 2, 6 on 3 and 5 on 4. The folded strip is 4 squares long, with piles (1, 8), (2, 7), (3, 6) and (4, 5). The second fold lays its right half on its left half: pile (4, 5) lands on pile (1, 8), and pile (3, 6) lands on pile (2, 7). So the stack over square 1 holds squares 1, 8, 4 and 5, and the hole goes through all four. Check: the holes 1, 4, 5 and 8 sit symmetrically about the middle of the strip, as the first fold requires. The transferable idea: record which pieces lie on top of each other after each fold, then unfold by reading the record backwards.
solutions.elegant: Unfold one step at a time, mirroring each hole in its fold line. Undoing the second fold mirrors the hole in square 1 across the line between squares 2 and 3, giving square 4. Undoing the first fold mirrors squares 1 and 4 across the middle of the strip, giving squares 8 and 5.

problems.whyOnTest: Paper folding questions test tracking layers: each unfold mirrors every hole in its fold line, so the holes double each time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each of Pia, Quin and Rae is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Pia says: "Quin and I are the same type." Quin says: "Rae is a knave." Rae says: "Exactly one of us three is a knight." Who are the knights?

choices.misconception: I worked out that Quin must be a knight and then called the other two knaves without checking Rae's statement.
I trusted Rae and made her the one knight, without checking Pia's statement, which would then be true.
I believed every statement and did not notice that Quin calls Rae a knave.
I decided they were all knaves and missed that Pia's sentence would then be true.

hints: Look at Pia's statement. What does it tell you about Quin, whichever type Pia is?
If Pia is a knight, Quin is the same type as her. If Pia is a knave, her statement is false, so Quin is the opposite type to her. Work out Quin in both cases, then use what Quin says.
Quin is a knight either way, so Rae is a knave and Rae's statement is false. Now test whether Pia could be a knave.

solutions.reliable: Start with Pia. If Pia is a knight, her statement is true, so Quin is a knight too. If Pia is a knave, her statement is false, so Quin is the opposite type to a knave, which is a knight. Either way Quin is a knight. Quin tells the truth, so Rae is a knave, and Rae's statement "exactly one of us three is a knight" must be false. If Pia were a knave, Quin would be the only knight and Rae's statement would be true, which cannot happen. So Pia is a knight. Check: Pia and Quin are the same type, as Pia says; Rae is a knave, as Quin says; and there are two knights, so Rae lies. The transferable idea: when a statement links the speaker to someone else, try both types for the speaker, and if both cases agree you have a fact to build on.
solutions.elegant: Whoever says "X and I are the same type" shows that X is a knight: a knight says it truthfully about a knight, and a knave says it falsely about a knight. So Quin is a knight and Rae is a knave. Rae's claim of exactly one knight is false, so there are two knights: Pia and Quin.

problems.whyOnTest: Truth-teller and liar puzzles test case checking: try each type for a speaker, follow it through every statement, and keep only what survives.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven whole numbers, each bigger than zero, add up to 50. Which of these must be true?

choices.text: Two of the numbers are equal.
choices.misconception: I thought seven numbers with such a small total had to include a repeat.

choices.text: At least one of the numbers is even.
At least one of the numbers is odd.
choices.misconception: I thought an even total could not be made from even numbers alone.

choices.text: One of the numbers is bigger than 8.
choices.misconception: I knew some number had to be at least 8 and read that as bigger than 8.

choices.text: All of the numbers are different.
choices.misconception: I assumed the numbers were all different because the question did not mention repeats.

hints: For each choice, try to build seven numbers that break it.
A statement must be true only if no example can break it. Look for counterexamples, and for the one choice where trying to break it leads to something impossible, think about odd and even.
Suppose all seven numbers were odd. Adding seven odd numbers gives an odd total, but 50 is even.

solutions.reliable: Hunt for counterexamples. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 29 adds to 50 with no two equal, so the first choice fails. 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 20, 20 adds to 50 with no odd number, so the third choice fails, and its repeats knock out the last choice. 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 2 adds to 50 with nothing bigger than 8, so the fourth choice fails. For the second choice, suppose no number is even, so all seven are odd. Odd numbers pair up into even sums, and seven odd numbers make three pairs with one left over, so their total is odd. But 50 is even, which is impossible. So at least one number must be even. The transferable idea: to show something must happen, imagine it does not and find the clash.
solutions.elegant: Only one choice survives the counterexamples above, so it must be the answer, and the odd-even clash shows why: an odd count of odd numbers always has an odd total.

problems.whyOnTest: Must-be-true questions test two moves: knock out choices with a counterexample, and prove the survivor by imagining it false.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 60 cm ribbon is cut into two pieces. The longer piece is 18 cm longer than the shorter piece. How long is the shorter piece?

choices.misconception: I split the ribbon in half and then took 18 cm off the 30 cm half.
I split the ribbon into two equal halves and ignored the 18 cm difference.
I found the longer piece instead of the shorter one.
I took the 18 cm away from 60 cm but forgot to share what was left between the two pieces.

hints: Draw two bars, one longer than the other by 18.
In a bar model the longer bar is a short bar plus an extra 18 cm. Remove the extra piece, and what is left is two equal short bars.
60 - 18 = 42 cm is two short pieces, so one short piece is half of 42.

solutions.reliable: Draw the short piece as a bar and the long piece as the same bar plus 18 cm. Together they make 60 cm. Take away the extra 18 cm: 60 - 18 = 42 cm is two equal short bars, so the short piece is 42 / 2 = 21 cm. Check: 21 + 39 = 60 and 39 - 21 = 18. The transferable idea: with a total and a difference, remove the difference first, then share equally.
solutions.elegant: Halfway is 30 cm, and each piece sits half the difference, 9 cm, away from halfway: the short piece is 30 - 9 = 21 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Sum-and-difference problems are a bar-model classic, and the trap is taking the 18 off one half.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The graph shows how far Zara was from home during a bike ride. How many kilometres did she ride altogether?

figure.alt: A line graph of distance from home in kilometres against time in hours, from 0 to 6 hours. The line rises from 0 km to 12 km in the first hour, stays flat at 12 km until hour 2, rises to 20 km at hour 3, stays flat at 20 km until hour 4, then falls steadily to 0 km at hour 6.

choices.misconception: I gave the length of the whole ride in hours instead of the distance.
I read only the first part of the ride, up to the first flat stretch.
I read the highest point on the graph, which is only the ride out, not the ride back.
I added the heights of the two flat stretches, 12 and 20.

hints: What does a flat part of this graph mean?
The graph shows distance from home, not distance ridden. Rising means riding away, falling means riding back, and flat means standing still. Add up every stretch she rode.
She rode 12 km out, then 8 km further out to reach 20 km, then 20 km back home.

solutions.reliable: Read each piece. Hour 0 to 1: from 0 to 12 km, so 12 km ridden. Hour 1 to 2: flat, so she stopped. Hour 2 to 3: from 12 to 20 km, so 8 km more. Hour 3 to 4: flat, stopped again. Hour 4 to 6: from 20 km back to 0, so 20 km. Total 12 + 8 + 20 = 40 km. The transferable idea: on a distance-from-home graph, add every rise and every fall, and treat flat parts as rests.
solutions.elegant: She finished where she started, so she rode back exactly as far as she rode out. The furthest point is 20 km, so the ride was 20 + 20 = 40 km.

problems.whyOnTest: Graph questions check that you know what the vertical axis measures: distance from home is not the same as distance travelled.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A baker makes 150 rolls. She sells two thirds of them in the morning and half of the remaining rolls in the afternoon. How many rolls are left at the end of the day?

choices.misconception: I took half of all 150 rolls in the afternoon instead of half of what was left, so it seemed none were left.
I stopped after the morning and forgot the afternoon sales.
I gave the number of rolls sold in the morning.
I gave the total number of rolls sold, not the number left.

hints: Do the morning first, then the afternoon.
Work in stages. Find what is left after the morning, and only then take half of that. The afternoon fraction is of the leftover rolls, not of all 150.
Two thirds of 150 is 100, which leaves 50. Half of those 50 are sold in the afternoon.

solutions.reliable: Morning: two thirds of 150 is 100 sold, so 150 - 100 = 50 remain. Afternoon: half of the 50 remaining is 25 sold, leaving 50 - 25 = 25. The transferable idea: in multi-step fraction problems each fraction applies to whatever is left at that stage, so update the amount after every step.
solutions.elegant: After the morning one third is left; after the afternoon half of that third is left, which is one sixth of 150, or 25.

problems.whyOnTest: Multi-step word problems test whether you track what each fraction is a fraction of.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Using each of the digits 0, 3, 5 and 8 exactly once, Ivo writes the largest four-digit number and the smallest four-digit number he can. What is their difference?

choices.misconception: I subtracted column by column, always taking the smaller digit from the larger one, instead of borrowing.
I borrowed from the hundreds column but forgot to make its digit one smaller.
I put the 0 at the front of the smallest number, making 0358, which is not a four-digit number.
I added the two numbers instead of finding their difference.

hints: Can a four-digit number start with 0?
For the largest number, put the digits from biggest to smallest. For the smallest, the smallest digit should go first, but a four-digit number cannot start with 0, so think about where the 0 goes.
The numbers are 8530 and 3058. Subtract carefully, borrowing where needed.

solutions.reliable: Largest: digits in decreasing order, 8530. Smallest: the first digit cannot be 0, so it is the smallest non-zero digit, 3, followed by the others in increasing order: 3058. Difference: 8530 - 3058 = 5472. Check by adding: 3058 + 5472 = 8530. The transferable idea: in place-value questions the leading digit carries the most weight and can never be 0.

problems.whyOnTest: Building the largest and smallest numbers tests place value, and the zero-in-front trap catches students who rush.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When the two digits of a certain two-digit number are swapped, the new number is 27 bigger. How many two-digit numbers have this property?

choices.misconception: I found that the units digit must be 3 more than the tens digit and gave that 3 as the answer.
I listed 14, 25, 36, 47 and 58 and stopped too soon, missing 69.
I also counted 03, which becomes 30, but 03 is not a two-digit number.
I counted every two-digit number whose digits differ by 3, including those that get smaller when swapped.

hints: Write the number as 10 times the tens digit plus the units digit.
Work out how much a number changes when its digits swap, in terms of its two digits. The change has a simple form that tells you how the digits must be related. Then list every number that fits.
Swapping changes the number by 9 times the difference of the digits, so the units digit must be exactly 3 more than the tens digit, and the tens digit cannot be 0.

solutions.reliable: Call the tens digit a and the units digit b, so the number is 10a + b. Swapped, it is 10b + a. The increase is (10b + a) - (10a + b) = 9b - 9a = 9 x (b - a). This must be 27, so b - a = 3. The tens digit a must be at least 1 and b at most 9, so a can be 1 to 6: 14, 25, 36, 47, 58, 69. That is 6 numbers. Check one: 41 - 14 = 27. The transferable idea: swapping two digits always changes a number by 9 times the difference of the digits.
solutions.elegant: Try one: 14 becomes 41, which is 27 bigger. Adding 11 raises both digits by 1 and keeps the gap of 3, so the list is 14, 25, 36, and so on up to 69, where the units digit reaches 9. That is 6 numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles reward writing a number as 10a + b; the rule that a swap changes a number by 9 times the digit gap comes up again and again.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The four-digit number 6_72 is divisible by both 4 and 9. Which digit goes in the gap?

choices.misconception: I used the test for 3 instead of the test for 9 and picked the smallest digit that passed.
I left the 7 out when adding the digits, so I made 6 + 2 + 1 = 9.
I thought a number divisible by 4 must have the digit 4 in it.
I left the 6 out when adding the digits, so I made 7 + 2 + 9 = 18.

hints: Each divisibility test looks at a different part of the number.
The test for 4 looks only at the last two digits; the test for 9 looks at the sum of all the digits. Check the test for 4, then make the digit sum a multiple of 9.
72 is a multiple of 4 whatever the missing digit is. The other digits add to 6 + 7 + 2 = 15, and the next multiple of 9 is 18.

solutions.reliable: Divisible by 4: the last two digits, 72, make a multiple of 4 (72 = 4 x 18), so every digit in the gap passes. Divisible by 9: the digit sum must be a multiple of 9. 6 + 7 + 2 = 15, so 15 plus the missing digit must be 18 (reaching 27 would need 12, which is not a digit). So the digit is 3, and indeed 6372 = 9 x 708 = 4 x 1593. The transferable idea: when a number must pass two tests, apply each test to the part of the number it looks at.

problems.whyOnTest: Missing-digit questions test the divisibility rules directly, and the rule for 3 is the tempting wrong tool.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The list 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, ... keeps repeating the block 1, 2, 3, 2. What is the sum of the first 50 numbers in the list?

choices.misconception: I counted 12 full blocks of 4 and forgot the 2 numbers left over.
I worked out 50 / 4 = 12.5 blocks and multiplied 12.5 by the block sum of 8, but the half block is 1 and 2, not half of 8.
I added the two leftover numbers as 2 and 3, starting the next block in the wrong place.
I rounded 12.5 up to 13 full blocks.

hints: What does one full block add up to?
Count how many complete blocks fit into the first 50 numbers and how many numbers are left over. Add the full blocks, then the leftover numbers, read from the start of a block.
Each block of 4 adds to 8. 50 = 12 x 4 + 2, so there are 12 blocks followed by 1 and 2.

solutions.reliable: One block 1, 2, 3, 2 adds to 8. 50 numbers make 12 full blocks (48 numbers) and 2 more. The 12 blocks add to 12 x 8 = 96. Numbers 49 and 50 start a new block, so they are 1 and 2. Total: 96 + 1 + 2 = 99. The transferable idea: split a long cycle into full blocks plus a remainder, and read the remainder from the start of the block.
solutions.elegant: The first 52 numbers are exactly 13 blocks, which add to 104. Numbers 51 and 52 are 3 and 2, so the first 50 add to 104 - 5 = 99.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeating-cycle questions test the remainder: where the cycle breaks off decides the last part of the sum.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ... are written in rows. Row 1 has one number, row 2 has two numbers, row 3 has three numbers, and so on. So row 1 is 1, row 2 is 2, 3, row 3 is 4, 5, 6 and row 4 is 7, 8, 9, 10. What is the first number in row 12?

choices.misconception: I found the first number of row 11 instead of row 12.
I found the last number of row 11 and forgot to move on to the next number.
I found the last number of row 12 instead of the first.
I worked out 11 x 12 = 132 for the numbers in rows 1 to 11, forgetting to halve it, then added 1.

hints: How many numbers are written before row 12 starts?
Rows 1 to 11 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 11 numbers altogether. Row 12 starts with the very next number.
To add 1 + 2 + ... + 11, pair 1 with 11, 2 with 10, and so on: each pair makes 12.

solutions.reliable: The last number in each row equals how many numbers have been written so far. Rows 1 to 11 hold 1 + 2 + ... + 11 numbers. Pairing 1 with 11, 2 with 10, 3 with 9, 4 with 8 and 5 with 7 makes five pairs of 12, with 6 left over: 60 + 6 = 66. So row 11 ends with 66, and row 12 starts with 67. Check against the rows shown: row 4 should start after 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 numbers, at 7, and it does. The transferable idea: in a table that grows row by row, the last number of a row is the running total of the row lengths.
solutions.elegant: Look at the ends of the rows: 1, 3, 6, 10, ... The gaps between them are 2, 3, 4, ..., so keep adding: 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66. That is the end of row 11, so row 12 starts at 67.

problems.whyOnTest: Table and grid patterns test finding a rule for where a row starts or ends, instead of writing out the whole table.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many two-digit numbers have a tens digit that is bigger than their units digit? For example, 52 is one of them, but 25 and 33 are not.

choices.misconception: I counted the possible tens digits, 1 to 9, instead of the numbers.
I forgot that the units digit can be 0, so I missed 10, 20, 30 and the other multiples of 10.
I also counted numbers like 33 and 77, where the two digits are equal.
I counted every two-digit number whose two digits are different, in either order.

hints: Split the numbers by their tens digit.
For each tens digit from 1 to 9, count the units digits that are smaller than it. Remember that 0 is a units digit too.
Tens digit 1 allows only units digit 0, tens digit 2 allows 0 and 1, and so on up to tens digit 9.

solutions.reliable: Do casework on the tens digit. With tens digit 1 the units digit must be 0: 1 number. With tens digit 2 it can be 0 or 1: 2 numbers. In general, tens digit d allows the d units digits 0 up to d - 1. Total 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 9 = 45. The transferable idea: pick one digit to split on, count each case, and add the cases.
solutions.elegant: Think of all 100 digit pairs from 00 to 99. Ten have equal digits, and the other 90 split evenly into those whose first digit is bigger and those whose second digit is bigger, so 45 have the first digit bigger. None of those 45 starts with 0, so all are real two-digit numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework questions test choosing a good thing to split on, then adding the cases without missing any.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sam tosses a coin three times and writes down H or T each time, in order, for example HTT. How many of the possible lists have more heads than tails?

choices.misconception: I counted only HHH, forgetting that two heads and one tail is also more heads.
I ignored the order, so HHT, HTH and THH counted as one list, plus HHH.
I counted only the lists with exactly two heads and forgot HHH.
I counted all the possible lists, not just those with more heads.

hints: List all the possibilities first.
A tree diagram splits into H and T at each toss, giving every possible list exactly once. Then pick out the lists where heads outnumber tails.
There are 8 lists. More heads means 3 heads, or 2 heads and 1 tail in any order.

solutions.reliable: A tree with two branches at each of three tosses gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 lists: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. More heads than tails means at least 2 heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH. That is 4 lists. The transferable idea: a tree diagram lists every outcome once, so you can sort them without missing any.
solutions.elegant: Swap every H for T and every T for H. This pairs each list with more heads with one with more tails, and with three tosses there are no ties, so exactly half of the 8 lists, 4, have more heads.

problems.whyOnTest: Tree diagrams make sure every ordered outcome is listed once, which is exactly what the order trap tests.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. A path 1 m wide runs all the way round the inside edge of the garden. What is the area of the path, in square metres?

choices.misconception: I took only 1 m off each side length, so I used an inside part of 11 m by 6 m and got 84 - 66.
I made all four strips of path 2 m shorter, 10 + 10 + 5 + 5, so the corner squares were not counted at all.
I multiplied the distance round the garden, 38 m, by the width of 1 m, so each corner square was counted twice.
I worked out the area of the part inside the path, 10 m by 5 m, instead of the area of the path itself.

hints: Sketch the garden and shade the path along all four edges.
Find the area of the whole garden and the area of the part inside the path, then subtract. Check on your sketch how much the path takes off each side.
The whole garden is 12 x 7 = 84 square metres. The path takes 1 m off both ends of each side, so the inside part is 10 m by 5 m.

solutions.reliable: The whole garden is 12 x 7 = 84 square metres. The path is 1 m wide on every side, so the part inside it loses 1 m at both ends of its length and of its width: it is 10 m by 5 m, which is 50 square metres. The path is 84 - 50 = 34 square metres. The transferable idea: a sketch shows that a border eats into both ends of every side, which is exactly where the corner squares hide.
solutions.elegant: Cut the path into two long strips 12 m by 1 m and two short strips that fit between them, 5 m by 1 m. Each corner square now belongs to one strip only, so the area is 12 + 12 + 5 + 5 = 34 square metres.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing the path shows its four corner squares, which get counted twice or not at all by anyone who works from the words alone.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle measures 8 cm by 5 cm. A 2 cm by 2 cm square is cut out of the middle of one of the 8 cm sides, leaving a notch that does not touch any corner. What is the perimeter of the shape that is left?

choices.misconception: I took away the 2 cm of edge where the square was removed and forgot the new edges inside the notch.
I thought cutting a piece out never changes the perimeter, which is only true for a corner cut.
I took off the 2 cm gap and added the two sides of the notch but forgot its bottom edge.
I worked out the area, 40 - 4, instead of the perimeter.

hints: Walk around the new edge. What happens at the notch?
Removing the square takes away a 2 cm piece of the long side but adds the three sides of the notch. Compare what is lost with what is gained.
The rectangle's perimeter is 26 cm. The notch loses 2 cm of edge and gains 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 cm.

solutions.reliable: The rectangle's perimeter is 2 x (8 + 5) = 26 cm. Cutting the notch removes 2 cm from the long side but adds three new edges of 2 cm each: the two sides of the notch and its bottom. So the perimeter is 26 - 2 + 6 = 30 cm. The transferable idea: when a piece is cut away, count edges lost and edges gained; a corner cut breaks even, but a notch in the middle of a side adds its two sides.
solutions.elegant: Slide the bottom of the notch back out to the edge in your mind: that edge plus the rest of the outline makes the original 26 cm, and the only extra length is the two 2 cm sides of the notch, so 26 + 4 = 30 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter questions test edge-by-edge thinking, and the belief that removing a piece shrinks the perimeter is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A team of 3 is chosen from 4 girls and 3 boys. The team must include at least one boy. How many different teams are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted the teams with no boys, which are the ones that are not allowed.
I counted only the teams with exactly one boy and forgot teams with two or three boys.
I counted every team of 3 and forgot the rule about including a boy.
I chose one boy first and then any 2 of the other 6, so teams with two or three boys got counted more than once.

hints: Is it easier to count the teams that break the rule?
Count all teams of 3 from the 7 people, then take away the teams that have no boys. This avoids splitting into cases by the number of boys.
There are 35 teams of 3 from 7 people. Teams with no boys come from the 4 girls only, and there are 4 of those.

solutions.reliable: Split by the number of boys. One boy: 3 choices of boy and 6 pairs of girls, so 18 teams. Two boys: 3 pairs of boys and 4 choices of girl, so 12 teams. Three boys: 1 team. Total 18 + 12 + 1 = 31. The transferable idea: when choosing a group with a condition, split into cases that do not overlap and add them.
solutions.elegant: Count the opposite. There are 35 teams of 3 from 7 people (7 x 6 x 5 / 6). Teams with no boy come only from the 4 girls, and there are 4 of them (leave one girl out). So 35 - 4 = 31 teams include a boy.

problems.whyOnTest: "At least one" signals counting the opposite, and choosing one boy first is the classic overcount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 is used exactly once to write two three-digit numbers. The first number is bigger than the second. What is the smallest possible difference between them?

choices.misconception: I made the bigger number as small as possible, 412, but wrote the smaller one as 356 instead of making it as large as possible.
I used the two largest digits, 6 and 5, as the hundreds digits, giving 612 - 543.
I paired each digit with its neighbour, making 642 - 531.
I split the digits in order, making 456 - 123.

hints: The hundreds digits matter most. How close can they be?
Make the hundreds digits differ by just 1. Then give the bigger number the smallest possible ending and the smaller number the largest possible ending. Try each pair of neighbouring hundreds digits.
With hundreds digits 4 and 3, the best is 412 - 365. Check the other neighbouring pairs, such as 2 and 1 or 5 and 4, to see that they do worse.

solutions.reliable: If the hundreds digits differ by 2 or more, the difference is at least 200 - 99 = 101, so they should differ by 1. For each such pair, the bigger number takes the two smallest leftover digits in increasing order and the smaller number takes the two largest in decreasing order. Hundreds 2 and 1: 234 - 165 = 69. Hundreds 3 and 2: 314 - 265 = 49. Hundreds 4 and 3: 412 - 365 = 47. Hundreds 5 and 4: 512 - 463 = 49. Hundreds 6 and 5: 612 - 543 = 69. The smallest is 47. The transferable idea: in digit-placing puzzles, settle the most valuable place first, then push the remaining digits to the extremes.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit-placing puzzles test place value with a goal: the hundreds decide almost everything, and the endings fine-tune.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three equal circles of radius 2 cm sit side by side in a row, each touching the next. A rectangle is drawn around them so that its top and bottom touch all three circles and its ends touch the end circles. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?

choices.misconception: I used the radius where I needed the diameter, so I worked with a 6 cm by 2 cm rectangle.
I added only the two long sides of 12 cm and forgot the two short ends.
I used the radius, 2 cm, for the height of the rectangle instead of the diameter.
I worked out the area, 12 x 4, instead of the perimeter.

hints: How wide is one circle?
The rectangle's length is three circle widths and its height is one circle width. A circle's width is its diameter, which is twice the radius.
The diameter is 4 cm, so the rectangle is 12 cm long and 4 cm high.

solutions.reliable: Each circle is 2 x 2 = 4 cm across. Three in a row make the rectangle 3 x 4 = 12 cm long, and its height is one diameter, 4 cm. Perimeter: 2 x (12 + 4) = 32 cm. The transferable idea: when circles touch a line or each other, measure across them using the diameter.

problems.whyOnTest: Circle questions test switching from radius to diameter whenever circles touch each other or a boundary.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia spent half of her money on a book. Then she spent a third of the money she had left on lunch. She had 10 euros left. How much money did Mia have at the start?

choices.misconception: I undid the lunch step but forgot to undo the book step.
I undid only the book step by doubling 10, and forgot about lunch.
I treated both steps as spending half, so I doubled twice.
I added the fractions she spent, a half and a third, to get five sixths, so I took 10 euros as one sixth of her money.

hints: Start from the 10 euros at the end and work backwards.
Undo the steps in reverse order. After lunch she had two thirds of what she had before lunch, and after the book she had half of what she started with.
10 euros is two thirds of the money she had before lunch, so before lunch she had 15 euros.

solutions.reliable: Work backwards. Lunch took a third of what she had, leaving two thirds, and those two thirds are 10 euros. So one third is 5 euros and before lunch she had 15 euros. The book took half of her money, leaving the other half, so 15 euros is half and she started with 30 euros. Check: half of 30 is 15, a third of 15 is 5, and 15 - 5 = 10. The transferable idea: each fraction is a fraction of what was there at that moment, so undo the steps one at a time from the end.
solutions.elegant: She kept a half, then two thirds of that half, so she kept a third of her money in all. That third is 10 euros, so she started with 30 euros.

problems.whyOnTest: Working-backwards questions test undoing the steps in reverse order, and the trap is treating every fraction as a fraction of the starting amount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class, the ratio of boys to girls is 4 : 7. There are 9 more girls than boys. How many children are in the class?

choices.misconception: I found the number of boys instead of the whole class.
I added the 9 extra girls to the 11 parts of the ratio.
I found the number of girls instead of the whole class.
I took the 9 extra girls to be one part, so I multiplied 9 by 11.

hints: Draw the boys as 4 equal bars and the girls as 7 bars that size.
The girls have 3 more parts than the boys. Those 3 parts are the 9 extra girls, which tells you the size of one part.
One part is 9 / 3 = 3 children, and the whole class is 4 + 7 = 11 parts.

solutions.reliable: Think of the class as equal parts: boys 4 parts, girls 7 parts. The girls have 7 - 4 = 3 parts more, and that difference is 9 children, so one part is 3 children. The class is 11 parts, so it has 11 x 3 = 33 children. Check: 12 boys and 21 girls give 12 : 21 = 4 : 7, and 21 - 12 = 9. The transferable idea: match the difference you are given to the difference in parts to find the size of one part.

problems.whyOnTest: Ratio-as-parts questions test matching a given number to the right number of parts, then scaling to the part you need.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square is divided into a 3 by 3 grid of equal small squares. How many rectangles of any size, including squares, can be traced along the lines of the grid?

choices.misconception: I counted only the nine smallest squares.
I counted only the squares, of sizes 1 by 1, 2 by 2 and 3 by 3.
I counted the long rectangles lying flat but not the same rectangles standing upright.
I forgot to count the whole big square as one of the rectangles.

hints: Sort the rectangles by their width and height.
Count by size: for each width and height from 1 to 3, count how many positions a rectangle of that size can slide into. Do not forget rectangles standing upright as well as lying flat.
1 by 1: 9. 1 by 2: 6 each way. 1 by 3: 3 each way. 2 by 2: 4. 2 by 3: 2 each way. 3 by 3: 1.

solutions.reliable: Count each size by sliding it around the grid. 1 by 1: 9. 1 by 2: 6 lying flat and 6 standing up, so 12. 1 by 3: 3 + 3 = 6. 2 by 2: 4. 2 by 3: 2 + 2 = 4. 3 by 3: 1. Total 9 + 12 + 6 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 36. The transferable idea: count hidden shapes by size and position, and remember that a rectangle that is not a square has two orientations.
solutions.elegant: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the 4 vertical lines for its sides and 2 of the 4 horizontal lines for its top and bottom. Each choice can be made in 6 ways, so there are 6 x 6 = 36 rectangles.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting hidden rectangles tests sorting by size, and the choose-two-lines trick turns a long list into one multiplication.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Nine children stand side by side in a line. Each is either a truth-teller, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Every child says: "Exactly one of the children next to me is a liar." The two children at the ends each have only one child next to them. How many truth-tellers are in the line?

choices.misconception: I worked out the line correctly but counted the liars instead of the truth-tellers.
I counted only the truth-tellers in the middle of the line and left out the two at the ends.
I guessed the line goes truth-teller, liar, truth-teller, liar, and so on, without checking that a truth-teller in the middle would then have two liars next to him.
I thought they must all tell the truth because they all say the same thing, but then nobody would have a liar next to them.

hints: Is the first child a truth-teller or a liar? What does that force next door?
A liar’s claim is false, so a liar has no liar or two liars beside him. The end child has one neighbour. Try the first child as a liar, then a truth-teller, walking along the line each time.
If the first child is a liar, the line is forced to go L, T, T, L, T, T, L, T, T, and then the last child's claim is false although he is a truth-teller. So the first child tells the truth.

solutions.reliable: Look at the first child, who has only one neighbour. Case 1: the first child is a liar. His claim is false, so child 2 is a truth-teller. Child 2 has exactly one liar beside him and child 1 is that liar, so child 3 tells the truth. Child 3 already has a truth-teller on one side, so child 4 must be the liar. Child 4 lies, and with child 3 telling the truth, child 5 cannot be a liar. Carrying on the same way gives L, T, T, L, T, T, L, T, T. But then child 9 is a truth-teller whose only neighbour, child 8, is not a liar, which contradicts his claim. So Case 1 is impossible. Case 2: the first child tells the truth, so child 2 is a liar. Walking along in the same way gives T, L, T, T, L, T, T, L, T, and child 9 tells the truth with liar child 8 beside him, so everything fits. Every child's statement checks out, and there are 6 truth-tellers. The transferable idea: when each person's type forces the next person's type, try both choices for the first person and follow the chain until it works or breaks.

problems.whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles test whether you turn each statement into a firm rule and follow it person by person, rejecting a starting guess the moment it leads to a contradiction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five people each fill a 3 by 3 grid with the numbers 1 to 9, using each number once. Each person then reports the three row totals of their grid. Exactly one report must contain a mistake. Which one?

choices.misconception: I thought 24 was too big for a single row, not noticing that 7 + 8 + 9 is exactly 24.
I thought two rows could never have the same total because all nine numbers are different.
I thought two rows of 18 would use up all the big numbers, so I never tried 3, 7, 8 and 4, 5, 9.
I thought a row of only 10 left too little room for rows of 17 and 18, so I never tried 1, 4, 5 then 2, 7, 8 and 3, 6, 9.

hints: Every number from 1 to 9 is in exactly one row.
Instead of building grids, find something every correct report must share. Adding the three row totals adds every number in the grid exactly once, so all correct reports have the same grand total.
1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, so the three row totals must add to 45. Add each report and look for the one that does not.

solutions.reliable: The three rows together contain every number from 1 to 9 exactly once, so the three row totals must add up to 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45. Check each report: 6 + 15 + 24 = 45, 14 + 14 + 17 = 45, 9 + 18 + 18 = 45, 10 + 17 + 18 = 45, but 13 + 16 + 17 = 46. A report that adds to 46 is impossible, so 13, 16, 17 must contain a mistake. (The others really can happen, for example rows 1, 2, 3 and 4, 5, 6 and 7, 8, 9 give 6, 15, 24.) The transferable idea: to prove something is impossible, find a quantity that is forced, then show the claim contradicts it.
solutions.elegant: Pair 1 with 9, 2 with 8, 3 with 7, 4 with 6, and 5 is left: four tens and a five make 45, so any report whose totals do not add to 45 contradicts itself.

problems.whyOnTest: Proving a claim impossible usually means finding one forced fact, like a fixed total, that the claim breaks.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A wooden rod 84 cm long is cut into three pieces. The middle-sized piece is twice as long as the shortest piece, and the longest piece is twice as long as the middle-sized piece. How long is the longest piece?

choices.misconception: I found the length of one box, the shortest piece, and stopped there.
I found the middle-sized piece instead of the longest one.
I cut the rod into three equal pieces, ignoring that the pieces have different lengths.
I left out the shortest piece and split 84 between the other two pieces in the ratio 2 : 4.

hints: Draw the shortest piece as one box.
Draw a bar model: the middle-sized piece is two of the same boxes, and the longest piece is twice the middle-sized one. Count how many equal boxes make up the whole 84 cm.
The longest piece is 4 boxes, so the rod is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 equal boxes and each box is 84 ÷ 7 = 12 cm.

solutions.reliable: Draw the shortest piece as one box. The middle-sized piece is twice as long, so 2 boxes, and the longest piece is twice the middle-sized one, so 4 boxes.
