Together that is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 equal boxes making 84 cm, so one box is 84 ÷ 7 = 12 cm. The longest piece is 4 × 12 = 48 cm. Check: 12 + 24 + 48 = 84, 24 is twice 12 and 48 is twice 24. The transferable idea: in a bar model, draw every piece in the same unit box, count all the boxes in the whole, and only then divide.

problems.whyOnTest: Part-whole questions test whether you draw every piece in the same unit and count all the equal parts before dividing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The chart shows how many books were borrowed from a class library on each school day of one week. On how many days were more books borrowed than the average number per day for that week?

figure.alt: A bar chart of books borrowed on five school days, with the vertical axis marked 0 to 14 in steps of 2. Monday 6, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 4, Thursday 12, Friday 8.

choices.misconception: I thought the average had to be the busiest day's 12 books, so no day could beat it.
I divided the week's total of 40 by 4 instead of by the 5 days, so I compared with 10.
I counted Friday, which is exactly equal to the average, as more than the average.
I compared each day with Wednesday, the quietest day, instead of with the average.

hints: First find the average, then compare each bar with it.
Read each bar against the axis, add the five values and divide by the number of days. Then count only the bars that are strictly taller than the average.
The bars show 6, 10, 4, 12 and 8, a total of 40, so the average is 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Now check which days beat 8, remembering that equal is not more.

solutions.reliable: Read the bars: Monday 6, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 4, Thursday 12, Friday 8. The total is 40 books over 5 days, so the average is 40 ÷ 5 = 8 books per day. More than 8 were borrowed on Tuesday (10) and Thursday (12). Friday's 8 is equal to the average, not more. So the answer is 2 days. The transferable idea: read every value before calculating, divide by the number of items actually shown, and re-read whether the question says "more than" or "at least".
solutions.elegant: Compare each bar with 8 and balance the differences: Monday -2, Tuesday +2, Wednesday -4, Thursday +4, Friday 0. They cancel to zero, which confirms 8 is the average, and only two differences are positive.

problems.whyOnTest: Chart questions test careful reading of every bar and of the exact comparison asked, here strictly more than the average.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bakery sells rolls at 3 euros each, in bags of 4 for 10 euros, or in boxes of 10 for 22 euros. Sam needs at least 17 rolls. What is the least amount he can pay?

choices.misconception: I worked out the box price per roll, 2.20 euros, and multiplied by 17, as if the shop sold any number at that price.
I bought a box and two bags to get 18 rolls without checking whether 3 single rolls would be cheaper than the second bag.
I bought four bags and one single roll and never tried using a box.
I bought all 17 rolls one at a time at 3 euros each.

hints: Start with the cheapest way to buy most of the rolls.
A box is the cheapest price per roll, then a bag, then single rolls. Take one box and work out the cheapest way to get the remaining rolls, then compare with plans that use no box or two boxes.
One box gives 10 rolls for 22 euros. For the other 7: a bag and 3 singles cost 10 + 9 = 19 euros, while two bags cost 20 euros and seven singles cost 21 euros.

solutions.reliable: Compare the plans in steps. Per roll, a box costs 2.20 euros, a bag 2.50 euros and a single 3 euros, so buy a box first: 10 rolls for 22 euros. Sam still needs 7 rolls. Two bags (8 rolls) cost 20 euros, one bag and 3 singles cost 10 + 9 = 19 euros, and 7 singles cost 21 euros, so the best is 19 euros, a total of 22 + 19 = 41 euros. Other plans are dearer: two boxes cost 44 euros, and without a box the best is four bags and a single for 43 euros. The least he can pay is 41 euros. The transferable idea: in a multi-step money problem, settle the big cheap block first, then compare every option for the leftover rather than assuming the next bulk deal is best.

problems.whyOnTest: Multi-step shopping problems test whether you compare every option for the leftover instead of grabbing the next bulk deal.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When the digit 1 is written in front of a two-digit number, the new three-digit number is exactly 5 times the original number. What is the sum of the digits of the original number?

choices.misconception: I added the digits of the new three-digit number, 125, instead of the original one.
I added the digits of both numbers, 25 and 125, together.
I found the original number and gave it instead of the sum of its digits.
I gave the new three-digit number instead of anything about the original.

hints: What does writing a 1 in front of a two-digit number add to it?
Writing 1 in the hundreds place adds exactly 100, so the new number is the old number plus 100. Use the fact that it is also 5 times the old number.
The old number plus 100 equals 5 times the old number, so 100 must be 4 times the old number.

solutions.reliable: Writing the digit 1 in front of a two-digit number puts 1 in the hundreds place, which adds 100. So the new number is (original + 100). It is also 5 times the original, so original + 100 = 5 × original, which means 100 = 4 × original, and the original is 25. Check: writing 1 in front gives 125, and 5 × 25 = 125. The digit sum of 25 is 2 + 5 = 7. The transferable idea: a digit placed in a position adds its place value, so turn a digit trick into "number plus place value".
solutions.elegant: Think of the new number as five copies of the old one. One copy is already inside it, so the other four copies must make up the extra 100, and each copy is 25.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value puzzles test whether you see that a digit in the hundreds place simply adds a hundred-sized chunk.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A two-digit number is equal to 4 times the sum of its digits. When its two digits are swapped, the new number is 27 more than the original number. What is the original number?

choices.misconception: I used only the rule about the sum of the digits and took the first number that worked.
I used only the rule about swapping the digits and took the first number that worked, since 41 - 14 = 27.
I used only the rule about the sum of the digits and took the largest number that worked.
I found the right number but gave the number with its digits swapped instead of the original.

hints: Use one rule at a time to make a short list.
Write the number as 10a + b, with tens digit a and units digit b. The sum rule links a and b, leaving only a few candidates. Then work out how much swapping the digits changes each one.
The sum rule says 10a + b = 4a + 4b, so b = 2a: the candidates are 12, 24, 36 and 48. Swapping the digits of a number makes it bigger by 9 times the difference of its digits.

solutions.reliable: Call the digits a (tens) and b (units), so the number is 10a + b. The sum rule says 10a + b = 4(a + b), so 6a = 3b and b = 2a. That leaves 12, 24, 36 and 48. Now test the swap rule: 21 - 12 = 9, 42 - 24 = 18, 63 - 36 = 27, 84 - 48 = 36. Only 36 gives 27. Check: 4 × (3 + 6) = 36, and swapping gives 63, which is 27 more. The transferable idea: when a number must satisfy two conditions, use the easier one to make a short list, then test the list against the other.
solutions.elegant: Swapping the digits changes 10a + b into 10b + a, a change of 9(b - a). So the digits differ by 3, and the candidates are 14, 25, 36, 47, 58 and 69. Only 36 equals 4 times its digit sum.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit-constraint puzzles with two rules test whether you write the number by place value and check every condition, not just the first one that gives a match.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the four-digit number 25★4, the star stands for a single digit. The number is divisible by 12. Which digit is the star?

choices.misconception: I checked only divisibility by 3 and took the first digit that worked.
I checked only divisibility by 4 and took the smallest digit that is not zero.
I checked only divisibility by 3 and took the largest digit that worked.
I checked only divisibility by 4 and took the largest digit that worked.

hints: 12 can be split into two numbers whose tests you know.
A number is divisible by 12 exactly when it is divisible by both 3 and 4. Use the digit-sum test for 3 and the last-two-digits test for 4, and find the digit that passes both.
For 3: 2 + 5 + ★ + 4 must be a multiple of 3, so ★ is 1, 4 or 7. For 4: the last two digits ★4 must be a multiple of 4, so ★ is even.

solutions.reliable: Divisible by 12 means divisible by 3 and by 4 (3 and 4 share no factor, and 3 × 4 = 12). For 3, the digit sum 2 + 5 + ★ + 4 = 11 + ★ must be a multiple of 3, so ★ is 1, 4 or 7. For 4, the number formed by the last two digits, ★4, must be a multiple of 4: 04, 24, 44, 64 and 84 work, so ★ must be even. The only digit in both lists is 4, giving 2544 = 12 × 212. The transferable idea: test divisibility by a composite number by splitting it into factors that share nothing, then apply each quick test.

problems.whyOnTest: Divisibility by 12 needs both the 3-test and the 4-test, and each test alone leaves several tempting digits.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The decimal for one seventh is 0.142857142857..., where the block 142857 repeats forever. What is the sum of the first 50 digits after the decimal point?

choices.misconception: I added eight full blocks and forgot the two extra digits after them.
I added eight full blocks and then three extra digits, 1, 4 and 2, instead of two.
I multiplied the block sum 27 by 50 ÷ 6, as if the digits were spread out evenly.
I rounded 50 ÷ 6 up to 9 and added nine full blocks, which is 54 digits.

hints: How many full blocks of six digits fit into 50 digits?
The digits repeat in blocks of 6, so split the 50 digits into full blocks plus a few left over. Each full block has the same digit sum; the leftover digits are the first few of the block.
50 = 8 × 6 + 2, so there are 8 full blocks and 2 extra digits. One block adds to 1 + 4 + 2 + 8 + 5 + 7 = 27.

solutions.reliable: The block 142857 has 6 digits adding to 1 + 4 + 2 + 8 + 5 + 7 = 27. Since 50 = 8 × 6 + 2, the first 50 digits are 8 full blocks followed by the first 2 digits of the next block, which are 1 and 4. The sum is 8 × 27 + 1 + 4 = 216 + 5 = 221. The transferable idea: for a repeating pattern, divide by the cycle length; the quotient counts full cycles and the remainder tells you exactly where you stop.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeating patterns test whether you use the remainder correctly instead of rounding the number of cycles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Numbers are written in rows. Row 1 is 1. Row 2 is 2, 3. Row 3 is 4, 5, 6. Each new row has one more number than the row before, and the counting continues. What is the first number in row 10?

choices.misconception: I thought each row starts with its own row number, because row 2 starts with 2.
I found the first number of row 9 instead of row 10.
I found how many numbers come before row 10 and gave that, forgetting to add 1.
I found the last number in row 10 instead of the first.

hints: Look at the last number in each row.
The last number in a row equals how many numbers have been written so far, which is 1 + 2 + 3 + ... up to that row. The first number of the next row is one more.
Rows 1 to 9 hold 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45 numbers, so row 9 ends with 45.

solutions.reliable: Row n has n numbers, so rows 1 to 9 together hold 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45 numbers. That means row 9 ends with 45, and row 10 starts with the next number, 46. Check with the start: row 3 starts at 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, as shown. The transferable idea: in a table that fills row by row, the last entry of a row counts everything written so far, so add up the row lengths.
solutions.elegant: Pair the row lengths: 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, 4 + 6 are four tens, plus 5 makes 45, so row 10 begins at 46.

problems.whyOnTest: Table patterns test whether you can find a position by counting everything that comes before it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Matchstick hexagons are laid in a row, each new hexagon sharing one side with the one before it. One hexagon uses 6 matchsticks and a row of two uses 11. How many hexagons are in a row that uses exactly 61 matchsticks?

choices.misconception: I divided 61 by 6, as if no sides were shared, and rounded down.
I took away the first hexagon's 6 sticks, divided 55 by 5 and forgot to count the first hexagon.
I divided 61 by 5, got 12.2, and rounded up because of the leftover stick.
I treated 61 as the number of hexagons and worked out how many sticks that row would need.

hints: How many new sticks does each extra hexagon need?
Each new hexagon shares one side, so it adds fewer than 6 sticks. Find how many sticks each extra hexagon adds, then work backwards from 61.
Each new hexagon adds 5 sticks, so n hexagons use 6 + 5(n - 1) = 5n + 1 sticks.

solutions.reliable: The first hexagon uses 6 sticks and each new one adds 5, because one of its sides is already there. So n hexagons use 6 + 5(n - 1) = 5n + 1 sticks. Set 5n + 1 = 61: then 5n = 60 and n = 12. Check: 12 hexagons use 6 + 11 × 5 = 61. The transferable idea: in a growing pattern, find the starting amount and the amount each step adds, then work backwards from the total.
solutions.elegant: Think of one starting stick, then each hexagon adds a group of 5 sticks. 61 = 1 + 5 × 12, so there are 12 groups.

problems.whyOnTest: Visual patterns test whether you spot the shared parts that make each step add less than a whole new shape.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three ordinary dice, on which opposite faces always add up to 7, are stacked in a tower on a table. The top face of the tower shows 5. What is the total of all the faces that touch another die or the table?

choices.misconception: I counted only the two hidden faces of the middle die.
I counted the bottom face of the top die and the middle die, but forgot the bottom die.
I counted the hidden pairs on the two lower dice but forgot the bottom face of the top die.
I used 5 for the bottom face of the top die, copying its top face instead of taking the opposite face.

hints: List the touching faces die by die.

Opposite faces add to 7. The top die has one touching face, opposite the 5. The middle and bottom dice each have their top and bottom faces touching something, and those two faces are opposite each other.
The top die's bottom face is 7 - 5 = 2. The middle die's top and bottom add to 7, and so do the bottom die's.

solutions.reliable: Go die by die. The top die touches the middle die with its bottom face, which is opposite the 5, so it shows 7 - 5 = 2. The middle die touches with both its top and bottom faces, a pair of opposite faces adding to 7. The bottom die touches the middle die with its top and the table with its bottom, another opposite pair adding to 7. Total: 2 + 7 + 7 = 16. The transferable idea: on a die, opposite faces add to 7, so any hidden top-and-bottom pair is worth 7 without knowing which numbers they are.
solutions.elegant: Each die has a top and bottom face adding to 7, so the six top and bottom faces of the tower total 3 × 7 = 21. Of those six faces only the very top one, the 5, touches nothing, so the touching faces total 21 - 5 = 16.

problems.whyOnTest: Dice questions test the opposite-faces rule, which lets you total hidden faces without knowing each one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square sheet of paper is folded in half, then folded in half again, and then folded in half a third time. One hole is punched through all the layers, away from every fold and edge. How many holes are there when the sheet is unfolded?

choices.misconception: I counted one hole for each fold.
I added two holes for each of the three folds.
I counted every hole twice, once on each side of the paper.
I multiplied the 8 layers by the 3 folds.

hints: How many layers does the hole go through?
Each fold in half doubles the number of layers. A single punch makes one hole in every layer, and each layer becomes a separate part of the unfolded sheet.
The layers go 1, then 2, then 4, then 8, so the punch goes through 8 layers.

solutions.reliable: Each fold in half doubles the number of layers: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8. A punch away from every fold and edge makes one hole in each layer, and unfolding spreads those layers back across the sheet, so there are 8 separate holes. The transferable idea: folding doubles the layers each time, so after n folds one punch makes n twos multiplied together, which is 8 holes for three folds.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding and punching problems test whether you track layers doubling rather than adding a fixed amount per fold.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At one point of a floor tiling, two regular hexagons and some equilateral triangles meet, fitting around the point exactly with no gaps and no overlaps. How many triangles meet at that point?

choices.misconception: I thought each corner of an equilateral triangle was 120 degrees.
I took each corner of a hexagon to be 90 degrees, like a square.
I used 60 degrees for a hexagon's corner, which is the turning angle outside it, not the angle inside.
I filled the whole 360 degrees with triangles and forgot the two hexagons.

hints: The angles around a point add to 360 degrees.
Find the angle at a corner of a regular hexagon and of an equilateral triangle. The corners meeting at the point must add up to exactly 360 degrees.
A hexagon corner is 120 degrees, so two hexagons take 240 degrees. That leaves 120 degrees for triangles, whose corners are 60 degrees each.

solutions.reliable: Angles around a point add to 360 degrees. A regular hexagon splits into 6 equilateral triangles meeting at its centre, so each corner is 2 × 60 = 120 degrees. Two hexagons take 240 degrees, leaving 360 - 240 = 120 degrees. Each equilateral triangle corner is 60 degrees, so 120 ÷ 60 = 2 triangles fit. The transferable idea: in any tiling, the corners meeting at a point must total exactly 360 degrees.
solutions.elegant: A hexagon is made of 6 triangles, and its corner holds 2 triangle corners. So two hexagons fill the space of 4 triangle corners, and the 6 triangle corners that fit around a point leave room for 2 real triangles.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions test the rule that corners meeting at a point add to 360 degrees, plus knowing polygon corner angles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two players play a match. Every game has a winner, and the first player to win 2 games wins the match. How many different orders of game winners can a match have?

choices.misconception: I counted only who wins the match, not the different ways the games can go.
I listed the ways one player can win the match and forgot the other player.
I listed only the ways two games can turn out and forgot that a match can need a third game.
I listed all the results of three games, even when the match was already over after two.

hints: Draw a tree: the first game, then the second.
Make a tree diagram. Each game branches two ways, but a branch stops as soon as someone has 2 wins. Count the ends of the branches.
After two games: AA and BB end the match. AB and BA each need a third game, which can go either way.

solutions.reliable: Call the players A and B and draw a tree. If one player wins both of the first two games the match ends: AA or BB. If the first two games are split, AB or BA, a third game decides it, giving ABA, ABB, BAA and BAB. That is 2 + 4 = 6 orders. The transferable idea: in a tree diagram, stop a branch the moment the outcome is decided, otherwise you count games that are never played.

problems.whyOnTest: Tree diagrams test whether you stop branches that are already finished instead of counting every possible sequence.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers have digits whose product is 24?

choices.misconception: I counted only the groups of three different digits, not the numbers they make.
I counted the groups of digits, such as 1, 3, 8, instead of the numbers made from them.
I missed one of the groups made of three different digits, so I lost its 6 numbers.
I forgot the group 2, 2, 6, which uses a repeated digit.

hints: First find which groups of three digits multiply to 24.

Split into cases by the set of digits used. No digit can be 0, and each digit is at most 9. For each set, count how many three-digit numbers it makes, remembering that a repeated digit gives fewer orders.
The sets are 1, 3, 8 and 1, 4, 6 and 2, 3, 4 and 2, 2, 6. Three different digits can be ordered in 6 ways; a set with a repeat in only 3.

solutions.reliable: No digit can be 0, and digits are at most 9. List the sets of three digits with product 24, smallest digit first. With a 1: the other two multiply to 24, giving 3 and 8, or 4 and 6 (2 and 12 is not allowed). With smallest digit 2: the other two multiply to 12 and are at least 2, giving 2 and 6, or 3 and 4. With smallest digit 3: the other two would multiply to 8 and both be at least 3, impossible. So the sets are 1, 3, 8; 1, 4, 6; 2, 3, 4; and 2, 2, 6. Each set of three different digits makes 6 numbers, and 2, 2, 6 makes 3 (226, 262, 622). Total: 6 + 6 + 6 + 3 = 21. The transferable idea: split by a clear case rule, here the smallest digit, so no case is missed, then count each case separately.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework is tested by problems where one quiet case, like a repeated digit, is easy to miss or overcount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Bus tickets cost 4 euros each. Mia has 30 euros and buys as many tickets as she can. How much money does she have left?

choices.misconception: I divided 30 by 4, got 7.5, and took the 0.5 after the decimal point as the money left over.
I worked out how many tickets she buys and gave that number instead of the money left.
I rounded 7.5 up to 8 tickets and gave the number of tickets.
I worked out how much she spends instead of how much she has left.

hints: Read the last sentence again: what is being asked?
First find how many whole tickets she can afford, then work out what those cost. The question asks for the money remaining, not the number of tickets or the amount spent.
7 tickets cost 28 euros, and 8 would cost 32, which is too much.

solutions.reliable: Mia can buy whole tickets only. 7 tickets cost 7 × 4 = 28 euros and 8 would cost 32 euros, more than she has, so she buys 7. She has 30 - 28 = 2 euros left. Note that 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5 does not mean 0.5 euros are left: the 0.5 is half of a ticket, worth 2 euros. The transferable idea: before answering, re-read what is asked, because a problem often makes you compute several numbers on the way and only one of them is the answer.

problems.whyOnTest: Contest questions often make you compute several numbers on the way; this checks you answer the one actually asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a contest, a wrong answer costs nothing. Each question has 5 answer choices and is worth 4 points. With one minute left, Ben guesses at random on his last 10 questions. On average, how many points will these guesses earn him?

choices.misconception: I thought random guesses earn nothing, so it is not worth answering.
I found how many questions he gets right on average and gave that instead of the points.
I thought a guess is right one time in ten, so one question right, worth 4 points.
I thought a guess is right half the time, so I gave 5 questions right.

hints: With 5 choices, how often is a random guess right?
A random guess picks the right answer one time in five. Work out how many of the 10 guesses are right on average, then turn that into points, remembering that wrong answers lose nothing.
One fifth of 10 guesses is 2 right answers on average, and each is worth 4 points.

solutions.reliable: With 5 choices, a random guess is right one time in five. Over 10 guesses that is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 right answers on average. Each is worth 4 points, so the guesses earn 2 × 4 = 8 points on average, and since wrong answers cost nothing there is nothing to subtract. The transferable idea: when there is no penalty for a wrong answer, a guess can only help, so never leave a question blank.

problems.whyOnTest: With no penalty for wrong answers, every blank throws away points; this makes the size of that gift concrete.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A train 200 m long travels at 20 m per second. It goes through a tunnel 600 m long. How many seconds pass from the moment the front of the train enters the tunnel until the back of the train leaves it?

choices.misconception: I worked out how long the train takes to pass a single point, using only its own length of 200 m.
I worked out how long the whole train is completely inside the tunnel, using 600 - 200 = 400 m.
I used only the length of the tunnel, 600 m, and forgot that the back of the train still has to come out.
I added the length of the train twice, once for going in and once for coming out, so I used 1000 m.

hints: Sketch the train at the start and again at the end.
Draw the train with its front at the tunnel entrance, then with its back at the exit. The distance the train moves between your two pictures is what the speed has to cover.
Between the two pictures the front of the train passes through the whole 600 m tunnel and then goes 200 m further.

solutions.reliable: Draw two pictures. At the start the front of the train is at the entrance. At the end the back of the train is at the exit, so the front is 200 m beyond it. The front has moved 600 + 200 = 800 m. At 20 m per second that takes 800 divided by 20 = 40 seconds. Check with the back of the train: it starts 200 m before the entrance and ends at the exit, also 800 m. The transferable idea: when something long passes something else, draw where it starts and where it ends and follow one point of it.

problems.whyOnTest: A sketch of the train at the start and at the end shows that it must cover the tunnel plus its own length, which the words alone hide.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers of stickers that Ana and Ben have are in the ratio 3 : 5. Then each of them is given 12 more stickers, and the ratio becomes 3 : 4. How many stickers did Ana have at first?

choices.misconception: I found how many stickers Ben had at first instead of Ana.
I found how many stickers Ana had at the end, after the 12 were added.
I found how many stickers Ben had at the end instead of what Ana had at first.
I treated the 12 new stickers as one part and gave Ana 3 parts.

hints: When both get the same number of stickers, what stays the same?
The difference between Ben's and Ana's stickers does not change. In 3 : 5 the difference is 2 parts, and in 3 : 4 it is 1 part, so compare the size of a part before and after.
One part after is the same as two parts before. Ana goes from 3 small parts to 3 big parts, which is 6 small parts, so the 12 new stickers are 3 small parts.

solutions.reliable: Giving both of them 12 stickers does not change the difference between their numbers. At first the ratio is 3 : 5, so the difference is 2 small parts. At the end the ratio is 3 : 4, so the difference is 1 big part. So 1 big part equals 2 small parts. Ana starts with 3 small parts and ends with 3 big parts, which is 6 small parts. The 12 new stickers made up the extra 3 small parts, so one small part is 4 stickers, and Ana had 3 × 4 = 12 at first. Check: Ana 12 and Ben 20 is 3 : 5, and after the gift Ana 24 and Ben 32 is 3 : 4. The transferable idea: in a changing-ratio problem, find the quantity that stays the same, here the difference, and match the parts through it.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve from the smallest choice: if Ana had 12, Ben had 20, and after the gift they have 24 and 32, which is 3 : 4. It works, so Ana had 12.

problems.whyOnTest: Ratio questions test whether you find what stays the same when both amounts change, here the difference between them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Today Lea is 7 years old and her brother is 3. In how many years will their ages add up to 30?

choices.misconception: I found the brother's age at that time instead of the number of years.
I found Lea's age at that time instead of the number of years.
I thought their total grows by 1 each year, forgetting that both of them get older.
I subtracted only Lea's age from 30.

hints: How much does the total of their ages grow each year?
Each year both children get one year older, so their total age grows by 2 every year. Find how much the total still has to grow.
Today the total is 7 + 3 = 10, so it must grow by 20, at 2 per year.

solutions.reliable: Today their ages add up to 7 + 3 = 10. Every year both get one year older, so the total grows by 2 each year. It must grow by 30 - 10 = 20, which takes 20 ÷ 2 = 10 years. Check: in 10 years Lea is 17 and her brother 13, and 17 + 13 = 30. The transferable idea: in age problems everyone ages at the same rate, so a total of several ages grows by one year per person per year.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems test whether you remember that every person gets older, so a total of ages grows faster than one person's age.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular card measures 10 cm by 7 cm. A square of side 3 cm is cut out of one of its corners. What is the perimeter of the shape that is left?

choices.misconception: I added the two new edges from the cut without taking away the two pieces of edge that were removed.
I added all four sides of the cut-out square to the rectangle's perimeter.
I worked out the area that is left, 70 - 9, instead of the perimeter.
I worked out the area of the whole card instead of the perimeter.

hints: Look closely at what happens to the edge at the cut corner.
Cutting a corner square removes two short pieces of the card's edge but adds two new edges of the same lengths. Compare what is lost with what is gained.
The card's perimeter is 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 cm. The cut removes 3 + 3 cm of edge and adds 3 + 3 cm of new edge.

solutions.reliable: The card has perimeter 10 + 7 + 10 + 7 = 34 cm. Cutting a 3 cm square from a corner removes 3 cm from each of two sides, but creates two new edges of 3 cm each, facing inward. The loss and the gain are equal, so the perimeter is still 34 cm. Check by walking around: 10 - 3, then 3, then 3, then 7 - 3, then 10, then 7: 7 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 10 + 7 = 34. The transferable idea: pushing a corner inward keeps every horizontal and vertical length, so the perimeter of a rectilinear shape can stay the same while its area shrinks.
solutions.elegant: Push the two new edges outward back onto the corner: they exactly fill the gap, so the shape has the same perimeter as the full card.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter and area are easily confused; cutting a corner changes the area but not the perimeter.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, point P is at 2.5 and point Q is at 4.1. Point R lies between them, one quarter of the way from P to Q. Where is R?

choices.misconception: I found how far R is from P and gave that distance instead of R's position.
I measured the quarter of the distance from P in the wrong direction, away from Q.
I wrote one quarter of 1.6 as 0.04 instead of 0.4 and added it to 2.5.
I found the point halfway between P and Q instead of a quarter of the way.

hints: How far apart are P and Q?
Find the distance from P to Q by subtracting. Take one quarter of that distance, then step that far from P towards Q.
The distance is 4.1 - 2.5 = 1.6, and a quarter of 1.6 is 0.4.

solutions.reliable: The distance from P to Q is 4.1 - 2.5 = 1.6. One quarter of 1.6 is 0.4. Starting at P and moving 0.4 towards Q gives 2.5 + 0.4 = 2.9. Check: the halfway point is 3.3, and 2.9 is halfway between 2.5 and 3.3, so it is one quarter of the way. The transferable idea: a fraction of the way from one point to another is the start plus that fraction of the gap.
solutions.elegant: Halve twice: halfway from 2.5 to 4.1 is 3.3, and halfway from 2.5 to 3.3 is 2.9.

problems.whyOnTest: Number line questions test the difference between a distance and a position, and decimal care with fractions of a gap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A strip is made of 4 equal squares in a row. How many rectangles of any size can be seen in the strip? A square counts as a rectangle.

choices.misconception: I counted only the four small squares.
I left out the four small squares because they are squares, even though squares count.
I counted the small squares and the two-square rectangles, then stopped.
I counted every size except the whole strip itself.

hints: Count the rectangles by how many squares long they are.
Every rectangle in the strip is a run of neighbouring squares. Count the runs that are 1, 2, 3 and 4 squares long separately, sliding along the strip each time.
There are 4 runs of length 1, 3 of length 2, 2 of length 3 and 1 of length 4.

solutions.reliable: Every rectangle in the strip is a block of neighbouring squares. Count by length: 4 blocks of 1 square, 3 blocks of 2 squares, 2 blocks of 3 squares and 1 block of 4 squares. That gives 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 rectangles. The transferable idea: count hidden shapes by size, and slide each size along the figure so that overlapping shapes are counted too.
solutions.elegant: A rectangle is fixed by choosing its left and right ends from the 5 vertical lines of the strip. There are 10 ways to choose 2 of 5 lines, so 10 rectangles.

problems.whyOnTest: Hidden-shape questions test whether you count overlapping shapes of every size, not just the pieces the figure is cut into.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Pia, Quinn and Rae have 70 shells altogether. Quinn has twice as many shells as Pia, and Rae has 10 more shells than Quinn. How many shells does Rae have?

choices.misconception: I found Pia's share, one block of 12, and gave that instead of Rae's.
I found Quinn's 24 shells and forgot that Rae has 10 more.
I drew Rae's bar as one block plus 10 instead of two blocks plus 10, so I split 60 into 4 blocks of 15.
I left out the extra 10 and split all 70 into 5 equal blocks of 14, then gave Rae two of them.

hints: Draw a bar for each person, starting with Pia.
Pia's bar is one block, Quinn's is two blocks, and Rae's is two blocks with an extra piece of 10. Take the extra 10 away from the total first, so that what is left is made of equal blocks only.
There are 5 blocks plus 10. So 5 blocks make 60, and one block is 12.

solutions.reliable: Pia is 1 block, Quinn is 2 blocks and Rae is 2 blocks plus 10. Altogether that is 5 blocks plus 10, which makes 70, so 5 blocks make 60 and one block is 12. Pia has 12, Quinn has 24 and Rae has 24 + 10 = 34. Check: 12 + 24 + 34 = 70. The transferable idea: in a bar model, take away the pieces that are not whole blocks first, then share what is left among the equal blocks.

problems.whyOnTest: Bar models test whether every comparison becomes blocks in the right place, and whether the extra 10 is taken away before sharing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The chart shows the number of rainy days in five months. In which month did the number of rainy days change the most compared with the month before?

figure.alt: A bar chart of rainy days per month, with the scale marked every 2 days and gridlines every day: March 4, April 10, May 12, June 5, July 7.

choices.misconception: I picked the month with the fewest rainy days instead of looking at changes between months.
I only looked at increases, so I found the jump of 6 into April and ignored the bigger drop.
I picked the tallest bar, which shows the most rain, not the biggest change.

choices.text: It cannot be told from the chart
choices.misconception: I thought a bar chart only shows amounts, so I did not see that the changes can be worked out by subtracting.

hints: A change can go up or down.
Read each bar's height carefully from the scale, then subtract each month from the next one. A drop counts as a change just as much as a rise, so compare the sizes of the differences.
The heights are 4, 10, 12, 5 and 7. The changes are 6 up, 2 up, 7 down and 2 up.

solutions.reliable: Reading the bars gives March 4, April 10, May 12, June 5 and July 7. The changes from one month to the next are 6 (into April), 2 (into May), 7 (into June) and 2 (into July). The biggest change is the drop of 7 from May to June, so the answer is June. The transferable idea: a question about change is about the gaps between bars, not the bars themselves, and a fall is as big a change as a rise.
solutions.elegant: Look for the biggest step between neighbouring bar tops: the cliff from the tallest bar, May, down to June stands out at once.

problems.whyOnTest: Charts test whether you read what is asked: the biggest change is a gap between bars, and the tallest bar is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A school buys 7 boxes of pens. Each box holds 12 packs, and each pack holds 5 pens. The pens are shared equally among 6 classes. How many pens does each class get?

choices.misconception: I shared the 84 packs among the classes and forgot that each pack holds 5 pens.
I worked out the pens in one box, 12 times 5, and stopped there.
I found the number of packs, 7 times 12, and never turned packs into pens.
I found the total number of pens but forgot to share them among the 6 classes.

hints: Find the total number of pens first.
Work in order: boxes to packs, packs to pens, then share the pens. Writing each step's unit next to its number stops you from sharing packs instead of pens.
7 boxes of 12 packs is 84 packs. 84 packs of 5 pens is 420 pens. Now share 420 among 6 classes.

solutions.reliable: 7 boxes times 12 packs is 84 packs. 84 packs times 5 pens is 420 pens. 420 shared among 6 classes is 70 pens each. The transferable idea: in a multi-step problem, label the unit at every step so you always know whether you are holding boxes, packs or pens.
solutions.elegant: Share before you multiply: 12 packs divided by 6 classes is 2 packs per class from each box, so each class gets 7 times 2 times 5 = 70 pens.

problems.whyOnTest: Multi-step word problems test whether you finish every step, and each choice here is a place where a student stopped too soon.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the number 47 385, the digits 7 and 5 swap places. By how much does the number decrease?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the two digits, 7 minus 5, and forgot that they stand in different places.
I treated the 7 as a hundreds digit, so the swap lost 200 and gained 2, giving 198.
I only looked at the thousands place falling from 7000 to 5000 and forgot the units place rose.
I added the 2 gained in the units place to the 2000 lost, instead of taking it away.

hints: Write the new number down before you subtract.
Each digit is worth its value times its place. Find how much the thousands place loses and how much the units place gains, then combine the two changes.
The new number is 45 387. The thousands place loses 2000 but the units place gains 2.

solutions.reliable: After the swap the number is 45 387. 47 385 - 45 387 = 1998. The transferable idea: a digit's worth depends on its place, so a swap changes two places at once and both changes must be counted.
solutions.elegant: The 7 in the thousands place becomes 5, a loss of 2000. The 5 in the units place becomes 7, a gain of 2. Overall the number drops by 2000 - 2 = 1998.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value is tested by asking what a digit is worth where it stands, not what the digit is.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A four-digit number has four different digits, and its digits add up to 10. What is the largest such number?

choices.misconception: I put 9 first and made the rest add to 1, without checking that two zeros repeat a digit.
I put 8 first and split the remaining 2 as 1 and 1, so the digit 1 appears twice.
I found that 7 must come first but then made the next digit as big as possible, which forced two zeros.
I used the four smallest different digits that add to 10 and put them largest first, without trying a bigger first digit.

hints: Make the first digit as big as you can.
To make a number largest, fix the digits from the left. For each choice of first digit, ask whether three different digits that are left can still make up the rest of the sum.
The three smallest different digits, 0, 1 and 2, add to 3. So the first digit can be at most 10 - 3 = 7.

solutions.reliable: Try first digits from 9 downward. With 9 first, the other three different digits must add to 1, but three different digits add to at least 0 + 1 + 2 = 3. The same problem stops 8, which leaves only 2. With 7 first, the rest must add to 3, which forces 0, 1 and 2, and the largest order is 7210. The transferable idea: build the largest number greedily from the left, but check at each step that the remaining digits can still meet every condition.
solutions.elegant: The three digits after the first add to at least 0 + 1 + 2 = 3, so the first digit is at most 7, and then the rest must be exactly 2, 1, 0 in that order.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles test whether you check every condition, here 'different digits', while greedily making a number as large as possible.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the four-digit number 4?52, the ? stands for one missing digit. The number is divisible by 3 but not by 9. How many different digits could replace the ?

choices.misconception: I thought every multiple of 3 is also a multiple of 9, so I decided no digit could work.
I stopped at the first digit that worked, 1, and did not test the others.
I found 1, 4 and 7 but forgot to throw out 7, which makes the number divisible by 9 as well.
I counted the digits that fail the test for 3 instead of the ones that pass it.

hints: Add up the digits you can see.
A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is a multiple of 3, and by 9 when its digit sum is a multiple of 9. So you want digit sums that are multiples of 3 but not 9.
The known digits add to 11. Adding the missing digit, you can reach 12, 15 or 18. One of those is a multiple of 9.

solutions.reliable: The known digits give 4 + 5 + 2 = 11. The missing digit d makes the sum 11 + d, from 11 to 20. The multiples of 3 in that range are 12, 15 and 18, so d is 1, 4 or 7. But 18 is a multiple of 9, so d = 7 gives a number divisible by 9 and must be removed. That leaves 1 and 4: 2 digits. The transferable idea: divisibility by 3 and by 9 both live in the digit sum, so a 'but not' condition is checked on the same sum.

problems.whyOnTest: Divisibility rules are tested with a 'but not' twist: every multiple of 9 is a multiple of 3, so one case must be removed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the value of 50 - 49 + 48 - 47 + ... + 4 - 3 + 2 - 1?

choices.misconception: I paired the numbers from 50 - 49 down to 4 - 3 and forgot the last pair, 2 - 1.
I thought each of the 49 gaps between neighbouring numbers gave a difference of 1.
I thought each of the 50 numbers gave a difference of 1, so I counted numbers instead of pairs.
I added all the numbers from 1 to 50 and ignored the minus signs.

hints: Look at the first two numbers together.
Group the terms in pairs, each a number minus the one just below it. Every pair has the same value, so the answer is that value times the number of pairs.
Each pair such as 50 - 49 or 2 - 1 equals 1. The 50 numbers make 25 pairs.

solutions.reliable: Group as (50 - 49) + (48 - 47) + ... + (2 - 1). Each bracket equals 1. There are 50 numbers, so there are 25 brackets, and the total is 25. The transferable idea: when signs alternate, pair neighbouring terms so each pair has the same simple value, then count the pairs carefully.
solutions.elegant: Add the two kinds of number separately: the even numbers 2 to 50 add to 650 and the odd numbers 1 to 49 add to 625, so the value is 650 - 625 = 25.

problems.whyOnTest: Long alternating sums are designed for regrouping, and the traps are counting numbers instead of pairs.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A paint colour is mixed from red, white and blue paint in the ratio 3 : 7 : 2. In one batch there are 12 litres more white paint than red paint. How many litres of blue paint are in the batch?

choices.misconception: I took the 12 litres to be the red paint's 3 parts, so a part was 4 and the blue was 8.
I found the red paint, 3 parts of 3 litres, instead of the blue.
I took the 12 litres as one part, so the blue's 2 parts came to 24.
I found the whole batch, 12 parts of 3 litres, instead of the blue paint.

hints: How many parts more white is there than red?
Draw the ratio as equal parts: 3 for red, 7 for white and 2 for blue. The 12 litres are not one colour, they are the gap between white and red, so count the parts in that gap.
White has 7 - 3 = 4 parts more than red, so 4 parts are 12 litres and one part is 3 litres.

solutions.reliable: White is 7 parts and red is 3 parts, so white has 4 parts more than red. Those 4 parts are the 12 litres, so one part is 3 litres. Blue is 2 parts, which is 6 litres. Check: red 9, white 21 and blue 6 litres are in the ratio 3 : 7 : 2, and 21 - 9 = 12. The transferable idea: in a ratio problem, first work out which parts a given amount stands for, then find the size of one part.

problems.whyOnTest: Ratio problems test whether you match a given amount to the right number of parts; here the 12 litres are a difference of 4 parts, not one share.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Roughly how many hours old is a child on their 11th birthday?

choices.misconception: I found 11 times 365 days and then divided by 24 instead of multiplying.
I counted the days, 11 times 365, and never turned days into hours.
I found the hours in one year, about 8760, and forgot to multiply by 11.
I multiplied by 60 as well, which gives minutes, not hours.

hints: Round the numbers before you multiply.
Chain the units: years to days, days to hours. Rounding each number to something friendly keeps the arithmetic quick, and only the size of the answer matters here.
11 years is about 4000 days, and each day has 24 hours, which is about 25.

solutions.reliable: 11 years is 11 times 365, about 4000 days. Each day has 24 hours, so the total is about 4000 times 24, which is close to 100 000 (the exact value is 96 360). The transferable idea: estimate by rounding to friendly numbers and tracking units, then pick the choice with the right number of digits.
solutions.elegant: A year is about 8760 hours, close to 9000, and 11 years is a little under 100 000 hours.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimation questions check you multiply through every unit change; each wrong choice stops at the wrong unit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, P is at 2.4 and Q is at 5.1. The point M is exactly halfway between P and Q. What number is at M?

choices.misconception: I found half the distance from P to Q and gave that instead of the position of M.
I found the distance from P to Q and gave that as the answer.
I added half the distance to Q instead of to P, which goes past Q.
I added the two positions together and forgot to halve the total.

hints: The halfway point must lie between 2.4 and 5.1.
Find how far apart P and Q are, take half of that distance, then step that far from P toward Q. Check that the answer really sits between the two points.
The distance is 5.1 - 2.4 = 2.7, and half of 2.7 is 1.35. Now start at P.

solutions.reliable: The distance from P to Q is 5.1 - 2.4 = 2.7. Half of that is 1.35. Starting at P, M is at 2.4 + 1.35 = 3.75. Check from Q: 5.1 - 1.35 = 3.75 as well. The transferable idea: a midpoint is the average of the two ends, and it must land between them.
solutions.elegant: The midpoint is the average: (2.4 + 5.1) divided by 2 = 7.5 divided by 2 = 3.75.

problems.whyOnTest: Number-line questions test whether you report a position or a distance; three choices here are distances or overshoots.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the addition ABC + ABC + ABC = BBB, each letter stands for a different digit, and ABC and BBB are three-digit numbers. What is A + B + C?

choices.misconception: I took ABC as 111, because three 111s make 333, and added 1 + 1 + 1 without checking that B has to be the same digit in both numbers.
I found that B is 4 and gave B instead of the sum of all three digits.
I added up the digits of BBB, which is 444, instead of the digits of ABC.
I tried B = 5 and got 185, but never checked that its middle digit should be B.

hints: BBB is B times 111.
Three times ABC equals BBB, and BBB is B times 111, which is B times 3 times 37. So ABC must be 37 times B. Test the values of B, remembering the middle digit of ABC has to be B.
ABC is 37 times B. Try B from 3 to 9 and look for a result whose middle digit is B.

solutions.reliable: Since BBB = B times 111 and 111 = 3 times 37, the equation says ABC = 37 times B. For ABC to have three digits, B is at least 3. Testing: 111, 148, 185, 222, 259, 296, 333 for B = 3 to 9. Only 148 has middle digit B = 4 and three different digits. Check: 148 times 3 = 444. So A + B + C = 1 + 4 + 8 = 13. The transferable idea: rewrite a repeated-digit number like BBB as B times 111, and factor 111 to shrink the search.
solutions.elegant: Column by column: 3 times C must end in B, and 3 times ABC is at most 999, so A is 1, 2 or 3. With A = 1, BBB lies between 300 and 599, so B is 3, 4 or 5, making C equal to 1, 8 or 5. Only 148 works with three different digits. The cases A = 2 and A = 3 fail the same quick test.

problems.whyOnTest: Cryptarithms reward one structural insight, here BBB = B times 111, and punish skipping the check that every letter fits.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The word PUZZLES is written over and over without spaces: PUZZLESPUZZLESPUZ... What is the 100th letter?

choices.misconception: I stopped one short and found the 99th letter.
I counted one letter past the remainder, so I found the 101st letter.
I forgot the double Z and counted PUZZLES as 6 letters, which made the remainder 4.
I thought 100 letters is a whole number of words, so the 100th letter ends a word.

hints: How long is one copy of the word?
The letters repeat in a cycle as long as the word. Find how many full copies fit in 100 letters; the remainder tells you how far into the next copy you are.
PUZZLES has 7 letters. 7 times 14 = 98, so the 98th letter ends a copy.

solutions.reliable: PUZZLES has 7 letters, counting both Zs. 14 full copies use 98 letters, so the 99th letter is P and the 100th is U. In terms of remainders, 100 divided by 7 is 14 remainder 2, and the 2nd letter is U. The transferable idea: in a repeating pattern, the position divided by the cycle length leaves a remainder that names the place in the cycle.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeating cycles test careful counting of the cycle and of the remainder; both slips appear among the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ... fill a grid along diagonals. Diagonal 1 is just 1 (row 1, column 1). Diagonal 2 holds 2 (row 1, column 2) then 3 (row 2, column 1). Each new diagonal is one longer, starts in row 1 and runs down to column 1. Which number is in row 3, column 5?

choices.misconception: I stepped down the diagonal three times from row 1 instead of twice, so I landed in row 4.
I went along the diagonal from the bottom, starting at column 1, instead of starting from row 1.
I gave the last number on that diagonal, the one in column 1, instead of the one in row 3.
I thought row 3, column 5 is on diagonal 8, because 3 + 5 = 8, so I started from 29.

hints: Sketch the first four diagonals.
Every square on one diagonal has the same row + column. Work out which diagonal row 3, column 5 lies on, find the number that starts that diagonal in row 1, then step down the diagonal to row 3.
Row + column is 2 on diagonal 1, 3 on diagonal 2, and so on, so row 3, column 5 is on diagonal 7. Diagonals 1 to 6 use 1 + 2 + ... + 6 = 21 numbers.

solutions.reliable: On diagonal 1 the row plus the column is 2, on diagonal 2 it is 3, and so on, so row 3, column 5 (3 + 5 = 8) is on diagonal 7. Diagonals 1 to 6 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21 numbers, so diagonal 7 starts with 22 in row 1, column 7. Going down it, 23 is in row 2, column 6 and 24 is in row 3, column 5. The transferable idea: in a grid filled by a rule, find something that stays the same along the path of the filling, here row + column, and use it to locate a square without drawing the whole grid.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid patterns test whether you find the rule that locates a square, here row + column naming the diagonal, instead of drawing the whole grid.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five people sit around a round table. Each is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Every one of them says: "Both people next to me are knaves." How many knights are at the table?

choices.misconception: I thought everyone could be a knave, without noticing their statements would then all be true.
I placed one knight and checked only the two people beside it, not the knaves on the far side.
I put knights in every other seat, 1, 3 and 5, forgetting that seats 5 and 1 are next to each other.
I believed every statement, so I made everyone a knight without checking that they would then be lying.

hints: What does a knave's statement tell you once you know it is false?

A knight must have two knaves beside it, so no two knights sit together. A knave's statement is false, so every knave must have at least one knight beside it. Find how many knights satisfy both rules.
Two knights cannot sit side by side, and with 5 seats that allows at most 2. Check whether 0 or 1 knight can leave every knave next to a knight.

solutions.reliable: A knight tells the truth, so both of its neighbours are knaves: no two knights are adjacent, which allows at most 2 knights in 5 seats around a circle. A knave lies, so at least one of its neighbours is a knight. With 0 knights every knave would be telling the truth, which is impossible. With 1 knight, the two people opposite it have only knave neighbours, so they would be telling the truth. With 2 knights in seats 1 and 3, the knaves in seats 2, 4 and 5 each sit next to a knight, and everything works. So there are exactly 2 knights. The transferable idea: turn each type's statement into a rule about its neighbours, then test the possible counts and check every person.

problems.whyOnTest: Knights-and-knaves puzzles test whether you use the liars' statements too, and around a table whether you remember the circle closes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A staircase is built from unit squares. Stage n has n squares in its bottom row, n - 1 in the row above, and so on up to 1 square at the top, with every row lined up on the left. Stage 1 is a single square. What is the perimeter of stage 10?

choices.misconception: I counted only the horizontal edges, the bottom and the tops of the steps, and missed the vertical ones.
I counted the squares in stage 10 instead of the edges around the outside.
I thought every new square adds 2 to the perimeter, but squares tucked into a step touch two others and add nothing.
I added the perimeters of all 55 squares, counting the shared inside edges as well.

hints: Work out the perimeters of stages 1, 2 and 3.

Try small cases and look for a pattern, or slide the steps' edges out to the edges of a rectangle around the staircase. The horizontal step edges together make the top, and the vertical ones make the right side.
Stages 1, 2 and 3 have perimeters 4, 8 and 12. Sliding the step edges outward turns the staircase's outline into a 10 by 10 square's outline.

solutions.reliable: The left side and the bottom are each 10 long. The tops of the steps are horizontal edges that together cover a length of 10, and the risers on the right are vertical edges that together cover a height of 10. So the perimeter is 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 40. The small cases 4, 8, 12 for stages 1, 2, 3 agree with the rule 4 times n. The transferable idea: the perimeter of a staircase shape equals the perimeter of the rectangle around it, because the steps can be pushed out to the rectangle's edges.
solutions.elegant: Push every step edge outward: the treads slide up to the top side and the risers slide right to the right side, so the outline has the same length as a 10 by 10 square, which is 40.

problems.whyOnTest: Growth patterns at 5 points need an idea, here that a staircase's perimeter equals its bounding square's, rather than counting squares.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five standard dice, whose opposite faces add up to 7, stand in a row on a table, each touching the next. Wherever two dice touch, the touching faces show the same number. The outer face of the left end die shows 3. What is the total of all the faces that touch another die?

choices.misconception: I added the two touching faces of each of the three middle dice, 7 each, and forgot that the end dice touch a neighbour too.
I thought every touching face shows 3, like the left end, so I did 8 faces times 3.
I added the left end die's touching face, 4, but forgot that the die at the right end touches a neighbour too.
I used the 3 on the outer face of the left die instead of the 4 on its touching face.

hints: Which faces of a middle die touch its neighbours?
A middle die touches its two neighbours with a pair of opposite faces, which add to 7. Each end die touches with only one face, so find those by following the row from the left end.
The three middle dice give 3 times 7 = 21. The left die's touching face is opposite its 3, so it shows 4.

solutions.reliable: Each of the three middle dice touches its neighbours with two opposite faces, worth 7 per die, so they give 21. The left die's touching face is opposite the 3, so it shows 4. Following the row: die 2 has 4 on its left and 3 on its right, die 3 has 3 and 4, and die 4 has 4 and 3, so die 5 touches with 3. The total is 21 + 4 + 3 = 28. The transferable idea: on a die, a pair of opposite faces always adds to 7, so whenever both faces of a pair are counted, their total is fixed without knowing the numbers.
solutions.elegant: Along the row the touching numbers alternate 4, 4, 3, 3, 4, 4, 3, 3. That is four 4s and four 3s, so the total is 4 times 7 = 28. With five dice the answer would be 28 whatever the left end showed.

problems.whyOnTest: Dice problems reward spotting that opposite faces add to 7, which turns tracking every face into a quick fixed total.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Cubes are stacked in towers on a 3 by 3 board. From the front, the tallest towers in the three columns look 3, 1 and 2 cubes high. From the right side, the tallest towers in the three rows look 2, 3 and 1 cubes high. What is the largest number of cubes there could be?

choices.misconception: I copied the front view into all three rows, which makes every row look 3 high from the side.
I gave each square the larger of its column's and its row's heights, which makes some views too tall.
I filled the whole board 3 cubes high and ignored both views.
I multiplied the totals of the two views, 6 times 6.

hints: Each square's tower is limited by two views.
A tower cannot be taller than the front view allows for its column, or than the side view allows for its row. Make every tower as tall as both limits allow, then add.
Each square can hold the smaller of its column height and its row height. Fill in the 3 by 3 table of these smaller values.

solutions.reliable: A square in a column of height c and a row of height r can hold at most the smaller of c and r. Making every square exactly that tall keeps both views correct. The row of height 2 gives 2, 1, 2 = 5. The row of height 3 gives 3, 1, 2 = 6. The row of height 1 gives 1, 1, 1 = 3. The total is 5 + 6 + 3 = 14. The transferable idea: when two views limit a stack, each tower is capped by the smaller limit, and the largest stack uses every cap.

problems.whyOnTest: Views-of-a-solid questions test whether you combine two views square by square rather than reading each view alone.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle 6 units by 8 units is covered exactly, with no gaps and no overlaps, by rectangular tiles that are 2 units by 3 units. How many tiles are used?

choices.misconception: I laid every tile with its 3 side along the 8 side, fitted only two per row, and ignored the strip left over.
I divided the 48 unit squares by 3 only, as if each tile covered 3 squares.
I divided the 48 unit squares by 2 only, as if each tile covered 2 squares.
I counted the unit squares in the rectangle instead of the tiles.

hints: How many unit squares does one tile cover?
When tiles cover a shape exactly, the shape's area equals the number of tiles times the area of one tile. Find both areas and divide.
The rectangle covers 6 times 8 = 48 unit squares, and one tile covers 2 times 3 = 6.

solutions.reliable: The rectangle has area 6 times 8 = 48 and each tile has area 2 times 3 = 6, so 48 divided by 6 = 8 tiles. A real layout exists: put the 3 sides along the 6 side (two tiles across) and the 2 sides along the 8 side (four tiles down), giving 2 times 4 = 8. The transferable idea: in an exact tiling, area divides evenly, and the tile count is the big area divided by the small one.
solutions.elegant: Two tiles fit across the 6 side and four fit along the 8 side, so 2 times 4 = 8 without working out any area.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions check that you compare areas, not lengths, and that a layout actually exists.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square sheet of paper is folded in half, and then in half again, to make a smaller square. The corner where the two folds meet is cut off with one straight cut, and one hole is punched through the middle of the small square. How many holes are in the paper when it is unfolded?

choices.misconception: I counted one hole from the cut and one from the punch, without thinking about the layers.
I thought two folds make only two layers, so the punch made 2 holes, plus 1 from the cut.
I thought cutting a corner only makes a notch, so I counted just the 4 punched holes.
I thought the cut corner makes 4 holes as well, one in each layer, like the punch.

hints: How many layers thick is the folded square?
Folding twice makes four layers, so a punch through the middle goes through all four. The folded corner, though, is the centre of the big sheet, where all four layers meet at one point.
The punch makes 4 holes, one in each quarter. The four cut corners all meet at the centre and join into a single hole.

solutions.reliable: Two folds make four layers, so the punch makes 4 holes, one in each quarter of the sheet. The corner where both folds meet is the centre of the original square. Cutting it off removes a small triangle from each of the four layers, and those four triangles fit together around the centre into one diamond-shaped hole. So there are 4 + 1 = 5 holes. The transferable idea: unfold step by step and track where each cut sits on the original sheet; cuts on a fold join up across it instead of making separate holes.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding and punching tests tracking layers, and noticing that a cut on the folds joins into one hole instead of several.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A digital clock shows times from 1:00 to 12:59, such as 7:05 or 11:40. It never shows 0 or 13 as the hour. Going once through all of these times, for how many of them do the digits shown add up to 4?

choices.misconception: I only used minute digits from 1 to 9 and forgot that a minute digit can be 0, as in 1:03.
I only looked at the hours 1 to 9 and forgot that 10, 11 and 12 have small digit sums too.
I forgot 4:00, where the minutes are 00 and add nothing to the sum.
I counted every time twice, once in the morning and once in the afternoon, but the question goes through the times only once.

hints: Sort the times by the hour.
Only hours whose digits add to 4 or less can work, and 10, 11 and 12 count. For each such hour, count the minutes whose two digits make up the rest of the sum, allowing 0 as a digit.
The hours that can work are 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11 and 12. For hour 1, the minute digits must add to 3: 03, 12, 21 and 30, which is 4 ways.

solutions.reliable: The hour's digits must add to at most 4, so the hour is 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11 or 12, with digit sums 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2 and 3. The minute digits must make up the rest. A sum of 3 can be made in 4 ways (03, 12, 21, 30), a sum of 2 in 3 ways (02, 11, 20), a sum of 1 in 2 ways (01, 10) and a sum of 0 in 1 way (00). So the hours give 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 for hours 1 to 4 and 4 + 3 + 2 for hours 10 to 12, a total of 10 + 9 = 19. The transferable idea: in casework, split by the most restricted part first, here the hour, so every case is a short, complete list.
solutions.elegant: Hours 10, 11 and 12 have the same digit sums as hours 1, 2 and 3, so they repeat those cases: (4 + 3 + 2 + 1) + (4 + 3 + 2) = 19.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework is tested by whether every case is listed, including easy-to-miss ones like the two-digit hours and minutes with a 0.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three different numbers are chosen from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 so that no two of the chosen numbers are next to each other (such as 3 and 4). How many such choices are there?

choices.misconception: I took away 6 neighbouring pairs times 5 choices of third number from 35, counting some choices twice.
I counted the choices that break the rule instead of the ones that keep it.
I only threw out choices where all three numbers are in a row, like 3, 4, 5.
I counted all the ways to choose three numbers and ignored the rule.

hints: List them, starting with the smallest number chosen.
Fix the smallest number, then the middle one, and count the possible largest ones. Keeping every list in increasing order stops you counting the same choice twice.
If the smallest is 1, the middle can be 3, 4 or 5, leaving 3, 2 and 1 choices for the largest.

solutions.reliable: List the choices in increasing order. Smallest 1: (1,3,5), (1,3,6), (1,3,7), (1,4,6), (1,4,7), (1,5,7), which is 6. Smallest 2: (2,4,6), (2,4,7), (2,5,7), which is 3. Smallest 3: (3,5,7), which is 1. Smallest 4 or more leaves no room. The total is 6 + 3 + 1 = 10. The transferable idea: count with a restriction by listing in a fixed order, so each choice appears exactly once.
solutions.elegant: Close up the gaps: if the chosen numbers are a, b, c, then a, b - 1, c - 2 are three different numbers from 1 to 5, and every such triple comes back to exactly one valid choice. So the count equals the number of ways to choose 3 from 5, which is 10.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting with restrictions is tested by tempting overcounts: subtracting neighbour pairs counts some choices twice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sam's bus leaves at 7:50 and the ride takes 25 minutes. From the bus stop he walks 8 minutes to school. School starts at 8:30. How many minutes early is Sam?

choices.misconception: I forgot the 8-minute walk and stopped when the bus arrived at 8:15.
I worked out that Sam arrives at 8:23 and gave the minutes of that time.
I added the ride and the walk to get the travel time, which is not what was asked.
I found the time from 7:50 to 8:30 and forgot the trip takes some of it.

hints: What exactly is the question asking for?
Find the time Sam arrives at school, then compare it with the start time. Re-read the question before choosing, because several times appear along the way.
The bus arrives at 8:15, and the walk brings Sam to school at 8:23.

solutions.reliable: The bus leaves at 7:50 and takes 25 minutes, so it arrives at 8:15. The 8-minute walk brings Sam to school at 8:23. School starts at 8:30, so he is 30 - 23 = 7 minutes early. The transferable idea: before answering, name the exact quantity asked for, because a problem with several steps hands you several tempting numbers.
solutions.elegant: From 7:50 to 8:30 is 40 minutes, and the trip uses 25 + 8 = 33 of them, so 40 - 33 = 7 minutes are left over.

problems.whyOnTest: Contest problems put every intermediate number among the choices; this tests that you answer the question actually asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ann took a third of the sweets in a bag. Then Ben took half of the sweets that were left. Cy took the last 6 sweets, and the bag was empty. How many sweets were in the bag at the start?

choices.misconception: I found how many sweets were left after Ann took hers, not how many there were at the start.
I undid Ann's step by adding a third of 12, but Ann took a third of the starting number, not of 12.
I undid Ann's step by doubling 12 again, as if she had taken half.
I thought Ann left a third instead of taking a third, so I tripled 12.

hints: Start with Cy and go backwards.
Undo the last step first. Cy's 6 sweets were what Ben left, and Ben took half. Then think about what fraction of the bag Ann left behind, because that is the amount you know.
Before Ben, there were 12 sweets. Ann took a third, so those 12 sweets are the two thirds she left.

solutions.reliable: Cy took what Ben left, and Ben took half, so before Ben there were 2 times 6 = 12 sweets. Ann took a third of the bag, so these 12 sweets are the other two thirds. One third is 6, and the bag held 3 times 6 = 18. Check: Ann takes 6 of the 18, leaving 12; Ben takes 6, leaving 6 for Cy. The transferable idea: work backwards from the end, and when someone takes a fraction, ask what fraction is left, because that is the amount you know.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards is tested with fractions of a changing amount: the number you know is what was left, not what was taken.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A lift starts on floor 60 of a very tall building. It goes up 1 floor, then down 2 floors, then up 3, then down 4, and so on, each trip 1 floor longer than the one before. Which floor is the lift on after its 51st trip?

choices.misconception: I found how many floors the lift ends up above where it started and gave that instead of the floor number.
I made one trip too many, stopping after the 52nd trip, which goes down.
I worked out where the lift is after 50 trips and forgot to make the 51st trip.
I thought each up trip and the down trip after it cancel out, so only the last trip of 51 floors counted.

hints: Work out which floor the lift is on after each of its first six trips.
Try small cases first. List the floors after trips 1 to 6 and look for a rule for the odd-numbered trips, since trip 51 is odd.
After trips 1, 3 and 5 the lift is on floors 61, 62 and 63. After trip 2k + 1 it is on floor 60 + (k + 1), and 51 = 2 × 25 + 1.

solutions.reliable: The floors after trips 1 to 6 are 61, 59, 62, 58, 63, 57. Each down trip is 1 longer than the up trip before it, so every pair (up, then down) takes the lift 1 floor lower. After 50 trips, which is 25 pairs, the lift is on floor 60 - 25 = 35. Trip 51 goes up 51 floors, to 35 + 51 = 86. The small cases agree: after trip 2k + 1 the lift is on floor 60 + k + 1, and k = 25 gives 86. The transferable idea: when a process runs for many steps, do the first few by hand and let the pattern tell you the rule.
solutions.elegant: Keep trip 1 on its own and pair the rest as (down 2, up 3), (down 4, up 5), and so on up to (down 50, up 51). That is 25 pairs, each taking the lift 1 floor higher. So the lift ends on floor 60 + 1 + 25 = 86.

problems.whyOnTest: Trying small cases turns a 51-step process into a pattern; the trap is pairing the trips in a way that leaves the last one out.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The number 333...33 is written with twenty 3s, and it is multiplied by itself. What is the sum of the digits of the answer?

choices.misconception: I kept adding the digits of the answer until only one digit was left, and that always comes to 9 here.
I added the digits of the number itself, twenty 3s, instead of the digits of its square.
I saw the pattern of 1s, a 0, 8s and a final 9, wrote nineteen 1s and nineteen 8s, but forgot the final 9.
I treated 33 × 33 as the first case of my pattern, so I added 9 one time too many and got 18 + 19 × 9.

hints: Square 3, 33 and 333, and add up the digits each time.
Try small cases. The squares follow a clear digit pattern, and so do their digit sums. Check the rule on one more case before you trust it for twenty 3s.

solutions.reliable: Small cases: 3 × 3 = 9 (digit sum 9), 33 × 33 = 1089 (18), 333 × 333 = 110889 (27), 3333 × 3333 = 11108889 (36). With n threes the square is n - 1 ones, then a 0, then n - 1 eights, then a 9. For twenty 3s that is nineteen 1s, a 0, nineteen 8s and a 9, so the digit sum is 19 + 0 + 19 × 8 + 9 = 19 + 152 + 9 = 180. The transferable idea: a problem with a huge number is usually a pattern problem in disguise, and three or four small cases reveal it.
solutions.elegant: Each extra 3 adds one more 1 and one more 8 to the square, which adds 1 + 8 = 9 to the digit sum. A single 3 gives 9, so twenty 3s give 9 × 20 = 180.

problems.whyOnTest: Nobody can multiply a 20-digit number by hand in a contest; trying 3, 33 and 333 first shows the pattern that makes the answer easy.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four different whole numbers, each bigger than 1, are multiplied together. Which of these could be the result?

choices.misconception: I used 2, 2, 3 and 5, repeating the 2, but the four numbers must all be different.
I used 2, 3, 3 and 5, repeating the 3, but the four numbers must all be different.
I used 1, 3, 4 and 8, forgetting that every number must be bigger than 1.
I used 1, 2, 5 and 10, forgetting that 1 is not allowed.

hints: What is the smallest result that four such numbers can give?
Bound the answer before testing anything. The smallest possible product uses the four smallest allowed numbers, and any choice below that bound is impossible.
The smallest product is 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 = 120, so every choice below 120 is out. Then check that the remaining choice really can be made.

solutions.reliable: The four different numbers are each at least 2, so in order they are at least 2, 3, 4 and 5. Their product is therefore at least 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 = 120. That rules out 60, 90, 96 and 100 at once. The last choice works: 144 = 2 × 3 × 4 × 6. The transferable idea: find the smallest (or largest) value possible first, and every choice beyond it can be crossed out without any searching.

problems.whyOnTest: Bounding the smallest possible product removes four choices in one step, faster than trying to factor each one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four children have different whole-number ages that add up to 30. The youngest is 3 years old. Which of these could be the age of the oldest?

choices.misconception: I spread the ages out as 3, 7, 8 and 9 without checking the total; they only add up to 27, not 30.
I let the two middle children both be 4, giving 3, 4, 4 and 19, but the ages must all be different.
I made the two middle children 1 and 2, forgetting that nobody can be younger than the youngest, who is 3.
I subtracted only the youngest child's age from 30 and forgot about the two middle children.

hints: How old can the oldest be at most? And at least?
Bound the answer from both sides. For the oldest to be as old as possible, make the middle two as young as allowed; for the oldest to be as young as possible, make them as old as allowed.
Most: 3 + 4 + 5 + 18 = 30, so the oldest is at most 18. Least: if the oldest is k, the total is at most 3 + (k - 2) + (k - 1) + k = 3k, and 3k must reach 30.

solutions.reliable: Upper bound: the middle two are at least 4 and 5, so the oldest is at most 30 - 3 - 4 - 5 = 18, and 3, 4, 5, 18 works. Lower bound: if the oldest is k, the other two are at most k - 1 and k - 2, so the total is at most 3 + (k - 2) + (k - 1) + k = 3k. This must be at least 30, so k is at least 10. The oldest is between 10 and 18. Only 18 lies in that range: 9 is too small, and 19, 24 and 27 are too big. The transferable idea: bounding from both sides narrows five choices to one without trying any particular set of ages.
solutions.elegant: Total = 3 + (the other three). The other three are different and bigger than 3, so they add up to at least 4 + 5 + k and at most (k - 2) + (k - 1) + k. So 12 + k is at most 30 and 3k is at least 30, giving k between 10 and 18.

problems.whyOnTest: Asking how big and how small the answer can be is often faster than solving, and here it leaves exactly one choice standing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to 6.9 × 4.1 + 8.2 × 2.9?

choices.misconception: I added all four numbers together instead of multiplying each pair.
I worked out only the second product, about 8 × 3, and forgot to add the first one.
I worked out only the first product, about 7 × 4, and forgot to add the second one.
I multiplied all four rounded numbers together, 7 × 4 × 8 × 3, instead of adding the two products.

hints: Round each number to the nearest whole number first.
The choices are far apart, so an estimate is enough. Round each number, multiply the pairs, then add the two products, doing the multiplications before the addition.
Rounded, the sum is 7 × 4 + 8 × 3 = 28 + 24.

solutions.reliable: Round each number: 6.9 is about 7, 4.1 about 4, 8.2 about 8 and 2.9 about 3. Then 7 × 4 + 8 × 3 = 28 + 24 = 52. The exact value is 28.29 + 23.78 = 52.07, so 52 is closest by far. The transferable idea: when the choices are spread out, a quick rounded estimate picks the answer and the exact arithmetic is wasted time.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimation is a decision about the choices: when they are far apart, rounding is enough, as long as the order of operations is kept.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A runner completes each lap of a track in 1 minute 58 seconds. About how long does she take to run 21 laps at this pace?

choices.misconception: I rounded each lap down to 1 minute and ignored the 58 seconds.
I worked out 21 × 118 = 2478 seconds and then read 2478 as about 24.8 minutes.
I treated 1 minute 58 seconds as 1.58 minutes, but a minute has 60 seconds, not 100.
I worked out 21 × 118 = 2478, treated it as minutes and divided by 60 to get hours.

hints: 1 minute 58 seconds is very close to a whole number of minutes.
The choices are far apart, so round the lap time to the nearest minute and multiply. Be careful: 58 seconds is almost a whole minute, not 0.58 of one.
1 minute 58 seconds is just under 2 minutes, so 21 laps take just under 21 × 2 = 42 minutes.

solutions.reliable: Each lap takes 2 seconds less than 2 minutes. So 21 laps take 21 × 2 = 42 minutes, minus 21 × 2 = 42 seconds, which is 41 minutes 18 seconds. The nearest choice is about 41 minutes. The transferable idea: round to a friendly number, estimate, and pick the nearest choice, but round minutes and seconds as time, not as decimals.
