problems.statement: Ali buys 4 identical pencils and pays with a 5-euro note. He gets 1.80 euros in change. Bea buys 7 of the same pencils. How much do Bea's pencils cost?

choices.misconception: I found the price of one pencil, 0.80 euros, and stopped there.
I worked out the cost of only the 3 extra pencils that Bea buys compared with Ali, 3 times 0.80 euros.
I treated the 1.80 euros change as the cost of 4 pencils, so one pencil was 0.45 euros and 7 cost 3.15 euros.
I worked out what Ali's 4 pencils cost, 3.20 euros, instead of Bea's 7.

hints: First find what Ali's pencils cost.
The change is what is left of the 5 euros, so the pencils cost the difference. Divide to find the price of one pencil, then scale up to 7.
Ali's 4 pencils cost $5 - 1.80 = 3.20$ euros, so one pencil costs 0.80 euros. Now multiply by 7.

solutions.reliable: Ali paid 5 euros and got 1.80 euros back, so his 4 pencils cost $5.00 - 1.80 = 3.20$ euros. One pencil costs $3.20 \div 4 = 0.80$ euros. Seven pencils cost $7 \times 0.80 = 5.60$ euros. Check: 5.60 is 3.20 for four pencils plus 2.40 for three more. The transferable idea: change is the money paid minus the cost, so subtract before you divide.
solutions.elegant: Bea buys 7 = 4 + 3 pencils. Four cost 3.20 euros and three cost three quarters of that, 2.40 euros, so 5.60 euros in all.

problems.whyOnTest: Money problems test whether you turn the change back into a cost before you divide, a step that is easy to skip under time pressure.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A frog sits at 0 on a number line. Each jump takes it exactly 3 units to the left or to the right. After exactly 7 jumps, which of these numbers could the frog be on?

choices.misconception: I thought the frog could jump right and left the same number of times and end back at 0, but 7 jumps cannot split into two equal groups.
I thought 2 more right jumps than left jumps was possible, but with 7 jumps the numbers of right and left jumps differ by an odd number.
I thought 4 more right jumps than left jumps was possible, giving 12, but with 7 jumps that difference must be odd.
I counted 6 jumps to the right as 18 and forgot about the seventh jump.

hints: Think about how many jumps go right and how many go left.
If r jumps go right and l go left, then r + l = 7 and the frog ends on 3 times (r - l). Ask whether r - l can be even when r + l is odd.
Since r + l = 7 is odd, r - l is odd too: 1, 3, 5 or 7, or minus one of these. So the frog ends on 3 times an odd number.

solutions.reliable: Say r jumps go right and l go left, so r + l = 7 and the frog ends on $3(r - l)$. Because r + l is odd, one of r and l is even and the other is odd, so r - l is odd. The possible positions are 3, 9, 15, 21 and their negatives. Of the choices only 9 works, for example with 5 jumps right and 2 jumps left: 15 - 6 = 9. The transferable idea: the sum and the difference of two whole numbers are always both even or both odd.
solutions.elegant: Each jump changes the frog's position by 3, an odd number, so every jump switches it between odd and even numbers. After an odd number of jumps from 0 it must be on an odd number, and 9 is the only odd choice.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity questions reward noticing that an odd number of odd-sized steps always lands on an odd number, which beats listing every route.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A row of square tiles follows a rule. Picture 1 is a black tile with an arrow pointing up. From each picture to the next, the arrow turns a quarter turn clockwise and the tile switches between black and white. So picture 2 is a white tile with an arrow pointing right. What does picture 23 look like?

choices.text: A black tile with the arrow pointing down
A white tile with the arrow pointing down
choices.misconception: I got the arrow right but thought the odd-numbered pictures are white.

choices.text: A black tile with the arrow pointing left
choices.misconception: I took the remainder 3 from 23 divided by 4 and turned the arrow 3 quarter turns from up, forgetting that picture 1 has had no turns yet.

choices.text: A white tile with the arrow pointing left
choices.misconception: I worked out picture 24 instead of picture 23.

choices.text: A black tile with the arrow pointing up
choices.misconception: I thought the arrow repeats every 2 pictures like the colour does, so every odd picture would match picture 1.

hints: Two things change at once. Track each one on its own.
The arrow repeats every 4 pictures and the colour every 2. Find where picture 23 falls in each cycle separately, then put the two answers together.
Pictures 1, 5, 9, ..., 21 have the arrow pointing up, so picture 22 points right and picture 23 points down. Odd-numbered pictures are black.

solutions.reliable: The arrow goes up, right, down, left and then repeats, so it has a cycle of 4. Picture 21 = 1 + 4 × 5 points up like picture 1, so picture 22 points right and picture 23 points down. The colour has a cycle of 2: odd pictures are black and even pictures are white, so picture 23 is black. Picture 23 is a black tile with the arrow pointing down. The transferable idea: when a pattern changes two things at once, find each cycle separately and then combine them.
solutions.elegant: Picture 23 comes after 22 changes. 22 quarter turns is 5 full turns and 2 more, so the arrow points down; 22 colour switches is an even number, so the tile is black, as at the start.

problems.whyOnTest: Visual patterns often change two features at once; this tests describing each change separately before choosing the next picture.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One angle of a parallelogram is 70 degrees. What is the sum of its two largest angles, in degrees?

choices.misconception: I found the size of one large angle, 110 degrees, but the question asks for the sum of two of them.
I added the two smallest angles, 70 + 70, instead of the two largest.
I added one large and one small angle, which sit next to each other and always make 180 degrees.
I subtracted 70 from 360, which gives the sum of the other three angles, not the two largest.

hints: Which angles of a parallelogram are equal?
In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add up to 180 degrees. Use that to find all four angles.
Going round the shape, the angles are 70, 110, 70 and 110 degrees.

solutions.reliable: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add up to 180 degrees, so the angle next to the 70 degree angle is 110 degrees. Opposite angles are equal, so the four angles are 70, 110, 70 and 110. The two largest add up to 110 + 110 = 220 degrees. Check: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360. The transferable idea: in a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add up to 180 degrees.
solutions.elegant: All four angles add up to 360 degrees and the two small ones are 70 each, so the two large ones together are 360 - 140 = 220 degrees.

problems.whyOnTest: Shape-property questions test whether you know which angles of a parallelogram match, and then answer exactly what is asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a square grid, the point P is at (3, 7). P is reflected in the horizontal line y = 4, and then the new point is reflected in the vertical line x = 5. Where does P end up?

choices.misconception: I did the first reflection, to (3, 1), and forgot the second one.
I skipped the reflection in y = 4 and only reflected (3, 7) in the line x = 5.
I moved the point onto each line instead of across it, first to (3, 4) and then to (5, 4).
I did the first reflection correctly, then moved the point 2 units, its distance from x = 5, but away from the line instead of across it.

hints: Do one reflection at a time.
A reflection in a horizontal line keeps x the same and puts the point the same distance away on the other side of the line. A reflection in a vertical line keeps y the same.
P is 3 units above y = 4, so its image is 3 units below, at (3, 1). Now (3, 1) is 2 units to the left of x = 5.

solutions.reliable: P = (3, 7) is 3 units above the line y = 4, so its reflection is 3 units below the line: (3, 1). That point is 2 units to the left of the line x = 5, so its reflection is 2 units to the right of it: (7, 1). The transferable idea: a reflection keeps the coordinate that runs along the mirror line and sends the point the same distance to the other side.
solutions.elegant: Reflecting in y = 4 sends y to 8 - y, and reflecting in x = 5 sends x to 10 - x. So (3, 7) goes to (10 - 3, 8 - 7) = (7, 1). In fact, two reflections in perpendicular lines make a half turn about the point where the lines cross, here (5, 4).

problems.whyOnTest: Reflection questions test whether you jump across the mirror line by the same distance, one step at a time, rather than sliding onto it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a square grid, a parallelogram has its corners at the grid points (0, 0), (5, 0), (7, 3) and (2, 3). What is its area, in grid squares?

choices.misconception: I used the triangle rule and halved the base times the height, but the shape is a parallelogram, not a triangle.
I counted only the 3 by 3 square between x = 2 and x = 5, where the shape fills the whole height, and left out the two slanted end pieces.
I drew the 7 by 3 box around the shape but took away only one of the two corner triangles outside it.
I took the area of the 7 by 3 box around the shape and forgot to remove the two corner triangles outside it.

hints: Can you cut off a piece at one end and move it to the other?
Cut the triangle off one slanted end and slide it to the other end. The pieces then make a rectangle, and cutting and moving does not change the area.
The triangle with corners (0, 0), (2, 0) and (2, 3) slides 5 units right to fill the gap at (5, 0), (7, 0), (7, 3). The result is a rectangle from x = 2 to x = 7, 3 squares tall.

solutions.reliable: Draw the box from (0, 0) to (7, 3); its area is 7 × 3 = 21. Outside the parallelogram but inside the box are two right triangles, one at the top left and one at the bottom right, each with legs 2 and 3. Each has area 2 × 3 / 2 = 3. So the area is 21 - 3 - 3 = 15 grid squares. The transferable idea: a slanted shape on a grid can be measured by cutting and moving pieces, or by subtracting from a box drawn around it.
solutions.elegant: Cut off the left-hand triangle and slide it 5 units to the right. The parallelogram becomes a 5 by 3 rectangle, so the area is 5 × 3 = 15.

problems.whyOnTest: Dissection questions test whether you see that cutting and sliding a piece keeps the area, turning a slanted shape into a rectangle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular pond is 10 m long and 4 m wide. A frog sits on one long edge, 3 m from a corner. It wants to reach the point directly opposite on the other long edge. It may not swim, but it can walk along the edge of the pond. What is the shortest distance it can walk?

choices.misconception: I measured straight across the pond, but the frog is not allowed to swim.
I thought going round to the opposite point always takes half the perimeter, 14 m, but that is only true when starting from the middle of a side.
I sent the frog round the far end: 7 m to that corner, 4 m across and 7 m back.
I walked the frog all the way round the pond, which is the whole perimeter, 28 m.

hints: Which corner is nearer to the frog?
The shortest route around a rectangle follows its edges, so the frog must go round one of the two ends. Work out both ways round and compare them.
Round the near end: 3 m to the corner, 4 m along the short side, then 3 m back along the other long side.

solutions.reliable: Going round the near end, the frog walks 3 m to the corner, 4 m along the short side and 3 m along the other long side to the point opposite: 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 m. Going round the far end it walks 7 + 4 + 7 = 18 m. The shortest walk is 10 m. The transferable idea: around an obstacle, the shortest path hugs the corners, so compare the possible ways round.
solutions.elegant: Both routes cross one short side of 4 m. The near route adds 3 m twice and the far route adds 7 m twice, so the shortest is 4 + 2 × 3 = 10 m.

problems.whyOnTest: Shortest-path questions test whether you respect the obstacle and compare the routes around it, instead of measuring the forbidden straight line.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a square grid, a triangle has its corners at the grid points (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4). How many grid points lie strictly inside the triangle, not on its edges?

choices.misconception: I also counted the point (3, 2), but it lies exactly on the slanted edge, not inside the triangle.
I worked out the area, 12, and thought the number of grid points inside must equal the area.
I counted the grid points inside the whole 6 by 4 rectangle instead of only inside the triangle.
I counted every grid point of the triangle, including the 12 points on its edges and corners.

hints: Go column by column.
For each x from 1 to 5, find how high the slanted edge is above that x, and count the whole-number heights above 0 and strictly below the edge. Take care with any point exactly on the edge.
The slanted edge drops 2 for every 3 across, so above x = 3 it is at height exactly 2. Above x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 its heights are 3 1/3, 2 2/3, 2, 1 1/3 and 2/3.

solutions.reliable: The slanted edge joins (0, 4) to (6, 0), dropping 2 for every 3 across. Column by column, its height is 3 1/3 above x = 1, 2 2/3 above x = 2, 2 above x = 3, 1 1/3 above x = 4 and 2/3 above x = 5. A point strictly inside has a height of at least 1 and below the edge, so the counts are 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 7. Above x = 3 the point (3, 2) is on the edge, so it does not count. The transferable idea: count grid points column by column, and check carefully for points that sit exactly on a slanted edge.
solutions.elegant: The 6 by 4 rectangle has 5 × 3 = 15 grid points inside it. Its diagonal from (0, 4) to (6, 0) passes through exactly one of them, (3, 2), and splits the other 14 into two matching halves. So the triangle has 14 / 2 = 7 points inside.

problems.whyOnTest: Lattice-point counting tests careful grid reasoning, especially spotting a point that lies exactly on a slanted edge.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The net in the picture is folded into a cube. At each corner of the cube, three faces meet. What is the largest possible total of the three numbers that meet at one corner?

figure.alt: A cube net of six squares. Four squares form a row, labelled 6, 1, 5 and 2 from left to right. A square labelled 4 is attached above the square labelled 1, and a square labelled 3 is attached below the square labelled 2.

choices.misconception: I found the smallest corner total, 1 + 3 + 5, instead of the largest.
I only looked at points where three squares already meet in the flat net, and the best of those was 6 + 1 + 4.
I saw that 6 and 5 are opposite, so I took 6 with the next biggest numbers, 4 and 3, without checking that 4 and 3 are opposite too.
I added the three biggest numbers, 6, 5 and 4, without checking that 6 and 5 land on opposite faces.

hints: First find which faces end up opposite each other.
Opposite faces never meet at a corner. Every corner uses exactly one face from each pair of opposite faces, so find the three opposite pairs first.
In the row of four, squares two apart fold to opposite faces: 6 with 5, and 1 with 2. That leaves 4 and 3 as the last pair.

solutions.reliable: In a row of four squares, the first and third fold to opposite faces, and so do the second and fourth, so 6 is opposite 5 and 1 is opposite 2. The two remaining squares, 4 and 3, are opposite each other. Each corner of the cube touches one face from each opposite pair, and every such choice of three faces meets at a corner. So the largest total takes the larger number from each pair: 6 + 2 + 4 = 12. The transferable idea: on a cube, three faces meet at a corner exactly when no two of them are opposite.

problems.whyOnTest: Net questions test whether you can find opposite faces before folding, because opposite faces can never share a corner.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ava, Ben, Cy, Dot and Eli all have different heights. Eli is taller than Ben, and Ben is taller than Cy. Dot is taller than Ben. Exactly two of the others are taller than Ava. Eli is not the tallest. Who is the second tallest?

choices.misconception: I found the tallest person, Dot, instead of the second tallest.
I thought having exactly two people taller than her put Ava in second place, but it puts her third.
I counted second from the wrong end and gave the second shortest person.
I thought the order of Dot and Eli is not fixed because no clue compares them directly, but the clue that Eli is not the tallest settles it.

hints: One clue fixes Ava's place exactly.
Ava is third. Ben has at least Eli and Dot above him, so think about where Ben and Cy can go. Then decide who is on top.
Ben must be fourth and Cy fifth, so Dot and Eli fill first and second place. Eli is not the tallest.

solutions.reliable: Exactly two people are taller than Ava, so Ava is third. Eli and Dot are both taller than Ben, and Ava is third, so Ben is fourth or fifth; since Ben is taller than Cy, Ben is fourth and Cy is fifth. Dot and Eli take first and second place, and Eli is not the tallest, so the order from tallest is Dot, Eli, Ava, Ben, Cy. The second tallest is Eli. The transferable idea: start with the clue that pins someone to an exact place, then fill in around it.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering puzzles test whether you start from the clue that fixes an exact position, then let the other clues squeeze everyone else into place.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag holds 7 red, 5 blue and 2 green marbles. Without looking, Leo takes marbles out one at a time. What is the smallest number of marbles he must take to be sure of having at least one marble of each colour?

choices.misconception: I thought 3 marbles are enough because there are 3 colours, but all 3 could be red.
I used one more than the number of colours, which is how many you need to be sure of two marbles of the same colour, not one of each.
I only imagined taking all 7 reds first, and forgot that the next marble could be blue rather than green.
I found the unluckiest case, all 7 red and all 5 blue marbles, but forgot that he needs one more marble to get a green one.

hints: Imagine Leo is as unlucky as possible.
Find the largest number of marbles he could take and still be missing a colour. To be sure, he needs one more than that.
The unluckiest start is all of the two biggest colours: 7 red and 5 blue marbles, and still no green.

solutions.reliable: In the unluckiest case Leo first takes all 7 red and all 5 blue marbles: 12 marbles and no green. The next marble must be green, so 13 marbles are enough. Fewer are not: with 12 marbles he might still have no green. Any 13 marbles must contain every colour, because leaving out one colour leaves at most 7 + 5 = 12 marbles. The transferable idea: to guarantee something, build the unluckiest case that avoids it, then add one.

problems.whyOnTest: Guarantee questions test worst-case thinking: find the unluckiest run that avoids the goal, then add one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three balances are level. On the first, 1 cube balances 3 balls. On the second, 2 balls balance 1 cone and 1 marble. On the third, 1 cone balances 3 marbles. All cubes weigh the same, and so do all balls, all cones and all marbles. How many marbles balance one cube?

choices.misconception: I found the weight of a ball, 2 marbles, instead of the weight of a cube.
I worked out what the 2 balls on the second balance weigh, 4 marbles, and took that as the weight of the cube.
I left out the marble on the second balance, so 2 balls balanced only a cone, 3 marbles, and a ball came out as 1.5 marbles.
I read the second balance as 1 ball balancing a cone and a marble, so a ball was 4 marbles and a cube 12.

hints: Start from the balance that uses only one kind of unknown object.
The third balance tells you a cone in marbles. Put that into the second balance to find a ball, then use the first balance to find a cube.
On the second balance, the cone and the marble together weigh 3 + 1 = 4 marbles, and that is the weight of 2 balls.

solutions.reliable: A cone weighs 3 marbles, so the right side of the second balance weighs 3 + 1 = 4 marbles. That is the weight of 2 balls, so one ball weighs 2 marbles. A cube balances 3 balls, which is 3 × 2 = 6 marbles. Check: 3 balls weigh 6 marbles, and 2 balls weigh 4 marbles, the same as a cone and a marble. The transferable idea: in a chain of balances, start with the one that has a single unknown and swap objects for marbles one step at a time.
solutions.elegant: Turn everything into marbles from the bottom of the chain up: cone = 3, so 2 balls = 3 + 1 = 4, so ball = 2, so cube = 3 × 2 = 6.

problems.whyOnTest: Balance puzzles test substitution: swapping each object for what it balances, one balance at a time, until everything is in the same unit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A board has 4 rows and 5 columns of squares. One domino is placed on the board so that it covers exactly two squares that share an edge. In how many different positions can it be placed?

choices.misconception: I only counted the dominoes lying along the rows, 4 in each of the 4 rows, and forgot the upright ones.
I thought every row and every column gives 4 positions, but a column has only 4 squares and so only 3 positions.
I gave every one of the 20 squares two dominoes, one going right and one going down, even for the squares on the right or bottom edge.
I counted from each square to each of its neighbours, which counts every domino twice, once from each end.

hints: Count lying-flat and standing-up positions separately.
A flat domino fits wherever two squares sit side by side in a row. Count the positions in one row, then multiply by the number of rows. Do the same for the columns.
A row of 5 squares has 4 places for a flat domino; a column of 4 squares has 3 places for an upright one.

solutions.reliable: Flat dominoes: each row of 5 squares has 4 places, and there are 4 rows, so there are 16. Upright dominoes: each column of 4 squares has 3 places, and there are 5 columns, so there are 15. In total there are 16 + 15 = 31 positions. The transferable idea: count the positions of a shape by where its first square can go, in each direction separately.
solutions.elegant: Every domino position matches one unit edge shared by two squares. Each of the 4 rows has 4 such edges between its squares, 16 in all, and each of the 3 lines between rows has 5, 15 in all. That makes 31.

problems.whyOnTest: Sliding-window counting tests counting the positions in each direction, rather than cutting the board into pieces or counting each pair twice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A number machine turns 2 into 6, 4 into 20 and 5 into 30. It uses the same rule every time. What does it turn 8 into?

choices.misconception: I built a rule from the first example only, multiply by 3, and did not test it on 4 or 5.
I used only the first two examples, which go up by 14 over 2 steps, and assumed every step of 1 adds 7, without checking that 5 would then give 27, not 30.
I found the rule, multiply the number by the next number, but multiplied 8 by 7, the number before it.
I multiplied 8 by itself but forgot to add 8.

hints: Test any rule you find on all three examples.
The outputs do not grow at a steady rate, so the rule is not just adding the same amount each time. Try writing each output as the input times some other number.

solutions.reliable: First check a steady-rate rule: from 2 to 4 the output goes up by 14, which is 7 for each step of 1, but from 4 to 5 it goes up by 10, so the rule does not add a fixed amount. Write each output as a product: 6 = 2 × 3, 20 = 4 × 5 and 30 = 5 × 6. Each time the number is multiplied by the next number. So 8 turns into 8 × 9 = 72. The transferable idea: a rule found from examples must fit every example, so test it on all of them before you use it.
solutions.elegant: Each output is the input squared plus the input: 4 + 2 = 6, 16 + 4 = 20 and 25 + 5 = 30. So 8 gives 64 + 8 = 72.

problems.whyOnTest: Rule-finding questions test checking a guessed rule against every example, since a rule that fits one or two examples often fails the third.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 5 by 5 by 5 cube is built from 125 unit cubes. A square tunnel, 3 cubes wide and 3 high, is cut straight through the middle from front to back, leaving a border 1 cube thick. A second tunnel of the same size is cut through the middle from left to right. How many unit cubes are left?

choices.misconception: I took away 45 cubes for each tunnel, 90 in all, but the two tunnels share a 3 by 3 by 3 block in the middle, so I removed those cubes twice.
I only took away the cubes of one tunnel, 45, and forgot the second tunnel.
I saw that the tunnels share a block of 27 cubes, but I took it off both tunnels, so I removed only 45 + 45 - 27 - 27 = 36 cubes.
I only took away the 27 cubes where the two tunnels cross.

hints: How many cubes does one tunnel remove, and do the two tunnels share any?
Each tunnel is 3 by 3 cubes across and 5 cubes long. Where the tunnels cross they share a block, and those cubes must be taken away only once.
Each tunnel has 3 × 3 × 5 = 45 cubes, and the shared block in the middle is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubes.

solutions.reliable: Each tunnel removes 3 × 3 × 5 = 45 cubes. The two tunnels cross in the middle of the cube, where they share a block of 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubes. So the number of different cubes removed is 45 + 45 - 27 = 63, and 125 - 63 = 62 cubes are left. The transferable idea: when two shapes overlap, add them and then take off the shared part once.
solutions.elegant: Count what is left directly. The top layer and the bottom layer are untouched: 25 + 25 = 50 cubes. In each of the 3 middle layers only the 4 corner cubes survive, because the two tunnels together cut out a plus shape of 21 squares. That is 4 × 3 = 12 more, so 50 + 12 = 62.

problems.whyOnTest: Hidden-cube questions test seeing inside the solid, here that two crossing tunnels share a block of cubes that must not be removed twice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six children share 50 sweets so that each child gets at least one sweet and no two children get the same number. What is the smallest possible number of sweets for the child who gets the most?

choices.misconception: I divided 50 by 6 to get about 8 and thought the biggest share could be as small as the average.
I divided 50 by 6 and rounded up to 9, thinking the biggest share only has to be just above the average.
I chose six numbers in a row ending at 10, but 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10 is only 45, not 50.
I gave the other five children as few as possible, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, which makes the biggest share as large as possible, not as small as possible.

hints: Suppose the biggest share is m. What is the largest possible total?
Everyone else has a different, smaller number, so at most m - 1, m - 2, and so on down to m - 5. Use this to find how small m can be, then build an example.
If the biggest share is m, the total is at most m + (m - 1) + (m - 2) + (m - 3) + (m - 4) + (m - 5) = 6m - 15, and this must reach 50.

solutions.reliable: Let the child with the most have m sweets. The others have different, smaller numbers, so the total is at most m + (m - 1) + (m - 2) + (m - 3) + (m - 4) + (m - 5) = 6m - 15. For m = 10 that is only 45, less than 50, so m = 10 is too small, and any smaller m is worse. For m = 11 an example works: 5 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10 + 11 = 50. So the answer is 11. The transferable idea: to make the largest value as small as possible, push all the other values up close to it, then build an example that reaches the bound.
solutions.elegant: Six different numbers bunched as tightly as possible are consecutive. Near the average, 5 to 10 add up to 45 and 6 to 11 add up to 51. So the top share is at least 11, and taking 1 away from the 6 gives 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, which add up to exactly 50.

problems.whyOnTest: Extremal questions need two halves: an argument that nothing smaller can work, and an example that reaches the bound.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the 5 by 5 grid shown, three squares are shaded. What is the smallest number of further squares that must be shaded so that both dashed diagonals are lines of symmetry of the pattern?

figure.alt: A 5 by 5 grid of squares with both diagonals drawn as dashed lines. Counting rows from the top and columns from the left, three squares are shaded: row 1 column 2, row 2 column 5, and row 4 column 4. The square in row 4 column 4 lies on the diagonal from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.

choices.misconception: I only made the pattern symmetric about the diagonal from the top left to the bottom right, which needs just 2 more squares.
I only made the pattern symmetric about the diagonal from the top right to the bottom left, which needs 3 more squares.
I reflected each shaded square once in each diagonal but did not reflect the new squares again, so I missed the square opposite each one through the centre.
I thought the square lying on a diagonal needs no partner at all, so I added 3 squares for each of the other two.

hints: Reflect each shaded square in both diagonals, and keep going.

Every reflection of a shaded square in either diagonal must be shaded, and so must the reflections of those new squares. Each shaded square brings a whole group with it, and a square on a diagonal brings a smaller group.
Row 1 column 2 brings row 2 column 1, row 4 column 5 and row 5 column 4. Row 2 column 5 brings three more squares. Row 4 column 4 brings only row 2 column 2.

solutions.reliable: Count rows from the top and columns from the left. Reflecting in the diagonal from top left to bottom right swaps the row and column numbers; reflecting in the other diagonal sends row r, column c to row 6 - c, column 6 - r. Row 1 column 2 forces row 2 column 1, row 4 column 5 and row 5 column 4: 3 new squares. Row 2 column 5 forces row 5 column 2, row 1 column 4 and row 4 column 1: 3 new squares. Row 4 column 4 lies on the first diagonal and forces only row 2 column 2: 1 new square. These 10 squares reflect onto each other in both diagonals, so 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 more squares are needed and enough. The transferable idea: a symmetric pattern is made of complete groups of squares that the symmetries move onto each other.
solutions.elegant: Two reflections in the diagonals together also give a half turn, so a square that is on neither diagonal belongs to a group of 4, and a square on one diagonal (other than the centre) belongs to a group of 2. The three groups hold 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 squares, and 3 are already shaded, so 7 more are needed.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetry completion tests whether you keep reflecting until nothing new appears, rather than reflecting each square only once.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 1 by 1 square stands on a line with corners at (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1), and there is a dot on the corner at (0, 1). The square rolls to the right: each roll is a quarter turn clockwise about its bottom-right corner. Where is the dot after 10 rolls?

choices.misconception: I tracked which corner of the square the dot is on, but forgot that the square itself moves 1 to the right with every roll.
I thought the dot comes back to the top-left corner every 2 rolls, so after an even number of rolls it would be back on top.
I thought the dot stays on the top edge as the square rolls, ending at the top-right corner of the last square.
I worked out the dot's position after 2 rolls, (3, 0), and multiplied both numbers by 5 for 10 rolls.

hints: Roll the square a few times and watch the dot.
After 4 rolls the square has made a full turn, so the dot is back on the same corner, just 4 units further right. Work out the first 4 rolls carefully, then use the cycle.
The dot goes from (0, 1) to (2, 1), then (3, 0), then stays at (3, 0), then (4, 1). After 4 rolls it is on the top-left corner again, 4 units further right.

solutions.reliable: Roll 1 turns about (1, 0) and sends the dot to (2, 1), the top-right corner. Roll 2 turns about (2, 0) and sends it to (3, 0), the bottom-right corner. Roll 3 turns about (3, 0) itself, so the dot stays at (3, 0), which is now the bottom-left corner. Roll 4 turns about (4, 0) and sends it to (4, 1), the top-left corner again. So every 4 rolls the dot returns to the top-left corner, 4 units further right. After 8 rolls it is at (8, 1); two more rolls repeat what rolls 1 and 2 did, giving (10, 1) and then (11, 0). The transferable idea: a repeated rotation has a cycle, so find one full cycle and then use the remainder.
solutions.elegant: After k rolls the square covers x = k to x = k + 1. The corners repeat every 4 rolls, and 10 = 8 + 2, so the dot is on the corner it reached after 2 rolls, the bottom-right one, which is now at (11, 0).

problems.whyOnTest: Rolling-shape questions test following a rotation carefully through one full cycle and then using the remainder, rather than guessing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square tile is cut into 4 triangles by its diagonals. Each triangle is painted red, blue or yellow, and each colour is used at least once. Two tiles count as the same if one can be turned, without flipping, to look exactly like the other. How many different tiles are possible?

choices.misconception: I only counted which colour is used twice and did not think about where the triangles go.
I also treated tiles that are mirror images of each other as the same, but the tiles may not be flipped over.

I counted 2 ways to place the two matching triangles and 2 orders for the other colours, 4 tiles for each repeated colour, but when the matching triangles are opposite, a half turn makes the two orders look the same.
I counted every way to paint the four triangles in place, forgetting that turning a tile can make two paintings look the same.

hints: With 4 triangles and 3 colours, one colour must be used twice.
Choose the colour that is used twice. Its two triangles are either side by side or opposite each other. In each case, ask whether swapping the other two colours gives a tile that a turn can match.

If the two matching triangles are opposite, a half turn swaps the other two triangles, so their order does not matter. If they are side by side, the two orders are mirror images, and turning cannot match them.

solutions.reliable: Four triangles and three colours, each used at least once, means exactly one colour is used twice, and there are 3 ways to choose it. Say red is used twice. If the two red triangles are opposite each other, the blue and yellow triangles are opposite too, and a half turn swaps them, so there is only 1 such tile. If the two red triangles are side by side, going clockwise after them comes either blue then yellow or yellow then blue; these are mirror images, and no turn changes the clockwise order, so they are 2 different tiles. That is 1 + 2 = 3 tiles for each repeated colour, and 3 × 3 = 9 in all. The transferable idea: when turning makes arrangements the same, sort them by a feature that turning keeps, then count each kind once.
solutions.elegant: There are 3 × 6 × 2 = 36 ways to paint the triangles in place: choose the repeated colour, choose 2 of the 4 triangles for it, then order the other two colours. A painting with all three colours never looks the same after a quarter or a half turn, because a quarter turn would need all four triangles the same colour and a half turn would need opposite triangles to match, using only two colours. So every tile appears in exactly 4 of the 36 paintings, and 36 / 4 = 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting up to symmetry tests spotting which arrangements a turn makes identical, and which ones are mirror images that a turn cannot match.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben, Cai and Dia live one per floor on floors 1 to 4. Each plays a different instrument: drum, flute, harp or piano. The harp player lives directly above Ben. Ana lives higher than the drummer, but not on the top floor. The flute player lives on floor 1. Dia lives on floor 4. Who plays the flute?

choices.misconception: I put Ana on floor 1 because the only limit I used was that she is not on the top floor, forgetting that she must live higher than the drummer.
I put Ben on floor 1 with the harp player on floor 2 above him, not noticing that floor 2 must be the drummer's floor.
I mixed up the top and the bottom of the building and put the flute player on floor 4, where Dia lives.
I left out the clue that Dia lives on floor 4, and without it two different arrangements fit.

hints: Where can Ana live?
Ana is on floor 2 or floor 3. If she were on floor 2, the drummer would be on floor 1, but floor 1 belongs to the flute player. Carry on like this, and use the harp clue last.
Ana is on floor 3, so the drummer is on floor 2. Ben is directly below the harp player, and floor 2 belongs to the drummer, so Ben must be on floor 2.

solutions.reliable: Dia is on floor 4 and Ana is not on the top floor, so Ana is on floor 2 or 3. If Ana were on floor 2, the drummer would be below her on floor 1, but floor 1 is the flute player's, so Ana is on floor 3 and the drummer is on floor 2. Ben and Cai share floors 1 and 2. If Ben were on floor 1, the harp player would be on floor 2, but that is the drummer, so Ben is on floor 2 and plays the drum, and the harp player is Ana on floor 3. Cai is on floor 1, so Cai plays the flute, and Dia plays the piano. The transferable idea: in a logic grid, test each case a clue allows and cross out the ones that clash.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination puzzles test trying each case a clue allows and ruling cases out by contradiction, rather than guessing a whole arrangement.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Exactly one of these five statements about a positive whole number n is false. (1) n is a multiple of 6. (2) n is a multiple of 9. (3) n is a multiple of 4. (4) n is less than 50. (5) n is odd. What is n?

choices.misconception: I trusted statement (5), so I kept the statements that fit an odd number, a multiple of 9 below 50, and picked 9, not noticing that two statements are then false.
I decided statement (2) was the false one and took the smallest multiple of both 6 and 4, forgetting that 12 is not odd either.
I decided statement (3) was the false one and took the smallest multiple of both 6 and 9, forgetting that 18 is not odd either.
I decided statement (4) was the false one and took the first multiple of 36 above 50, but 72 is even, so statement (5) is false too.

hints: Which statements cannot both be true?
An odd number cannot be a multiple of 6 or of 4. So if statement (5) were true, at least two statements would be false. Decide which statement is the false one first.
Statement (5) is the false one, so n is a multiple of 6, of 9 and of 4, and it is less than 50.

solutions.reliable: If n were odd, it could not be a multiple of 6 or of 4, so statements (1) and (3) would both be false, which is one too many. So statement (5) is the false one, and the other four are true. Then n is a multiple of 6, 9 and 4, which means a multiple of 36, and n is less than 50. The only such positive whole number is 36. Check: 36 is a multiple of 6, 9 and 4, it is less than 50, and it is not odd, so exactly one statement is false. The transferable idea: when exactly one statement is false, find two statements that clash; the false one must be among them.

problems.whyOnTest: 'Exactly one is false' puzzles test reading the condition precisely and finding statements that cannot all hold together.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle BAC is 40 degrees. The point D lies on side AC so that BD = BC, as marked. How many degrees is angle ABD?

figure.alt: Triangle ABC with A at the top and base BC, with sides AB and AC the same length. Point D lies on side AC, a little closer to C than to A, and is joined to B. Segments BD and BC each carry two tick marks, showing they are equal. The angle at A is marked 40 degrees.

choices.misconception: I put the two equal angles of triangle BCD at B and D instead of at D and C, so angle DBC came out as 55 degrees and 70 - 55 = 15.
I found angle DBC, 40 degrees, which is the other part of angle ABC, not angle ABD.
I found angle ABC, 70 degrees, the whole angle at B, instead of only the part between BA and BD.
I found angle ADB, 110 degrees, instead of angle ABD.

hints: Look for isosceles triangles in the figure.
Triangle ABC has AB = AC, and triangle BCD has BD = BC. In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Start from the 40 degree angle at A.
Angles ABC and ACB are both 70 degrees. In triangle BCD, angle BDC equals angle BCD, so angle DBC = 180 - 70 - 70 = 40.

solutions.reliable: In triangle ABC, AB = AC, so angles ABC and ACB are equal: each is (180 - 40) / 2 = 70 degrees. In triangle BCD, BD = BC, so the angles opposite those sides are equal: angle BDC = angle BCD = 70 degrees. So angle DBC = 180 - 70 - 70 = 40 degrees. Then angle ABD = angle ABC - angle DBC = 70 - 40 = 30 degrees. Check with triangle ABD: angle ADB = 180 - 70 = 110, and 40 + 110 + 30 = 180. The transferable idea: equal sides give equal opposite angles, and a chain of isosceles triangles passes angles from one triangle to the next.
solutions.elegant: Angle BDC = 70 degrees is an outside angle of triangle ABD, so it equals the sum of the two inside angles at A and B: 40 + angle ABD = 70, giving angle ABD = 30.

problems.whyOnTest: Triangle-property questions test spotting isosceles triangles from equal sides and passing angles from one triangle to the next.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven whole numbers are written around a circle. For each pair of neighbours, Pia adds the two numbers together, which gives seven sums. At most how many of the seven sums can be odd?

choices.misconception: I split the seven numbers into separate pairs of neighbours, which only gives 3 pairs, but every number belongs to two neighbouring pairs.
I paired each odd number with just one neighbour, so with 4 odd and 3 even numbers I counted only 4 odd sums.
I alternated odd and even around the circle and thought the place where the pattern breaks spoils the pair on each side of it.
I alternated odd and even all the way round, not noticing that with seven numbers the first and last are both odd and sit next to each other.

hints: When is the sum of two numbers odd?
A sum is odd exactly when one number is odd and the other is even. Walk round the circle and count how many times you switch between odd and even. You must end where you started.
Going all the way round brings you back to the number you started from, so the number of switches is even. It cannot be 7.

solutions.reliable: A sum of two neighbours is odd exactly when one is odd and the other is even, that is, wherever you switch between odd and even as you walk round the circle. Walking all the way round brings you back to the starting number, so you switch an even number of times. So at most 6 of the 7 sums are odd. Six is possible: the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in order around the circle give the sums 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 8, and only 8 is even. The transferable idea: going round a closed loop, the number of switches between two states is always even.
solutions.elegant: Add up all seven sums. Each number is used in two sums, so the total is twice the sum of the numbers, which is even. Seven odd sums would add up to an odd total, so at least one sum must be even. The example 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 shows that 6 odd sums can happen.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity arguments show what is impossible: around a circle of odd length, odd and even numbers cannot alternate all the way round.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A large robot mower can cut a field on its own in 3 hours. A small robot mower can cut the same field on its own in 6 hours. The small mower starts alone. After 2 hours the large mower joins it, and they finish the field together. How long does the whole job take, counted from the start?

choices.misconception: I worked out how long the two mowers take together from the very start, and left out the 2 hours the small mower worked alone.
I thought two mowers finish the rest in half the time the small one would need alone, so 4 hours became 2 more hours.
I thought the whole job takes the average of 3 hours and 6 hours.
I added the small mower's 2 hours to the 3 hours the large mower takes on its own.

hints: Think about what fraction of the field each mower cuts in one hour.
Work in fractions of the field. Find how much the small mower has cut before help arrives, then how fast the two mowers cut together, and divide the part that is left by that combined speed.
In 2 hours the small mower cuts 2/6 = 1/3 of the field, so 2/3 is left. Together they cut 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 of the field per hour, so 2/3 takes (2/3) ÷ (1/2) = 4/3 hours.

solutions.reliable: Per hour, the large mower cuts 1/3 of the field and the small one cuts 1/6. In the first 2 hours the small mower alone cuts 2 × 1/6 = 1/3, leaving 2/3. Working together they cut 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 of the field per hour, so the remaining 2/3 takes (2/3) ÷ (1/2) = 4/3 hours, which is 1 hour 20 minutes. The whole job takes 2 hours + 1 hour 20 minutes = 3 hours 20 minutes. The transferable idea: in work problems, add speeds (fractions of the job per hour), never times.
solutions.elegant: Count in small-mower hours: the large mower does as much in one hour as the small mower does in two. The field is 6 small-mower hours of work. After 2 hours, 4 small-mower hours remain, and together they do 3 small-mower hours each hour, so they need 4/3 hours more. Total 3 hours 20 minutes.

problems.whyOnTest: Combined work at 4 points adds a twist: one worker starts alone, so you must split the job before adding rates.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A father is 40 years old. His three children are 13, 10 and 5 years old. In how many years will the father's age be equal to the sum of his three children's ages?

choices.misconception: I thought the gap closes by 3 + 1 = 4 years every year, adding the father's year instead of taking it away.
I added 3 years a year to the children's total but forgot that the father gets older too.
I thought the gap of 12 years closes by just 1 year every year.
I found the right moment but gave the father's age then instead of the number of years.

hints: How much does the children's total grow each year? And the father's age?
Find the gap between the father's age and the children's total today. Then work out by how much that gap shrinks each year, because the two amounts grow at different speeds.
Today the children's total is 13 + 10 + 5 = 28, which is 12 less than 40. Each year the total grows by 3 and the father grows by 1, so the gap shrinks by 2 a year.

solutions.reliable: Today the children's ages add up to 13 + 10 + 5 = 28, and the father is 40, a gap of 12. Every year each child gets one year older, so their total grows by 3, while the father's age grows by 1. The gap shrinks by 3 - 1 = 2 each year, so it closes after 12 ÷ 2 = 6 years. Check: in 6 years the father is 46 and the children are 19, 16 and 11, which add up to 46. The transferable idea: when two amounts grow at different speeds, divide the gap by the difference of the speeds.
solutions.elegant: Try the choices: after 6 years the father is 46 and the children total 28 + 18 = 46, a match. After 3 or 4 years the father is still ahead, and after 12 the children's total is past him.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems test whether you track how every quantity changes over time, here a total of three ages against one age.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sara has plenty of 2-euro coins and 5-euro notes, and no other money. She wants to pay exactly 23 euros without getting any change. What is the smallest total number of coins and notes she can use?

choices.misconception: I counted only the 5-euro notes and forgot to add the coins.
I counted only the 2-euro coins and forgot to add the notes.
I used as many notes as possible, four of them, and then two coins, without checking that this makes 24 euros, not 23.
I used one note and nine coins, the first way I found, and did not look for a way with fewer pieces.

hints: Can she use an even number of 5-euro notes?
Try each possible number of 5-euro notes and check whether the rest can be paid in 2-euro coins. Then compare the totals and keep the smallest.
The coins always make an even amount, so the notes must make an odd amount: 1 note or 3 notes. With 3 notes, 8 euros are left, which is 4 coins.

solutions.reliable: The 2-euro coins always add up to an even number of euros, and 23 is odd, so the 5-euro notes must make an odd amount: 1 note (5 euros) or 3 notes (15 euros). With 1 note, 18 euros are left, which needs 9 coins, so 10 pieces. With 3 notes, 8 euros are left, which needs 4 coins, so 7 pieces. Four notes would already be 20, leaving 3 euros that coins cannot make. The smallest number is 7. The transferable idea: use parity to cut down the cases before you count.

problems.whyOnTest: Money problems at 3 points check that you test every combination, not just the greedy one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A counter starts at 0 on a number line. It makes 10 moves. The first move is 1 step, the second move is 2 steps, and so on, up to 10 steps on the tenth move. Each move can go either left or right. Which of these numbers could the counter finish on?

choices.misconception: I thought the moves could cancel each other out in pairs, so the counter could come back to 0.
I thought that after an even number of moves the counter always lands on an even number.
I thought turning the first move round takes just 1 away from 55, which gives 54.
I only checked that the number is odd and forgot that the counter can get at most 55 steps away.

hints: If every move went right, where would the counter end up?
Start from all moves going right. Think about what happens to the finishing point when one move is turned round to go left. Does it change the parity of the finishing number?
All moves right gives 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55. Turning a move of k steps round changes the end by 2k, an even amount, so the end is always odd and at most 55.

solutions.reliable: If every move goes right, the counter ends at 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55. Turning a move of k steps round from right to left moves the finish 2k to the left, which is an even change. So every possible finish is 55 minus an even number: it is always odd, and it is never more than 55 or less than -55. That rules out 0, 20 and 54 (even) and 57 (too far). For 37, turn only the 9-step move round: 55 - 18 = 37. The transferable idea: changing a sign in a sum changes the total by an even amount, so the parity never changes.
solutions.elegant: The sum ±1 ± 2 ± ... ± 10 always has the same parity as 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55, because a minus sign instead of a plus changes the total by twice that number. Only odd numbers up to 55 can appear, and 37 is the only choice that fits.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity at 4 points: the trick is to see that swapping a direction changes the end point by an even amount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular board is 84 cm long and 60 cm wide. It is to be covered exactly by equal square tiles, without cutting any tile. The side of each tile is a whole number of centimetres. What is the largest possible side length of a tile, in centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found a tile size that fits both sides, 6, but did not check for a bigger one.
I subtracted 60 from 84 and took the difference as the tile size.
I found the right tile but gave how many tiles are needed, 7 times 5, instead of the side length.
I found the smallest number that both 84 and 60 divide into, instead of the largest number that divides both.

hints: The tile side must fit exactly along both the long side and the short side.
The side length must be a factor of 84 and also a factor of 60. List the factors of the smaller number and find the largest one that also divides the bigger number.
Factors of 60, from the top: 60, 30, 20, 15, 12, ... The first one that also divides 84 is 12, because 84 = 7 × 12.

solutions.reliable: A square tile of side s fits a whole number of times along 84 cm and along 60 cm only if s divides both 84 and 60. Going down the factors of 60: 60, 30, 20 and 15 do not divide 84, but 12 does, since 84 = 7 × 12 and 60 = 5 × 12. So the largest tile has side 12 cm, and 7 × 5 = 35 of them cover the board. The transferable idea: the biggest equal piece that fits two lengths exactly is their greatest common factor.
solutions.elegant: Split both numbers into primes: 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 and 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. They share 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

problems.whyOnTest: This tests the greatest common factor in a picture, where students often grab the least common multiple instead.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the units digit of $2^1 + 2^2 + 2^3 + \dots + 2^{10}$?

choices.misconception: I added the units digits in groups of four, 2 + 4 + 8 + 6 = 20 each, and forgot the two powers left over.
I added the units digits of only the first nine powers.
I gave the units digit of the last power, $2^{10}$, instead of the whole sum.
I thought the sum was equal to $2^{11}$, which ends in 8.

hints: Write down the units digits of the first few powers of 2.
The units digits of powers of 2 repeat in a short cycle. Add the units digits of one full cycle, count how many full cycles there are and what is left over.
The units digits go 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4. Two full cycles give 20 + 20 = 40, and the last two terms add 2 + 4 = 6.

solutions.reliable: Only units digits matter. The units digits of $2^1$ to $2^{10}$ are 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, because the cycle 2, 4, 8, 6 repeats. Their sum is 20 + 20 + 2 + 4 = 46, so the units digit of the whole sum is 6. Check: the actual sum is 2 + 4 + 8 + ... + 1024 = 2046, which ends in 6. The transferable idea: for last digits, keep only last digits and use the repeating cycle.
solutions.elegant: Doubling the sum and taking it away from itself: the sum equals $2^{11} - 2 = 2048 - 2 = 2046$, so the units digit is 6.

problems.whyOnTest: Last-digit cycles at 4 points: here the cycle must be summed, and the leftover terms are the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the calculation $1 + 2 + 3 - 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 - 8 + \dots + 21 + 22 + 23 - 24$, every fourth number is subtracted and all the others are added. What is the result?

choices.misconception: I only added up the numbers that are subtracted, 4 + 8 + ... + 24.
I grouped the numbers in fours, but I only made five groups instead of six.
I added all the numbers to get 300 and then took away the multiples of 4 only once.
I added all the numbers from 1 to 24 and ignored the minus signs.

hints: Look at the numbers in groups of four.
Group the terms in fours, each group ending with a subtracted number. Work out what each group is worth and look for a pattern in those values, then add them up.
The groups give 1 + 2 + 3 - 4 = 2, 5 + 6 + 7 - 8 = 10, 9 + 10 + 11 - 12 = 18, and so on. There are six groups, worth 2, 10, 18, 26, 34 and 42.

solutions.reliable: Group the terms in fours: (1 + 2 + 3 - 4) + (5 + 6 + 7 - 8) + ... + (21 + 22 + 23 - 24). The groups are worth 2, 10, 18, 26, 34 and 42, six groups going up by 8. Pair them from the outside in: 2 + 42 = 10 + 34 = 18 + 26 = 44, so the sum is 3 × 44 = 132. Second method: all numbers from 1 to 24 add to 300, and the multiples of 4 add to 4 + 8 + ... + 24 = 84. Each multiple of 4 is subtracted instead of added, which takes away twice its value: 300 - 2 × 84 = 132. The transferable idea: group terms so the pattern repeats, and check by a second grouping.
solutions.elegant: Every subtracted number is counted with the wrong sign, so start from the full total and take each of them away twice: 300 - 2 × 84 = 132.

problems.whyOnTest: Clever regrouping: pairing or tripling terms turns a long sum into a short pattern you can add in your head.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A water tank is three quarters full. After 12 litres are used, it is half full. How many litres does the tank hold when it is full?

choices.misconception: I took 1/2 from 3/4 by working out 3 - 1 and 4 - 2, which gives 2/2, so I thought 12 litres was the whole tank.
I thought the 12 litres used were three quarters of the tank.
I gave how much water is in the tank now that it is half full.
I gave how much water was in the tank at the start, when it was three quarters full.

hints: What fraction of the tank do the 12 litres make up?
Find the difference between three quarters and one half. That fraction of the tank is the 12 litres, so scale it up to the whole tank.
Three quarters minus one half is one quarter, so 12 litres is one quarter of the tank. The whole tank is four quarters.

solutions.reliable: The water level drops from 3/4 of the tank to 1/2 of the tank, which is a drop of 3/4 - 2/4 = 1/4 of the tank. That quarter is the 12 litres, so the full tank holds 4 × 12 = 48 litres. Check: 3/4 of 48 is 36, and 36 - 12 = 24, which is half of 48. The transferable idea: the change in a fraction matches the change in the amount.

problems.whyOnTest: A fractions-of-a-quantity check: the given amount matches a difference of two fractions, not either fraction itself.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a club, 60% of the members are boys. Then 15 girls join the club and nobody leaves. Now 40% of the members are boys. How many boys are in the club?

choices.misconception: I found that the club started with 30 members, but then took 40% of 30, the new percentage, instead of 60%.
I worked out the new total of 45 members, but took 60% of it, the old percentage.
I gave the number of members at the start instead of the number of boys.
I thought the 15 new girls made the drop of 20%, so 20% of the club was 15 members and 60% was 45.

hints: Which number stays the same when the girls join?
The number of boys does not change. Compare it with the size of the club before and after, using the two percentages, and find how much the club grew in terms of the boys.
Boys are 60% of the old club, so the old club is 5/3 of the boys. Boys are 40% of the new club, so the new club is 5/2 of the boys. The difference, 15 members, is 5/2 - 5/3 = 5/6 of the boys.

solutions.reliable: Let the club start with T members. The boys are 60% of T, and after 15 girls join they are 40% of T + 15. The number of boys has not changed, so 0.6T = 0.4(T + 15), which gives 0.6T = 0.4T + 6, so 0.2T = 6 and T = 30. The boys are 60% of 30 = 18. Check: after the girls join there are 45 members, and 18 is 40% of 45. The transferable idea: when a percentage changes, find the quantity that stays fixed and build the equation around it.
solutions.elegant: Think in ratios: 60% boys means boys to girls is 3 : 2, and 40% boys means 2 : 3. Keep the boys fixed at 6 parts: 6 : 4 before and 6 : 9 after. The 15 new girls are 5 parts, so one part is 3 and there are 6 × 3 = 18 boys.

problems.whyOnTest: Percentages at 5 points: the whole changes, so you must anchor on the part that stays the same.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to $0.49 \times 812 \div 0.198$?

choices.misconception: I rounded 0.198 to 0.2 but then divided by 20 instead of by 0.2.
I multiplied by 0.2 instead of dividing by it.
I thought dividing by 0.2 is the same as dividing by 2.
I worked out 0.49 × 812 is about 400 and forgot to divide by 0.198.

hints: Round each number to something easy before calculating.
Replace 0.49 by a half, 812 by 800 and 0.198 by 0.2. Remember that dividing by a number smaller than 1 makes the answer bigger.
Half of 800 is 400. Dividing by 0.2 is the same as multiplying by 5, so the answer is about 400 × 5.

solutions.reliable: Round: 0.49 is about 1/2, 812 is about 800 and 0.198 is about 0.2. So the value is about 1/2 × 800 ÷ 0.2 = 400 ÷ 0.2. Dividing by 0.2 means asking how many fifths fit, which is multiplying by 5, so the value is about 2000. The exact value is about 2009, so 2000 is clearly the closest choice. The transferable idea: dividing by a small decimal makes a number bigger, so estimate with friendly fractions.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimation checks number sense with decimals, especially that dividing by a number below 1 makes things bigger.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Kai's mean score on his tests so far is 14. If he scores 20 on his next test, his mean will go up to 15. What score would he need on that next test to make his mean 16 instead?

choices.misconception: I thought he only needs to score the new mean, 16, on the next test.
I thought each extra point on the mean needs just one extra point on the test, so 20 + 1.
I found he has taken 5 tests, but I added 5 extra points to 20 instead of 6, forgetting the new test counts too.
I found the total he needs over all six tests, 96, and gave that instead of the score on the new test.

hints: First work out how many tests Kai has already taken.
Scoring 20 instead of 14 lifts every test's share of the mean. Use that to find the number of tests. Then work out the total needed for the new mean and subtract what he already has.

The 6 extra points above 14 raise the mean by 1 for all the tests including the new one, so there are 6 tests in all, 5 so far. For a mean of 16 over 6 tests he needs a total of 96, and he has 5 × 14 = 70.

solutions.reliable: Say Kai has taken n tests, with total 14n. After a score of 20 there are n + 1 tests with mean 15, so 14n + 20 = 15(n + 1) = 15n + 15, which gives n = 5. So far his total is 5 × 14 = 70. For a mean of 16 over 6 tests he needs 6 × 16 = 96 in total, so the next score must be 96 - 70 = 26. Check: (70 + 26) ÷ 6 = 16. The transferable idea: work with totals, because a mean is a total shared out.
solutions.elegant: Every point above the old mean of 14 is shared among all 6 tests. Raising the mean by 1 takes 6 extra points (20 = 14 + 6), so raising it by 2 takes 12: he needs 14 + 12 = 26.

problems.whyOnTest: Means at 5 points: the count of tests is hidden, and you have to recover it from how one score moves the mean.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Figure 1 is a plus sign made of 5 squares: one square in the centre and one square on each of its four sides. To make each new figure, one square is added to the end of each of the four arms. How many squares make up figure 12?

choices.misconception: I worked out 1 + 4 × 11, counting one step too few.
I counted the four arms of 12 squares each but forgot the centre square.
I started from figure 1's 5 squares and added 4 squares twelve times, one time too many.
I multiplied figure 1's 5 squares by 12.

hints: How long is each arm in figure 1, figure 2 and figure 3?
Split each figure into the centre square and four equal arms. Work out how long one arm is in figure n, then put the pieces back together.
In figure 1 each arm has 1 square, in figure 2 each arm has 2, so in figure 12 each arm has 12 squares. Add the four arms and the centre.

solutions.reliable: Figure n is a centre square with four arms of n squares each, so it has 1 + 4n squares. Check with the small cases: figure 1 has 1 + 4 = 5 and figure 2 has 1 + 8 = 9, which matches adding 4 each time. Figure 12 has 1 + 4 × 12 = 49 squares. The transferable idea: describe a growing figure by its parts, a fixed piece plus pieces that grow with n.

problems.whyOnTest: Visual patterns at 3 points check that you can turn a picture rule into a count without an off-by-one slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sequence A is 2, 7, 12, 17, ..., going up by 5 each time. Sequence B is 3, 7, 11, 15, ..., going up by 4 each time. How many numbers smaller than 250 appear in both sequences?

choices.misconception: I divided 250 by 20 and rounded down, without checking where the shared numbers start.
I saw that 7 and 27 both end in 7 and counted every number ending in 7 below 250.
I thought the shared numbers go up by 5 + 4 = 9, so I counted 7, 16, 25, and so on.
I counted the numbers of sequence A from 7 upwards and never checked them against sequence B.

hints: Find the first two numbers that are in both sequences.
Once one shared number is found, the next shared number must be a jump that is a whole number of 5s and a whole number of 4s. Find that jump, then count the terms of the new sequence below 250.
The shared numbers start 7, 27, 47, ..., going up by 20, the smallest number that is a multiple of both 5 and 4. The largest one below 250 is 247.

solutions.reliable: Sequence A is the numbers that leave remainder 2 when divided by 5, and sequence B is the numbers that leave remainder 3 when divided by 4. The first number in both is 7. To stay in both sequences, the next jump must be a multiple of 5 and of 4, so the shared numbers go up by 20: 7, 27, 47, ..., 247. These are 7 + 20k for k = 0, 1, ..., 12, which is 13 numbers. The next one, 267, is too big. The transferable idea: the numbers common to two arithmetic sequences form a new arithmetic sequence whose step is the least common multiple of the two steps.

problems.whyOnTest: Arithmetic sequences meet the least common multiple here, a classic two-step 4-point problem.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A large equilateral triangle with 6 cm sides is made from 1 cm matchsticks, which divide it into small equilateral triangles with 1 cm sides. A triangle with 2 cm sides made this way uses 9 matchsticks, 3 of them inside it rather than on its edge. How many matchsticks lie inside the large triangle, not on its edge?

choices.misconception: I counted the matchsticks on the edge, 3 × 6, instead of the ones inside.
I counted the small triangles, 36 of them, instead of the matchsticks.
I counted the inside matchsticks in rows of 2, 3, 4 and 5 for each direction, leaving out the row with a single matchstick.
I counted every matchstick in the large triangle and forgot to leave out the 18 on the edge.

hints: Every matchstick points in one of three directions.
Sort the matchsticks by direction, for example the horizontal ones. Count how many lie in each row, decide which rows are on the edge, then use symmetry for the other two directions.

The horizontal matchsticks lie in rows of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 from the top. Only the bottom row of 6 is on the edge, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 horizontal ones are inside, and the other two directions look the same.

solutions.reliable: Every matchstick is parallel to one of the three sides. Count the horizontal ones first: going down from the top, the horizontal rows have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 matchsticks. Only the bottom row lies on the edge, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 horizontal matchsticks are inside. Turning the triangle shows that the other two directions also have 15 inside each, so 3 × 15 = 45 matchsticks are inside. Check with the given case: side 2 gives 3 × 1 = 3 inside, which matches. The transferable idea: count edges in a grid by sorting them into directions.
solutions.elegant: Each upward-pointing small triangle owns exactly 3 matchsticks, and every matchstick belongs to exactly one upward triangle. There are 1 + 2 + ... + 6 = 21 upward triangles, so there are 3 × 21 = 63 matchsticks in all. The edge has 3 × 6 = 18 of them, leaving 63 - 18 = 45 inside.

problems.whyOnTest: Growth patterns at 5 points need an organising idea, here counting matchsticks by direction and then separating the inside from the edge.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A list starts with 49. Each new number is the sum of the digits of the number before it, plus 5. So the list begins 49, 18, 14, 10, ... What is the 100th number in the list?

choices.misconception: I gave the 99th number instead of the 100th.
I let the repeating block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 start at the second number instead of the third.
I let the repeating block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 start at the first number instead of the third.
I put 49 and 18 into the repeating block, using a block of eleven numbers, but 49 and 18 never come back.

hints: Write out the first twelve or so numbers and watch for a repeat.
Once a number comes back, the list repeats from there forever. Find where the repeating block starts and how long it is, then work out where the 100th number falls in the block.
The list is 49, 18, 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9, 14, ... From the 3rd number on, the block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 repeats. The 100th number is the 98th number of this repeating part.

solutions.reliable: Following the rule: 49, 18, 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9, 14, ... After 9 comes 9 + 5 = 14 again, so from the 3rd number onwards the block 14, 10, 6, 11, 7, 12, 8, 13, 9 of length 9 repeats, and 49 and 18 never return. The 100th number is number 98 of the repeating part. Since 98 = 10 × 9 + 8, it is the 8th number of the block, which is 13. The transferable idea: when a rule makes a list repeat, find where the cycle starts and how long it is, then use remainders.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules often fall into a cycle. Spotting it, and noticing that the first two numbers are outside it, is the 4-point skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A secret rule turns two numbers into one number. Using the rule, $5 \otimes 3 = 16$, $4 \otimes 1 = 15$, $6 \otimes 5 = 11$ and $3 \otimes 3 = 0$. What is $7 \otimes 2$ using the same rule?

choices.misconception: I only matched the first example: I added the two numbers and doubled the result.
I guessed the first number times itself minus the second number, without checking it against the examples.
I squared both numbers but added the squares instead of taking one from the other.
I added the two numbers and then squared the result.

hints: Why might two equal numbers give 0?
Equal numbers giving 0 suggests the rule takes something away. Try combining the sum and the difference of the two numbers, or their squares, and test your guess on every example.
Each answer is the first number squared minus the second number squared: 25 - 9 = 16, 16 - 1 = 15, 36 - 25 = 11 and 9 - 9 = 0.

solutions.reliable: Test a guess on all four examples. The rule 'square the first number, square the second, subtract' works: 25 - 9 = 16, 16 - 1 = 15, 36 - 25 = 11 and 9 - 9 = 0. So 7 ⊗ 2 = 49 - 4 = 45. Second method: the same values come from (sum) × (difference): 8 × 2 = 16, 5 × 3 = 15, 11 × 1 = 11 and 6 × 0 = 0, so 7 ⊗ 2 = 9 × 5 = 45. The transferable idea: a guessed rule only counts once it fits every example.
solutions.elegant: The example 3 ⊗ 3 = 0 hints that the difference of the numbers is a factor. Dividing each answer by the difference gives 8, 5 and 11, which are the sums. So the rule is sum times difference, and 7 ⊗ 2 = 9 × 5 = 45.

problems.whyOnTest: Inferring a rule at 5 points: several rules fit one example, and only careful checking against all of them finds the real one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In Mila's school, every child who plays in the orchestra also sings in the choir. Tom goes to Mila's school, and he does not sing in the choir. Which of these must be true?

choices.text: Tom does not play in the orchestra.

choices.misconception: I mixed up the two groups and thought that a child who does not sing must play in the orchestra instead.

choices.text: Every child who sings in the choir also plays in the orchestra.
choices.misconception: I turned the rule round: every orchestra player sings, so I thought every singer plays too.

choices.text: Some children who sing in the choir do not play in the orchestra.
choices.misconception: I thought the choir must have singers outside the orchestra, but the rule allows every singer to play as well.

choices.text: Nothing can be said about whether Tom plays in the orchestra.
choices.misconception: I thought the rule only talks about orchestra players, so it says nothing about a child who does not sing.

hints: Imagine Tom were in the orchestra. What would the rule say about him?
The rule says the orchestra sits completely inside the choir. Picture two circles, one inside the other, and decide where a child outside the bigger circle can be.
If Tom played in the orchestra, the rule would make him sing in the choir, but he does not. So he cannot be in the orchestra.

solutions.reliable: Draw the orchestra as a circle inside the bigger circle of the choir, because every orchestra player also sings. Tom is outside the choir circle, so he is outside the orchestra circle too: Tom does not play in the orchestra. The rule does not say every singer plays, so the third statement need not be true, and nothing in it forces the choir to have singers outside the orchestra, so the fourth need not be true either. The transferable idea: 'every A is a B' means anything that is not a B cannot be an A.

problems.whyOnTest: Reading a logical statement precisely: 'every orchestra player sings' does not mean 'every singer plays'.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev each go to a different club: chess, judo, swimming or tennis, which meet one per day, Monday to Thursday. Tennis is on Thursday. Chess is the day before Ben's. Swimming is later than chess. Cleo's club is earlier than Ana's, and Ana's earlier than Dev's. Cleo does not play chess. Which club is Ben's?

choices.misconception: I mixed up the clue and made Ben the chess player, instead of the child whose club comes the day after chess.
I let Cleo play chess on Monday, missing the clue that she does not, and then gave Ben judo on Tuesday.
I read 'the day just before' as 'some day before', so I let Ben go on Thursday and play tennis.
I forgot the clue that swimming is later than chess, so I found more than one way to fit everything.

hints: On which days could Ben's club meet?
Ben cannot be on Monday, since chess comes the day before his club. Try each of the other days for Ben and see which clue breaks. The order of Cleo, Ana and Dev fixes the rest.
If Ben is on Thursday, chess is Wednesday and swimming has no later free day. If Ben is on Tuesday, chess is Monday, but Cleo must be on Monday and she does not play chess. So Ben is on Wednesday.

solutions.reliable: Ben's club cannot be on Monday, because chess is the day before it. If Ben is on Thursday, he plays tennis and chess is on Wednesday, but then swimming would have to be on Thursday too, which is impossible. If Ben is on Tuesday, chess is on Monday, and the other three children fill Monday, Wednesday and Thursday in the order Cleo, Ana, Dev, so Cleo is on Monday playing chess, which the last clue forbids. So Ben is on Wednesday, chess is on Tuesday, and Cleo, Ana and Dev are on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday. Ana plays chess, Dev plays tennis, swimming must be after Tuesday, so it is Ben's Wednesday club, and Cleo does judo. The transferable idea: in an elimination puzzle, test the cases for the most constrained person and let each contradiction remove one case.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination at 5 points: two lists to match at once, and each clue removes a case only when combined with another.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben, Cy, Dot and Eli stand in a line, one behind another, all facing the front. Exactly two children stand between Ana and Dot. Ben stands directly behind Eli. Dot is somewhere in front of Ben. Cy is not at the front. Who is second from the front?

choices.misconception: I found the right line but counted second from the back instead of from the front.
I read 'Ben stands directly behind Eli' as Ben standing just in front of Eli.
I read 'exactly two children between Ana and Dot' as Ana and Dot being two places apart, with only one child between them.
I forgot the clue that Cy is not at the front and used the line Cy, Dot, Eli, Ben, Ana.

hints: Where can Ana and Dot stand if exactly two children are between them?
Number the places 1 to 5 from the front. List the few ways to place Ana and Dot, then try to fit Eli and Ben as a pair next to each other, and check the last clues.
Ana and Dot use places 1 and 4 or places 2 and 5. Dot must be ahead of Ben, and Eli and Ben need two places next to each other. Only Dot 1, Ana 4 survives, with Eli 2 and Ben 3.

solutions.reliable: Number the places 1 (front) to 5 (back). With exactly two children between them, Ana and Dot are in places 1 and 4 or in places 2 and 5. Dot cannot be in place 5, because Dot is ahead of Ben. If Dot is in place 4 and Ana in place 1, Ben must be in place 5 and Eli in place 4, but place 4 is taken. If Dot is in place 2 and Ana in place 5, the free places are 1, 3 and 4, so Eli and Ben take 3 and 4 and Cy is at the front, which is not allowed. So Dot is in place 1 and Ana in place 4. The free places are 2, 3 and 5: Eli and Ben take 2 and 3, and Cy takes 5. The line is Dot, Eli, Ben, Ana, Cy, so Eli is second. The transferable idea: start with the clue that allows the fewest positions and test each one against the rest.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering from clues at 5 points: several clues must be combined, and each case is ruled out by a different clue.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a balance, 1 red brick and 2 blue bricks balance 11 marbles. On another balance, 2 red bricks and 1 blue brick balance 13 marbles. All red bricks weigh the same, all blue bricks weigh the same and all marbles weigh the same. How many marbles balance 1 red brick and 1 blue brick together?

choices.misconception: I worked out the weight of a blue brick and gave that instead of a red and a blue brick together.
I worked out the weight of a red brick and gave that instead of a red and a blue brick together.
I thought one red and one blue brick must sit halfway between the two balances, so I took the average of 11 and 13.
I put both balances together, 3 red and 3 blue bricks against 24 marbles, and gave 24 without sharing it into three equal groups.

hints: What happens if you put everything from both balances onto one balance?
Put both left pans together and both right pans together, and the balance still holds. Count the red and blue bricks that are then on the left, and split them into equal groups.
Together the pans hold 3 red bricks and 3 blue bricks against 11 + 13 = 24 marbles. That is three groups of one red and one blue brick, so each group balances 24 ÷ 3 marbles.

solutions.reliable: Put both balances together: 3 red bricks and 3 blue bricks balance 11 + 13 = 24 marbles. These bricks make three equal groups of 1 red and 1 blue brick, so each group balances 24 ÷ 3 = 8 marbles. Check by finding each brick: the second balance has one more red brick and one fewer blue brick than the first, and 2 more marbles, so a red brick is 2 marbles heavier than a blue one. Then 1 red and 2 blue bricks are as heavy as 3 blue bricks and 2 marbles, which is 11 marbles, so a blue brick is 3 marbles, a red brick is 5 marbles, and 5 + 3 = 8.
