solutions.reliable: Take the doors one at a time. For the first door, in the worst case the first 5 keys fail, and then you know the 6th key opens it without trying, so 5 tries are enough. That leaves 5 keys for the second door, which needs at most 4 tries, then at most 3, 2 and 1 for the next doors, and the last key must fit the last door with no try at all. So 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 tries are always enough. Fewer are not always enough: a failed try only rules out one key for one door, and with bad luck each try fails until only one possibility is left, so the unlucky person really does need all 15. The transferable idea: for a guarantee, follow the worst possible luck, and notice when the last option no longer needs testing.

problems.whyOnTest: Worst-case counting: you must follow the unluckiest order of events and also see that the last remaining key never needs testing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle measures 10 cm by 6 cm. A 2 cm by 2 cm square is cut away from each of its four corners. What is the perimeter of the shape that is left?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 4 cm at each corner for the two 2 cm pieces removed, and forgot the new edges.
I subtracted 2 cm for each of the four corners.
I worked out the area left, 60 - 16 = 44, instead of the perimeter.
I added the new inner edges but forgot to remove the cut-away parts of the outer edges.

hints: What happens to the boundary at one corner?
At each corner, two pieces of the old boundary are removed and two new edges appear. Compare their lengths before computing anything.
Each corner loses two 2 cm pieces of boundary and gains two new 2 cm edges.

solutions.reliable: At each corner, 2 cm is removed from each of the two sides, but two new edges of 2 cm each are exposed. The loss and the gain balance, so the perimeter equals that of the rectangle: 2 x (10 + 6) = 32 cm. The transferable idea: cutting a rectangle out of a corner moves edges inward without changing the total perimeter.
solutions.elegant: Push each notched edge back out to the original rectangle: the horizontal edges still add up to 10 + 10 and the vertical ones to 6 + 6, so 32 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter versus area: corner cuts reduce the area but not the perimeter, and the wrong choices come from treating the two alike.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A regular hexagon has an area of 54 square centimetres. Joining every second corner of the hexagon makes an equilateral triangle. What is the area of this triangle, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found the area of one of the six triangles around the centre and stopped.
I thought the triangle covered only two of the six triangles around the centre.
I thought the triangle covered four of the six triangles around the centre.
I thought each corner piece cut off was half of a centre triangle, so I took 3 x 4.5 from 54.

hints: Join the centre of the hexagon to its six corners.
Compare each corner piece cut off outside the triangle with a piece inside it. Joining the centre to the triangle's corners splits the triangle into three pieces; look for a reflection matching them.
Folding each cut-off corner across the triangle's side lands it exactly on one of the three pieces inside.

solutions.reliable: Call the hexagon ABCDEF with centre O, and the triangle ACE. ABCO has four equal sides (each equals the side of the hexagon), so it is a rhombus, and its diagonal AC cuts it into two equal halves: triangle ABC outside the big triangle and triangle AOC inside it. The same happens at the other two corners. So the hexagon is six equal pieces, three inside the triangle and three outside, and the triangle has area 54 / 2 = 27 square centimetres. The transferable idea: show two regions are equal by matching pieces, and the area follows without any lengths.
solutions.elegant: The six centre triangles each have area 9. The hexagon is three rhombi like ABCO, each of area 18, and each side of the big triangle is a diagonal cutting one rhombus in half. So the triangle has area 3 x 9 = 27.

problems.whyOnTest: Area by dissection: matching each cut-off piece with an equal piece inside shows the triangle is exactly half, with no lengths needed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A triangle has two sides of length 5 cm and 12 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths are possible for the third side?

choices.misconception: I assumed the 12 cm side had to be the longest side.
I allowed the third side to be 7 cm, but then 5 + 7 just equals 12 and the triangle is flat.
I allowed both 7 cm and 17 cm, where the triangle collapses into a straight line.
I only checked that the third side is shorter than 5 + 12 = 17.

hints: How short and how long can the third side be?
In any triangle, each side is shorter than the other two put together. Use this twice: once with the third side as the longest, and once with the 12 cm side as the longest.
The third side must be more than 12 - 5 = 7 and less than 12 + 5 = 17.

solutions.reliable: The third side x must satisfy x < 5 + 12 = 17, and also 12 < 5 + x, that is x > 7. The whole numbers from 8 to 16 work, which is 9 lengths. The transferable idea: the third side of a triangle lies strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two sides.

problems.whyOnTest: The triangle inequality, with the boundary cases as traps: a third side equal to the sum or the difference gives a flat triangle, not a real one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two circles, with radii 9 cm and 4 cm, touch each other. Both circles also touch the same straight line and lie on the same side of it. How far apart are the two points where the circles touch the line?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the radii, 9 - 4.
I took the square root of 9 x 4 = 36 and forgot to double it.
I took the distance between the centres, 13, and subtracted the difference in heights, 5, instead of using Pythagoras.
I gave the distance between the centres, 9 + 4, instead of the distance along the line.

hints: Draw it: join the centres, and drop radii to the line.

The radii to the line are perpendicular to it, and the segment joining the centres passes through the point where the circles touch. Cut off a right-angled triangle from this shape and use Pythagoras.
The centres are 9 + 4 = 13 apart, and their heights above the line differ by 9 - 4 = 5.

solutions.reliable: The radii to the touching points are perpendicular to the line. The segment joining the centres passes through the point where the circles touch, so it has length 9 + 4 = 13. Draw a line parallel to the given line from the smaller centre to the larger radius: it makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13 and vertical side 9 - 4 = 5. Its horizontal side equals the distance between the touching points, which is the square root of 169 - 25 = 144, so 12 cm. The transferable idea: for touching circles, join the centres and drop radii to the tangent line to make a right-angled triangle.
solutions.elegant: As soon as the diagram is drawn, a 5, 12, 13 triangle appears: 13 between the centres and 5 difference in height leave 12 along the line.

problems.whyOnTest: Touching circles: the distance between the centres is the sum of the radii, and radii meet tangent lines at right angles, which builds a Pythagoras triangle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A coach says: 'Everyone who made the team came to every practice.' If the coach is right, which of the following must be true?

choices.text: Ana came to every practice, so she made the team.
choices.misconception: I reversed the statement, as if coming to every practice guaranteed a place on the team.

choices.text: Ben missed a practice, so he did not make the team.
Cleo did not make the team, so she missed a practice.
choices.misconception: I assumed not making the team means a missed practice, but Cleo may have come every time and still not been picked.

choices.text: Everyone who came to every practice made the team.
choices.misconception: I turned 'everyone who made the team came' into 'everyone who came made the team'.

choices.text: At least one person made the team.
choices.misconception: I assumed the statement says someone made the team, but it would still be true if nobody did.

hints: Which kind of person would make the coach wrong?
A statement of the form 'everyone who is P is Q' is broken only by someone who is P but not Q. For each choice, ask whether it could fail while the coach is still right.
If Ben missed a practice and made the team anyway, the coach would be wrong.

solutions.reliable: The coach's claim says there is nobody who made the team but missed a practice. Ben missed a practice, so if he had made the team the claim would be false; hence he did not make the team, and B must be true. A and D reverse the claim. C fails because Cleo could have come to every practice and still not been picked. E fails because the claim is also true if nobody made the team. The transferable idea: 'every P is Q' also means 'not Q means not P', but it does not mean 'Q means P'.

problems.whyOnTest: Reading 'everyone who ...' precisely: the contrapositive must hold, while the reversed statement and its opposite are the common traps.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben, Cara and Dev each play a different one of four instruments: piano, violin, drums and flute. Ana plays neither piano nor drums. Ben plays neither violin nor piano. Cara plays neither violin nor drums. Dev plays neither violin nor flute. Cara is the pianist's cousin. Who plays the flute?

choices.misconception: I gave Ana the flute because her clue left violin or flute, without seeing that nobody else can play the violin.
I did not use the cousin clue, and took the set-up where Cara plays piano and Ben plays flute.
I lost track of Dev's own clue, which rules out the flute, and gave him the last instrument I had not placed.
I missed that the cousin clue means Cara is not the pianist, so I thought two set-ups were possible.

hints: Which instrument can only one person play?
In an elimination grid, look for a row or column with a single possible entry, fill it in, and cross it out everywhere else. Repeat, and make sure every clue gets used, including the last one.
Only Ana can play the violin. The cousin clue tells you Cara is not the pianist.

solutions.reliable: The violin is ruled out for Ben, Cara and Dev, so Ana plays the violin. Cara cannot be her own cousin, so she is not the pianist; with violin and drums also ruled out, Cara plays the flute. Then Ben, who cannot play piano, plays drums, and Dev plays piano. Every clue checks. The flute player is Cara. The transferable idea: in a logic grid, hunt for a row or column with only one possibility left, and make sure every clue is used.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination grids reward finding the forced cell first; leaving out one clue leaves two possible set-ups, which is the trap here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven children stand in a single line, one behind another. Lea has exactly 4 children in front of her. Max has exactly 5 children behind him. How many children stand between Lea and Max?

choices.misconception: I took '4 children in front of her' to mean Lea is 4th in line.
I subtracted the places, 5 - 2 = 3, which measures the gap instead of counting the children in it.
I counted Lea and Max as well as the children between them.
I added the 4 children and the 5 children.

hints: Turn each clue into a place counted from the front.
Number the places 1 to 7 from the front of the line. Each clue fixes one child's place exactly. Then count the places strictly between the two.
Lea is in place 5. Max has 5 children behind him out of 7, so he is in place 2.

solutions.reliable: With 4 children in front, Lea is 5th. With 5 children behind out of 7, Max is in place 7 - 5 = 2. The places strictly between 2 and 5 are 3 and 4, so 2 children stand between them. The transferable idea: convert every ranking clue into an exact position before comparing.
solutions.elegant: The 4 children in front of Lea include Max, and the 5 behind Max include Lea, so together the two groups cover all 7 children. Since 4 + 5 = 9, exactly 2 children are counted twice, and those are the children between Max and Lea.

problems.whyOnTest: Ranking clues are easiest as exact positions; the off-by-one between 'children in front' and 'place in line' is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 12 are written on a board. In each step, you erase any two numbers and write down their sum minus 3. You continue until only one number is left. What is that number?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 3 once for each of the 12 numbers instead of once for each step.
I subtracted 3 only ten times, miscounting the number of steps.
I thought the minus 3 happened only once, at the very end.
I thought replacing two numbers by their sum keeps the total the same, and forgot the minus 3.

hints: What happens to the total of all the numbers in one step?
Instead of following one particular order of steps, track a quantity that changes in the same way at every step, whichever two numbers are chosen. The total on the board is such a quantity.
Each step lowers the total by exactly 3, and going from 12 numbers to 1 takes 11 steps.

solutions.reliable: The total starts at 1 + 2 + ... + 12 = 78. Erasing a and b and writing a + b - 3 lowers the total by exactly 3, whichever numbers are chosen. Each step removes one number from the board, so going from 12 numbers to 1 takes 11 steps, and the final number is 78 - 11 x 3 = 45. The transferable idea: when a process allows many choices, look for a quantity that changes predictably whatever the choices.
solutions.elegant: Subtract 3 from every number on the board. A step then just adds two of these reduced numbers together, so their total never changes. It starts at 78 - 12 x 3 = 42, so at the end the last number minus 3 is 42, and the last number is 45.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariants: with free choices at every step, the answer must come from a quantity the steps change predictably, here the total on the board.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Doubling a number and then adding 7 gives the same result as tripling the number and then subtracting 5. What is the number?

choices.misconception: I wrote 2n + 7 = 3n + 5, treating the subtraction as an addition.
I added 7 and 5 and then divided by 2 + 3 = 5, combining the two sides instead of comparing them.
I found the number correctly but then gave the result 2 x 12 + 7 instead.
I reached -n = -12 and then dropped only one of the two minus signs.

hints: Call the number n and write down both sides.
Translate each half of the sentence into an expression with n, set the two equal, then collect the n terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
2n + 7 = 3n - 5. Subtracting 2n from both sides leaves 7 = n - 5.

solutions.reliable: Let the number be n. Then 2n + 7 = 3n - 5. Subtract 2n from both sides: 7 = n - 5, so n = 12. Check: 2 x 12 + 7 = 31 and 3 x 12 - 5 = 31. The transferable idea: translate each phrase into symbols, then check the answer against the original words.
solutions.elegant: Going from double to triple adds one more copy of the number, and that extra copy has to make up the change from adding 7 to subtracting 5, which is 7 + 5 = 12. So the number is 12.

problems.whyOnTest: Translating words into an equation, where the classic slip is a sign on the subtraction and checking catches it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A grandmother is 7 times as old as her granddaughter. In 6 years, she will be 4 times as old as her granddaughter. How old is the grandmother now?

choices.misconception: I found the granddaughter's age and gave that instead.
I gave the granddaughter's age in 6 years.
I gave the grandmother's age in 6 years, not her age now.
I added 6 years to the granddaughter but not to the grandmother, solving 7g = 4(g + 6).

hints: Both people get 6 years older.
Use one letter for the granddaughter's age now. Write both ages in 6 years, remembering that the grandmother ages too, and set up the 'four times' equation.
With the granddaughter aged g now: 7g + 6 = 4(g + 6).

solutions.reliable: Let the granddaughter be g years old, so the grandmother is 7g. In 6 years: 7g + 6 = 4(g + 6) = 4g + 24, so 3g = 18 and g = 6. The grandmother is 7 x 6 = 42. Check: in 6 years they are 48 and 12, and 48 = 4 x 12. The transferable idea: in age problems everyone ages by the same amount, and the question may ask about either person at either time.
solutions.elegant: The age gap never changes. Now it is 6 times the granddaughter's age, and in 6 years it is 3 times her age then. So 6g = 3(g + 6), giving g = 6, a gap of 36 years and a grandmother of 42.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems hinge on everyone ageing equally; the wrong choices are the right numbers for the wrong person or the wrong year.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a four-digit number, the third digit equals the sum of the first two digits, and the fourth digit equals the sum of the second and third digits. For example, 1347 is one such number. How many such four-digit numbers are there?

choices.misconception: I assumed the four digits must all be different.
I assumed no digit could be 0.
I let the first digit be 0, which does not give a four-digit number.
I only checked that the third digit stays at most 9 and forgot about the fourth digit.

hints: Write every digit using only the first two.
If the first two digits are a and b, the other two are fixed by the rule. Write them in terms of a and b, then count the pairs for which every digit stays at most 9.
The digits are a, b, a + b and a + 2b, so you need a + 2b at most 9, with a at least 1.

solutions.reliable: With first digits a and b, the number reads a, b, a + b, a + 2b. The last digit is the largest, so the only conditions are a + 2b at most 9, a at least 1 and b at least 0. Count by b: b = 0 allows a = 1 to 9 (9 numbers); b = 1 allows a = 1 to 7 (7); b = 2 allows 1 to 5 (5); b = 3 allows 1 to 3 (3); b = 4 allows only a = 1 (1). Total 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 25. The transferable idea: when later digits are forced by earlier ones, count the free choices and apply one condition to the largest forced digit.
solutions.elegant: Counting by the second digit gives the odd numbers 9, 7, 5, 3, 1, and the first five odd numbers add up to 5 x 5 = 25.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles where some digits are forced: reduce to free choices plus one condition, and watch for leading zeros and zero digits.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + ... + 100! is divided by 9? (Here n! means 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x n, so for example 4! = 24.)

choices.misconception: I thought every factorial from 2! onwards is a multiple of 9, so only 1! counted.
I thought every factorial from 3! onwards is a multiple of 9, since each one contains a factor 3.
I thought every factorial from 5! onwards is a multiple of 9 because 5! = 120 ends in 0.
I treated n! as 1 + 2 + ... + n instead of 1 x 2 x ... x n.

hints: From which point is every term a multiple of 9?
A factorial is a multiple of 9 once it contains two factors of 3. Every term from that point on adds nothing to the remainder, so only a few small terms need adding up.
6! contains both 3 and 6, so 6! and every later term are multiples of 9. Add 1! to 5!.

solutions.reliable: 6! = 720 = 80 x 9, and every later factorial is a multiple of 6!, so all the terms from 6! onwards are multiples of 9. The remaining terms add to 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 + 120 = 153 = 17 x 9. So the whole sum is a multiple of 9 and the remainder is 0. The transferable idea: in a long sum, find where the terms stop mattering for the remainder, then handle the few that are left.
solutions.elegant: Work with remainders on division by 9 from the start: 1!, 2!, 3!, 4!, 5! leave 1, 2, 6, 6, 3, and every later term leaves 0. Since 1 + 2 + 6 + 6 + 3 = 18 is a multiple of 9, the remainder is 0.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders of huge sums: most terms vanish, and the trap is deciding too early where they start to vanish.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A ticket machine takes only 5-cent, 10-cent and 20-cent coins. In how many different ways can you put in exactly 50 cents, if only the number of each coin matters and not the order?

choices.misconception: I only counted the ways that use no 20-cent coin at all.
I listed the ways but missed the one that uses only 5-cent coins.
I counted the ways with no 20-cent coin and with one, but forgot the ways with two.
I thought every way had to use at least one coin of each kind.

hints: Sort the ways by how many 20-cent coins they use.
Systematic listing: fix the biggest coin first, then the next biggest, and let the 5-cent coins fill whatever is left. Each case becomes a short, complete list you can check.
With no 20s, use 0 to 5 tens. With one 20, 30 cents remain: 0 to 3 tens. With two 20s, 10 cents remain: 0 or 1 ten.

solutions.reliable: Fix the number of 20-cent coins. None: the 10-cent coins can number 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, with 5-cent coins making up the rest, so 6 ways. One: 30 cents remain, and 0 to 3 tens gives 4 ways. Two: 10 cents remain, and 0 or 1 ten gives 2 ways. Total 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. The transferable idea: list by the largest item first, so each case is short and nothing is missed or repeated.
solutions.elegant: Once the 20s and 10s are chosen, the 5-cent coins are forced, so you are really counting how many tens fit in 50, 30 and 10 cents: 6 + 4 + 2.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing a small set of combinations without gaps or repeats is the core skill, and the trap is a missing case at one end of a list.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers have digits that add up to 5?

choices.misconception: I counted every string of three digits that adds to 5, including ones that start with 0.
I only counted numbers with no zero digit, like 113 and 221.
I worked through first digits 1 to 4 and forgot 500.
I counted the different sets of digits, like 4, 1, 0, instead of the numbers they make.

hints: Split into cases by the first digit.
Casework on the hundreds digit: once it is fixed, the other two digits must add to what is left, and you can count those pairs directly. Remember zero is allowed after the first digit.
If the first digit is 1, the last two add to 4: 04, 13, 22, 31, 40, which is 5 ways. Continue for first digits 2, 3, 4, 5.

solutions.reliable: Fix the hundreds digit a, from 1 to 5. The tens and units digits must add to 5 - a, and two digits adding to k can be chosen in k + 1 ways (0 and k, 1 and k - 1, up to k and 0). So the counts are 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 for a = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, giving 15. The transferable idea: casework on the most restricted position turns a vague count into a short sum.
solutions.elegant: Count all digit strings of length three adding to 5 (21 of them, by stars and bars), then remove the 6 that start with 0, since those are two-digit strings adding to 5: 21 - 6 = 15.

problems.whyOnTest: Casework on one digit at a time is a standard Kangaroo route, and the traps are leading zeros and the forgotten end case.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cafe offers 7 different toppings for its pancakes. A plate comes with exactly 2 different toppings. How many different plates are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted choosing a first topping and then a second, so each pair got counted twice.
I multiplied the 7 toppings by the 2 toppings on each plate.
I also counted plates with the same topping twice, even though the toppings must be different.
I chose each of the two toppings from all 7, ignoring both order and repeats.

hints: Does the order of the two toppings matter?
This is a selection, not an arrangement. Count ordered choices first, then divide by the number of orders each pair appears in.
There are 7 x 6 = 42 ordered choices, and each plate appears twice in that list.

solutions.reliable: Choose a first topping in 7 ways and a different second topping in 6 ways: 42 ordered choices. Each plate, such as honey with banana, was counted twice (honey then banana, banana then honey), so there are 42 / 2 = 21 plates. The transferable idea: when order does not matter, count with order and divide by how many orders each choice has.
solutions.elegant: Each plate is a pair, just like a handshake between two of 7 people: 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo checks whether you can tell a selection from an arrangement, and 42 is waiting for anyone who forgets to divide.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The streets of a town form a square grid. Sam walks from one corner to the opposite corner, going 4 blocks east and 4 blocks north in some order, always moving east or north. The crossing exactly in the middle (2 blocks east and 2 north of the start) is closed. How many routes can Sam take?

choices.misconception: I counted the routes that go through the closed crossing instead of the ones that avoid it.
I counted every route and forgot to take out the ones through the closed crossing.
I assumed exactly half of all routes pass through the middle.
I removed 6 + 6 routes for the closed crossing instead of 6 x 6.

hints: Count all routes, then the bad ones.
Complementary counting: a route is a string of 4 Es and 4 Ns. Count all such strings, then count the routes through the middle crossing by splitting each into a first half and a second half.
All routes: choose which 4 of the 8 steps go east, 70 ways. Routes through the middle: 6 ways to get there, then 6 ways on.

solutions.reliable: A route is an ordering of 4 east steps and 4 north steps, so there are 70 routes in total (choose positions for the 4 east steps among 8). A route through the middle crossing reaches it in 6 ways (2 east and 2 north in some order) and continues in 6 ways, giving 6 x 6 = 36. So 70 - 36 = 34 routes avoid it. The transferable idea: when a restriction blocks a point, count everything and subtract the routes forced through that point.
solutions.elegant: Label each crossing with the number of routes to it, adding the numbers from the left and from below, and write 0 at the closed crossing. The corner ends at 34, with no subtraction needed.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid paths with a blocked point test both path counting and the decision to count the complement, and 36 punishes stopping halfway.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six couples meet at a party. Each person shakes hands once with every other person except their own partner. How many handshakes are there?

choices.misconception: I counted handshakes between all 12 people and forgot that partners do not shake hands.
I took away one handshake for each of the 12 people instead of one for each of the 6 couples.
I said each person shakes 10 hands and multiplied by 12, without halving.
I multiplied 12 by 11 and forgot both to halve and to remove the partners.

hints: How many hands does one person shake?
Handshakes and pairs: count from each person's point of view, then remember that every handshake has two people in it, so that total counts each handshake twice.
Each of the 12 people shakes 10 hands, which gives 120, but each handshake was counted by both people.

solutions.reliable: Each of the 12 people shakes hands with everyone except themselves and their partner, so 10 people. That gives 12 x 10 = 120, but each handshake is counted once by each of the two people, so there are 60 handshakes. The transferable idea: count from each person, then divide by 2 because every pair was counted from both ends.
solutions.elegant: If everyone shook hands, there would be 12 x 11 / 2 = 66 handshakes. Exactly 6 are missing, one per couple, so 66 - 6 = 60.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting pairs with a restriction checks whether you halve correctly and remove the right number of missing pairs.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A chessboard has 8 rows and 8 columns of small squares. How many different 3 by 3 squares, made of 9 small squares, can be found on it?

choices.misconception: I cut the board into separate 3 by 3 blocks that do not overlap.
I thought a 3 by 3 square can start in 8 - 3 = 5 places across.
I thought a 3 by 3 square can start in 7 places across, one fewer than 8.
I counted one square for each small square as its top left corner, even near the edges.

hints: The squares are allowed to overlap.
Sliding window: a 3 by 3 square is fixed by where its top left corner sits. Count the possible starting columns and rows separately, then multiply.
Across, the left column of the square can be column 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.

solutions.reliable: The left edge of a 3 by 3 square can sit at column 1 up to column 6, because columns 6, 7 and 8 are the last three. That is 6 positions across, and likewise 6 positions down, so there are 6 x 6 = 36 squares. The transferable idea: a window of width k slides into n - k + 1 positions along a row of n.
solutions.elegant: Check with a smaller case: on a 3 by 3 board, n - k + 1 = 1, and there is exactly one 3 by 3 square. That confirms the plus one.

problems.whyOnTest: Sliding window counts are everywhere in Kangaroo, and the two traps are cutting into blocks and the off-by-one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: From the top corner of a triangle, 3 straight lines are drawn to the bottom side, dividing that side into 4 parts. Then one straight line is drawn across the triangle, parallel to the bottom side, crossing all of these lines. How many triangles of any size can be found in the figure?

choices.misconception: I only counted the triangles whose base lies on the bottom side.
I counted only the triangles one slice wide: the 4 small ones above the parallel line and the 4 tall thin ones that reach the bottom side.
I also counted the 4 pieces between the parallel line and the bottom, but they are four-sided, not triangles.
I counted only the 4 small triangles at the top.

hints: Every triangle in the figure has the same top corner.
Counting shapes in a figure: describe each triangle by its two sides through the top corner and the line its base lies on. Count the choices of each, then multiply.
There are 5 lines through the top corner, so 10 ways to choose two of them. The base can be on either of 2 horizontal lines.

solutions.reliable: Two horizontal lines are parallel, so no triangle can use both; every triangle has two sides along lines through the top corner and a base on one horizontal line. There are 5 lines through the top corner (the two sides of the big triangle and the 3 drawn lines), so 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 pairs. Each pair, with the bottom side, makes a triangle, and with the parallel line makes another. That gives 10 x 2 = 20. The transferable idea: describe a shape by the lines that form it, then count choices of lines.
solutions.elegant: For one horizontal line, the triangles are 4 of width one, 3 of width two, 2 of width three and 1 of width four: 10. The parallel line gives a second, smaller copy of the same picture: 20.

problems.whyOnTest: Hidden-figure counting rewards a system over staring, and naming each triangle by its lines is the system that never misses one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A tower of unit cubes stands on a table: a 5 by 5 bottom layer, a 3 by 3 middle layer centred on it, and one cube centred on top. A cube is hidden if none of its faces can be seen. Faces on the table or against another cube cannot be seen. How many cubes are hidden?

choices.misconception: I found the hidden cubes in the bottom layer but forgot the centre of the middle layer, covered by the top cube.
I counted the cubes that can be seen instead of the hidden ones.
I only counted the cube directly under the top cube.
I took the inside of an n by n layer to be (n - 1) by (n - 1), giving 16 + 4 + 0.

hints: Go layer by layer. Which cubes have their top face covered?
A cube is hidden only if it is not on the outside edge of its layer and the layer above covers its top. Work through each layer separately and count the cubes that pass both tests.
In the bottom layer, the inner 3 by 3 cubes are not on the edge, and the middle layer covers all their tops.

solutions.reliable: Bottom layer: the 16 cubes around the edge show a side face. The inner 3 by 3 block of 9 cubes has no side showing, and the middle layer sits exactly on top of them, so all 9 are hidden. Middle layer: the 8 edge cubes show a side, and the centre cube is covered by the top cube, so 1 is hidden. The top cube is visible. Total 9 + 1 = 10. The transferable idea: count hidden cubes one layer at a time, checking sides and tops separately.
solutions.elegant: There are 25 + 9 + 1 = 35 cubes. The visible ones are the 16 edge cubes of the bottom layer, the 8 edge cubes of the middle layer and the top cube, 25 in all, so 35 - 25 = 10 are hidden.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting cubes you cannot see is a Kangaroo favourite, and it rewards a layer-by-layer check over guessing from the outside.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cyclist rides 6 km up a hill at 12 km per hour, then comes straight back down the same road at 24 km per hour. What is her average speed for the whole trip, in km per hour?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two speeds, 12 and 24.
I added the two speeds together.
I divided only the one-way distance, 6 km, by the total time of 45 minutes.
I divided the whole 12 km by the uphill time of half an hour only.

hints: Average speed is total distance over total time.
The quick average of 12 and 24 is tempting. Check it a second way by working out the actual times for each half and using total distance divided by total time.
Uphill takes 6 / 12 = 0.5 hours and downhill takes 6 / 24 = 0.25 hours. The trip is 12 km.

solutions.reliable: Going up takes 6 / 12 = 0.5 hours, coming down takes 6 / 24 = 0.25 hours, so the whole trip is 12 km in 0.75 hours. Average speed is 12 / 0.75 = 16 km per hour. The transferable idea: when a fast answer comes from averaging rates, check it with total distance over total time, because she spends longer at the slower speed.
solutions.elegant: She spends twice as long going up as coming down, so the average is weighted 2 to 1 toward 12: (2 x 12 + 1 x 24) / 3 = 16. That second method confirms the first.

problems.whyOnTest: Averaging two speeds is a classic trap, and a second check with real times exposes 18 before you commit to it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 20 cm. One of its sides is 4 cm long. How long is each of its two equal sides?

choices.misconception: I made the 4 cm side one of the equal pair and did not check that 4, 4 and 12 cannot form a triangle.
I made 4 cm one of the equal sides and then gave the length of the third side.
I subtracted the 4 cm side from the perimeter and stopped.
I halved the 20 cm perimeter, as if the triangle had only the two equal sides.

hints: There are two cases. Does each one really make a triangle?
Properties of triangles: the 4 cm side is either one of the equal pair or the odd side. Find the lengths in each case, then check that any two sides add to more than the third.
If the equal sides were 4 cm, the third side would be 12 cm, but 4 + 4 is less than 12.

solutions.reliable: Case 1: the two equal sides are 4 cm. Then the third side is 20 - 8 = 12 cm, but 4 + 4 = 8 is less than 12, so the two short sides cannot meet: no triangle. Case 2: 4 cm is the base. The other two sides share 16 cm equally, so each is 8 cm, and 4, 8, 8 is a real triangle. The answer is 8 cm. The transferable idea: when a figure allows two cases, test each against the triangle inequality before accepting it.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo likes problems with two apparent cases where one quietly fails, and this one probes the triangle inequality.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three circles have radii 2 cm, 3 cm and 10 cm. Each circle touches the other two from the outside. What is the area of the triangle whose corners are the three centres, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found a right triangle with legs 5 and 12 but forgot to halve.
I used diameters, so my triangle had sides 10, 24 and 26.
I used the sides 5 and 13 as the base and height.
I used the sides 12 and 13 as the base and height.

hints: When two circles touch, how far apart are their centres?

For circles touching from outside, the line between centres passes through the point of contact, so its length is the sum of the radii. Find all three side lengths, then look for something special about them.
The sides are 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 10 = 13 and 2 + 10 = 12. Is 5, 12, 13 a right triangle?

solutions.reliable: Touching circles have centres a distance apart equal to the sum of their radii, so the sides are 2 + 3 = 5, 2 + 10 = 12 and 3 + 10 = 13. Since 5 x 5 + 12 x 12 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13 x 13, the triangle has a right angle between the sides 5 and 12. Its area is 5 x 12 / 2 = 30. The transferable idea: touching circles turn into a triangle of radius sums, and Pythagorean triples are worth spotting.
solutions.elegant: Without spotting the right angle, Heron's formula with half-perimeter 15 gives the square root of 15 x 10 x 3 x 2 = 900, which is 30 again.

problems.whyOnTest: This probes the fact that touching circles have centres one radius sum apart, then rewards recognising a right triangle hidden in the numbers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four squares with sides 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm stand in a row from smallest to largest, with their bottom edges on the same line and each square touching the next one along a side. What is the perimeter of the staircase shape they make?

choices.misconception: I added the perimeters of the four squares and forgot that the edges where two squares touch are inside the shape.
I took away each touching edge once, but each one was counted in two squares' perimeters, so it had to come off twice.
I found the area of the shape, 1 + 4 + 9 + 16, instead of its perimeter.
I added the bottom and the steps along the top, 10 + 10, but forgot the vertical edges.

hints: Walk around the outline and sort the edges into horizontal and vertical.

Perimeter of rectilinear shapes: the step tops together are as long as the bottom edge. The upward edges, the left side and the rises, together are as tall as the tallest square, which is the right side’s height.
The bottom is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 cm, so the step tops also total 10 cm. The left side and the rises add to 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 cm, the same as the 4 cm right side.

solutions.reliable: Add the four square perimeters: 4 + 8 + 12 + 16 = 40 cm. Where two squares touch, the shared part is as long as the smaller square's side: 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm. Each shared part was counted in both squares, and none of it is on the outline, so subtract 2 x (1 + 2 + 3) = 12 cm. The perimeter is 40 - 12 = 28 cm. The transferable idea: when shapes are joined, every touching edge leaves the perimeter twice, once from each shape.
solutions.elegant: Push the steps out to the bounding rectangle, 10 cm wide and 4 cm tall. The top steps still add to 10 cm across and the rises still add to 4 cm up, so the perimeter equals that rectangle's: 2 x (10 + 4) = 28 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter of rectilinear shapes rewards matching horizontal and vertical edges, and the trap is counting the edges where shapes touch.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A regular hexagon has an area of 48 square centimetres. The midpoints of its six sides are joined in order to make a smaller hexagon inside it. What is the area of the smaller hexagon, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I thought each corner piece, whose sides are half as long as those of the triangle made by three neighbouring corners, had half of that triangle's area instead of a quarter.
I thought the six corner pieces together were as big as one of the six central triangles.
I found the total area of the six corner pieces instead of the hexagon left in the middle.
I worked out the area of one corner piece, 2, but took it away only once instead of six times.

hints: Split the big hexagon into six equal triangles from its centre. How big is each?
Area by dissection: the small hexagon is the big one with six corner pieces cut off. Compare one corner piece with the triangle formed by three neighbouring corners of the big hexagon.

Call three neighbouring corners A, B and C, and the centre O. The rhombus OABC is two central triangles, 16, and its diagonal AC halves it, so triangle ABC is 8. The corner piece at B joins the midpoints of AB and BC.

solutions.reliable: Lines from the centre O to the six corners cut the hexagon into six equal triangles of area 8. Take three neighbouring corners A, B, C. The rhombus OABC is two of those triangles, area 16, and the diagonal AC cuts it into two equal halves, so triangle ABC has area 8. The corner piece cut off at B is the triangle joining B to the midpoints of BA and BC. It is triangle ABC shrunk to half the size in every direction, so it has a quarter of the area: 2. Six corner pieces total 12, leaving 48 - 12 = 36. The transferable idea: break the shape into pieces you can compare, and remember that halving every length quarters the area.
solutions.elegant: Each corner piece is a quarter of a triangle ABC, and triangle ABC is a sixth of the hexagon, so each piece is 1/24 of it. Six pieces are 6/24 = 1/4, and the small hexagon is 3/4 of 48, which is 36.

problems.whyOnTest: Area by dissection asks you to compare a piece with one you already know, and the hexagon's six central triangles are the natural units to count in.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The point (2, 5) is reflected in the line y = x, where the two coordinates are equal. The new point is then rotated a quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin (0, 0). Where does it end up?

choices.misconception: I did the reflection but forgot the rotation.
I rotated a quarter turn clockwise instead of anticlockwise.
I rotated the original point and forgot to reflect it first.
I turned the reflected point a half turn instead of a quarter turn.

hints: Do one move at a time and sketch the point after each.
Reflecting in y = x swaps the two coordinates. A quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin sends a point in the top right quarter to the top left quarter. Apply them in the order given.
After the reflection the point is (5, 2). A quarter turn anticlockwise sends (x, y) to (negative y, x).

solutions.reliable: Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates: (2, 5) becomes (5, 2). A quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin sends (x, y) to (negative y, x), so (5, 2) goes to (negative 2, 5). Check by sketching: (5, 2) points right and a little up; a quarter turn anticlockwise points it up and a little left. The transferable idea: break a combined transformation into single moves and track a point through each.
solutions.elegant: Track any point: (x, y) becomes (y, x) and then (negative x, y). So the two moves together act like a single reflection in the y-axis, and (2, 5) lands on (negative 2, 5).

problems.whyOnTest: Combining a reflection with a rotation tests careful order and direction, and every one-mistake answer is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev each own one different pet: a cat, a dog, a fish and a rabbit. Neither Ben nor Dev owns the dog. Ana owns neither the fish nor the dog. Dev and the cat's owner are cousins. Neither Ben nor Dev owns the rabbit. Who owns the cat?

choices.misconception: I stopped before using the last clue, when Ana could still have had the cat.
I gave the cat to Cleo because the cat clue does not mention her.
I took the cousins clue to mean Dev owns the cat.
I missed that the last clue leaves only one arrangement, so I thought two were possible.

hints: Pin down the dog first.
Elimination grid: make a table of people against pets, cross out each pair the clues forbid, and whenever a row or column has one space left, fill it and cross out the rest of that column or row.
The dog cannot be Ben's, Dev's or Ana's, so it is Cleo's. Now Dev is not the dog, cat or rabbit.

solutions.reliable: The dog is not Ben's or Dev's, and not Ana's, so Cleo owns the dog. Dev is not the dog's owner, not the cat's owner (Dev is the cousin of that person) and not the rabbit's owner, so Dev owns the fish. That leaves the cat and the rabbit for Ana and Ben, and Ben does not own the rabbit, so Ana owns the rabbit and Ben owns the cat. The transferable idea: fill the grid square that is forced, then let each new fact eliminate more.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination grids test reading every clue precisely, including a clue that rules someone out without naming the pet directly.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Twenty-five people stand in a queue. Ana is 9th from the front and Ben is 6th from the back. How many people are standing between them?

choices.misconception: I put Ben in place 25 - 6 = 19, one place too far forward.
I subtracted their positions and added 1, which counts both Ana and Ben.
I removed the 9 and the 6 from 25, then wrongly removed Ana and Ben a second time.
I subtracted their positions, 20 - 9, which counts Ben but not Ana.

hints: Find Ben's place counting from the front.
Ordering and ranking: turn both positions into places from the front, then count the places strictly between them. Check with a tiny queue so the plus or minus one is right.
6th from the back of 25 is 20th from the front, since 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 is six places.

solutions.reliable: Ben is 6th from the back, so he is in place 25 - 6 + 1 = 20 from the front. The people strictly between places 9 and 20 are in places 10 to 19, which is 10 people. The transferable idea: convert both rankings to the same end, then count the gap carefully with a small example.
solutions.elegant: The first 9 people include Ana and the last 6 include Ben. Everyone else is between them: 25 - 9 - 6 = 10.

problems.whyOnTest: Ranking from both ends is a reliable Kangaroo question, and its only real difficulty is the off-by-one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Eleven lamps are all switched off. In one move you must flip the switches of exactly 3 different lamps: each of those 3 lamps that is off goes on, and each that is on goes off. What is the smallest number of moves needed to have all 11 lamps on at the same time?

choices.misconception: I divided 11 by 3 and rounded down, so some lamps were never switched on.
I rounded 11 divided by 3 up to 4 and missed that every move changes the number of lamps that are on by an odd amount, so after 4 moves it is even.
I saw that 4 moves fail, then thought the number of moves had to be even, so I jumped to 6.
I thought each lamp could be switched only once, and 11 is not a multiple of 3.

hints: In one move, by how much can the number of lamps that are on change?

Invariants and parity: each move flips 3 lamps, so the number that are on changes by 3 or by 1. Track whether that number is odd or even after each move, then check the smallest leftover count can be reached.
After every move the parity of the number of lamps on switches, so to reach 11 (odd) you need an odd number of moves. Three moves flip only 9 switches, which is too few.

solutions.reliable: Each move flips 3 lamps, so the number of lamps that are on changes by 3 or by 1, an odd amount. Starting from 0, it is odd after 1 move, even after 2, odd after 3, and so on, so reaching 11 needs an odd number of moves. Three moves flip only 9 switches, fewer than 11 lamps, so 3 is not enough, and 4 is even, so the answer is at least 5. Five moves do work: label the lamps 1 to 11 and flip 1, 2, 3; then 1, 2, 4; then 1, 2, 5; then 6, 7, 8; then 9, 10, 11. Lamps 1 and 2 are flipped three times and end on, and every other lamp is flipped once. The transferable idea: a parity argument rules out the tempting answer, and an explicit example shows the next answer works.
solutions.elegant: Try a small case first: with 5 lamps, rounding 5 / 3 up suggests 2 moves, but 2 moves always leave an even number of lamps on. Three moves work: flip 1, 2, 3, then 1, 2, 4, then 1, 2, 5. The same pattern, parity first and then two lamps flipped three times, gives 5 moves for 11 lamps.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity is the simplest invariant, and here it is the only thing that rules out the tempting 4, while an explicit example confirms 5.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a game, Lina thinks of a number. She adds 4, multiplies the result by 3, subtracts 6 and then halves what she has. She ends with 12. What number did she think of?

choices.misconception: I applied her steps forward to 12 instead of undoing them.
I forgot to undo the halving, so I started undoing from 12 instead of 24.
I undid the last step wrongly by adding 4 instead of subtracting it.
I undid all the steps except the first one, adding 4.

hints: Start at 12 and go back.
Working backwards: undo the steps in reverse order, using the opposite operation each time. Doubling undoes halving, adding undoes subtracting, and so on.
Double 12 to get 24, add 6 to get 30, then divide by 3.

solutions.reliable: Undo each step from the last: double 12 to get 24, add 6 to get 30, divide by 3 to get 10, subtract 4 to get 6. Check forward: 6 + 4 = 10, 10 x 3 = 30, 30 - 6 = 24, 24 / 2 = 12. The transferable idea: to reverse a chain of operations, undo them in reverse order with inverse operations, then check forward.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards through a chain of operations is a basic Kangaroo move, and order and inverse slips each give a listed answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A father and his son have ages that add up to 48 years. Six years ago, the father was 5 times as old as his son. How old is the father now?

choices.misconception: I found the son's age now and gave that.
I gave the father's age six years ago.
I took 6 years off the father's age but not off the son's.
I took 6 years off the son's age but not off the father's.

hints: Six years ago, both of them were 6 years younger.
Age problems: call the son's age now s, so the father is 48 - s. Write both ages six years ago, then turn the second sentence into an equation.
Six years ago they were s - 6 and 42 - s, so 42 - s = 5(s - 6).

solutions.reliable: Let the son be s years old now, so the father is 48 - s. Six years ago they were s - 6 and 42 - s, so 42 - s = 5(s - 6) = 5s - 30, which gives 6s = 72 and s = 12. The father is 48 - 12 = 36. Check: six years ago they were 30 and 6, and 30 is 5 times 6. The transferable idea: in age problems, move every person by the same number of years, then answer the question actually asked.
solutions.elegant: Six years ago their ages added to 48 - 12 = 36, and the father had 5 parts to the son's 1, so 6 parts made 36. The son was 6 and the father 30, so the father is 36 now.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems test moving both people back in time by the same amount, and the distractors are the other ages met on the way.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When the whole number N is divided by 9 the remainder is 4. When the whole number M is divided by 9 the remainder is 7. What is the remainder when N x M is divided by 9?

choices.misconception: I added the remainders and did not reduce the answer.
I multiplied the remainders but forgot to divide 28 by 9.
I added the remainders instead of multiplying them.
I subtracted the smaller remainder from the larger.

hints: Try N = 4 and M = 7.
Remainders: the remainder of a product depends only on the remainders of the factors. Multiply the remainders, then take the remainder of that result.

solutions.reliable: Write N = 9a + 4 and M = 9b + 7. Every part of the product N x M is a multiple of 9 except 4 x 7 = 28, and 28 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9. So N x M leaves remainder 1. The transferable idea: multiply remainders, then reduce, because the multiples of the divisor drop out.
solutions.elegant: Test real numbers: N = 13 and M = 16 give 208 = 23 x 9 + 1. Remainder 1 again.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders of products are the heart of modular reasoning, and the trap is forgetting to reduce the product of the remainders.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the three-digit number 495, the middle digit 9 is the sum of the other two digits, 4 + 5. How many three-digit numbers have this property?

choices.misconception: I forgot that the last digit is allowed to be 0, as in 110.
I chose the first and last digits freely and did not check that their sum stays a single digit.
I only counted the numbers whose middle digit is 9.
I let the first digit be 0 as well, which does not give a three-digit number.

hints: Choose the first and last digits; the middle one is then forced.
Digit constraints: the middle digit is decided by the other two, but it must be a single digit. Do casework on the first digit and count the last digits that keep the sum at most 9.
If the first digit is 1, the last digit can be 0 to 8, which is 9 numbers. If it is 2, the last digit can be 0 to 7.

solutions.reliable: Let the digits be a, b, c with b = a + c. The first digit a is 1 to 9, and c can be any digit from 0 up to 9 - a so that b is a single digit. That gives 9, 8, 7, ..., 1 numbers for a = 1, 2, ..., 9, which adds to 45. The transferable idea: when one digit is determined by the others, count the free choices and keep the forced digit in range.
solutions.elegant: Count by the middle digit instead: if b = k, then a can be 1 to k and c = k - a, so there are k numbers. Adding k from 1 to 9 gives 45 again.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles test translating a condition into limits on each digit, then counting without dropping zeros or letting a leading zero in.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts 1, 3, and after that every term is the previous term minus the one before it. So the third term is 3 - 1 = 2. What is the sum of the first 100 terms?

choices.misconception: I found the 100th term instead of the sum of the first 100 terms.
I added one term too few after the complete blocks of six.
I saw that every block of six terms adds to 0 and ignored the terms left over after the blocks.
I added one term too many after the complete blocks of six.

hints: Write out the first ten terms.
Recursive rules often repeat. Generate terms until the starting pair comes back, find the length of the cycle and the sum of one cycle, then deal with the leftover terms.
The terms go 1, 3, 2, negative 1, negative 3, negative 2, then 1, 3 again. One cycle of 6 adds to 0.

solutions.reliable: The terms are 1, 3, 2, negative 1, negative 3, negative 2, 1, 3, ..., repeating every 6 terms because the pair 1, 3 comes back. Each block of 6 adds to 0. Since 100 = 16 x 6 + 4, the first 96 terms add to 0, and the remaining 4 terms are 1, 3, 2, negative 1, which add to 5. The transferable idea: a rule that uses the last two terms repeats as soon as a pair repeats, so find the cycle and handle the remainder.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo regularly asks about the 100th or 2026th step of a rule, which can only be done by finding the cycle and the remainder.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A round badge is divided into 5 equal sectors, like slices of a pie. Each sector is painted red or blue. The badge can be turned, but not flipped over. Two badges count as the same if one can be turned to look exactly like the other. How many different badges are there?

choices.misconception: I counted every colouring of the 5 sectors and forgot that turned badges are the same.
I only counted how many sectors are red, from 0 to 5, and not where they are.
I divided 32 by 5 and rounded up.
I thought two red sectors could be arranged in 3 different ways, and the same for two blue sectors.

hints: Sort the badges by how many sectors are red.
Counting up to symmetry: for each number of red sectors, list the arrangements that cannot be turned into each other. Turning around a circle means only the gaps between red sectors matter.
With 2 red sectors they are either next to each other or separated by one sector on the short side. Separated by two is the same as by one.

solutions.reliable: Count by the number of red sectors. 0 red: 1 badge. 1 red: 1 badge. 2 red: the two reds are either side by side or have one blue between them on the shorter way round, so 2 badges. 3 red: same as 2 blue, so 2 badges. 4 red: 1 badge. 5 red: 1 badge. Total 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 8. The transferable idea: when turns make things equal, sort by a feature turning cannot change, then count shapes within each group.
solutions.elegant: Of the 32 colourings, 2 are all one colour and do not change when turned. The other 30 come in groups of 5 turns, giving 6 badges. Adding the 2 single-colour badges gives 8.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting up to rotation separates careful listers from those who divide blindly, and 7 and 32 catch both kinds of shortcut.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An ordinary die, whose opposite faces add up to 7, sits on a table with 1 on top, 2 facing you and 3 on the right. It is rolled a quarter turn to the right, tipping over its right bottom edge, then a quarter turn away from you, then another quarter turn to the right. What is now on top?

choices.misconception: I tracked the rolls correctly but gave the face on the bottom instead of the top.
I stopped after the first roll.
I thought the two rolls to the right cancel each other out, so I only did the roll away from me.
I gave the face that ends up facing me instead of the face on top.

hints: First write down all six faces: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
Opposite faces add to 7, so the start is top 1, bottom 6, front 2, back 5, right 3, left 4. Rolling right sends the left face up; rolling away sends the front face up.
After the first roll the top is 4 and the left is 6. After the roll away the top is 2, and the left face is still 6.

solutions.reliable: Start: top 1, bottom 6, front 2, back 5, right 3, left 4. Rolling to the right moves the top to the right, the right to the bottom, the bottom to the left and the left to the top, so the top becomes 4 and the left becomes 6, while front and back stay. Rolling away moves the front to the top, so the top becomes 2, and the left and right faces do not move: left is still 6. The last roll to the right brings the left face, 6, to the top. The transferable idea: record all six faces and update them roll by roll, using opposite pairs adding to 7.
solutions.elegant: Only the left face matters for the last roll to the right. The left face is 4 at the start, the first roll puts the bottom, 6, on the left, and the roll away does not touch the left and right faces. So 6 comes to the top.

problems.whyOnTest: Rolling a die checks whether you can track all six faces at once, using the rule that opposite faces add to 7.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bracelet has 7 equally spaced beads on a loop: 3 are black and 4 are white. Two bracelets count as the same if one can be turned or flipped over to look exactly like the other. How many different bracelets are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted every way to choose which 3 of the 7 places are black, treating turned and flipped bracelets as different.
I counted every way to share the 4 white beads among the 3 gaps between black beads, keeping the gaps in a fixed order, so I counted turned copies again.
I allowed turning the bracelet but forgot it can also be flipped, so I counted a pattern and its mirror image separately.
I sorted the bracelets into all three blacks together, exactly two together, or none together, and missed that exactly two together can happen in two different ways.

hints: Look at the white beads sitting between the black ones.
Do not count positions; count shapes. The 3 black beads split the 4 white beads into 3 gaps. Turning or flipping only moves the gaps around, so list the possible gap sizes.
The gap sizes can be 4, 0, 0 or 3, 1, 0 or 2, 2, 0 or 2, 1, 1. Check that each set of gap sizes gives just one bracelet.

solutions.reliable: The 3 black beads cut the loop into 3 gaps, and the 4 white beads are shared among those gaps. Turning the bracelet just moves the gaps round the circle, and flipping reverses their order. With only 3 gaps, any order of three gap sizes can be turned or flipped into any other, so a bracelet is fixed by its set of gap sizes alone. The possible sets are 4, 0, 0 and 3, 1, 0 and 2, 2, 0 and 2, 1, 1, so there are 4 bracelets. The transferable idea: when arrangements count as equal up to turning and flipping, describe each one by a feature that turning and flipping cannot change, rather than by positions.
solutions.elegant: Without flips there are 5 patterns, because the gaps 3, 1, 0 and 3, 0, 1 go round the circle in opposite directions and cannot be turned into each other. A flip joins exactly that pair, leaving 4.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting up to symmetry punishes counting positions, and the wrong choices come from forgetting turns, forgetting flips, or merging two different shapes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten people sit evenly spaced around a round table. Each person shakes hands once with every other person except the two people sitting directly next to them. How many handshakes take place?

choices.misconception: I counted 7 handshakes for each of the 10 people and forgot that every handshake involves two people, so each was counted twice.
I counted every pair of the 10 people and forgot to leave out the pairs of neighbours.
I left out only one neighbour per person, giving 8 handshakes each, and then halved 10 x 8.
I took all 45 pairs and subtracted 20 neighbour pairs, counting each neighbouring pair once from each side.

hints: Count from one person's point of view first.
Overcount, then correct: count the handshakes each person makes and multiply by the number of people, then fix the fact that each handshake was seen from both ends.
Each person shakes 10 - 1 - 2 = 7 hands, so 10 x 7 = 70 counts every handshake twice.

solutions.reliable: Each person skips themselves and their two neighbours, so shakes 7 hands. Ten people times 7 is 70, but each handshake has been counted once by each of the two people in it, so there are 70 / 2 = 35. The transferable idea: count from each person, then divide by the number of times each object was counted.
solutions.elegant: There are 45 pairs of people in total, and exactly 10 of them are neighbours around the table, one pair per gap. 45 - 10 = 35.

problems.whyOnTest: Handshake problems test whether you notice that counting from each person counts every handshake twice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag holds 30 tiles numbered 1 to 30. Without looking, you take out tiles one at a time. What is the smallest number of tiles you must take to be certain that two of the tiles you hold add up to a multiple of 3?

choices.misconception: I thought two tiles with the same remainder on division by 3 always add up to a multiple of 3, so I used 3 remainder boxes plus 1.
I forgot that one multiple of 3 can join a safe handful, so I thought 10 tiles was the most that could avoid a good pair.
I thought the pair had to include a multiple of 3, so I planned to take all 20 other tiles and then one more to be sure of holding one.
I imagined the luckiest draw, where the very first two tiles already work.

hints: Sort the tiles by their remainder when divided by 3.
Imagine the unluckiest possible handful. Work out which remainders can live together without two of them summing to a multiple of 3, make that handful as large as possible, then add one.
Remainders 1 and 2 cannot both appear, and at most one tile with remainder 0 is allowed. So take all ten of one class plus one multiple of 3.

solutions.reliable: There are ten tiles with each remainder 0, 1 and 2. Two tiles add to a multiple of 3 exactly when their remainders are 0 and 0, or 1 and 2. A safe handful can therefore hold at most one multiple of 3, and cannot mix remainder 1 with remainder 2. The biggest safe handful is all ten tiles of remainder 1 (or of remainder 2) plus one multiple of 3: 11 tiles. The next tile must complete a pair, so 12 tiles guarantee it. The transferable idea: for a guarantee, build the worst possible collection, then add one.

problems.whyOnTest: Worst-case questions reward building the largest bad collection, and the trap here is assuming equal remainders are what matter.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle measures 8 cm by 5 cm. A 2 cm by 2 cm square is cut out from the middle of one of the long sides, leaving a notch. What is the perimeter, in cm, of the shape that remains?

choices.misconception: I thought cutting out a square never changes the perimeter, which is only true when the square comes from a corner.
I subtracted the 2 cm gap in the long side and forgot the three new edges of the notch.
I added all four sides of the small square, 8 cm, instead of the three new edges minus the gap.
I worked out the area of the shape, 40 - 4, instead of its perimeter.

hints: Trace the edge of the new shape with your finger.
Start from the rectangle's perimeter. Ask what the cut removes from the outline and what it adds: the notch removes part of one side but creates new edges inside the shape.
The rectangle has perimeter 26. The cut removes 2 cm of the long side and adds three edges of 2 cm.

solutions.reliable: The rectangle's perimeter is 2 x (8 + 5) = 26 cm. Cutting the notch removes 2 cm of the long side but adds the notch's two side walls and its floor, 3 x 2 = 6 cm. The new perimeter is 26 - 2 + 6 = 30 cm. The transferable idea: when a shape is cut, track what leaves the outline and what joins it, instead of assuming the perimeter shrinks with the area.
solutions.elegant: Push the notch's floor back out to the long side and it exactly fills the gap, so only the two 2 cm walls are extra: 26 + 4 = 30.

problems.whyOnTest: Perimeter and area move in opposite directions here, and the corner-cut fact students remember gives the wrong answer for a notch.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The midpoints of the sides of a square of side 10 cm are joined to make a second square. The midpoints of the sides of the second square are joined to make a third square. What is the area of the third square, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I stopped after making the second square and gave its area.
I halved the area three times, once for each square including the first.
I thought each new square has half the side of the one before, so I squared 2.5.
I thought the four corner triangles cut off at each step make up only a quarter of the square, so I multiplied by three quarters twice.

hints: Look at the four triangles cut off from the corners.
Area by dissection: fold the four corner triangles inwards across the sides of the inner square and see how much of the inner square they cover. That tells you the fraction kept at each step.
The four corner triangles fold in to cover the inner square exactly, so each new square has half the area of the one before.

solutions.reliable: Folding each corner triangle inwards along a side of the inner square lands it exactly on a quarter of the inner square, so the inner square has the same area as the four corner triangles together. Each step therefore keeps half the area. The first square has area 100, the second 50, and the third 25 square centimetres. The transferable idea: a dissection that matches pieces one to one gives a ratio of areas without any lengths.
solutions.elegant: Joining midpoints twice gives a square turned back upright whose side is exactly half of 10, so its area is 5 x 5 = 25.

problems.whyOnTest: Midpoint squares appear often because the halving can be seen by folding, and the distractors catch halving the side instead of the area.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A stick 12 cm long is cut into three pieces, each a whole number of centimetres long. The three pieces are then used as the sides of a triangle. How many different triangles can be made this way? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as the same.

choices.misconception: I counted every way to cut the stick into three whole-number pieces and did not check which ones can make a triangle.
I also accepted pieces where the two shorter ones add up exactly to the longest, like 3, 3 and 6, but those lie flat and make no triangle.
I counted the same three lengths in a different order as a different triangle.
I forgot that all three pieces can be the same length, 4, 4 and 4.

hints: Can any three lengths make a triangle?
Use the triangle inequality: the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side. With a total of 12, that means the longest side must be less than half of 12.
The longest piece must be shorter than 6 cm, so it is 4 or 5 cm. List the other two pieces for each case.

solutions.reliable: For a triangle, the two shorter sides must add up to more than the longest. Since all three add up to 12, the longest side must be less than 6 cm, and it must be at least 4 cm because three pieces of at most 3 cm reach only 9. With longest side 4 the only choice is 4, 4, 4. With longest side 5 the other two add to 7 and neither is more than 5, giving 5, 5, 2 and 5, 4, 3. That makes 3 triangles. The transferable idea: turn the triangle inequality into a bound on the longest side, then list systematically from there.

problems.whyOnTest: This checks that you test the triangle inequality strictly, since pieces whose short sides exactly reach the long side cannot form a triangle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A large circle has radius 6 cm. Inside it, two circles of radius 3 cm touch each other at the centre of the large circle, and each touches the large circle. A small circle is drawn inside the large circle so that it touches the large circle and both 3 cm circles. What is its radius, in cm?

choices.misconception: I made the small circle fill the whole gap from the centre of the large circle up to its edge, a diameter of 6, without checking that it would then overlap the 3 cm circles.
I found the radius correctly and then doubled it, giving the diameter.
I set the height of the small circle's centre equal to 3 plus its radius, forgetting that the line between the two centres is slanted, so it needs Pythagoras.
I used 6 cm, the large radius, as the sideways distance between the small circle's centre and a 3 cm circle's centre, instead of 3 cm.

hints: Join the centres of circles that touch.
When two circles touch, the distance between their centres is the sum of the radii, or the difference if one is inside the other. Call the small radius r and look for a right-angled triangle.
The small centre is 6 - r above the large centre, 3 cm sideways from a 3 cm circle's centre, and 3 + r away from it.

solutions.reliable: Call the small radius r. Its centre lies straight above the centre O of the large circle, because the picture is symmetric. It touches the large circle from inside, so its centre is 6 - r from O. It touches a 3 cm circle from outside, whose centre is 3 cm to the side of O, so the distance between those two centres is 3 + r. These form a right-angled triangle with legs 3 and 6 - r and slanted side 3 + r, so 9 + (6 - r) x (6 - r) = (3 + r) x (3 + r). Expanding, 45 - 12r = 9 + 6r, so 18r = 36 and r = 2 cm. The transferable idea: touching circles turn into distances between centres, and a right angle from symmetry gives the equation.

problems.whyOnTest: Touching circles are solved by joining centres, and the distractors come from guessing the size from the picture or treating a slanted distance as straight.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these shapes can be turned through less than a full turn about its centre to land exactly on itself, but has no line of symmetry?

choices.text: A kite with sides 3 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm
choices.misconception: I mixed up the two kinds of symmetry: a kite has a mirror line but no turning symmetry, and I read it the wrong way round.

choices.text: An isosceles trapezium with parallel sides 3 cm and 5 cm
choices.misconception: I thought a half turn maps an isosceles trapezium onto itself because its two slanted sides are equal.

choices.text: A parallelogram with sides 3 cm and 5 cm and no right angle
A rectangle measuring 3 cm by 5 cm
choices.misconception: I checked that a half turn works and stopped, without checking for mirror lines, which a rectangle has.

choices.text: An equilateral triangle with sides of 5 cm
choices.misconception: I knew a third of a turn maps it onto itself and assumed a shape with turning symmetry cannot also have mirror lines.

hints: Check each shape twice: once for turning, once for folding.
A shape needs to pass the turning test and fail every folding test. Turning symmetry comes from a centre point; line symmetry means folding along a line makes the halves match exactly.
A half turn about the centre maps a parallelogram onto itself, but folding along either diagonal or across the middle never matches its slanted corners.

solutions.reliable: The rectangle and the equilateral triangle have turning symmetry but also mirror lines. The kite and the isosceles trapezium have a mirror line but no turning symmetry. The parallelogram with unequal sides and no right angles is mapped onto itself by a half turn about the point where its diagonals cross, yet no fold matches it: folding along a diagonal fails because the sides are unequal, and folding across the middle fails because the angles are not right angles. The transferable idea: line symmetry and turning symmetry are independent, so test for each one separately.

problems.whyOnTest: Line and rotational symmetry are tested separately at this level, and the parallelogram is the standard shape that has one without the other.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The point P(4, negative 2) is reflected in the y-axis. Its image is then reflected in the line y = x. What are the coordinates of the final point?

choices.misconception: I did the reflection in the y-axis and forgot to do the second reflection.
I skipped the reflection in the y-axis and only reflected in the line y = x.
I did the two reflections in the opposite order, y = x first and then the y-axis.
I thought reflecting in the y-axis changes the sign of both coordinates, which is really a half turn, and then swapped them.

hints: Do the two reflections one at a time, in order.
Know the rule for each mirror: reflecting in the y-axis changes the sign of the first coordinate only, and reflecting in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates.
The first reflection gives (negative 4, negative 2). Now swap the two coordinates.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting (4, negative 2) in the y-axis keeps the second coordinate and changes the sign of the first, giving (negative 4, negative 2). Reflecting that in the line y = x swaps the coordinates, giving (negative 2, negative 4). The transferable idea: learn each reflection as a rule on coordinates, and apply a chain of transformations strictly in the order given, because order matters.

problems.whyOnTest: Combined transformations test both the coordinate rules and the order, and each distractor is one rule or one step done wrongly.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A net of a cube is made of 6 squares joined edge to edge and cut out as one piece. To fold it into a cube, edges of its outline are taped together in pairs, one piece of tape per pair. How many pieces of tape are needed?

choices.misconception: I counted all the edges of the cube, forgetting that some of them are folds that are already joined.
I counted the fold lines inside the net instead of the edges that must be taped.
I counted the edges on the outline of the net but forgot that each piece of tape joins two of them.
I thought one piece of tape is needed for each face of the cube.

hints: Every edge of the finished cube is either a fold or a taped seam.
Count the fold lines in any net: six squares held together in one piece need a certain number of shared edges. Then compare with the number of edges a cube has.
Six squares in one piece share exactly 5 edges, which become folds. A cube has 12 edges.

solutions.reliable: Count the outline: 6 squares have 6 x 4 = 24 sides. The 5 shared edges inside the net use up 10 of these sides, leaving 14 sides on the outline. Taping joins them in pairs, so 14 / 2 = 7 pieces of tape. The transferable idea: count the same thing two ways, edges of the net and edges of the solid, and the difference tells you what is missing.
solutions.elegant: A cube has 12 edges. Five of them are already folds in the net, so the other 12 - 5 = 7 must be taped, whichever of the cube's nets you use.

problems.whyOnTest: Nets questions are usually about which net folds; this one checks that you see a net as a cube with some edges cut.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When the whole number N is divided by 7, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when N x N is divided by 7?

choices.misconception: I doubled the remainder instead of squaring it, and 8 leaves remainder 1.
I thought the remainder stays the same when the number is multiplied by itself.
I squared the remainder but forgot to divide 16 by 7 again.
I found that 16 is 2 more than 14, then gave 7 - 2, the distance up to the next multiple of 7.

hints: Try a real number that leaves remainder 4, such as 11.
Write N as a multiple of 7 plus 4. Squaring it, every part containing the multiple of 7 stays a multiple of 7, so only 4 x 4 matters, and that must be reduced again.
4 x 4 is 16, which is not yet a remainder on division by 7.

solutions.reliable: Write N = 7k + 4. Then N x N = 49k x k + 56k + 16. The first two parts are multiples of 7, and 16 = 14 + 2, so N x N leaves remainder 2. Check with N = 11: 11 x 11 = 121 = 119 + 2, and 119 = 7 x 17. The transferable idea: remainders multiply, but the product must be reduced again before it is a remainder.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainder arithmetic is a core 7-8 idea, and the classic slip is forgetting to reduce after multiplying.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers have a middle digit larger than both their first digit and their last digit? For example, 362 counts but 326 does not.

choices.misconception: I did not allow the last digit to be 0, so I used the same choices for the last digit as for the first.
I let the first digit be 0, which does not give a three-digit number.
I found 240 and then halved it, thinking each number had been counted twice.
I allowed the first and last digits to equal the middle digit instead of being smaller.

hints: Fix the middle digit first.
Use casework on the middle digit. For each possible middle digit, count the choices for the first digit and the last digit separately, remembering the first digit cannot be 0 but the last can.
With middle digit m, the first digit has m - 1 choices and the last digit has m choices. Add m(m - 1) for m = 2 to 9.
