solutions.reliable: Let the middle digit be m. The first digit must be from 1 to m - 1, giving m - 1 choices, and the last digit from 0 to m - 1, giving m choices. Adding m(m - 1) for m = 2, 3, ..., 9 gives 2 + 6 + 12 + 20 + 30 + 42 + 56 + 72 = 240. The transferable idea: in digit problems, fix the digit with the most constraints first, then count the others for each case.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit-constraint counting rewards fixing the most constrained digit, and the traps are the first-digit zero rule and strict versus non-strict inequality.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a jar of marbles, two fifths of the marbles are red. Then 12 red marbles are taken out and nothing else changes. Now one quarter of the marbles in the jar are red. How many marbles were in the jar at the start?

choices.misconception: I solved correctly but gave the number of marbles left in the jar after the 12 were taken out.
I solved correctly but gave the number of red marbles at the start instead of all the marbles.
I got as far as three fifths of the starting number being 36 and gave 36 without finishing.
I took the quarter as a quarter of the starting number, not of the marbles left after 12 were taken out.

hints: Which marbles are not touched at all?
The marbles that are not red never change. Write what fraction of the jar they are before and after, and compare the two totals.
The other marbles are three fifths of the start and three quarters of what is left.

solutions.reliable: Let the jar start with T marbles, so 2T/5 are red. After 12 red ones go, there are T - 12 marbles and 2T/5 - 12 of them are red, which must be a quarter: 2T/5 - 12 = (T - 12)/4. Multiplying by 20 gives 8T - 240 = 5T - 60, so 3T = 180 and T = 60. Check: 24 of 60 are red; after removing 12, 12 of the 48 left are red, which is one quarter. The transferable idea: a fraction is always a fraction of something, so write down which total each fraction refers to.
solutions.elegant: The non-red marbles do not change. They are three fifths of the start and three quarters of the end, so the start and end totals are in the ratio 5 to 4. The 12 marbles removed are therefore one fifth of the start, which is 60.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of a changing total are a standard trap, because students take every fraction of the starting amount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pack of 480 sheets of paper is 5.1 cm thick. Which of these is closest to the height of a pile of one million of these sheets?

choices.misconception: I divided a million by about 500 and got 200 packs instead of 2,000.
I found that about 2,000 packs are needed but forgot to multiply by the 5 cm thickness of each pack, so I took the pile to be 2,000 cm.
I changed about 10,000 cm into metres by dividing by 10 instead of by 100.
I multiplied a million by 5.1 cm, as if each single sheet were 5.1 cm thick.

hints: Round 480 and 5.1 to easy numbers.
Estimate to the nearest choice: treat a pack as 500 sheets and 5 cm thick, find how many packs make a million sheets, then convert the height into metres.
A million sheets is about 2,000 packs of 500, and each pack is about 5 cm.

solutions.reliable: Round a pack to 500 sheets and 5 cm. A million sheets is 1,000,000 / 500 = 2,000 packs, so the pile is about 2,000 x 5 = 10,000 cm, which is 100 m. The exact height is about 106 m, so 100 m is clearly the closest choice. The transferable idea: when the choices differ by factors of 10, round hard, and then track the zeros and the units carefully.

problems.whyOnTest: Order-of-magnitude choices test estimation, and the slips happen when counting zeros and converting units.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four villages A, B, C and D lie along one straight road. B is 5 km from A, C is 3 km from B, D is 7 km from C, and D is 9 km from A. How far is C from A, in km?

choices.misconception: I put the villages in the order A, B, C and added 5 + 3, without checking that D can then be 9 km from A.
I put C 7 km beyond D, so 9 + 7, and did not check whether B could then be 5 km from A and 3 km from C.
I found the right order but gave the distance from B to C instead of from A to C.
I found the two places 7 km from D, at 2 km and at 16 km from A, and did not use the clues about B to rule one of them out.

hints: Draw the road as a line and put A at 0.
Place the villages using the clues one at a time. Fix A and D first, since their distance is given, then find the possible places for C, and test each against the clues about B.
With A at 0 and D at 9, C is at 2 or at 16. Only one of these is 3 km from a point 5 km from A.

solutions.reliable: Put A at 0 on the road and D at 9. C is 7 km from D, so C is at 2 or at 16. B is 5 km from A, so B is at 5 or at negative 5. B must also be 3 km from C: the point 5 is 3 km from 2, while neither 5 nor negative 5 is 3 km from 16. So C is at 2, and the order along the road is A, C, B, D. C is 2 km from A. The transferable idea: place the most definite clues first, list the few possible positions, and test each one against every remaining clue.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering from clues rewards drawing the line and testing every case, and the wrong choices come from assuming the order the letters are listed in.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At each of three shops, Lina spends half of the money she has and then 2 euros more. After the third shop she has 1 euro left. How many euros did she have before the first shop?

choices.misconception: I worked backwards through only two of the three shops.
I worked backwards through only the last shop.
I undid each shop by doubling first and then adding 2, which undoes the steps in the wrong order.
I ignored the extra 2 euros and just doubled three times.

hints: Start from the 1 euro at the end.
Work backwards. At each shop she halved her money and then subtracted 2, so undo the last operation first: add 2, then double. Repeat for each shop in reverse order.
Before the third shop she had (1 + 2) x 2 = 6 euros. Repeat this step twice more.

solutions.reliable: Undo each shop by adding 2 and then doubling. Before the third shop: (1 + 2) x 2 = 6. Before the second: (6 + 2) x 2 = 16. Before the first: (16 + 2) x 2 = 36. Check forwards: 36 becomes 18 - 2 = 16, then 8 - 2 = 6, then 3 - 2 = 1. The transferable idea: to work backwards, reverse both the operations and their order.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards is the fastest route when the end state is known, and the trap is undoing the operations in the wrong order.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts with 3. Each term after the first is found by doubling the term before it and then subtracting 1, so the sequence begins 3, 5, 9, 17. What is the 20th term?

choices.misconception: I wrote the nth term as 2 to the power n - 1, plus 1, without checking it against the first term, so I got the 19th term.
I saw that the terms are close to powers of 2 and dropped the extra 1.
I applied the rule 20 times starting from 3, which gives the 21st term.
I thought the terms go up by 2 each time, as they do from 3 to 5, so I added 19 twos to 3.

hints: Subtract 1 from each term and look again.
Find a simpler sequence hiding inside: subtract 1 from every term, see what the rule does to those new numbers, then write the nth term directly instead of stepping 19 times.
Each term minus 1 gives 2, 4, 8, 16, so the nth term is 2 to the power n, plus 1.

solutions.reliable: Subtract 1 from each term: 3, 5, 9, 17 become 2, 4, 8, 16. If a term is t, the next is 2t - 1, and 2t - 1 - 1 = 2(t - 1), so the numbers one less than the terms double every step. They start at 2, so the nth of them is 2 to the power n, and the nth term is 2 to the power n, plus 1. Check: the 1st term is 2 + 1 = 3. Since 2 to the power 10 is 1,024, 2 to the power 20 is 1,024 x 1,024 = 1,048,576, so the 20th term is 1,048,577. The transferable idea: shift a recursive sequence by a constant to turn it into one you recognise.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules are slow to step through by hand, and spotting the hidden doubling gives any term at once, while off-by-one slips give the neighbouring terms.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The whole numbers 1, 2, 3, ... are written in rows. Row 1 holds 1 number, row 2 holds the next 2 numbers, row 3 holds the next 3 numbers, and so on. What is the first number in row 20?

choices.misconception: I added up the lengths of rows 1 to 19 but forgot to add 1, so I gave the last number of row 19.
I added up the lengths of rows 1 to 20, which gives the last number of row 20.
I added up the lengths of rows 1 to 20 and then added 1, which is the start of row 21.
I added the row lengths 1 to 19 as 19 x 20 without halving, and then added 1.

hints: What is the last number in each row?
The last number in a row equals how many numbers have been written so far. Use the formula for the sum of the first few whole numbers, then step to the next number.
Rows 1 to 19 hold 1 + 2 + ... + 19 = 19 x 20 / 2 numbers.

solutions.reliable: The last number in row n is 1 + 2 + ... + n, because that is how many numbers have been written. Rows 1 to 19 hold 19 x 20 / 2 = 190 numbers, so row 19 ends with 190 and row 20 starts with 191. Check on a small case: row 3 should start just after 1 + 2 = 3, at 4, which matches 1 / 2 3 / 4 5 6. The transferable idea: in a triangular table, the ends of the rows are the triangular numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Triangular arrangements are common, and every wrong choice is an off-by-one between the end of one row and the start of the next.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five years ago, Tom was 3 times as old as his sister. In five years' time, he will be twice as old as she will be then. How old is Tom now?

choices.misconception: I added 5 years to Tom's age in the future clue but forgot to add them to his sister's age.
I solved correctly but gave Tom's age five years ago.
I solved correctly but gave Tom's age in five years' time.
I solved correctly but gave his sister's age instead of Tom's.

hints: Both people's ages change by the same number of years.
Translate into equations: call the ages now t and s, write each clue using t - 5 and s - 5 for the past and t + 5 and s + 5 for the future, then solve together.
t - 5 = 3(s - 5) and t + 5 = 2(s + 5). Write t from each and set them equal.

solutions.reliable: Let Tom be t and his sister s now. Five years ago: t - 5 = 3(s - 5), so t = 3s - 10. In five years: t + 5 = 2(s + 5), so t = 2s + 5. Then 3s - 10 = 2s + 5, so s = 15 and t = 35. Check: five years ago they were 30 and 10, and 30 is 3 times 10; in five years they will be 40 and 20, and 40 is twice 20. The transferable idea: shift every person's age by the same number of years, then reread the question to see whose age, and when.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve from the choices: if Tom is 35, five years ago he was 30, so his sister was 10 and is now 15. In five years they will be 40 and 20, which works.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems test setting up equations at different times, and most wrong choices answer for the wrong person or the wrong year.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A fish tank is 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm tall. It is filled to the top using a jug that holds 2 litres. How many full jugs of water are needed?

choices.misconception: I found the tank holds 60 litres and forgot that each jug holds 2 litres.
I thought 1 litre is 100 cubic centimetres, so I found 600 litres and divided by 2.
I thought 1 litre is 1 cubic centimetre, so I divided 60,000 by 2.
I found the tank holds 60 litres and multiplied by 2 instead of dividing.

hints: How many cubic centimetres make one litre?
Find the volume of the tank in cubic centimetres, convert it to litres using 1 litre = 1,000 cubic centimetres, then share it out into 2-litre jugs.
The tank holds 50 x 30 x 40 = 60,000 cubic centimetres.

solutions.reliable: The tank holds 50 x 30 x 40 = 60,000 cubic centimetres. One litre is 1,000 cubic centimetres, so that is 60 litres. Each jug holds 2 litres, so 60 / 2 = 30 jugs are needed. The transferable idea: get every quantity into the same unit before dividing, and know that a litre is the volume of a 10 cm cube.
solutions.elegant: A 2-litre jug is 2,000 cubic centimetres, and 60,000 / 2,000 = 30.

problems.whyOnTest: Volume conversion is where students slip, because a litre is 1,000 cubic centimetres, not 100 and not 1.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five different positive whole numbers have an average of 9. What is the largest possible value of the second-largest of them?

choices.misconception: I found the best set, 1, 2, 3, 19 and 20, but gave the largest number instead of the second-largest.
I made the largest number as big as possible, 45 - 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 = 35, instead of the second-largest.
I forgot that the numbers must be different, used 1, 1 and 1, and split the remaining 42 equally into 21 and 21.
I gave the average instead of the largest possible value of the second-largest number.

hints: The five numbers add up to 5 x 9.
Use the extremal principle: make the three smallest numbers as small as the rules allow, then share what is left between the two largest so the smaller of them is as big as possible.
The three smallest are 1, 2 and 3, leaving 39 for the two largest, which must be different.

solutions.reliable: An average of 9 for five numbers means they add up to 45. To make the second-largest big, the three smallest should be as small as possible: different positive whole numbers, so at least 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. That leaves 39 for the two largest. The largest must be bigger than the second-largest, so the second-largest is less than half of 39, at most 19. The set 1, 2, 3, 19, 20 shows that 19 works. The transferable idea: push everything you are not maximising to its limit, then check that the extreme case really exists.

problems.whyOnTest: Extremal questions reward pushing everything else to its limit, and the distractors come from ignoring a word like different or answering for the wrong number.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Eleven cups stand upside down on a table. In one move you must turn over exactly three cups, any three you choose. What is the smallest number of moves needed to get all eleven cups the right way up?

choices.misconception: I divided 11 by 3 and rounded up, without checking that 4 moves make 12 turns, an even number, while eleven cups that each need an odd number of turns need an odd total.
I thought each cup needs its own move.
I divided 11 by 3 and rounded down, but 3 moves turn over only 9 cups.
I thought that since 11 is not a multiple of 3 the cups can never all end up the right way, forgetting that a cup can be turned more than once.

hints: How many times must each single cup be turned over?
Look at something that changes in a fixed way: each cup must be turned an odd number of times, so think about whether the total number of turns is odd or even, and compare with 3 turns per move.
Eleven odd numbers add up to an odd total, so the number of moves must be odd and at least 4.

solutions.reliable: Each cup starts upside down, so it must be turned over an odd number of times. Eleven odd numbers add up to an odd number, so the total number of turns is odd. Each move makes 3 turns, so after m moves there have been 3m turns, and 3m is odd only when m is odd. Also 3m must be at least 11, so m is at least 4. The smallest odd number that is at least 4 is 5. Five moves do work: turn cups 1, 2, 3, then 4, 5, 6, then 7, 8, 9, then 10, 1, 2, and finally 11, 1, 2. The transferable idea: when a process allows many choices, track a quantity whose parity changes in a fixed way, then show the bound can be reached.
solutions.elegant: Count the cups that are upside down. Each move changes that count by 1 or 3, an odd amount, so its parity switches every move. It starts at 11, which is odd, and must reach 0, which is even, so the number of moves is odd. Four is too few to reach every cup, so the answer is 5.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity invariants show that tempting answers like 4 are impossible, and the test is whether you prove the bound and also show it can be reached.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A very large floor is tiled with regular hexagons and equilateral triangles, all with the same side length. Every side of every hexagon is shared with a triangle, and every side of every triangle is shared with a hexagon. Ignoring the edges of the floor, how many triangles are there for each hexagon?

choices.misconception: I saw that two triangles and two hexagons meet at every corner, so I thought there must be equally many of each shape.
I counted the 6 triangles around each hexagon but forgot that each triangle also touches 3 hexagons, so every triangle was counted 3 times.
I counted the 3 hexagons around each triangle and gave that as the number of triangles for each hexagon.
I counted the sides correctly but turned the ratio upside down, giving hexagons for each triangle.

hints: Count the sides where a hexagon meets a triangle.
Overcount, then correct: count the shared sides once from the hexagons and once from the triangles. Both counts describe the same sides, so set them equal.
Each hexagon has 6 shared sides and each triangle has 3, and every shared side belongs to exactly one of each.

solutions.reliable: Every side on the floor is shared by one hexagon and one triangle. Counting these sides from the hexagons gives 6 for each hexagon, and counting them from the triangles gives 3 for each triangle. Both counts describe the same sides, so 6 x (number of hexagons) = 3 x (number of triangles), and there are 2 triangles for each hexagon. The transferable idea: count the same things from two sides and set the counts equal.
solutions.elegant: Count corners instead. Each hexagon has 6 corners and each corner is shared by 2 hexagons, so there are 3 corners for each hexagon. Each triangle has 3 corners, each shared by 2 triangles, so there are 1.5 corners for each triangle. Hence triangles are twice as many as hexagons.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions often hide a double count, and the tempting wrong answers count each shared tile more than once or read the ratio backwards.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square is cut by its two diagonals and by the two lines that join the midpoints of opposite sides, making 8 small triangles. How many triangles of any size can be found in the figure, with all three sides along the drawn lines?

choices.misconception: I counted only the eight smallest triangles.
I counted the 8 small triangles and the 4 halves of the square, but missed the 4 triangles made of two small ones that meet at the centre.
I counted the small triangles and the ones made of two small triangles, but for the halves of the square I used only one diagonal and found 2 instead of 4.
I counted every set of three of the nine points where lines meet, as long as they were not in a line, even when the sides are not drawn.

hints: Sort the triangles by how many small triangles they contain.
Count systematically by size: a triangle in this figure is made of 1, 2 or 4 small triangles. Count each size separately, checking that every side lies on a drawn line.
There are 8 triangles of 1 piece, 4 of 2 pieces meeting at the centre, and the halves of the square cut off by each diagonal.

solutions.reliable: Every triangle here is made of 1, 2 or 4 of the small triangles. One piece: the 8 small triangles. Two pieces: the two small triangles on either side of a line from the centre to the midpoint of a side together form a triangle, with one whole side of the square as its base and the centre as its top, and there are 4 of these. Two small triangles that meet along part of a diagonal make a small square instead. Four pieces: each diagonal cuts the square into 2 halves, giving 4 such triangles. No other group of pieces is a triangle. The total is 8 + 4 + 4 = 16. The transferable idea: count hidden shapes by size, so that no size is missed and none is counted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Hidden-triangle counts reward sorting by size, and the wrong choices come from missing one size or counting shapes whose sides are not drawn.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two standard dice are stacked on a table, one on top of the other. On each die, opposite faces add up to 7. A face is hidden if it touches the table or the other die, and every other face can be seen. What is the largest possible total number of dots on the visible faces?

choices.misconception: I treated both dice as hiding a full opposite pair worth 7, but the upper die hides only its bottom face.
I took off the 7 hidden on the lower die but forgot that the bottom face of the upper die is hidden too.
I thought each die hides just one face and put the 1 face down on both dice, taking off only 2.
I took off only the face touching the table and forgot the two faces where the dice touch each other.

hints: Work out which faces are hidden, one die at a time.
The lower die hides its top and its bottom, which are opposite faces, so its hidden total is fixed. Only the hidden face of the upper die can be chosen, so make it as small as possible.
Each die has 21 dots. The lower die hides exactly 7 dots and the upper die hides at least 1 dot.

solutions.reliable: Each die has 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21 dots, so 42 in all. The lower die hides its top and bottom faces, which are opposite, so it always hides exactly 7. The upper die hides only its bottom face, which can be the 1. The largest visible total is 42 - 7 - 1 = 34. The transferable idea: a hidden pair of opposite faces always costs exactly 7, so only the unpaired hidden faces can be chosen.
solutions.elegant: The lower die shows its four side faces, which are two opposite pairs, so 14 dots. The upper die shows everything except its bottom, at most 21 - 1 = 20. Together that is 34.

problems.whyOnTest: Dice questions reward knowing that opposite faces sum to 7, which turns a hidden pair into a fixed amount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid is made of stacks of identical cubes on a 3-by-3 square base. From the front, the three columns, left to right, look 2, 3 and 1 cubes tall. From the right side, the three rows, front to back, look 3, 1 and 2 cubes tall. What is the greatest number of cubes the solid can contain?

choices.misconception: I found the smallest number of cubes that gives these two views, not the greatest.
I added the 6 cubes I can see from the front to the 6 cubes I can see from the side.
I made each stack as tall as the larger of its two view heights instead of the smaller one.
I made every one of the nine stacks 3 cubes tall, the tallest height in either view.

hints: Each stack is limited by two views at once.
Each stack is capped by the front-view height of its column and the side-view height of its row. For the most cubes, build every stack to the smaller of its two caps, then check both views.
Front row (limit 3): heights 2, 3, 1. Middle row (limit 1): 1, 1, 1. Back row (limit 2): 2, 2, 1.

solutions.reliable: Give each stack its column (front view) and its row (side view). Its height can be at most the smaller of the two view values. Front row, limit 3: heights 2, 3, 1, total 6. Middle row, limit 1: 1, 1, 1, total 3. Back row, limit 2: 2, 2, 1, total 5. Every column and every row still reaches its stated height, so both views are right, and the greatest total is 6 + 3 + 5 = 14. The transferable idea: two views only cap each stack at the smaller of its two readings, and filling every stack up to its cap gives the maximum.

problems.whyOnTest: Views questions test whether you see that each view only caps a stack, so the most and the fewest cubes are different questions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A wooden block measuring 3 by 4 by 5 is painted on all of its outside faces and then cut into 60 unit cubes. How many of the unit cubes have paint on exactly two of their faces?

choices.misconception: I counted the corner cubes, but those have paint on three faces, not two.
I counted the cubes with exactly one painted face, the ones in the middle of each face of the block.
I removed only one corner cube from each edge instead of the cubes at both ends.
I counted every cube along the 12 edges, corners included, as 4 x (3 + 4 + 5).

hints: Paint on exactly two faces means the cube sits on an edge of the block.
Cubes with exactly two painted faces lie along the 12 edges of the block, but not at the corners, where cubes have three painted faces. Count each edge's cubes without its two ends.
There are four edges each of length 3, 4 and 5, giving 1, 2 and 3 cubes each once the corners are left out.

solutions.reliable: The block has 12 edges: four of length 3, four of length 4 and four of length 5. On each edge the two end cubes are corners with three painted faces, so an edge of length L gives L - 2 cubes with exactly two painted faces. That is 4 x (1 + 2 + 3) = 24. The transferable idea: in a painted block, corner cubes have three painted faces, other edge cubes two, other face cubes one, and the hidden core none.

problems.whyOnTest: Painted-cube questions check that you can sort small cubes by where they sit: corner, edge, face or hidden centre.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At one point of a floor, a square and two copies of the same regular polygon fit together exactly, with no gaps and no overlaps. How many sides does that polygon have?

choices.misconception: I found the outside angle of 45 degrees correctly but divided 180 by 45 instead of 360 by 45.
I thought the three tiles must share the 360 degrees equally, 120 each, and chose the hexagon, whose angles are 120 degrees.
I worked out the outside angle of the polygon, 45 degrees, and gave that instead of its number of sides.
I found the angle each polygon must fill at the point and gave that angle instead of the number of sides.

hints: The angles meeting at the point must add up to 360 degrees.
Take the square's angle away from 360 and share what is left equally between the two matching polygons. Then turn that angle into a number of sides through the outside angle.
360 - 90 = 270, so each polygon has angles of 270 / 2 = 135 degrees, and outside angles of 180 - 135 = 45 degrees.

solutions.reliable: The square fills 90 degrees, leaving 360 - 90 = 270 degrees for the two matching polygons, so each has angles of 135 degrees. The outside angle is then 180 - 135 = 45 degrees, and the outside angles of any polygon add up to 360, so it has 360 / 45 = 8 sides. The transferable idea: to find a regular polygon from its angle, go through the outside angle, which must divide 360 exactly.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions check that the angles around a point total 360 and that a regular polygon is found fastest from its outside angle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A long strip of paper is folded in half, then in half again, then in half a third time, each fold bringing the two ends together. One straight cut is then made across the middle of the folded strip, at right angles to its length, through all the layers. Into how many pieces does the paper fall?

choices.misconception: I thought one straight cut always makes two pieces, however many layers it passes through.
I thought each fold adds just one extra piece, so one cut and three folds give 1 + 3 = 4.
I counted the 8 layers the scissors pass through and took each layer as one piece.
I thought each of the 8 layers is cut into two separate pieces, giving 8 x 2.

hints: Count how many cuts the unfolded strip actually receives.
Three folds stack 8 layers, so the single cut slices the long strip at 8 different places. A strip cut at several places falls into one more piece than there are cuts, just like a ribbon.
Unfolded, the strip has 8 separate cuts along its length.

solutions.reliable: Folding in half three times stacks 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 layers. The cut goes through every layer, so the unfolded strip is cut at 8 different places along its length. A strip cut at 8 places falls into 8 + 1 = 9 pieces; most of them are folded loops that stay in one piece because they are joined at a fold. The transferable idea: unfold in your head and count the cuts on the flat strip, then pieces = cuts + 1.
solutions.elegant: Try small cases. One fold: 2 layers, 2 cuts, 3 pieces. Two folds: 4 cuts, 5 pieces. The pieces are always the layers plus 1, so three folds give 8 + 1 = 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding-and-cutting questions reward unfolding in your head and counting cuts on the flat strip, not layers in the stack.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A post is a cylinder 7 dm tall, and the distance around it is 12 dm. A string starts at a point on the bottom edge, winds exactly twice around the post, and ends at the point on the top edge directly above its start. What is the shortest possible length of the string, in dm?

choices.misconception: I took the string once around the bottom, 12 dm, and then straight up 7 dm, as if it wound only once.
I counted only the two trips around the post, 2 x 12, and forgot that the string also has to climb 7 dm.
I took the string twice around the bottom and then straight up, 24 + 7, instead of along a slant.
I unrolled the two turns into a 24 by 7 rectangle and got 25, then doubled it again for the two turns.

hints: Imagine cutting the post open and laying its surface flat.

Unrolling the curved surface gives a flat rectangle. Going twice around becomes a horizontal distance of two times around the post, and the shortest string becomes a straight line across that rectangle.
The flattened string is the diagonal of a rectangle 24 dm wide and 7 dm tall.

solutions.reliable: Cut the post along the vertical line through the start and unroll it twice, side by side. The surface becomes a rectangle 2 x 12 = 24 dm wide and 7 dm tall, and the shortest string is its diagonal. By Pythagoras, 24 x 24 + 7 x 7 = 576 + 49 = 625, so the string is 25 dm long. The transferable idea: a shortest path on a curved or folded surface becomes a straight line once the surface is flattened.

problems.whyOnTest: Shortest-path questions test whether you flatten the surface so the route becomes a straight line and Pythagoras applies.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sign on a shelf says: 'Every box on this shelf contains a red pen.' The sign turns out to be false. Which of these statements must be true?

choices.text: At least one box on the shelf contains no red pen.
No box on the shelf contains a red pen.
choices.misconception: I thought the opposite of 'every box has one' is 'no box has one', but the sign is already false if a single box is missing a red pen.

choices.text: Exactly one box on the shelf contains no red pen.
choices.misconception: I pictured the smallest way the sign could fail and assumed it was the only way, but several boxes could be missing a red pen.

choices.text: Every box on the shelf contains a pen of another colour.
choices.misconception: I read 'no red pen' as 'a pen of a different colour', but a box could hold no pen at all.

choices.text: At least one box on the shelf contains a red pen.
choices.misconception: I assumed that if not every box has a red pen then some box still does, but the sign is also false when no box has one.

hints: What is the least that has to happen for the sign to be false?
A claim about every box fails as soon as one single box breaks it. For each option, ask whether it holds in every situation where the sign is false, or only in some of them.
The sign is false whenever one or more boxes have no red pen, and nothing else is known.

solutions.reliable: 'Every box contains a red pen' is false exactly when at least one box contains no red pen, so the first statement must be true. 'No box', 'exactly one box' and 'at least one box has a red pen' each describe only some of the ways the sign can fail: perhaps one box lacks a red pen, perhaps all of them do. 'A pen of another colour' adds something never said, since a box could be empty. The transferable idea: the opposite of 'every one does' is 'at least one does not', not 'none does'.

problems.whyOnTest: Logic questions often hinge on denying 'every' correctly, and the trap is swinging all the way to 'none'.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Fern, Gus, Hana and Ivo each do a different one of these sports: chess, judo, rowing and tennis. Hana plays chess. Gus walks to training with the rower and the judo player. Fern does not play tennis. Ivo does not row. Who does judo, and who rows?

choices.misconception: I used Gus's clue to rule out only rowing for him, not judo, so I gave Gus the judo and Ivo the tennis.
I read 'Gus walks to training with the rower' as saying Gus is the rower, and then Fern was left with judo.
I read the clue 'Ivo does not row' the wrong way round, as 'Ivo rows', which left judo for Fern.

choices.text: It cannot be decided from the clues.
choices.misconception: I stopped when each clue ruled out only some sports and decided there was not enough information, without combining the clues.

hints: Find the person who has only one sport left.

Draw a grid of people against sports and cross out every pairing a clue forbids. Someone who walks with the rower and the judo player is neither of them. When a person has one sport left, it is theirs.
Hana plays chess, and Gus does neither rowing nor judo, so Gus plays tennis.

solutions.reliable: Hana plays chess. Gus walks with the rower and the judo player, so he is neither of them, and chess is taken, so Gus plays tennis. That leaves judo and rowing for Fern and Ivo. Ivo does not row, so Ivo does judo and Fern rows. The clue that Fern does not play tennis agrees. The transferable idea: in an elimination grid, look for a row or column with only one option left, fill it in, and repeat.

problems.whyOnTest: Elimination grids test combining clues: each clue alone settles little, but crossing them off together forces every answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five friends, Pia, Quin, Rosa, Sam and Tom, all have different heights. Pia is taller than Quin but shorter than Rosa. Sam is shorter than Quin. Tom is taller than Pia, but he is not the tallest of the five. Who is the second tallest?

choices.misconception: I put Pia straight below Rosa because the first clue names them together, and forgot that Tom must also fit in above Pia.
I counted second from the shortest end instead of second from the tallest.
I ignored the clue that Tom is not the tallest, put Tom first and so had Rosa second.

choices.text: It cannot be decided from the clues.
choices.misconception: I saw that no clue compares Tom with Rosa directly, so I thought either could be taller, and missed that 'not the tallest' settles it.

hints: Who can possibly be the tallest?
Turn each clue into a chain of 'taller than' links. Then rule people out of the top place one by one: anyone with someone taller than them cannot be the tallest.
Pia, Quin and Sam each have someone taller than them, and Tom is not the tallest, so Rosa is the tallest.

solutions.reliable: The clues give Rosa above Pia, Pia above Quin and Quin above Sam. Pia, Quin and Sam each have someone taller, and Tom is not the tallest, so Rosa is the tallest. Tom is taller than Pia, so Tom is above Pia but below Rosa. The full order, tallest first, is Rosa, Tom, Pia, Quin, Sam, so Tom is second tallest. The transferable idea: in ordering puzzles, settle an extreme place first by ruling out everyone who cannot be there.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering questions reward finding the one forced position first, usually an end of the line, then letting the rest fall into place.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The nine numbers 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ..., 1/9 are written on a board. In one move you erase any two numbers a and b and write the single number a + b + ab in their place. After eight moves only one number is left. What is it?

choices.misconception: I found that the product of all the (1 + number) values is 10, then subtracted 1 for every one of the nine numbers instead of once.
I cancelled the product of the (1 + number) values down to 9 instead of 10, then subtracted 1.
I multiplied all the (1 + number) values correctly but forgot to subtract 1 at the end.
I found the product of all the (1 + number) values was 10 and then added 1 instead of subtracting it.

hints: Try adding 1 to the new number a + b + ab.
Since a + b + ab + 1 = (a + 1)(b + 1), adding 1 to every number turns each move into multiplying two of them. The product of all the (number + 1) values never changes.

solutions.reliable: Because a + b + ab + 1 = (a + 1)(b + 1), the product of (x + 1) over all the numbers x on the board is the same after every move. At the start it is 2/1 x 3/2 x 4/3 x ... x 10/9, and everything cancels except 10/1 = 10. At the end there is one number N with N + 1 = 10, so N = 9. The transferable idea: when a repeated operation looks messy, look for a quantity it never changes, then compare the start with the end.
solutions.elegant: Combine in order. 1 and 1/2 give 1 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 2. Then 2 and 1/3 give 2 + 1/3 + 2/3 = 3. Each time, n and 1/(n + 1) give n + 1, so the last number is 9. The invariant shows that any other order gives 9 too.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariant questions describe a process too long to simulate and test whether you can find the quantity that never changes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 3 to the power 51, the product of 51 threes, is divided by 7?

choices.misconception: I divided the power 51 by 7 and gave that remainder, 2, instead of working with 3 to the power 51.
I found that 51 is 3 more than a multiple of 6 and gave the position 3 instead of the remainder at that position.
I counted one step too far along the cycle 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 and landed on 4.
I worked out the last digit of 3 to the power 51, which is 7, instead of the remainder on dividing by 7.

hints: Find the remainders of 3, 9, 27, ... when they are divided by 7.

Each remainder comes from the one before by multiplying by 3 and taking the remainder again, so the remainders must repeat in a cycle. Find the length of the cycle and where the 51st power falls in it.
The remainders go 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 and then repeat, a cycle of length 6.

solutions.reliable: Multiply by 3 and take the remainder on division by 7 each time: 3, then 9 gives 2, then 6, then 18 gives 4, then 12 gives 5, then 15 gives 1. After that the cycle 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 repeats every 6 powers. Since 51 = 6 x 8 + 3, the 51st power has the same remainder as the 3rd power, which is 6. The transferable idea: remainders of powers always cycle, so find the cycle and reduce the power by its length.
solutions.elegant: 3 to the power 3 is 27, which is one less than 28, a multiple of 7. So each block of three 3s leaves remainder 6, which behaves like -1. The 51 threes make 17 such blocks, and 17 copies of -1 multiply to -1, so the remainder is 7 - 1 = 6.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders of big powers test spotting a repeating cycle, and the traps give the cycle position or mix it up with the last digit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A snail crawls 3 millimetres every second. Moving at this steady speed, how many metres does it travel in one hour?

choices.misconception: I multiplied by 60 only, which turns seconds into minutes, so I found the distance for one minute.
I used 360 seconds in an hour instead of 3600.
I divided 10800 millimetres by 100, thinking a metre is 100 millimetres.
I found the distance in millimetres and forgot to change it into metres.

hints: Find the distance in millimetres first, then convert.
An hour is 60 minutes of 60 seconds each. Multiply to get the millimetres travelled in an hour, then remember how many millimetres make one metre.
3 x 3600 = 10800 millimetres, and a metre is 1000 millimetres.

solutions.reliable: One hour is 60 x 60 = 3600 seconds, so the snail crawls 3 x 3600 = 10800 millimetres. A metre is 1000 millimetres, so that is 10800 / 1000 = 10.8 metres. The transferable idea: convert in small named steps and write the unit at every step, because each slip changes the answer by a power of ten.

problems.whyOnTest: Unit conversion questions check that time and length are converted with the right factors, and every slip gives one of the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the number 5,384,926, the value of the digit 8 is how many times the value of the digit 2?

choices.misconception: I compared the digits 8 and 2 themselves and ignored the places they stand in.
I counted the 8 as only two places to the left of the 2, so I used 100 instead of 1000 for the places.
I compared the places correctly but forgot that 8 is itself 4 times 2.
I counted the 8 as four places to the left of the 2, one place too many, so I used 10000 for the places.

hints: Write down what each of the two digits is actually worth.
A digit's value depends on its place. Find the place of the 8 and the place of the 2 by counting from the right, write both values in full, then divide.
The 8 is in the ten-thousands place and the 2 is in the tens place.

solutions.reliable: Counting from the right, 5,384,926 has 6 ones, 2 tens, 9 hundreds, 4 thousands and 8 ten-thousands. So the 8 is worth 80,000 and the 2 is worth 20. Then 80,000 / 20 = 4000. The transferable idea: each step one place to the left multiplies a digit's value by 10, so compare both the digits and the number of places between them.
solutions.elegant: The 8 stands three places to the left of the 2, which multiplies by 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000, and the digit 8 is 4 times the digit 2, so the answer is 4 x 1000 = 4000.

problems.whyOnTest: Place-value questions check that a digit's value depends on its position, and the traps miscount the places or compare only the digits.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Nadia's father was 30 years old when she was born. Four years ago, he was 4 times as old as she was then. How old is her father now?

choices.misconception: I found Nadia's age four years ago and gave that instead of her father's age now.
I found Nadia's age now and gave that instead of her father's age.
I treated 'four years ago' as 'in four years', so I made Nadia 6 and her father 36 today.
I gave the father's age four years ago, which is the moment the 4 times clue describes, not his age now.

hints: The age gap between two people never changes.
The gap is always 30 years. When the father was 4 times as old as Nadia, the gap was 3 times her age at that moment. Find her age then, then move forward to today.
Four years ago Nadia was 30 / 3 = 10 years old.

solutions.reliable: Let Nadia have been n years old four years ago, so her father was 4n. The gap is 4n - n = 3n, and the gap is always 30, so n = 10. Four years ago they were 10 and 40, so today they are 14 and 44. Her father is 44. Check: 44 - 14 = 30, and 40 is 4 times 10. The transferable idea: the age gap is fixed, so use it to turn a 'times as old' fact into one equation, then answer for the person and the moment asked about.

problems.whyOnTest: Age questions reward using the fixed age gap, and the traps offer the other person's age or the right person at the wrong time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven whole numbers add up to 50. At most how many of them can be odd?

choices.misconception: I thought an even total means every one of the numbers has to be even.
I thought at most half of the seven numbers can be odd, and rounded down.
I thought the number of odd numbers has to be odd, so I took the largest odd count below 7.
I did not check the parity: seven odd numbers always add up to an odd total, never 50.

hints: What kind of total do you get from an odd number of odd numbers?
A sum of whole numbers is even exactly when it contains an even number of odd terms. So the count of odd numbers here must be even, and it cannot be more than 7.
The count of odd numbers must be even and at most 7. Test whether 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 and 44 works.

solutions.reliable: A sum is even only when it contains an even number of odd terms. Since 50 is even, the number of odd numbers is even, so 7 is impossible and the most is 6. Six odd numbers really do work: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 44 = 50. The transferable idea: parity often rules out the obvious answer, and then a single example shows the next one is possible.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity questions test that the number of odd terms decides whether a sum is odd or even.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In an orchard, three fifths of the trees are apple trees and the rest are pear trees. A storm damages one third of the apple trees and one half of the pear trees. What fraction of all the trees in the orchard is damaged?

choices.misconception: I multiplied one third by one half instead of taking each fraction of its own group of trees.
I took the average of one third and one half, as if there were as many apple trees as pear trees.
I worked out the damaged apple trees correctly but took half of the pear trees to be half of the whole orchard.
I added one third and one half as if both were fractions of the whole orchard.

hints: Each fraction is a fraction of a different group of trees.
Find what fraction of the whole orchard the pear trees are. Then work out the damaged apple trees and the damaged pear trees each as a fraction of the whole orchard, and add.
The pear trees are two fifths of the orchard. One third of three fifths is one fifth.

solutions.reliable: The pear trees are 1 - 3/5 = 2/5 of the orchard. Damaged apple trees: 1/3 of 3/5 = 1/5 of the orchard. Damaged pear trees: 1/2 of 2/5 = 1/5 of the orchard. Together 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5. The transferable idea: when fractions are taken of different groups, turn each into a fraction of the whole before adding.
solutions.elegant: Pretend there are 15 trees: 9 apple and 6 pear. The storm damages 3 apple trees and 3 pear trees, 6 in all, and 6 out of 15 is 2/5.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of different groups test whether you convert each to a fraction of the whole, and the classic slip adds or averages them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to 2 to the power 20, the product of twenty 2s?

choices.misconception: I multiplied 2 by 20 instead of multiplying twenty 2s together.
I worked out 20 x 20, swapping the 2 and the 20.
I doubled 2 to the power 10, about 1000, instead of multiplying it by itself.
I thought that ten more 2s multiply the answer by 10, so I took 1024 x 10.

hints: Start from a smaller power of 2 that is close to a round number.
Twenty 2s are two groups of ten 2s, so 2 to the power 20 is 2 to the power 10 multiplied by itself. Round 2 to the power 10 to a nearby round number first.
2 to the power 10 is 1024, which is about 1000.

solutions.reliable: Ten 2s multiply to 1024, which is about 1000. Twenty 2s are two groups of ten, so 2 to the power 20 is 1024 x 1024, about 1000 x 1000 = 1,000,000. The exact value is 1,048,576, far closer to 1,000,000 than to any other choice. The transferable idea: 2 to the power 10 is about 1000, so every ten 2s add about three zeros.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimation questions offer numbers of very different sizes, so the test is keeping track of size, here with the rule that ten 2s make about 1000.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Moving only right or up along the lines of a square grid, you travel from the point (0, 0) to the point (4, 3). The one-unit stretch of line from (2, 1) up to (2, 2) is closed, though both of those points can still be visited. How many different routes are there?

choices.misconception: I counted the routes that use the closed stretch instead of the ones that avoid it.
I treated the whole point (2, 1) as closed, so I also removed routes that pass through it and then go right.
I added the 3 routes up to the closed stretch and the 3 routes after it, 3 + 3 = 6, instead of multiplying them.
I counted every route from (0, 0) to (4, 3) and forgot to remove the ones that use the closed stretch.

hints: Count all the routes first, then remove the bad ones.
Each route has 4 steps right and 3 up, fixed by choosing which steps go up. A route using the closed stretch reaches (2, 1), steps up to (2, 2), then carries on: multiply the counts before and after.
There are 35 routes in all. There are 3 routes from (0, 0) to (2, 1), and 3 routes from (2, 2) to (4, 3).

solutions.reliable: A route is 7 steps, and choosing which 3 of them go up fixes it, so there are 35 routes in all. A route using the closed stretch goes from (0, 0) to (2, 1), which takes 3 steps with 1 up, so 3 ways; then up to (2, 2); then to (4, 3), which takes 3 steps with 1 up, so 3 ways. That is 3 x 3 = 9 bad routes, leaving 35 - 9 = 26. The transferable idea: count routes through a forbidden step by multiplying the ways before and after it, then subtract from the total.
solutions.elegant: Write at each grid point the number of routes reaching it, which is the number from the left plus the number from below, but do not add from below at (2, 2). Filling in row by row, the point (4, 3) gets 26.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid route questions test multiplying the counts before and after a step, and a closed street rewards counting the complement.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Twelve people meet, and every two of them shake hands once, except that three particular people, who met earlier that day, do not shake hands with one another. How many handshakes take place?

choices.misconception: I took away 3 handshakes for each of the three people, 9 in all, though only 3 pairs are missing.
I counted each of the 3 missing handshakes twice, once for each person, and took away 6.
I counted all the handshakes between twelve people and forgot to remove the missing ones.
I worked out 12 x 11 = 132 without halving, so every handshake was counted twice, then took off the 3 missing ones counted twice as well.

hints: Count all the possible handshakes, then remove the ones that do not happen.
Each of the 12 people would shake 11 hands, but that counts every handshake from both ends. Then think about how many pairs the three people form among themselves.
Everyone together would make 12 x 11 / 2 = 66 handshakes. Three people form 3 pairs.

solutions.reliable: If everyone shook hands with everyone, there would be 12 x 11 / 2 = 66 handshakes. The three people form 3 pairs among themselves, so 3 handshakes are missing, and 66 - 3 = 63 take place. The transferable idea: count pairs among n people as n x (n - 1) / 2, and remove a small group's own pairs in the same way.

problems.whyOnTest: Handshake questions test counting each pair once, and the traps forget to halve or remove too many missing pairs.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle is divided by grid lines into 3 rows of 5 equal small squares. How many squares of any size have all four sides on these lines?

choices.misconception: I counted only the 15 small squares.
I counted only squares of each size that do not overlap, so I found 2 two-by-two squares and 1 three-by-three square instead of 8 and 3.
I counted the small squares and the 2 by 2 squares but forgot the 3 by 3 squares.
I counted every rectangle on the grid, not only the squares.

hints: Sort the squares by size.
A square of a given size can slide to many positions, and they may overlap. For each size, count how many places its top-left corner can sit across and how many down, then multiply.
1 by 1: 3 x 5 positions. 2 by 2: 2 x 4 positions. 3 by 3: 1 x 3 positions.

solutions.reliable: Sort by size. A 1 by 1 square fits in 3 x 5 = 15 places. A 2 by 2 square can start in 2 rows and 4 columns, so 2 x 4 = 8 places. A 3 by 3 square fills all 3 rows and can start in 3 columns, so 3 places. No larger square fits. Total 15 + 8 + 3 = 26. The transferable idea: count hidden squares size by size, and let each size slide to every position, overlaps included.

problems.whyOnTest: Hidden-shape counts test organised counting, size by size, and the traps miss a size or forget that squares can overlap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A coaster is an equilateral triangle. Each of its three corners is painted one of 4 colours, and colours may be repeated. The coaster can be turned but not flipped over, and two coasters count as the same if one can be turned to look exactly like the other. How many different coasters can be made?

choices.misconception: I counted the coasters with all corners the same and with two corners the same, but forgot the ones with three different colours.
I counted each set of three different colours once, but those three colours can go round the triangle in two different ways.
I thought two corners of one colour and one of another could be arranged in two different ways, but turning makes them all the same.
I counted all 4 x 4 x 4 colourings without treating turned coasters as the same.

hints: Sort the coasters by how many different colours they use.
Turning cannot change which colours a coaster uses, so count one, two and three colours separately. In each group, ask how many arrangements are really different once turning is allowed.
With three different colours A, B and C, going round the corners you can meet them as A, B, C or as A, C, B.

solutions.reliable: One colour: 4 coasters. Two colours, with two corners of one colour and one corner of the other: choose the doubled colour (4 ways) and the single colour (3 ways), and turning makes every placement the same, so 12 coasters. Three different colours: choose which colour is left out (4 ways), and the three colours can go round clockwise in 2 different orders, which no turn can swap, so 8 coasters. Total 4 + 12 + 8 = 24. The transferable idea: when turned copies count as the same, sort by a feature that turning cannot change and count inside each group.
solutions.elegant: There are 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 colourings. A coaster with all corners one colour looks the same after every turn and appears once among them; every other coaster appears 3 times, once per turn. So there are 4 + (64 - 4) / 3 = 4 + 20 = 24 coasters.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetry counting tests that you neither count turned copies separately nor divide blindly by the number of turns.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pencil case holds 5 red, 7 blue and 9 black pens. Without looking, you take out pens one at a time. What is the smallest number you must take out to be certain of having at least two pens of each colour?

choices.misconception: I counted two pens of each colour, 3 x 2 = 6, which is only enough if you are lucky.
I built the worst case from the two smallest groups, all the red and blue pens, and then added 2 black pens.
I took all the black and blue pens as the worst case but forgot that I still need two red pens.
I took all the black and blue pens as the worst case and then added only one red pen.

hints: Imagine the unluckiest order the pens could come out in.
The worst case delays the colour you are short of for as long as possible. Decide which colour can be held back longest, and count how many pens can come out before you have two of it.
You could take all 9 black and all 7 blue pens before a single red one.

solutions.reliable: The unluckiest draw takes every pen of the two largest colours first: 9 black and 7 blue, 16 pens, and still no red. The next two pens must then both be red, so 18 pens are needed. And 18 is always enough: among 18 pens at most 16 are not red, at most 14 are not blue and at most 12 are not black, so there are at least two of each. The transferable idea: for 'certain to have', build the worst case by emptying the largest groups first, then add what is still needed.

problems.whyOnTest: Worst-case questions test thinking like the unluckiest drawer, and the traps hold back the wrong colour or stop one pen short.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a sequence, every term from the third onwards is the mean of the two terms just before it. The first term is 0 and the fifth term is 15. What is the second term?

choices.misconception: I added the two terms before each term instead of taking their mean, so the terms were 0, x, x, 2x and 3x.
I set the fourth term equal to 15 instead of the fifth, so I solved 3/4 of x = 15.
I set the third term equal to 15 instead of the fifth, so I solved half of x = 15.
I thought each new term was half of the term just before it, so I made the fifth term x / 8 and solved x / 8 = 15.

hints: Call the second term x and write out the terms one by one.
Each term is half the sum of the two before it. Keep the first term as 0 and the second as x, write the next three terms as fractions of x, and set the fifth equal to 15.
The terms are 0, x, x / 2, 3x / 4 and 5x / 8.

solutions.reliable: With second term x, the third term is (0 + x) / 2 = x / 2, the fourth is (x + x / 2) / 2 = 3x / 4, and the fifth is (x / 2 + 3x / 4) / 2 = 5x / 8. So 5x / 8 = 15, giving x = 15 x 8 / 5 = 24. Check: 0, 24, 12, 18, 15. The transferable idea: when a rule builds each term from earlier ones, carry an unknown through the rule and solve one equation at the end.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve from the choices. Starting 0, 24 the sequence runs 0, 24, 12, 18, 15, which reaches 15 at the fifth term.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive sequences test applying the exact rule step by step, and an unknown term can be carried along until one equation remains.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A large circle has centre O and radius 12. Inside it lie two smaller circles, with radii 4 and r. Each small circle touches the large circle from the inside, and the two small circles touch each other from the outside. The lines from O to the centres of the two small circles are perpendicular. What is r?

choices.misconception: I put the right angle at the centre of the circle with radius 4 instead of at O.
I found the distance from O to the centre of the circle with radius 4, 12 - 4 = 8, and gave that.
I found the distance between the centres of the two small circles, 4 + 6 = 10, and gave that instead of r.
I took the distance between the centres of the two small circles as r - 4, the difference of the radii, instead of the sum 4 + r.

hints: When one circle touches another from the inside, how far apart are their centres?
Centres of circles touching from the inside are a difference of radii apart, and from the outside a sum. Write the sides of the triangle of centres in terms of r, then use the right angle at O.
The sides are 12 - 4 = 8 and 12 - r, meeting at the right angle, and 4 + r opposite it. So 8 x 8 + (12 - r) x (12 - r) = (4 + r) x (4 + r).

solutions.reliable: Call the small centres B (radius 4) and C (radius r). Touching from the inside gives OB = 12 - 4 = 8 and OC = 12 - r, and touching from the outside gives BC = 4 + r. The right angle is at O, so BC is the longest side: 64 + (12 - r)(12 - r) = (4 + r)(4 + r). Expanding, 64 + 144 - 24r = 16 + 8r, so 192 = 32r and r = 6. Check: the sides are 8, 6 and 10, and 64 + 36 = 100. The transferable idea: for touching circles, join the centres; the distances are sums or differences of radii and the problem becomes a triangle problem.
solutions.elegant: Try the choices. With r = 6 the triangle has sides OB = 8, OC = 6 and BC = 10, which is the 3-4-5 right triangle doubled, with the right angle at O as required.

problems.whyOnTest: Touching-circle questions test joining the centres, since each distance is a sum or a difference of radii and the picture becomes a triangle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 5-by-5 board of squares is to be covered by twelve dominoes, each covering two squares that share a side, so that exactly one square is left uncovered. How many of the 25 squares could be the one left uncovered?

choices.misconception: I assumed that any square could be the one left over, since 24 squares remain whichever one is removed.
I coloured the board like a chessboard but counted the colour with fewer squares instead of the colour with more.
I thought only a corner square could be left out, because corners are the hardest squares to cover.
I assumed only the centre square works, because the board is symmetric about it.

hints: Colour the board like a chessboard, with the corners dark.
This is a colouring argument: every domino covers one square of each colour. Count how many squares of each colour the dominoes must cover, and decide which colour the uncovered square has to be.
With dark corners there are 13 dark squares and 12 light ones. Twelve dominoes cover 12 of each, so the uncovered square must be dark. Check that every dark square really can be the gap.

solutions.reliable: Colour the board in a chessboard pattern with dark corners: 13 dark squares and 12 light ones. Every domino covers one dark and one light square, so twelve dominoes cover exactly 12 of each, and the uncovered square must be dark. That rules out all 12 light squares. Every dark square does work. Number rows and columns 1 to 5. If the gap is in an odd row and an odd column, the rows above and below it come in even numbers (cover them with upright dominoes), and in its own row an even number of squares lies on each side (cover them with flat dominoes). If the gap is in an even row and an even column, make it the centre of a 3-by-3 block, cover that block's ring of 8 squares with four dominoes, and the rest splits into strips of even width. So 13 squares are possible. The transferable idea: a colouring turns 'can this be covered?' into a count that every piece must respect.
solutions.elegant: One count does all the elimination: 13 dark squares against 12 light ones. Testing squares one at a time without the colouring would take far longer.

problems.whyOnTest: Colouring arguments turn a covering question into a count, and the trap answers come from forgetting which colour is in the majority.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lena had some stickers. She gave half of them to her brother, then gave 4 to a friend, and then bought 10 more. She now has 30 stickers. How many stickers did she have at the start?

choices.misconception: I undid the steps but in the original order: I doubled first, then added 4, then took away 10.
I undid the purchase and the gift to the friend but forgot to undo the halving.
I applied her steps forwards to the 30 instead of undoing them.
I undid the gift to the friend by taking away 4 instead of adding the 4 back.

hints: Start from the 30 and walk through the story in reverse.
Work backwards: undo the last step first, and undo each step with its opposite operation. Buying becomes giving back, giving away becomes getting back, and halving becomes doubling.
Before buying 10 she had 20. Before giving 4 away she had 24. Those 24 are the half she kept.

solutions.reliable: Undo the steps from last to first. Before buying 10 she had 30 - 10 = 20. Before giving 4 away she had 20 + 4 = 24. Those 24 were the half she kept, so she started with 2 x 24 = 48. Check forwards: 48, then 24, then 20, then 30. The transferable idea: to work backwards, reverse both the order of the steps and each operation.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards needs the steps reversed in order and in operation, and each half-reversed attempt gives one of the other choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A card has seven sentences on it, numbered 1 to 7. Sentence number k says: 'At most k of the sentences on this card are true.' How many of the seven sentences are true?

choices.misconception: I noticed that sentence 7 must be true and assumed that all seven sentences are therefore true.
I worked out that sentences 1, 2 and 3 are false and gave the number of false sentences instead of true ones.
I decided only sentence 7, the weakest claim, is true, without checking that this would make sentence 1 true as well.
I thought sentences that talk about themselves can never be true, so I said none of them are.

hints: Suppose exactly T sentences are true. Which sentences does that make true?
Assume a value and look for a contradiction. If exactly T sentences are true, work out which numbered sentences that makes true, count them, and see whether the count comes back to T.
If exactly T are true, sentence k is true exactly when k is T or more. That is sentences T to 7, which is 8 - T sentences. Set 8 - T equal to T.

solutions.reliable: Suppose exactly T sentences are true. Sentence k is true exactly when T is at most k, so the true sentences are numbers T, T + 1, ..., 7, and there are 8 - T of them. For the card to be consistent, 8 - T = T, so T = 4: sentences 4 to 7 are true and sentences 1 to 3 are false. Every other value contradicts itself; for example, if all 7 were true, sentence 1 would be claiming that at most one sentence is true. The transferable idea: assume a value, follow its consequences, and keep only the value that does not contradict itself.
solutions.elegant: Sentence 7 is certainly true, and if sentence k is true so is every later one. So the true sentences form a block ending at 7, and the block must start at its own length. A block from T to 7 has 8 - T members, and only the block 4, 5, 6, 7 starts at its length.

problems.whyOnTest: Self-referring sentences are settled by assuming a count and hunting for a contradiction, which is the core move of informal proof.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Nine different positive whole numbers add up to 100. What is the smallest possible value of the largest of the nine numbers?

choices.misconception: I divided 100 by 9 and rounded up, forgetting that the nine numbers must all be different.
I divided 100 by 9 and rounded down to get a typical size for the numbers.
I took the nine numbers from 7 to 15 as the tightest set and did not notice that they only add up to 99.
I found how large the biggest number could be, by making the other eight 1 to 8, instead of how small.

hints: If the largest number is M, how big can the total possibly be?

Use extremal thinking: nine different numbers, none above M, total at most the nine consecutive numbers ending at M. Find the first M whose ceiling reaches 100, then check it can actually be achieved.
With largest 15 the total is at most 7 + 8 + ... + 15 = 99, which is too small. With largest 16, try 10 to 16 together with two smaller numbers that add up to 9.

solutions.reliable: If the largest number is M, the nine different numbers are at most M, M - 1, ..., M - 8, whose sum is 9M - 36. We need 9M - 36 to be at least 100, so M is at least 136 / 9, which is about 15.1. So 15 is impossible (7 + 8 + ... + 15 = 99) and 16 is the candidate. It works: 1, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16 add up to 100. The transferable idea: bound the extreme value using the most crowded case, then show that the bound is actually reached.

problems.whyOnTest: Minimising the largest of several different numbers needs a bound and an example, and simple averaging ignores the 'all different' condition.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pen costs 3 euros more than a pencil. Four pencils and two pens cost 18 euros altogether. How much does one pen cost?

choices.misconception: I found the price of a pencil and gave that as the answer instead of the price of a pen.
I shared the 18 euros equally among the six items, ignoring the difference in price.
I wrote 4p + 2p = 18 without the extra 3 euros, got 3 for the pencil and then added 3.
I wrote 4p + 2p + 3 = 18, adding the extra 3 euros once instead of once for each pen.

hints: Let the price of a pencil be p. What is the price of a pen?
Translate the sentence into one equation: write the cost of four pencils and the cost of two pens using the pencil's price, add them, and set the total equal to 18.
4p + 2(p + 3) = 18 simplifies to 6p + 6 = 18. Solve for p, then remember the question asks about the pen.

solutions.reliable: Let a pencil cost p euros, so a pen costs p + 3 euros. Then 4p + 2(p + 3) = 18, so 6p + 6 = 18 and p = 2. A pen costs 2 + 3 = 5 euros. Check: 4 x 2 + 2 x 5 = 18. The transferable idea: name one unknown, write every other quantity in terms of it, and reread the question before answering.
solutions.elegant: Take away the extra 3 euros on each of the two pens: 18 - 6 = 12 euros would buy six items at the pencil price, so a pencil costs 2 euros and a pen costs 5.

problems.whyOnTest: Writing a sentence as an equation is the skill, and the trap is forgetting that 'more than' applies to every pen bought.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Today Marta is 40 years old and her son is 12. In how many years' time will Marta be exactly twice as old as her son?

choices.misconception: I worked out how old the son will be at that moment and gave his age instead of the number of years.
I added the years to the son's age but not to Marta's, so I solved 40 = 2 x (12 + x).
I worked out how old Marta will be at that moment instead of how many years away it is.
I halved the 28-year age gap, thinking the son only has to make up half of it.

hints: Does the difference between their ages ever change?
Age problems have one fixed quantity: the age gap. When Marta is twice as old as her son, the gap between them equals the son's age at that moment.
The gap is 40 - 12 = 28 years, so at that moment the son will be 28. How many years from now is that?

solutions.reliable: In x years Marta will be 40 + x and her son 12 + x. Twice as old means 40 + x = 2(12 + x) = 24 + 2x, so x = 16. Check: in 16 years they will be 56 and 28, and 56 is twice 28. The transferable idea: in age problems every person gets older by the same number of years.
solutions.elegant: The age gap is always 28 years. When Marta is twice her son's age, the gap equals the son's age, so he will be 28. He is 12 now, so that is 16 years away.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems reward spotting that the age gap never changes, and each trap answer either ages only one person or answers a different question.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular water tank measures 2 m long, 1 m wide and 50 cm deep. It is filled using a jug that holds 2.5 litres. How many jugfuls of water are needed to fill the tank? (1 litre = 1000 cubic centimetres.)

choices.misconception: I changed 50 cm into 0.05 m instead of 0.5 m, so the tank came out ten times too small.
I changed cubic metres into cubic centimetres by multiplying by 100 x 100, as for square units, instead of 100 x 100 x 100.
I multiplied the 1000 litres by 2.5 instead of dividing by the size of the jug.
I used 50 for the depth without changing the centimetres into metres.

hints: Put every length in centimetres before you multiply anything.
Unit conversion: convert the lengths first and find the volume in cubic centimetres, then change it into litres using the conversion given, and only then divide by the jug.
In centimetres the tank is 200 by 100 by 50, which is 1 000 000 cubic centimetres.

solutions.reliable: In centimetres the tank is 200 by 100 by 50, so its volume is 200 x 100 x 50 = 1 000 000 cubic centimetres. That is 1 000 000 / 1000 = 1000 litres. Each jug holds 2.5 litres, so 1000 / 2.5 = 400 jugfuls are needed. The transferable idea: convert lengths before multiplying them, because one cubic metre is 100 x 100 x 100 cubic centimetres.
solutions.elegant: One cubic metre is exactly 1000 litres. The tank is 2 x 1 x 0.5 = 1 cubic metre, so it holds 1000 litres, which is 400 jugs of 2.5 litres.

problems.whyOnTest: Volume units cube the conversion factor, and each wrong choice comes from converting a length, an area or a volume by the wrong factor.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The bar chart shows how many people visited a small museum on each day from Monday to Friday. On Saturday the number of visitors was 50% more than the mean number of visitors per weekday. How many people visited on Saturday?

figure.alt: A bar chart of museum visitors per day, on an axis labelled every 10 with gridlines every 5: Monday 40, Tuesday 25, Wednesday 35, Thursday 30, Friday 50.

choices.misconception: I found the mean for the five weekdays and forgot to add the extra 50 percent.
I added 50 percent to Friday, the busiest day, instead of to the mean.
I took 50 percent of the five-day total of 180 instead of working from the mean.
I added 50 percent to the five-day total of 180 instead of to the mean.

hints: Read all five bars carefully, including the two that end between labels.
First find the mean: total the five readings and share the total equally among the days. Then '50% more' means the mean plus half of the mean again.
The five bars total 180, so the mean is 36. Half of 36 is 18.

solutions.reliable: From the chart: 40 + 25 + 35 + 30 + 50 = 180 visitors, so the mean is 180 / 5 = 36 per weekday. Fifty percent more is 36 + 18 = 54. The transferable idea: read every value before calculating, and apply a percentage to exactly the quantity the sentence names.

problems.whyOnTest: Reading a chart and then applying a percentage to the right base (the mean, not the total or the tallest bar) is a two-step data skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cafe bakes 15 cakes every day and uses 4 eggs in each cake. Eggs come in boxes of 6. How many boxes of eggs does the cafe use in one week?

choices.misconception: I worked out the number of boxes for one day and forgot to multiply by the seven days.
I found the number of eggs used in the week and forgot to change it into boxes.
I counted only the five weekdays instead of all seven days of the week.
I multiplied by 6 for the boxes instead of dividing by 6.

hints: How many eggs does one day need?
Break it into steps: eggs per day, then eggs per week, then boxes. Write the unit after each step, so that you divide by the box size at the right moment and do not stop early.
One day uses 15 x 4 = 60 eggs, which is 10 boxes.

solutions.reliable: Each day uses 15 x 4 = 60 eggs, which is 60 / 6 = 10 boxes. Over 7 days that is 7 x 10 = 70 boxes. The transferable idea: label the unit after each step (eggs per day, eggs per week, boxes) so you never stop one step short.

problems.whyOnTest: Multi-step word problems reward tracking units; each wrong choice stops at, skips or reverses one of the three steps.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When the digits of a certain three-digit number are written in reverse order, the result is 594 more than the original number. How many three-digit numbers have this property?

choices.misconception: I found the three possible pairs of first and last digits and forgot that the middle digit can be anything.
I allowed the first digit to be 0, which also let 0 and 6 be the outer digits.
I let the middle digit run from 1 to 9 and forgot that it can also be 0.
I found one pair of outer digits that works and counted only its ten middle digits.

hints: Write the number as 100a + 10b + c. What happens to b on reversing?

Use place value: reversing swaps the hundreds digit and the units digit and leaves the tens digit where it is, so the difference depends only on the outer digits. Find which outer digits work, then count the middle digits.
The difference is 99(c - a) = 594, so c - a = 6. The first digit a cannot be 0.

solutions.reliable: With digits a, b, c the number is 100a + 10b + c and its reverse is 100c + 10b + a. The difference is 99c - 99a = 99(c - a), and 594 = 99 x 6, so c = a + 6. The first digit a is at least 1 and c is at most 9, so the outer digits are 1 and 7, 2 and 8, or 3 and 9. The middle digit is free, with 10 choices. That gives 3 x 10 = 30 numbers. Check one: 147 reversed is 741, and 741 - 147 = 594. The transferable idea: write a number by place value, and the digits that do not move cancel out.

problems.whyOnTest: Writing the digits by place value shows the middle digit cancels, so the question collapses to one equation and a careful count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many two-digit numbers are equal to 7 times the sum of their own digits?

choices.misconception: I found one example by trial and assumed it was the only one.
I reached 'tens digit = 2 x units digit' and let the units digit run from 1 to 9, without checking the tens digit stays a single digit.
I also counted 0, written as 00, alongside the four real two-digit answers.
I tested only the multiples of 7 below 70, so I never reached the fourth answer.

hints: Write the number as 10a + b, with digits a and b.

Turn the condition into an equation in the two digits and simplify it. It becomes a simple link between the tens digit and the units digit; then list every digit pair that fits, remembering both must be single digits.
10a + b = 7a + 7b simplifies to 3a = 6b, that is, a = 2b. The tens digit a is from 1 to 9.

solutions.reliable: With tens digit a and units digit b, 10a + b = 7(a + b), so 3a = 6b and a = 2b. Since a is a single digit from 1 to 9, b can be 1, 2, 3 or 4, giving 21, 42, 63 and 84. Check 84: its digits add to 12 and 7 x 12 = 84. So there are 4 such numbers. The transferable idea: write a digit puzzle in place-value form, and the equation usually shows exactly how the digits are tied together.
solutions.elegant: Each such number is a multiple of 7, and dividing it by 7 gives its digit sum. Testing the multiples of 7 from 14 to 98 finds 21, 42, 63 and 84 quickly, and the equation a = 2b explains why the list stops there.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit puzzles reward writing 10a + b, which turns trial and error into a short list that you can be sure is complete.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A plus sign or a minus sign is placed in front of each of the numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 10, and the ten signed numbers are added together. How many different results are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted the ways of choosing the ten signs, but many different choices give the same result.
I counted every whole number from minus 55 to 55, not noticing that the result is always odd.
I counted only the positive odd results and forgot the negative ones.
I counted the whole numbers from 1 to 55 as the possible results.

hints: Is the result odd or even, whatever signs you choose?

Think about parity. Switching a sign from plus to minus changes the total by twice that number, an even amount, so every result shares the all-plus total's parity. Then find the range and check which values in it occur.
The all-plus total is 55, so every result is odd and lies from minus 55 to 55. Switching numbers whose sum is S gives 55 - 2S, and S can be any whole number from 0 to 55.

solutions.reliable: With all plus signs the total is 55. Changing the signs of some numbers whose sum is S lowers the total by 2S, giving 55 - 2S. Every whole number S from 0 to 55 is a sum of different numbers from 1 to 10 (take 10 if it fits, then 9 if it fits, and so on down), so the results are exactly the odd numbers from minus 55 to 55. There are 28 positive ones and 28 negative ones, 56 in all. The transferable idea: flipping a sign changes a sum by an even amount, so the parity is fixed and only the range needs checking.
