problems.whyOnTest: Sign-flipping problems hide a parity invariant: half of the whole numbers in the range are impossible, and the other half all occur.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When 2026 is divided by a certain whole number d, the remainder is 6. How many different values could d have?

choices.misconception: I counted every divisor of 2020 and forgot that the divisor must be bigger than the remainder 6.
I left out d = 2020, because I did not think a divisor that large could leave a remainder.
I counted the pairs of numbers that multiply to give 2020 instead of the divisors themselves.
I listed the divisors of 2026 instead of the divisors of 2026 - 6.

hints: If 2026 leaves remainder 6 when divided by d, what does d divide exactly?
Remainders: d must divide 2026 - 6 exactly, and a remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by. List the divisors of that number and keep only the allowed ones.
2020 = 2 x 2 x 5 x 101. Its divisors are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 101, 202, 404, 505, 1010 and 2020. Which of them are bigger than 6?

solutions.reliable: Remainder 6 means 2026 = q x d + 6 for some whole number q, so d divides 2020 exactly. Also a remainder must be smaller than the divisor, so d is bigger than 6. Since 2020 = 2 x 2 x 5 x 101, its divisors are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 101, 202, 404, 505, 1010 and 2020. Throwing out 1, 2, 4 and 5 leaves 8 values. Check one: 2026 = 2 x 1010 + 6. The transferable idea: a remainder condition becomes a divisibility condition, plus the rule that the remainder is smaller than the divisor.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainder questions often turn into divisor questions, and the trap is forgetting that a remainder must be smaller than the divisor.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two-thirds of the pupils in a class are girls. A quarter of the girls wear glasses, and 4 girls wear glasses. How many pupils are in the class?

choices.misconception: I found the number of girls and stopped there instead of going on to the whole class.
I found the number of boys instead of the number of pupils in the whole class.
I used one third instead of two thirds when going from the girls to the whole class.
I doubled the 16 girls, as though the girls were half of the class.

hints: First find how many girls there are.
Work backwards through the fractions: the 4 girls are a known fraction of the girls, and the girls are a known fraction of the class. Undo one fraction at a time.
4 is a quarter of the girls, so there are 16 girls. 16 is two thirds of the class, so one third of the class is 8.

solutions.reliable: 4 girls are a quarter of the girls, so there are 16 girls. 16 is two thirds of the class, so one third is 8 and the whole class is 24. Check: two thirds of 24 is 16, and a quarter of 16 is 4. The transferable idea: undo fractions one layer at a time, finding one part before the whole.
solutions.elegant: The girls with glasses are a quarter of two thirds, that is one sixth, of the class. So the class has 6 x 4 = 24 pupils.

problems.whyOnTest: Fractions of fractions are undone layer by layer, and each wrong choice stops at, or mishandles, one of the layers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to the number of seconds in 13 years?

choices.misconception: I stopped after converting the years to hours and did not change the hours into seconds.
I multiplied by 60 only once after reaching hours, so I found minutes rather than seconds.
I used 3600 seconds for a whole day, forgetting to multiply by the 24 hours in it.
I multiplied by 60 one time too many, going past seconds.

hints: Round as you go: about 365 days a year, 24 hours a day.

Estimate to the nearest choice: chain the conversions from years to days to hours to minutes to seconds, rounding each step. The choices are far enough apart that rough numbers decide it, as long as no step is skipped.
A day has 24 x 3600 = 86 400 seconds, roughly 90 000. A year of about 365 days is roughly 30 million seconds.

solutions.reliable: A day has 24 x 60 x 60 = 86 400 seconds. A year has about 365 days, so about 31.5 million seconds. Thirteen years is about 13 x 31.5 million, roughly 410 million. The transferable idea: when the choices differ by large factors, round boldly and spend your care on counting the conversion steps.
solutions.elegant: A year is very close to 31.5 million seconds, a number worth remembering. Thirteen years is then a little over 400 million.

problems.whyOnTest: When the choices are many times apart, estimating beats exact work, and each wrong choice drops or repeats one conversion.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The first term of a sequence is 3. Every later term is equal to the sum of all the terms before it. What is the 10th term?

choices.misconception: I assumed every term is double the one before it, starting from the first, so I did not notice that the second term is also 3.
I worked out the terms correctly but stopped at the 9th term.
I added 3 each time, as though each new term grew by the first term only.
I doubled 3 ten times, once for every term, instead of following the rule.

hints: Write out the first five terms carefully. What is the second term?
A recursive rule: compare each new term with the one just before it. The sum of everything before term n + 1 is term n plus the sum of everything before term n, which is term n again.
The terms go 3, 3, 6, 12, 24, ... From the second term on, each term is double the one before.

solutions.reliable: The second term is the sum of the terms before it, which is just 3. The third is 3 + 3 = 6, the fourth is 3 + 3 + 6 = 12, and the fifth is 24. From the third term on, each term equals the previous term plus everything before the previous term, which is the previous term again, so each term doubles. The terms are 3, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384, 768, so the 10th term is 768. The transferable idea: write out the first few terms of a recursive rule by hand before trusting a pattern.
solutions.elegant: From the second term on the terms double, and the second term is 3. The 10th term is 8 doublings after the second: 3 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 3 x 256 = 768.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules reward writing out the first few terms, and the trap here is assuming the doubling starts from the very first term.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a 10-by-10 multiplication table, the entry in row r and column c is r x c, for every r and c from 1 to 10. What is the sum of all 100 entries?

choices.misconception: I added the whole numbers from 1 to 100, as though the table held each of them once.
I added only the entries on the diagonal, 1 + 4 + 9 + ... + 100.
I added the entries of the last row, 10 + 20 + ... + 100, and stopped there.
I took 1 + 2 + ... + 10 to be 45, leaving out the 10, and squared that.

hints: Add up one row first. How do the other rows compare with it?
Look for the pattern in the table: each row is a multiple of the first row, so each row sum is the same multiple of the first row's sum. Then add the row sums in the same way.
Row r adds up to 55 x r, so the total is 55 x (1 + 2 + ... + 10).

solutions.reliable: Row 1 is 1, 2, ..., 10, with sum 55. Row r is r times row 1, so it sums to 55r. Adding all ten rows gives 55 x (1 + 2 + ... + 10) = 55 x 55 = 3025. The transferable idea: in a table built by a rule, sum one row, see how the other rows relate to it, and the grand total factorises.
solutions.elegant: Multiplying out (1 + 2 + ... + 10) x (1 + 2 + ... + 10) produces every product r x c exactly once, so the sum is 55 x 55 = 3025.

problems.whyOnTest: Summing a structured table by noticing that each row scales the first replaces 100 additions with one multiplication.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The operation ★ follows one rule, which you can work out from these examples: 2 ★ 3 = 8, 4 ★ 1 = 8 and 5 ★ 5 = 30. What is 6 ★ 3?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the two numbers without testing that rule on the examples.
I found the rule a + b + 3, which fits the first two examples, and did not test it on the third.
I found the right kind of rule but added the second number instead of the first, using a x b + b.
I added the two numbers without testing that rule on the examples.

hints: Compare each result with the product of its two numbers.

A rule must fit every example, not just one or two. Compare each result with a simple combination of its two numbers, look at what is left over each time, and see how the leftover is linked to the numbers.
The products are 6, 4 and 25. The leftovers are 2, 4 and 5, which are the first numbers.

solutions.reliable: The products are 2 x 3 = 6, 4 x 1 = 4 and 5 x 5 = 25. The results are bigger by 2, 4 and 5, which is the first number each time. So a ★ b = a x b + a, and 6 ★ 3 = 18 + 6 = 24. Note that a + b + 3 fits the first two examples but gives 13, not 30, for 5 ★ 5. The transferable idea: test a candidate rule against every example before using it.
solutions.elegant: Each result is the first number times one more than the second: 2 x 4 = 8, 4 x 2 = 8, 5 x 6 = 30. So 6 ★ 3 = 6 x 4 = 24.

problems.whyOnTest: Inferring a rule rewards checking every example; each wrong choice comes from a rule that fits only some of the examples or none of them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square frame has inside edges of length 20 cm. A coin of radius 3 cm rolls all the way around the inside of the frame, always touching it, until it is back where it started. How long is the path traced by the centre of the coin?

choices.misconception: I used the side of the frame, as if the centre of the coin ran right along the edge.
I moved each side of the path in by one radius in total, instead of by one radius at each end.
I added a quarter circle at each corner, which happens when a coin rolls around the outside of a square, not the inside.
I took a whole diameter off each end of every side instead of a radius.

hints: How far is the centre of the coin from a side it is touching?

Touching means the distance from the centre to the side equals the radius. So the centre always stays 3 cm away from the sides; find the shape the centre moves along, and check what happens at a corner.
The centre moves along a smaller square. Each of its sides is 20 - 3 - 3 cm long, and at a corner the centre simply changes direction.

solutions.reliable: While the coin touches a side, its centre is 3 cm from that side. So the centre moves along a square whose sides are 3 cm inside the frame on every side, which makes each side 20 - 3 - 3 = 14 cm long. At a corner the coin touches two sides at once, and the centre just turns through a right angle without any curve. The path is 4 x 14 = 56 cm. The transferable idea: a circle touching a line has its centre exactly one radius from the line, so track the centre instead of the rim.

problems.whyOnTest: Touching circles are handled through their centres, and the trap is borrowing the curved corners that appear only when a coin rolls around the outside.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rhombus has one angle of 60 degrees. Its shorter diagonal is 7 cm long. What is the perimeter of the rhombus?

choices.misconception: I found the perimeter of one of the two triangles that the diagonal makes, not of the rhombus.
I treated the rhombus as a square, so I took each side to be the diagonal divided by √2.
I added the diagonal to the four sides, although it is not part of the outside edge.
I added the perimeters of both triangles, so the diagonal was counted twice.

hints: The shorter diagonal cuts the rhombus into two triangles. What kind of triangles are they?
Use the properties of a rhombus: all four sides are equal. Each triangle has two sides of the rhombus and a 60 degree angle between them, so work out its other two angles.
Each triangle is isosceles with a 60 degree angle between its equal sides, so its other angles are also 60 degrees, and it is equilateral.

solutions.reliable: All four sides of a rhombus are equal. The shorter diagonal joins the two ends of the sides that meet at the 60 degree angle, so it cuts off a triangle with two equal sides and 60 degrees between them. Its other two angles are equal and add up to 120 degrees, so each is 60 degrees and the triangle is equilateral. So each side of the rhombus equals the diagonal, 7 cm, and the perimeter is 4 x 7 = 28 cm. The transferable idea: an isosceles triangle with a 60 degree angle is always equilateral.
solutions.elegant: A rhombus with a 60 degree angle is two equilateral triangles glued along the shorter diagonal, so every side is 7 cm and the perimeter is 28 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Knowing the properties of a rhombus, and spotting the equilateral triangles inside it, turns one diagonal into the side length.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two regular pentagons and one more regular polygon fit together around a single point, with no gaps and no overlaps. How many sides does the third polygon have?

choices.misconception: I assumed the third polygon is another pentagon without checking that three pentagons leave a gap.
I used 120 degrees for the pentagon's angle, which is really the hexagon's, so the gap came out as 120 degrees.
I divided 360 by the exterior angle of 36 degrees and then added 2, mixing in the angle-sum formula.
I remembered that octagons fill gaps in tilings and chose the octagon without working out the gap.

hints: The angles meeting at the point must add up to 360 degrees.

Fitting tiles around a point: find the interior angle of a regular pentagon, work out the angle left for the third polygon, then find which regular polygon has that interior angle, going through its exterior angle.
A regular pentagon's angles are 108 degrees, so 360 - 108 - 108 = 144 degrees is left. An interior angle of 144 degrees means an exterior angle of 36 degrees.

solutions.reliable: The angles of a pentagon add up to 3 x 180 = 540 degrees, so each angle of a regular pentagon is 108 degrees. Two of them use 216 degrees, leaving 360 - 216 = 144 degrees. A regular polygon with interior angle 144 degrees has exterior angle 180 - 144 = 36 degrees, and the exterior angles of a polygon add up to 360, so it has 360 / 36 = 10 sides. The transferable idea: angles meeting at a point add up to 360, and the exterior angle is the quickest route from an angle to a number of sides.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions are angle sums at a point, and turning an interior angle into a number of sides via the exterior angle is the step tested.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At a meeting, every two people shook hands exactly once, except for two people who refused to shake hands with each other. There were 44 handshakes in total. How many people were at the meeting?

choices.misconception: I found how many handshakes there would have been if everyone had shaken hands, and gave that number.
I counted the handshakes as 1 + 2 + ... + n instead of 1 + 2 + ... + (n - 1), so the 45 handshakes gave me 9 people.
I thought the missing handshake stood for one extra person, so I added 1 to the 10 people.
I found the 10 people and then added the two who refused, counting them a second time.

hints: How many handshakes would there be if nobody had refused?
Count pairs: with n people every pair shakes hands once, so the full count is n times (n - 1), halved. Add back the missing handshake, then find the n that fits.
Without the refusal there would be 45 handshakes, so n x (n - 1) = 90.

solutions.reliable: Had everyone shaken hands there would have been 44 + 1 = 45 handshakes. With n people that number is n(n - 1) / 2, so n(n - 1) = 90 = 10 x 9, giving n = 10. The transferable idea: count all the pairs first, then adjust for the exceptions.
solutions.elegant: Let people arrive one at a time and shake hands with everyone already there: the second shakes 1 hand, the third 2, and so on. 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, so the tenth person completes the 45 pairs.

problems.whyOnTest: Pair counting with one exception checks that you can count the full set of pairs and then correct for what is missing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A cube has 8 corners. A straight segment is drawn between every pair of corners. How many of these segments pass through the inside of the cube, rather than lying along an edge or across a face?

choices.misconception: I counted every pair of corners without removing the edges and the face diagonals.
I removed the 12 edges from the 28 pairs but forgot to remove the face diagonals.
I counted the diagonals across the faces, two on each of the six faces, instead of the inside ones.
I gave each corner its one inside segment but did not notice that every segment had been counted from both ends.

hints: From one corner, how many segments go to each kind of other corner?

Overcount, then correct: count segments corner by corner, sort them into edges, face diagonals and inside segments, and remember each segment has two ends. Or subtract the edges and face diagonals from all the pairs.
From each corner there are 3 edges, 3 face diagonals and 1 inside segment. Eight corners give 8 ends of inside segments.

solutions.reliable: There are 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 pairs of corners. Of these, 12 are edges and 12 are face diagonals (two on each of the six faces). The rest go through the inside: 28 - 12 - 12 = 4. The transferable idea: count everything and subtract what you do not want, or count from each end and halve.
solutions.elegant: Each corner has exactly one opposite corner, and every inside segment joins a corner to its opposite. Counting from all 8 corners counts each segment twice, so there are 8 / 2 = 4.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting from each end and halving, or counting all pairs and subtracting, are the two standard ways to correct an overcount.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A closed box measures 1 cm by 2 cm by 4 cm. An ant walks on the outside surface of the box from one corner to the corner furthest from it. How long is the shortest possible route?

choices.misconception: I walked along the edges, 1 + 2 + 4, instead of cutting across the faces.
I used the straight line through the inside of the box, which the ant cannot walk along.
I unfolded the two faces so that the 1 cm and 4 cm edges lined up, which is not the shortest unfolding.
I unfolded the two faces so that the 2 cm and 4 cm edges lined up, which gives the longest of the three routes.

hints: Unfold the box so the ant's route becomes a straight line.

Shortest paths on a surface: unfold the two faces the ant crosses into one flat rectangle, and the shortest route across them is its diagonal. There are three different ways to do this; compare them all.
The unfolded rectangles are (1 + 2) by 4, (1 + 4) by 2 and (2 + 4) by 1. Use Pythagoras on each one.

solutions.reliable: The ant crosses two neighbouring faces; unfolding them flat makes a rectangle whose diagonal is the route. The three choices of the shared edge give rectangles 3 by 4, 5 by 2 and 6 by 1, with diagonals √25 = 5, √29 and √37. The shortest is 5 cm. The transferable idea: unfold a surface to turn a shortest path into a straight line, then compare every unfolding.
solutions.elegant: Put the two shortest edges side by side: a (1 + 2) by 4 rectangle has diagonal 5, from the 3, 4, 5 right triangle. Joining the two shortest edges always gives the shortest unfolding.

problems.whyOnTest: Unfolding a solid turns a path on its surface into a straight segment, and the trap is stopping at the first unfolding you try.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two different whole numbers, both greater than 8, have greatest common divisor 8 and least common multiple 480. How many such pairs of numbers are there? (A pair counts once, whichever order its numbers are written in.)

choices.misconception: I forgot to rule out the pair 8 and 480, even though 8 is not greater than 8.
I listed every way to write 60 as a product of two numbers without checking that the two parts share no common factor, and I kept the pair 8 and 480.
I listed every factor pair of 60 without checking that the two parts share no common factor, then removed the pair 8 and 480.
I counted every pair twice, once in each order, and I also kept the pair 8 and 480.

hints: Write both numbers as 8 times something.
With the numbers written as 8m and 8n, m and n share no common factor and the least common multiple is 8 x m x n. Split m x n into two parts with no common factor.
From 8 x m x n = 480 you get m x n = 60. The splits of 60 into two parts with no common factor are 1 x 60, 3 x 20, 4 x 15 and 5 x 12.

solutions.reliable: Both numbers are multiples of 8, so write them as 8m and 8n. Their greatest common divisor is exactly 8 only if m and n share no common factor, and then their least common multiple is 8mn. So 8mn = 480 and mn = 60. The factor pairs of 60 are 1 x 60, 2 x 30, 3 x 20, 4 x 15, 5 x 12 and 6 x 10; the pairs 2 x 30 and 6 x 10 share a factor, so they fail. That leaves m, n = 1 and 60, 3 and 20, 4 and 15, 5 and 12, giving 8 and 480, 24 and 160, 32 and 120, 40 and 96. Both numbers must be greater than 8, so 8 and 480 is out, leaving 3 pairs. The transferable idea: take the greatest common divisor out first, and what remains must be coprime parts of the quotient.
solutions.elegant: Since the GCD times the LCM equals the product of the two numbers, the product is 8 x 480. After dividing each number by 8, the two quotients have product 60 and no common factor. Each of the prime powers 4, 3 and 5 must go wholly to one side, which gives 4 unordered splits; dropping the split 1 and 60 (the pair 8 and 480) leaves 3.

problems.whyOnTest: GCD and LCM questions are really about splitting prime factors between two numbers, and the traps are forgetting the coprime condition or the stated restriction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is (1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 49) - (2 + 4 + 6 + ... + 48)? The first bracket holds every odd number from 1 to 49, and the second holds every even number from 2 to 48.

choices.misconception: I paired each even number with the odd number just above it, got 24 differences of 1, and forgot the 1 left over at the start.
I assumed both brackets had the same number of terms that would cancel out, leaving 0.
I subtracted the odd total from the even total, reversing the order of the two brackets.
I cancelled each even number against the odd number just below it as if they were equal, which left only 49.

hints: Count how many terms are in each bracket.
Do not add each bracket on its own. Pair every even number with a nearby odd number so that each pair has the same small difference, then see what is left over.
Pair 3 with 2, 5 with 4, and so on up to 49 with 48. Each pair gives 1, and the 1 at the very start has no partner.

solutions.reliable: There are 25 odd numbers from 1 to 49 and 24 even numbers from 2 to 48. Group them as 1 + (3 - 2) + (5 - 4) + ... + (49 - 48). There are 24 brackets, each worth 1, giving 24, and the unpaired 1 at the start makes the total 25. The transferable idea: regroup a long sum into pairs that each give the same simple value, and watch for the term with no partner.
solutions.elegant: The odd numbers from 1 to 49 add to 25 x 25 = 625 and the even numbers from 2 to 48 add to 2 x (1 + 2 + ... + 24) = 600, so the difference is 25.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo arithmetic is rarely about long sums: pairing terms turns the work into counting, and the leftover term is the usual trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the addition KAN + KAN = ROOK, each letter stands for a digit, different letters stand for different digits, and no number starts with 0. What number is KAN?

choices.misconception: I forgot that different letters must stand for different digits, and let A and K both be 8.
I found 613 + 613 = 1226, which has the right pattern, but I let A be 1 even though R is already 1.
I solved the puzzle correctly but gave the answer ROOK instead of KAN.
I found 668 + 668 = 1336, which has the right pattern, but I let A be 6 even though K is already 6.

hints: What is the largest possible value of KAN + KAN?
Fix R first. In the units column K is the last digit of N + N, so K is even. Test the few values of K, carrying carefully, and check that every letter gets its own digit.
R = 1 and K is even and at least 5, so K is 6 or 8. Try K = 8: then N is 4 or 9, and the hundreds column needs O to be 6 or 7.

solutions.reliable: Two three-digit numbers add to less than 2000, so R = 1. ROOK is at least 1000, so K is at least 5, and K is the last digit of N + N, so K is even: K = 6 or K = 8. In the hundreds column K + K plus any carry equals 10 + O. If K = 6, then O is 2 or 3 and N is 3 or 8; checking the tens column, every option is either impossible or forces A to repeat a digit already used (A = 1 or A = 6), so K = 6 fails. If K = 8, then O is 6 or 7 and N is 4 or 9. With N = 4 there is no carry from the units, so A + A = O with no carry into the hundreds, giving O = 6 and A = 3. With N = 9 the tens column forces A = 8, which repeats K. So KAN = 834, and indeed 834 + 834 = 1668. The transferable idea: in a letter sum, settle the leading digit and the units column first, then test the few cases left.

problems.whyOnTest: Cryptarithms reward working column by column with carries, and the classic slip is accepting a solution that reuses a digit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five test scores have a mean of 82. When the lowest of them is removed, the remaining four scores have a mean of 86. What was the lowest score?

choices.misconception: I thought the lowest score was 4 below the mean, because the mean went up by 4.
I thought the removed score had to make up a rise of 4 for all five scores, so I put it 5 x 4 = 20 below the old mean.
I subtracted 4 x 4 = 16 from the new mean, 86, instead of from the old mean, 82.
I gave the change in the mean instead of working out the score.

hints: Turn each mean back into a total.
A mean times the number of values gives the total. Find the total of all five scores and the total of the four that are left; the removed score is the difference.
The five scores total 5 x 82 = 410 and the four scores total 4 x 86 = 344.

solutions.reliable: The five scores total 5 x 82 = 410. The four remaining scores total 4 x 86 = 344. The removed score is 410 - 344 = 66. The transferable idea: when a mean changes, work with totals, never with the means directly.
solutions.elegant: The four remaining scores average 4 above the old mean of 82, so together they sit 4 x 4 = 16 above it. Across all five scores the amounts above and below 82 balance out, so the removed score must sit 16 below 82, at 66.

problems.whyOnTest: Mean problems test switching between means and totals, and each wrong answer comes from reasoning about the means without the totals.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many four-digit numbers have at least two digits that are the same? For example, 1231 and 5559 count, but 1234 does not.

choices.misconception: I counted the four-digit numbers whose digits are all different and gave that count instead of the rest.
I counted the numbers with all digits different as 10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5040, letting the first digit be 0, and subtracted that from 9000.
I counted the numbers with all digits different as 9 x 8 x 7 x 6, forgetting that 0 can be used after the first digit.
I subtracted 4536 from 10,000, thinking there are 10,000 four-digit numbers instead of 9000.

hints: It is easier to count the numbers that do not count.
Complementary counting: find how many four-digit numbers have all four digits different, and subtract from the total number of four-digit numbers. Watch out for the digit 0 in the first place.
There are 9000 four-digit numbers. With all digits different, the first digit has 9 choices (not 0), then 9, 8 and 7 choices for the others.

solutions.reliable: Four-digit numbers run from 1000 to 9999, so there are 9000 of them. Count those with all four digits different: the first digit can be 1 to 9 (9 choices), the second any of the 9 digits not yet used (0 is now allowed), the third 8 choices and the fourth 7. That gives 9 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 4536. The rest have at least one repeated digit: 9000 - 4536 = 4464. The transferable idea: when "at least one" invites many cases, count the opposite and subtract.

problems.whyOnTest: At least one questions invite messy casework; the test is seeing that the complement is a single clean product, then handling the zero correctly.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 5 by 5 by 5 cube is made of 125 unit cubes. Three straight tunnels are drilled right through it, each removing one full line of unit cubes and joining the centres of two opposite faces: front to back, top to bottom and left to right. How many unit cubes are removed?

choices.misconception: I added the three tunnels of 5 cubes each without noticing that they cross.
I subtracted one cube for each pair of tunnels, but all three pairs share the same single centre cube.
I saw that the centre cube was counted more than once but subtracted it only once, though it was counted three times.
I worked out how many cubes are left in the big cube instead of how many are removed.

hints: Where do the three tunnels meet?
Each tunnel is a line of 5 cubes, but the lines may share cubes. Add the three lines, then correct for any cube you counted more than once.
All three tunnels pass through the very centre cube, and they share no other cube. That cube was counted three times in 5 + 5 + 5.

solutions.reliable: Each tunnel removes a line of 5 unit cubes, and 3 x 5 = 15 counts every removed cube at least once. The three lines all pass through the centre cube of the big cube and share no other cube. The centre cube was counted three times instead of once, so subtract 2: 15 - 2 = 13. The transferable idea: when shapes overlap, count each piece and then fix every cube that was counted more than once.
solutions.elegant: Count the centre cube once, then each tunnel adds the 4 cubes it has besides the centre: 1 + 3 x 4 = 13.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting cubes in a solid tests careful handling of overlaps, and every wrong choice is a different mistake about the shared centre cube.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle measures 12 cm by 8 cm. A point P is chosen anywhere on its top side, and P is joined to the two bottom corners, making a triangle. What is the total area of the parts of the rectangle outside this triangle?

choices.misconception: I treated the triangle as a quarter of the rectangle, 24 square cm, and subtracted that from 96.
I found the area of only one of the two leftover corner triangles, assuming each is half of what is left.
I thought the triangle and the two pieces beside it each take up a third of the rectangle.

choices.text: It depends on where P is
choices.misconception: I thought sliding P along the top side changes the area of the triangle.

hints: What are the base and the height of the triangle?
Area by subtraction: find the area of the rectangle and the area of the triangle, then subtract. Ask whether the triangle area depends on where P sits.
The triangle has the 12 cm bottom side as its base and the full 8 cm height of the rectangle, wherever P is.

solutions.reliable: The rectangle has area 12 x 8 = 96 square cm. The triangle has base 12 cm (the bottom side) and height 8 cm (from the bottom side up to P), so its area is 12 x 8 / 2 = 48 square cm, wherever P is on the top side. The area outside it is 96 - 48 = 48 square cm. The transferable idea: a shaded region is often the whole minus a shape whose area is easy, even when its position is not fixed.
solutions.elegant: Draw a vertical line from P down to the bottom side. It cuts the rectangle into two smaller rectangles, and the triangle takes exactly half of each. So the triangle is half the rectangle, and so is the outside.

problems.whyOnTest: Area by subtraction rewards noticing that a triangle's area depends only on its base and height, so the free point P does not matter.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A transparent 3 by 3 by 3 box has 27 cube-shaped cells. Some cells are filled with solid cubes, which may float with empty cells below them. Seen straight from the front, from the top and from the right side, each view shows all 9 of its squares dark. What is the smallest number of cubes needed?

choices.misconception: I filled every cell, not seeing that cubes hidden behind other cubes add nothing to any view.
I made the front, top and right-hand faces of the box solid, which uses every cell except the 8 that touch none of those faces.
I filled the bottom layer and then built columns of cubes on one diagonal, believing that was the fewest.
I put 3 cubes along a long diagonal of the box, thinking each one darkens a whole row of every view.

hints: How many squares of the front view can one cube darken?
First find a lower bound: each cube darkens exactly one square of the front view. Then try to reach that bound by placing cubes so that no two line up in any of the three directions.
At least 9 cubes are needed. Try putting 3 cubes in each horizontal layer, with no two in the same row or column, shifting the pattern from layer to layer.

solutions.reliable: Lower bound: the front view has 9 squares, and each cube darkens exactly one of them, so at least 9 cubes are needed. Construction: label cells by (column, depth, layer) and place cubes at (1,1,1), (2,2,1), (3,3,1) in the bottom layer, (1,2,2), (2,3,2), (3,1,2) in the middle layer and (1,3,3), (2,1,3), (3,2,3) in the top layer. In each layer the three cubes use every column and every depth once, so the front and side views are full in every layer; across the three layers every column and depth pair appears once, so the top view is full. So 9 cubes suffice and the answer is 9. The transferable idea: prove a lower bound by counting what each piece can do, then build an example that meets it.
solutions.elegant: Each cube darkens one square in each of the three views, and there are 9 squares per view, so 9 is the least possible if no two cubes ever hide each other. Arranging the cubes like a Latin square in every layer achieves exactly that.

problems.whyOnTest: Views questions at the 5-point level ask for an extreme value, which needs both a bound and an example that reaches it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many points whose coordinates are both whole numbers lie strictly inside the triangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 6), not on any of its sides?

choices.misconception: I included the points on the slanted side, where x + y = 6, as if they were inside.
I included the points on the two sides along the axes, where x or y is 0.
I counted every whole-number point in the triangle, including all the points on its three sides.
I worked out the area of the triangle, 18, and took it as the number of points.

hints: Write down the conditions that a point strictly inside must satisfy.
A point inside has x at least 1, y at least 1, and lies below the slanted side x + y = 6. Count column by column, one value of x at a time.
Strictly inside means x and y are at least 1 and x + y is at most 5. For x = 1 there are 4 values of y.

solutions.reliable: A whole-number point (x, y) is strictly inside when x is at least 1, y is at least 1 and x + y is less than 6, so at most 5. For x = 1, y can be 1 to 4 (4 points); for x = 2, 3 points; x = 3, 2 points; x = 4, 1 point; x = 5, none. Total 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. The transferable idea: turn a region into inequalities and count one column at a time, deciding carefully whether boundary points are in.
solutions.elegant: Pick's theorem gives the same count: the area 18 equals the number of interior points plus half the 18 boundary points minus 1, so the interior count is 18 - 9 + 1 = 10.

problems.whyOnTest: Lattice-point counts test reading strictly inside precisely, and each wrong choice includes a different part of the boundary.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A clock with hands but no numbers hangs opposite a mirror. In the mirror, the clock seems to show 2:40. What time does the clock really show?

choices.misconception: I read the time straight from the mirror image without reversing it.
I reversed the hour hand but kept the minute hand where it looked, at 40 minutes.
I thought a mirror turns the clock half way round, so I added 6 hours.
I worked out 12 - 2 = 10 for the hours and 60 - 40 = 20 for the minutes separately, forgetting to borrow an hour.

hints: Where does the minute hand really point?
A mirror swaps left and right, so each hand is reflected in the line through 12 and 6. Reflect the minute hand first, then work out where the hour hand must be at that minute.
The minute hand really points at the 4, so it is 20 minutes past. The real time and the mirror time always add up to 12 hours.

solutions.reliable: A mirror reflects each hand in the vertical line through 12 and 6. In the mirror the minute hand points at the 8 (40 minutes), so really it points at the 4: 20 minutes past. In the mirror the hour hand is two thirds of the way from 2 to 3, so really it is two thirds of the way from 10 back to 9, which is a third of the way from 9 to 10, as it should be at 20 past 9. The real time is 9:20. Check: 9:20 + 2:40 = 12:00. The transferable idea: a mirror image of a clock shows the time that adds to the real time to make 12 hours.
solutions.elegant: The real time and the mirror time add to 12:00, so the real time is 12:00 - 2:40 = 11:60 - 2:40 = 9:20.

problems.whyOnTest: Mirror clocks test reflecting both hands, and the classic slip is subtracting hours and minutes separately without borrowing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten people sit around a round table. Each is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Every one of them says: "The person on my left is a knave, and the person on my right is a knight." How many knights are at the table?

choices.misconception: I seated knights and knaves alternately, which makes each knight's left neighbour a knave, but I did not check the right neighbour.
I saw that a knight forces the person on its right to be a knight, followed this round the table and stopped one person short of coming back to the start.
I took everyone's statement as true, not noticing that each would then be calling a knight a knave.
I placed a single knight with a knave on its left and assumed everyone else could be a knave, without checking the knight's right neighbour.

hints: Suppose one person is a knight. Who must sit on their right?

If anyone is a knight, both halves of their sentence are true. Follow what that forces around the table, person by person, until you come back to where you started. Then check whether all knaves works.
A knight has a knight on its right, and that knight has a knight on its right, and so on all the way round. But the first knight also needs a knave on its left.

solutions.reliable: Suppose someone is a knight. Then the person on their right is a knight. That person is a knight too, so the person on their right is a knight, and so on all the way round the table: everyone is a knight. But then the first knight's left neighbour is a knight, not a knave, so its statement is false, a contradiction. So nobody is a knight. Check that all knaves works: each knave says the person on the right is a knight, which is false, so the whole sentence is false, as a knave's must be. There are 0 knights. The transferable idea: assume one case, follow what it forces step by step, and look for a contradiction.

problems.whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles test chasing consequences around a cycle; one knight would force a chain that collides with itself.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 9 are written in a 3 by 3 grid, one number in each square. Of the three rows and the three columns, at most how many can have an even sum?

choices.misconception: I assumed the numbers could be arranged so that every row and every column had an even sum.
I saw that the three rows cannot all be even but forgot that the same argument applies to the columns.
I only considered the rows and forgot that the columns count too.
I thought that with five odd numbers to place, at least three of the six lines would have to contain an odd number of odd numbers.

hints: Add up the three row sums. What do you get?
Suppose all three rows had even sums and look for a contradiction with the total of 1 to 9. Then apply the same argument to the columns, and finally check that the bound can actually be reached.
The three row sums add to 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, which is odd, so not all three rows can be even. The same holds for the columns.

solutions.reliable: The three row sums together are 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, which is odd. If all three row sums were even, their total would be even, a contradiction; so at most 2 rows have an even sum. The same argument shows at most 2 columns do. So at most 4 lines are even. This is reached by the grid with rows 1, 3, 2 / 5, 7, 4 / 6, 8, 9: the row sums are 6, 16 and 23, and the column sums are 12, 18 and 15, so two rows and two columns are even. The answer is 4. The transferable idea: assume the best case and show it forces an impossible total, then build an example for the next best case.

problems.whyOnTest: Proof by contradiction shows up as an at most question: assuming the maximum leads to an odd total that cannot be even.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A balance has two pans. You have three weights: 1 g, 3 g and 8 g. The object goes on one pan, and each weight can go on either pan or be left off. How many different whole-number masses, in grams, can be weighed exactly in a single weighing?

choices.misconception: I only put weights on the pan opposite the object, which gives just the 7 different totals of the weights.
I allowed one weight against one other weight but never two weights against one, so I missed 6 and 10.
I counted the 27 ways to place the weights, removed the empty one and halved for mirror images, without checking that every result is different.
I counted every way of placing each weight left, right or off, apart from all off, without noticing that many give a repeated or negative mass.

hints: A weight on the same pan as the object counts as a minus.

Each mass you can weigh is a total of the form plus or minus 1, plus or minus 3, plus or minus 8, with some weights left out. List the positive totals systematically, starting with the masses up to 12.
The heaviest mass is 1 + 3 + 8 = 12. Check each of 1 to 12: for example 2 = 3 - 1, 5 = 8 - 3, 6 = 8 + 1 - 3 and 10 = 8 + 3 - 1.

solutions.reliable: Putting a weight beside the object subtracts it, so the masses you can weigh are the positive values of a x 1 + b x 3 + c x 8 where each of a, b, c is 1, 0 or -1. The largest is 12. Going through 1 to 12: 1, 2 = 3 - 1, 3, 4 = 3 + 1, 5 = 8 - 3, 6 = 8 + 1 - 3, 7 = 8 - 1, 8, 9 = 8 + 1, 10 = 8 + 3 - 1, 11 = 8 + 3 and 12 = 8 + 3 + 1. Every whole number from 1 to 12 works and nothing larger does, so 12 masses. The transferable idea: in balance puzzles a weight on the object's pan subtracts, which turns sums into signed sums.
solutions.elegant: The weights 1 and 3 alone give every mass from -4 to 4. Adding 8 on the other side then covers 4 to 12, and 1 to 4 are already covered, so every mass from 1 to 12 is possible.

problems.whyOnTest: Balance puzzles test seeing that weights on both pans subtract as well as add, which roughly doubles what a small set can measure.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two friends start together from the same point on a circular track 600 m long. One walks at 2 m per second and the other runs at 4 m per second, in opposite directions around the track. After how many seconds do they first meet?

choices.misconception: I used the difference of the two speeds, as if they were going the same way round.
I used only the runner's speed, as if the walker stood still.
I thought they meet when together they have covered half the track.
I averaged the two speeds to 3 m per second and divided the track length by that.

hints: Together, how much of the track have they covered when they meet?
When two people move towards each other, the gap between them closes at the sum of their speeds. Here the gap to close is the whole length of the track.
They close the 600 m gap at 2 + 4 = 6 m every second.

solutions.reliable: Moving in opposite directions, they first meet when the distances they have covered add up to the full 600 m. Together they cover 2 + 4 = 6 m each second, so they meet after 600 / 6 = 100 seconds. Check: the walker has gone 200 m and the runner 400 m, which add to 600 m. The transferable idea: when two movers approach each other, add their speeds; when one chases the other, subtract them.

problems.whyOnTest: Meeting questions test whether speeds should be added or subtracted, and each wrong choice uses the wrong combination.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A school takes 148 people on a trip. A coach seats 40 people and costs 300 euros to hire; a minibus seats 15 people and costs 130 euros. Everyone must have a seat. What is the lowest possible total cost?

choices.misconception: I used coaches only, since they are cheaper per seat, and needed 4 of them.
I divided 148 by 40 to get 3.7 coaches and paid 3.7 x 300, as if part of a coach could be hired.
I hired 3 coaches and 1 minibus, which seat only 135 people, forgetting the last 13.
I used minibuses only and needed 10 of them.

hints: Coaches are cheaper per seat, but empty seats still cost money.
Try each possible number of coaches, from 4 down to 0, and for each one work out how many minibuses are needed to seat the rest. Compare the totals.
Three coaches seat 120, leaving 28 people, who need 2 minibuses. Compare that with 4 coaches.

solutions.reliable: Go through the number of coaches. 4 coaches seat 160: cost 1200. 3 coaches seat 120, and the other 28 people need 2 minibuses: cost 900 + 260 = 1160. 2 coaches seat 80, and the other 68 need 5 minibuses: cost 600 + 650 = 1250. 1 coach and 8 minibuses: 300 + 1040 = 1340. No coaches and 10 minibuses: 1300. The lowest is 1160 euros. The transferable idea: when vehicles come in whole units, list the few combinations and compare, rather than trusting the cheapest rate.

problems.whyOnTest: Multi-step word problems test rounding up to whole vehicles and comparing options, rather than trusting the best price per seat.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Matchsticks are used to build a large triangle divided into small triangles. A triangle of side 1 uses 3 matches, a triangle of side 2 (made of 4 small triangles) uses 9 matches, and a triangle of side 3 (made of 9 small triangles) uses 18 matches. How many matches does a triangle of side 10 use?

choices.misconception: I counted only the matches around the outside of the triangle, 3 x 10.
I assumed the count goes up by 6 each time, as it does from side 1 to side 2.
I used 3 x 10 x 10 / 2 instead of 3 x 10 x 11 / 2.
I added 1 + 2 + ... + 11 instead of 1 + 2 + ... + 10, then multiplied by 3.

hints: Sort the matches by the direction they point.
Every match lies in one of three directions. Count the matches lying flat, row by row, and use symmetry for the other two directions. Check your rule against sides 1, 2 and 3.
In a triangle of side n, the flat matches come in rows of 1, 2, ..., n. The same is true in each of the other two directions.

solutions.reliable: Each match points in one of three directions. In a triangle of side n, the horizontal matches form rows of 1, 2, 3, ..., n, so there are 1 + 2 + ... + n of them, and by symmetry the same number point in each of the other two directions. So the total is 3 x (1 + 2 + ... + n). Check: n = 3 gives 3 x 6 = 18. For n = 10 the total is 3 x 55 = 165. The transferable idea: count a growing figure by sorting its pieces into types, then check the formula on the small cases you were given.
solutions.elegant: The counts go 3, 9, 18, ..., increasing by 6, 9, 12, ..., so the side-10 count is 3 + 6 + 9 + ... + 30 = 3 x (1 + 2 + ... + 10) = 165.

problems.whyOnTest: Growth patterns test finding a rule that fits every given stage, and the traps are extending the first jump or slipping by one row.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A machine takes two numbers and gives back one, always by the same rule. It turns 2 and 3 into 13, it turns 1 and 4 into 17, and it turns 3 and 1 into 10. What does it turn 5 and 2 into?

choices.misconception: I guessed the rule involved squaring but squared the sum 5 + 2 instead of adding the two separate squares.
I subtracted the square of the second number from the square of the first instead of adding them.
I found a rule that fits only the first example, multiply the numbers and add 7, and used it to get 5 x 2 + 7.
I fitted only the first example with 2 times the first number plus 3 times the second, which gives 10 + 6.

hints: Check any rule you guess against all three examples.
A rule is only right if it fits every example, not just the first. Try combining the squares of the two numbers, then test your idea on all three pairs before using it.
2 x 2 + 3 x 3 = 13, 1 x 1 + 4 x 4 = 17 and 3 x 3 + 1 x 1 = 10. Each output is the sum of the two squares.

solutions.reliable: Test the idea of adding squares: 4 + 9 = 13, 1 + 16 = 17 and 9 + 1 = 10, so the rule fits all three examples. For 5 and 2 the machine gives 25 + 4 = 29. Other rules that fit the first example, such as multiplying and adding 7, fail on the second (1 x 4 + 7 = 11, not 17). The transferable idea: a guessed rule is only a rule once it fits every example you are given.

problems.whyOnTest: Rule-finding questions punish fitting only the first example; the test is checking a guess against every case before using it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: From a tree, Rosa walks 3 km north, then 4 km east, then 6 km south, then 8 km west. How far is she now from the tree, in a straight line?

choices.misconception: I added up all four distances she walked instead of finding how far she ended from the tree.
I found she ended 3 km south and 4 km west of the tree, then added those two distances instead of using the straight line.
I added the north and south distances and the east and west distances instead of subtracting opposite directions, then used a right triangle with sides 9 and 12.
I used only the last two legs, 6 and 8, as the sides of a right triangle.

hints: Sketch her path and mark where she ends.
Draw the walk on a grid with the tree at the start. Opposite directions cancel, so find how far south and how far west she ends up, then join her end point straight to the tree.
North 3 then south 6 leaves her 3 km south; east 4 then west 8 leaves her 4 km west. The straight line is the long side of a right triangle with sides 3 and 4.

solutions.reliable: Treat north-south and east-west separately. Going 3 km north and then 6 km south leaves Rosa 3 km south of the tree. Going 4 km east and then 8 km west leaves her 4 km west. Her straight-line distance is the long side of a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, which is 5 km, since 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 25 = 5 x 5. The transferable idea: when directions are described in words, draw them; opposite moves cancel and the picture shows the triangle.

problems.whyOnTest: Direction problems are easy once drawn, and the wrong choices come from adding legs that should cancel or skipping the sketch.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sheet of paper is cut into 3 pieces. Then one of the pieces is cut into 3 pieces, then one of the pieces is cut into 3, and so on: each cut turns one piece into 3. After 20 cuts in total, how many pieces are there?

choices.misconception: I thought each cut makes 3 pieces, so 20 cuts make 3 x 20.
I added 3 pieces for every cut to the 1 sheet I started with.
I saw that each cut adds 2 pieces but forgot to count the sheet I started with.
I thought each cut adds one more piece, as when a piece is cut in two.

hints: Count the pieces after 1, 2 and 3 cuts.
Try small cases first: work out the number of pieces after the first few cuts and look at how much each cut changes the count. Then extend that pattern to 20 cuts.
After 1 cut there are 3 pieces, after 2 cuts 5, after 3 cuts 7. Each cut removes one piece and adds three.

solutions.reliable: Small cases: 0 cuts give 1 piece, 1 cut gives 3, 2 cuts give 5, 3 cuts give 7. Each cut takes away one piece and puts back three, a gain of 2. After 20 cuts there are 1 + 2 x 20 = 41 pieces. The transferable idea: when a process repeats many times, run it two or three times by hand and find how much each step changes the count.
solutions.elegant: The number of pieces is always odd and grows by 2 each cut, so after n cuts it is 2n + 1, and 2 x 20 + 1 = 41.

problems.whyOnTest: Large repeated processes are a signal to try small cases first; the traps are counting pieces made instead of pieces gained, or forgetting the start.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is equal to 47 x 53 x 61?

choices.misconception: I multiplied 2491 by 60 and forgot to add the last 2491 needed to make 61 lots.
I multiplied 2491 by 6 instead of 60 and then added 2491, losing a place value.
I worked out 47 x 53 as 2500 + 9 = 2509 instead of 2500 - 9, then multiplied by 61.
I rounded 47 x 53 to 50 x 50 = 2500 and multiplied that by 61.

hints: You may not need to multiply at all: look at the last digits.
Eliminate choices with cheap checks: a product of odd numbers is odd, its last digit comes only from the last digits of the factors, and its size is close to 50 x 50 x 60.
The last digit is the last digit of 7 x 3 x 1, which is 1. Only one choice ends in 1.

solutions.reliable: Multiply carefully: 47 x 53 = 2491 (it is 50 x 50 - 3 x 3), and 2491 x 61 = 2491 x 60 + 2491 = 149,460 + 2491 = 151,951. The transferable idea: before grinding through a long calculation, check whether a quick test like the last digit already picks out the answer.
solutions.elegant: The last digit of the product is the last digit of 7 x 3 x 1 = 21, which is 1. Of the choices, only 151,951 ends in 1, so no long multiplication is needed. Its size also fits the estimate 50 x 50 x 60 = 150,000.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo rewards checking choices against cheap facts like parity, last digit and size before doing long arithmetic.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

choices.misconception: I thought the two products were equal because both pairs of numbers add up to 2000.
I saw that the products are 1000 x 1000 - 1 and 1000 x 1000 - 4, but subtracted the wrong way round.
I saw that the products are 1000 x 1000 - 1 and 1000 x 1000 - 4, but added the 1 and the 4 instead of subtracting.
I took the answer to be the change in how far apart the numbers are, from 2 apart to 4 apart.

hints: Both pairs of numbers sit evenly around 1000.
The numbers are suspiciously close to 1000, which is a signal to look for a trick before grinding. Write each factor as 1000 plus or minus a small number and multiply out.

solutions.reliable: Grinding works: 999 x 1001 = 999,999 and 998 x 1002 = 999,996, and the difference is 3. The quicker way is to see that both pairs are centred on 1000. Then 999 x 1001 = 1000 x 1000 - 1 x 1 = 999,999 and 998 x 1002 = 1000 x 1000 - 2 x 2 = 999,996, so the difference is 4 - 1 = 3. The transferable idea: when the numbers are suspiciously close to a round number, spend ten seconds looking for the trick before you start long multiplication.
solutions.elegant: For two numbers placed symmetrically around 1000, the product is 1000 x 1000 minus the square of their distance from 1000. The distances are 1 and 2, so the answer is 2 x 2 - 1 x 1 = 3.

problems.whyOnTest: Some questions are built to be ground out slowly or seen at once; the test is spotting the structure that makes the big numbers cancel.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each question on a test has 5 choices, scores 5 points if correct and loses nothing if wrong. Sam has 10 questions left and no time. On 6 he can rule out 3 wrong choices; on the other 4 he can rule out nothing. If he guesses on all 10, how many points should he expect on average?

choices.misconception: I thought a guess is as likely to cost points as to earn them, so on average guessing gains nothing.
I gave every guess a 1 in 5 chance, ignoring the choices Sam can rule out.
I only counted the 6 questions where he narrowed it down to two choices and left out the other 4.
I counted every guess as a correct answer.

hints: How many choices are left on each kind of question?
Since a wrong answer costs nothing, each guess is worth its chance of being right times 5 points. Work out that average for each kind of question and add them up.
With two choices left, a guess is worth half of 5 points, 2.5 on average. With all five choices left, it is worth a fifth of 5 points, 1 on average.

solutions.reliable: On the 6 questions with two choices left, each guess is right half the time, worth 5 / 2 = 2.5 points on average, so 6 x 2.5 = 15 points. On the 4 questions with all five choices, each guess is right one time in five, worth 1 point on average, so 4 points. Altogether Sam expects 15 + 4 = 19 points, compared with 0 for leaving them blank. The transferable idea: with no penalty, a guess is never worse than a blank, and ruling out choices makes it worth much more.

problems.whyOnTest: With no penalty for wrong answers, every blank throws away points; this checks that you can value a guess after ruling out choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular sign is 1.2 m long and 40 cm wide. What is its area in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I multiplied 1.2 by 40 without changing the metres into centimetres.
I worked in metres and gave the area in square metres, not in square centimetres.
I found the perimeter in centimetres instead of the area.
I changed 1.2 m into 12 cm instead of 120 cm.

hints: Put both lengths in the same unit before multiplying.
Re-read what is asked: area, in square centimetres. Convert the length to centimetres first, remembering that 1 m is 100 cm, then multiply.
1.2 m is 120 cm, so the area is 120 x 40 square centimetres.

solutions.reliable: Convert first: 1.2 m = 120 cm. The area is 120 x 40 = 4800 square centimetres. Check: in metres the area is 1.2 x 0.4 = 0.48 square metres, and 1 square metre is 10,000 square centimetres, which again gives 4800. The transferable idea: before choosing an answer, check that it is the quantity asked for and in the unit asked for.

problems.whyOnTest: Unit slips cost easy points: every wrong choice here is a correct calculation of the wrong thing or in the wrong unit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: With 20 minutes left, Lina reaches the last eight questions: each is worth 5 points, has 5 choices and costs nothing if wrong. They would take her 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 14 and 15 minutes. She solves as many as she can in time, all correctly, and guesses the rest. What is her expected score on these eight?

choices.misconception: I counted only the questions she solves and left the other five blank instead of guessing.
I gave each guess one fifth of a point instead of one fifth of 5 points.
I counted every one of the eight questions as worth 5 points, whether solved or guessed.
I thought she also had time for the 8-minute question after the 3, 5 and 6 minute ones.

hints: To solve as many as possible, which questions should she pick?
Pick the quickest questions first until the time runs out, and check that no other choice fits more into 20 minutes. Then add the average value of the guesses on the rest.
The three quickest take 3 + 5 + 6 = 14 minutes, and any four take at least 22. Each guess is right one time in five.

solutions.reliable: To fit the most questions into 20 minutes she should take the quickest ones: 3 + 5 + 6 = 14 minutes. Any four questions take at least 3 + 5 + 6 + 8 = 22 minutes, so she can solve at most 3, worth 15 points. She guesses the other 5, and each guess earns 5 points one time in five, which is 1 point on average, so 5 more points. Her expected score is 15 + 5 = 20. The transferable idea: in the 5-point block, read everything first, take the quickest wins, and never leave the rest blank.

problems.whyOnTest: The 5-point block is won by choosing which questions to solve and guessing the rest, so this checks both the choosing and the guessing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three consecutive even numbers add up to 78. What do you get when you multiply the smallest of the three by the largest?

choices.misconception: I found the middle number, 26, and stopped there instead of answering the question that was asked.
I used consecutive numbers 25, 26 and 27 instead of consecutive even numbers, so I multiplied 25 by 27.
I thought the smallest times the largest is the same as the middle number squared, $26 \times 26$.
I divided 78 by 3 and took 26 as the smallest number, so I used 26, 28 and 30 and multiplied 26 by 30.

hints: Find the three numbers first, then reread what the question wants.
Three evenly spaced numbers have their mean in the middle. Once you have the middle one, step 2 down and 2 up, then do exactly what the last sentence asks.
The middle number is $78 \div 3 = 26$, so the numbers are 24, 26 and 28. Now multiply the smallest by the largest.

solutions.reliable: The three numbers are evenly spaced, so the middle one is their mean: $78 \div 3 = 26$. The numbers are 24, 26 and 28 (check: $24 + 26 + 28 = 78$). The question asks for the smallest times the largest: $24 \times 28 = 672$. The transferable idea: after finding the natural quantity, reread the last sentence, because the question often asks for one more step.
solutions.elegant: With middle number 26, the product is $(26 - 2)(26 + 2) = 26^2 - 4 = 676 - 4 = 672$. This also shows why 676, the square of the middle number, is close but wrong.

problems.whyOnTest: The natural answer, the middle number, is not what is asked: this tests reading the final question before bubbling.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangular pool measures 12 m by 5 m. A path 1 m wide runs all the way around the outside of the pool. What is the area of the path, in square metres?

choices.misconception: I added 1 m to the length and to the width instead of 2 m, so I worked out $13 \times 6 - 60 = 18$.
I multiplied the pool's perimeter, 34 m, by the 1 m width and forgot the four corner squares of the path.
I multiplied the outer perimeter, 42 m, by the 1 m width, which counts each corner square twice.
I found the area of the whole outer rectangle, $14 \times 7$, and forgot to take away the pool.

hints: Sketch the pool with the path around it and label the outer measurements.
Draw the diagram: the path is the big outer rectangle minus the pool. Work out how much the path adds to each side length, remembering that it sits on both sides.
The outer rectangle is 14 m by 7 m, because the path adds 1 m at each end. Subtract the pool's $12 \times 5$.

solutions.reliable: The path adds 1 m at both ends of each side, so the outer rectangle is $12 + 2 = 14$ m by $5 + 2 = 7$ m, with area $14 \times 7 = 98$ square metres. The pool covers $12 \times 5 = 60$ square metres. The path is $98 - 60 = 38$ square metres. The transferable idea: a quick sketch with the numbers written on it shows that the path sticks out past the pool at both ends.
solutions.elegant: Split the path into pieces: two long strips $12 \times 1$, two short strips $5 \times 1$ and four $1 \times 1$ corner squares. That is $24 + 10 + 4 = 38$, and the sketch makes the four corners impossible to forget.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing the path around the pool exposes the corner squares, which is exactly where most mental answers go wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The number $N$ is written with thirty 3s: $N = 333\ldots3$. What is the sum of the digits of $N \times N$?

choices.misconception: I tried only the smallest case, $3 \times 3 = 9$, and assumed the digit sum stays 9 for any number of 3s.
I thought the digit sum of $N \times N$ is the same as the digit sum of $N$, which is $30 \times 3 = 90$.
I saw the pattern of ones, a 0, eights and a final 9, with 29 ones and 29 eights, but I left out the final 9: $29 + 29 \times 8 = 261$.
I thought $N \times N$ has 30 ones and 30 eights before the final 9, so I got $30 + 240 + 9 = 279$.

hints: Work out $3^2$, $33^2$ and $333^2$ before thinking about thirty 3s.
Try small cases first: square the numbers made of one, two, three and four 3s, add up the digits of each result, and look for a rule linking the digit sum to the number of 3s.
$33^2 = 1089$, $333^2 = 110889$ and $3333^2 = 11108889$. The digit sums are 9, 18, 27 and 36: always 9 times the number of 3s.

solutions.reliable: Small cases: $3^2 = 9$ (digit sum 9), $33^2 = 1089$ (18), $333^2 = 110889$ (27), $3333^2 = 11108889$ (36). With $k$ threes, the square is $k - 1$ ones, then a 0, then $k - 1$ eights, then a 9, so its digit sum is $(k - 1) + 8(k - 1) + 9 = 9k$. For $k = 30$ the digit sum is $9 \times 30 = 270$. The transferable idea: when a problem is far too big to calculate, do the sizes 1, 2, 3 and 4 and let the pattern do the work.
solutions.elegant: There is no shortcut that beats the small cases here, but one more case makes the rule safe to trust: $33333^2 = 1111088889$, with digit sum $4 + 0 + 32 + 9 = 45 = 9 \times 5$. So thirty 3s give $9 \times 30 = 270$.

problems.whyOnTest: Nobody can square a 30-digit number in a contest; the problem rewards trying 3, 33 and 333 and spotting the rule.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A shop sells pencils in small packs of 3 for 2 euros and in big packs of 5 for 3 euros. Tom bought 41 pencils and paid 26 euros. How many big packs did he buy?

choices.misconception: I used only the money: 4 small packs and 6 big packs cost 26 euros, and I did not check that they hold 42 pencils, not 41.
I worked out the packs correctly but gave the number of small packs instead of the number of big packs.
I used only the money: 1 small pack and 8 big packs cost 26 euros, and I did not check that they hold 43 pencils.
I found 7 small packs and 4 big packs and then gave the total number of packs.

hints: Each answer choice is a number of big packs. Test one.
Back-solve: pick a choice for the number of big packs, work out how many pencils are left for small packs, and check whether the cost comes to 26 euros. Both conditions must hold.

Try 7 big packs: 35 pencils, leaving 6 pencils for 2 small packs, costing $21 + 4 = 25$ euros, 1 euro short. Choices 6 and 8 leave a number of pencils that small packs cannot make, and 11 big packs are already too many pencils. Check 4.

solutions.reliable: Test the choices. 11 big packs hold 55 pencils, too many. 8 big packs leave 1 pencil and 6 big packs leave 11 pencils, and neither is a whole number of packs of 3. 7 big packs leave 6 pencils, so 2 small packs, costing $7 \times 3 + 2 \times 2 = 25$ euros, not 26. 4 big packs leave 21 pencils, so 7 small packs, costing $4 \times 3 + 7 \times 2 = 12 + 14 = 26$ euros. So Tom bought 4 big packs. The transferable idea: when solving forwards needs two equations, testing the five choices is often faster and safer.
solutions.elegant: Forwards: with $s$ small and $b$ big packs, $3s + 5b = 41$ and $2s + 3b = 26$. Doubling the first gives $6s + 10b = 82$ and tripling the second gives $6s + 9b = 78$. Subtracting, $b = 4$, and then $s = 7$.

problems.whyOnTest: Two conditions must both hold; testing the choices against both is quicker than algebra and catches answers that satisfy only one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is equal to $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{7}$?

choices.misconception: I added the tops and added the bottoms, getting $\frac{6}{27} = \frac{2}{9}$.
I used 840 as the common denominator but changed each fraction as if the denominator were 420, so I got $\frac{669}{840} = \frac{223}{280}$.
I lost the $\frac{1}{2}$ while rewriting over a common denominator and added only $\frac{1}{3}$ up to $\frac{1}{7}$.
I lost the $\frac{1}{7}$ and added only $\frac{1}{2}$ up to $\frac{1}{6}$, which gives $\frac{29}{20}$.

hints: Before adding, ask roughly how big the total must be.
Bound it: the first three fractions are easy to add exactly, and each of the last three lies between $\frac{1}{7}$ and $\frac{1}{5}$. That traps the sum between two numbers, and only one choice fits.
$\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{13}{12}$, and the last three add to between $\frac{3}{7}$ and $\frac{3}{5}$. So the sum is between about 1.51 and 1.68.

solutions.reliable: First, $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{13}{12} \approx 1.08$. Each of $\frac{1}{5}$, $\frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{7}$ is at least $\frac{1}{7}$ and at most $\frac{1}{5}$, so together they are between $\frac{3}{7} \approx 0.43$ and $\frac{3}{5} = 0.6$. The sum is therefore between about 1.51 and 1.68. Now $\frac{2}{9} \approx 0.22$, $\frac{223}{280} \approx 0.80$, $\frac{153}{140} \approx 1.09$ and $\frac{29}{20} = 1.45$ are all too small, which leaves $\frac{223}{140} \approx 1.59$. An exact check over 420: $210 + 140 + 105 + 84 + 70 + 60 = 669$, and $\frac{669}{420} = \frac{223}{140}$. The transferable idea: a rough lower and upper bound can remove four choices without any exact arithmetic.
solutions.elegant: Only a lower bound is needed: the sum is more than $\frac{13}{12} + \frac{3}{7}$, which is more than 1.5, and only one choice is bigger than 1.5.

problems.whyOnTest: Exact addition over 420 is slow and error-prone; bounding the sum between 1.5 and 1.7 picks the answer in seconds.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A circular running track has a diameter of 64 m. Which of these is closest to the distance, in kilometres, that a runner covers in 5 laps?

choices.misconception: I forgot about $\pi$ and just multiplied the diameter by 5, getting 320 m.
I worked out each lap as $\pi$ times the radius, $3.14 \times 32$, which gave about 500 m for 5 laps.
I treated 64 m as the radius, so I worked out $2 \times 3.14 \times 64 \times 5$, about 2000 m.
I got about 1000 m but divided by 100 instead of 1000 to change metres into kilometres.

hints: One lap is the distance around the circle. Round $\pi$ to 3.
Estimate to the nearest choice: the choices are far apart, so use $\pi \approx 3$ for the distance around, multiply by the number of laps, then change metres into kilometres carefully.
One lap is about $3 \times 64 \approx 190$ m, so 5 laps are about 960 m.

solutions.reliable: One lap is the circumference, $\pi \times 64 \approx 3.14 \times 64 \approx 201$ m. Five laps are about $5 \times 201 = 1005$ m, which is about 1.005 km. The closest choice is 1. The transferable idea: when the choices differ by large factors, a rough estimate with $\pi \approx 3$ is enough to decide.
solutions.elegant: With $\pi \approx 3$: $3 \times 64 \times 5 = 960$ m, just under 1 km. The neighbouring choices, 0.5 and 2, are a factor of 2 away, far more than the rounding error.

problems.whyOnTest: The choices are so far apart that an estimate with pi about 3 decides it; the traps are radius and diameter mix-ups and unit slips.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the value of $1^2 - 2^2 - 3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2 - 6^2 - 7^2 + 8^2 + \dots + 97^2 - 98^2 - 99^2 + 100^2$? The signs repeat in the pattern plus, minus, minus, plus.

choices.misconception: I ignored the squares and worked out $1 - 2 - 3 + 4 = 0$ for each group of four, so I thought everything cancels.
I found that the first group, $1 - 4 - 9 + 16$, equals 4, and gave that as the answer.
I counted the 25 groups of four and gave the number of groups as the answer.
I found that each group of four adds to 4, but then multiplied 4 by the 100 terms instead of by the 25 groups.

hints: Work out the first group of four, then the second group of four.
Spot the trick rather than grind: a hundred squares is far too slow. Group the terms in fours, following the sign pattern, and check whether every group has the same value.

solutions.reliable: Group the terms in fours: $(1^2 - 2^2 - 3^2 + 4^2) + (5^2 - 6^2 - 7^2 + 8^2) + \dots$. The first group is $1 - 4 - 9 + 16 = 4$ and the second is $25 - 36 - 49 + 64 = 4$. Expanding shows this always happens: $n^2 - (n^2 + 2n + 1) - (n^2 + 4n + 4) + (n^2 + 6n + 9) = 4$. The 100 terms make 25 groups, so the total is $25 \times 4 = 100$. The transferable idea: when the long calculation is hopeless, spend a minute hunting for a repeating block before deciding to grind.
solutions.elegant: Use differences of neighbouring squares inside each group: $(n+3)^2 - (n+2)^2 = 2n + 5$ and $n^2 - (n+1)^2 = -(2n + 1)$. These add to 4 for every group, so 25 groups give 100.

problems.whyOnTest: Grinding fifty pluses and minuses of squares is hopeless; the problem tests deciding quickly to look for a repeating block.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Zoe has 30 minutes left and six unstarted questions. She would solve each correctly in this time: P (3 points, 4 min), Q (3 points, 6 min), R (4 points, 9 min), S (4 points, 14 min), T (5 points, 5 min), U (5 points, 11 min). Counting only questions she finishes, what is the most points she can score?

choices.misconception: I did the 5-point questions first, then the 4-point ones, and stopped as soon as the next one did not fit: T, U and R make 14 points.
I did the quickest questions first, P, T, Q and R, and stopped when U no longer fitted, which gives 15 points.
I picked the questions with the most points per minute first, T, P, Q and then U, which left too little time for R and gave 16 points.
I left out only the slowest question, S, and did not check that the other five take 35 minutes, which is more than 30.

hints: She cannot do all six. Think about which questions to leave out.
Time triage: all six take 49 minutes, so at least 19 minutes of questions must be skipped. Find the set of skipped questions that frees enough time while losing as few points as possible.
Skipping one question frees at most 14 minutes, so at least two must go. Compare the pairs that free 19 minutes or more by the points they cost.

solutions.reliable: All six take $4 + 6 + 9 + 14 + 5 + 11 = 49$ minutes, so questions worth at least 19 minutes must be left out, losing as few of the 24 available points as possible. One question frees at most 14 minutes, so at least two must go. The pairs that free 19 minutes or more are S and Q (20 min, 7 points), S and T (19 min, 9 points), S and R (23 min, 8 points), S and U (25 min, 9 points) and R and U (20 min, 9 points). The cheapest is S and Q. Leaving out three questions loses at least $3 + 3 + 4 = 10$ points, which is worse. So Zoe does P, R, T and U: 29 minutes and $3 + 4 + 5 + 5 = 17$ points. The transferable idea: deciding what to skip is a calculation in its own right, and simple rules like biggest first or quickest first can cost points.
solutions.elegant: Think about what to skip rather than what to do. S is by far the worst value, under 0.3 points per minute, so drop it; then 35 minutes of work remain for 30 minutes of time, and the cheapest way to free 5 more minutes is to drop Q (3 points, 6 minutes). That leaves 17 points.

problems.whyOnTest: Choosing which questions to leave is a real exam skill; the greedy rules students use each lose at least a point here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On the last four questions of a test, each with 5 choices, Mia has no idea of the answers. Wrong answers cost nothing, so she guesses at random on all four instead of leaving them blank. What is the probability that she gets at least one of them right?

choices.misconception: I worked out the chance of getting all four right, $\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^4$, instead of at least one.
I thought each guess has a 1 in 5 chance, so the chance for the four questions together is also 1 in 5.
I found the chance that all four guesses are wrong, $\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^4$, and forgot to take it away from 1.
I added $\frac{1}{5}$ four times, which counts the outcomes with two or more right answers more than once.

hints: 'At least one right' has many cases. What is the only case that fails?
Use the complement: find the chance that every guess is wrong, then subtract it from 1. The four guesses are independent, so their chances multiply.
Each guess is wrong with probability $\frac{4}{5}$, so all four are wrong with probability $\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^4 = \frac{256}{625}$.

solutions.reliable: Each guess is wrong with probability $\frac{4}{5}$. All four are wrong with probability $\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{256}{625}$. Every other outcome has at least one right answer, so the probability is $1 - \frac{256}{625} = \frac{369}{625}$, a little more than a half. The transferable idea: four blind guesses with no penalty give better than an even chance of at least one extra correct answer, so a blank is never the better choice.
solutions.elegant: Count outcomes: the four answers can be filled in $5^4 = 625$ ways, and $4^4 = 256$ of them avoid every correct choice. So $625 - 256 = 369$ of the 625 equally likely ways get at least one right.

problems.whyOnTest: With no penalty, guessing has only upside; this puts a number on it using the complement of all wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A leaking tap drips once every 2 seconds, and 20 drops make 1 millilitre. How many litres of water drip from the tap in one day?

choices.misconception: I worked out the water for one hour, 1800 drops or 90 millilitres, and forgot to multiply by 24.
I counted one drop every second instead of one drop every 2 seconds.
I thought 1 litre is 100 millilitres, so I divided 2160 by 100.
I got 2160 millilitres and forgot to change millilitres into litres.

hints: How many seconds are there in a day?
Check units: go from seconds to drops, from drops to millilitres, then from millilitres to litres. Write the unit after every number so the last step is not skipped.
A day has $24 \times 3600 = 86\,400$ seconds, so there are $43\,200$ drops, which is $43\,200 \div 20 = 2160$ millilitres.

solutions.reliable: A day has $24 \times 60 \times 60 = 86\,400$ seconds. One drop every 2 seconds gives $43\,200$ drops. At 20 drops per millilitre that is $43\,200 \div 20 = 2160$ millilitres. Since 1 litre is 1000 millilitres, this is 2.16 litres. The transferable idea: before bubbling, ask whether the number is in the unit the question asked for.
solutions.elegant: Work per hour to keep the numbers small: 1800 drops, which is 90 millilitres. Per day: $24 \times 90 = 2160$ millilitres, which is 2.16 litres.

problems.whyOnTest: Every step is easy; the marks are lost by stopping at millilitres or at one hour, so this tests the final units check.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The price of a bike was raised by 25%. Later, the new price was lowered by 20%. The bike now costs 240 euros. What was its price before both changes?
