choices.misconception: I undid only the 25% rise, $240 \div 1.25 = 192$, and forgot about the 20% cut.
I undid the changes by adding 20% to 240, which gave 288, and then taking 25% off 288.
I combined the two changes into a 5% rise and took 5% off 240.
I undid only the 20% cut, $240 \div 0.8 = 300$, and forgot about the 25% rise.

hints: Undo the last change first, then the one before it.
Work backwards, then sanity-check with a second method: push your answer forwards through both changes and see whether you land on 240 euros.
A 20% cut multiplies the price by 0.8 and a 25% rise multiplies it by 1.25. What is $1.25 \times 0.8$?

solutions.reliable: Working backwards: before the 20% cut the price was $240 \div 0.8 = 300$ euros, and before the 25% rise it was $300 \div 1.25 = 240$ euros. A second method confirms it: start from 240, raise it by 25% to 300, then lower that by 20%; 20% of 300 is 60, giving 240 again. So the original price was 240 euros. The transferable idea: when an answer looks surprising, check it a different way, for example by plugging it back in, instead of rereading the first method.
solutions.elegant: The two changes multiply the price by $1.25 \times 0.8 = 1$, so together they change nothing, and the price before was the same 240 euros.

problems.whyOnTest: The answer looks too simple to be right, so a forward check is what gives the confidence to bubble it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five houses stand in a row. Each house is painted one of 3 colours, and any two houses next to each other must be different colours. In how many different ways can the row be painted?

choices.misconception: I multiplied $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2$ and missed one of the five houses.
I gave every house 2 choices, $2^5$, forgetting that the first house can be any of the 3 colours.
I added the choices, $3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2$, instead of multiplying them.
I ignored the rule about neighbours and counted $3^5$ ways.

hints: Paint the houses one at a time, from left to right.
The multiplication principle: count the colour choices for each house in turn, given the house just before it, then multiply, because all the choices happen together.
The first house has 3 choices. Every later house only has to differ from the house on its left, so it has 2 choices.

solutions.reliable: Paint from left to right. The first house can be any of 3 colours. Each later house must differ from its left neighbour, which leaves 2 choices whatever happened before. So there are $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 48$ ways. The transferable idea: when choices are made one after another and the number of options at each step is fixed, multiply.
solutions.elegant: Check with small cases: 2 houses give $3 \times 2 = 6$ ways, which is easy to list, and each extra house doubles the count, so 5 houses give $6 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 48$.

problems.whyOnTest: Neighbour rules look as if they need casework, but each house only has to avoid one colour, so the multiplication principle applies.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five students, including Ana and Ben, stand in a row for a photo. In how many of the possible orders is Ana somewhere to the left of Ben? (They do not have to stand next to each other.)

choices.misconception: I chose the 2 places for Ana and Ben, 10 ways, but forgot that the other three students can stand in different orders.
I only counted orders where Ana stands right next to Ben on his left, treating them as one block: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$.
I took all 120 orders and removed the 48 orders where Ana and Ben stand next to each other.
I counted all the possible orders of the five students and forgot the condition about Ana and Ben.

hints: First ignore Ana and Ben: how many orders of the five students are there?
Arrangements of a few objects: count all the orders of five students, then use the symmetry between Ana and Ben instead of listing cases.
There are $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$ orders. Swapping Ana and Ben turns every order with Ana on the left into one with Ana on the right.

solutions.reliable: Choose the 2 places for Ana and Ben: there are 10 pairs of places, and in each pair Ana must take the left place, so there is only 1 way to put them in. The other three students fill the remaining 3 places in $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ ways. That gives $10 \times 6 = 60$ orders. The transferable idea: place the people with a condition first, then arrange everyone else.
solutions.elegant: All $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$ orders split into pairs by swapping Ana and Ben, and in each pair exactly one order has Ana on the left. So the answer is $120 \div 2 = 60$.

problems.whyOnTest: Symmetry halves the count instantly; the traps are forgetting the other students or treating Ana and Ben as a block.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 3-digit code uses the digits 0 to 9 and may start with 0. The code must contain at least one 7, and no digit may appear twice in a row: 737 is allowed, but 377 is not. How many such codes are there?

choices.misconception: I placed the 7 in one of the 3 positions and gave each other position 9 choices, $3 \times 9 \times 9$, ignoring the rule about repeats.
I counted the codes with at least one 7, $1000 - 729$, and forgot the rule that no digit appears twice in a row.
I fixed the 7 in the first position and counted only $1 \times 9 \times 9$ codes.
I counted all codes with no digit twice in a row, $10 \times 9 \times 9$, and forgot that a 7 is required.

hints: Think about the codes that break only the 'at least one 7' rule.
Counting with restrictions: first count all codes with no digit twice in a row, then subtract those that contain no 7 at all. Both counts come from the multiplication principle.
No digit twice in a row: $10 \times 9 \times 9 = 810$ codes. No digit twice in a row and no 7: $9 \times 8 \times 8 = 576$ codes.

solutions.reliable: Codes with no digit twice in a row: 10 choices for the first digit, then 9 for each later digit (anything except the digit before), so $10 \times 9 \times 9 = 810$. Of these, the codes with no 7 have 9 choices for the first digit, then 8 for each later digit (not 7 and not the digit before), so $9 \times 8 \times 8 = 576$. The codes with at least one 7 number $810 - 576 = 234$. The transferable idea: when 'at least one' meets another rule, count everything that obeys the other rule and subtract the ones with none.
solutions.elegant: Casework on where the 7s are. Exactly one 7 in the middle: $9 \times 9 = 81$. Exactly one 7 at the start: the middle is not 7 (9 ways) and the last digit is neither 7 nor the middle digit (8 ways), so 72. Exactly one 7 at the end: also 72. Two 7s must be 7, then a non-7, then 7: 9 codes. Total $81 + 72 + 72 + 9 = 234$.

problems.whyOnTest: Two rules interact here; the reliable move is to count the codes obeying one rule and subtract the unwanted ones.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a corner of a room, 30 unit cubes are stacked: a 4 by 4 layer on the floor, then 3 by 3, then 2 by 2, then 1 cube, each layer pushed into the corner against both walls. Every cube face not touching the floor, a wall or another cube is painted. How many cubes have no paint?

choices.misconception: I counted the cubes that do get paint, 16, instead of the cubes with no paint.
I only counted the hidden cubes in the bottom layer and forgot the hidden cubes in the layers above it.
I forgot the walls and counted as if the stack stood in the middle of the floor, so the cubes against the walls looked painted.
I counted only the cube surrounded by other cubes on all six sides and forgot that faces against a wall or the floor are not painted either.

hints: Which faces of a cube in this stack could ever get paint?

Count cubes in a stack layer by layer: because of the walls and floor, a cube can only show its top face and its two outward side faces. Decide, for each layer, which cubes have all three of those covered.
A cube with another cube on top of it also has cubes in front of it and beside it, so it shows nothing. In the bottom layer, that is the 3 by 3 block under the next layer.

solutions.reliable: Only the top, the front and the outer side of a cube can be painted: its back and other side touch a wall or a cube, and its bottom touches the floor or a cube. In each layer, the cubes covered by the layer above also have cubes in front of them and beside them, because each layer is one cube wider than the one above, so they show nothing. That is $3 \times 3 = 9$ cubes in the bottom layer, $2 \times 2 = 4$ in the second and 1 in the third, while the top cube is painted. So $9 + 4 + 1 = 14$ cubes have no paint. The transferable idea: count a stack layer by layer, deciding for each layer which cubes are hidden.
solutions.elegant: A cube gets paint exactly when nothing sits on top of it. Looking down from above you see a 4 by 4 square, so 16 cubes have nothing on top and get paint. The other $30 - 16 = 14$ cubes have none.

problems.whyOnTest: Hidden cubes in a stack must be reasoned about layer by layer, and the walls change which faces can be seen.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A model of a car is built at a scale of 1 to 25, so every length on the model is $\frac{1}{25}$ of the real length. The roof of the model has an area of 40 square centimetres. What is the area of the real car's roof, in square metres?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the area by 25 as if it were a length, getting 1000 square centimetres, which is 0.1 square metres.
I got 25 000 square centimetres but thought that 1 square metre is 1000 square centimetres.
I multiplied by 25 three times, as for a volume, and got 625 000 square centimetres.
I got 25 000 square centimetres but thought that 1 square metre is 100 square centimetres.

hints: If every length grows 25 times, how does an area grow?
Scaling: areas scale by the square of the length factor. After scaling, change square centimetres into square metres, remembering that 1 m is 100 cm in both directions.
The real roof is $40 \times 25 \times 25 = 25\,000$ square centimetres, and 1 square metre is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ square centimetres.

solutions.reliable: Every length of the real car is 25 times the model's, so every area is $25 \times 25 = 625$ times as big: $40 \times 625 = 25\,000$ square centimetres. One square metre is $100 \text{ cm} \times 100 \text{ cm} = 10\,000$ square centimetres, so the roof is $25\,000 \div 10\,000 = 2.5$ square metres. The transferable idea: lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$.
solutions.elegant: Picture a 1 cm by 1 cm square on the model: on the car it is 25 cm by 25 cm, which is $\frac{1}{4}$ m by $\frac{1}{4}$ m, or $\frac{1}{16}$ of a square metre. Forty such squares make $\frac{40}{16} = 2.5$ square metres.

problems.whyOnTest: Area scales by the square of the length factor, and square units need squaring too: two separate chances to slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Through how many degrees does the hour hand of a clock turn between 9:40 in the morning and 1:10 in the afternoon of the same day?

choices.misconception: I moved the hour hand 6 degrees per hour, the way the minute hand moves in one minute.
I counted only the 3 full hours from 10:00 to 1:00 and ignored the extra minutes.
I counted from 9 to 1 as 4 whole hours and ignored the minutes.
I worked out how far the minute hand turns, $3.5 \times 360$, instead of the hour hand.

hints: How long is it from 9:40 to 1:10?
Clock geometry: the hour hand turns a full 360 degrees in 12 hours. Find the time that passes, then turn it into degrees for the hour hand.
From 9:40 to 1:10 is 3 hours 30 minutes, and the hour hand turns $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees each hour.

solutions.reliable: From 9:40 to 1:10 is 3 hours 30 minutes, which is 3.5 hours. The hour hand goes once round (360 degrees) in 12 hours, so it turns 30 degrees per hour. In 3.5 hours it turns $3.5 \times 30 = 105$ degrees. The transferable idea: the hour hand turns half a degree every minute, so the minutes matter.
solutions.elegant: The hour hand turns half a degree per minute. The time is 210 minutes, so it turns $210 \div 2 = 105$ degrees.

problems.whyOnTest: The hour hand keeps moving between the numbers; the test is whether the extra minutes are turned into degrees too.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five people sit together. Each is a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Each person says how many knaves there are among the other four. Their answers are 1, 3, 3, 4 and 4. How many knights are there?

choices.misconception: I trusted one of the people who said 4, so I decided there were 4 knaves and 1 knight, without checking the two people who said 3: as knaves they would each see exactly 3 knaves and be telling the truth.
I worked out that there are 3 knaves and gave the number of knaves instead of the number of knights.
I thought only the odd one out, the person who said 1, was lying, so I counted 4 knights.
I forgot that a knave does not count himself, so 'all five are knaves' also seemed to work, and I thought the answer could not be decided.

hints: Who sees more knaves among the other four: a knight or a knave?
Truth-tellers and liars: suppose there are $K$ knaves in total. A knight sees exactly $K$ knaves among the others, but a knave sees only $K - 1$. Test each value of $K$ suggested by the answers.
All knights give the same true answer $K$. Try $K = 3$: the two people who said 3 are the knights and the other three are knaves. Check that each knave's answer is false.

solutions.reliable: Say there are $K$ knaves. A knight is not a knave, so a knight sees exactly $K$ knaves among the other four and says $K$; a knave sees $K - 1$ knaves and must say something else. If $K = 1$, only the person who said 1 could be a knight, leaving at least 4 knaves, not 1. If $K = 3$, there are 2 knights, and only the two who said 3 can be knights; the three knaves then each see 2 knaves but say 1, 4 and 4, all false. This works. If $K = 4$, there is 1 knight, but then each knave sees 3 knaves, so the two people who said 3 would be telling the truth. If there are no knights at all, all 5 are knaves and each sees 4, so the people who said 4 would be telling the truth. Any other $K$ would need knights who said a number nobody said. So $K = 3$ and there are $5 - 3 = 2$ knights. The transferable idea: knights all give the same true answer, so sort the speakers by what they said and test each case.

problems.whyOnTest: The key is that a knave does not count himself; that one-person shift is what leaves exactly one consistent case.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four stacks each hold 10 coins. Each stack is all real (10 g each) or all fake (11 g each), and any number of them, even none, may be fake. You weigh some coins from each stack together, once, on an exact scale. What is the fewest coins in total that always tells you which stacks are fake?

choices.misconception: I took one coin from each stack, but then the scale only shows how many stacks are fake, not which ones.
I took 0, 1, 2 and 4 coins, thinking the stack I took nothing from could be worked out at the end, but nothing tells me whether it is fake.
I took 1, 2, 3 and 4 coins, but then the first two stacks being fake adds the same extra weight as the third stack alone.
I took 1, 2, 4 and 7 coins, checking only that no amount is the sum of two others, but $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$.

hints: The extra grams on the scale equal the number of fake coins weighed.
Weighing puzzles: every possible set of fake stacks must give a different reading. Count how many sets there are, then ask how large the largest reading must be.
There are $2^4 = 16$ possible sets of fake stacks, so 16 different extra weights are needed, starting at 0. The largest, when all four stacks are fake, must be at least 15.

solutions.reliable: The scale shows the extra weight above 10 g per coin, which equals the number of fake coins weighed. Each of the $2^4 = 16$ possible sets of fake stacks must give a different extra weight. These are 16 different whole numbers, the smallest being 0, so the largest is at least 15. The largest extra weight happens when all four stacks are fake, and it then equals the total number of coins taken, so at least 15 coins are needed. Taking 1, 2, 4 and 8 coins works: every number from 0 to 15 is a sum of some of these in exactly one way, so the reading tells you exactly which stacks are fake. Each amount is at most 10, so the coins are available. The transferable idea: count how many situations must be told apart, and make sure the weighing can give that many different readings.
solutions.elegant: A pure counting argument gives the bound: 16 situations need 16 different readings, and the readings can only run from 0 up to the number of coins taken, so at least 15 coins. Powers of 2 meet the bound exactly, just as every number from 0 to 15 has one way of being written in binary.

problems.whyOnTest: A single weighing can only separate as many cases as it has readings; counting the cases gives the bound, and powers of 2 meet it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pump fills an empty pool in 6 hours. A drain empties a full pool in 10 hours. The pump is switched on with the pool empty, but the drain is left open for the first 3 hours and then closed. How long after the pump is switched on is the pool full?

choices.misconception: I worked out the time needed after the drain was closed, 4.8 hours, and forgot to add the first 3 hours.
I worked out that the drain let out $\frac{3}{10}$ of the pool and added $\frac{3}{10}$ of an hour, 18 minutes, instead of the time the pump needs to replace that water.
I added the 3 hours with the drain open on top of the 6 hours, as if the pump did nothing during them.
I used the combined rate $\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{15}$ for the whole time, as if the drain were never closed.

hints: How much of the pool does the drain let out while it is open?
Combined work rates: in the first 3 hours the pump and the drain both act, so use their combined rate; after that only the pump works. Measure everything in fractions of the pool per hour.

With both working, the pool gains $\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{15}$ of its volume each hour, so after 3 hours it is $\frac{1}{5}$ full. The pump fills the remaining $\frac{4}{5}$ at $\frac{1}{6}$ of the pool per hour.

solutions.reliable: With both working, each hour the pool gains $\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{5 - 3}{30} = \frac{1}{15}$ of its volume. After 3 hours it is $\frac{3}{15} = \frac{1}{5}$ full. The pump alone fills the remaining $\frac{4}{5}$ in $\frac{4}{5} \times 6 = 4.8$ hours, which is 4 hours 48 minutes. The total is $3 + 4.8 = 7.8$ hours, or 7 hours 48 minutes. The transferable idea: add rates as fractions of the job per hour, with a minus sign for anything that undoes the job.
solutions.elegant: In its 3 open hours the drain lets out $\frac{3}{10}$ of a pool. The pump needs $\frac{3}{10} \times 6 = 1.8$ hours to replace that, so the whole job takes $6 + 1.8 = 7.8$ hours, which is 7 h 48 min.

problems.whyOnTest: Rates combine with a minus sign when one machine undoes the other, and here the rate changes partway: two steps, one trap each.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Whole numbers are written in a square spiral on squared paper. 1 is in the centre, 2 is to its right, 3 is above 2, then 4 and 5 go to the left, 6 and 7 go down, 8, 9 and 10 go to the right, 11 goes up, and so on, turning anticlockwise. Which number is directly below 2026?

choices.misconception: I thought the spiral turns downward after 2026, so the next number, 2027, would be below it.
I thought the odd square 2025 sits directly under 2026, when in fact it is just to its left.
I thought every perfect square, not only the odd ones, sits on the bottom-right diagonal, so I used $46^2 = 2116$.
I added one full lap of the next ring, $8 \times 23 = 184$, to 2026.

hints: Where do the numbers 9, 25 and 49 sit in the spiral?
Patterns in grids: the odd squares 1, 9, 25, 49 and so on lie on one diagonal, each at the bottom-right corner of a ring. Find the odd square just before 2026, then work out what lies around it.
$45^2 = 2025$ is the bottom-right corner of a ring, and 2026 starts the next ring, one step to its right. The square directly below 2026 is the bottom-right corner of that new ring.

solutions.reliable: In the spiral, 9 is at the bottom-right corner of the first ring around 1, 25 at the bottom-right corner of the next ring, and in general each odd square sits one step down and to the right of the previous odd square. Since $45^2 = 2025$, the number 2025 is a bottom-right corner, and 2026 is one step to its right, starting the next ring, which then goes up. The square directly below 2026 is one step down and to the right of 2025, so it is the next bottom-right corner: $47^2 = 2209$. The transferable idea: find the numbers that sit on a simple diagonal, then locate everything else from them.
solutions.elegant: Check the rule on a small case first: 9 is a corner, 10 is to its right, and directly below 10 is 25, the next odd square. In the same way, below $45^2 + 1 = 2026$ is $47^2 = 2209$.

problems.whyOnTest: Locating a big number in a spiral is hopeless by counting; the odd squares on the diagonal turn it into a short pattern argument.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A board 48 cm by 60 cm is to be covered exactly with identical square tiles, without cutting or overlapping any tile. The tiles are to be as large as possible. How many tiles are needed?

choices.misconception: I found the side of each tile, 12 cm, and gave that instead of the number of tiles.
I used 6 cm tiles, which fit but are not the largest possible, so I got $8 \times 10 = 80$.
I used 4 cm tiles, a common factor of 48 and 60 but not the greatest one, so I got $12 \times 15 = 180$.
I divided the board's area, 2880 square centimetres, by 12 instead of by the tile's area, $12 \times 12$.

hints: The side of a tile must divide both 48 and 60.
Factors and the greatest common factor: the largest square tile that fits exactly has a side equal to the greatest common factor of 48 and 60. Then count the tiles along each side.
The greatest common factor of 48 and 60 is 12, so the tiles are 12 cm by 12 cm.

solutions.reliable: The tile side must divide both 48 and 60, and it should be as large as possible, so it is the greatest common factor. The factors of 48 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24 and 48, and the largest that also divides 60 is 12. So there are $48 \div 12 = 4$ tiles along one side and $60 \div 12 = 5$ along the other, making $4 \times 5 = 20$ tiles. The transferable idea: 'the largest piece that fits exactly' means the greatest common factor.
solutions.elegant: Check by area: the board is $48 \times 60 = 2880$ square centimetres, each tile is $12 \times 12 = 144$, and $2880 \div 144 = 20$.

problems.whyOnTest: The largest tile that fits both sides is the greatest common factor in disguise; the traps are a smaller common factor or dividing an area by a length.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four standard dice, whose opposite faces add up to 7, are placed on a table in a 2 by 2 square, so that each die touches two others face to face. A face is hidden if it touches the table or another die. What is the smallest possible total of the dots on all the faces that are not hidden?

choices.misconception: I thought the two visible side faces of each die are opposite each other, so they add up to 7, giving $1 + 7 = 8$ per die.
I thought each die touches only one other die, so I counted the top and three sides: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ per die.
I found the largest possible total, $4 + 5 + 6 = 15$ per die, instead of the smallest.
I added all the faces of all four dice, $4 \times 21$, forgetting that some faces are hidden.

hints: For one die, which three faces show, and where do they meet?
Dice face relationships: each die shows its top and two outer sides, and these three faces meet at one corner, so no two of them are opposite. Find the smallest possible corner total.
The faces 1, 2 and 3 have opposites 6, 5 and 4, so no two of them are opposite, and they can meet at a corner. That gives 6 per die.

solutions.reliable: Each die has its bottom on the table and two side faces against its neighbours, and those two side faces are next to each other, not opposite. So it shows its top and its two outer sides: three faces that meet at one corner, no two of them opposite. The three smallest numbers, 1, 2 and 3, contain no pair adding to 7, so they can meet at a corner: turn each die so that 1, 2 and 3 are the faces showing. Each die then shows 6 dots, and the smallest total is $4 \times 6 = 24$. The transferable idea: on a die, the faces that meet at a corner never include an opposite pair.
solutions.elegant: Count what is hidden instead: each die hides three faces that meet at a corner, worth at most $6 + 5 + 4 = 15$ dots, so it shows at least $21 - 15 = 6$. The total is at least $4 \times 6 = 24$, and this can be reached.

problems.whyOnTest: Seeing which faces of a die meet at a corner, and so can never be opposite, is the key spatial fact behind most dice problems.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ola has taken some tests. If she scores 100 on her next test, the mean of all her scores will be 86. If she scores 60 on it instead, the mean will be 81. What is the mean of her scores so far?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two possible new means, 86 and 81.
I found the number of tests she has already taken, 7, and gave that instead of the mean.
I divided the new totals by the number of earlier tests instead of including the new test, so I solved $8m + 100 = 8 \times 86$.
I found that 8 tests share the 40-point difference, but then took 8 as the number of tests before the next one, so I solved $8m + 100 = 9 \times 86$.

hints: The two cases differ only in the next score. Compare them.

Means and working backwards: changing one score by 40 changes the total by 40, and the mean by 40 divided by the number of tests including the new one. That gives the number of tests, and then the totals.
The means differ by $86 - 81 = 5$, so there are $40 \div 5 = 8$ tests in all, including the next one. With a score of 100, the 8 scores total $8 \times 86 = 688$.

solutions.reliable: The two cases differ only in the next score, by $100 - 60 = 40$ points, and the means differ by $86 - 81 = 5$. Since the mean is the total divided by the number of tests, there are $40 \div 5 = 8$ tests including the next one, so Ola has taken 7 so far. If the next score is 100, the 8 scores total $8 \times 86 = 688$, so her 7 scores so far total $688 - 100 = 588$, and their mean is $588 \div 7 = 84$. Check with the other case: $(588 + 60) \div 8 = 648 \div 8 = 81$. The transferable idea: changing one value changes the mean by that change divided by how many values there are.
solutions.elegant: Let her mean so far be $m$. With 8 tests in all, a score of 100 raises the mean by $\frac{100 - m}{8}$, so $m + \frac{100 - m}{8} = 86$. Multiplying by 8 gives $8m + 100 - m = 688$, so $7m = 588$ and $m = 84$.

problems.whyOnTest: One score change shifting the mean reveals how many values there are; working backwards from a mean is the skill being tested.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a calendar, the days of a month are written in rows of 7, from Monday to Sunday. This month has 31 days, and the 1st is a Wednesday. How many different 2 by 2 squares of four dates can be drawn on the calendar, with every box of the square holding a date?

choices.misconception: I counted 6 squares for each of the 4 pairs of neighbouring weeks, as if every week were complete.
I counted the squares between the full weeks but included only one of the two short weeks, $6 + 6 + 4$.
I counted 7 squares across each pair of weeks, one for each day, but a 2 by 2 square needs two neighbouring columns.
I only counted squares inside the three complete weeks and ignored both short weeks.

hints: Sketch the calendar and mark where the first and last weeks start and stop.

Counting by position: a 2 by 2 square is fixed by its top-left date. Count the possible top-left positions for each pair of neighbouring weeks separately, taking care with the short first and last weeks.
Week 1 is Wednesday to Sunday (1 to 5) and week 5 is Monday to Friday (27 to 31). Weeks 2, 3 and 4 are complete.

solutions.reliable: The weeks are: 1 to 5 (Wednesday to Sunday), 6 to 12, 13 to 19, 20 to 26 (complete), and 27 to 31 (Monday to Friday). A 2 by 2 square uses two neighbouring weeks and two neighbouring days, and every box must hold a date. Weeks 1 and 2 share the five days Wednesday to Sunday, giving 4 squares. Weeks 2 and 3: 7 days, giving 6 squares. Weeks 3 and 4: 6 squares. Weeks 4 and 5: Monday to Friday, 5 days, giving 4 squares. Total $4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 20$. The transferable idea: in sliding-window counting, label each window by its starting position and count the starting positions row by row.
solutions.elegant: Two neighbouring weeks that share $n$ days in a row give $n - 1$ squares, one for each pair of neighbouring days: $(5 - 1) + (7 - 1) + (7 - 1) + (5 - 1) = 20$.

problems.whyOnTest: Sliding windows are counted by their starting position; the short first and last weeks are where careless counts go wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A quiz team of 3 is chosen from 5 girls and 4 boys. The team must have exactly 2 girls and 1 boy. How many different teams are possible?

choices.misconception: I chose any 3 of the 9 children and forgot the team needs exactly 2 girls and 1 boy.
I picked a first girl in 5 ways and a second girl in 4 ways, so every pair of girls was counted twice: $5 \times 4 \times 4 = 80$.
I added the 10 ways to pick the girls and the 4 ways to pick the boy instead of multiplying them.
I counted teams with 2 boys and 1 girl, $6 \times 5 = 30$, mixing up which group gives two members.

hints: Pick the girls and the boy as two separate jobs.

Count the pairs of girls, remembering that the order inside a pair does not matter. Then count the choices of boy, and combine with the multiplication principle, because every pair can go with every boy.
There are $5 \times 4 \div 2 = 10$ pairs of girls and 4 boys, and each pair can go with each boy.

solutions.reliable: Choose the two girls first. A first girl in 5 ways and a second in 4 ways gives $5 \times 4 = 20$, but each pair has been counted twice (Ana then Bea is the same pair as Bea then Ana), so there are 10 pairs. Any of the 4 boys can join any pair, so there are $10 \times 4 = 40$ teams. The transferable idea: split a selection into independent parts, count each part as an unordered choice, then multiply.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests choosing an unordered group in parts: halving the ordered count of girl pairs, then multiplying by the choices for the boy.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A lock code is 3 letters long. Each letter is one of A, B, C, D and E, and letters may repeat, so AAB and CEC are both codes. How many codes contain at least one vowel (A or E)?

choices.misconception: I counted the codes with no vowel at all, $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$, and forgot to subtract them from the total.
I counted only the codes with exactly one vowel and missed the codes with two or three vowels.
I took away the codes made only of vowels, $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$, instead of the codes with no vowels: 125 - 8 = 117.
I chose a place for a vowel, a vowel, and any letters for the other two places, $3 \times 2 \times 25 = 150$, so codes with several vowels were counted more than once.

hints: Which codes are the easy ones to count here?
Counting 'at least one' directly needs several cases. Instead count all the codes, count the codes with no vowel at all, and subtract.
There are $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$ codes in all, and $3 \times 3 \times 3$ codes that use only B, C and D.

solutions.reliable: All codes: $5^3 = 125$. A code with no vowel uses only B, C and D in each place: $3^3 = 27$ codes. Every other code has at least one vowel, so the answer is 125 - 27 = 98. Check by cases: exactly one vowel $3 \times 2 \times 9 = 54$, exactly two vowels $3 \times 4 \times 3 = 36$, exactly three $2^3 = 8$, and 54 + 36 + 8 = 98. The transferable idea: when a condition says 'at least one', count the opposite and subtract from the total.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests complementary counting: 'at least one' is messy to count directly but easy as everything minus none.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many of the whole numbers from 1 to 60 are divisible by 4 or by 6, or by both?

choices.misconception: I added the 15 multiples of 4 and the 10 multiples of 6 and forgot that some numbers were counted twice.
I thought the numbers counted twice were the multiples of $4 \times 6 = 24$, so I took away only 2 instead of 5.
I counted only the numbers divisible by both 4 and 6, which are the multiples of 12.
I worked out how many numbers are divisible by neither 4 nor 6 and gave that instead.

hints: Some numbers are multiples of 4 and of 6 at the same time.
Count the multiples of 4, count the multiples of 6, and subtract the numbers counted twice. A number divisible by both 4 and 6 is a multiple of their least common multiple.
There are 15 multiples of 4 and 10 multiples of 6. The numbers in both lists are the multiples of 12.

solutions.reliable: Multiples of 4 up to 60: 60 / 4 = 15. Multiples of 6: 60 / 6 = 10. A number is in both lists exactly when it is a multiple of 12 (not 24: 12 itself is divisible by both), and there are 60 / 12 = 5 of those. So the count is 15 + 10 - 5 = 20. The transferable idea: add the two groups, subtract the overlap once, and find the overlap with the least common multiple.
solutions.elegant: The pattern repeats every 12 numbers. From 1 to 12 the numbers that work are 4, 6, 8 and 12, which is 4 of them. There are five blocks of 12 in 60, so $5 \times 4 = 20$.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests two-set inclusion-exclusion with numbers, where the overlap comes from the least common multiple, not the product.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Using the digits 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, with no digit used more than once, how many even three-digit numbers can be made? (A number cannot start with 0.)

choices.misconception: I forgot that 0 is even, so I only let the number end in 2 or 4.
I chose the even last digit in 3 ways, then gave the first digit 4 choices and the middle 3, forgetting that the first digit cannot be 0: $3 \times 4 \times 3 = 36$.
I counted all the three-digit numbers with different digits, $4 \times 4 \times 3 = 48$, and forgot they must be even.
I only counted the numbers ending in 0 and forgot that 2 and 4 are even too.

hints: Fill the most restricted place first. Which digit is special here?
The last digit must be even and the first digit cannot be 0, and the digit 0 affects both rules. Split into two cases: the number ends in 0, or it ends in 2 or 4.
Ending in 0: $4 \times 3$ numbers. Ending in 2 or 4: the first digit can be neither 0 nor the last digit, which leaves 3 choices.

solutions.reliable: Case 1, last digit 0: the first digit is any of 1, 2, 3, 4 (4 ways) and the middle is any of the 3 digits left, so 12 numbers. Case 2, last digit 2 or 4 (2 ways): the first digit cannot be 0 or the last digit, so 3 ways, and the middle can be any of the 3 digits left, including 0, so $2 \times 3 \times 3 = 18$ numbers. Total 12 + 18 = 30. The transferable idea: when one digit is involved in two restrictions, split into cases on that digit.
solutions.elegant: Count the opposite: there are $4 \times 4 \times 3 = 48$ three-digit numbers with different digits. The odd ones end in 1 or 3 (2 ways), then the first digit has 3 choices (not 0 and not the last digit) and the middle 3, giving 18. So 48 - 18 = 30 are even.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests counting with two restrictions that share the digit 0, where the multiplication principle only works after splitting into cases.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A large 4 by 4 by 4 cube is built from 64 unit cubes. How many different 2 by 2 by 2 cubes, each made of 8 of the unit cubes, can be found inside it? They are allowed to overlap.

choices.misconception: I cut the big cube into separate 2 by 2 by 2 blocks that do not overlap and counted only those.
I thought the small cube could start at any of 4 positions in each direction, $4 \times 4 \times 4$, but from the last position it would stick out.
I found 3 positions in each direction but added them, 3 + 3 + 3, instead of multiplying.
I found the 9 positions in one layer and multiplied by 4 layers, but there are only 3 positions going up as well.

hints: Slide a block 2 units long along an edge 4 units long. How many stops?
A 2 by 2 by 2 cube is fixed by where its corner nearest you sits. Count the possible positions in each of the three directions and multiply, because the directions are independent.
Along an edge of 4 units, a block 2 units long can start at 3 places.

solutions.reliable: In one direction, a block of length 2 inside a length of 4 can start at position 1, 2 or 3, so there are 4 - 2 + 1 = 3 places. The same is true across and up. Each choice of the three starting positions gives a different 2 by 2 by 2 cube, so there are $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$. The transferable idea: count overlapping blocks by sliding, with $n - k + 1$ positions in each direction.
solutions.elegant: Each 2 by 2 by 2 cube has a centre point where 8 of its unit cubes meet, and that point is a corner of the unit grid strictly inside the big cube. Those inside grid corners form a 3 by 3 by 3 array, so there are 27 such cubes.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests the sliding-window count in three dimensions, where the classic slip is cutting the cube into separate pieces.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid 4 by 4 by 4 cube of 64 unit cubes sits in a corner of a room, with its bottom on the floor and two side faces flat against the two walls. A unit cube is hidden if none of its faces can be seen from anywhere in the room. How many unit cubes are hidden?

choices.misconception: I counted only the cubes that are not on the outside of the big cube at all, a 2 by 2 by 2 block, and forgot that the floor and walls hide faces too.
I counted the unit cubes that can be seen instead of the ones that are hidden.
I took away 16 cubes for each of the three faces that can be seen, 64 - 48 = 16, but cubes on the shared edges were taken away more than once.
I forgot the two walls and only treated the floor as hiding faces, which left a 2 by 2 by 3 block hidden.

hints: Which of the big cube's six faces can actually be seen?
Only three faces of the big cube are open: the top and two sides. A unit cube is hidden exactly when it touches none of these three faces. Peel off those three layers and see what block is left.
Removing the top layer and the two open side layers leaves a block that is 3 cubes long in each direction.

solutions.reliable: The floor and the two walls cover three faces of the big cube, so only the top, the front and the open side can be seen. A unit cube can be seen exactly when it is in the top layer, the front layer or the open side layer. Remove those three layers: what remains is a block 3 cubes long, 3 wide and 3 tall, tucked against the floor and both walls. None of its cubes shows a face, so $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ cubes are hidden. Check by counting the visible cubes: the three open faces hold 16 + 16 + 16 cubes, minus 4 + 4 + 4 counted twice along the shared edges, plus the 1 corner cube taken away three times, which gives 48 - 12 + 1 = 37, and 64 - 37 = 27. The transferable idea: a hidden region is what is left after peeling away every layer that can be seen.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests counting hidden cubes, where faces against a floor or wall are hidden too, and peeling the visible layers avoids double counting.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Different whole numbers are chosen from 1 to 20. What is the smallest number of them you must choose to be sure that two of the chosen numbers differ by exactly 5?

choices.misconception: I sorted the numbers into 5 groups by their remainder on division by 5 and said 6 numbers force two into one group, but two numbers in a group can differ by 10 or 15.
I found that 10 numbers can be chosen with no two differing by 5 and gave 10, forgetting that the answer is one more than that.
I counted the 15 pairs of numbers from 1 to 20 that differ by 5 and thought I needed one more number than there are pairs.
I sorted the numbers into 5 groups by their remainder on division by 5 and answered with the number of groups.

hints: How many numbers can you choose while still avoiding a difference of 5?
Make boxes so that two numbers in the same box always differ by exactly 5. Count the boxes to see when two chosen numbers must share one, and find a big set that avoids it.

solutions.reliable: First, 10 numbers are not enough: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 has no two numbers differing by 5 (differences inside each block are at most 4, and between blocks at least 6). Next, any 11 numbers work. Split 1 to 20 into the ten pairs (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 8), (4, 9), (5, 10), (11, 16), (12, 17), (13, 18), (14, 19), (15, 20), which use every number exactly once. With 11 numbers in 10 pairs, some pair has both of its numbers chosen, and they differ by 5. So the answer is 11. The transferable idea: for a 'be sure' question, find the largest set that avoids the event; the answer is one more, and pigeonhole boxes prove it.
solutions.elegant: Think in chains where neighbours differ by 5: (1, 6, 11, 16), (2, 7, 12, 17), and so on, five chains of 4. From a chain of 4 you can take at most 2 numbers without taking neighbours, so at most $5 \times 2 = 10$ numbers avoid a difference of 5, and an 11th always creates one.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests the pigeonhole principle with well-chosen boxes, pairs that differ by 5, plus an example showing one fewer is not enough.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A straight segment joins the points (2, 3) and (14, 21). How many points with both coordinates whole numbers lie on this segment, including its two ends?

choices.misconception: I found the 6 equal steps between the whole-number points and counted the steps instead of the points.
I found the right points but left out both ends of the segment.
I thought there is a whole-number point above every whole number x from 2 to 14, which gave 13.
I thought there is a whole-number point beside every whole number y from 3 to 21, which gave 19.

hints: How far does the segment go across, and how far up?
From one end to the other is 12 across and 18 up. The whole-number points split it into equal steps, each a whole number across and a whole number up. Use the greatest common divisor.
The greatest common divisor of 12 and 18 is 6, so each step is 2 across and 3 up.

solutions.reliable: From (2, 3) to (14, 21) the segment goes 12 across and 18 up, so every 2 across it goes 3 up. A whole-number point on the segment must be a whole number of these 2-across, 3-up steps from (2, 3), because 2 and 3 have no common factor. That gives (2, 3), (4, 6), (6, 9), (8, 12), (10, 15), (12, 18), (14, 21): 6 steps and 7 points. The transferable idea: a segment between lattice points going a across and b up contains $\gcd(a, b) + 1$ lattice points.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests lattice reasoning: whole-number points on a segment come in equal steps set by the greatest common divisor of the run and the rise.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Square ABCD has side 12 cm, with its corners in the order A, B, C, D around the square. Point E lies on side BC with BE = 8 cm, and point F lies on side CD with DF = 3 cm. What is the area of triangle AEF, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found the total area of the three corner triangles and gave that instead of what is left.
I assumed that a triangle drawn from a corner of the square always takes up half of it.
I forgot to halve the 4 by 9 rectangle for the triangle at corner C, so I took away 36 there instead of 18.
I mixed up BE and EC and used BE = 4 cm, which changes two of the corner triangles.

hints: Triangle AEF is the square with three right-angled triangles cut off.
Draw the square and mark E and F. The three corner triangles at B, C and D are right-angled, so their areas are easy. Subtract them from the area of the square.
The corner triangles have legs 12 and 8, then 12 and 3, then EC = 4 and FC = 9.

solutions.reliable: The square has area 144. Around triangle AEF are three right-angled triangles: ABE with legs 12 and 8, area 48; ADF with legs 12 and 3, area 18; and ECF with legs EC = 12 - 8 = 4 and FC = 12 - 3 = 9, area 18. So triangle AEF has area 144 - 48 - 18 - 18 = 60 square centimetres. The transferable idea: a slanted triangle inside a rectangle is often easiest as the rectangle minus right-angled corner pieces.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests area by subtraction: a tilted triangle is hard to measure directly but easy as a square minus three right-angled corners.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. At each corner, an exterior angle is made by extending one side beyond that corner. What is the size of the smallest exterior angle, in degrees?

choices.misconception: I gave the smallest interior angle instead of the smallest exterior angle.
I found the largest interior angle, 80 degrees, and stopped there.
I thought the smallest exterior angle sits at the smallest interior angle, so I worked out 180 - 40.
I used 360 degrees as the angle sum of a triangle, which made the angles 80, 120 and 160 and the smallest exterior angle 180 - 160.

hints: An exterior angle and the interior angle beside it make a straight line.
Split 180 degrees in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 to find the interior angles. Each exterior angle is 180 minus its interior angle, so the largest interior angle gives the smallest exterior angle.
The interior angles are 40, 60 and 80 degrees.

solutions.reliable: The ratio has 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts sharing 180 degrees, so one part is 20 degrees and the angles are 40, 60 and 80. Each exterior angle is 180 minus the interior angle at that corner: 140, 120 and 100. The smallest is 100 degrees. The transferable idea: the biggest interior angle has the smallest exterior angle beside it.
solutions.elegant: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles at the other corners. The smallest exterior angle is at the largest interior angle, so it equals the two smaller angles together: 2 + 3 = 5 parts of 20 degrees, which is 100 degrees.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests angles on a straight line and in a triangle, and the trap that the smallest exterior angle sits at the largest interior angle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a 4 by 4 grid, rows are numbered 1 to 4 from the top and columns 1 to 4 from the left. The squares at row 1, column 1 and row 1, column 2 are shaded. At least how many more squares must be shaded so the pattern looks the same after a quarter turn about the grid's centre?

choices.misconception: I made the pattern look the same after a half turn only, which needs just the 2 squares opposite the shaded ones.
I counted all 8 squares of the finished pattern, including the 2 that were already shaded.
I only copied the corner square to the other three corners and forgot that the second shaded square needs copies too.
I turned the pattern a quarter turn twice and shaded the new squares each time, but forgot the third quarter turn.

hints: Where does each shaded square go after one, two and three quarter turns?
For the pattern to survive a quarter turn, every shaded square must come with the three squares it lands on after one, two and three quarter turns. Track each shaded square around the grid.
The corner square lands on the other three corners. The square in row 1, column 2 lands on row 2, column 4, then row 4, column 3, then row 3, column 1.

solutions.reliable: Turn the grid clockwise a quarter turn at a time. The corner square in row 1, column 1 visits the other three corners, so 3 more squares are needed. The square in row 1, column 2 visits row 2, column 4, then row 4, column 3, then row 3, column 1, so 3 more again. These six squares are all different, so 6 further squares must be shaded, and the finished 8-square pattern does look the same after a quarter turn. The transferable idea: under quarter-turn symmetry, squares come in groups of four (apart from a centre square), so complete every group.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests rotational symmetry: every shaded square must come with all of its images under a quarter turn, and it is easy to stop short.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A point starts at (1, 2). It is reflected in the line x = 3, then in the line x = 7, then in x = 3 again, then in x = 7 again, and so on, taking turns. Where is the point after 10 reflections?

choices.misconception: I thought each pair of reflections moves the point by the distance between the lines, 4, instead of twice that distance.
I thought every single reflection moves the point 8 to the right, so I added 80.
I thought reflecting twice always brings a point back to where it started, so 10 reflections change nothing.
I found that each pair of reflections moves the point 8 units, but I moved it to the left instead of the right.

hints: Work out the first two reflections carefully. Where does the point end up?
Reflecting in two parallel lines one after the other is the same as a slide. Find how far and which way one pair of reflections moves the point, then use that five times.
After two reflections the point is at (9, 2): it has moved 8 to the right.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting (1, 2) in x = 3 gives (5, 2), since 1 is 2 to the left of the line and 5 is 2 to the right of it. Reflecting (5, 2) in x = 7 gives (9, 2). So one pair of reflections moves the point 8 to the right. The 10 reflections are 5 such pairs, so the point moves $5 \times 8 = 40$ to the right and ends at (41, 2). Checking the next pair: (9, 2) goes to (-3, 2) and then to (17, 2), again 8 further right. The transferable idea: two reflections in parallel lines make a slide of twice the distance between the lines.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests composing transformations: two reflections in parallel lines combine into a slide of twice the gap, not a return to the start.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The net shown is folded to make a cube. What is the sum of the numbers on the four faces that share an edge with the face numbered 1?

figure.alt: A cube net of six squares in a staircase of three steps. Top row: square 1 with square 2 to its right. Middle row: square 3 directly below 2, with square 4 to its right. Bottom row: square 5 directly below 4, with square 6 to its right.

choices.misconception: I thought the two ends of the staircase, 1 and 6, finish opposite each other, so I added 2, 3, 4 and 5.
I thought squares that touch only at a corner in the net, like 1 and 3, finish opposite each other, so I added 2, 4, 5 and 6.
I added all five other numbers, forgetting that one face of a cube is opposite face 1 and does not touch it.
I thought 5, which lies on the same slanting line as 1, two steps down, finishes opposite 1, so I added 2, 3, 4 and 6.

hints: Only one face of the cube does not touch face 1. Which one?
Find the face opposite 1 by folding one square at a time in your head: keep 1 flat as the floor and see where each square lands as you fold along the joins. Then add the other four.
With 1 as the floor, 2 and 3 fold up as two walls that meet at a corner, and 4 then folds over the top as the roof.

solutions.reliable: Keep face 1 flat as the floor. Square 2 is joined to the right edge of 1, so it folds up into a wall. Square 3 is joined to the bottom edge of 2, so it folds round into a second wall, meeting wall 2 at a corner. Square 4 is joined to the edge of 3 that is now at the top, so 4 folds over to become the roof, opposite the floor. Squares 5 and 6 then fill the last two walls. So 4 is opposite 1, and the four faces sharing an edge with 1 are 2, 3, 5 and 6, with sum 2 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 16. The transferable idea: fold a net one square at a time from a fixed base; the face opposite the base is the only one that does not touch it.
solutions.elegant: Squares 1, 2, 3 and 4 form a Z shape: across, down, across. The two end squares of a Z always finish opposite each other, because the two middle squares fold up as walls that meet at a corner and the end squares become the floor and the roof. So 4 is opposite 1, and in the same way the Z made by 3, 4, 5 and 6 puts 3 opposite 6, which leaves 2 opposite 5. The faces touching 1 are 2, 3, 5 and 6, with sum 16.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests folding a net in your head on the trickiest net shape, and the trap of pairing the two ends of the staircase as opposite faces.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a standard die, opposite faces add up to 7. At each of the 8 corners of the die, three faces meet, and the three numbers on those faces are added. How many different totals are there among the 8 corners?

choices.misconception: I allowed any three different numbers, including opposite ones like 1 and 6, so every total from 6 to 15 seemed possible.
I counted all the ways to choose 3 of the 6 faces, $6 \times 5 \times 4 \div 6 = 20$, but most of those groups never meet at a corner.
I thought opposite corners of the die always have the same total, so I only counted 4 pairs of corners.
I saw that 8 is impossible as a total, but I missed that 13 is impossible too.

hints: Can the faces 1 and 6 ever meet at a corner?
Opposite faces never meet, so a corner uses one face from each pair: 1 or 6, 2 or 5, 3 or 4. Each of these 8 choices is a real corner. List the 8 totals and look for repeats.
The totals with 1 are 1 + 2 + 3, 1 + 2 + 4, 1 + 5 + 3 and 1 + 5 + 4. Each total with 6 is 5 more than one of these.

solutions.reliable: Opposite faces never meet, so a corner takes one number from each of the pairs 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4. There are $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ such choices and a die has 8 corners, so each choice is exactly one corner. The totals are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, 1 + 5 + 3 = 9, 1 + 5 + 4 = 10, and with 6 instead of 1: 11, 12, 14 and 15. All 8 are different, so there are 8 different totals. The transferable idea: on a cube, the three faces at a corner take one face from each pair of opposite faces.
solutions.elegant: The totals using 1 are 6, 7, 9 and 10, and swapping the 1 for a 6 adds 5, giving 11, 12, 14 and 15. The first four are all at most 10 and the last four are all at least 11, so no two totals match, and there are 8.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests the key die fact that the three faces at a corner take one face from each opposite pair, followed by careful listing of the totals.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid is built by stacking 1 cm cubes on a 4 by 4 grid on a table. The stack heights, back row first, each row left to right, are 3, 2, 2, 1; 2, 2, 1, 1; 2, 1, 1, 0; 1, 1, 0, 0. What is its surface area in square centimetres, including the faces on the table?

choices.misconception: I added the areas of the top, front and side views but forgot the matching bottom, back and other side.
I used the whole 4 by 4 square, 16, for the views from above and below, though three squares of the grid are empty.
I counted 6 faces for each of the 20 cubes and forgot that faces glued to another cube are hidden.
I left out the 13 faces resting on the table.

hints: Look at the solid from each of the six directions.
The stacks never get taller as you move forward or to the right, so the solid has no hollows: each square seen from any of the six directions is exactly one face. Add up the six views.
From above and from below you see 13 squares. From the front and from the back you see 3 + 2 + 2 + 1. From either side you see 3 + 2 + 2 + 1.

solutions.reliable: Count the faces direction by direction. Top: each of the 13 non-empty stacks shows one top face, and the bottom also has 13 faces on the table. Front: in each column the stacks get no taller towards the front, so every step down shows its own faces and the column shows as many front faces as its tallest stack: 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8, and the back also shows 8. Each side, in the same way, shows 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8. Total 13 + 13 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 58 square centimetres. The transferable idea: for a solid with no hollows, the surface area is twice the sum of the top, front and side views.
solutions.elegant: Check by gluing: the 20 cubes have 120 faces. There are 7 places where one cube sits on another and 24 places where two cubes touch side by side, 31 joins in all, and each join hides 2 faces. So 120 - 62 = 58.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests reading a solid from its views: with no hollows, each view shows each outer face once, so the six views give the whole surface.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid block measuring 2 by 3 by 4 is made of 24 unit cubes. What is the smallest number of unit cubes that must be added to it to make a solid cube?

choices.misconception: I found the 4 by 4 by 4 cube but forgot that 24 of its unit cubes are already there.
I aimed for a 3 by 3 by 3 cube, which has 27 unit cubes, but the block is 4 long and cannot fit inside it.
I added two layers of 3 by 4 to turn the 2 into 4, but forgot that the 3 still had to become 4.
I added one layer of 2 by 4 to turn the 3 into 4, but forgot that the 2 still had to become 4.

hints: The cube must be at least as long as the block's longest edge.
The block has an edge of length 4, so the cube needs edges of at least 4. Count the unit cubes in a 4 by 4 by 4 cube and take away the ones you already have.
A 4 by 4 by 4 cube has 64 unit cubes.

solutions.reliable: A cube that contains the block needs every edge at least 4 long, so the smallest is 4 by 4 by 4, with 64 unit cubes. The block already has $2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24$, so 64 - 24 = 40 must be added. The transferable idea: the target shape is fixed by the largest dimension, and what is missing is found by subtraction.
solutions.elegant: Build it in steps as a check: two layers of 3 by 4 turn the 2 into 4, adding 24 cubes and making a 4 by 3 by 4 block; one layer of 4 by 4 then turns the 3 into 4, adding 16 more. 24 + 16 = 40.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests building with unit cubes: the smallest cube is fixed by the longest edge, and the cubes needed are found by subtraction.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five friends sit in a row of 5 seats for a photo. Mia insists on sitting at one of the two ends of the row. In how many different orders can the five friends sit?

choices.misconception: I only let Mia sit at the left end and forgot she could sit at the right end too.
I counted all the orders of the five friends and ignored Mia's wish.
I worked out the orders where Mia is not at an end, 120 - 48, instead of the ones where she is.
I placed Mia in 2 ways and then added the choices for the other seats, 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, instead of multiplying them.

hints: Seat Mia first.
Mia has a choice of seats. Once she is seated, the other four friends fill the remaining four seats in any order. Use the multiplication principle.
Mia has 2 choices. The other four can be arranged in $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ ways.

solutions.reliable: Mia can take the left end or the right end: 2 ways. Then the other four friends fill the 4 remaining seats: 4 choices for the first free seat, 3 for the next, then 2, then 1, which is 24 ways. So there are $2 \times 24 = 48$ orders. The transferable idea: place the restricted person first, then arrange everyone else.
solutions.elegant: Over all 120 orders, Mia is in each of the 5 seats equally often, so 2 out of every 5 orders put her at an end: $120 \times 2 \div 5 = 48$.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests arrangements with one restriction: place the restricted person first, then multiply by the arrangements of the rest.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A flag has 3 horizontal stripes. Each stripe is coloured with one of 5 colours, and two stripes that touch must have different colours. The top and bottom stripes may match. How many different flags are possible?

choices.misconception: I made all three stripes different colours, $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$, though the top and bottom stripes may match.
I let every stripe be any of the 5 colours and ignored the rule about touching stripes.
I remembered that the middle stripe must differ from the top one, but gave the bottom stripe all 5 colours: $5 \times 4 \times 5 = 100$.
I added the choices for the stripes, 5 + 4 + 4, instead of multiplying them.

hints: Colour the stripes from top to bottom.
Count the choices for each stripe in turn, given the stripe just above it. Each stripe only has to avoid one colour, and the choices multiply.
Top: 5 choices. Middle: anything except the top colour. Bottom: anything except the middle colour.

solutions.reliable: Colour from the top. The top stripe has 5 choices. The middle must differ from the top: 4 choices. The bottom must differ only from the middle (it may match the top): 4 choices. So there are $5 \times 4 \times 4 = 80$ flags. The transferable idea: when each choice only has to avoid its neighbour, count the choices in order and multiply.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests the multiplication principle when each choice depends only on the one before it, without overcounting or overrestricting.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Squares of size 2 by 2 are to be cut out of a 7 by 7 sheet of squared paper, cutting only along the grid lines. What is the largest number of 2 by 2 squares that can be cut out?

choices.misconception: I divided the 49 small squares by 4 and rounded down, as if hardly any paper had to be wasted.
I thought only one strip 1 square wide had to be wasted, leaving 42 small squares, and 42 / 4 rounds down to 10.
I counted all the places where a 2 by 2 square can be drawn, $6 \times 6 = 36$, forgetting that the pieces cannot overlap.
I marked the 16 squares with an odd row number and an odd column number, and since each 2 by 2 square covers one of them, I said 16 could fit.

hints: Mark small squares so that every 2 by 2 square must cover one.

Number the rows and columns 1 to 7 and mark each small square whose row and column numbers are both even. Every 2 by 2 square covers exactly one mark, so the marks limit the count. Then reach that limit.
There are 3 even numbers from 1 to 7, so there are $3 \times 3 = 9$ marked squares.

solutions.reliable: Number the rows and columns 1 to 7 and mark the 9 small squares whose row and column numbers are both even. A 2 by 2 square covers two neighbouring rows, exactly one of which is even, and two neighbouring columns, exactly one of which is even, so it covers exactly one marked square. Pieces that do not overlap cover different marked squares, so at most 9 pieces can be cut. And 9 is possible: cut the top left 6 by 6 part into a 3 by 3 arrangement of 2 by 2 squares, wasting the strips along the right and bottom edges. The answer is 9. The transferable idea: to show that more pieces are impossible, mark or colour squares so that every piece must use up one mark.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests a marking argument: the area suggests 12, but marking squares that every piece must cover proves that 9 is the most.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A shop mixes peanuts costing 6 euros per kilogram with cashews costing 15 euros per kilogram. It makes 12 kg of mix, worth exactly 9 euros per kilogram. How many kilograms of cashews are in the mix?

choices.misconception: I found the amount of peanuts in the mix instead of the amount of cashews.
I assumed that the mix must be half peanuts and half cashews.
I divided the whole cost of the mix, $12 \times 9 = 108$ euros, by the cashew price, as if all the money went on cashews.
I took the cashew share as the 3 euro gap between the mix and peanut prices divided by the cashew price, 3/15 of 12.

hints: Is 9 euros nearer to the peanut price or the cashew price?
Write the total value two ways: 12 kg at 9 euros, or peanuts at 6 euros plus cashews at 15 euros. Or compare the gaps: the mix price is 3 above the peanut price and 6 below the cashew price.
If c kg are cashews, then $6(12 - c) + 15c = 108$.

solutions.reliable: Let c be the number of kilograms of cashews, so 12 - c kilograms are peanuts. The mix is worth $12 \times 9 = 108$ euros, so $6(12 - c) + 15c = 108$, which gives 72 + 9c = 108, so 9c = 36 and c = 4. Check: 8 kg of peanuts cost 48 euros and 4 kg of cashews cost 60 euros, 108 euros in all. The transferable idea: in a mixture, the value of the parts adds up to the value of the whole.
solutions.elegant: Balance the gaps: each kilogram of peanuts is 3 euros below the mix price and each kilogram of cashews is 6 euros above it. The amounts below and above must cancel, so there must be twice as much peanut as cashew: 8 kg and 4 kg.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests a weighted average: the mix price sits nearer the larger ingredient, and the gaps to each price give the ratio.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid chocolate egg weighs 40 g and needs exactly 2 g of foil to cover its surface. A larger solid chocolate egg has exactly the same shape and needs exactly 18 g of the same foil to cover its surface. How much does the larger egg weigh, in grams?

choices.misconception: I thought the weight grows in the same way as the foil, so I multiplied 40 by 9.
I found that the larger egg is 3 times as long and multiplied the weight by 3.
I halved 9 instead of taking its square root, so I used a length factor of 4.5 and multiplied 40 by $4.5^3$.
I worked out that the larger egg is 27 times as heavy, then gave 27 as the answer instead of $27 \times 40$.

hints: Foil covers a surface. Weight fills a volume.

The foil needed grows with the area, which grows by the square of the length factor. The weight grows with the volume, which grows by the cube of the length factor. Find the length factor from the foil first.
The foil grows by a factor of 9, so every length grows by a factor of 3.

solutions.reliable: The foil covers the surface, so the ratio of foil is the ratio of areas: 18 / 2 = 9. Areas of similar shapes grow by the square of the length factor, so the length factor is 3, since $3 \times 3 = 9$. Weight is proportional to volume, which grows by the cube of the length factor, $3^3 = 27$. So the larger egg weighs $27 \times 40 = 1080$ g. The transferable idea: for similar solids, if lengths scale by k then areas scale by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$, so always go through the length factor.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests scaling of similar solids: from an area ratio back to the length factor, then forward to the volume ratio.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Eight parcels all have different weights. A balance compares two parcels at a time, one on each pan, and shows which one is heavier. What is the smallest number of weighings that is certain to find the heaviest parcel, however the results turn out?

choices.misconception: I counted the rounds of a knockout, 8 to 4 to 2 to 1, instead of the weighings, but each round needs several weighings.
I counted only the first round, pairing the 8 parcels into 4 weighings, and forgot that the winners must be compared too.
I thought every parcel had to be weighed once, so I counted one weighing per parcel.
I compared every pair of parcels, $8 \times 7 \div 2 = 28$ weighings, which is far more than needed.

hints: After a weighing, which parcel can no longer be the heaviest?
Each weighing can rule out at most one parcel, the lighter one, from being the heaviest. Count how many parcels must be ruled out, and check that a knockout really manages it in that many weighings.
Seven parcels must be ruled out, and each weighing rules out only one.

solutions.reliable: A knockout works: weigh any two parcels, keep the heavier, weigh it against a new parcel, and so on. Each weighing knocks out one parcel, so after 7 weighings only one is left, and it has beaten every other parcel directly or through a chain. Fewer weighings are not enough: a weighing only shows that one parcel is lighter than another, so it rules out at most one parcel. To be sure which parcel is heaviest, all 7 others must have lost at least once, which needs at least 7 weighings. The answer is 7. The transferable idea: when each test can eliminate at most one candidate, you need at least as many tests as candidates to eliminate.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests balance reasoning: each weighing can only eliminate one candidate, so a knockout is best, and rounds are not the same as weighings.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 5 by 5 table is filled in with numbers. Every square in the top row and every square in the left column holds 1. Every other square holds the sum of the number directly above it and the number directly to its left. What number is in the bottom right square?

choices.misconception: I stopped one square too early and gave the number just to the left of the bottom right square.
I thought each square holds its row number times its column number, so I gave $5 \times 5 = 25$.
I added up the whole bottom row, 1 + 5 + 15 + 35 + 70 = 126, instead of taking only its last square.
I thought every step right or down adds just 1, so the bottom right square holds 5 + 5 - 1 = 9.

hints: Start filling in the table, one row at a time.
Each row is built from the row above it: every square adds the number above to the number on its left. Work along each row from left to right, and look for a pattern in the rows as they grow.
The first three rows are 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, then 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.

solutions.reliable: Fill the table row by row, working from left to right, since each square needs the square above it and the square to its left. Row 1 is 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Row 2 is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Row 3 is 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Row 4 is 1, 4, 10, 20, 35. Row 5 is 1, 5, 15, 35, 70. So the bottom right square holds 70. The transferable idea: when a table is defined by a rule, fill it in a careful order so that every square you need is already known.
solutions.elegant: The number in each square counts the routes from the top left square to it, moving one square right or down at a time: every route arrives from the square above or the square to the left, so the counts add, just like the rule. A route to the bottom right square makes 4 moves right and 4 moves down, 8 moves in all, and is fixed by choosing which 4 of the 8 are moves right: $\frac{8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 70$.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests filling a table from a rule and spotting its structure: each row is built from the row above, and every entry counts routes through the grid.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A clock face is marked with the hours 0 to 23 around its edge. Its hour hand turns once every 24 hours and points straight up at midnight. Its minute hand turns once every hour, as on an ordinary clock. What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 16:20, in degrees?

choices.misconception: I moved the hour hand on by half a degree per minute, as on an ordinary clock, but on this dial it moves only a quarter of a degree per minute.
I put the hour hand exactly on the 16 and forgot that it moves on during the 20 minutes.
I treated the clock as an ordinary 12-hour clock showing 4:20.
I found the larger angle between the hands, 360 - 125, instead of the smaller one.

hints: How many degrees does this hour hand turn in one hour?
The usual clock facts do not work on this dial. Work out how many degrees each hand turns per minute, find where each hand points, measured clockwise from straight up, and subtract.
The hour hand turns 360 / 24 = 15 degrees per hour, a quarter of a degree per minute, so at 16:20 it is at $16 \times 15 + 20 \times 0.25$ degrees. The minute hand is at $20 \times 6$ degrees.

solutions.reliable: Measure clockwise from straight up. The hour hand moves 360 / 24 = 15 degrees per hour, which is 0.25 degrees per minute. At 16:20 it is at $16 \times 15 + 20 \times 0.25 = 240 + 5 = 245$ degrees. The minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute, so it is at $20 \times 6 = 120$ degrees. The angle between them is 245 - 120 = 125 degrees, and since that is less than 180 it is the smaller angle. The transferable idea: for any clock, find each hand's speed in degrees per minute and locate both hands from the same starting line.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests clock geometry from first principles: the usual 30 and 0.5 degree facts fail on this dial, so each hand's speed must be worked out.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The table shows how many goals a hockey team scored in each of its 16 matches this season. $$\begin{array}{l|ccccc} \text{Goals in a match} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline \text{Number of matches} & 2 & 6 & 3 & 1 & 4 \end{array}$$ What is the median number of goals per match?

choices.misconception: I gave the number of goals that happened most often, which is the mode, not the median.
I took the 9th match on its own as the middle, instead of averaging the 8th and 9th of the 16.
I found the median of the bottom row, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6, instead of the median number of goals.
I gave the largest number in the bottom row, which is how many matches had the most common score.

hints: Imagine all 16 scores written in order from smallest to largest.
With 16 values, the median is halfway between the 8th and 9th values in order. Use the table to find which score sits in each of those places, counting through the columns.
The first 2 values are 0, the next 6 (places 3 to 8) are 1, and the next 3 (places 9 to 11) are 2.

solutions.reliable: List the 16 scores in order: places 1 and 2 are 0, places 3 to 8 are 1, places 9 to 11 are 2, place 12 is 3, and places 13 to 16 are 4. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle ones, the 8th and the 9th: (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5. The transferable idea: in a frequency table, count through the columns to find the middle places, and with an even count average the two middle values.

problems.whyOnTest: Tests reading a frequency table: the median is a position among all 16 matches, not a value read straight off one row.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid clay figure is 6 cm tall and weighs 40 g. A second solid figure has exactly the same shape, is made of the same clay and is 15 cm tall. How much does the second figure weigh, in grams?

choices.misconception: I scaled the weight by the height ratio $\frac{15}{6}$ once, as if weight grew like a length.
I used the extra height, 9 cm compared with 6 cm, and cubed $\frac{9}{6}$ instead of $\frac{15}{6}$.
I multiplied by the square of $\frac{15}{6}$, as if weight grew like an area.
I cubed only the 5 in $\frac{5}{2}$ and forgot to cube the 2, so I multiplied 40 by $\frac{125}{2}$.

hints: Weight depends on the amount of clay. How does volume grow?
Similar solids: if every length is multiplied by a scale factor, every volume, and so every weight of the same material, is multiplied by the cube of that factor.
The scale factor is $\frac{15}{6} = \frac{5}{2}$, so the volume is multiplied by $\frac{5}{2} \times \frac{5}{2} \times \frac{5}{2} = \frac{125}{8}$.

solutions.reliable: Every length of the big figure is $\frac{15}{6} = \frac{5}{2}$ times the matching length of the small one. Volume uses three lengths multiplied together, so the volume, and with the same clay the weight, is multiplied by $\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{125}{8}$. The weight is $40 \times \frac{125}{8} = 5 \times 125 = 625$ g. The transferable idea: lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$.
solutions.elegant: Measure in units of 3 cm: the small figure is 2 units tall and the big one is 5 units tall. Their volumes compare like $2^3 = 8$ to $5^3 = 125$. So 8 parts weigh 40 g, one part weighs 5 g, and 125 parts weigh 625 g.

problems.whyOnTest: Scaling a solid tests whether you know weight follows volume, so it grows with the cube of the length ratio, not the ratio itself.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Walls X and Y meet at a right angle. On the floor, P is 1 m from X and 5 m from Y; Q is 4 m from X and 7 m from Y. A ball rolls straight from P, bounces off X, then off Y, and stops at Q. What is the shortest possible path, in metres?

choices.misconception: I reflected P in wall X and measured straight to Q, which leaves out the bounce off wall Y.
I sent the ball straight into the corner where the walls meet, thinking that touches both walls in the shortest way.
I reflected only Q in wall Y and measured straight from P, which leaves out the bounce off wall X.
I unfolded the path into a 5 by 12 right triangle correctly, but added the two short sides instead of finding the long side.

hints: Can you replace a bounce by a mirror image?
Reflecting a point in a wall turns a path that bounces off that wall into a straight line of the same length. Reflect P in wall X and Q in wall Y, then join the two images.
Put the corner at $(0, 0)$ with wall X along one axis: P is $(1, 5)$ and Q is $(4, 7)$. Their images are $(-1, 5)$ and $(4, -7)$, which are 5 apart across and 12 apart up and down.

solutions.reliable: Put the corner at the origin, with wall X on the line $x = 0$ and wall Y on the line $y = 0$. Then P is $(1, 5)$ and Q is $(4, 7)$. Reflecting P in wall X gives $P' = (-1, 5)$, and reflecting Q in wall Y gives $Q' = (4, -7)$. Any path P, then wall X, then wall Y, then Q has the same length as a path from $P'$ to the same two wall points to $Q'$, and that is shortest when it is straight. The straight segment from $P'$ to $Q'$ crosses wall X 2.6 m from the corner and then wall Y $\frac{13}{12}$ m from the corner, so the bounces happen in the right order. Its length is $\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ m. The transferable idea: a bounce is a reflection, so unfold the path into a straight line.
solutions.elegant: Unfold both bounces from Q's end: reflecting Q in wall Y and then in wall X is the same as a half turn about the corner, which sends $Q = (4, 7)$ to $(-4, -7)$. The path is at least as long as the straight line from $P = (1, 5)$ to $(-4, -7)$, which is $\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13$, and the straight line is reached. Going through the corner instead gives $\sqrt{26} + \sqrt{65} \approx 13.16$, a little longer.

problems.whyOnTest: Shortest bouncing paths reward the reflection trick: mirror the endpoints, draw one straight line, and a hard minimum becomes Pythagoras.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Between 1:00 pm and 5:00 pm on the same afternoon, how many times do the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock make an angle of exactly $90^\circ$?

choices.misconception: I counted only the times when the minute hand is a quarter turn behind the hour hand.
I counted only the times when the minute hand is a quarter turn ahead of the hour hand.
I counted two right angles in each of the four hours and then added one more for 3:00.
