problems.statement: Books stand in a single row on a shelf. The red book is 9th from the left end and the blue book is 14th from the right end. The red book is to the left of the blue book, and exactly three books stand between them. How many books are on the shelf?

choices.misconception: I put the blue book to the left of the red one, so it was 5th from the left, which gives 5 + 14 - 1 = 18.
I added 9 and 14 and forgot the three books between the red book and the blue book.
I placed the blue book three places after the red one, 12th from the left, instead of four places after, and got 12 + 14 - 1.
I added 9, 3 and 14 and then added the red and blue books again, counting them twice.

hints: First work out the blue book's place counted from the left.
Draw the shelf as a row of boxes. Three books between red and blue put the blue book four places after the red one. Then use the blue book's place from the right to find the total.
The blue book is 9 + 4 = 13th from the left and 14th from the right, so 12 books are to its left and 13 to its right.

solutions.reliable: The red book is 9th from the left. Three books stand between red and blue, so the blue book is 9 + 3 + 1 = 13th from the left. Being 14th from the right means 13 books stand to its right. The total is 12 to its left, the blue book, and 13 to its right: 12 + 1 + 13 = 26. The transferable idea: when one item's place is counted from both ends, the total is (place from the left) + (place from the right) - 1.
solutions.elegant: Split the shelf into three blocks: the red book and the 8 to its left (9 books), the 3 in between, and the blue book with the 13 to its right (14 books). Then 9 + 3 + 14 = 26, with nothing counted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering questions test careful counting of positions from both ends, where off-by-one errors are the main trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven children of different heights stand in a row. Each child counts how many of the children to their left are taller than them. From left to right, the counts are 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 2, 5. In which position, counting from the left, is the tallest child?

choices.misconception: I assumed the first child, with nobody on the left, must be the tallest.
I mixed up taller and shorter and found the shortest child, who stands in 2nd place.
I assumed the child with the biggest count, 5, is the tallest, but a big count means many taller children.
I thought the counts do not give enough information to fix the order of the heights.

hints: What count must the tallest child have?
Nobody is taller than the tallest child, so its count is 0. Also, every child to the right of the tallest has at least one taller child on their left. Use both facts.
Only the children in positions 1 and 4 count 0. If the tallest stood in position 1, what would the child in position 4 have counted?

solutions.reliable: Nobody is taller than the tallest child, so the tallest child counts 0: that leaves position 1 or position 4. If the tallest child were in position 1, the child in position 4 would have a taller child on the left and could not count 0. So the tallest child is in position 4. Check: the children in positions 5, 6 and 7 all count at least 1, which fits, since the tallest stands to their left. In fact the counts fix the whole order: from tallest to shortest the positions are 4, 1, 6, 3, 5, 7, 2. The transferable idea: in ordering puzzles, start from the extreme item and ask what clue it must produce.
solutions.elegant: The tallest child counts 0, and every child to its right counts at least 1, so the tallest is always the last child in the row who counts 0. Here that is position 4.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering from clues rewards starting with the extreme case: the tallest child counts 0, so it must be the last 0 in the list.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A frog sits at 0 on a number line. It makes ten jumps: the first of length 1, the second of length 2, and so on, up to the tenth of length 10. Each jump goes left or right, as the frog chooses. How many different numbers could the frog finish on?

choices.misconception: I counted only the odd numbers to the right of 0, from 1 to 55, and forgot the same numbers on the left.
I counted the odd numbers strictly between -55 and 55, thinking the two ends could not be reached, though jumping right every time reaches 55.
I counted every whole number from -55 to 55, forgetting that the finishing number is always odd.
I counted the 1024 ways of choosing the ten directions, as if different choices always finish on different numbers.

hints: Is the finishing number odd or even?

Turning one jump from right to left lowers the finish by twice that jump, so its parity never changes. Find the parity and the range, then check whether every number of that parity in the range can be reached.
Jumping right every time gives 55. Sending jumps with total length s to the left instead gives 55 - 2s, and s can be any whole number from 0 to 55.

solutions.reliable: If every jump goes right, the frog ends at 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55. Sending a set of jumps left instead, with lengths adding up to s, changes the finish to 55 - 2s. So the finish is always odd and lies between -55 and 55. Every s from 0 to 55 is possible: from 1 to 10 use a single jump, and larger totals can be built from the largest lengths (for example 11 = 10 + 1 and 30 = 10 + 9 + 8 + 3). So every odd number from -55 to 55 can be reached. There are 28 odd numbers from 1 to 55 and 28 from -55 to -1, so 56 in all. The transferable idea: a parity argument shows which values are impossible; then check that all the others really occur.
solutions.elegant: The finish is 55 - 2s, where s is the total length of the jumps sent left, and s can be any whole number from 0 to 55. Different values of s give different finishes, so there are 56 of them.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity questions test spotting what never changes, here the oddness of the finishing point, before counting what can be reached.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are written on a board. A step means erasing two of the numbers, say $a$ and $b$, and writing the number $ab - a - b + 2$ instead. After six steps only one number is left. What is that number?

choices.misconception: I found that the product of the numbers each minus 1 never changes, and it is 0 here, but I forgot that the last number is that product plus 1.
I assumed the sum of the numbers stays the same, as it would if each step wrote a + b.
I multiplied 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 × 6, one less than each of the numbers 2 to 7, leaving out the factor 0 that comes from the number 1, and then added 1.
I assumed the product of all the numbers stays the same, 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 × 6 × 7.

hints: Rewrite $ab - a - b + 2$ as a product plus something.
Look for a quantity that does not change from step to step. Factorise ab - a - b + 1, and think about each number on the board minus 1.
ab - a - b + 2 = (a - 1)(b - 1) + 1. So if you think of each number x on the board as x - 1, a step just multiplies two of these together.

solutions.reliable: The new number is $(a - 1)(b - 1) + 1$, so the new number minus 1 equals $(a - 1)(b - 1)$. Hence the product of (x - 1) over all the numbers on the board never changes. At the start it is (1 - 1)(2 - 1)(3 - 1)...(7 - 1) = 0, because of the number 1. At the end there is one number N with N - 1 = 0, so N = 1, whatever order the steps are done in. The transferable idea: when a process allows many choices but the question expects one answer, look for a quantity that never changes.
solutions.elegant: Since the answer cannot depend on the order, pick an easy order. Combining 1 with any number b gives b - 1 - b + 2 = 1. So combine 1 with 2 to get 1, then that 1 with 3, and so on: the last number is 1.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariant questions test finding a hidden quantity that never changes, so a long process with many choices has one forced outcome.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bishop is a chess piece that moves any number of squares diagonally. A bishop starts in a corner square of a board with 7 rows and 9 columns, coloured like a chessboard. Making as many moves as it likes, how many squares of the board can it visit, including its starting square?

choices.misconception: I counted only the squares on the one diagonal through the corner, forgetting that the bishop can change direction.
I halved the 63 squares and rounded down, not noticing that the colour of the corners is the one with the extra square.
I thought every row had 5 squares of the corner's colour, so 7 × 5, but the rows alternate between 5 and 4.
I thought the bishop could reach every square if it made enough moves.

hints: What happens to the colour of the bishop's square on each move?
A diagonal move never changes the colour of the square, so the bishop is stuck on squares of its starting colour. Count those, and check that it can really reach all of them.
In each row of 9 the colours alternate. Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 start with the corner's colour, rows 2, 4 and 6 start with the other colour.

solutions.reliable: A diagonal move always lands on a square of the same colour, so the bishop only ever visits squares of the corner's colour. Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 start with that colour and contain 5 such squares each; rows 2, 4 and 6 contain 4 each. That is 4 × 5 + 3 × 4 = 32. On a board this size the bishop can zigzag to every square of its colour, so all 32 can be visited. The transferable idea: colour the board so that a move always keeps (or always switches) the colour, then count by colour.
solutions.elegant: The 63 squares split into 32 of one colour and 31 of the other. With an odd number of rows and of columns, all four corners share a colour, and that is the colour with the extra square: 32.

problems.whyOnTest: Colouring arguments test noticing a property that a move can never change, here the colour of the square the bishop stands on.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Eleven teams play in a league. Every two teams play each other exactly once; each match has a winner, who gets 1 point, and a loser, who gets 0. At the end, ten of the teams have the same number of points (the eleventh may or may not have that number too). How many points does the eleventh team have?

choices.misconception: I assumed the team that is different from the others must have lost every match.
I assumed the team that is different from the others must have won every match.
I gave each of the ten teams 4 points and the remaining 55 - 40 = 15 to the eleventh team, forgetting that it plays only 10 matches.
I thought many different results were possible, so I did not look for a reason why only one score fits.

hints: How many points are handed out in the whole league?
Count the matches to get the total number of points. If the ten equal teams have p points each, write the total using p and the eleventh team's score, and remember how many matches each team plays.
There are 55 matches, so 10p + q = 55, where q is the eleventh team's score and q is between 0 and 10.

solutions.reliable: Each match gives out exactly 1 point, and there are 11 × 10 ÷ 2 = 55 matches, so the points add up to 55. If the ten teams have p points each and the eleventh has q, then 10p + q = 55. The eleventh team plays only 10 matches, so q is between 0 and 10. Since 55 - q must be a multiple of 10, q ends in 5, and the only such number from 0 to 10 is 5. Then p = 5 as well, so in fact all eleven teams finish level. This can really happen: place the teams around a circle and let each team beat the next five teams clockwise. The transferable idea: suppose a different value and show that it breaks a total you know exactly.
solutions.elegant: The ten teams' points add up to a multiple of 10, so the eleventh team's score has the same last digit as 55. A score from 0 to 10 that ends in 5 must be 5.

problems.whyOnTest: Proof by contradiction tests ruling out every other value with a fixed count, here the 55 points shared out in the league.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A passenger sits by the window of a train travelling at 70 km/h. A train 150 m long passes in the opposite direction, taking exactly 6 seconds from the moment its front reaches her window until its back passes it. What is the speed of the other train, in km/h?

choices.misconception: I worked out 150 ÷ 6 = 25 metres per second and forgot both to change it into km/h and to take away the speed of her own train.
I thought the two trains share the closing speed of 90 km/h equally, so each has half of it.
I found the closing speed of the two trains, 90 km/h, and forgot to take away the speed of her own train.
I added the 70 km/h of her own train to the closing speed of 90 km/h instead of subtracting it.

hints: How fast does the other train move past her window, in metres per second?

From her seat, the other train goes past at the two speeds added, because the trains move in opposite directions. Find that closing speed from the length and the time, change it to km/h, then remove her own speed.
The other train moves 150 m past her in 6 seconds: 25 metres per second, which is 90 km/h.

solutions.reliable: Relative to the passenger, the other train moves its own length, 150 m, in 6 seconds, so the closing speed is 25 metres per second. One metre per second is 3.6 km/h, so this is 25 × 3.6 = 90 km/h. The trains move in opposite directions, so the closing speed is the sum of their speeds: 70 + v = 90, which gives v = 20 km/h. The transferable idea: in passing problems, use the speed of one object relative to the other, and remember that opposite directions add.

problems.whyOnTest: Passing questions test relative speed and unit changes together: closing speed from length and time, then convert and subtract.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The ages of the five members of a family, in whole years, add up to 80 today. Exactly four years ago, the ages of the family members who had already been born added up to 61. How old is the youngest member of the family today?

choices.misconception: I noticed the total grew by 19 instead of 20 and took the missing 1 as the youngest's age.
I assumed the youngest was born exactly four years ago, but then the total would have grown by the full 20.
I subtracted 61 from 80 and gave the difference as the youngest's age.
I expected all five ages to grow by 4, making 20, so I thought a growth of 19 was impossible, forgetting that someone may not have been born yet.

hints: Had all five been alive four years ago, how much would the total grow?
Each person alive four years ago adds exactly 4 to the total. Someone born more recently adds only their present age. Compare 80 - 61 with what you would expect.
The total grew by 19, not 20. Four people who were alive four years ago account for 16 of it.

solutions.reliable: If all five had been born four years ago, the total would have grown by 5 × 4 = 20, but it grew by 80 - 61 = 19. So someone was born less than four years ago. Each person who was alive four years ago adds exactly 4. If four were alive then, they add 16, and the newest member adds their present age, 19 - 16 = 3, which is under 4, so it fits. If only three were alive, they add 12 and the two youngest would need ages adding up to 7, but each is at most 3, so that is impossible. So the youngest is 3. The transferable idea: in age problems everyone alive ages by the same amount, so compare the real change in a total with the expected change.

problems.whyOnTest: Age problems test that everyone alive ages equally, so a total that grows by less than expected reveals someone not yet born.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten straight lines are drawn in the plane. No two of them are parallel, and no three of them pass through the same point. Into how many regions do the ten lines divide the plane?

choices.misconception: I thought each new line adds just one region, as it would if all the lines were parallel.
I thought each line adds two regions, one on each side of it.
I added 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55 for the regions the lines add, but forgot the one region the plane was before any line was drawn.
I saw that 1 line and 2 lines make 2 and 4 regions and assumed the number keeps doubling, but 3 lines make only 7.

hints: Count the regions for 1, 2, 3 and 4 lines.
Find a rule for how many new regions one more line creates. The new line crosses every earlier line, and each piece of the new line between crossings splits one old region in two.
The 4th line crosses the 3 earlier lines at 3 different points, so it is cut into 4 pieces and adds 4 regions. In the same way the k-th line adds k regions.

solutions.reliable: With no lines the plane is 1 region. The k-th line crosses each of the k - 1 earlier lines exactly once, since no two are parallel, and at k - 1 different points, since no three meet at a point. These points cut the new line into k pieces, and each piece splits one old region into two, so the k-th line adds k regions. The counts are 2, 4, 7, 11, ... for 1, 2, 3, 4 lines, and for ten lines the total is 1 + (1 + 2 + ... + 10) = 1 + 55 = 56. The transferable idea: for a count that grows step by step, find how one more object changes it, then add up the changes.
solutions.elegant: Count what creates regions: the plane starts as 1 region, each line adds 1 region when it is drawn on its own, and each crossing point adds 1 more. Ten lines have $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ crossing points, so there are 1 + 10 + 45 = 56 regions.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive counting tests finding how one more line changes the total, instead of guessing a pattern from the first two cases.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sheet of paper 0.1 mm thick is cut in half and one half is put on top of the other. The two-sheet stack is cut in half and stacked again in the same way, and so on, 20 cuts in all. Roughly how tall is the final stack?

choices.misconception: I added 0.1 mm for each of the 20 cuts instead of doubling the thickness every time.
I thought 20 doublings make 2 to the power 10 plus 2 to the power 10, about 2000 sheets, instead of 2 to the power 10 times 2 to the power 10.
I found about 100 000 mm but divided by 100 instead of by 1000 to change millimetres into metres.
I found about 100 000 mm and then read it as 100 000 m, forgetting to change the units.

hints: How many sheets are in the stack after 20 cuts?
Each cut doubles the number of sheets, so after 20 cuts there are 2 to the power 20 sheets. Estimate this using 2 to the power 10 ≈ 1000, multiply by the thickness, and change units carefully.
$2^{20} = 2^{10} \times 2^{10} \approx 1000 \times 1000$, so about a million sheets, each 0.1 mm thick.

solutions.reliable: Each cut doubles the number of sheets, so after 20 cuts there are $2^{20}$ sheets. Since $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 1000$, $2^{20}$ is about 1 000 000 (exactly 1 048 576). The height is about 1 000 000 × 0.1 mm = 100 000 mm. There are 1000 mm in a metre, so this is about 100 m (more exactly 104.9 m), the height of a tall building. The transferable idea: repeated doubling grows by a factor of about 1000 every 10 steps.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimation questions test handling repeated doubling with the benchmark 2 to the 10th ≈ 1000, then converting units without slipping a factor of 10.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A six-digit number is made by writing the same two-digit number three times in a row, such as 474747 or 101010. Which of these numbers divides every six-digit number made in this way?

choices.misconception: I saw that the digit sum is three times the digit sum of the two-digit number and thought that made it a multiple of 9, but it only makes it a multiple of 3.
I thought a repeating pattern of digits always passes the test for 11, but the alternating sum is 3 times the difference of the two digits, which is usually not 0.
I remembered that four-digit numbers like 4747 are multiples of 101 and assumed the same holds for six digits.
I mixed this up with numbers like 474474, a three-digit block written twice, which are multiples of 1001.

hints: Write 474747 as 47 times something.
Writing a two-digit number three times in a row is the same as multiplying it by one fixed number. Find that number and factorise it.
474747 = 47 × 10101, and the same multiplier works for every two-digit block. Now factorise 10101.

solutions.reliable: If the two-digit block is n, the six-digit number is n × 10000 + n × 100 + n = n × 10101. Now 10101 = 3 × 3367 = 3 × 7 × 481 = 3 × 7 × 13 × 37, so every such number is a multiple of 3, 7, 13 and 37. Of the choices, only 7 always divides. The others fail for n = 10: 101010 has digit sum 3, so it is not a multiple of 9; 101010 ÷ 11 is not a whole number; 101010 ÷ 101 is not a whole number; and 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 would need a factor 11. The transferable idea: write a digit pattern as a block times a fixed multiplier, then factorise the multiplier.

problems.whyOnTest: Divisibility questions about digit patterns test writing the pattern as a block times a fixed number, here 10101 = 3 × 7 × 13 × 37.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a pond, 80% of the fish are carp. Some of the carp are taken out, and no other fish are added or removed. Now 50% of the fish in the pond are carp. What percentage of the carp were taken out?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 50 from 80, treating the drop in percentage points as the share of carp removed.
I thought the carp went from 80 to 50 out of the same 100 fish, so 30 of the 80 carp were removed.
I found that 40 fish are left out of the original 100 and gave that instead.
I found that 60 fish were removed and gave that as a percentage of all the fish, not of the carp.

hints: Which fish do not change in number?
Imagine 100 fish at the start. The other fish are not touched, so their number stays the same, but they become a larger share of the pond. Use them to find the new total.
There are 20 other fish. After the removal they make up 50% of the pond, so the pond holds 40 fish.

solutions.reliable: Start with 100 fish: 80 carp and 20 others. The 20 others stay, and afterwards they make up 50% of the pond, so the pond now holds 40 fish, of which 20 are carp. So 80 - 20 = 60 carp were taken out, which is 60/80 = 75% of the carp. The transferable idea: when percentages change, anchor on the quantity that does not change.

problems.whyOnTest: Percentage-change questions test anchoring on the part that stays fixed, because the total itself changes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four friends sit in a row of seven empty chairs, one person per chair. In how many ways can they sit so that at least two of them are next to each other? (It matters who sits in which chair.)

choices.misconception: I counted the seatings where nobody sits next to anybody, which is the opposite case, and forgot to subtract it from the total.
I counted sets of four chairs, 35 - 1, and forgot that the four friends can be arranged in those chairs in 24 ways.
I counted all the seatings, 7 × 6 × 5 × 4, without removing those where nobody sits next to anybody.
I chose a pair of neighbouring chairs, seated two friends there and the other two anywhere, which counts many seatings more than once.

hints: Count the opposite: when does nobody sit next to anybody?
Count all the seatings, then subtract those in which no two friends sit side by side. With four people and only seven chairs, very few choices of chairs keep everyone apart.
All seatings: 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 840. Four chairs out of seven with no two next to each other must be chairs 1, 3, 5 and 7.

solutions.reliable: All seatings: 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 840. If no two friends are neighbours, the four chairs need an empty chair between each pair, which uses at least 4 + 3 = 7 chairs, so the chairs must be 1, 3, 5 and 7, and the friends can sit in them in 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways. So at least two friends are neighbours in 840 - 24 = 816 seatings. The transferable idea: "at least" conditions are usually easier through the opposite case.

problems.whyOnTest: Complementary counting tests turning a messy "at least" condition into a total minus one small, clean case.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Twenty children stand in a circle, numbered 1 to 20 clockwise. Going clockwise round and round, starting with child 1, the children still standing are passed in turn and every second one sits down: child 1 stays up, child 2 sits, child 3 stays up, child 4 sits, and so on. Which child is the last one standing?

choices.misconception: I tried 2, 4 and 8 children, where child 1 is always the last one standing, and assumed the same happens with 20.
I knew child 1 is last with 16 children, but I started adding 2 from 17 children instead of from 16, so I added only three steps of 2.
I treated each trip round the circle separately, and from the second trip on I started by sitting down the first child still standing.
I saw that all the even-numbered children sit down on the first trip round and assumed the last odd number, 19, would be left.

hints: Play the same game with fewer children first.
Find the last child standing for 1, 2, 3, up to about 10 children, and look for a pattern. Pay special attention to what happens with 2, 4, 8 and 16 children.
For 1 to 8 children the last one standing is child 1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 5, 7, 1. The answer is child 1 whenever the number of children is a power of 2, and it goes up by 2 for each extra child after that.

solutions.reliable: Small cases give, for 1 to 8 children, the winners 1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 5, 7, 1. Here is why the powers of 2 matter. If an even number of children are standing and child 1 is next to be passed, one trip round sits down every second child and comes back to child 1, who is passed again, with half as many children left. Starting from 16, this halves to 8, 4, 2 and 1, and child 1 is never the one who sits. Now take 20 = 16 + 4 children. After four children sit down (children 2, 4, 6 and 8), 16 remain and the next child to be passed, staying up, is child 9. From here the game is exactly a game of 16 starting with child 9, so child 9 is last. The transferable idea: small cases reveal the pattern, but check enough of them, because a pattern can reset, as this one does at each power of 2.
solutions.elegant: Write the number of children as a power of 2 plus a remainder: 20 = 16 + 4. Once 4 children have sat down, 16 remain and child 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 is first in line, and in a game with a power of 2 children the first in line always wins. So child 9 is last.

problems.whyOnTest: Small cases reveal a pattern that resets at each power of 2, and a student who stops after 2, 4 and 8 children falls into the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A triangle has its corners at the points (1, 1), (7, 3) and (3, 9). What is its area?

choices.misconception: I used the coordinate formula for the area correctly but forgot to halve at the end.
I assumed the triangle covers exactly half of the 6 by 8 rectangle around it.
I worked out the three right-angled triangles around the outside and gave their total instead of subtracting it from the rectangle.
I gave the area of the 6 by 8 rectangle that surrounds the triangle.

hints: Draw the smallest rectangle, with sides along the grid lines, that contains the triangle.
Box the triangle in a rectangle, then cut away the right-angled triangles in the corners. Check the answer with a second method, such as the shoelace formula.
The rectangle runs from x = 1 to 7 and from y = 1 to 9, so it is 6 by 8. The three corner triangles have areas 6, 12 and 8.

solutions.reliable: The smallest rectangle around the triangle has opposite corners (1, 1) and (7, 9), so it measures 6 by 8 and has area 48. Inside the rectangle but outside the triangle are three right-angled triangles: below the side from (1, 1) to (7, 3), with shorter sides 6 and 2 and area 6; to the right of the side from (7, 3) to (3, 9), with shorter sides 6 and 4 and area 12; to the left of the side from (3, 9) to (1, 1), with shorter sides 2 and 8 and area 8. So the triangle has area 48 - 26 = 22. A second method as a check: the shoelace formula gives half of |1(3 - 9) + 7(9 - 1) + 3(1 - 3)| = half of |-6 + 56 - 6| = 22. The transferable idea: when two independent methods agree, you can mark the answer with confidence.

problems.whyOnTest: Checking with a second method catches slips like a forgotten half: box-and-subtract and the shoelace formula must agree.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two joggers start together from opposite ends of a straight 400 m path and run towards each other at 5 metres per second and 3 metres per second. On reaching an end, each jogger turns round at once and keeps the same speed. After how many seconds do they meet for the second time?

choices.misconception: I found the first meeting, when together they have covered 400 m, and stopped there.
I thought they would meet again when the faster jogger reached the far end and turned round.
I doubled the time of the first meeting, as if together they covered only one more path length before meeting again.
I thought the faster jogger had to catch the slower one from behind, so I worked out 400 ÷ (5 - 3).

hints: Between two meetings, how far do the two joggers run altogether?
Draw a time line. Before the first meeting they cover one path length together. After it, each runs on to an end and turns back, so together they cover more before meeting again.
From the first meeting to the second, together they cover two path lengths, 800 m, at a combined 8 metres per second.

solutions.reliable: Together the joggers cover 8 m every second, so they first meet after 400 ÷ 8 = 50 s. After that, each runs on to the end ahead and turns back, and they meet again when together they have covered two more path lengths, 800 m, which takes 100 s. So the second meeting is at 150 s. Check positions: at 150 s the faster jogger has run 750 m, that is 400 m out and 350 m back, so it is 50 m from where it started; the slower one has run 450 m, that is 400 m and then 50 m back, so it is also 50 m from the faster one's starting end. Could the faster one catch the slower one from behind earlier? From 80 s both head for the same end, but the slower one turns at about 133 s, long before it could be caught. The transferable idea: for meetings on a back-and-forth path, track the total distance the two cover together.
solutions.elegant: Unfold the path: meeting head-on happens when together they have covered 1, 3, 5, ... path lengths. The second time is at 3 × 400 = 1200 m together, which at 8 metres per second is 150 s.

problems.whyOnTest: Meeting questions on a back-and-forth path test combined distance: after the first meeting the joggers must together cover two more path lengths.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Some cells of a 5 by 5 grid are painted so that every row and every column contains an even number of painted cells (zero counts as even). What is the largest possible number of painted cells?

choices.misconception: I thought an even number of painted cells in a row meant exactly two.
I left one whole row and one whole column empty and painted the 4 by 4 block that remains, which works but is not the most.
I left out a single cell, which fixes its own row and column but leaves the other four rows and columns with 5 painted cells.
I painted every cell, forgetting that 5 is an odd number.

hints: How many painted cells can one row hold at most?
Each row has 5 cells and needs an even number painted, so at most 4. That gives an upper bound for the whole grid. Then try to reach it while keeping every column even too.
At most 4 per row gives at most 20. Try leaving exactly one unpainted cell in each row and in each column.

solutions.reliable: A row has 5 cells and must contain an even number of painted ones, so it has at most 4. Five rows give at most 20 painted cells. Twenty is possible: leave the five cells of one diagonal unpainted and paint all the others. Then every row and every column has exactly 4 painted cells, which is even. The transferable idea: a parity condition can cap each line, giving a bound; then a symmetric construction shows the bound is reached.
solutions.elegant: Count the unpainted cells instead: each row and each column needs an odd number of unpainted cells, so at least 1, which means at least 5 unpainted cells. The 5 cells of a diagonal are enough, leaving 20 painted.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity questions test turning 'even in every row' into a bound, at most 4 of 5, and then finding a grid that reaches it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two circles, each of radius 5 cm, have centres 8 cm apart, so they cross at two points. How long is the straight line joining these two crossing points, in centimetres?

choices.misconception: I found the distance from the midpoint to one crossing point and forgot to double it.
I gave the distance from a centre to the midpoint of the common chord, which is half of 8.
I assumed the common chord is as long as the distance between the centres.
I took the common chord to be a diameter of one of the circles.

hints: Draw both circles, the line joining the centres and the line through the crossing points.
The line joining the crossing points is cut in half, at right angles, by the line joining the centres. Find a right-angled triangle that has a radius as its longest side.
Each centre is 4 cm from the midpoint of the chord, and a radius of 5 cm reaches from a centre to a crossing point.

solutions.reliable: Call the centres A and B and the crossing points P and Q. By symmetry PQ is perpendicular to AB, and the two segments cut each other in half at a point M, with AM = MB = 4. In the right-angled triangle AMP, AP = 5 and AM = 4, so MP = 3. Hence PQ = 2 × 3 = 6 cm. The transferable idea: draw the diagram with its line of symmetry, and a right-angled triangle usually appears.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing the diagram reveals the hidden right-angled triangle; without a sketch the common chord is easy to confuse with other lengths.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven numbers have a mean of 12. One of them, $x$, is replaced by $3x$, and the mean of the seven numbers becomes 14. What is $x$?

choices.misconception: I found how much the total went up, 14, and gave that as $x$, forgetting the increase is $3x - x = 2x$.
I thought the number itself went up by 2, the same as the mean, so I solved $2x = 2$.
I found the new number $3x$ instead of the original number $x$.
I thought the total went up by $3x$ instead of by $3x - x$, so I solved $3x = 14$.

hints: How much did the total of the seven numbers go up?
Turn both means into totals. The change in the total comes only from replacing $x$ by $3x$, so compare the increase in the total with $3x - x$.
The total rose from $7 \times 12 = 84$ to $7 \times 14 = 98$, an increase of 14.

solutions.reliable: The total was $7 \times 12 = 84$ and becomes $7 \times 14 = 98$, so it rose by 14. Replacing $x$ by $3x$ raises the total by $3x - x = 2x$, so $2x = 14$ and $x = 7$. Check: changing 7 to 21 adds 14 to the total. The transferable idea: a change in the mean times the count gives the change in the total.

problems.whyOnTest: Means questions test converting between means and totals; here the trap is mixing up the increase in the total with the number itself.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When Leo was born, his mother was 28. Today her age is 4 less than three times Leo's age. In how many years from now will she be exactly twice as old as Leo?

choices.misconception: I found Leo's age today and stopped there.
I found how old Leo will be when his mother is twice his age, not how many years away that is.
I found the mother's age today instead of the number of years.
I found the mother's age at the moment she is twice as old as Leo.

hints: The difference between their ages is always 28.
First use today's information, with the fixed gap of 28, to find Leo's age. Then ask: when is someone twice as old as a person 28 years younger?
Today $L + 28 = 3L - 4$, so Leo is 16 and his mother is 44. She is twice his age when he is 28.

solutions.reliable: Let Leo be $L$ today; his mother is $L + 28$. Then $L + 28 = 3L - 4$, so $L = 16$ and she is 44. In $t$ years, $44 + t = 2(16 + t)$, so $t = 12$. Check: in 12 years they are 28 and 56. The transferable idea: name the unknown the question asks for, then answer that, not a quantity found along the way.
solutions.elegant: A person 28 years older is exactly twice as old when the younger one is 28, because then the gap equals the younger age. Leo is 16 now (from $L + 28 = 3L - 4$), so that happens in $28 - 16 = 12$ years. The transferable idea: 'twice as old' happens when the younger age equals the gap.

problems.whyOnTest: Two-stage age questions reward tracking the fixed age gap and answering the exact question asked, here a number of years, not an age.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A course grade is worked out as 40% of the homework score plus 60% of the exam score. Lina's homework score is 90. What exam score does she need for a course grade of 75?

choices.misconception: I treated the grade as the plain average of homework and exam, so I solved $(90 + x) \div 2 = 75$.
I swapped the weights and used 60% for the homework and 40% for the exam.
I worked out how many points of the 75 the exam must supply, 39, and gave that instead of the exam score.
I thought she needs 75 on the exam to get 75 overall, whatever her homework score.

hints: How many of the 75 points come from her homework?
A weighted grade adds each score times its weight. Find the homework's share of the grade, then work out what exam score, times 0.6, makes up the rest.
The homework supplies $0.4 \times 90 = 36$ points, so the exam must supply $75 - 36 = 39$ points.

solutions.reliable: The grade is $0.4 \times 90 + 0.6x = 36 + 0.6x$. Setting $36 + 0.6x = 75$ gives $0.6x = 39$, so $x = 65$. Check: $0.4 \times 90 + 0.6 \times 65 = 36 + 39 = 75$. The transferable idea: in a weighted average, each part counts in proportion to its weight.
solutions.elegant: Her homework is 15 points above the target of 75 with weight 0.4, worth $0.4 \times 15 = 6$ points. The exam, with weight 0.6, must be 6 points' worth below 75: $6 \div 0.6 = 10$ below, so 65. The transferable idea: weighted deviations from the target must balance.

problems.whyOnTest: Weighted averages appear in grades, mixtures and prices; this checks you weight each part instead of taking a plain average.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Jug A holds 3 litres of a drink that is 40% juice. Jug B holds 4 litres of a drink that is 90% juice. Drink is poured from B into A until the drink in A is 60% juice. Then 1 litre is poured from A back into B. What percentage of the drink in B is now juice?

choices.misconception: I just averaged the two strengths, 90% and 60%, without considering how much of each is in jug B.
I forgot that 2 litres had already left jug B, so I added the returned litre to the full 4 litres.
I added up the juice in jug B correctly but divided by the original 4 litres instead of the 3 litres now in it.
I swapped the weights and mixed one part at 90% with two parts at 60%.

hints: First work out how much drink was poured from B into A.
Track litres of juice, not percentages. After the first pour, find jug A's volume and juice; then follow the litre poured back and recount the juice and the volume in jug B.
Pouring $x$ litres gives $1.2 + 0.9x = 0.6(3 + x)$, so $x = 2$, and jug B is left with 2 litres of its 90% drink.

solutions.reliable: Jug A starts with $0.4 \times 3 = 1.2$ litres of juice. Pouring $x$ litres from B adds $0.9x$ litres of juice, so $1.2 + 0.9x = 0.6(3 + x)$, which gives $0.3x = 0.6$ and $x = 2$. Jug B now holds 2 litres containing 1.8 litres of juice. One litre of A's 60% drink adds 0.6 litres of juice, so B holds 3 litres containing 2.4 litres of juice, and $2.4 \div 3 = 0.8$, which is 80%. The transferable idea: in mixture problems, follow the amount of the ingredient, not the percentage.
solutions.elegant: Jug B ends with 2 litres at 90% and 1 litre at 60%. Its strength is a weighted average, two thirds of the way from 60 towards 90 because there is twice as much of the 90% drink: $60 + 20 = 80$. The transferable idea: a two-part mixture's strength lies closer to the larger part, in proportion to the amounts.

problems.whyOnTest: Mixture questions test whether you track the actual amount of an ingredient through several pours rather than averaging percentages.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many six-digit numbers that use each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 exactly once are divisible by 12?

choices.misconception: I only checked that the number is even, so I counted every arrangement ending in 2, 4 or 6.
I thought the last two digits had to form a multiple of 12, so I only used the endings 12, 24 and 36.
I checked only divisibility by 3, which every arrangement passes, so I counted all the arrangements.
I thought a number is divisible by 4 when its last digit is 4, so I counted the arrangements ending in 4.

hints: Split 12 into two divisibility tests that are easier to check.
A number is divisible by 12 exactly when it is divisible by 3 and by 4. See what the digit sum tells you, then count the possible last two digits.
The digit sum is 21, so divisibility by 3 is automatic. List the two-digit endings made of different digits from 1 to 6 that are multiples of 4.

solutions.reliable: Since $12 = 3 \times 4$ and 3 and 4 share no factor, the number must be divisible by 3 and by 4. The digit sum is $1 + 2 + \dots + 6 = 21$, so every arrangement is divisible by 3. For 4, the last two digits must form a multiple of 4 using two different digits from 1 to 6: 12, 16, 24, 32, 36, 52, 56, 64, which is 8 endings. The other four digits can go in front in $4! = 24$ ways, so there are $8 \times 24 = 192$ numbers. The transferable idea: test divisibility by a composite number through factors that share nothing and have simple rules.

problems.whyOnTest: Divisibility by 12 needs two rules at once, for 3 and for 4; this probes whether you pick the right pair and apply the last-two-digits rule fully.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers is divisible by 24?

choices.misconception: I tested divisibility by 4 and by 6, because $24 = 4 \times 6$, and 5652 passes both.
I tested divisibility by 8 by looking only at the last two digits, 16, as in the test for 4.
I checked that 5384 is divisible by 8 and forgot that it must also be divisible by 3.
I saw that the digits add up to 24 and thought that makes the number divisible by 24.

hints: Write 24 as a product of two numbers that share no factor.
Use $24 = 3 \times 8$: the number must pass the test for 3 (digit sum) and the test for 8 (last three digits). Splitting 24 as $4 \times 6$ fails, because 4 and 6 share the factor 2.
Only one choice has a digit sum divisible by 3 and last three digits forming a multiple of 8.

solutions.reliable: Divisibility by 24 means divisibility by 3 and by 8, because $3 \times 8 = 24$ and 3 and 8 share no factor. 5832 has digit sum 18 and ends in 832, and $832 = 8 \times 104$, so both tests pass; indeed $5832 = 24 \times 243$. 5652 ends in 652 and 3516 ends in 516, neither a multiple of 8. 5384 has digit sum 20, not a multiple of 3. 6738 ends in 738, not a multiple of 8. The transferable idea: split a divisor into factors with no common factor before applying the simple tests.

problems.whyOnTest: Divisibility tests combine only through factors that share nothing; this checks you split 24 as 3 times 8 and use the last three digits for 8.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many of the 100 square numbers $1^2, 2^2, 3^2, \dots, 100^2$ leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 8?

choices.misconception: I thought only numbers leaving remainder 1 or 7 when divided by 8 have squares leaving remainder 1.
I thought $n^2$ leaves remainder 1 only when $n$ itself leaves remainder 1.
I only looked at the square numbers up to 100, which are 1, 9, 25, 49 and 81.
I knew squares leave remainder 0, 1 or 4 on division by 8 and assumed each happens equally often, about a third of 100.

hints: Try the squares of 1, 3, 5 and 7.
The remainder of $n^2$ on division by 8 depends only on the remainder of $n$. Check all eight possible remainders, or look at what happens to every odd number.
$1^2, 3^2, 5^2, 7^2$ are 1, 9, 25 and 49, and each leaves remainder 1. Even squares leave remainder 0 or 4.

solutions.reliable: The remainder of $n^2$ depends only on the remainder of $n$ on division by 8. Remainders 0 to 7 give squares 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, which leave remainders 0, 1, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 1. So remainder 1 happens exactly when $n$ is odd, which is 50 of the numbers from 1 to 100. The transferable idea: to study remainders of a formula, check one representative of each remainder class.
solutions.elegant: An odd number is $2k + 1$, and $(2k + 1)^2 = 4k(k + 1) + 1$. Since $k(k + 1)$ is even, $4k(k + 1)$ is a multiple of 8, so every odd square leaves remainder 1, while every even square is a multiple of 4 and leaves 0 or 4. The answer is the 50 odd numbers. The transferable idea: the product of two consecutive numbers is always even.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainder questions reward checking each remainder class once; here every odd square leaves remainder 1, which surprises students who only test a few cases.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Thirteen posts, numbered 0 to 12 in order, stand evenly around a circular track. A runner starts at post 0. In the first minute she runs forward 1 post, in the second minute 2 posts, in the third minute 3 posts, and so on. At which post is she after 100 minutes?

choices.misconception: I found the remainder of 100, the number of minutes, divided by 13, instead of using the total number of posts run.
I divided the total of 5050 posts by 12, because the posts go up to 12, instead of by the 13 posts.
I worked out $1 + 2 + \dots + 100$ as $100 \times 100 \div 2 = 5000$ instead of 5050.
I found the right remainder, 6, but counted the starting post as post 1 instead of post 0.

hints: How many posts does she pass in total?
Going once round the track brings her back to post 0, so only the remainder of her total distance, measured in posts, on division by 13 matters. Find the total first.
The total is $1 + 2 + \dots + 100 = 5050$ posts.

solutions.reliable: In 100 minutes she runs $1 + 2 + \dots + 100 = \frac{100 \times 101}{2} = 5050$ posts forward. Every 13 posts bring her back to post 0, and $5050 = 13 \times 388 + 6$, so she is at post 6. The transferable idea: positions around a circle of $n$ places are remainders on division by $n$.

problems.whyOnTest: Cyclic positions are remainders in disguise; the test is finding the total distance first and then dividing by the right number of places.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What are the last two digits of $7^{2026}$?

choices.misconception: I only tracked the last digit, 9, and assumed the tens digit would be 0.
I noticed that $7^4 = 2401$ ends in 01 and assumed every large power of 7 ends in 01.
I listed the cycle 01, 07, 49, 43 starting from $7^0$ and took its second entry because 2026 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 4.
I counted the powers left over after $7^{2024}$ as three instead of two.

hints: Work out the last two digits of the first few powers of 7.
Only the last two digits matter when you keep multiplying by 7. Look for a power of 7 whose last two digits are 01; after that the pattern of last two digits repeats.
$7^4 = 2401$ ends in 01, so the last two digits repeat every 4 powers: 07, 49, 43, 01.

solutions.reliable: The last two digits of $7^1, 7^2, 7^3, 7^4$ are 07, 49, 43, 01. Since $7^4$ ends in 01, multiplying by $7^4$ does not change the last two digits, so they repeat every 4 powers. As $2026 = 4 \times 506 + 2$, $7^{2026}$ ends in the same two digits as $7^2 = 49$. The transferable idea: a power ending in 01 makes the last two digits cycle.
solutions.elegant: $7^{2026} = (7^4)^{506} \times 7^2 = 2401^{506} \times 49$. Every power of 2401 ends in 01, and a number ending in 01 times 49 ends in 49. The transferable idea: split the exponent around a power that ends in 01.

problems.whyOnTest: Last-digit cycles extend to the last two digits once you find a power ending in 01; the trap is tracking only the final digit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: For how many whole numbers $n$ from 1 to 100 does $n^n$ end in the digit 6?

choices.misconception: I only counted the numbers ending in 6, since every power of such a number ends in 6.
I counted the numbers ending in 4 or 6 and forgot that numbers ending in 2 or 8 can work too.
I counted every number ending in 2, 4, 6 or 8, thinking all of their powers end in 6 when the exponent is even.
I thought powers of a number ending in 4 end in 6 only when the exponent is a multiple of 4, like the cycles for 2 and 8.

hints: Only the last digit of $n$ and the exponent matter.
Sort $n$ by its last digit. For each last digit, find the cycle of last digits of its powers and see which exponents give 6. Remember that the exponent is $n$ itself.
Last digit 6: always. Last digit 4: the cycle is 4, 6, so even exponents work. Last digits 2 and 8: cycles of length 4 that reach 6 at exponents that are multiples of 4.

solutions.reliable: Odd $n$ give odd $n^n$, and $n$ ending in 0 gives last digit 0, so only $n$ ending in 2, 4, 6 or 8 can work. Ending in 6: every power ends in 6, giving 10 numbers. Ending in 4: powers end in 4, 6, 4, 6, ..., so even exponents give 6, and every such $n$ is even, giving 10. Ending in 2: the cycle is 2, 4, 8, 6, so $n$ must be a multiple of 4: 12, 32, 52, 72, 92, giving 5. Ending in 8: the cycle is 8, 4, 2, 6, so again $n$ must be a multiple of 4: 8, 28, 48, 68, 88, giving 5. Total: $10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 30$. The transferable idea: when the exponent changes too, sort by last digit and use each cycle's length.

problems.whyOnTest: Here the exponent changes with the base, so you must combine last-digit cycles with casework on the last digit; skipping or overcounting a case is the usual loss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A jacket is reduced by 30%. At the till, a further 10% is taken off the reduced price, and the shopper pays 63 euros. What was the original price?

choices.misconception: I added the two discounts to make 40% off and divided 63 by 0.6.
I only undid the 30% reduction, dividing 63 by 0.7.
I only undid the 10% reduction, dividing 63 by 0.9.
I added 40% of 63 back on, instead of dividing by the fraction of the price that was paid.

hints: The second discount is taken from the reduced price, not the original.
Each discount multiplies the price: 30% off means paying 0.7 of it, then 10% off means paying 0.9 of that. Work out the combined multiplier, then undo it.
The shopper pays $0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63$ of the original price.

solutions.reliable: After both discounts the shopper pays $0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63$ of the original price $P$. So $0.63P = 63$, giving $P = 100$ euros. The transferable idea: successive percentage changes multiply, and undoing a change means dividing by its multiplier.
solutions.elegant: Check by going forwards from a choice: 100 euros minus 30% is 70 euros, and 10% off 70 euros leaves 63 euros. The transferable idea: back-solving from a choice confirms a chain of percentages quickly.

problems.whyOnTest: Stacked discounts multiply rather than add, and undoing a percentage means dividing; both traps are on offer here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Over one year, the number of fiction books in a library rose by 50%, the number of non-fiction books stayed the same, and the total number of books rose by 20%. What percentage of the books were fiction at the start of the year?

choices.misconception: I found the percentage of fiction books at the end of the year instead of at the start.
I found the percentage of non-fiction books at the start instead of fiction books.
I found the ratio of fiction to non-fiction books, $2 : 3$, and turned the fraction $\frac{2}{3}$ into a percentage.
I subtracted the 20% rise from the 50% rise and took the difference as the fiction share.

hints: Let there be $f$ fiction and $n$ non-fiction books at the start.
Write the end-of-year total in two ways: from the 50% rise in fiction with non-fiction unchanged, and from the overall 20% rise. Setting them equal gives the ratio of fiction to non-fiction.

solutions.reliable: With $f$ fiction and $n$ non-fiction books, the end of the year has $1.5f + n$ books, which is also $1.2(f + n)$. So $0.3f = 0.2n$, and $f : n = 2 : 3$. Fiction was $\frac{2}{5}$ of the books, which is 40%. Check with 200 fiction and 300 non-fiction: at the end there are 300 and 300, 600 books, which is 20% more than 500. The transferable idea: an overall percentage change is a weighted average of the group changes.
solutions.elegant: The whole collection grew by 20%, a weighted average of fiction's 50% and non-fiction's 0%. Since 20 is $\frac{20}{50} = \frac{2}{5}$ of the way from 0 to 50, fiction was $\frac{2}{5}$ of the books: 40%. The transferable idea: a combined rate sits between the group rates, in proportion to the group sizes.

problems.whyOnTest: Percentage-change questions often hide a weighted average; this checks you set up both totals and answer for the right moment.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to $\sqrt{50} + \sqrt{99}$?

choices.misconception: I added under the square root first, working out $\sqrt{50 + 99} = \sqrt{149}$.
I thought $\sqrt{50}$ is 5, half of $\sqrt{100}$, because 50 is half of 100.
I rounded both square roots up, to 8 and 10.
I used the square roots of the perfect squares just below, $\sqrt{25} = 5$ and $\sqrt{81} = 9$.

hints: Which perfect squares are close to 50 and to 99?
Compare each number with the nearest perfect square: 50 is just above 49 and 99 is just below 100. Square roots of sums cannot be split, so estimate each root separately.
$\sqrt{50}$ is a little more than 7 and $\sqrt{99}$ is a little less than 10.

solutions.reliable: Since $49 < 50$, $\sqrt{50}$ is a little more than 7 (about 7.07), and since $99 < 100$, $\sqrt{99}$ is a little less than 10 (about 9.95). The sum is about 17.02, so 17 is closest. The transferable idea: estimate a square root from the nearest perfect square, and never add under the root sign.

problems.whyOnTest: Estimation questions reward anchoring square roots to nearby perfect squares; adding under the root sign is the classic trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five numbers have a mean of 20. If one of them is removed, the other four have a mean of 18. If instead a different one of the five is removed, the other four have a mean of 23. What is the difference between the two numbers that were removed?

choices.misconception: I found the difference between the two new means and stopped there.
I multiplied the 5-point difference in means by 5, the original count, instead of by 4.
I only found the first number that was removed.
I only found the second number that was removed.

hints: Turn each mean into a total.
Mean times count gives a total. Subtracting each removed number from the total of all five gives a total of four numbers; compare the two four-number totals.
The five numbers total 100, and the two groups of four total 72 and 92.

solutions.reliable: The five numbers total $5 \times 20 = 100$. Removing the first leaves $4 \times 18 = 72$, so it was 28. Removing the second leaves $4 \times 23 = 92$, so it was 8. The difference is $28 - 8 = 20$. The transferable idea: convert means to totals before adding or removing items.
solutions.elegant: Both groups of four come from the same five numbers, so the difference between the removed numbers equals the difference between the four-number totals: $4 \times (23 - 18) = 20$. The transferable idea: when two cases share the same total, compare their differences directly.

problems.whyOnTest: Means questions test that you convert to totals; this one rewards spotting that only the difference of the two four-number totals matters.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six different positive whole numbers have a mean of 10. What is the largest possible value of their median?

choices.misconception: I forgot the numbers must all be different, so I made the four largest numbers as equal as possible, such as 1, 1, 14, 14, 15, 15.
I took the median of six numbers to be the fourth number and made that as large as possible.
I made the two middle numbers equal, wrote $1 + 2 + c + c + (c + 1) + (c + 2) = 60$ and got $c = 13.5$.
I thought the median of a list must be equal to its mean.

hints: The median of six numbers is the average of the third and fourth.

The total is fixed at 60. To push the middle two numbers up, make every other number as small as the rules allow: the two smallest as small as possible, and the two largest only just above the fourth.
With the list $1, 2, c, d, d + 1, d + 2$, the total is $c + 3d + 6 = 60$, and $c < d$.

solutions.reliable: Order the numbers $a < b < c < d < e < f$, with total 60 and median $\frac{c + d}{2}$. Make the others as small as possible: $a = 1$, $b = 2$, $e = d + 1$, $f = d + 2$. Then $c + 3d = 54$, so $c + d = 54 - 2d$, which is largest when $d$ is smallest. But $c < d$ means $54 - 3d < d$, so $d \ge 14$. With $d = 14$ and $c = 12$, the list 1, 2, 12, 14, 15, 16 totals 60 and has median 13. A median of 13.5 would need $c + d = 27$ with $d \ge 14$, and then the total is at least $1 + 2 + 27 + 15 + 16 = 61$, which is too much. The transferable idea: to make one part of a fixed total as large as possible, squeeze every other part to its minimum.

problems.whyOnTest: Extremal questions about averages test whether you squeeze the other values while respecting every condition, here that the numbers are all different.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In an arithmetic sequence, the 3rd term is 20 and the 8th term is 5. Which term is the first negative term of the sequence?

choices.misconception: I wrote the $n$th term as $26 - 3n$ instead of $26 - 3(n - 1)$, which made the 9th term look negative.
I stepped down from the 8th term but counted three steps to get from 5 to $-1$ instead of two.
I counted 6 steps from the 3rd term to the 8th, so I used a step of 2.5 instead of 3, and stepping down from 20 at the 3rd term I reached 0 at the 11th term.
I found the value of the first negative term instead of its position in the sequence.

hints: How many steps are there from the 3rd term to the 8th?
Between two terms, the number of steps is the difference of their positions. Find the size of each step, then keep stepping down from a known term until you go below zero.
Five steps take 20 down to 5, so each step is $-3$: the terms go 20, 17, 14, 11, 8, 5, ...

solutions.reliable: From the 3rd to the 8th term is 5 steps, and $5 - 20 = -15$, so each step is $-3$. Continuing from the 8th term: the 9th is 2 and the 10th is $-1$, the first negative term. Check with the first term: $20 + 2 \times 3 = 26$, and $26 - 3(n - 1) < 0$ first holds for $n = 10$. The transferable idea: the number of steps from term $m$ to term $n$ is $n - m$, and the answer should be the kind of quantity asked for.

problems.whyOnTest: Arithmetic sequence questions test counting steps between positions correctly and answering with a position when a position is asked for.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In an arithmetic sequence, the first 10 terms add up to 175 and the next 10 terms add up to 475. What is the common difference?

choices.misconception: I thought each of the next 10 terms is only one step more than its partner in the first 10, so I divided 300 by 10.
I thought each term of the second group is 20 steps more than its partner, so I divided 300 by 200.
I divided the difference of the sums, 300, by the 20 terms.
I found the first term instead of the common difference.

hints: Pair the 1st term with the 11th, the 2nd with the 12th, and so on.
Each term in the second group is a fixed number of steps further on than its partner in the first group. Compare the two sums pair by pair instead of finding the first term.
Each of the 10 pairs differs by 10 steps, so the sums differ by $10 \times 10 = 100$ steps.

solutions.reliable: Pair the $k$th term with the $(k + 10)$th term: each pair differs by $10d$, and there are 10 pairs, so $475 - 175 = 100d$, giving $d = 3$. Check: the first term $a$ satisfies $10a + 45 \times 3 = 175$, so $a = 4$; the terms 11 to 20 run from 34 to 61, and $\frac{10 \times (34 + 61)}{2} = 475$. The transferable idea: compare blocks of an arithmetic sequence term by term.
solutions.elegant: Alternatively, the mean of the first 10 terms is 17.5, the average of the 5th and 6th terms, and the mean of the next 10 is 47.5, the average of the 15th and 16th. These are 10 steps apart, so $10d = 30$ and $d = 3$. The transferable idea: the mean of a block of an arithmetic sequence sits at its middle.

problems.whyOnTest: Arithmetic sequence questions reward pairing terms; this checks you count how many steps separate partners and how many pairs there are.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts with 1. Each later term is the previous term plus the last digit of the previous term, so the sequence begins 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 22, 24, ... What is the 100th term?

choices.misconception: I stopped one step early and gave the 99th term.
I thought each step adds 5 on average, so I worked out $1 + 99 \times 5$.
I counted 25 full blocks of four steps, each adding 20, starting from the first term 1.
I lined the blocks of four up from the second term but stopped at the start of a block, which is the 98th term.

hints: Look at the last digits of the terms from 2 onwards.
From the second term on, the last digits cycle 2, 4, 8, 6, so every four steps add the same amount. Find that amount, then count carefully how many full blocks fit before the 100th term.
The terms 2, 22, 42, ... are the 2nd, 6th, 10th, ... terms: every four steps add $2 + 4 + 8 + 6 = 20$.

solutions.reliable: From the 2nd term, the last digits repeat 2, 4, 8, 6, and each block of four steps adds $2 + 4 + 8 + 6 = 20$. So the 2nd, 6th, 10th, ... terms are 2, 22, 42, ..., and the $(4k + 2)$th term is $2 + 20k$. The 98th term ($k = 24$) is 482; then 484 is the 99th and 488 the 100th. The transferable idea: when a rule depends on the last digit, look for a cycle in the last digits and the fixed growth per cycle.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules often settle into a cycle after a few terms; the test is spotting where the cycle starts and counting the terms exactly.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence of positive whole numbers starts with any two such numbers. From then on, each term equals the term before it plus twice the term two places before it. The sixth term is 500. How many such sequences are there?

choices.misconception: I allowed one of the first two terms to be 0, which adds the sequence starting 50, 0.
I miscounted the terms and wrote my equation for the fifth term, $6a + 5b = 500$.
I used the simpler rule 'add the two terms before', which gives the sixth term $3a + 5b = 500$.
I miscounted the terms and wrote my equation for the seventh term, $22a + 21b = 500$.

hints: Call the first two terms $a$ and $b$, and write the sixth term using them.
Build the terms one at a time with the rule. You get one equation in $a$ and $b$; then count its solutions in positive whole numbers by checking which values of $b$ make $a$ a positive whole number.

solutions.reliable: With first terms $a$ and $b$, the sequence is $a$, $b$, $b + 2a$, then $(2a + b) + 2b = 2a + 3b$, then $(2a + 3b) + 2(2a + b) = 6a + 5b$, then $(6a + 5b) + 2(2a + 3b) = 10a + 11b$. So $10a + 11b = 500$. Then $11b$ must end in 0, so $b$ is a multiple of 10, and $11b < 500$ leaves $b = 10, 20, 30, 40$, with $a = 39, 28, 17, 6$. That is 4 sequences. The transferable idea: write the terms of a recursive sequence in its starting values, then solve in whole numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursion problems often reduce to one equation in the starting values; building each term carefully and then counting whole-number solutions is the skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A machine turns whole numbers into other numbers. The inputs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 give the outputs 5, 7, 11, 17 and 25. The gaps between the outputs keep growing in the same pattern. What output does the input 10 give?

choices.misconception: I kept adding the last gap, 8, instead of letting the gaps keep growing.
I continued the gaps but stopped one step early, which gave the output for the input 9.
I thought doubling the input doubles the output, so I doubled 25.
I guessed the rule 'square and add 1' from the input 4 alone, without checking it against the others.

hints: Look at the gaps between the outputs.
The gaps are 2, 4, 6, 8: they grow by 2 each time. Either keep adding the next gaps up to the input 10, or find a formula that fits every example and check it.
The next gaps are 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18.

solutions.reliable: The gaps are 2, 4, 6, 8, so the next gaps, for the inputs 6 to 10, are 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. The output for 10 is $25 + 10 + 12 + 14 + 16 + 18 = 95$. The transferable idea: when the gaps grow steadily, list them until you reach the term you need.
solutions.elegant: The rule $n^2 - n + 5$ fits every example: 5, 7, 11, 17, 25. For $n = 10$ it gives $100 - 10 + 5 = 95$. The transferable idea: steadily growing gaps point to a squared term, and a formula must be checked against all the examples.

problems.whyOnTest: Rule-finding questions check whether you test a guessed rule against every example and follow how the gaps change instead of assuming they stay constant.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A screen shows the number 2027. In one move you may add 12 to the number on the screen or subtract 33 from it, but the number on the screen must always stay positive. What is the smallest number that can appear on the screen?

choices.misconception: I only subtracted 33 as many times as possible and never used the additions.
I treated each pair of moves as one step down of 21 and stopped when I could not take another 21.
I thought the smallest number would be 3 itself, since every move changes the number by a multiple of 3.
I thought that by mixing additions and subtractions the number could be brought all the way down to 1.

hints: What do 12 and 33 have in common?
Both moves change the number by a multiple of 3, so the remainder on division by 3 never changes. That rules out many numbers; then check that the smallest allowed one really can be reached.
2027 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3, so every number that appears does too.

solutions.reliable: Each move adds or subtracts a multiple of 3, so the remainder on division by 3 never changes. 2027 leaves remainder 2, so the screen can never show 1 or 3, and 2 is the best possible. It can be reached: subtracting 33 sixty-one times gives $2027 - 2013 = 14$. From 14, add 12 twice and subtract 33 to get 5; add 12 three times and subtract 33 to get 8; do that again to get 11; then add 12 twice and subtract 33 to get 2. The number stays positive throughout. The transferable idea: an invariant shows what is impossible, and a construction shows the best remaining value is possible.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariant questions ask what never changes under the moves; here the remainder on division by 3 is fixed, and you must also show the bound is reached.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Some different positive whole numbers add up to 1000, and the product of any two of them is even. What is the largest possible number of numbers?

choices.misconception: I allowed one odd number, 1, together with 31 even numbers, without checking whether the total could still be 1000.
I ignored the condition on the products and used as many small numbers as possible, since $1 + 2 + \dots + 44 = 990$.
I forgot that the numbers must be different and used 500 twos.
I halved 1000 to allow for the numbers being even and then also used $2 + 4 + \dots + 2k = k(k + 1)$, so I solved $k(k + 1) \le 500$.

hints: How many of the numbers can be odd?
Two odd numbers have an odd product, so at most one number is odd. Ask what a single odd number would do to the parity of the total, then use the smallest possible numbers to bound the count.
With exactly one odd number the total would be odd, so every number is even. And $2 + 4 + \dots + 64 = 1056$ is more than 1000.

solutions.reliable: If two of the numbers were odd, their product would be odd, so at most one is odd. If exactly one were odd, the total would be odd, not 1000. So all the numbers are even. Then $k$ different even numbers add up to at least $2 + 4 + \dots + 2k = k(k + 1)$, and $32 \times 33 = 1056 > 1000$, so $k \le 31$. Thirty-one works: $2 + 4 + \dots + 60 = 930$, and $930 + 70 = 1000$, so take 2, 4, ..., 60 and 70. The transferable idea: rule out cases by contradiction, then bound the count using the smallest possible values.

problems.whyOnTest: Proof by contradiction trims the cases; here ruling out a single odd number by parity is the step most solvers miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana walks from home to school at 4 km/h. Her brother leaves home 10 minutes after her, cycles the same route at 12 km/h, and reaches the school at the same moment as Ana. How far is the school from home?

choices.misconception: I used 10 minutes as 0.1 hours instead of $\frac{1}{6}$ of an hour.
I multiplied the difference in speeds, 8 km/h, by the 10 minutes, as if that were the distance to the school.
I found how far Ana walks during her 10-minute head start, not the length of the route.
I found how far her brother cycles in 10 minutes instead of solving for the distance.

hints: Her brother's trip takes 10 minutes less than Ana's.
Write each journey time as distance divided by speed, in hours. The two times differ by 10 minutes, which is $\frac{1}{6}$ of an hour.

solutions.reliable: Ana takes $\frac{d}{4}$ hours and her brother $\frac{d}{12}$ hours, and the difference is 10 minutes, which is $\frac{1}{6}$ of an hour. So $\frac{d}{4} - \frac{d}{12} = \frac{d}{6} = \frac{1}{6}$, giving $d = 1$ km. Check: Ana takes 15 minutes and her brother 5 minutes, 10 minutes apart. The transferable idea: convert minutes to hours before mixing them with km/h.
solutions.elegant: Her brother is 3 times as fast, so his trip takes a third of Ana's time. The 10-minute difference is two thirds of Ana's time, so she walks for 15 minutes, and at 4 km/h that is 1 km. The transferable idea: over a fixed distance, time is inversely proportional to speed.

problems.whyOnTest: Rate questions test unit control and setting up the time difference; turning 10 minutes into 0.1 hours is the classic slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: At noon a cyclist leaves town A for town B, and at the same moment a walker leaves B for A along the same road. Both keep steady speeds. They pass each other at 12:40, and the cyclist reaches B at 13:00. At what time does the walker reach A?

choices.misconception: I assumed the walker needs as long after the meeting as before it, another 40 minutes.
I thought the walker is a third as fast as the cyclist, because 20 minutes is a third of 60 minutes.
I added the cyclist's whole journey time, 60 minutes, to the meeting time.
I worked out how long the walker still needs after the meeting, not the time when the walker arrives.

hints: Compare the cyclist's last 20 minutes with the walker's first 40 minutes.
At the meeting point, the stretch the cyclist still has to ride is exactly the stretch the walker has already walked. Comparing the times each needs for that stretch gives the ratio of their speeds.
The cyclist rides the walker's 40-minute stretch in 20 minutes, so the walker is half as fast as the cyclist.

solutions.reliable: After the meeting, the cyclist needs 20 minutes for the stretch the walker covered in 40 minutes, so the walker's speed is half the cyclist's. The cyclist rides the whole road in 60 minutes, so the walker needs 120 minutes and arrives at 14:00. Check: after the meeting the walker must cover the cyclist's 40-minute stretch at half speed, which takes 80 minutes, and 12:40 plus 80 minutes is 14:00. The transferable idea: at a meeting point, each traveller's remaining distance is the other's distance covered so far.

problems.whyOnTest: Rate questions often hide a speed ratio in the times; this checks you compare the same stretch of road and then answer with a clock time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: When Ann was as old as Bo is now, Bo was 6. When Bo is as old as Ann is now, Ann will be 30. How old is Ann now?

choices.misconception: I found Bo's age now instead of Ann's.
I assumed Ann's age now is exactly halfway between 6 and 30.
I found the age gap between Ann and Bo and gave that as Ann's age.
I gave Ann's age at the later moment, not her age now.

hints: The gap between their ages is always the same.
Draw a line of ages with four marks: Bo's age back then, Bo's age now, Ann's age now and Ann's age later. Each pair of neighbouring marks is exactly one age gap apart.
The ages 6, Bo's age now, Ann's age now and 30 are equally spaced, so there are three equal gaps from 6 to 30.

solutions.reliable: Let the age gap be $g$. Ann was Bo's current age $g$ years ago, when Bo was 6, so Bo is now $6 + g$ and Ann is $6 + 2g$. Bo reaches Ann's current age in $g$ years, when Ann will be $6 + 3g = 30$. So $g = 8$, Bo is 14 and Ann is 22. Check: 8 years ago Ann was 14 and Bo was 6; in 8 years Bo will be 22 and Ann 30. The transferable idea: in 'when A was as old as B is now' problems, each shift in time is exactly one age gap.

problems.whyOnTest: Tangled age statements become simple once you see that every shift in time is one age gap; the test is turning the words into equally spaced ages.
